entries.name: Acorn Barnacle
entries.heroTitle: Acorn Barnacle — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A crustacean that spends its adult life glued head-down inside a white cone of plates on intertidal rock. When the tide covers it, the top plates part and six pairs of feathery legs comb the water; as the sea drains away they shut tight, sealing in enough moisture to last until the next tide.
identification: White to grey cone built from six wall plates
Diamond-shaped opening closed by two pairs of movable plates
Base is a soft membrane rather than a chalky plate
Usually no more than about 15 millimetres across
Crowded individuals grow tall, narrow and columnar
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic. Hard surfaces between the tides on cold-water rocky shores of the North Atlantic: bare rock, boulders, pier pilings and the shells of mussels and snails. It often forms dense sheets across the middle shore, especially where waves keep the water well mixed.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_atlantic. Hard surfaces between the tides on cold-water rocky shores of the North Atlantic: bare rock, boulders, pier pilings and the shells of mussels and snails. It often forms dense sheets across the middle shore, especially where waves keep the water well mixed.

behaviorTraits: White to grey cone built from six wall plates
Diamond-shaped opening closed by two pairs of movable plates

whyInteresting: On a Scottish shore in the 1950s, Joseph Connell showed experimentally that this barnacle crowds a smaller Chthamalus barnacle out of the lower shore.
Settling larvae search the rock and prefer spots where adults of their own species already live, detecting a chemical cue the adults leave behind.
Experiments have shown it can survive part of its body water freezing during winter low tides.
Like other crustaceans it moults, but only its soft inner cuticle; the shell plates grow by adding material at their edges.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Phytoplankton, especially diatoms, with small zooplankton and fine detritus. The legs are beaten rhythmically through still water or held open as a net in a current, and trapped particles are scraped to the mouth.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: The dog whelk is a major predator, drilling through the plates or forcing them apart; sea stars, shore crabs and fish such as the shanny also feed on it. Its only defence is to close the plates and hold fast.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day and night make little difference to it: it feeds at any hour whenever the sea covers it. A sleep state is not known in barnacles.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically about 3 to 5 years; studies have found that barnacles high on the shore, where predators are fewer, can live longer than those near low water.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating takes place in autumn, and each animal broods thousands of embryos inside its shell through the winter. Larvae hatch in late winter or spring, as the plankton bloom starts, and after several swimming stages a cyprid larva settles and cements itself to rock.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: There are no separate sexes: each barnacle is a hermaphrodite carrying both male and female organs. Individuals usually fertilise neighbours rather than themselves, reaching them with a very long, extensible penis.

entries.name: Acorn Weevil
entries.heroTitle: Acorn Weevil — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Female Acorn Weevils use elongated rostrums to bore into acorns and lay eggs. The larva develops protected inside the seed, turning one precise tool into a nursery strategy.
identification: Rounded, pear-shaped body about 4 to 8 millimetres long
Brown body mottled with pale, golden-grey scales
Very long, thin, downcurved snout
Elbowed antennae set partway along the snout
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe. Oak woodland, wood pasture, parkland and hedgerows with mature, acorn-bearing oaks across much of Europe, mostly in the lowlands.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe. Oak woodland, wood pasture, parkland and hedgerows with mature, acorn-bearing oaks across much of Europe, mostly in the lowlands.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 35/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Rounded, pear-shaped body about 4 to 8 millimetres long
Brown body mottled with pale, golden-grey scales
Very long, thin, downcurved snout
Elbowed antennae set partway along the snout
whyInteresting: The female drills by turning her whole head from side to side, rotating the snout into the acorn.
After drilling, the female turns round and places an egg into the shaft with her ovipositor.
Acorns only partly eaten by a larva can still germinate if the embryo has not been damaged.
Acorns holding a larva are often reported to fall from the tree earlier than sound ones.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults feed mainly on developing acorns, chewing into the kernel with tiny jaws at the tip of the snout, and may also take oak buds and young shoots. The larva eats the kernel from inside the acorn.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds pick adults from oak foliage, and mice, jays and other acorn eaters consume larvae inside the nut. Adults drop from leaves and keep still when disturbed, and parasitic wasps are recorded attacking the larvae.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are active on oak foliage by day in warm weather and shelter among leaves and bark at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most of the life is spent as a larva in the soil, usually one to two years, and possibly longer in some larvae. Adults live for a few months from late spring into autumn.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid in summer in young, still-green acorns, usually one per acorn. When the acorn falls, the grown larva chews a round exit hole, burrows into the soil and later pupates there. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The female's snout is longer, often about as long as her body, and her antennae join it further from the tip. The male has a noticeably shorter snout.

entries.name: Acorn Woodpecker
entries.heroTitle: Acorn Woodpecker — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Cooperative family groups of this clown-faced woodpecker drill holes in a granary, often a dead trunk or a pole, and wedge a single acorn into each. Their stores reach thousands of nuts and carry the group through winter.
identification: Pale staring eye in a black-and-white clown face
Glossy black back and wings with a white rump
White wing patches that flash in flight
Black breast band streaked into a white belly
Loud, laughing waka-waka calls from the group
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Acorn Woodpecker belongs in oak woodland, pine-oak forest, dead trees, utility poles, and communal granary sites.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america. Acorn Woodpecker belongs in oak woodland, pine-oak forest, dead trees, utility poles, and communal granary sites.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 28/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Pale staring eye in a black-and-white clown face
Glossy black back and wings with a white rump
White wing patches that flash in flight
Black breast band streaked into a white belly
Loud, laughing waka-waka calls from the group
whyInteresting: Females that share a nest often remove and destroy eggs already laid by their co-breeders before they start laying themselves.
Studies found that young birds staying in their home group rarely breed while a parent of the opposite sex is still a breeder there.
It often catches flying insects in the air, sallying out from a high perch like a flycatcher.
When a breeding place falls vacant, birds from other groups gather and fight for it, sometimes for days.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Acorn Woodpecker feeds on acorns, insects, sap, fruit, and cached nuts from drilled holes.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Cooper's and sharp-shinned hawks take adults, while snakes and squirrels raid nest cavities. Group members keep watch from high perches, give harsh alarm calls, and chase jays and squirrels away from the granary.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Acorn Woodpecker rests in tree cavities and defended granary territories. It is active by day, and at dusk several group members often roost together in one cavity.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults that reach breeding age often live several years, and some ringed birds have been recorded at more than 15 years old.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Clutches are usually about four or five eggs, but where two or three females share a nest one cavity can hold many more. Incubation lasts roughly 11 days, and the whole group, including grown young from earlier years, feeds the chicks until they fledge at about a month.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In males the red crown meets the white forehead; in females a black band separates the white forehead from a smaller red patch.

entries.name: Common Sandpiper
entries.heroTitle: Common Sandpiper — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A small brown-and-white shorebird that works the edges of rivers and lakes, constantly bobbing its rear end. In flight it skims low over the water on stiff, flickering wings, giving a sharp, piping call. It breeds along stony shores from Europe into Asia and winters on coasts and inland waters far to the south.
identification: Constant tail-bob while walking the shore
Stiff-winged flight low over water
Sharp, piping call in flight
Brown upperparts with clean white underparts
White wing-bar visible in flight
analysis.habitat: Breeds beside stony rivers, lake shores and shingle banks with open margins and sparse cover. Outside the breeding season it uses coastal creeks, harbours, reservoirs and other inland waters with muddy or rocky edges for feeding.
analysis.nativeRange: Breeds beside stony rivers, lake shores and shingle banks with open margins and sparse cover. Outside the breeding season it uses coastal creeks, harbours, reservoirs and other inland waters with muddy or rocky edges for feeding.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 12/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Constant tail-bob while walking the shore
Stiff-winged flight low over water
Sharp, piping call in flight
Brown upperparts with clean white underparts
White wing-bar visible in flight
whyInteresting: The rear end bobs almost continuously as the bird walks, even when it pauses to pick prey.
In flight the wings beat in a stiff, flickering pattern close above the water, unlike the looser action of many larger waders.
A usual clutch is four eggs laid in a shallow scrape among stones or short plants beside water.
After breeding, many birds leave inland rivers for coasts and inland waters across Africa, southern Asia and Australia.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small insects, spiders, worms and other invertebrates picked from mud, stones and shallow water along the shore.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and chicks are taken by foxes, crows, gulls and other ground predators along open shores. Adults face sparrowhawks, falcons and similar raptors, especially when flushed into the open.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day along shorelines, feeding and bobbing as it walks. At night it rests on sheltered banks, islands or quiet water edges away from traffic.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Birds that reach breeding age typically live about 8 years. The longest ringed bird lived 15 years, 1 month and 5 days.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The nest is a shallow scrape among stones or short vegetation near water. The usual clutch is four eggs; both parents incubate, and the chicks leave soon after hatching to feed along the shore.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in the field: brown above, white below, with a white wing-bar in flight.

entries.name: Common Bluetail
entries.heroTitle: Common Bluetail — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A slender damselfly barely 3 centimetres long, and one of the commonest across Africa and warm parts of Asia. It thrives where many damselflies cannot, breeding in rice paddies, drainage ditches, garden ponds and even slightly brackish water.
identification: Slender body roughly 3 centimetres long
Male thorax black above with green to blue-green sides
Male has a bright blue band near the abdomen tip
Clear wings held closed above the back at rest
Weak, fluttering flight low among plants
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, north_africa_middle_east, south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia. Still or slow water with plenty of emergent grasses and reeds: ponds, marsh edges, ditches, rice fields, reservoirs and garden pools, mainly in the lowlands.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, north_africa_middle_east, south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia. Still or slow water with plenty of emergent grasses and reeds: ponds, marsh edges, ditches, rice fields, reservoirs and garden pools, mainly in the lowlands.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 15/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Slender body roughly 3 centimetres long
Male thorax black above with green to blue-green sides
Male has a bright blue band near the abdomen tip
Clear wings held closed above the back at rest
Weak, fluttering flight low among plants
whyInteresting: Females come in more than one inherited colour form, and those that resemble males are thought to receive fewer unwanted mating attempts.
Mating pairs form a wheel shape, and in this genus copulation can last an hour or more.
It is one of the most widespread damselflies of the Old World, ranging from Africa to southern Japan.
Its name senegalensis refers to Senegal in West Africa, the region from which the species was first described.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults snatch small flying insects such as midges, gnats, mosquitoes and aphids from the air or pick them off leaves. The aquatic larvae ambush water fleas, mosquito larvae and other tiny animals with an extendable lower jaw.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, frogs, spiders and larger dragonflies take adults; fish, water bugs and dragonfly larvae eat the larvae. Adults escape with short, low flights into dense vegetation, and larvae hide among submerged stems.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, mostly from mid-morning to afternoon in sunshine. At night and in dull weather adults roost clinging to grass stems and reeds near the water, while larvae stay among submerged plants.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults typically live roughly two to four weeks. In warm climates the larval stage may last only one to two months, allowing several generations a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs alone, without the male attached, inserting them into the stems and leaves of floating or submerged plants. Larvae hatch within days, moult many times underwater, then climb a stem to emerge as adults.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a black thorax with green stripes and a bright blue band near the tail tip. Females come in several colour forms, some patterned like males and others greenish, olive or brownish.

entries.name: African Forest Buffalo
entries.heroTitle: African Forest Buffalo — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: African Forest Buffalo AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: The smallest form of African buffalo, less than half the weight of a big savanna bull, it is adapted to life in rainforest. Each small herd tends to stay within a limited home range centred on a few favoured grassy clearings, which its grazing is thought to help keep open.
identification: Red-brown to chestnut coat, darker in some males
Short horns swept back and up, without a heavy boss
Large ears fringed with long hair tufts
Compact body, roughly 1 to 1.3 metres at the shoulder
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Lowland rainforest and forest-savanna mosaic of West and Central Africa, especially where grassy clearings, marshy glades, riverbanks and old logging roads break the canopy.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Lowland rainforest and forest-savanna mosaic of West and Central Africa, especially where grassy clearings, marshy glades, riverbanks and old logging roads break the canopy.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 63/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Red-brown to chestnut coat, darker in some males
Short horns swept back and up, without a heavy boss
Large ears fringed with long hair tufts
Compact body, roughly 1 to 1.3 metres at the shoulder
whyInteresting: Herds are small, often under about 20 animals, compared with savanna buffalo herds of hundreds.
Forest buffalo and savanna buffalo interbreed where their ranges meet, producing animals of intermediate size and colour.
It often travels along trails made by forest elephants through otherwise dense undergrowth.
Adults usually weigh roughly 250 to 320 kilograms.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly grasses and sedges grazed in clearings and along rivers, with some herbs, leaves and shoots browsed at forest edges.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards take calves and sometimes adults, and lions where forest meets savanna. People hunting for meat are the biggest threat. Groups bunch together, and adults face threats or charge.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds mostly in the early morning, late afternoon and at night, and rests in shaded forest or thick cover during the hottest hours, often lying down together.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly documented; about 15 to 20 years is a commonly given figure.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Details for the forest form are poorly known. As in other African buffalo, a single calf is born after a pregnancy of about 11 months; it can follow its mother within hours, stays close to her in the herd, and suckles for several months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are larger and heavier, often darker, with thicker horn bases. Females are usually redder with slimmer horns.

entries.name: African Grey Hornbill
entries.heroTitle: African Grey Hornbill — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: African Grey Hornbill AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: African Grey Hornbills move through savanna woodland and dry forest edges, feeding on insects, fruit, seeds, and small animals. Their survival is shaped by calling, pair contact, and the protected logic of nest cavities.
identification: Grey-brown plumage with pale stripes above and below the eye
Down-curved bill with a small ridge-like casque
Pale edges to the wing feathers
Buoyant, dipping flight between trees
Piping whistled call given with head thrown back
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Dry savanna and open woodland, including acacia, mopane and broad-leaved woodland, across much of Africa south of the Sahara. It avoids dense rainforest and true desert.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Dry savanna and open woodland, including acacia, mopane and broad-leaved woodland, across much of Africa south of the Sahara. It avoids dense rainforest and true desert.

Down-curved bill with a small ridge-like casque
Pale edges to the wing feathers
Buoyant, dipping flight between trees
Piping whistled call given with head thrown back
whyInteresting: While the female is sealed in, the male brings food and passes it to her through a narrow slit in the wall.
The entrance is plastered shut from inside, mainly with droppings and food remains.
It belongs to Lophoceros, a genus of smaller dry-country hornbills once included in Tockus.
Some populations move seasonally, following rains across the savanna.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly insects such as grasshoppers and caterpillars, gleaned from branches and sometimes caught in flight, plus small lizards and fruit. It forages mainly in the tree canopy.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks and eagles hunt adults, and tree-climbing snakes and small carnivores can threaten nests. Birds give loud alarm calls and fly to cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and roosts at night on branches in the tree canopy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Reliable wild lifespan series for Lophoceros nasutus are still scarce. Females seal themselves into tree cavities while males deliver food through a narrow slit.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually two to four white eggs are laid in a natural tree hole. The female moults her flight feathers while inside, incubating for about four weeks. She later breaks out, the chicks reseal the entrance, and both parents feed them until they fledge.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The male's bill is blackish with a creamy stripe at the base. The female's bill has a creamy-yellow base and a dark red tip to the upper mandible.

entries.name: African Harrier-Hawk
entries.heroTitle: African Harrier-Hawk — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: African Harrier-Hawk teaches Flexible Reach through legs that bend where other raptors are rigid. Hanging off a trunk with wings beating for balance, it feels into holes and nests that stay closed to sharper, faster hunters.
identification: Intertarsal joints that bend both forward and sideways
Clambers and hangs on trunks and nests, wings flapping for balance
Bare facial skin that flushes from yellow to red
Grey plumage with a single broad white band across a long tail
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Woodland, forest edge, riverine trees, palm stands and wooded gardens across sub-Saharan Africa suit African Harrier-Hawks because Flexible Reach needs surfaces to cling to and cavities to search. The place rewards the bird that can work a trunk rather than only the open air.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. whyInteresting: Its double-jointed legs let it reach into cavities, crevices and weaver nests that other raptors cannot open.
The bare skin of its face changes colour, flushing red when the bird is excited or displaying.
It is one of very few raptors that regularly eats fruit, taking the oily flesh of oil palm nuts.
It is also called the Gymnogene, a name describing that bare face.
Two eggs are often laid, but usually only one chick is raised.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Nestlings, eggs, geckos, bats, frogs, insects and oil palm fruit.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger eagles, and nest predators taking eggs or young. Its answer is not speed but placement: nests set high in a tree fork, and a body that can hold onto awkward surfaces where pursuit is difficult.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: African Harrier-Hawks are diurnal, working trees and cliffs through the day. Their rhythm is a slow search rather than a fast chase, quartering slowly and stopping to investigate anything that could hold prey.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: A typical lifespan is unpublished; birds that extract nestlings with double-jointed tarsi among African palms are rarely aged by rings.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay one to three eggs on a stick platform built in a tree fork, and both parents feed the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are slightly larger than males, and the two are otherwise closely alike. The difference is small because both sexes need the same specialised reach to feed themselves.

analysis.summary: African Palm Civet teaches Quiet Reward through a tree-climber that finds sweetness after dark. Nocturnal eyes, flexible body, spotted coat, fruit foraging, and canopy movement show that some rewards belong to the one who moves quietly where others stop looking.
identification: Arboreal Foraging: climbing lets the civet search fruiting trees and forest layers.
Night Movement: darkness protects the quiet search for sweet resources.
Fruit-Linked Role: feeding on fruit can help move seeds through the forest.
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Tropical forests, gallery forests, dense woodland, plantations, and fruiting tree edges.

Night Movement: darkness protects the quiet search for sweet resources.
Fruit-Linked Role: feeding on fruit can help move seeds through the forest.
whyInteresting: African Palm Civets are nocturnal mammals that spend most of their time climbing and feeding high in forest trees.
They feed heavily on fruit but may also eat small animals and other foods.
Despite the name, they are in their own family, Nandiniidae, not true civets.
Genetic studies place their family as an early branch of the cat-like carnivores, separate from cats, civets, and hyenas.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruits, berries, small mammals, insects, eggs, and other foods. Sweetness is found by climbing, smelling, and returning to fruiting places.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, large snakes, crowned eagles, humans, and habitat loss create pressure. Tree movement, night activity, and concealment help the civet avoid direct confrontation.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: African Palm Civets are nocturnal, resting by day in trees or cover and moving after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive records exceed fifteen years (AnAge); wild ages stay scarce for this nocturnal fruit-eater of African forest canopy.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to small litters in sheltered places, often using dense vegetation or tree cover.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are similar in general appearance, though males may be larger.

entries.name: African Penguin
entries.heroTitle: African Penguin — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The only penguin that breeds in Africa, nesting in colonies on islands and a few mainland beaches of Namibia and South Africa. Pairs usually stay together for years and return to the same nest site, taking turns to guard the eggs while the other feeds at sea. Bare pink skin above the eyes sheds heat in the sun.
identification: Black facial mask bordered by a broad white band
Single black horseshoe band across the white chest
Bare pink skin patch above each eye
Scattered black chest spots, different on every bird
Loud, donkey-like braying call
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, south_atlantic. Rocky offshore islands and sheltered mainland beaches from central Namibia to Algoa Bay in South Africa, in the cold, fish-rich water of the Benguela system. Nests are burrows in guano or sand, or hollows under boulders and bushes.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, south_atlantic. Rocky offshore islands and sheltered mainland beaches from central Namibia to Algoa Bay in South Africa, in the cold, fish-rich water of the Benguela system. Nests are burrows in guano or sand, or hollows under boulders and bushes.

Single black horseshoe band across the white chest
Bare pink skin patch above each eye
Scattered black chest spots, different on every bird

whyInteresting: After the 2000 Treasure oil spill near Cape Town, about 19,000 oiled penguins were cleaned, and a similar number of un-oiled birds were moved away.
Guano harvesting removed the deep deposits it once burrowed into, leaving many nests exposed to sun and flooding.
Numbers are estimated to have fallen by more than 95 per cent since the early 1900s, and the species was listed as Critically Endangered in 2024.
The Boulders Beach colony near Cape Town was founded by just two pairs in the early 1980s.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Sardines and anchovies are the staple, with round herring, horse mackerel and squid. It hunts by pursuit diving, usually to less than 30 metres though dives past 100 metres are recorded, and small groups often herd shoals together.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Cape fur seals and sharks catch adults at sea. On land, kelp gulls take eggs and small chicks, and at some mainland colonies mongooses, genets and caracals have been recorded taking penguins. Adults defend the nest with sharp jabs of the bill.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It feeds at sea by day and returns to land around dusk, resting at night in the burrow or among the colony. During the annual moult of about three weeks it stays ashore and fasts.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 10 to 15 years on average in the wild, with some reaching their late twenties; birds in zoos have lived past 30.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Two eggs are laid and incubated by both parents in shifts for about 38 to 40 days. Chicks are guarded for the first month, then gather in crèches, and go to sea at roughly 60 to 130 days depending on food supply.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is identical. Males are slightly larger with a deeper, heavier bill, a difference usually clear only when a pair stands side by side.

entries.name: African Pygmy Hedgehog
entries.heroTitle: African Pygmy Hedgehog — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: African Pygmy Hedgehog AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: African Pygmy Hedgehog teaches Spined Night Foraging through a small nocturnal body built for cautious exploration. Spines, sniffing, insect hunting, curled defense, and night movement show how curiosity can keep working when protection is always close.
identification: Albino coloring makes vulnerability visible without removing defense
Keratin spines turn a small body into a clear boundary
Nocturnal caution lets smell and hearing guide movement
Curling behavior protects the softest parts first
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Dry savanna, grassland and open scrub across a broad belt of Africa south of the Sahara, from the west of the continent east to Sudan and south into East Africa. It avoids dense forest and wet ground, and also lives on farmland and in gardens. By day it shelters under rocks and in holes, termite mounds and leaf litter.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, worms, small invertebrates, and occasional soft foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, snakes, carnivores, and rough handling threaten hedgehogs. The predator story matters because the spines and curl are not aggression; they are a boundary that tells danger the soft center is not easily reached.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hedgehogs are mainly nocturnal.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They often live about 3 to 5 years in the wild and longer in good care.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to small litters of hoglets that are born helpless with soft spines that harden after birth.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, so the main visible lesson is not display but body-wide defense. Sexing usually depends on anatomy, showing that this animal’s identity is built around protection more than ornament.

analysis.summary: Pygmy Kingfisher expresses Flashperch through tiny bright body, watchful perch, sudden darting strike, and small-prey focus make the Flashperch principle specific rather than generic; body, habitat, and pressure all point back to the same lesson.

whyInteresting: About 12 centimetres long and weighing roughly 10 to 14 grams, it is one of Africa's smallest kingfishers.
It resembles the Malachite Kingfisher, but its blue crown stops above the eye and it has a lilac wash across the cheeks.
In southern Africa it is a summer visitor, arriving with the rains around October and leaving by about April.
It migrates by night, and birds are regularly found stunned or killed after flying into lit windows.
Nest tunnels become foul-smelling, because droppings and food remains build up inside while the chicks grow.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Prey recorded includes insects, small fish, frogs, and aquatic or terrestrial invertebrates. Grasshoppers, mantids, beetles, caterpillars and spiders make up most of it, and small lizards are taken occasionally.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sparrowhawks, goshawks and other small hawks take adults, while snakes, monitor lizards and mongooses can reach eggs and chicks in the nest burrow. A threatened bird keeps still on a shaded perch or darts into thick cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: This kingfisher is diurnal, resting on small perches and hunting in bursts. At night it is thought to roost alone in dense foliage.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: SAFRING recoveries list a maximum of three years ten months for Ispidina picta, a tiny woodland kingfisher that hunts insects from low perches.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Both partners dig a short tunnel, about 30 centimetres long, into a sandy bank, the wall of an aardvark burrow or a termite mound. The 3 to 6 white eggs hatch after about 18 days, and both parents feed the chicks until they fledge at around three weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike. Juveniles are duller, with a blackish bill in place of the adult's bright red one.

entries.name: African Sharptooth Catfish

analysis.summary: This large, eel-shaped catfish breathes air as well as water. A branching, tree-like organ above the gills absorbs oxygen from gulps taken at the surface, so it survives in warm, stagnant swamps and drying pools where most fish would suffocate.
identification: Long, eel-like body with a broad, flattened bony head
Four pairs of long barbels around the mouth
Very long dorsal and anal fins reaching almost to the tail
No adipose fin behind the dorsal fin
Grey to olive-brown back, often mottled, with pale belly
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, north_africa_middle_east. Lakes, slow rivers, swamps, floodplain pools and irrigation channels across much of Africa and parts of the Middle East. It favours muddy bottoms, dense vegetation and shallow, warm water.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, north_africa_middle_east. Lakes, slow rivers, swamps, floodplain pools and irrigation channels across much of Africa and parts of the Middle East. It favours muddy bottoms, dense vegetation and shallow, warm water.

whyInteresting: In fish farming it is often crossed with the vundu, Heterobranchus longifilis, to produce a fast-growing hybrid.
The largest fish have been reported at about 1.5 to 1.7 metres long, though most caught are far smaller.
It is one of the most widely farmed fish in Africa and has been taken to fish farms in Asia, Europe and South America.
Escaped fish have become established in several countries outside Africa, where it is treated as an invasive predator of native fish.
Its skin has no scales and is coated in thick mucus that helps keep it moist out of water.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An opportunistic omnivore that eats fish, insects, crustaceans, snails, frogs, small birds, carrion and plant matter. It hunts mainly at night by touch and taste using its barbels, sucking prey into its wide mouth.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Crocodiles, fish eagles, herons, cormorants, otters and large fish take young or medium-sized catfish, and people fish for it heavily. Stout, lockable spines in the pectoral fins make it hard to swallow, and it hides in mud or vegetation.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal. By day it rests quietly in deeper water, under vegetation or in burrows and hollows in the mud, becoming active and moving into shallows after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Reliable ages for wild fish are scarce; figures of around 8 to 15 years are sometimes quoted, and very large individuals are probably older.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning follows the first heavy rains, when pairs move onto newly flooded shallows at night. A large female can release many tens of thousands of sticky eggs, and the biggest well over a hundred thousand, onto submerged plants; they hatch within about a day or two, and the young receive no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a long, pointed genital papilla just behind the vent; in females it is short and rounded, and ripe females have a swollen belly.

analysis.summary: A fast-running hunting spider that catches prey by searching and grabbing rather than with a web. It is one of the most common spiders in North American crops and orchards, where it eats many pest insects.
identification: Pale yellow to light green body without a strong pattern
Dark tips to the feet
Dark jaws that stand out against the pale body
First pair of legs the longest

whyInteresting: Its bite is painful but usually causes only redness and mild swelling; earlier claims of skin necrosis are not well supported.
Adults measure only about 5 to 10 mm in body length, not counting the legs.
Spiders of this genus have been observed feeding on plant nectar as well as prey.
Adult males wander more widely than females, especially when searching for mates.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Eats small insects such as moth larvae, aphids and flies, as well as insect eggs and other small spiders, which it grabs and bites after finding them by touch on leaves and stems at night.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, wasps that stock nests with spiders, and larger spiders take them. When disturbed, it runs fast and will bite if grabbed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal, from dusk until shortly before dawn. In cold weather it becomes inactive, often overwintering in a thicker silk retreat under bark, in plant debris or inside buildings.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one year; most live through a single season, with adults usually dying after breeding.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female lays a few dozen eggs in a silk sac inside her retreat and stays with them until the spiderlings hatch and leave. She may produce several egg sacs over the season.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are slimmer with relatively longer legs and swollen palps; females have a larger, rounder abdomen.

entries.name: Alderfly
entries.heroTitle: Alderfly — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Alderfly spends nearly a year as a predatory larva in silt at the bottom of slow water, then a few days as a weak-flying adult that barely feeds. Almost all of its life is the waiting part, and that is where the work gets done.
identification: Smoky dark brown wings held steeply roof-like over the body
Heavy, fluttering, reluctant flight over a few metres at most
Long thread-like antennae and a broad head
Rests on waterside vegetation and stonework rather than flying
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, central_asia. Slow rivers, canals, lakes and ponds with soft silt beds and vegetated, undisturbed banks. Both halves are required — the silt for the long larval hunt, the bank for pupation.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe, central_asia. Slow rivers, canals, lakes and ponds with soft silt beds and vegetated, undisturbed banks. Both halves are required — the silt for the long larval hunt, the bank for pupation.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 24/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Smoky dark brown wings held steeply roof-like over the body
Heavy, fluttering, reluctant flight over a few metres at most

whyInteresting: Larvae are fully aquatic predators with seven pairs of feathery abdominal gills, hunting midge larvae and worms in the silt for most of a year.
The larva leaves the water to pupate in damp soil on the bank, so the species needs both the water and an undisturbed margin.
Adults live only a few days to a couple of weeks and feed very little or not at all.
Egg masses are laid in dense brown patches of several hundred on vegetation and structures directly above water, so the hatchlings drop straight in.
Anglers imitate both the larva and the adult, and an alderfly hatch is a well-known trigger for surface feeding on lowland rivers.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Larvae are active predators of midge larvae, worms and other soft-bodied invertebrates in the sediment. Adults barely feed at all; the entire energy budget for the flying stage was earned underwater.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish take both larvae and any adult that lands on the water, and birds take adults off waterside vegetation. The larva's defence is to stay in the silt, and the adult's is to be brief.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are sluggish by day and rest on vegetation, becoming most active in the late afternoon and evening; larvae hunt in the dark of the sediment regardless of time.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Roughly one year in total, of which about eleven months are spent as a larva and only days to a fortnight as a winged adult.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay dense brown egg masses of several hundred on leaves and stonework directly over water; larvae drop straight in on hatching and begin hunting immediately.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike; females are usually a little larger and heavier-bodied, most obviously when carrying eggs.

entries.name: Alpine Chough
entries.heroTitle: Alpine Chough — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Alpine Choughs are intelligent mountain corvids that move in flocks, play in strong winds, and search for insects, berries, and human scraps around cliffs and alpine settlements. Their survival comes from curiosity, group awareness, and comfort in high exposed places.
identification: Glossy black plumage all over
Short, slightly curved yellow bill
Bright coral-red legs in adults
Rippling, high-pitched calls from the flock
Long tail and rounded wings in soaring flight
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, central_asia, south_asia, east_asia. High mountains from southern Europe and North Africa east to the Himalayas and China, mostly between about 1,500 and 5,000 metres. It uses alpine grassland, cliffs, scree and gorges, moving down to valleys in harsh winter weather.

whyInteresting: Pairs usually stay together for years and return to the same nest site each season.
Juveniles have duller, black legs and gain the adult's red legs as they mature.
It has been reported nesting above 6,000 metres in the Himalayas, one of the highest breeding altitudes recorded for any bird.
Outside the breeding season, large flocks gather at good feeding sites.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: In summer it probes turf and turns over stones for beetles, grasshoppers, larvae and snails. In autumn and winter it switches largely to fruit such as rose hips, juniper and other berries.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Golden eagles and peregrine falcons take adults, and eagle owls and ravens are probably also predators. Flocks call loudly on spotting a raptor and often mob it together in the air.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active through the day. At night it roosts in caves, deep cliff crevices or sheltered rock ledges, often communally, and in winter may fly many kilometres from valley feeding sites back up to these roosts.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult survival is high, and birds can live well over a decade in the wild, though most live fewer years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs nest in cliff crevices, caves or buildings, lining a stick nest with grass and wool. The female incubates three to five eggs for about two weeks, and the young fledge at roughly a month old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes share the glossy black plumage, yellow bill and red legs. Males average slightly larger and heavier, a difference that cannot be judged reliably in the field.

entries.name: Alpine Marmot
entries.heroTitle: Alpine Marmot — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A heavy ground squirrel of high European mountains that lives in family groups sharing one burrow system. The group spends summer feeding and carrying dry grass underground for bedding, then plugs the entrances in early autumn and hibernates together for about six months. Huddling with older animals helps the juveniles survive the winter.
identification: Family groups on grassland above the treeline
Grey-brown coat with yellowish flanks and darker crown
Piercing whistle given in alarm
Short bushy tail with a black tip
Sits upright on boulders beside burrow entrances
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe. Alpine and subalpine grassland on sunny slopes with deep soil for digging and scattered boulders for lookouts, mostly between the treeline and about 3,000 metres and locally lower. Native to the Alps and the Tatra Mountains, and introduced or reintroduced in the Pyrenees, parts of the Carpathians and other ranges.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe. whyInteresting: Alarm whistles vary with the danger: a single sharp whistle tends to mark a sudden, close threat such as an eagle overhead, and a series of whistles a less urgent one.
Body temperature during hibernation falls to around 5 °C and breathing slows to one to three breaths a minute.
Adults weigh about 3 kilograms on emerging in spring and can approach double that before hibernation.
Young usually stay with the family for at least two years before leaving to seek a territory of their own.
Marmot fat was long rendered into an ointment in Alpine folk medicine, one reason the animals were hunted.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, sedges, herbs and flowers are grazed near the burrow, with some roots, seeds and occasional insects and worms. It picks young, tender shoots, and feeding is heaviest in the weeks before hibernation, when the fat for winter is laid down.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Golden eagles are a major threat, with red foxes, wolves and dogs on the ground. A sharp whistle from any colony member sends others racing to the nearest burrow entrance.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hibernation in a grass-lined chamber lasts from about October to April. In summer it feeds above ground in the morning and late afternoon, retreating underground in midday heat and at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Up to about 15 years in the wild, though many die in their first winters; captive animals have reached about 17.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually only the dominant female breeds. Mating takes place soon after emergence in spring, gestation lasts about 33 to 34 days, and a litter of typically 2 to 5 young first appears above ground at around 40 days old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes wear the same grey-brown coat, and no feature separates them reliably by sight, though males average slightly heavier.

Small, agile body for steep Himalayan and alpine forest terrain.
Musk scent glands that shape communication and human pressure.
Secretive browsing life in cold slopes and scrub.

Musk deer are valued and threatened for musk, which has caused heavy hunting pressure.
They are solitary and secretive compared with many herd deer.
They browse leaves, grasses, lichens, and mountain vegetation.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snow leopards, lynx, wolves, foxes, humans, and habitat loss threaten them. Secrecy, slope movement, and low profile help protect a body built differently.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Alpine Musk Deer are crepuscular or nocturnal in many areas, feeding when cover and quiet reduce risk.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Poorly documented for this species. Musk deer in general are thought to live about 10 to 14 years in the wild, and captive animals have occasionally reached about 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to hidden fawns that rely on camouflage and stillness.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have prominent tusks and musk glands, while females lack the same display tools. The sex difference is central to the alternative strategy.

entries.name: Alpine Swift
entries.heroTitle: Alpine Swift — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The largest swift in Europe, brown above with a white belly and throat split by a dark breast band. Tiny data loggers fitted to Swiss breeding birds showed them staying in the air for around 200 days without landing while they wintered over West Africa.
identification: long scythe wings
high-speed aerial feeding
cliff nesting
and extended airborne life

Breeds on mountain cliffs, sea cliffs and tall old buildings in southern Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, southern Asia, parts of Africa and Madagascar. It feeds high over valleys, forests and towns. European and western Asian birds winter over sub-Saharan Africa; many African and Indian populations are largely resident.

high-speed aerial feeding
cliff nesting

whyInteresting: Its call is a loud, rising and falling trill, very different from the scream of the Common Swift.
Its wingspan is about 55 to 60 centimetres, as wide as a small falcon's.
It was long placed in the genus Apus but is now put in Tachymarptis, together with the Mottled Swift of Africa.
Adults weigh roughly 80 to 120 grams, about twice as heavy as a Common Swift.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It eats flying insects and airborne spiders caught in continuous flight. Flies, beetles, bugs and flying ants are gathered high over valleys, often far from the colony.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: In the air and at colonies, falcons, hawks, owls, and nest predators threaten Alpine Swift. Speed and height protect adults, and nests hidden deep in crevices keep eggs and chicks out of reach of most climbers.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It is highly diurnal in flight and able to remain airborne for very long periods outside breeding duties. During the breeding season adults spend the night clinging inside the colony crevices.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Individuals can live many years, with some swifts reaching a decade or more. Ringing records suggest a few Alpine Swifts pass 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After pairing, females lay eggs in cliff or building crevice nests where both parents feed aerial-caught insects to chicks. Clutches are usually of 2 or 3 white eggs, incubated by both parents for about three weeks, and the young stay in the nest for about 7 to 10 weeks, longer in poor weather.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is the same in both sexes; females are not reliably separable from males even in the hand.

entries.name: Amano Shrimp
entries.heroTitle: Amano Shrimp — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A translucent freshwater shrimp from the streams of Japan and Taiwan, about 3 to 5 centimetres long. Adults live in fresh water but their larvae can only develop in brackish or salt water, so each generation is swept down to the sea and the young must make their way back upstream.
identification: Translucent grey body with a pale stripe along the back
Rows of reddish-brown dots or dashes along the sides
Large for a dwarf shrimp, up to 5 centimetres
Small bristle-tipped claws in constant motion while feeding
Long antennae and a fan-shaped tail
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: east_asia. Clear, fast-flowing streams and small rivers running to the sea in Japan and Taiwan, over rock, gravel and leaf litter in fresh water.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: east_asia. Clear, fast-flowing streams and small rivers running to the sea in Japan and Taiwan, over rock, gravel and leaf litter in fresh water.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 19/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Translucent grey body with a pale stripe along the back
Rows of reddish-brown dots or dashes along the sides
Large for a dwarf shrimp, up to 5 centimetres
Small bristle-tipped claws in constant motion while feeding
Long antennae and a fan-shaped tail
whyInteresting: The common name honours the Japanese aquarist Takashi Amano, who popularised the shrimp in planted tanks in the 1980s for its appetite for algae.
It was long known as Caridina japonica, until a 2006 revision showed that the older name Caridina multidentata applied to the same animal.
Many shrimp in the trade are collected from the wild, because the larvae are difficult to rear in captivity.
It sheds its shell in one piece to grow, leaving an empty, shrimp-shaped skin that is often mistaken for a dead animal.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Algae, the film of microbes on rocks and wood, and decaying plant matter, plus dead animals and small invertebrates when it finds them. Food is picked and scraped up with the first two pairs of legs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Stream fish, eels, freshwater crabs and wading birds eat the adults, and the drifting larvae are taken by plankton feeders. A nearly transparent body, hiding under stones and leaf litter, and a sudden backward flick of the tail are its defences.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly nocturnal in the wild, sheltering under stones and among leaf litter by day and coming out to graze after dark. Where there are no predators, as in aquaria, it feeds openly in daylight.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Aquarium shrimp usually live about 2 to 3 years, sometimes longer; how long they last in the wild is less certain.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female carries up to a few thousand tiny eggs under her abdomen for about a month or more, fanning them with her swimming legs. The hatched larvae drift downstream and must reach brackish or salt water to develop.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger, up to about 5 centimetres against roughly 3.5 for males, and the lower row of markings on their flanks is drawn out into dashes. Males have evenly spaced round dots.

analysis.summary: The largest river dolphin, with males reaching about 2.5 metres, it swims into flooded forest when rivers rise. Its neck vertebrae are not fused as in ocean dolphins, so it can bend its head sideways and twist its long body around submerged trunks and roots while hunting.

Small eyes and a rounded, bulging forehead

Known in Brazil as the boto, it appears in Amazonian folklore as a shape-shifter that takes human form at night.
Dolphins in the Bolivian river system are sometimes treated as a separate species, Inia boliviensis, a split that is still debated.
Killing for use as bait in the piracatinga catfish fishery has driven steep declines in parts of the Brazilian Amazon.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active at any hour, with feeding often busiest in the morning and late afternoon. Rest appears to be taken in short spells near the surface in slow, quiet water rather than in one long night-time sleep.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and heavier than females and usually much pinker, largely because scar tissue from fights with other males builds up on their skin.

Sold as a small algae eater, it grows to the length of an arm and outlives most tanks it is bought for.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal, wedged under wood or into a bank tunnel through the day and grazing after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Amazon Sailfin Catfish live 10 to 15 years or more, long enough to outlast several dry seasons in the same stretch of water.

Species look so alike from the shell that many can be identified reliably only by dissecting the reproductive organs.
Amber snails have reached remote Pacific islands such as Hawaii, where dozens of species found nowhere else have evolved.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Decaying plant material, algae, fungi and the film of microbes on wet leaves and mud, rasped off with the radula, a ribbon of tiny teeth. Some species also graze soft living leaves.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, frogs, ground beetles, marsh fly larvae and small mammals eat them. The thin shell is little defence, and in some species the body cannot withdraw fully, so they depend on dull colouring and on staying within dense, wet vegetation.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most active at night and on humid or rainy days. In dry or cold spells they rest sealed to stems or under litter, and temperate species spend the winter dormant in soil or plant debris.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one to two years in the species that have been studied; many temperate populations are close to annual.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Each snail is a hermaphrodite and pairs exchange sperm. Eggs are laid in gelatinous clusters of a few to several dozen on damp soil, litter or plant bases, and hatch in roughly two to four weeks into tiny shelled young. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: There are no separate sexes. Every individual is a hermaphrodite with both male and female organs, and adults look alike.

analysis.summary: The American Black Bear runs its whole year on what the season offers — green shoots in spring, insects in summer, then a single-minded autumn of eating up to twenty thousand calories a day before denning. It is not one strategy but four, in order.

Despite the name a black bear may be cinnamon, blond, blue-grey or white — the white Kermode bears of coastal British Columbia are the same species.
Short curved claws make it a much better climber than a Grizzly, and cubs go up a tree at the first sign of trouble.

It moults inside a protected chamber in soil or rotten wood, and may eat the shed skin afterwards.
Tiny mites often ride on its body; they are thought to be mostly harmless passengers.
Its defensive fluid seeps from a row of small pores running along each side of the body.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds on decaying plant matter: dead leaves, soft rotting wood and the fungi and microbes growing on them, which it scrapes and chews with its mouthparts as it moves slowly through the litter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, shrews, skunks, raccoons and some beetles attack millipedes of this kind. Its first response is to coil into a tight spiral that shields the legs and soft underside, lying still until the danger passes.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active at night and after rain, when the air is humid. By day it lies hidden in leaf litter, under logs or in soil, and in cold months it becomes dormant deeper in the ground or in rotting wood.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Individuals are reported to live several years, perhaps up to about 10, taking a few years to reach maturity; wild lifespan is poorly documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in the soil, reportedly coating each one in a small capsule of chewed soil or plant matter. Young hatch with only a few segments and legs, adding more with each moult as they grow, with no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males have the legs of the seventh body ring modified into mating structures called gonopods, leaving a visible gap in the leg row there. Females have a complete leg row and can be slightly bulkier.

entries.name: American Kestrel
entries.heroTitle: American Kestrel — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A compact falcon of open country that watches the ground with intense focus, dropping onto prey it has spotted from a perch many metres away. Like other falcons it kills with a bite, driving a tooth-like notch on the upper bill into the neck of its victim.
identification: Small falcon, about the size of a mourning dove
Two black vertical stripes on each side of a pale face
Males have blue-grey wings; females have rufous, barred wings
Rufous back and tail, the male's tail tipped with a black band
Hovers into the wind or bobs its tail while perched on wires

Two dark spots on the back of the head may act as false eyes, deterring attackers approaching from behind.
It readily nests in boxes, and nest-box programmes are used to monitor its populations across North America.
Surplus prey is often cached in grass clumps, tree crevices or fence posts and eaten later.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Large insects such as grasshoppers, crickets, beetles and dragonflies dominate in warm months; voles, mice, small birds, lizards and small snakes matter more in winter and when chicks are being fed. Most prey is caught on the ground.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Cooper's hawks, red-tailed hawks, goshawks, great horned owls and other larger raptors kill adults, while rat snakes, raccoons and squirrels raid nests. Kestrels mob predators with shrill calls and nest inside cavities that are hard to reach.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, hunting most in the morning and late afternoon. At night it roosts alone in tree cavities, dense foliage, building ledges or nest boxes, often using the same spot for weeks.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most wild birds live only 1 to 5 years; the oldest ringed bird on record was about 14 years old.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually 4 or 5 eggs are laid in a bare cavity with no nest material and incubated for about 29 to 31 days, mostly by the female. The male brings food; chicks fledge at about four weeks and depend on the parents for a further couple of weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are a little larger and heavier than males. Unlike most raptors, the sexes can be told apart by plumage even in the nest once feathers grow, and young males have more heavily streaked breasts than adult males.

entries.name: American Lobster
entries.heroTitle: American Lobster — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: American Lobster grows power slowly, using cold water, shelter competition, claws, and repeated molts to build long-term dominance.
identification: Two unequal front claws: a heavy crusher and a slimmer toothed cutter
Greenish-brown to dark olive shell in life, turning red only when cooked
Long reddish antennae that can exceed the body length
Small pincers on the first two pairs of walking legs
Spiny, pointed rostrum projecting between the eyes

Lobsters release urine from openings near the antennae and jet it forward at rivals and mates as a chemical signal.
Blue lobsters, caused by a genetic change in shell pigment, are often quoted as about one in two million; yellow and split-coloured animals are rarer.
The heaviest recorded American lobster, caught off Nova Scotia in 1977, weighed about 20 kilograms.
Warming water has caused sharp declines at the southern end of the range, such as Long Island Sound, while catches rose farther north in Maine.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Crabs, mussels, clams, sea urchins, marine worms, small fish and some algae are eaten, along with carrion. It finds food mainly by smell, using chemical sensors on its short inner antennae and on the hairs of its walking legs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Cod, wolffish, sculpins, striped bass, seals and large crabs eat lobsters, above all small juveniles and animals left soft after moulting, and people trap them in vast numbers. It backs into a crevice or dug burrow with claws raised, or shoots backwards with a flick of the tail.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Largely nocturnal: it stays in a crevice or burrow by day and emerges around dusk to forage, returning before dawn. Activity slows sharply in winter cold.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Age is hard to measure because the shell is shed at every moult. Many are thought to live several decades, and the largest wild lobsters may be 50 years old or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating follows the female's moult, and she stores sperm until she extrudes eggs onto the swimmerets under her tail. She carries several thousand to tens of thousands of eggs, depending on her size, for about 9 to 12 months; hatched larvae drift in the plankton for weeks before settling.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Under the tail, the first pair of swimmerets is hard and grooved in males but soft and feathery in females. Females also have a broader tail, while males of the same length carry larger claws.

entries.name: American Pika
entries.heroTitle: American Pika — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A small, round-eared relative of rabbits, the pika spends the brief alpine summer as a hay-maker. It makes many trips a day into the meadow, returning with mouthfuls of grasses and flowers, and piles them under boulders as a store that feeds it through winter.
identification: Rounded, egg-shaped body with no visible tail
Short, round ears edged with pale fur
Greyish-brown to buff fur, paler underneath
Roughly 16 to 22 cm long, about the size of a fist
Sits hunched and still on rocks between trips

Studies in Colorado found that pikas store plants rich in bitter compounds, which keep well in the pile and become more palatable over winter.
Young pikas usually settle close to where they were born, so animals on isolated rocky slopes can be cut off from other populations.
Some populations live well below the high peaks, in cool lava fields such as Craters of the Moon in Idaho.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, sedges, wildflowers and shrub leaves near the talus edge. In summer it gathers plants into haypiles under rocks, and, since it does not hibernate, the stored hay feeds it through winter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Weasels are among its most dangerous predators because they can follow it into the rock pile; martens, coyotes, foxes, hawks and golden eagles catch it in the open. Pikas give short alarm calls and dive into gaps between the rocks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. It retreats into cool gaps deep in the rock pile during warm middays and overnight. It does not hibernate, and stays active beneath the snow all winter.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually up to about 3 years in the wild; a few individuals have been recorded reaching around 6 or 7 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding starts in spring. After a pregnancy of about a month, the female gives birth to usually 2 to 4 young, which are weaned within about a month. A second litter is sometimes started, but in studied populations it is rarely weaned, and juveniles must claim a territory before winter.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike and are about the same size.

entries.name: American Red Squirrel
entries.heroTitle: American Red Squirrel — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: American Red Squirrel AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: The American Red Squirrel is the small, noisy tree squirrel of North America's conifer forests, rusty above and white below with a bold white eye ring. Each one lives alone on a territory built around a store of cones, and scolds almost anything that walks beneath it.
identification: Rusty red-brown back and tail
White belly, often edged by a black side stripe
Bold white ring around each dark eye
Small compact body with a slim, lightly bushed tail
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Spruce, fir, pine and hemlock forest across Canada, Alaska, the northern United States and down the Rockies and Appalachians, along with mixed woods and conifer-planted parks. It needs cone-bearing trees and a cool shaded spot where a midden will not dry out.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america. Spruce, fir, pine and hemlock forest across Canada, Alaska, the northern United States and down the Rockies and Appalachians, along with mixed woods and conifer-planted parks. It hangs mushrooms in the forks of branches to dry before storing them.
In late winter it bites into sugar maple bark, leaves the sap to evaporate and returns later to lick the concentrated sugar.
The rattle is a territorial advertisement, and each squirrel's rattle is measurably different from its neighbours'.
A female is receptive to males for only about one day in each breeding season.
The Douglas Squirrel of the Pacific coast is its closest relative and lookalike, but has an orange-buff belly where the American Red Squirrel is white.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds of conifer cones are the staple, supplemented by buds, flowers, berries, fungi, tree sap, insects and occasionally birds' eggs and nestlings. Cones are cut green and stored closed, which is why the larder has to be built in a few busy weeks and then held all winter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: American martens, fishers, lynx, bobcats, foxes, weasels, goshawks, red-tailed hawks and owls all hunt it. A squirrel on a long-held territory knows every escape route through the branches, which is another return on staying put.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day all year and does not hibernate, though it stays in the nest through the worst cold and storms. Nests are in tree cavities, in balls of grass and shredded bark among the branches, or in tunnels inside the midden itself.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Many die in their first year; those that win a territory commonly live three to five years, with a few reaching eight or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After about five weeks of pregnancy a female bears a litter of usually three or four, raised alone in a nest. Young must find or inherit a territory with a midden before their first winter, and some mothers hand over part or all of their own to one of them.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are alike in size and colour, and both sexes hold and defend individual territories. Only on a female's single day of receptivity do males leave their own ground and gather on hers.

analysis.summary: North America's largest thrush, grey-brown above with a brick-orange breast, breeding from Alaska and Canada south into Mexico. Males are among the first birds to sing each morning, starting well before sunrise with a carolling run of rising and falling phrases.

Yellow bill, often dusky at the tip

Robins found dying on lawns after DDT spraying against Dutch elm disease became a central example in Rachel Carson's Silent Spring.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few predators. Gulls, ravens, coyotes, foxes and great horned owls take eggs and chicks. Nesting on islands keeps most land predators away, and colonies may abandon nests after repeated human disturbance.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the same plumage. Males are larger, with noticeably longer bills.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, including shrikes and small falcons, lizards, praying mantises and large spiders prey on it. Grey-brown colouring hides it against bark while it keeps still; if approached it leaps and flies off, showing smoky-banded hindwings before dropping into cover.

entries.name: Mottled Duck
entries.heroTitle: Mottled Duck — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Most birds never migrate, unusual among North American ducks: they spend the whole year in the same coastal and freshwater marshes of Florida and the Gulf of Mexico coast. This warm-brown dabbler is a close relative of the Mallard, but the drake lacks bright breeding plumage.

Many pairs form in autumn and early winter, months before the spring nesting season.
A separate population in coastal South Carolina descends from birds released there in the 1970s and 1980s.
Florida birds and those of the western Gulf coast form two separate populations, often treated as distinct subspecies, fulvigula and maculosa.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Dabbles and up-ends in shallow water for the seeds of grasses, sedges and other marsh plants, with snails, insects, crayfish and small fish. Laying females and ducklings take more animal food, especially in spring.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Alligators, raccoons, skunks, snakes and fire ants take eggs and ducklings, and hawks and owls kill adults. Hens nest hidden in dense grass and slip away low when a predator approaches, and flightless moulting adults keep deep in cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds mostly in the early morning and late afternoon, and sometimes at night. Between feeding bouts it rests on banks, mudbars or open water, often within dense marsh cover.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: An average wild lifespan is not well established. Hunting, predators and flooded nests remove many birds each year, yet banding recoveries show that a few survive past their tenth year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female lines a ground nest in dense grass near water with down and lays about 8 to 12 creamy to greenish eggs. She incubates alone for roughly 25 to 27 days, and the ducklings leave the nest within a day and feed themselves under her guard.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is alike, but bill colour separates them: males have a bright yellow to olive-yellow bill, females a duller orange or olive bill with dark spotting along the top. Males are also slightly larger.

In Canada it is listed as endangered, with only a small and scattered population.

The tadpoles are distasteful to many fish, so they can use ponds where fish are present.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Beetles, ants, crickets, caterpillars, spiders and other small invertebrates. It sits and waits at night, snapping up anything small that moves within reach with a flick of the sticky tongue.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hognose snakes specialise in eating toads; garter snakes, herons, raccoons and some birds also take them. Glands on the skin, especially the large ones behind the eyes, release distasteful toxins, and a threatened toad may puff up, flatten or play dead.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active at night in warm weather. By day it digs backwards into loose sand or shelters under logs and debris, and it spends winter buried deep in sand below the frost line.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most wild adults probably live only a few years, perhaps up to about 5; captive toads can live longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay several thousand eggs in long gelatinous strings wound around plants in shallow water, mostly from April to June. The eggs hatch within about a week, and small black tadpoles transform into tiny toadlets in roughly one to two months. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger. Breeding males have a dark grey or blackish throat and dark pads on the inner fingers for gripping the female; females have pale throats.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few natural predators of adults are known. Domestic dogs kill some, and herders sometimes kill it in the belief that it takes livestock; mining and roads break up its habitat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Andean Mountain Cat rests in rock dens, caves, ledges, and hidden cliff shelters. Activity varies between areas: camera traps have recorded it mostly at night and around dawn and dusk, yet many sightings are by day.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Reproduction is poorly known. Litters are thought to be of one or two kittens, born in rock dens, with births reported from spring into summer.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike, and too few animals have been measured to describe any size difference.

Short crest often raised when excited

Some populations breed almost all year, while others at high altitude or in the far south nest in a single season.
Young birds leave the nest before they can fly well and hide in low cover while the parents keep feeding them.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly seeds of grasses and weeds picked from bare or short-grass ground, with insects and other small invertebrates taken especially when feeding young. It forages by hopping and scratching on the ground, often near people.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, falcons, cats and nest robbers such as snakes take adults, eggs and chicks. Nests are often parasitised by the Shiny Cowbird. Birds flush into shrubs with a sharp alarm note when threatened.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Males often begin singing before sunrise, and birds keep foraging until dusk. The night is spent perched out of sight in dense shrubs or thick vegetation.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly documented; like most small sparrows it probably lives about 2 to 5 years, with some individuals surviving longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The cup nest is built on the ground under a tuft of grass or low in a shrub. Clutches are usually 2 or 3 speckled eggs, incubated for about two weeks; both parents feed the chicks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike. Juveniles lack the rufous collar and bold head stripes and are streaked brown below.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Anegada Rock Iguana is diurnal, basking and sheltering in burrows during heat.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults grow slowly and are believed to live for several decades, though no wild iguana on Anegada has been followed through its whole life.

analysis.summary: The Freshwater Angelfish is built tall and flat rather than streamlined, which is slow in open water and ideal among flooded roots and stems. It gave up speed for the ability to turn on the spot in a vertical world.

whyInteresting: The body shape is an adaptation to vegetation, letting the fish slip between vertical stems and roots where a torpedo-shaped fish would be blocked.
The vertical barring breaks up the outline against reed stems and shifts in intensity with stress and dominance.
Pairs bond and both parents guard the eggs, fanning them and moving fry between prepared surfaces.
Eggs are laid on a cleaned vertical surface — a leaf, a stem or a piece of slate — rather than in a scrape.
It comes from the slow blackwater tributaries of the Amazon basin, and nearly every ornamental variety traces to that wild form.
