fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small invertebrates, crustaceans and fish fry taken with quick, precise strikes from a hovering position. Ambushing from among stems needs manoeuvring rather than pursuit, which is what the body is for.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger cichlids, catfish and birds. The barred pattern against vertical stems, and the ability to turn where a faster fish cannot follow, are the whole defence.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, becoming still and drifting close to cover at night, when the barring often pales noticeably.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around ten years, and longer in good aquarium conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A bonded pair cleans a vertical surface and lays several hundred eggs on it, then both parents fan and guard them and move the fry between sites until they are free-swimming.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Very hard to tell apart outside breeding. Males may develop a slightly steeper forehead; the reliable difference is only visible at spawning, when the female's breeding tube is broader and blunter.

entries.name: Ankole-Watusi Cattle
entries.heroTitle: Ankole-Watusi Cattle — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A breed of domestic cattle descended from the long-horned Ankole herds of East Africa, carrying some of the largest horns of any cattle. They can span about 2.4 metres from tip to tip, and blood circulating through their honeycombed cores sheds heat before returning to the body.

The Ankole-Watusi name is used for the breed developed in the United States from animals imported through European zoos during the twentieth century.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: In East Africa lions, leopards and spotted hyenas take cattle, calves especially. Adults face a threat with lowered horns, and herders traditionally pen the animals overnight. On farms elsewhere disease matters more than predation.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Grazes by day, mostly in the cooler morning and late afternoon, and lies up to chew the cud around midday. The herd beds down close together on open ground after dark.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females and young explain why secrecy matters: birth sites, nests, calves, or hidden juveniles depend on cover before they can handle open risk.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes carry large horns. Bulls are heavier, about 450 to 730 kilograms against about 410 to 540 for cows, with a thicker neck and a small hump over the shoulders.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators of this species have not been studied directly. Birds, wasps and larger spiders hunt small jumping spiders in general, and animals that have learned to avoid ants are thought to leave convincing mimics alone.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active in daylight, mostly in sunshine. At night and in cold or wet weather it shelters in a small silk cell spun under a stone, in a curled leaf or among grass stems, and it passes the winter in a similar retreat.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: As in other jumping spiders, the female probably lays her eggs in a silk retreat and guards them. How many eggs she lays and how long the young take to hatch and mature are not known.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males have greatly enlarged jaws that project forwards, nearly as long as the front half of the body. Females have short jaws and a fuller abdomen.

entries.name: Antarctic Petrel
entries.heroTitle: Antarctic Petrel — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Antarctic Petrel expresses Frostwing through cold-ocean flight, Antarctic breeding, colony nesting, and repeated return through severe weather make the Frostwing principle specific rather than generic; body, habitat, and pressure all point back to the same lesson.

colony nesting

whyInteresting: It is the only member of the genus Thalassoica.
Its plumage is dark brown above, with a broad white band across the rear of each wing and a white tail tipped brown.
One colony, at Svarthamaren in Dronning Maud Land, has been estimated at a few hundred thousand breeding pairs.
Its wingspan is roughly one metre, and it flies with stiff wingbeats broken by long glides.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Its food is krill, fish, squid, and marine carrion found over cold seas. Antarctic krill makes up most of the diet in many studies, and birds snatch prey at the surface, often feeding in flocks near the ice edge.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Blizzards can bury nests or chill chicks, and south polar skuas take eggs and chicks from exposed ledges, even at colonies far inland. When threatened, adults and chicks reportedly spit foul stomach oil.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: In summer it rests on cliffs or sea surface between foraging flights, active around long polar daylight. Outside the breeding season it stays in the pack ice zone and roosts on icebergs and floes.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Long-lived, like most petrels: high yearly adult survival suggests breeding adults typically live well over a decade, though reliable maximum ages have not been published.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Late in the southern spring, females lay one egg in a rocky nest, and both parents share incubation and feeding. The egg hatches after about six weeks, and the chick fledges roughly six to seven weeks later.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike; males are reported to average slightly larger, but they cannot be told apart in the field.

entries.name: Common Carpet Beetle
entries.heroTitle: Common Carpet Beetle — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Common Carpet Beetle AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A small, rounded beetle, about 3 to 4 millimetres long, patterned with black, white and orange-red scales. Adults feed on pollen at flowers, while the bristly larvae, known as woolly bears, feed on wool, fur, feathers and other dead animal material.
identification: Small, oval, convex body about 3 to 4 millimetres long
Black with irregular white scale patches
Orange-red scales along the midline where the wing cases meet
Short, clubbed antennae
Larva is a brown, bristly woolly bear with long tail tufts
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, central_asia. Outdoors, adults visit flowers in meadows, hedgerows and gardens; larvae develop in bird and wasp nests and animal remains, and indoors in carpets, wardrobes and stored woollens.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, central_asia. Outdoors, adults visit flowers in meadows, hedgerows and gardens; larvae develop in bird and wasp nests and animal remains, and indoors in carpets, wardrobes and stored woollens.

whyInteresting: Larvae can survive long periods without food and moult repeatedly, and their shed bristly skins are often the first sign of an infestation.
The bristly hairs of the larvae can cause an itchy rash in some people, sometimes called carpet beetle dermatitis.
Introduced accidentally to North America in the nineteenth century, it became known there as the buffalo carpet beetle.
When disturbed, adults often pull in their legs and antennae and lie still, feigning death.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults eat pollen and nectar from flowers. Larvae digest keratin, feeding on wool, fur, feathers, hides and dead insects in bird nests, animal remains and stored textiles.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders, predatory beetles and parasitic wasps take adults and larvae. The larva's arrow-tipped bristles detach and tangle the mouthparts of attacking ants and spiders; adults drop and play dead when disturbed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are active by day, visiting flowers in sunshine. Larvae stay hidden in nests, carcasses or stored materials. Winter is usually passed as a larva, with pupation in spring.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: The life cycle usually takes about a year, most of it as a larva. Adults live a few weeks.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After mating on flowers, females seek out bird nests, animal remains or buildings and lay eggs on keratin-rich material. Larvae moult repeatedly over many months and pupate inside the last larval skin. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look almost identical; females are on average slightly larger, and reliable sexing needs close examination.

entries.name: Brown-throated Sunbird
entries.heroTitle: Brown-throated Sunbird — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Rather than specialising on a few deep flowers, this sunbird takes nectar from the blossoms of many different plants, from palms and fruit trees to garden shrubs. At long tubular flowers it has been recorded piercing the base of the corolla to reach the nectar directly instead of probing from the front.
identification: Short, fairly straight bill for a sunbird
Male: glossy green and purple crown and back
Male: brown throat above a bright yellow belly
Female: olive upperparts, yellow underparts and a pale eye-ring
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, sumatra, borneo. Lowland open country with scattered trees: coastal scrub, mangrove edges, coconut groves, plantations, parks, village gardens and secondary growth at forest edges. It is uncommon inside closed forest.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia, sumatra, borneo. Lowland open country with scattered trees: coastal scrub, mangrove edges, coconut groves, plantations, parks, village gardens and secondary growth at forest edges. It is uncommon inside closed forest.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 20/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Short, fairly straight bill for a sunbird
Male: glossy green and purple crown and back
Male: brown throat above a bright yellow belly

whyInteresting: It is also known as the Plain-throated Sunbird, a name used in many field books.
The nest is a hanging, pear-shaped pouch of fibres and plant down with a side entrance, slung from a twig or palm frond.
The female lays one or two eggs and does most or all of the incubation.
It adapts well to towns and is one of the commonest sunbirds in gardens and parks in Malaysia and Singapore.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Nectar from many kinds of flowers, including coconut, banana and hibiscus, together with small insects and spiders. It usually feeds while perched, gleaning prey from leaves and bark and sometimes hovering briefly.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predation on this species is little studied. Like other small garden birds, its hanging nests are probably raided by snakes, crows and squirrels, and adults may be caught by small hawks and cats. Pairs call sharply and flit around intruders that come near the nest.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, feeding from first light and busiest in the morning. At night it roosts perched among dense leaves in shrubs and trees.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan for Anthreptes malacensis is unpublished; it takes nectar from many plant species and may pierce tubular flowers at the base.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female builds a hanging, pear-shaped purse of plant fibre, cobweb and debris with a side entrance, often shaded by a small porch. She lays one or two eggs and does the incubation; the male is reported to help feed the chicks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes differ strongly: males are glossy and iridescent, while females lack any gloss and are the plainer bird. Young males at first resemble females.

entries.name: Apostlebird
entries.heroTitle: Apostlebird — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Apostlebird teaches Twelve-Strong Forage through soft ashy-grey plumage, a short dark bill, a long dark tail, and the habit of moving as a noisy cooperative flock over open woodland ground.
identification: Soft ashy-grey body with a darker long graduated tail.
Short dark bill suited to ground foraging.
Almost always seen in small cooperative family groups.
Mud-nester proportions shared with White-winged Chough relatives.
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Open woodland, farmland edges, and inland eastern Australian country where cooperative flocks can forage on the ground together.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Open woodland, farmland edges, and inland eastern Australian country where cooperative flocks can forage on the ground together.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 28/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Soft ashy-grey body with a darker long graduated tail.
Short dark bill suited to ground foraging.
Almost always seen in small cooperative family groups.
Mud-nester proportions shared with White-winged Chough relatives.
whyInteresting: Apostlebird is Struthidea cinerea, an Australian endemic mud-nester in Corcoracidae.
Groups are often around a dozen birds, which inspired the common name.
They forage mostly on the ground for insects and seeds in inland eastern woodland and farmland.
Helpers in the flock share nest building and chick care, so Twelve-Strong Forage is social as well as physical.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, seeds, and other ground litter food taken while the flock scrapes and watches together.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors and terrestrial predators pressure exposed ground foragers, so flock vigilance keeps Twelve-Strong Forage useful.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal; flocks settle and roost together after daytime foraging.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild longevity is measured in years within stable family groups; cooperative care supports successive nesting seasons.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding is cooperative: several adults may help build the mud nest and feed nestlings.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike; flock behavior and overall mud-nester shape are clearer than sex cues in most field photos.

entries.name: Apple Snail
entries.heroTitle: Apple Snail — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: These mostly large freshwater snails of warm regions carry both a gill and a lung, so they can breathe underwater and also breathe air. This lets many live in stagnant, oxygen-poor water, and some species can outlast a dry season buried in mud for months.
identification: Large, globe-shaped shell with a low spire
Operculum that closes the shell opening
Very long, thread-like tentacles
Fleshy breathing tube extended to the water surface
Egg clusters laid above the water in many species
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america, south_asia, southeast_asia, sub_saharan_africa. Still or slow-moving fresh water: ponds, swamps, marshes, ditches, rice paddies and the weedy margins of lakes and rivers in warm parts of the Americas and Southeast Asia. Most prefer shallow water with soft mud and plenty of plants.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, south_america, south_asia, southeast_asia, sub_saharan_africa. Still or slow-moving fresh water: ponds, swamps, marshes, ditches, rice paddies and the weedy margins of lakes and rivers in warm parts of the Americas and Southeast Asia. Most prefer shallow water with soft mud and plenty of plants.

whyInteresting: The golden apple snail was taken from South America to Asia around 1980 as a food animal and became a serious pest of rice.
Pomacea eggs are brightly coloured and contain toxic proteins, and very few animals eat them.
The snail kite has a slender, deeply hooked bill that fits inside the shell opening to cut the snail free.
Apple snails can carry rat lungworm, a parasite that infects people who eat the snails raw or undercooked.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Most graze on aquatic plants, algae and decaying matter, rasping food with a toothed tongue called a radula. Some, such as the golden apple snail, eat tender rice seedlings, and many will scavenge dead animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snail kites and limpkins in the Americas and openbill storks in Asia specialise in apple snails, and fish, turtles, alligators, herons and rats also eat them. A disturbed snail lets go of its perch, sinks, and pulls the operculum shut.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most species are chiefly active at night and around dusk, spending the day buried in mud or tucked among plants.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Roughly 1 to 4 years in the well-studied Pomacea species, shorter in warm water where they grow fast. Figures for many other members of the family are not well known.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pomacea females climb out of the water, usually at night, to glue clutches of a few hundred to over a thousand pink or orange eggs to stems and walls. These hatch in about two to three weeks. Pila species lay in damp hollows on the bank.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are separate, unlike in many land snails. Males and females look much alike from outside; females are often slightly larger, and in some Pomacea the male has a rounder shell opening.

entries.name: Military Macaw
entries.heroTitle: Military Macaw — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A large green macaw of dry mountain forests and canyons. Mated pairs stay together within the flock, perching side by side and preening each other's head and neck feathers, the places a bird cannot reach with its own bill.
identification: Mostly bright green with a red forehead patch
Bare pinkish-white face lined with rows of tiny dark feathers
Blue flight feathers and a long red-brown and blue tail
Olive-yellow underside to the wings and tail
Heavy black hooked bill
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Arid and humid forest in foothills and mountains, including pine-oak woodland, dry tropical forest and steep canyons with cliffs, mostly between about 500 and 2,500 metres. It ranges patchily from Mexico to north-western Argentina.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Arid and humid forest in foothills and mountains, including pine-oak woodland, dry tropical forest and steep canyons with cliffs, mostly between about 500 and 2,500 metres. It ranges patchily from Mexico to north-western Argentina.

whyInteresting: It is listed as Vulnerable, having declined through forest loss and capture of young birds for the pet trade.
Its loud, raucous calls carry far across canyons and are often the first sign of a flock passing overhead.
The name military is thought to refer to its green plumage, like the colour of old military dress uniforms.
Three subspecies are recognised: one in Mexico, one from Venezuela and Colombia south to Peru, and one in Bolivia and north-western Argentina.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, nuts, fruits and flowers taken in the treetops, with the powerful hooked bill used to crack hard shells. In parts of its South American range it visits exposed clay banks to eat soil.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predation on wild adults is rarely recorded; large raptors are the likeliest natural predators, and nests may be raided by climbing mammals and snakes. Trapping for the pet trade and forest loss are the main threats. Flocks call loudly in alarm and fly off together.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At night, mated pairs and family groups sleep close together on cliff ledges or in tall trees, often returning to the same roost site night after night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is not well known. Captive birds often live several decades, and ages of 50 years or more have been reported.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests in cliff crevices or hollows high in large trees. The female lays usually 2 or 3 eggs and incubates them for about 26 days; both parents feed the chicks, which fledge at roughly three months old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in plumage. Males may average slightly larger with a heavier bill, but birds cannot be reliably sexed in the field.

entries.name: Arabian Oryx
entries.heroTitle: Arabian Oryx — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Hunted out of the wild by 1972, this desert antelope survived only in captive herds, and animals bred from them were released in Oman from 1982. In 2011 it became the first animal once extinct in the wild to recover to Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. In hot weather its body temperature rises by day and falls at night, saving water otherwise spent on cooling.
identification: pale reflective coat
long straight horns
desert walking
and water-efficient grazing
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_africa_middle_east. Arabian desert plains, gravel flats, dunes, and sparse scrub.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_africa_middle_east. Arabian desert plains, gravel flats, dunes, and sparse scrub.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 66/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: pale reflective coat
long straight horns
desert walking
and water-efficient grazing
whyInteresting: It is the smallest of the oryx species, with adults typically weighing about 70 kilograms.
Seen side-on, the two horns can appear to merge into one, which may have fed the unicorn legend.
In 2007 Oman's Arabian Oryx Sanctuary became the first site ever removed from the UNESCO World Heritage List, after its protected area was greatly reduced.
In 1962 a rescue effort called Operation Oryx caught a few of the last wild animals to start a captive breeding herd in the United States.
It is known in Arabic as al-maha and is the national animal of Qatar.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds on grasses, herbs, roots, tubers, and desert plants located after rain. Its hooves scrape out roots and bulbs, and moisture from plants and dew lets it go weeks without drinking.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Arabian wolves were its chief natural predator and may still take calves in places. Poaching for meat and for live sale has set back reintroduced herds, notably in Oman. An adult can defend itself with its long, sharp horns.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Grazing happens mainly in the early morning, late afternoon and at night; it rests in shade or shallow scrapes during heat, moving more in cooler hours.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 15 to 20 years in the wild; animals in captivity have lived beyond 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a pregnancy of about eight months, females give birth to a single calf that hides before joining the herd. Calves are weaned at roughly four months, and births can occur in any season.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look very similar; both sexes carry long horns, with males often heavier and more territorial. Females' horns tend to be slightly thinner.

entries.name: Limpkin
entries.heroTitle: Limpkin — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The only living member of its family, a long-legged brown marsh bird related to cranes and rails. Its long, slightly down-curved bill has a small gap near the tip, and in many birds the tip is twisted slightly to one side, which helps it pull apple snails from their shells.
identification: Chocolate-brown plumage streaked and spotted with white on the head, neck and back
Bill yellowish at the base with a dark tip
Long dark grey legs
Flies with stiff, jerky upstrokes and legs trailing
About 65 centimetres long, the size of a small heron
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Freshwater marshes, swamps, spring runs, slow rivers and lake shores with dense emergent and floating plants and plenty of apple snails, mainly in lowlands from Florida and southern Georgia through Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean to Argentina.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Freshwater marshes, swamps, spring runs, slow rivers and lake shores with dense emergent and floating plants and plenty of apple snails, mainly in lowlands from Florida and southern Georgia through Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean to Argentina.

whyInteresting: The common name is thought to come from its halting, limping-looking gait.
Its loud, wailing scream, often heard at night, earned it the Florida name crying bird.
Introduced non-native apple snails have given it a new food supply, and it has recently spread into new parts of the south-eastern United States.
It regularly perches high in trees and on posts, unusual for a long-legged marsh bird.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Apple snails make up most of the diet. It finds them by walking through shallow water and probing among plants, carries each to a bank, log or tussock, and extracts the body. Freshwater mussels, other snails, frogs, insects and worms are also eaten.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and chicks are probably taken by raccoons, snakes and birds of prey; predation on adults is poorly documented. Adults escape by running into dense cover or flying low with legs dangling, and pairs call loudly when an intruder nears the nest.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and partly at night, when it sometimes feeds. It rests standing in marsh vegetation or perched in trees and shrubs.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild has not been documented in any detail, as few Limpkins have been followed through banding.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The nest is a bulky pile of plant material in marsh vegetation, a shrub or a tree, usually near water. Typically 4 to 8 buff, brown-blotched eggs are incubated by both parents for about 4 weeks, and the downy chicks follow the adults soon after hatching.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in plumage. Males are on average a little larger, which is hard to judge except when a pair stands together.

entries.name: Map Butterfly
entries.heroTitle: Map Butterfly — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Its two yearly generations look like different species. Adults emerging in spring are orange with black spots; the summer brood is black with a white band. Day length experienced by the caterpillar decides which form the pupa will produce.
identification: Underside brown with a fine network of pale lines
Flies low and settles often on flowers and leaves
Basks on sunlit leaves with wings spread flat
Small, with a wingspan of roughly 3 to 4 cm
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, central_asia, east_asia. Woodland rides, clearings and edges, damp meadows, river valleys and scrub where patches of stinging nettle grow in partial shade. Mostly lowland and hill country across Europe and temperate Asia to Japan.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe, central_asia, east_asia. Woodland rides, clearings and edges, damp meadows, river valleys and scrub where patches of stinging nettle grow in partial shade. Mostly lowland and hill country across Europe and temperate Asia to Japan.

behaviorTraits: Underside brown with a fine network of pale lines
Flies low and settles often on flowers and leaves
Basks on sunlit leaves with wings spread flat

whyInteresting: Linnaeus described the spring and summer forms as two separate species, and the names levana and prorsa are still used for them.
Rearing under intermediate conditions can produce a form between the two, called porima, which is also found occasionally in the wild.
Over the last century it has spread into parts of northern and western Europe where it was not previously recorded.
Butterflies released in England in the early twentieth century are said to have been deliberately destroyed by a collector who objected to them.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars feed on common stinging nettle. Adults take nectar from flowers such as bramble, hogweed and other umbellifers, and thistles.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders and dragonflies take adults, and parasitic wasps and flies attack caterpillars. Caterpillars are protected by branched spines, and adults close their wings to show the brown, net-patterned underside, which blends with leaves.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Flies only in sunshine and rests overnight under leaves, often high on shrubs or trees. Winter is passed as a pupa.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults live about two to three weeks. The overwintering pupa lasts several months, so a spring-generation insect lives most of a year from egg to death.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid in stacked chains of up to about a dozen under nettle leaves. Caterpillars are black and spiny with two horns on the head and feed in groups when young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are slightly larger with broader, more rounded wings; in both seasonal forms the sexes share the same pattern.

entries.name: Arctic Char
entries.heroTitle: Arctic Char — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Arctic Char turns cold water into an advantage, shifting between lakes, rivers, and sea while reading temperature, depth, and season better than most fish.
identification: Pale pink or cream spots on a darker back
White leading edges on the lower fins
Slightly forked tail and very small scales
Silvery sides in fish fresh from the sea
Small fleshy fin between dorsal fin and tail
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, europe, central_asia, east_asia, arctic_antarctic, north_atlantic, north_pacific, arctic_ocean. Cold, clear, well-oxygenated lakes and rivers of the Arctic and subarctic, from shallow tundra lakes to deep basins where it keeps to cold water below the warm surface layer in summer. Sea-run stocks also feed along cold coasts.

Cold, clear, well-oxygenated lakes and rivers of the Arctic and subarctic, from shallow tundra lakes to deep basins where it keeps to cold water below the warm surface layer in summer. Sea-run stocks also feed along cold coasts.

whyInteresting: No other freshwater fish lives as far north; it occurs in Lake Hazen on Ellesmere Island, at nearly 82 degrees north.
A single lake can hold two to four distinct forms that differ in size, diet and depth; Thingvallavatn in Iceland has four.
Sea-run fish spend only a few weeks of summer in salt water and return to rivers and lakes each autumn, whether or not they will spawn.
Southern landlocked populations are relicts, cut off from the sea since the ice sheets retreated more than 10,000 years ago.
Inuit have long caught migrating char at stone weirs built across rivers.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insect larvae, zooplankton, snails and small crustaceans in fresh water, with larger individuals taking fish, including younger char. Sea-run fish feed heavily on amphipods, krill and small fish such as capelin during their time at sea.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Seals, otters, larger char and trout, and fish-eating birds such as divers, mergansers and gulls all take char, and people net and hook them. Young fish keep to the bottom among stones, where large fish cannot follow.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Activity follows season and light rather than a fixed daily cycle. In the far north fish feed through the continuous daylight of summer, and feeding slows greatly under winter ice.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly 10 to 20 years; slow-growing fish in cold Arctic lakes have been aged at about 30 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning takes place in autumn over gravel or stony shoals. The female digs a nest and buries from a few hundred to several thousand eggs, depending on her size; they hatch in spring. In the far north many females spawn only every second or third year.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Breeding males turn bright red or orange on the belly and lower fins, and develop a hooked lower jaw. Females colour up less strongly and look plumper with eggs. Outside the spawning season the sexes are similar.

entries.name: Arctic Fox
entries.heroTitle: Arctic Fox — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A small fox of the far north with some of the best-insulating fur measured in any mammal. In winter coat it has been found to need no extra heat production until the air falls to around minus 40 degrees Celsius. Most turn white in winter and grey-brown in summer, while a darker blue form, commoner on coasts, stays dark all year.
identification: Short muzzle, short rounded ears and short legs
Thick fur on the soles of the feet
A long, very bushy tail curled over the face at rest
A compact body about the size of a large house cat

Some den sites are used by generation after generation, and a few in Canada are thought to be centuries old.
In winter it often follows polar bears across the sea ice to scavenge what is left of their seal kills.
It hunts lemmings under the snow by listening for them, then leaping high and plunging nose first through the crust.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves, red foxes, eagles, polar bears, humans, and climate change threaten Arctic Foxes; camouflage and caching protect them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active across day and night depending on season and prey, with winter darkness and summer daylight changing the rhythm.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild Arctic Foxes often live a few years, though some survive longer; timing matters because harsh seasons sort the careless quickly.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females raise litters in dens, sometimes large when lemming numbers are high, with both parents often provisioning pups.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males may be slightly larger; coat color and season are more visible than sex.

analysis.summary: During hibernation its body temperature falls below freezing, to about -3 °C, the lowest recorded in any mammal. One of the largest ground squirrels in North America, it lives on tundra and mountain meadows as far north as the Arctic coast, and in north-east Siberia.

Sits bolt upright beside its burrow
Stocky body about 35 to 40 centimetres long, tail included

Males stock their hibernation burrows with seeds and eat them after they wake in spring, before fresh plants grow.
Seeds from an ancient cache in Siberian permafrost, thought to have been made by Arctic ground squirrels about 32,000 years ago, were used to grow Silene stenophylla plants.
It lives in colonies where each squirrel keeps its own set of burrows, and a single colony can hold dozens of animals.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, grasses, leaves, berries, and roots.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Red and Arctic foxes, grizzly bears, wolves, wolverines, ermine, golden eagles and other raptors hunt it. It stays close to burrow entrances and gives distinct alarm calls for aerial and ground predators.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day during the short summer, sheltering in its burrow overnight even under the midnight sun. It hibernates for seven to eight months, rewarming briefly every few weeks.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live fewer than 3 years in the wild; a few reach about 8 to 10.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating follows spring emergence. After a gestation of about 25 days the female bears a litter of about 5 to 10 young, which first leave the burrow at around 4 weeks old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike, though males are slightly larger. Males end hibernation weeks before females and stay below ground while their testes develop.

entries.name: Arctic Hare
entries.heroTitle: Arctic Hare — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A heavy, thick-furred hare of the far north, often 3 to 5 kilograms. When it runs it can rise onto its hind legs and bound upright like a small kangaroo, and has been reported to reach about 60 kilometres an hour across open tundra.
identification: Coat pure white in winter
Black tips to the ears
Ears short for a hare
Broad hind feet with dense fur on the soles
Sits in a compact, rounded hunch

Its long, straight front teeth help it pull out tough, frozen woody plants.
It was once treated by some authorities as a form of the mountain hare of Eurasia.
Although plants make up almost all of its diet, it has been recorded eating meat, including bait from traps.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Arctic willow is the staple: twigs, bark, buds and roots. It also eats crowberry, sedges, grasses, mosses and lichens, digging through snow with its forefeet to reach plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Arctic wolves, arctic and red foxes, gyrfalcons and snowy owls hunt it; stoats take young. It first crouches motionless, trusting its coat, then bolts in a zigzag when a predator comes close.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds in bouts across day and night, especially in the constant light of summer. It rests in a shallow scrape, snow hollow or the lee of a rock.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably about 3 to 5 years in the wild; few individuals live longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: One litter a year, typically of 2 to 8 leverets, born in late spring or early summer after about 50 days. They are born furred with eyes open, are nursed in short visits, and become independent within about two months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in the field; females may average slightly heavier.

entries.name: Argali
entries.heroTitle: Argali — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Argali Sheep teaches Highhorn through massive horns, open highland movement, herd awareness, and horizon-level vigilance. Power is steadier when vigilance stays wider than pride.

Large pale rump patch around a short tail
Tall, long-legged build for a wild sheep
Lower legs usually paler than the body, often whitish

whyInteresting: Argali are large wild sheep of Central Asian highlands, known for massive horns, open-country vigilance, and rugged movement.
Several subspecies are recognised, differing in size, colour and the spread of the rams' horns.
The IUCN Red List classes the argali as Near Threatened across its range.
Rams clash head-on in the rut; as in other wild sheep, a thick, double-layered skull helps absorb the impact.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, shrubs, herbs, and tough highland plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves are the chief predator, with snow leopards in rugged areas and eagles or foxes taking lambs. Hunting and competition with livestock threaten many herds. Argali rely on keen eyesight and run fast across open ground.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeding happens mostly in the morning and late afternoon, with midday rest spent lying on open slopes. At night herds bed down on high ground with a wide view.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually about 10 to 13 years in the wild; males tend to die younger than females.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Rutting runs from about October to January. After roughly five months, ewes give birth to one lamb, sometimes twins, in spring, hiding in rocky cover for the first days before rejoining the herd.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Rams may weigh more than twice as much as ewes and carry massive horns spiralling forward in a full curl. Ewes have much shorter, lightly curved horns.

whyInteresting: Wild populations come in several natural colour forms, including green, gold and red, often linked to particular river systems.
It is listed on CITES Appendix I, and only registered captive-bred fish, often microchipped, may be traded internationally.
It belongs to the bony-tongue family, named for the toothed bone on the floor of the mouth that works against teeth on the roof.
Its closest relatives, also in the genus Scleropages, live in northern Australia and New Guinea.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly insects and spiders that fall or rest near the water surface, plus small fish, shrimps, crabs and occasionally small frogs, seized in its large, upturned mouth.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural enemies. People are the main threat, through collecting for the ornamental fish trade and clearance of peat swamps. Juveniles are exposed to larger fish and birds and stay close to cover among roots.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Wild activity patterns are poorly studied. It hunts near the surface in daylight and twilight and appears to rest by holding still close to submerged roots and plants.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive fish commonly live 20 years or more; lifespan in the wild has not been well documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The male broods. After spawning he takes the few, large, yolky eggs into his mouth and carries eggs and then young for roughly two months, until the fry can swim and feed independently.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are hard to tell apart. Mature males tend to be slimmer, with a deeper mouth for brooding, while females are rounder in the body.

analysis.summary: Each forewing of this slim tan moth is split into two narrow, scale-fringed lobes, and each hindwing into three. At rest it rolls them into a thin stick held out at right angles to the long body, leaving the outline of a dry grass stem.

Weak, fluttering flight over short distances

whyInteresting: It is one of the main insect pests of globe artichokes in the coastal farming districts of California.
Wild thistles act as a reservoir from which moths move into cultivated artichoke fields.
Traps baited with the female's scent chemicals have been used by growers to monitor the moth in artichoke fields.
Most moths appear to travel only short distances between host plants rather than dispersing widely.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars feed on globe artichoke, thistles and related plants, eating leaves and then boring into stems and flower heads. Adult feeding has not been well documented.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Parasitic wasps and flies attack the caterpillars, and birds and spiders take adults; bats probably catch some in flight. Larvae are shielded inside the plant tissue they tunnel through.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults fly mainly at dusk and at night and rest through the day on host plants or nearby vegetation.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult lifespan has not been well documented, though adults probably live from one to a few weeks. A full generation, from egg to adult, probably takes roughly one to two months in warm weather and longer in cool conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs singly on leaves of the host plant, usually on the underside. The caterpillars tunnel into the plant and pupate in it or in debris near the base, and there are several generations a year where the climate allows.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot reliably be told apart in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds, mammals, larger frogs, road traffic, drying pools, and pollution can threaten them. Toxic skin and night activity improve survival.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly nocturnal, hiding by day in damp shelters and emerging after dusk or rain to feed and call.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay strings of eggs in ponds, ditches, or temporary water. Tadpoles develop quickly when warm shallow water remains long enough.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually smaller and call during breeding periods, while females grow larger and carry eggs. The differences become clearest around wet-season breeding.

analysis.summary: Generally regarded as the largest tortoise native to mainland Asia: the northern form can exceed 50 centimetres in shell length and 20 kilograms in weight. Molecular studies usually recover its genus, Manouria, as an early-branching lineage among the living tortoises.

Forelimbs armoured with large, overlapping pointed scales

whyInteresting: It is sometimes called the six-legged tortoise because the spurred scales on each thigh look like extra small legs.
Two forms are recognised: a northern one in Myanmar and Thailand, and a southern one on the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Borneo.
Other names include Asian brown tortoise, and the northern form is often called the Burmese mountain tortoise.
It lives up to about 1,000 metres in hill forest and tolerates cooler, wetter conditions than most tropical tortoises.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly plants: fallen leaves, bamboo shoots, grasses, fruit and fungi gathered on the forest floor. It also eats snails, worms and other small invertebrates when found.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and hatchlings are probably taken by predators such as monitor lizards and civets, but adults have few natural enemies. Hunting for food and trade by people has made it globally threatened. It withdraws into its shell when disturbed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Activity peaks in the early morning, the late afternoon and after rain. The night and the hottest part of the day are spent resting beneath fallen logs or in dense ground cover.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been measured. Captive individuals are reported to have lived more than 20 years, and much longer lives are thought likely.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female scrapes leaf litter into a mound and lays about 20 to 50 eggs inside, then guards the mound for days, pushing and hissing at intruders. Eggs take roughly two to three months to hatch.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Tail length is the clearest guide: long and thick in males, short in females. Males also show a slight dip in the underside of the shell.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators are poorly recorded. Hawks and falcons probably take adults, and tree-climbing snakes, crows and cats are likely to raid nests. Feeding and roosting in tight flocks means many eyes watch for danger, and nests are placed in holes out of reach.

whyInteresting: When a hornet hovers at the entrance, the guard bees shake their abdomens in unison, a signal that the hunter has been seen.
It is the original host of the Varroa mite; workers groom the mites off one another and remove infested brood, so colonies usually survive infestation.
In Japan the flowers of the orchid Cymbidium floribundum draw in whole swarms of this bee, and beekeepers set the plant out to catch them.
Colonies are smaller than those of the western honey bee, usually a few thousand to around 20,000 workers, and store less honey.
It has been kept for centuries in hollow logs, clay pots and cavities built into house walls.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Nectar and pollen from a wide range of wild flowers, crops and trees, mostly gathered within about a kilometre of the nest. Nectar is ripened into honey and stored in the combs; pollen feeds the developing larvae.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hornets are the chief enemy, picking off workers at the entrance and sometimes raiding the whole nest. Bee-eaters, honey buzzards, weaver ants, wax moths, martens and bears take bees, brood or honey. Guards sting and hiss, and a harassed colony may abandon the nest and move elsewhere.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Foragers fly from soon after sunrise until dusk. At night the whole colony stays on the combs inside the nest. In regions with cold winters the bees cluster together and live on stored honey until spring.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: As in other honey bees, workers live a few weeks in the flying season and several months when overwintering; queens can live for two years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The queen lays nearly all the eggs, placing one in each wax cell. Workers feed the larvae and cap the cells for pupation; a worker takes about 19 to 20 days from egg to adult. New colonies form by swarming.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Queens are the largest, with a long, tapered abdomen. Workers are smaller, sterile females with a sting and pollen baskets. Drones, the males, are stout and dark, with very large eyes that meet on top of the head, and have no sting.

Nests are built high in trees, in shrubs, or under roofs and eaves.

Larvae give adult workers droplets of a sugary secretion in return for the food brought to them.
Colonies that start in a small, low nest often move in summer to a much larger nest higher up.
A large nest in autumn may produce several hundred new queens.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults drink nectar, sap and juice from ripe fruit. Workers hunt flies, wasps and above all honeybees, often hovering in front of a hive to seize returning foragers. Prey is chewed into a paste and carried back to feed the larvae.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Honey buzzards tear open nests to eat the larvae and pupae, and some other birds catch adults. Lone foragers escape by fast flight; the sting, painful and dangerous to people with allergies, is used mainly in defence of the nest.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Workers forage by day and return to the nest at night, where the colony clusters on the combs. Activity slows in cool weather. Mated queens pass the winter alone and dormant in sheltered crevices, soil or rotting wood.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Workers live for a few weeks in summer; a queen lives about a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single queen founds a small nest in spring and rears the first workers herself. Workers then take over building and feeding while the queen only lays eggs. In late summer and autumn the colony rears males and new queens, which mate before the old colony dies.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Queens are the largest, up to about 3 cm; workers, also female, are about 2 to 2.5 cm. Males appear in autumn, have longer antennae and cannot sting.

analysis.summary: A large termite of Southeast Asia that raises hard earthen mounds in forests, plantations and gardens. A mature colony releases winged males and females in mass flights, usually reported after rain and after dark, and neighbouring mounds tend to fly on the same nights.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Workers collect dead wood, leaf litter and dry grass and carry it into the nest. The chewed material is built into sponge-like combs on which a Termitomyces fungus grows, and the termites eat the fungus and the broken-down comb.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Ants are the main enemy, raiding foraging parties and breached mounds. Pangolins, lizards, toads, birds and bats take workers or flying adults. Large-jawed soldiers block openings and bite while workers seal the gap with wet soil.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No daily sleep cycle has been described. Work inside the mound continues at all hours, and foragers travel out through underground galleries.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: The lifespan of queens, kings and colonies has not been measured for this species. Workers and soldiers are short-lived compared with the reproductive pair, which founds and heads the colony.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The queen lays eggs continuously in a thick-walled clay cell near the centre of the mound. Workers carry the eggs to nursery chambers and feed the larvae, which moult into workers, soldiers or, seasonally, winged reproductives.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Winged males and females look alike. Once a colony is established the queen's abdomen swells to several centimetres long with eggs, while the king stays close to his original size.

Released or escaped fish have formed wild populations in Hawaii and the south-eastern United States, where they are treated as invasive.
It is commonly sold alive in markets, in trays holding very little water.
Genetic studies suggest that the fish grouped under this name are several similar-looking species, not one.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A night-time predator of worms, insect larvae, shrimps, crayfish, snails, tadpoles, frogs and small fish. It waits at a burrow entrance or noses through mud and plants, seizing prey with a quick sucking gulp.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Herons, egrets, storks, snakeheads, water snakes, otters and monitor lizards take them, and people trap them widely for food. Slippery mucus, a burrow to retreat into and nocturnal habits are its main protection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hunting happens mostly at night. Daylight hours are spent resting inside a burrow in the bank or bottom mud, or tucked under dense plants.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan is not well documented in the wild or in captivity. Because most fish change from female to male as they age, the largest fish, usually males, tend to be the oldest.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning takes place in the warm, wet months. The male blows a nest of bubbles at the mouth of a burrow or among plants, the eggs are placed in it, and he guards the eggs and the newly hatched young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Every fish matures first as a female and later changes into a male, passing through an intersex stage. As a result males are the larger, older fish, and small adults are almost all female.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Its enemies are those of small land snails in general, among them ground beetles, rats and ground-feeding birds. It pulls back into the shell when touched.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural enemies, and the predators of its eggs and chicks are poorly documented. Hunting and the draining of wetlands are the main threats. Adults flush to high perches or soar away when approached.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At night it roosts high in tall trees, often in small groups, and it may rest on a perch or loaf on a sandbank through the heat of midday.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild has not been documented for this species.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs usually nest on their own rather than in colonies, building a large stick platform high in a tree. The clutch is about 2 to 4 eggs, incubated by both parents for roughly a month; chicks stay in the nest for about two months.

Larvae develop in decaying wood and other decomposing plant material, while adults feed on palms and other vegetation.

whyInteresting: It reached Samoa in 1909, reportedly in a shipment of rubber seedlings from Sri Lanka, and spread from there to other islands.
Males release a scent that draws both sexes to a breeding site, and a synthetic copy is used to bait traps.
A virus found in Malaysian beetles in the 1960s was released on Pacific islands as a control and greatly reduced damage there.
A disturbed adult makes a hissing squeak by rubbing the tip of its abdomen against the inside of its wing cases.
A palm has a single growing point, so a beetle that bores deep enough to destroy it kills the whole tree.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults chew the soft tissue of unopened fronds for its sap and leave the fibre unswallowed. Coconut and oil palm are attacked most, with date, betel-nut and ornamental palms also taken. Grubs eat rotting wood, compost, sawdust and dung.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pigs, rats and domestic fowl dig grubs out of the breeding sites, ants take eggs and small grubs, and scoliid wasps lay their eggs on larger ones. Adults are protected mainly by their thick armour.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal. Adults fly from dusk and through the early night, and often come to lights. By day they stay in their feeding tunnels or buried in the rotting material where they breed.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults are reported to live for several months, in some records up to about nine. Counting the months spent as a grub, the whole life usually lasts about a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female lays roughly 50 to 100 eggs over her life, a few at a time, in rotting palm trunks or similar material. Eggs hatch in about 8 to 12 days. The white, C-shaped grubs pass through three stages over several months, then pupate in a cell of packed fibre.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes carry a horn; it is longer on average in males, but sizes overlap. The tip of the abdomen is the surer guide: females have a dense tuft of reddish-brown hairs there, while males are bare and shiny.

The species was described in 1956 by the arachnologist Ray Forster, at first under the genus Archaea.
Many Australian assassin spiders are confined to a single mountain range or patch of wet forest.
Members of the family are also called pelican spiders, from the outline of the neck and jaws.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: No predators of this species have been recorded, and its defensive behaviour has not been described. At only a few millimetres long in leaf litter and low foliage, it is presumably exposed to the small hunters of the rainforest floor.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Assassin spiders are thought to hunt mainly at night, moving slowly through litter and low foliage, and to hang still beneath dead leaves or twigs by day. The daily rhythm of this species has not been studied.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males can be recognised under a hand lens by their enlarged palps. Other differences between the sexes, such as in size or the proportions of the neck, have not been described in a way that helps in the field.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike. Only close to spawning do they differ, as females swell with roe and males with milt.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sea lice spreading from salmon farms weaken and kill young fish on their way to sea, adding to losses from dams and warming rivers. Seals and large fish hunt adults at sea, while trout, eels, pike, herons, goosanders, cormorants and otters take eggs and young.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Spawning males develop a hooked lower jaw and darker, coppery-red colouring, while females stay more bronze. Some males mature while still small parr in the river and sneak into spawning pairs to fertilise eggs.

Although it looks like a weak flier, it has reached and settled many remote islands in the south-west Pacific.
The flightless takahe of New Zealand is a close relative, descended from a much earlier arrival of swamphens.
It is a legal game bird in New Zealand, where flocks can damage crops and pull up newly planted seedlings.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly plants: the soft shoots, stem bases and seeds of reeds, rushes, sedges, grasses and clover, pulled up with the bill. It also takes insects, snails, frogs, eggs, ducklings and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Swamp harriers take chicks and sometimes adults. Introduced stoats, ferrets and cats raid nests in New Zealand, as foxes do in Australia. Groups mob a harrier noisily, and a frightened bird runs for cover, taking flight only when pressed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeding goes on through the day, most visibly in the early morning and late afternoon. After dark it roosts on platforms of trampled reeds or in dense swamp vegetation, and groups often call loudly during the night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not well documented. Long-term studies of New Zealand breeding groups show established adults can hold the same territory for several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding groups often share one nest, a bowl of trampled reeds in which two or more females may lay. Each lays about 4 to 6 buff, blotched eggs, incubated for 23 to 27 days. The black, downy chicks leave the nest within days and are fed by the whole group.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is the same in both sexes. Males are larger on average, with a heavier bill and frontal shield, but the difference is hard to judge unless birds stand side by side.

Vinegar poured on a sting stops unfired stinging cells from discharging, though it does not relieve venom already injected.
Stinger nets are set off many northern Australian beaches during the season when it is inshore.
It is named after Hugo Flecker, a Queensland doctor who investigated a fatal sting in 1955.
An antivenom raised in sheep is made in Australia, though how much it helps remains debated.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Prawns make up most of the prey of large individuals, with small fish also taken. Prey that brushes the trailing tentacles is killed within seconds by venom, and the tentacles contract to carry it up into the bell to be digested.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few predators are documented; sea turtles and some fish are reported to eat box jellyfish, but this is poorly studied. The swimming stage steers around obstacles and swims away from disturbance rather than drifting passively.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Tracking studies in Queensland found individuals hunting actively by day and lying still on the sandy bottom for much of the night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: The swimming stage lives about one season, a few months, dying off as the wet season ends. How long the polyp stage survives has not been measured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Adults spawn late in the season, and fertilised eggs develop into larvae that settle as small polyps in estuaries. In the following warm season each polyp transforms into a single young swimming jellyfish that moves out to the coast.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are separate but look alike; they cannot be told apart in the field.

The venom that is dangerous to humans and other primates is much less potent to most other mammals.
Females may live for many years in the same burrow, while males die within months of maturing.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Centipedes, scorpions, parasitic wasps and birds take funnel-webs, and wandering males are the most exposed of all. The burrow is the defence: inside it, the spider faces one narrow approach at a time.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Funnel-webs are nocturnal, sitting at the burrow mouth after dark and retreating deep during the day. Their rhythm keeps them in humid darkness, because they lose water quickly in the open.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Females can live fifteen years or more in one burrow, while males mature at three or four years and then die within months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females stay with an egg sac inside the burrow and guard the spiderlings until they disperse.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are smaller and longer-legged with a mating spur on each second leg, and they are the ones that wander. The difference matters because the dangerous encounters almost always involve the roaming male.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few predators; eggs and chicks are taken by gulls, raptors and foxes. Colonies on islands and remote lake edges are the answer, putting distance between the nest and anything that walks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Australian Pelicans are diurnal, fishing through the day and loafing in groups on sandbars. Their rhythm is long stretches of rest broken by short bouts of cooperative fishing.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for a couple of decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay two or three eggs in a shallow scrape on bare ground, and both parents feed the young by regurgitation.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger with a longer bill; otherwise the sexes look alike. The difference matters little because both feed the same way.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Australian Pineapplefish shelter in caves and under ledges through the day and come out over open sand to hunt at night.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The queen builds the first small comb alone, lays an egg in each cell and feeds that first brood herself. Once these workers emerge she only lays eggs. Males and new queens are reared in late summer, and the rest of the colony dies with the first hard frosts.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Queens are larger than workers, and both are female and carry a sting. Males, which develop from unfertilised eggs, have longer antennae and no sting.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Ball pythons are mainly nocturnal or crepuscular, moving when darkness improves cover and prey activity.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: In captivity they can live for decades, and wild adults can also be long-lived compared with many small predators.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs and coil around the clutch during incubation. The same body that constricts prey can become a ring of warmth and protection around the future.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often heavier or larger than males, which supports egg production and brooding. The difference is not decorative; it is reproductive capacity expressed through body mass.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Banteng feeds on grasses, bamboo, leaves, shoots, fruit, and browse shaped by seasonal heat.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hunting for meat and horn trophies, and clearance of dry forest, have cut wild numbers sharply, and interbreeding with domestic cattle dilutes some wild populations. Herds are wary: a snorted alarm sends the whole group crashing into cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Banteng rests in forest shade, thickets, and herd resting sites near grazing grounds. Where undisturbed it feeds mostly in the early morning and late afternoon, but under hunting pressure herds shift to grazing at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly documented, probably around 20 years at most; captive animals have lived to about 25 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single calf is born after a gestation of about 9 to 10 months. Calves can follow the herd soon after birth, are weaned at around 9 months, and cows usually first breed at 2 to 3 years.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Strongly different. In most populations adult bulls turn dark chestnut to blue-black, with a shoulder hump and heavy horns rising from a bare, horny patch on the forehead; cows and young stay bright chestnut with short, tightly curved horns.

entries.name: Bar-headed Goose
entries.heroTitle: Bar-headed Goose — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Twice a year this pale grey goose crosses the Himalaya between the high lakes of Central Asia and the lowlands of South Asia. Its haemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly than that of lowland geese and its flight muscles are densely supplied with capillaries, so it can keep flapping in air that holds about half the oxygen available at sea level.
identification: Two black bars cross the back of the white head
A white stripe runs down each side of the dark neck
The body is pale silvery grey
Bill and legs are orange-yellow; the bill tip is black
In flight, dark wing tips contrast with pale grey forewings
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: central_asia, south_asia. Breeds beside lakes, marshes and rivers on high Central Asian plateaus, including the Tibetan Plateau, where many colonies lie above 4,000 metres, and in Mongolia. Winters on lowland lakes, reservoirs, river sandbanks and nearby farmland across the Indian subcontinent.

whyInteresting: Tracked geese leaving the Indian lowlands have climbed several thousand metres in about eight hours, with no pause to adjust to the thinner air.
The highest altitude logged by a tracked goose is about 7,290 metres; older reports of flocks above the summit of Everest have not been confirmed.
Most crossings are made at night and in the early morning, when the air is colder, denser and calmer.
Some females lay eggs in the nests of neighbouring pairs, which then incubate and rear the extra goslings.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grazes on grasses and sedges around the breeding lakes, also pulling up roots and tubers. In winter it feeds largely on farmland, taking young wheat, barley and other crop shoots and fallen rice grain.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, ravens, crows, gulls and eagles take eggs and goslings, so colonies favour islands that ground predators cannot reach, and both parents guard the brood. Hunting, egg collecting, wetland loss and outbreaks of bird flu also kill many.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds mainly by day on the breeding lakes. Wintering flocks often rest on sandbanks and open water through the middle of the day and fly to fields to graze around dusk and into the night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not well measured in the wild; about 15 to 20 years is usually quoted, and captive birds can live longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs nest in colonies from about May. The female lays 3 to 8 eggs and incubates them for roughly four weeks while the male stands guard. Goslings walk and feed themselves within a day or two and fly at about seven to eight weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females have the same plumage. Males average slightly larger and heavier, a difference hard to see unless a pair stands side by side.

entries.heroTitle: Bar-tailed Godwit — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: This long-billed shorebird nests on Arctic tundra and winters on coasts far to the south. Satellite-tagged birds from the Alaskan breeding population have flown to New Zealand and eastern Australia without stopping, covering around 11,000 to 13,500 kilometres in eight to eleven days, among the longest nonstop flights recorded for any bird.

On the way north from Australasia most birds stop in the Yellow Sea, where loss of tidal flats is a serious threat.
Tracked birds tend to set off on days with favourable tailwinds.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Bar-tailed Godwit feeds on marine worms, clams, crustaceans, insects, and mudflat invertebrates probed with a long bill.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Peregrine falcons strike roosting and feeding flocks on the coast. On the tundra, skuas, gulls and Arctic foxes take eggs and chicks. Parents fly at intruders with loud calls, and flocks bunch tightly and twist in the air when a falcon attacks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It forages by day or night whenever the tide uncovers the mudflats. Bar-tailed Godwit rests in open mudflat roosts, tundra cover, and flock resting sites. At high tide it packs into dense roosts, often on one leg with the bill tucked in.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults that survive their first migrations typically live around 8 to 12 years; ringed birds have been recorded at over 20 years old.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The nest is a shallow scrape on open tundra, usually holding four eggs. Both parents incubate for about three weeks. The chicks leave the nest within a day of hatching and find their own food while the parents guard them, flying at about four weeks old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger than males, with a noticeably longer bill. In breeding plumage males are deep brick-red below, while females are much paler buff or washed rufous. Outside the breeding season both sexes are grey-brown.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, now very rare in its range, were the main natural predator, and caracals, jackals and golden eagles may take lambs. Hunting and competition with livestock are the main threats today. It escapes by climbing broken cliffs where pursuers cannot follow.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It rests on cliffs or shaded slopes, feeding during cooler hours. Nights are spent on ledges or among boulders, and in hot weather it lies up in rock shade through the middle of the day.

The middle stretch of many European rivers is called the barbel zone, after the fish typical of it.
Most adults weigh 1 to 4 kilograms, but exceptional fish can exceed about 9 kilograms.
In England it is native only to some east-flowing rivers, but anglers have stocked it into many others.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds on the bottom with a downturned, protrusible mouth, finding insect larvae, freshwater shrimps, snails, worms, crayfish and small fish, often turning over stones and sifting gravel.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Otters, pike and cormorants take barbel, mostly younger fish, and herons catch fry in the shallows. Adults shelter in deep holes and under weed or snags; weirs, silt and pollution are the main threats to populations.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most active at dusk and through the night, it spends much of the day lying quietly in small shoals under weed, overhanging trees or in deeper pools, though it feeds by day in coloured water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly 15 to 20 years; some fish have been aged at over 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning takes place in late spring and early summer, when fish move upstream onto shallow gravel runs. Females shed thousands of sticky eggs among the stones, which hatch in about 1 to 2 weeks with no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females grow larger and heavier. In the spawning season males develop rows of small white tubercles on the head and back.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Natural predation is poorly documented; forest hawks and eagles are the likely threat to adults. Clearance of the lowland forest it uses outside the breeding season is the main pressure on the population.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are glossy black with a tall crest and a bare scarlet throat patch and wattle that swell during display. Females are smaller and duller, with a shorter crest and no red skin.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Once a female accepts a nest she lays 2 to 4 white eggs and incubates them alone for about 14 to 17 days. Chicks leave the nest at around 17 days. Males may go on to build further nests for other females.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Breeding males become brighter yellow; females are duller.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Herons, egrets, kingfishers, snakeheads, water snakes and large aquatic insects. In weedy shallows it hides among stems, and it can jump between puddles when a pool shrinks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and rests at night, often lying on a leaf near the surface or wedged among plants, with colours noticeably paler while it sleeps.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Bicolor Angelfish are active by day and retreat into reef crevices at night, wedging into cover before dark.

By protecting mealybugs from their enemies, it can worsen mealybug wilt disease in pineapple crops.
Its genus, Pheidole, is one of the largest ant genera, with more than a thousand described species.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Takes dead insects, small live invertebrates, seeds and sugary food such as nectar and fruit juices. Large prey is often cut up where it lies and carried back in pieces, and colonies tend aphids, scale insects and mealybugs for their honeydew.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Like other small ants, workers and winged queens are taken by spiders, other ants, and ant-eating birds and lizards. A colony holds many queens and, where the ant is invasive, spreads through many linked nests, so losing one nest rarely destroys it; workers seldom sting people.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Colonies may forage by day and by night in warm weather, slowing during cool spells. In ants that have been studied, workers rest in many short bouts rather than one long sleep, and the same is probably true here.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Individual lifespans are not well documented. Workers are thought to live only a few months, queens longer, and colonies persist far longer because many queens keep laying.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Many queens lay eggs in each colony. Workers feed the legless larvae, and nutrition during development largely decides whether a larva becomes a minor, a major or a queen. New colonies usually form by budding, with queens and workers walking to a new nest site.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Workers are all sterile females. Queens are much larger, with a bulkier thorax and wings shed after mating; males are winged, slender and short-lived.

entries.name: Bighorn Sheep

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Cougars are the main predator, with wolves, coyotes and bears also taking sheep and golden eagles taking lambs. fieldGuide.sleepPattern: At night it beds down in scraped hollows on ledges and high ground, often reused for years. By day it feeds in the morning and again towards evening, lying up to chew the cud at midday.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Rams are much heavier, up to about 140 kilograms in the Rockies, and carry thick horns that curl round past the cheek. Ewes weigh roughly half as much and have short, slender horns with only a slight curve.

whyInteresting: Scallops have dozens of small eyes along the mantle edge, each focusing light with a curved mirror made of crystals.
Mussels anchor themselves with byssus threads, protein fibres strong enough to hold against breaking waves.
Pearls form when a bivalve coats an irritant or trapped tissue with layers of nacre, the same material that lines many shells.
Shipworms are bivalves with a tiny shell used as a drill; they bore through wood, which bacteria in their gills help them digest.
Growth bands in the shells of long-lived species are counted like tree rings and used to reconstruct past sea temperatures.
