fieldGuide.dietSummary: Most filter plankton and suspended organic particles from water pumped across the gills, sorting food with cilia and mucus. Some suck up deposits from the sediment surface, some reef and deep-sea species gain food from symbiotic algae or bacteria, and a few deep-water species catch small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sea stars, drilling snails such as whelks, crabs, fish, oystercatchers and other shorebirds, sea otters and people all eat bivalves. Defences vary: most clamp the shell shut, burrowers dig deeper, and scallops escape by clapping their valves to swim off in jerks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: With no brain, bivalves have no sleep cycle in the usual sense. Many follow tidal or daily rhythms instead, opening to feed and closing when exposed at low tide or disturbed.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Varies enormously: many small clams live a year or a few years, freshwater pearl mussels can exceed 100 years, and an ocean quahog from Iceland was aged at 507 years, the oldest non-colonial animal whose age is precisely known.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Most release eggs and sperm into the water, where fertilised eggs become drifting larvae that settle after days to weeks; one oyster can shed millions of eggs. Some brood young in the gills, and many freshwater mussels release larvae that live for days to months as parasites on the gills or fins of fish.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Varies across the class. Most species have separate sexes that look identical from outside, although in some the ripe gonad differs in colour between males and females. Others, including many oysters, are hermaphrodites or change sex during life.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasshoppers, bees, wasps, flies and moths that blunder into the web make up most meals. The spider rushes out, swathes the prey in broad bands of silk thrown with the hind legs, then bites it and feeds.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards and mud dauber wasps, which paralyse spiders to stock their nest cells, are the main enemies. A threatened spider pumps its web back and forth until its outline blurs, or drops to the ground and hides among the plants.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Stays on the hub through the day and much of the night, with no separate retreat away from the web. Web building and repair often take place at night or in the early morning.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one year from egg to death: spiderlings emerge in spring, mature by late summer, and adults die with the first hard frosts of autumn.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In late summer or autumn the female spins one to a few brown, papery egg sacs, each holding several hundred to over a thousand eggs, and hangs them in the web or nearby plants. The young hatch in autumn but mostly overwinter inside the sac, dispersing in spring without any care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are far smaller than females, with a body under 1 cm against the female's 2 to 3 cm, and are paler and browner. In late summer they build small webs at the edge of, or close to, a female's web.

It is not aggressive and rarely stings people, even close to its nest.
Carried by shipping and trade, it has become established in Europe and on Pacific islands, far from its North American home.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal; females gather mud and hunt spiders by day, resting in shelter when light and temperature fade.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females build and provision nests and have stingers; males lack stingers and do not perform the same nesting labor.

analysis.summary: The Odorous House Ant runs one colony across many nests and many queens at once, shifting brood and workers between them whenever conditions change. No single nest is the colony, which is exactly why the colony is so hard to remove.

whyInteresting: Crushing one releases a coconut-like smell from glands at the rear of the abdomen, which is what gives the species its name.
A single colony can hold dozens of queens and many thousands of workers spread across separate nests that all belong to the same society.
Colonies split and relocate readily, sometimes several times in a season, which is why slow bait works on them and spraying does not.
They farm aphids and scale insects for honeydew and will defend those herds from ladybirds and lacewings.
Native right across North America, and one of the most frequently encountered ants inside houses there.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Honeydew from tended aphids and scale insects, plus nectar, small insects and almost anything sweet indoors. Foraging runs on shared scent trails, so the colony locates and empties a food source far faster than any single ant could.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders, larger ants and ground-feeding birds take foragers off the trail. The colony's answer is not defence but redundancy: losing a nest, or even a queen, does not end it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: There is no colony-wide rest. Workers run in overlapping shifts around the clock, with foraging heaviest through the evening and night in warm weather.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Workers live a few months and queens several years, but because a colony carries many queens at once it continues well past the life of any of them.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Several queens lay into the same colony and brood is carried between nests as conditions shift, so no single queen's output decides whether the colony continues.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Workers are all sterile females and look alike. Males are winged, appear only for mating flights and die soon after; queens are noticeably larger and shed their wings once mated.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Omnivorous. It takes grasshoppers, beetles and other insects, carrion, small rodents, eggs and nestlings, grain, seeds and berries, foraging mostly on the ground with a confident walk.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks such as goshawks and Cooper's hawks, great horned owls and golden eagles take adults; crows and ravens raid nests, and squirrels are thought to as well. Groups gather to mob predators with harsh calls.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. In winter it gathers at dusk into communal roosts in dense trees or thickets, dispersing again at first light.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Both partners build a bulky domed stick nest with a side entrance and a mud-lined cup. The female lays about 5 to 8 eggs and incubates them for roughly 16 to 18 days; chicks leave the nest at around four weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes share the same plumage; males are somewhat larger, with longer tails.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, American mink, stoats, crows and larger gulls take eggs and chicks, and peregrines take adults. Colonies rise together, screaming, and dive at intruders, driving off many would-be raiders.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. In the evening birds fly in long lines to roost communally on open water such as reservoirs, lakes and estuaries, resting afloat or on mudbanks until dawn.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically around 10 years for birds that survive their first year. Ringed individuals have been recorded at over 30 years old.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests are heaps of vegetation on the ground or among reeds. The usual clutch is two or three mottled eggs, incubated by both parents for about 24 days, and chicks fly at about five weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the same plumage in every season. Males are slightly larger on average, with a heavier bill, but the difference is hard to judge in the field.

entries.name: Black Horse Fly

analysis.summary: One of the biggest horse flies in eastern North America, this all-black fly reaches about 2.5 centimetres long. Females need a blood meal to mature their eggs, and one brushed off a horse or cow will circle back and land again within moments.
identification: Stout body entirely black, often with a bluish sheen
Wings dark and smoky, held out to the sides
Very large dark eyes covering most of the head
Short, stiff antennae projecting forward
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Black Horse Flies are native to eastern North America. They are associated with wetlands, marshes, river valleys, woodland edges, pastures and other humid areas where larvae develop in wet soil and adults can find large mammal hosts.

whyInteresting: Like other horse flies, it can carry diseases such as equine infectious anaemia from one host to the next on blood left on its mouthparts.
Large, dark, moving shapes and the carbon dioxide in breath help females home in on a host.
Tabanus larvae are known to eat one another when crowded, and this is thought to apply to this species too.
Heavy horse fly attacks are known to lower weight gain and milk yield in cattle, as the animals bunch up and stop grazing.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Females slice the skin of cattle, horses, deer and other large mammals with blade-like mouthparts and lap the pooled blood. Both sexes also take nectar and plant juices; males do not bite.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults are caught by dragonflies, robber flies, kingbirds and other flycatching birds, and by sand wasps that stock their nests with horse flies. Swishing tails and skin twitches of hosts also kill many. Its main defence is fast, agile flight.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: A daytime flier, most active in hot sunshine. At night and in cool or overcast weather it rests on the undersides of leaves and on stems in vegetation.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults live a few weeks. Most of the life is spent as a larva, and the whole cycle often takes a year or longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid in layered masses of several hundred on plants or objects overhanging water or wet ground. Larvae drop into mud, where they hunt other invertebrates, then pupate in drier soil. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The large eyes of males meet across the top of the head, while those of females are separated by a narrow gap.

entries.name: Black-legged Kittiwake

analysis.summary: Black-legged Kittiwake expresses Cliffcall through black legs, cliff ledge nests, noisy colonies, and repeated sea-foraging trips make the Cliffcall principle specific rather than generic; body, habitat, and pressure all point back to the same lesson.

Outside the breeding season it lives far out over the open ocean.

whyInteresting: The name kittiwake imitates its nasal call, a drawn-out kitti-waaake repeated endlessly at the breeding ledges.
The hind toe is tiny or missing altogether, which is what the species name tridactyla, meaning three-toed, refers to.
Young birds in their first winter carry a bold black zigzag across the upper wings and a dark half-collar on the nape.
Tracking has shown that some birds from British and Norwegian colonies cross the Atlantic to winter off Newfoundland and Labrador.
Steep population declines led to the species being listed as Vulnerable on the global Red List.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It feeds on small fish, marine invertebrates, and planktonic prey from surface waters. Sandeels, capelin, young herring and krill are typical, snatched while hovering low or taken in shallow plunges, and it also follows fishing boats for scraps.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Great skuas, large gulls, ravens and eagles take eggs, chicks and sometimes adults, and Arctic foxes raid any ledge they can reach. Sheer nest sites keep most ground predators out. Storms and shortages of prey fish, especially sandeels, cause widespread breeding failure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: An adult rests on cliffs or at sea, with intense colony activity during breeding. Feeding trips continue through the long northern days and into twilight, and outside the breeding season birds sleep afloat far offshore.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults commonly live about 10 to 15 years once they survive their first years at sea; ringed birds have been recorded at more than 25 years old.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Paired females lay eggs on cliff nests built from mud, vegetation, and sea material. The clutch is usually two eggs, sometimes one or three, incubated by both parents for about four weeks, and both parents feed the chicks until they fly.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the same plumage. Males average slightly larger, with a heavier head and bill, but the difference is hard to judge in the field.

entries.name: Common Molly

analysis.summary: A small livebearing fish native to Mexico and Central America. It tolerates a wider spread of water than most freshwater fish, living in inland streams and brackish lagoons, and it can be acclimatised to full seawater.

Short dorsal fin, not a tall sail
Rounded, fan-shaped tail fin
Wild fish silvery grey with rows of small spots
Stocky body, usually under 10 centimetres long

Wild fish live in warm, shallow, slow or still water from Mexico through Central America: lowland streams, ditches, ponds, coastal lagoons and mangrove creeks, fresh or brackish, usually over mud with plenty of algae. Domesticated forms are kept in heated aquaria worldwide.

Many mollies sold in shops are hybrids between this species and the larger sailfin mollies, so their exact parentage is often unknown.
Released aquarium fish have founded feral populations in warm waters outside the native range, including parts of Asia.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger fish, herons, kingfishers and water snakes are the likely predators of adults, and aquatic insects of fry. Mollies keep to the shallows in loose shoals and dart into weed or under the bank when alarmed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At night it rests almost motionless near the bottom or among plants and is slow to react.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 3 to 5 years in aquaria. Wild fish probably live less, but no reliable figures exist.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Young are born about four weeks after mating, in broods of roughly 20 to 100 depending on the size of the female. The fry swim and feed at once and get no care; adults eat any they catch, so survivors hide in dense plants.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are smaller and slimmer, and their anal fin is narrowed into a rod, the gonopodium, used to transfer sperm. Females are larger, deeper in the belly, and keep a fan-shaped anal fin.

entries.name: Black-naped Oriole
entries.heroTitle: Black-naped Oriole — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Black-naped Oriole is brilliant golden-yellow and still extremely hard to see. High in dense canopy that yellow reads as sunlit leaf, so almost everyone who finds one has heard the fluted whistle first.
identification: Brilliant golden-yellow body with black flight feathers
Broad black band running through the eye and around the nape
Deep pink-red bill, obvious at close range
Clear fluting two- or three-note whistle from high cover

The nape band is what separates it from other yellow orioles across its range, and gives the species its name.
Pairs will mob crows and drongos that come near an active nest, well above their weight.
The nest is a deep woven cup slung in a horizontal fork, often high and towards the outside of the canopy.
Northern populations migrate south for winter while tropical ones stay put year-round.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, especially figs, plus nectar and large insects and caterpillars taken in the canopy. Feeding high in foliage keeps the bird in exactly the light conditions where its colour disappears.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Crows, treepies and raptors take eggs and nestlings; snakes and monitor lizards reach nests in lower trees. Adults are rarely caught, mostly because they are rarely located.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, roosting in dense canopy overnight, with most calling early in the morning and again before dusk.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around eight to twelve years in the wild.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Two to three eggs in a deep woven cup high in a fork, both parents feeding the young. Nest sites are chosen for the same dense sunlit foliage the adults feed in.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Similar, but females are duller and more olive-toned on the back with slightly less clean black in the wing, and juveniles are streaked below.

whyInteresting: Its other common name, roof rat, reflects its habit of nesting high in lofts, roof spaces and trees rather than in burrows.
In towns where brown rats became established, black rats often declined, and in Britain they are now among the rarest mammals.
Introduced black rats have caused extinctions of island birds, reptiles and insects, and are a main target of island eradication programmes.
Females can breed from about three to four months old and raise several litters a year, usually of five to eight young.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An omnivore with a taste for plant food: seeds, grain, fruit, nuts and stored produce, plus insects, snails, eggs and nestling birds. It forages largely off the ground, climbing into trees, roofs and stores.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, especially barn owls, take many, along with cats, dogs, snakes, stoats, weasels and other small carnivores. People also trap and poison it. It escapes by climbing and by staying high in buildings and trees.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly nocturnal. By day it rests in nests of shredded material in roof spaces, wall cavities, dense vines or tree hollows, and on islands sometimes in ball-shaped tree nests. It does not hibernate.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild rats rarely survive much beyond a year. In captivity they can live about three to four years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a pregnancy of about three weeks the female gives birth to a litter of typically five to ten blind, hairless young in a nest. They are weaned at three to four weeks, and several litters can follow each year where food allows.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in colour and shape. Males are on average slightly larger, and adult males have a visible scrotum at the base of the tail.

Spawning takes place in spring and summer, and the tiny eggs drift in the water for a few days before hatching.
It is an important commercial and recreational catch, taken with traps, hook and line, and trawls.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sharks, spiny dogfish, larger groupers and other big predatory fish eat it, and it is a popular target for recreational and commercial fishing. It stays close to structure and darts into holes when threatened.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active mainly by day, feeding around structure; at night it settles close to rocks and wrecks. Northern fish move offshore into deeper shelf water for the winter and return inshore in spring.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Breeding males are larger and show a blue nuchal hump and bright blue and white face markings; females are plainer brown to grey with no hump.

analysis.summary: Confined to mid-mountain forest in eastern Papua New Guinea, this bird-of-paradise has a display unlike its relatives'. The male hangs upside down from a branch, spreads a fan of violet-blue flank plumes edged in maroon and black, pulses it, and gives a low, mechanical-sounding song.

Pale ivory bill against a black head
Bright blue wings and tail in both sexes
Male's two long, ribbon-like central tail feathers
Female's rufous underparts with dark barring

Blue Bird-of-paradise turns dense leaves into a living theatre, so Inverted Radiance exists because the environment gives contrast and timing somewhere to land.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit and insects matter because the bird must fuel movement, color, and display without abandoning the trees. The diet explains why Inverted Radiance is not empty glamour: the body earns its signal by constantly finding energy in the canopy.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators are not well documented; raptors and tree-climbing nest raiders are likely threats. The main danger is clearing of its mid-mountain forest for gardens and settlements, and males have also been hunted for their plumes.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, with males displaying mainly in the morning. It roosts at night in the forest canopy and is resident all year, with no seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild is not well documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female builds the nest, incubates and cares for the young alone. The nest is a shallow cup in a tree, and clutches of one egg have been recorded; many other breeding details remain poorly known.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have black underparts, violet-blue flank plumes and two long ribbon-like central tail feathers. Females lack plumes and ribbons and have rufous underparts with dark barring.

whyInteresting: Despite the name it is not a true jellyfish but a hydrozoan, a group that also includes the Portuguese man o' war.
The float is a disc of gas-filled chambers that keeps the colony at the surface.
Its sting is weak but can cause mild skin irritation, so stranded colonies are best not handled.
Single-celled algae living in its tissues are thought to add to the golden-brown colour of the float.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Catches small drifting prey such as copepods, larval fish and fish eggs with stinging tentacle-like polyps, then passes it to a single central feeding polyp beneath the float.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eaten by the blue sea slug Glaucus and violet sea snails of the genus Janthina, which drift with it at the surface. Its stinging cells give some protection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It has no sleep or rest cycle in the sense that animals with a brain do; the colony drifts and feeds continuously.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan of the floating colony has not been documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Reproductive polyps under the float bud off tiny free-swimming medusae. These produce eggs and sperm, and the young that result are thought to grow into new floating colonies.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The floating colony is not male or female. Sex belongs to the tiny medusae it releases, which are not seen in the field.

entries.name: Blue Crane

analysis.summary: Long dark grey wing plumes trail behind this pale blue-grey crane almost to the ground, like a tail. Standing about a metre tall, it is the national bird of South Africa, where almost the entire world population lives.

No bare red skin anywhere on the head
Long dark legs and a fairly short bill
Dark grey flight feathers contrasting with the paler body in flight

whyInteresting: A small, isolated population lives around Etosha Pan in northern Namibia, far from the main range.

Its call is a far-carrying, rattling croak, given often in flight and during displays.
The species is listed as Vulnerable after marked declines in parts of its range during the late twentieth century.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, roots and waste grain, with grasshoppers, caterpillars and other insects, frogs and small reptiles. It picks food from the ground while walking slowly across open fields.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Mammalian carnivores such as jackals are thought to take eggs and chicks; healthy adults have few natural enemies. Poisoning, collisions with overhead cables and loss of grassland are the main threats. Parents defend chicks by charging intruders and by distraction displays.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal. At night it roosts standing in shallow water at wetlands and dams, gathering in communal roosts outside the breeding season.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive birds have been reported to live more than 20 years, and wild adults are probably long-lived as well, as in other cranes, though no reliable wild figure is known.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually two eggs are laid on bare ground or among short grass, with little or no nest. Both parents incubate for about 30 days, and the chicks walk away from the nest within a day or two, following their parents until they can fly at around three months or more.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike. Males average slightly larger, so in a pair standing together the bigger bird is usually the male.

analysis.summary: Hanging upside down from a twig like a bat is how this sparrow-sized green parrot, only about 12 centimetres long, spends the night. It grips the perch with its feet and can stay suspended, body dangling, for long periods.

whyInteresting: Young birds are reported to resemble adult females and lack the male's red throat patch.
It is a popular cage bird and has been widely trapped in parts of its range.
Its flight is quick and straight, and flocks move rapidly between flowering trees.
Despite trapping, it remains widespread and is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Takes nectar and pollen from flowering trees, soft fruits such as figs, flower parts and small seeds. It clambers acrobatically through the canopy to reach blossoms.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Little is known about what preys on it, and no predator has been described in detail. Small and leaf-green, it is hard to pick out while it feeds among blossoms.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day in the canopy. At night it roosts on thin outer branches hidden among foliage, alone or in small groups.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been documented, and reliable captive records for this species are scarce.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests in tree holes. The female lines the cavity with leaf pieces, carrying them tucked among her rump feathers. Clutches are usually 3 or 4 white eggs, incubated by the female for about 20 days.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a red throat patch and a clearer blue crown spot. Females lack the red throat and have a duller or smaller blue crown.

Long treated as part of one widespread blue-crowned motmot, it is now usually recognised as a separate species of north-eastern Mexico.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: From a low perch it sallies out to snatch large insects, spiders, small lizards and frogs, beating bigger prey against a branch before swallowing. Fruit is also eaten.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predation on this species has been little studied. Its earth-bank nest tunnels are probably the most exposed point, open to snakes and small mammals that can crawl inside.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and often most vocal before sunrise, it perches quietly through the middle hours and roosts at night on a branch in dense cover.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: There are no reliable figures for how long this motmot lives in the wild.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs dig a nesting tunnel, often over a metre long, into an earth bank or ravine side. The clutch is reported as three or four white eggs, and both parents incubate and feed the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot be told apart in the field.

Pairs are thought to stay together for years, flying wing to wing even inside large flocks.
Captive birds are well known for mimicking human speech and household sounds.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Eats fruit, seeds, nuts, flowers and buds from trees and cacti, handling food with its feet and cracking hard shells with its strong hooked bill. Flocks sometimes raid crops such as citrus and maize.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large hawks and eagles take adults, while monkeys, snakes and other climbers raid nests. Poaching of chicks for the pet trade is the most serious threat. Flocks watch from treetops and burst away calling when danger appears.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. Birds gather at communal roosts in tall trees at dusk and fly out in noisy pairs and small groups soon after dawn.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly known, probably several decades at most. In captivity birds can live 40 years or more, and some are reported to have exceeded 60.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests in a tree cavity, laying usually 3 or 4 eggs. The female incubates for about 4 weeks while the male feeds her; chicks leave the nest at about 2 months old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike, and pairs cannot be told apart reliably by sight.

entries.name: Blue Glaucus
entries.heroTitle: Blue Glaucus — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Most nudibranch sea slugs crawl over the seabed, but this one spends its adult life adrift in the neuston, the thin surface layer of the open ocean. Adults are rarely more than about 3 cm long.

Silvery-grey back, the opposite surface to the blue
Fan-like clusters of slender finger-shaped cerata along each side
Tapering, pointed tail behind the last cerata

analysis.nativeRange: Warm and temperate oceans, including Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Ocean regions.

Fan-like clusters of slender finger-shaped cerata along each side

whyInteresting: It stores unfired stinging cells from its prey in the tips of its cerata, so handling one can give a painful sting.
A bubble of air held in the stomach keeps it floating upside down at the sea surface.
Like most nudibranchs it is a hermaphrodite, and both partners in a mating pair go on to lay eggs.
Onshore winds sometimes strand large numbers on beaches together with the floating prey they drift among.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Eats floating cnidarians, chiefly the Portuguese man o' war, the by-the-wind sailor and the blue button. It grips the prey with its jaws and toothed radula and bites off tentacles and tissue, and it has been recorded eating other glaucus.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators have rarely been recorded, and how often fish or seabirds take it is unknown. Wind is the clearer danger: it cannot swim against it, and onshore gales strand many on beaches, where they soon die.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No sleep or rest cycle has been described. It drifts day and night at the surface, feeding whenever wind and currents carry it into floating prey.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild age is unpublished and thought short, probably under a year; adults drift in the ocean surface film feeding on Portuguese man o' war and related floaters.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After mating, each slug lays strings of eggs attached to floating objects such as driftwood or the remains of its prey. The eggs hatch into tiny shelled larvae that drift in the plankton before changing into the adult form.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Hermaphroditic, so each individual carries both reproductive roles.

respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults drink nectar while larvae eat paralyzed spiders. The diet fits because the adult’s own energy and the offspring’s future meal are different tasks, showing preparation as two kinds of care.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, parasitic flies, and other wasps can threaten adults or nests. The pressure explains why sealed mud chambers matter: protection is built before the danger arrives.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mainly diurnal, working in warm daylight when mud can be gathered and spiders hunted. The rhythm fits because preparation requires usable weather and repeated trips.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults often live one season, with the species continuing through nest chambers and developing young.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: She rarely builds a new nest, instead reopening cells left by the black-and-yellow mud dauber and softening them with water she carries in. One egg goes into each stocked cell before it is sealed with mud. The larva spins a cocoon after feeding, and late broods pass the winter inside.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes are the same metallic blue. Males are usually a little smaller, have one more antennal segment, and lack a sting.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike to the human eye, though the male's blue crown is usually slightly brighter. Males also reflect more ultraviolet from the crown, a difference visible to blue tits but not to people.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually put at about four years in the wild, a figure that rests on few studies. Aquarium fish often die sooner because their natural diet is hard to replace.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are released into the water column after spawning, leaving larvae to develop as plankton before settling on reefs.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Many cleaner wrasses can change sex, usually with dominant individuals becoming male when social conditions shift.

Large, scissor-like jaws that open outward from the mouth
Every segment bears a pair of bristly side lobes

whyInteresting: Many individuals are about a metre long, and specimens of around 3 metres have been reported.
In 2009 a large eunicid worm, widely reported as a bobbit worm, was found in a tank at an aquarium in Cornwall, having arrived hidden in live rock.
Fossil burrows about 20 million years old from Taiwan suggest that large worms were ambushing prey from the seabed in a similar way.
Many worms photographed as bobbit worms may belong to other large Eunice species, and the group's classification is still unsettled.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly small fish, along with other worms and invertebrates that stray over the burrow. Prey is gripped by the jaws, reportedly with enough force to cut a fish in two, and dragged down into the sediment.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: What eats it is poorly documented; larger fish are presumed to be the main threat. It exposes only the head and antennae and snaps back into its burrow the instant it is disturbed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hunts mainly at night from the mouth of its burrow. By day it usually stays buried out of sight in the sediment.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long Eunice aphroditois lives in a burrow is still unrecorded in the field. Large adults can reach body lengths of several metres when fully extended.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs and sperm are presumed to be released into open water, with larvae developing in the plankton as in many eunicid worms; spawning in this species has not been observed.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Separate sexes are presumed, but males and females cannot be told apart from the outside.

entries.name: Bocage's Wall Lizard

analysis.summary: A small, slender lacertid, usually about 5 to 7 centimetres from snout to vent. Its back is a fine mesh of dark flecks over a green, olive or brown ground colour, a pattern that blends closely with lichen-crusted granite and mossy stone walls.

Pale, yellowish or orange belly
Long, thin tail about twice the body length

Like other wall lizards, it can shed its tail when seized; the regrown tail is usually shorter and plainer.
Females are reported to lay small clutches of roughly two to eight eggs, sometimes more than once in a season.
In the mild Atlantic climate of its range it can be seen basking on sunny days in almost any month.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small insects and spiders make up most of the diet, including flies, beetles, ants, caterpillars and grasshoppers, caught by active searching among low plants and stones or by a quick dash from a basking spot.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Kestrels and other birds of prey, snakes and domestic cats take it. It forages close to crevices and dense plants and darts into cover at the first sudden movement nearby.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, basking in early sunshine before foraging, and retiring at night into wall crevices, rock cracks or holes under stones. In the colder months it is largely inactive, though mild sunny days may bring some out.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not well documented. A long-term study in north-west Spain found populations made up mostly of young lizards, though some adults survive several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay small clutches of soft-shelled eggs, usually only a handful, in loose soil or under stones in late spring and summer, and may lay more than once a season. There is no parental care, and hatchlings are independent at once.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males have larger, broader heads and are usually greener with bolder dark netting; females are more often brown, with pale and dark stripes along the back and flanks.

Many sites stay suitable only where grazing or cutting keeps shrubs and trees from shading the wetland.
It is listed as Threatened under the US Endangered Species Act and Critically Endangered by the IUCN.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Omnivorous: beetles, caterpillars, snails, slugs, earthworms and other invertebrates, along with seeds, berries and carrion. Food is taken on land or in shallow rivulets.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Burying itself in soft mud is its main response to danger. Raccoons, skunks, foxes and opossums dig up nests and eat eggs and young, and herons and snakes take small turtles; drainage of its wetlands and illegal collecting have caused steep losses.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and often basks on tussocks in the morning. Nights and hot spells are spent buried in mud, and from about October to April it hibernates in spring-fed muck, root tangles or old muskrat burrows.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Long-lived: wild individuals are commonly estimated to live about 30 to 40 years, and some may live longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nesting is in June. The female lays usually 1 to 6 eggs, often about three, in the top of a sedge tussock or moss. They hatch after roughly 6 to 8 weeks, with no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a concave plastron and a longer, thicker tail with the vent beyond the shell edge; females have a flat plastron.

entries.name: Bolas Spider
entries.heroTitle: Bolas Spider — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The adult female builds no capture web. After dark she hangs from a single horizontal thread and lets down a short line tipped with a sticky globule, swinging it at any moth that flies close.
identification: Large, rounded abdomen dwarfing the small front body
Short, stout legs drawn in tight around the body at rest
Blotched brown, cream and white colouring with no bright markings
Front body usually with a pair of low bumps on top

whyInteresting: Young females and males use no globule; they grab tiny moth flies with the front legs after luring them by scent.
The sticky globule holds moths even though the loose scales on their wings let them slip free of ordinary spider webs.
The common name comes from the bolas, a South American throwing weapon of weights on a cord, which its weighted line resembles.
It belongs to the orb-weaver family Araneidae, though the adult female never spins an orb web.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Bolas Spider feeds on male moths attracted by mimicked pheromones and caught with a sticky silk droplet.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Its main defence against predators is disguise. By day the female sits motionless on a leaf, her lumpy, glossy, mottled body passing for a bird dropping, so hunters that search by sight tend to pass her over.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: The female spends the day pressed to the underside of a leaf and comes out onto her hunting line only after dark, going back to cover before dawn.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one year. Females mature by late summer, lay eggs and die with the autumn frosts; males mature and die much sooner.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In late summer and autumn the female makes several tough, brown, papery egg sacs and hangs them near her daytime leaf. The young are thought to stay inside through the winter, dispersing in spring; there is no further care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are tiny, only a small fraction of the female's size. Only adult females hunt with the sticky globule.

analysis.summary: A stout black jumping spider, 6 to 15 millimetres long, with white spots on the abdomen and metallic green or blue jaws. It walks up on prey and leaps onto it from several body lengths away, straightening its rear legs by a sudden rise in internal fluid pressure and trailing a silk safety line.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, dragonflies, larger spiders, and mud-dauber and spider wasps hunt it. It backs away or jumps clear on its silk line and hides in a silk shelter. Cornered spiders raise the front legs and show the metallic jaws.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hunts only in daylight. At night and in bad weather it stays inside a small, closed silk sac spun under bark, in a rolled leaf or in a corner. Nearly grown juveniles spend the winter in these sacs.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 1 to 2 years. Most individuals overwinter as nearly grown juveniles, mature in spring and die by autumn; females outlive males.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female lays her eggs inside a thick silk nest, commonly 30 to 170 per sac and sometimes several sacs in a season, and stays to guard them. Spiderlings moult once inside the nest, then emerge and disperse after about a month.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger, about 8 to 15 millimetres long against 6 to 13 in males. Males are blacker with sharper white markings, swollen pedipalps and fringed front legs, which they raise and wave in courtship.

analysis.summary: Pseudoscorpion explains Pincer through a body and routine shaped for its exact problem. Pseudoscorpions are tiny arachnids with pincer-like pedipalps and no tail, hunting small prey in leaf litter, bark, and hidden spaces. Females carry their eggs in a brood sac under the abdomen and nourish the embryos with a fluid they secrete.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders, centipedes and ground beetles eat it, and drying out is a constant risk. When disturbed it holds its pincers forward and scuttles rapidly backwards into a crack.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active at night, hunting over shelves, walls and bedding. By day it hides in crevices, behind books or under bark, sometimes inside a small silk chamber.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Roughly 2 to 3 years, based mainly on observations of animals kept in captivity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females produce eggs, and the young develop through small, exposed stages. For Pincer, reproduction shows how even tiny placement, host choice, substrate, or timing can decide survival.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females can differ in size, display, tools, or reproductive behavior. Those differences matter to Pincer when they change mating, egg placement, defense, or dispersal.

entries.name: Bootlace Worm

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike externally; the sexes can be told apart only when ripe gonads show through the body wall.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Alarmed groups scatter with sharp grunts into dense cover. Hunting for meat is the heaviest pressure over much of Borneo, and a recent African swine fever outbreak killed very large numbers.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Bornean Bearded Pig rests in dense forest cover, wallows, and shaded resting places. It can be active at any hour, with peaks around dawn and late afternoon, and groups under heavy hunting become more nocturnal.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Boars are larger than sows, with a heavier beard and more obvious warts on the snout. Both sexes carry the beard, so lone adults can be hard to sex.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat grasses, leaves, bark, fruit, palms, and other vegetation.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators, but calves can be vulnerable, and humans are the major threat through habitat loss, conflict, and fragmentation. Their defense is herd protection, size, and memory of routes, showing that strength depends on connected land.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are active across day and night depending on heat, food, and disturbance, often moving long distances.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Asian elephants can live for many decades, often 50 years or more in good conditions. Such longevity makes pathmaking a generational force: memory becomes part of strength.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to a single calf after a long pregnancy, and the herd helps protect and guide the young. Offspring learn gentleness and power through social contact, not isolation.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow larger and may disperse or live more separately as adults, while females form the core of family herds. The sex difference matters socially: gentle force is carried by matriarchal memory and male power in different ways.

analysis.summary: One of the few venomous mammals. Like other slow lorises, when threatened it is thought to raise its arms above its head and lick a gland on the inner elbow; mixed with saliva, the secretion makes its bite painful and slow to heal.

Pale stripe running down the nose between the eyes
Dense, woolly fur
Tail reduced to a short stub hidden in the fur

analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Bornean Slow Loris belongs in Bornean rainforest, secondary forest, gardens, vines, and night canopy pathways.

Pale stripe running down the nose between the eyes
Dense, woolly fur

whyInteresting: It was recognised as a separate species in 2013, after researchers compared facial mask markings among Bornean lorises.
Its eyes reflect torchlight strongly, so at night a bright eyeshine in the vines often reveals it.
Bites from slow lorises have caused severe allergic reactions, including shock, in some people.
Lorises sold as pets often have their teeth clipped out, which can cause fatal infections.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Bornean Slow Loris feeds on tree gum, nectar, fruit, insects, small vertebrates, and plant exudates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Reticulated pythons, birds of prey and, reportedly, orangutans take slow lorises. Far heavier losses come from people, through forest clearance and capture for the pet trade. When disturbed it freezes, curls into a ball or edges slowly out of sight rather than running.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Bornean Slow Loris rests in tree hollows, dense foliage, vines, and hidden day sleeping sites. Strictly nocturnal, it becomes active after dusk and settles before dawn, usually sleeping curled into a tight ball.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been documented for this species; slow lorises in general have lived around 20 years in captivity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Little has been recorded for this species. In slow lorises generally, a single infant, occasionally twins, is born after about six months' gestation, and the mother may leave it clinging to a branch while she forages.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot be told apart in the field.

entries.name: Zebu
entries.heroTitle: Zebu — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Humped cattle descended from the Indian aurochs and domesticated in South Asia roughly 8,000 years ago. Compared with European cattle they have more and larger sweat glands, a short glossy coat and a lower metabolic rate, so they keep grazing in heat that stops other breeds. Their skin also resists ticks and biting flies better.
identification: Fatty, muscular hump over the shoulders
Long, pendulous dewlap hanging below the neck
Large ears that droop in many breeds
Short, sleek coat, often grey, white or red
Twitches its loose skin to shake off flies
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: domestic_global. Kept on hot pasture, savanna, scrub and farmland across the tropics and subtropics, from South Asia, where it originated, to Africa and South America. It copes with dry rangeland, seasonal drought and humid lowlands, usually within walking distance of a well, river or village.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: domestic_global. Kept on hot pasture, savanna, scrub and farmland across the tropics and subtropics, from South Asia, where it originated, to Africa and South America. It copes with dry rangeland, seasonal drought and humid lowlands, usually within walking distance of a well, river or village.

whyInteresting: Humped bulls are carved on stone seals of the Indus Valley civilisation that are more than 4,000 years old.
Brahman cattle were bred in the United States from Indian breeds including the Guzerat, Nelore and Gir.
Brazil's Nelore herd, descended from Ongole cattle imported from India, is among the largest populations of any cattle breed.
Sanga cattle of Africa, including the long-horned Ankole, are thought to have arisen from crosses between humped and humpless cattle.
Miniature zebu stand only about a metre tall at the shoulder and are among the smallest cattle in the world.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grazes grasses and browses shrubs, crop stubble and straw, doing well on coarse forage of poor quality. Like all cattle it ruminates, bringing food back up to chew again so that microbes in the rumen can break down the fibre.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Most herds are guarded by people, so disease, drought and parasites cause more losses than predators. Near wild country, lions, tigers, leopards, hyenas and wolves take calves and sometimes adults; the cattle bunch together and face the threat with their horns.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, grazing mainly in the cooler early morning and late afternoon and resting in shade to chew the cud through the midday heat. At night the herd lies down together, often inside a pen.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly 15 to 20 years when allowed to live out a natural life; farmed and working animals are usually slaughtered or retired much earlier.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Cows carry a single calf for about nine and a half months, slightly longer than European breeds, and twins are rare. The calf stands and suckles within hours and is usually weaned at six to nine months. Heifers tend to mature later than European cattle.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Bulls are heavier, with a much larger hump, a thicker neck and a deeper dewlap. Cows are lighter and finer-boned, with a smaller hump and a visible udder. Both sexes can carry horns, depending on the breed.

entries.name: Bowfin
entries.heroTitle: Bowfin — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A heavy-bodied fish with a gas bladder lined with blood vessels that works like a lung. When warm, stagnant water runs short of oxygen, it rises to gulp air at the surface, surviving in shallows that suffocate most other fish.
identification: Long dorsal fin running over half the length of the back
Rounded, fan-shaped tail fin
Bony plate on the underside of the chin
Short tube-like nostrils
Olive, mottled body with a large mouth
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Swamps, backwaters, oxbow lakes, slow rivers and weedy lake margins of eastern North America, especially the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plains. It favours warm, still water with dense vegetation and soft, muddy bottoms.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america. Swamps, backwaters, oxbow lakes, slow rivers and weedy lake margins of eastern North America, especially the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plains. It favours warm, still water with dense vegetation and soft, muddy bottoms.

whyInteresting: Its family has a fossil record going back more than 100 million years, to the age of dinosaurs.
It can swim forwards or backwards by rippling its long dorsal fin, keeping the body almost still.
In 2022 scientists split bowfins into two species, keeping Amia calva for the coastal plain populations.
Local names include dogfish, mudfish, grinnel and choupique, reflecting its long familiarity to anglers.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish and aquatic insects make up most of the diet, along with crayfish, frogs and other small animals. It hunts mostly at night, lurking in weeds and seizing prey with a sudden rush and a powerful bite.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger fish, including gars and bass, eat eggs and young, and herons take small bowfin. Adults have few natural predators; people take them by angling and bowfishing.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most active at dusk and through the night. By day it tends to rest among dense weeds or near the bottom in sheltered water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically around 10 years in the wild, though figures vary; captive fish have been reported to reach about 30 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In spring the male clears a nest among vegetation in shallow water, where one or more females lay thousands of adhesive eggs. The male guards the eggs, and after hatching he shepherds the dense ball of fry for several weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Breeding males turn bright green on the fins and belly. In bowfins generally, males show a dark, orange- or yellow-ringed eyespot at the tail base, while in females it is usually faint or missing. Females grow larger.

entries.name: Brahminy Kite
entries.heroTitle: Brahminy Kite — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: One of the most familiar raptors of tropical Asian waterfronts, this chestnut-and-white kite spends much of the day in slow, buoyant flight, twisting its tail to steer. Small items snatched from the water are often eaten in the air, passed from foot to bill without the bird landing.

Chestnut body and wings
Black wingtips on the outer flight feathers
Rounded tail, not forked
Young birds are mottled brown

They are strongly associated with coasts, estuaries, mangroves, rivers, wetlands, harbours, and other waterside habitats.

It has been called the red-backed sea-eagle in Australia.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Takes dead and dying fish, crabs, frogs, snakes and small mammals, plus offal and refuse around harbours and fish markets. It often steals prey from other kites, crows and fishing birds.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators. Crows and other raptors mob it and compete for food. Threats come mainly from pesticides, poisoning and loss of mangroves and wetlands.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Spends much of the day hunting and soaring, often on thermals from mid-morning. Birds head to roost trees in late afternoon, sometimes forming large communal roosts near water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly documented, with no reliable published figures.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Both birds build a stick nest lined with leaves in a tall tree, often in mangroves. The clutch is usually two eggs, incubated mainly by the female for about four weeks. Young fledge at roughly seven to eight weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in plumage; females are slightly larger, but this is hard to judge in the field.

Grey to brown back finely speckled with pale and dark spots
Tail often faintly banded

whyInteresting: Males bob their heads and do push-up displays from rocks and walls to warn rivals off their territory.
It has been recorded eating cactus fruit and passing the seeds, so it may help disperse some plants.
Pockets in the skin folds at the sides of the neck often hold clusters of parasitic mites.
Besides insects, it has been recorded eating small lizards, including young of its own species.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Ants, beetles, termites, spiders and other small invertebrates make up most of the diet, taken on the ground and on rock and wall surfaces. It also eats flowers and fruit.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Likely predators include birds of prey, snakes and, in towns, domestic cats. It escapes by sprinting into rock crevices, holes or dense vegetation, and a seized lizard can shed its tail, which later regrows.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hunts through the sunny hours of the day. At night it shelters in rock crevices, under loose bark or in holes in walls.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably only a few years in the wild: lizards can mature within their first year and field populations appear to turn over quickly. A maximum age has not been established.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay small clutches, often about three to six eggs, in soil or sand, and may lay more than one clutch in a season. Breeding is concentrated in the warm, wet months, and there is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger with broader heads and black patches under the thighs and on the flap in front of the vent; females usually lack these patches.

entries.name: Brazilian Treehopper
entries.heroTitle: Brazilian Treehopper — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Brazilian Treehopper shows that structure can be signal. Its strange form is not wasted decoration; it changes the rules of attention.

Thin upright stalk rising from the back
Several round, hairy balls held on side branches
Clear, veined wings folded along the body

whyInteresting: The whole ornament is an outgrowth of the pronotum, the plate that covers the first segment of the thorax.
Its function is not settled; suggested roles include deterring predators, mimicking a fungus-infected insect, or acting as a sensory structure.
A 2011 study proposed that treehopper helmets are modified wings, but other researchers have disputed that interpretation.
Treehoppers commonly signal to one another with vibrations passed through plant stems, and this species is presumed to do the same.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds on plant sap, piercing stems with needle-like mouthparts and drinking from the vascular tissue. Like other treehoppers it probably excretes sugary honeydew, which can attract ants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, spiders and predatory insects are likely predators, though records for this species are few. Like many treehoppers, it probably sidles round the stem out of sight when disturbed, and it can also jump or fly off.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Its daily activity has not been studied. It spends long periods perched on a host stem while feeding, moving little by day or night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Nymph-to-adult lifespan for Bocydium globulare has not been timed in published field studies. Adults carry a globe-and-stalk pronotal structure above the head.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding in this species has been little studied. In treehoppers generally, females lay eggs into plant tissue and the nymphs pass through five moults before reaching adult form.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Visible differences between males and females are not well documented for this species. In treehoppers generally, females tend to be slightly larger than males.

Brazil produces an antivenom against Phoneutria bites, and the venom's toxins are studied for possible medical uses.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spider-hunting wasps paralyse it to feed their larvae, and birds, lizards, frogs and small mammals are reported to eat it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal. It spends the day hidden in crevices, under logs and bark, in banana bunches or in dark corners of buildings, and comes out after dark to hunt.

Wild hybrids between brill and turbot have been recorded, and the two are closely related members of the same genus.
It is a valued food fish, taken mostly as bycatch in trawl and net fisheries aimed at other flatfish.
Most adults are about 30 to 50 centimetres long, and exceptional fish reach roughly 75 centimetres.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Young brill in shallow nursery waters are taken by larger fish and seabirds; grown fish have fewer natural enemies, and trawl fishing is the main threat. Its defence is to stay flat and motionless until danger is very close, then burst away.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Much of each day is spent lying still on the bottom, and its daily rhythm of feeding and rest has not been studied in detail.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the same colour and shape; females are reported to grow larger on average, but the sexes cannot be told apart reliably by eye.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars feed only on buckthorns, in north-west Europe chiefly buckthorn and alder buckthorn. Adults drink nectar with a long tongue, from primroses, dandelions and sallow catkins in spring and from thistles, knapweeds and teasels in late summer.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Like most butterflies, it is eaten by birds at every stage of life, and many caterpillars are killed by parasitic wasps and flies that develop inside them. The green caterpillar rests pressed along a leaf midrib, where its colour matches the leaf.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are bright sulphur yellow; females are a pale greenish white and can be mistaken for a white butterfly in flight.

Small for a pleco at around 13 to 15 cm

The male guards the eggs alone in his cave and fans them with his fins, eating almost nothing until they hatch.
It rasps wood as well as algae, and needs driftwood in the water to digest properly.
It is kept in aquariums specifically as an algae grazer, which is why it is one of the most widely traded freshwater fish.
Unlike the common pleco it stays small, which is the whole reason the hobby prefers it.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Algae, biofilm and rasped wood taken off submerged surfaces, with detritus and the occasional invertebrate. This diet supports the principle because food is scraped off the same timber the cave is cut into — a guarding male never has to leave home to eat.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger catfish, cichlids and birds take them where cover runs out. Their answer is armour, a body wedged into a hole facing outward, and spines raised at the gill covers that make a small fish hard to swallow.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal. It stays wedged in wood or under rock through daylight and comes out to graze after dark, which is why aquarium keepers often go weeks without seeing one.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Bristlenose Pleco live around five to eight years, long enough for a male to hold and defend the same hollow through many clutches.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female lays a cluster of orange eggs inside the male's cave and then leaves; everything after that is his. Fry stay attached to the cave walls by their own suckermouths for days after hatching.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males carry the branched snout bristles and are the ones that hold caves; females are plainer and slightly rounder. The difference is the principle made visible — the bristles grow on the sex that does the guarding.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have the basal segments of the front feet broadened into pads, used to grip the female during mating; females have slender front feet. Females are on average slightly larger and broader.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live about 2 to 3 years, and few survive beyond 4.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry from about a thousand to several thousand eggs glued beneath the tail, for several weeks in summer and up to about three months in winter. The larvae drift in the plankton for weeks, moulting several times, before settling on the bottom in shallow water.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females grow larger than males, and the biggest shrimps in a catch are almost always females. Otherwise the sexes look very similar.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Takes insects, spiders and other arthropods probed from bark, moss and epiphytes with its long curved bill, and also eats fruit, especially from canopy trees and shrubs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Natural predators are poorly documented and likely include raptors. People have long hunted males for their tail plumes, used in highland headdresses, though the species remains fairly widespread.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, feeding mainly in the middle and upper forest layers. Night roosts are in trees, but roosting sites have rarely been described.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long brown sicklebills live is not known; no reliable ages from wild or captive birds have been reported.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Males take no part in nesting. The female builds a cup nest in a tree and raises the young alone; clutches are typically a single egg.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are blackish above with iridescent blue and purple gloss and dull brownish underparts, with an enormously long, graduated tail. Females are brown with a rufous crown, finely barred underparts and a much shorter tail.

Warning Without Pursuit fits because the spider possesses a serious defensive weapon while relying primarily on retreat and concealment.

The species is generally less aggressive than many people assume from the widow name.
Females produce distinctive spiky egg sacs that look like small cream-coloured burrs.
Brown Widows have spread widely through tropical and subtropical regions around the world.
They frequently live around buildings, fences, outdoor furniture and other sheltered human-made structures.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wasps, birds, reptiles and other spiders can prey on Brown Widows. Their main defence is concealment, web retreat and venom when physically threatened.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal. Brown Widows remain concealed in or near their web during daylight and become more active after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Females can live roughly one to several years depending on climate and conditions, while males generally live shorter lives.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females produce multiple egg sacs, each containing many eggs. The distinctive pointed or tufted surface of the egg sac is one of the easiest field clues separating Brown Widow nests from many other widow spiders.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are much larger with a bulbous abdomen and medically important venom apparatus. Males are smaller, more slender and generally much less conspicuous.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Strictly nocturnal. It spends the day perched upright in dense foliage high in a tall tree, often close to its mate, and begins hunting at dusk.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually lays 1 or 2 eggs in a tree hollow, a rock ledge or on the ground at the base of a tree. The female incubates while the male brings food, and both parents tend the downy owlets.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes have the same plumage. Females are somewhat larger than males, a difference that is hard to judge in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, snakes and dingoes take mulgaras, and introduced foxes and feral cats are considered a serious threat, particularly where fire has cleared the spinifex that gives it cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal, resting by day in a burrow it digs in sandy soil. In cool weather it may bask in the sun near the entrance, and it can drop into short bouts of torpor to save energy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably 3 to 6 years; males are reported to survive to breed in a second season in some cases, unlike many small carnivorous marsupials.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating takes place in the cooler months, and young are born after about five to six weeks. Females have six teats, so a litter is at most six. The pouch is shallow, and young are left in the burrow once too large to carry, weaning at around three to four months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are noticeably larger and heavier than females, but both share the same sandy colouring and brush-tipped tail. Females have six teats, which become obvious when they are carrying young.

Wild flocks have no fixed migration, and numbers in one district can swing from none to many thousands between years.
The yellow feathers of the crown and cheeks fluoresce under ultraviolet light, and experiments suggest that birds use this glow when choosing mates.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, falcons, snakes, cats, and nest predators threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Small parties fly to water soon after dawn to drink, then feed on the ground among the grasses. The hottest hours are spent quietly in shade, and the birds roost in trees at night.

whyInteresting: Colonies are small by the standards of social bees, typically from a few dozen to a few hundred workers, and in temperate species last a single season.
In many species the founding queen builds a thimble-sized wax pot beside her first brood and fills it with nectar to draw on in cold or wet spells.
Studies have shown that foraging bumblebees leave scent traces from their feet on flowers, and other bees can use these marks to skip blooms that were recently emptied.
Experiments with buff-tailed bumblebees showed they can sense the weak electric field around a flower, which changes briefly after another bee has visited.
Its sting lacks the large barbs that anchor a honeybee's, so a bumblebee can pull it free and sting more than once.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Nectar supplies the sugar that fuels flight, and pollen the protein fed to growing larvae. Tongue length differs between species: long-tongued bumblebees work deep flowers such as clovers and foxgloves, while some short-tongued ones bite through the base of a flower to steal nectar.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, robber flies, skunks, and parasites threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, often from early morning until dusk. At night workers stay in the nest, while males, which do not return to it, and foragers caught out late often rest clinging under a flower head until morning.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Workers live weeks; queens can overwinter. Most workers survive about two to six weeks in summer, depending on species and workload, and a mated queen usually lives about a year, much of it dormant underground; males live a few weeks.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In most temperate species a lone queen founds the colony in spring, building wax cells stocked with pollen, laying her first eggs and lying across the brood to keep it warm. The first workers emerge about four to five weeks later; late in the season the colony rears males and new queens.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females have pollen baskets and stingers; males do not sting.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults are mainly fish-eaters, taking sculpins, perch, whitefish and other bottom fish, plus crayfish. Young burbot eat insect larvae and small crustaceans. It hunts close to the bottom, largely by smell and touch.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and young are eaten by pike, perch and larger burbot, which are often cannibalistic. Adults have few natural enemies besides big pike, while fishing and river damming are the main human threats.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Chiefly nocturnal. During daylight it lies hidden under rocks, in crevices or among roots, coming out after dark to hunt along the bottom.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning happens in midwinter, often under ice, when many fish gather at night in writhing balls over sand or gravel. A large female sheds hundreds of thousands of tiny eggs; there is no nest or parental care, and hatching takes several weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike; females tend to grow larger and heavier than males of the same age.

Its venom is not considered dangerous to people, though the long fangs can give a painful puncture wound.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly large invertebrates such as earthworms, beetles, cockroaches and other spiders, with occasional frogs, lizards and small rodents. Prey is killed with venom and the fangs, then softened with digestive fluid. Birds are rarely if ever taken.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tarantula hawk wasps, which paralyse tarantulas as food for their larvae, are likely enemies, along with large snakes and ground-foraging mammals. Its main defence is to flick a cloud of barbed, irritating hairs from its abdomen with the hind legs.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Spends the daylight hours deep inside its burrow and becomes active after dark. Before moulting it may seal the entrance with silk and soil and stay hidden for days or weeks.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is not documented. In captivity females are reported to live 15 to 20 years or more, while males mature at around three to four years and usually die within a year or two afterwards.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females produce a silk egg sac and guard it inside the burrow for several weeks until the spiderlings emerge, after which the young disperse. Clutch sizes reported from captive breeding range from several dozen to over a hundred.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Mature males are lighter and longer-legged than females and carry swollen, bulb-tipped pedipalps used to transfer sperm. Females are bulkier, with a larger abdomen.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: The violet sea snail, the blue sea dragon nudibranch and the nudibranch Fiona pinnata feed on it. It cannot escape, and relies only on its stinging cells.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars eat the leaves of cabbage, mustard, radish and other cabbage-family plants, first grazing in groups under silk webbing and then boring into the growing heart. Adult feeding is not well documented.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Parasitic wasps and flies attack the eggs and caterpillars, and spiders, ants, predatory bugs and birds take larvae. The caterpillars shelter inside their webs and in the hearts of plants.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are active at night and come to lights, resting hidden among foliage by day. Caterpillars may feed at any hour.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: In warm tropical conditions the whole cycle from egg to adult takes about 3 to 4 weeks; adults live around 1 to 2 weeks.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in flat, overlapping clusters on the undersides of leaves, often dozens in one mass. When fully grown, the caterpillars drop to pupate in a silk cocoon in the soil. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look broadly alike in the field. Reliable separation needs close examination of the moth.

Its lesson is that independence works best when it still knows where to rest.

Wild Muscovies nest in tree cavities several metres up, and the day-old ducklings jump to the ground to follow their mother to water.
Drakes do not quack at all; the sound is a breathy hiss, which makes a flock far quieter than mallard-type ducks.
Feral populations breed freely in Florida, Texas and other warm places where birds escaped or were released.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, dogs, raccoons and large raptors take adults, and rats, crows and snapping turtles take eggs and ducklings. Roosting off the ground at night, with clawed feet that grip a branch, is its main answer.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Drakes are close to twice the weight of ducks, roughly 5 to 7 kg against 2.5 to 4 kg, with larger red caruncles and a low hiss in place of a quack. Ducks give a quiet trill.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike; males may be slightly larger, but there is no reliable visible difference in the field.

analysis.summary: California Scrub-Jays are corvids known for caching acorns and other food. Their survival depends on memory, social awareness, and turning small finds into future options.

Grey-brown patch on the back
Streaked white throat framed by a blue necklace
Thin white eyebrow above a dark cheek
Loud, harsh, rising scolding call
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Oak woodland, chaparral, coastal sage scrub and riparian scrub from Washington through Oregon and California into Baja California, mostly from sea level into the foothills. It has adapted well to suburban gardens and parks with oaks and shrubs.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america. whyInteresting: In experiments, jays watched while hiding food later moved their caches in private, and only birds that had stolen caches themselves did this.
Captive jays remembered what they had hidden and when, recovering perishable worms sooner than nuts.
Acorns that are never recovered can sprout, so the jays help spread oaks.
Jays gather and call loudly around a dead jay, then avoid feeding at that spot for a time.
It was split from Woodhouse's Scrub-Jay in 2016; together they had been called the Western Scrub-Jay.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Acorns, pine seeds and other nuts in autumn and winter; insects, spiders, fruit, and sometimes eggs, nestlings, small lizards and mice in spring and summer. It forages on the ground and in shrubs, hammering hard seeds open while holding them with its feet.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Cooper's and sharp-shinned hawks and owls take adults; snakes, crows, ravens, raccoons and cats raid nests. Jays give loud rasping alarm calls and gang up to mob hawks, snakes and cats near the territory.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active from dawn to dusk. Pairs roost at night in dense shrubs or leafy trees within their year-round territory.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults commonly live several years; banding records include birds of about 15 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A pair builds a twig cup lined with rootlets in a shrub or small tree. The female lays 3 to 6 greenish, spotted eggs and incubates them for about 16 to 18 days while the male feeds her; young fledge at about 18 days and stay with the parents for weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in plumage; males average slightly larger, but the difference cannot be judged in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Orcas, great white sharks, disease, fishing gear, and human disturbance create pressure. The sea lion’s answer is group awareness, fast swimming, hauled-out rest, and constant adjustment between sea and shore.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: California Sea Lions rest both on land and in water, while feeding trips may happen at different times depending on prey.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly about 15 to 25 years in the wild; animals in zoos and aquariums have been recorded living past 30.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An omnivore and scavenger that crushes mussels, snails, clams and sea urchins with its strong mouthparts. It also takes crabs, worms, dead animals and some algae.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: California sheephead, giant sea bass, octopuses, moray eels and people are its main enemies, and sea otters take it in the north. It backs into crevices, faces threats head-on, rasps loudly and escapes by flipping its tail backwards.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly nocturnal, it spends the day wedged into crevices and under ledges, often sharing a den with other lobsters, and leaves to forage after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Large individuals are thought to be 30 or more years old, but ages are uncertain because lobsters moult and are hard to age directly.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The male sticks a sperm packet to the female's underside; she scratches it open as her eggs emerge. She carries tens of thousands to several hundred thousand eggs under her tail for about 10 weeks, and the flat, transparent larvae drift for many months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females have a small pincer on the last pair of walking legs and broader swimmerets for holding eggs. Males grow larger, with longer front walking legs.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are nocturnal, flying from dusk through the night, and spend the daylight hours resting on foliage, bark or walls.
