fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly seeds of grasses and other steppe plants, with green shoots and insects in summer. It forages on the ground, sniffing out fallen seeds among the bases of grass clumps.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, hawks and falcons, foxes, polecats and weasels hunt it, and probably Pallas's cats too. It relies on its burrow, freezing when alarmed in the open and bolting for the nearest entrance.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal and crepuscular, emerging around dusk and foraging through the night. By day it sleeps in a nest chamber lined with grass inside its burrow.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 1.5 to 2 years in captivity, occasionally 3; most wild individuals probably live less than a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a pregnancy of about 18 to 21 days the female gives birth to a litter of usually 4 to 8 blind, hairless young. The pups are weaned at about three weeks, and the female can mate again soon after giving birth.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in colour and build; males have a longer gap between the anus and genital opening, which is how keepers tell them apart.

entries.name: Candy-striped Leafhopper

analysis.summary: Most leafhoppers are the colour of the leaf they sit on. The Candy-striped Leafhopper is the opposite: a hard, bright signal on a green stem, so a bird that has tried one remembers the taste and the pattern together.
identification: Wedge-shaped hopper, 8-9 mm, banded red, blue and yellow
Head pointed, with two small black spots on the crown
Jumps explosively when approached, then lands in the open again
Often sits on the upper surface of a leaf rather than underneath

whyInteresting: The pattern is aposematic. Distasteful hopper sap and a colour a bird can learn are cheaper than armour.
It feeds on a wide range of woody plants — oak, maple, elm, rose — by tapping xylem and phloem, and is common in gardens as well as woodland.
Males sing with vibration through the leaf, a signal you feel more than hear, which is how pairs find each other on a large tree.
It is native to North America and is one of the leafhoppers most often photographed because it does not hide.
Several Graphocephala species look similar; this one is the widespread eastern candy-stripe, not the blue-green sharpshooter of the West.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Xylem and phloem sap from a wide range of deciduous trees and shrubs. Feeding in the open on the upper leaf is how the colour does its job.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, jumping spiders and damsel bugs take hoppers that sit too long. The first line of defence is the colour; the second is a jump that puts a stem between them and the threat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day on sunlit foliage, stiller in cool weather, with the vibrational calling concentrated in warm hours.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults live several weeks in summer. There are usually two generations a year in the north of the range.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are inserted into leaf or stem tissue. Nymphs are paler and gain the full stripe pattern as they moult, so the warning is earned rather than present from the first instar.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the same colours. Males are slightly slimmer and are the ones sending vibrational calls through the leaf.

entries.name: Cape Buffalo
entries.heroTitle: Cape Buffalo — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Cape Buffalo expresses Herdline through heavy horns, strong herd defense, grass grazing, and collective alertness make the Herdline principle specific rather than generic; body, habitat, and pressure all point back to the same lesson.

strong herd defense
grass grazing

whyInteresting: Oxpeckers ride on buffalo and feed on their ticks, and the birds' hissing alarm calls can warn the host of danger.
Old bulls that spend their days in mud wallows are nicknamed dagga boys, after a Zulu word for mud.
The small, reddish forest buffalo of West and Central African rainforest weighs about half as much as the savanna form.
Before a herd moves, resting cows stand, face one way and lie down again, and the herd later sets off in the direction most had faced.
It has never been domesticated, unlike the Asian water buffalo, which belongs to a different genus.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A bulk grazer of grasses and other rough vegetation, often needing regular water. Herds usually drink every day and stay within a day's walk of water. The wide muzzle and mobile tongue crop tall, coarse grass that many other grazers leave.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Lions are the main predator of adults; spotted hyenas take calves, crocodiles seize drinking animals, and people hunt them. Herds bunch with calves in the middle, and groups of adults charge predators. Rinderpest killed huge numbers in the 1890s, and bovine tuberculosis is now established in some southern African herds.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Grazing is heaviest in the cool of evening, night and early morning. Through the midday heat it rests and ruminates in herds between grazing movements, often near water. Shade and mud wallows are used for cooling.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: An adult can live around 15 to 25 years in the wild. Few wild animals pass 20, and captive buffalo have reached almost 30.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a gestation of about 11 months, females give birth to one calf that stays within herd protection. Births peak in the rainy season. Calves suckle for up to a year, and daughters usually remain in the mother's herd.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are larger with heavier horn bosses; females form the stable herd core. Cows have slimmer horns that do not meet across the forehead, and old bulls often leave to live alone or in small bachelor groups.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly small aquatic animals such as insect larvae, small crustaceans and water snails, with seeds and other plant material. Food is taken from the top few centimetres of water and from soft mud.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: African marsh-harriers and Cape eagle-owls take Cape teal; adults escape by flying low and fast over water, while ducklings hide in vegetation or dive.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds mainly by day, with rest periods through the middle of the day spent loafing on mud spits or floating on open water. It also roosts at night on open water or bare shorelines, usually in pairs or small groups.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild has not been well documented for this species.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The nest is a down-lined hollow hidden in grass or under a bush, usually near water and often on an island. Clutches are typically about 6 to 9 eggs, incubated by the female for roughly four weeks; the male has been reported helping to guard the brood.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in plumage; the male is slightly larger, but the sexes are hard to separate in the field.

analysis.summary: Stocky, cat-sized monkeys of the genera Cebus and Sapajus, with dexterous hands and large brains for their size. Bearded capuchins in dry parts of Brazil crack palm nuts with stone hammers on rock or log anvils, choosing stones by weight, and the young watch adults for years before they succeed.

Hands constantly probing bark, leaves and fruit
Tufts or crests of crown hair in robust species

They use all levels from the ground to the canopy.

Hammer stones used by bearded capuchins often weigh about a kilogram, a third or more of the body weight of the monkey lifting them.
They rub crushed millipedes, ants, citrus and other pungent plants into their fur, which probably repels insects.
Capuchin friars gave these monkeys their name, because the dark cap of fur recalls the hood of the brown robe.
The tail can grip and brace the animal while it feeds, but adults seldom hang from it alone.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Omnivorous: fruit, nuts, seeds, flowers, insects, spiders, eggs and small vertebrates such as lizards, frogs and nestlings; coastal groups eat crabs and shellfish. Much food is extracted by hand, by stripping bark, breaking dead twigs, unrolling leaves and pounding hard items open.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Harpy eagles and other large raptors, jaguars, ocelots, tayras and large snakes hunt them. In the species studied, group members give different alarm calls for threats from the air and from the ground. Capuchins also dive into dense cover and mob snakes and cats.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Groups set off around sunrise and forage through the day, with a lull in the midday heat. They spend the night high in tall trees, in some areas in palms.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 15 to 25 years in the wild; captive animals commonly reach 40 and a few have passed 50.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: One infant is born after a pregnancy of about five to six months, usually at intervals of around two years. It rides on the mother's back, is often carried by other group members, and is weaned during its second year.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are noticeably larger and heavier than females, with longer canine teeth. In some tufted species the crown tufts are fuller in males, but young males and females are hard to tell apart.

Some other members of its genus live inside sponges and rarely clean, whereas this species lives mainly on coral and cleans regularly.
Genetic studies suggest that many of its young settle on reefs not far from where they hatched, despite their time in open water.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Colonies are mainly nocturnal, with heavy canopy foraging after dark and only sparse floor traffic by day.

whyInteresting: They can shake pollen out of flowers such as tomatoes by vibrating their flight muscles, a technique called buzz pollination.
In many species territorial males hover in one spot near nest sites or flowers and chase off other insects that come close.
In some species a gallery is reused and extended by later generations, so one piece of wood can hold many tunnels.
Females of many Old World species carry mites in a special pouch in the abdomen, and the mites appear to live harmlessly in the nests.
In some species several females share one nest, with one laying eggs while others guard the entrance.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults drink nectar and gather pollen from a wide range of flowers. Some species bite a slit at the base of long tubular flowers to reach nectar without entering the bloom.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Woodpeckers break into nests to reach larvae, and bee-eaters, shrikes and other birds catch adults. Parasitic flies and wasps attack the brood. Females can sting in defence but seldom do unless handled.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most species fly by day in warm sunshine and spend the night and cool weather inside the nest tunnel. A few tropical species forage mainly at dawn and dusk, and some have been recorded flying at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About a year in many temperate species, with adults emerging in late summer, overwintering in the tunnel and breeding the next spring; in some species females have been recorded surviving into a second breeding season.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Larvae feed and pupate in their sealed cells over several weeks, the timing depending on species and temperature. Brood size varies by species and with the length of the tunnel. In many species the mother stays with the nest, and the new adults may remain in it with her before dispersing.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males cannot sting. In many species males have pale or yellow markings on the face and larger eyes, while in some, such as the valley carpenter bee, males are golden brown and females black.

whyInteresting: Silphidae are widely known as Carrion Beetles because many species feed and breed on dead animals.
Many species detect chemicals released during decomposition and travel to carcasses.
Carrion Beetles are important recyclers because they help move animal nutrients back into ecosystems.
Some members of the family also prey on fly larvae and other small animals attracted to carcasses.
Burying beetles in the genus Nicrophorus go further and bury small vertebrate carcasses underground.
Burying beetles often carry hitchhiking mites to carcasses, where the mites eat fly eggs that would compete with the beetle larvae.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Carrion, decomposing animal material and associated organisms are central foods for many Silphidae. Some also prey heavily on fly maggots and other invertebrates found at carcasses. Feeding varies within the family, so AnimalDex does not claim that every Silphid follows exactly the same diet.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, mammals, reptiles and larger arthropods may prey on Carrion Beetles. Dark coloration, chemical defences in some species, hiding under carcasses or litter, and nocturnal activity can reduce exposure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Many Carrion Beetles are active in dim light or at night, especially when searching for carrion, although activity patterns vary substantially across the family.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: There is no defensible single lifespan for the entire Silphidae family, so AnimalDex does not apply one species' lifespan to the whole group.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Reproductive behaviour varies dramatically across Silphidae. Burying beetles such as Nicrophorus provide exceptional parental care around buried carcasses, while other Carrion Beetles follow less elaborate reproductive strategies. That distinction is preserved rather than generalized across the family.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are often subtle and species-specific. There is no single external male-female character that can safely describe all Silphidae.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A scavenger that feeds mainly on the bodies of insects and other arthropods that have died from heat stress, also taking live prey and some sugary liquids. Food is carried back to the nest in the mandibles.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Lizards, spiders, robber flies, antlions and birds take foragers. Workers face high risk outside the nest and reduce it by running fast and keeping foraging trips short.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, most strongly from late morning into the afternoon. At night and in the cooler hours the whole colony stays inside the underground nest.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Colonies are headed by one or more queens, which lay most of the eggs. Workers rear the larvae and pupae in underground chambers, and winged queens and males are produced once the colony is established.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: All foragers are non-reproductive female workers. Winged males are produced only for mating, differ from workers in body shape, and are seldom seen above ground.

analysis.summary: Long, mostly flattened predators with one pair of legs on each body segment, centipedes kill with a weapon found in no other animals. House centipedes have compound eyes and very long legs, and can run at around 40 centimetres a second.
Fossil centipedes are known from rocks more than 400 million years old, placing them among the earliest predators on land.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, shrews, toads, snakes, ground beetles, spiders and other centipedes eat them. Defences include bolting for cover, a venomous bite, and in many species shedding a leg that has been seized; some soil centipedes give off sticky or glowing secretions.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal. By day they shelter in soil or under stones, bark and logs, where it stays damp, and come out to hunt after dark. House centipedes may also be seen by day inside dim buildings.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Many species live several years, long for an arthropod, commonly about 2 to 6. House centipedes are reported to reach 3 to 7 years and large Scolopendra around 10 in captivity, though these upper figures are poorly documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Males leave a sperm packet that the female picks up. Many species lay roughly 10 to 60 eggs. Scolopendra and the soil centipedes coil around eggs and hatchlings to guard them, while stone and house centipedes lay eggs singly in soil and leave them.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in most species and usually cannot be told apart in the field. In some groups males have modified last legs, and in soil centipedes males often have slightly fewer leg pairs than females.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Young fish are eaten by larger pickerel, bass and wading birds, and adults are taken by ospreys, otters and herons. Cover in dense weed and quick escape bursts are the main defences.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike. Females tend to grow larger, but size alone cannot tell a single fish's sex.

analysis.summary: A limpet-shaped sea snail with a single oval hole at the peak of its shell. Water flows in under the shell edge, passes over the gills and leaves through that hole, while a broad muscular foot holds the animal to wave-washed rock as it grazes.

In very young shells the opening is thought to begin as a notch at the shell margin, becoming enclosed as the shell grows.
Wastes leave through the hole in the shell with the outgoing water, so they are carried away from the gills.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sea stars and crabs prey on it, and shorebirds and octopuses probably do too. When a sea star touches it, it lifts the shell and spreads its soft mantle up over it, leaving the star little to grip.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Movement follows the tide rather than a sleep cycle: it grazes while submerged, apparently most often at night, and sits clamped and still when the water drops.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike from outside and cannot be told apart in the field.

entries.name: Cherry Shrimp
entries.heroTitle: Cherry Shrimp — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Cherry Shrimp graze biofilm off every surface all day, and shift tone with the substrate and their own condition. The wild animal is a translucent brown; every vivid colour in a tank is something people selected for, not something the shrimp chose.
identification: Small shrimp, 2.5-4 cm, females larger and more strongly coloured
Constantly picking at surfaces with paired feeding claws
Translucent brown in the wild; red and other morphs are bred
A saddle of developing eggs visible behind the head in females

whyInteresting: The wild form is a mottled translucent brown. Fire red, blue and yellow morphs are all products of selective breeding in the aquarium trade.
Chromatophores let an individual darken or pale over hours to match a substrate, but they cannot produce the bred colours to order.
Neocaridina davidi breeds entirely in fresh water with no marine larval stage, which is why it establishes so easily in tanks and, where released, in the wild.
A female carries 20-30 eggs under her tail for about a month, fanning them constantly with her swimmerets.
Native to eastern China and Taiwan, and now feral in several warm-water systems worldwide.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Biofilm, algae, decaying leaves and detritus, grazed continuously from every available surface. It is unselective, low-value food available everywhere, which is exactly what makes constant quiet work viable.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Almost any fish large enough to fit one in its mouth, plus dragonfly larvae and larger shrimp. Cover and low contrast do the defending — there is no escape response beyond a tail-flick into leaf litter.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Grazes on and off around the clock with no true rest, though activity dips in the brightest part of the day and rises at dawn and dusk.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: One to two years, with females reaching breeding size at around four to five months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry the eggs under the abdomen until they hatch as fully formed miniature shrimp. There is no larval stage at all, so young start grazing the same surfaces the adults do immediately.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger, deeper-bodied and more strongly coloured, with a curved underside to the abdomen for holding eggs. Males are smaller, slimmer and paler.

analysis.summary: A tiny blood-feeding mite of poultry and wild birds, found wherever chickens are kept. It hides in cracks by day and climbs onto roosting birds at night, turning from grey to red after a meal. It can survive for months without feeding.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Nymphs and adults suck the blood of birds, mainly chickens but also pigeons, sparrows and other wild birds, climbing onto them at night to feed. They also bite people but cannot breed on them.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predatory mites, including species used in biological control on poultry farms, eat all stages. Poultry keepers are its main threat, through cleaning and treatments. It survives by hiding deep in crevices.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds at night on roosting birds and hides in crevices by day. In cold weather it becomes inactive and can go many months without food.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a blood meal the female lays a small batch of eggs in a crevice, repeating this after each feed. Six-legged larvae hatch within days, then pass through two nymph stages, which feed on blood, before becoming adults.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger and more often seen. Males are smaller, with mouthparts modified for transferring sperm.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, robber flies and dragonflies take small grassland moths such as this one by day, and bats hunt them at night; parasitic wasps and flies attack the caterpillars. When disturbed the caterpillar is thought to hold itself stiff and straight, like a stem.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have feathery antennae, while females have simple thread-like ones; otherwise the sexes share the same yellow and pink colouring and similar size.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, snakes and small carnivores are likely enemies of adults and nestlings, and trapping for the cage-bird trade has reduced numbers in places. When alarmed it scolds harshly from deep cover and slips away through the undergrowth rather than flying far.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, other mantises and parasitic wasps that lay eggs in its egg cases all take a toll. When threatened it may flare its wings, raise its forelegs and sway to look bigger, or simply rely on camouflage.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are heavier with a broad abdomen that often extends past the wings when full of eggs. Males are slimmer, fly more readily, and have more visible abdominal segments.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Chews the leaves of rice, other cultivated grasses and wild grasses on field banks. Nymphs and adults both feed on foliage, biting ragged notches from leaf edges.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Frogs, birds, spiders and praying mantises take nymphs and adults, and ducks kept in paddies are reported to eat them too. When disturbed it leaps away or slips round to the far side of a stem.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, feeding and moving most in warm sunshine. At night and in cold or wet weather it stays still, clinging to rice leaves and grass stems.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually one generation a year in cooler parts of the range, where the egg stage lasts through winter and adults live a few months. Warmer regions can support two generations a year, so each individual lives less than a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females push the abdomen into moist soil, often in paddy banks, and lay eggs in a frothy pod holding roughly a few dozen eggs. The nymphs dig out, receive no care, and pass through several moults to adulthood over roughly one to two months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are noticeably larger and stouter than males, and the tip of the female's abdomen carries short, pointed egg-laying valves. The smaller male has a blunt, upturned tip to the abdomen.

entries.name: Chinook Salmon
entries.heroTitle: Chinook Salmon — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: It is the largest of the Pacific salmon, known in Alaska and Canada as the king salmon. Fat stored at sea fuels some of the longest salmon runs anywhere: Yukon River fish travel up to about 3,000 kilometres upstream to spawn.

Blue-green to grey back with silver sides at sea
Commonly about 60 to 90 centimetres long, sometimes much larger

analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_pacific. Large, cold rivers and their tributaries on both sides of the North Pacific, spawning in deeper, faster water with coarser gravel than other salmon. At sea it lives in coastal and offshore water, often deeper than other salmon.

whyInteresting: Some young head to sea within months of hatching, while others stay in fresh water for a year or more.
Several runs, including the Sacramento River winter run, are listed as endangered under the US Endangered Species Act.
The species name tshawytscha comes from a local name for the fish in Kamchatka.
Some chinook, known as white kings, have pale flesh because they cannot store the red pigments from their food in their muscle.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: At sea it is mainly a fish-eater, and larger chinook take larger prey: herring, anchovies and sand lance, with squid and krill. In rivers and estuaries the young pick off drifting insects and small crustaceans. Returning spawners eat nothing.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Killer whales, seals, sea lions and sharks hunt it at sea, and one population of killer whales depends heavily on it. Bears and eagles take spawners; fish and birds eat the young. Dams, habitat loss and fishing have caused steep declines.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Counts at fish ladders on large rivers show upstream migrants moving mostly in daylight. Between bouts of travel they rest out of the main current, behind boulders, in eddies or under cut banks.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most spawn at 3 to 5 years old, some as late as 7 or more, and all die soon after spawning.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Chinook eggs are among the largest of any Pacific salmon, and a female typically lays around 3,000 to 7,000 of them, fewer in small fish. She covers each batch with gravel and stays to guard the nest until she dies. Fry emerge in late winter or spring.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Spawning males darken to olive-brown or maroon and grow a hooked jaw with large teeth. Some males, called jacks, return after only one year at sea at a much smaller size.

entries.name: Chital

Dark stripe running along the spine
White throat, belly and underside of the tail
Stags carry slender three-tined antlers
Tail raised to show white when fleeing

whyInteresting: Chital gather beneath trees where grey langurs are feeding to eat the fruit and leaves the monkeys drop, and each species reacts to the other's alarm calls.
Stags shed and regrow their antlers every year but not in step with one another, so some stags in hard antler can be seen in any month.
Stags often rear up on their hind legs to pull down foliage that is out of reach from the ground.
Animals taken abroad for parks and hunting have founded wild herds in Texas, Hawaii and northern Queensland.
The name chital comes from a Hindi word meaning spotted, and the species is also called the axis deer.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, leaves, fruit, and fallen browse.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tigers, leopards, dholes, crocodiles, and humans threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most grazing is done in the early morning and late afternoon, with some feeding after dark. The herd lies up in shade through the midday heat and rests again for part of the night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild animals are thought to live roughly 5 to 10 years, few reaching their teens. Captive chital have lived more than 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually a single fawn, rarely twins, born after a gestation of about seven and a half months. The fawn lies hidden in cover for its first days while the mother feeds nearby, then follows the herd, and is weaned at roughly four to six months.

whyInteresting: In most years very few young crabs survive to come ashore, but in occasional years they emerge from the sea in vast numbers.
Whale sharks gather off Christmas Island around spawning time and are thought to feed on the crab larvae.
During the migration rangers close some roads, and fences, underpasses and a bridge built for crabs steer them safely across others.
Where the crabs are numerous the forest floor stays almost bare of fallen litter, and few seedlings survive beneath the trees.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Introduced yellow crazy ants form supercolonies, spray formic acid and are estimated to have killed ten million or more crabs. Robber crabs take some adults, and vehicles crush many on the roads. Crabs caught in open sun dry out, so migrating animals stop in shade through the hottest hours.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, mainly in damp early mornings and late afternoons. Christmas Island Red Crab rests in forest burrows and moist retreats outside migration windows. In the dry season it stays underground for long periods, the entrance plugged with leaves.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not precisely known. Crabs first breed at about 4 to 5 years old and are thought to live at least 12 years, with some estimates of 20 or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After mating, the female broods up to about 100,000 eggs beneath her abdomen in a damp burrow near the shore for roughly two weeks. The eggs hatch on touching sea water, and the larvae drift for about a month before coming ashore as tiny crabs.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow larger and have bigger claws. Females have a much broader abdomen, which becomes obvious at about three years old and holds the eggs.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Tiny cilia on the plume filaments drive water through them, trapping phytoplankton and fine particles. Food is sorted by size and passed down grooves to the mouth; oversized particles are rejected.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Reef fish nip at exposed plumes. The worm detects passing shadows and changes in water movement, and after a scare it waits a short time before slowly extending the plumes again.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: The plumes stay out to feed through both day and night, and no daily rest period has been described.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Estimates from coral growth around the tubes suggest many live 10 to 30 years or more; exact ages are hard to confirm.

Tilapias are cichlids and are among the most widely farmed fish in the world.
Discus parents feed their newly free-swimming young on a nutritious mucus produced on their skin.
Some small Lake Tanganyika cichlids live and breed inside empty snail shells on the lake bed.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger fish, including other cichlids, and birds such as kingfishers, cormorants, herons and fish eagles take many, and otters and snakes some. They hide among rocks and plants. In Lake Victoria the introduced Nile perch is thought to have eliminated or greatly reduced hundreds of native species.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most are active by day and rest at night close to the bottom or in rock crevices and plant cover, often in paler or duller colours than during daylight.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Many small species live about 3 to 5 years, while larger ones such as the oscar commonly reach 10 to 15 years in aquariums. Wild lifespans are poorly documented for most species.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Parental care is found throughout the family. Substrate spawners lay sticky eggs on rock or leaves and fan and guard them; mouthbrooders, usually the female, carry eggs and fry in the mouth for weeks. Clutches range from roughly a few dozen to over a thousand eggs.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Varies across the family. In many species males are larger and brighter with longer fin tips, and in many species where the female mouthbroods, males bear egg-like spots on the anal fin; in others the sexes look alike, and in a few females are the more colourful.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Nymphs and adults suck phloem sap from stems, twigs and leaves of hundreds of plant species, including grapevine, citrus, maples and roses. Surplus sugar is passed out as sticky honeydew.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders, lacewing larvae, ladybirds, birds and parasitic wasps attack it; in Europe the wasp Neodryinus typhlocybae has been released to control it. Adults escape by jumping or flying off when disturbed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nymphs and adults stay settled on the same stem or leaf underside for long spells while feeding, and adults take flight mostly on warm days. Its night-time activity is undocumented.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults live from about midsummer until autumn, after a nymphal stage of roughly two months. Eggs laid in autumn hatch the following spring, so there is a single generation each year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females push their eggs singly into bark crevices on twigs in late summer and autumn, where they overwinter. Nymphs hatch in late spring and pass through five stages, often feeding in groups; there is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes share the same grey to brownish, waxy wings, and females are slightly larger. They are hard to tell apart without examining the tip of the abdomen.

Ants, including the Argentine ant, tend colonies for their sugary excretions and drive off parasitoids and predators in return.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: The mealybug destroyer ladybird Cryptolaemus montrouzieri, lacewing larvae, hoverfly larvae and parasitoid wasps such as Leptomastix dactylopii and Anagyrus species attack it. Its wax coat repels water and sprays, and ants tending colonies for honeydew drive enemies away.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No distinct daily activity cycle has been described; females and older nymphs stay mostly settled and feeding. It has no true dormancy, but development slows sharply in cold weather, and in cool climates it survives mainly indoors or in greenhouses.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: One generation takes roughly a month in warm conditions and much longer in cool weather. Adult males live only a few days, as they cannot feed.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After mating, a female lays several hundred eggs into a cottony wax sac beneath and behind her body, then dies. Tiny crawlers hatch within about a week and wander to new feeding sites; females pass through three nymphal stages before maturing.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult females are wingless, oval and wax-covered, much like large nymphs. Adult males are tiny, winged and gnat-like, with two long white tail filaments and no working mouthparts.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: A daytime bird that roosts at night among the dense branches of conifers, often close to the trunk.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Many live several years; a banded wild bird has been recorded at about 17 years old.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nesting starts in late winter while snow lies deep. Usually two or three eggs are laid and incubated for about 16 to 18 days; the young fledge at about three weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females wear identical grey, black and white plumage. Males are a little larger on average, with slightly longer bills, but a lone bird cannot be sexed by sight.

entries.name: Click Beetle
entries.heroTitle: Click Beetle — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Most members of this large family are slender, often brown or black beetles, and their larvae, known as wireworms, live in soil or rotting wood. Most adults can throw themselves into the air: a peg under the thorax is braced against the rim of a groove, then slips in with an audible click, snapping the body so that a beetle stranded on its back often lands upright.

Sharp, backward-pointing corners on the plate behind the head
Loose hinge between the front and rear of the body
Short, saw-toothed antennae in many species
Audible click when held or turned over

Almost any land habitat with soil or dead wood, from temperate grassland, farmland and woodland to tropical rainforest. Larvae of most species live in soil, leaf litter or decaying timber; the soil-dwelling wireworms of the genus Agriotes are often most numerous under long-established grassland.

The eyed click beetle of eastern North America carries two large black false eyes ringed with white on its thorax.
About 10,000 species have been described, and their wireworm larvae include some of the most damaging soil pests of potatoes and cereals.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Larvae, called wireworms, feed on roots, seeds and tubers in many soil-living species, while those living in dead wood often prey on other insect larvae. Adults of many species take nectar, pollen, sap or soft leaves, and some eat little.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, shrews, toads, lizards, spiders and ground beetles eat adults, and crows, starlings and moles dig out the larvae. A disturbed adult tucks in its legs, drops and lies still; if seized, the sudden snap of its body can jolt it free.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Many species are nocturnal and come to lights, while others are active on flowers and foliage in daytime sunshine. Inactive adults shelter under bark, in leaf litter, grass tussocks or soil, and some pass the winter there.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Larvae take from one to about five years to develop, depending on species and climate. Adults usually live a few weeks to a few months, though some overwinter and survive most of a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs singly or in small groups in soil, under bark or in rotting wood; crop-pest Agriotes species lay a few dozen to a few hundred. Eggs hatch within a few weeks, the larvae grow through many moults, and pupation takes place in a cell in soil or wood.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look much alike in most species. Females are often slightly larger and broader, and in some species males have longer, more strongly toothed or comb-like antennae.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mornings and late afternoons are its busiest times in hot weather, with a midday rest in shade. Nights are spent in a nest in a rock crevice or burrow, and winter brings long spells of torpor, with some activity reported on mild days.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly documented; most individuals are thought to live only a few years, and few probably exceed five.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike; females are reported to be slightly larger on average.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, feeding in flight. During the breeding season adults, and later the fledged young, roost in the colony's nests at night.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike and cannot be told apart in the field.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males have a bright yellow face and crest. Females have a mostly grey face washed with yellow and keep pale barring under the tail, which young males lose at their first moult.

whyInteresting: Coho introduced to the Great Lakes in the 1960s established a large sport fishery there, kept going partly by continued stocking.
Small early-maturing males called jacks slip in beside spawning pairs and fertilise eggs instead of fighting the large territorial males.
Spawned-out carcasses carry marine nitrogen and phosphorus into streams, feeding insects, bankside trees and the next generation of juveniles.
Coho recognise their home stream largely by smell, a memory imprinted as the young fish leave for the sea.
Several coho populations in California and Oregon are listed as threatened or endangered under United States law.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Young coho pick drifting insects from the current, both aquatic larvae and insects falling from bankside plants. At sea they eat mainly fish such as herring and sand lance, along with shrimp-like crustaceans. Returning adults stop feeding in fresh water.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Trout, sculpins, kingfishers and mergansers take eggs and young; seals, sea lions and killer whales hunt adults at sea, and bears, otters and eagles catch spawners in shallow streams. Juveniles stay close to logs and undercut banks for cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Fish do not sleep as mammals do. Juveniles feed by day and settle into slow water under cover at night; upstream migrants often move in darkness or murky high water and hold in deep pools between runs.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live about three years from egg to spawning, and nearly all die within a few weeks of spawning once.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female digs a gravel nest, or redd, with sweeps of her tail and lays roughly 2,000 to 4,500 eggs in several pockets, guarding the site until she dies. Eggs hatch after about six to eight weeks, and the young stay in the gravel for several more weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: At sea both sexes are silver. Spawning males turn deep red on the sides with a dark greenish back and grow a strongly hooked jaw; females colour less intensely and keep a rounder snout.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Across the tundra, foxes, snowy owls, skuas, weasels, and other Arctic predators threaten Collared Lemming. The snowpack gives cover through winter, and in summer it dives into burrows under rocks and hummocks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It does not hibernate and is active in tunnels and under snow as well as on the surface, depending on season. Activity comes in short bouts around the clock, with rest in grass-lined nests.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: It is often short-lived, commonly one to two years, with survival tied to rapid breeding.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Gestation lasts about three weeks, and a litter usually holds three to five young born in a grass nest. Breeding can continue under the snow, a female may raise several litters in a good year, and young are weaned at about three weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes wear the same coats and change colour at the same time; they cannot be distinguished in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars and pumas are the main natural predators, with coyotes and bobcats taking young in the north; people hunt it widely. A threatened herd usually scatters into dense cover, but a cornered animal will turn and bite.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Usually active in the early morning, late afternoon and evening, resting through the heat of the day. In hot desert summers it becomes largely nocturnal, lying up by day in shade, caves or hollows under banks.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are similar in size and colour, and both carry short, straight canine tusks, so the sexes are hard to tell apart in the field.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike. In breeding plumage the male's black line around the throat and dark area in front of the eye are usually a little stronger than the female's.

It walks on modified fins rather than swimming, and can jet water from its gill openings to move.
The lure is a modified dorsal spine, waved to imitate a small worm or shrimp.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish and crustaceans drawn in by the lure and taken in a single extremely fast strike.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger reef predators, though few take an animal that looks so exactly like sponge. Its answer is disguise so complete that it is rarely recognised as prey at all.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Commerson's Frogfish sit almost motionless day and night, holding position on sponge or rock rather than resting elsewhere.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They live for several years, and because colour change is slow, an individual's appearance records where it has been sitting.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning is in open water, where the eggs are released embedded in a floating jelly-like mass, or raft, that drifts until they hatch. The larvae live in the plankton before settling on the reef as tiny juveniles, and neither parent cares for the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are noticeably larger than males, and swell visibly with eggs before spawning. The size difference is reproductive rather than a display.

entries.name: Common Backswimmer
entries.heroTitle: Common Backswimmer — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Backswimmers are aquatic insects with oar-like hind legs and a reversed swimming posture. They hunt near the water surface, carrying air and striking prey from an angle most pond animals do not use.
identification: Keeled, boat-shaped body about 14 to 16 mm long
Pale back and darker underside, the reverse of most animals
Hind legs fringed with dense swimming hairs
Large eyes wrapping round the sides of the head
Short, pointed beak folded back beneath the head
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe. Still or slow fresh water such as ponds, lake margins, ditches, gravel pits, garden ponds and even cattle troughs, often with open water above submerged plants.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe. Still or slow fresh water such as ponds, lake margins, ditches, gravel pits, garden ponds and even cattle troughs, often with open water above submerged plants.

whyInteresting: Its store of air makes it lighter than water, so it floats back up unless it keeps swimming or clings to a plant.
Flying adults find new ponds by the polarised light reflected from water, detected by the lower part of each eye.
In Britain it is widely known as the greater water boatman.
Its species name, glauca, comes from the Latin for blue-grey.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Hunts aquatic insects and their larvae, mosquito larvae, tadpoles, small fish fry and insects trapped on the surface film, which it detects by the ripples. It grips prey with the front legs and injects saliva that liquefies the tissues before sucking them out.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, frogs, water birds and dragonfly nymphs eat backswimmers. When disturbed they dive and cling to plants, and adults simply fly to another pond. Handled carelessly, they can give a painful stab with the beak.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: There is no known sleep cycle. Between hunts it hangs motionless at the surface, head angled down and legs spread, and it is active day and night; adults can stay active through winter, even under ice.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About a year from egg to death: adults emerge in late summer, overwinter, breed the following spring and die soon after.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In late winter and spring the female cuts slits in submerged plant stems with her ovipositor and inserts the eggs singly. Nymphs hatch after a few weeks and pass through five wingless stages, reaching adulthood in mid to late summer.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in the field. They can be told apart only by the structures at the tip of the abdomen.

entries.name: Common Bed Bug
entries.heroTitle: Common Bed Bug — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Common Bed Bug AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A flat, wingless bug that lives alongside people almost worldwide and feeds only on blood. Adults are about 4 to 7 millimetres long, hide in cracks near sleeping places by day, and emerge at night to feed. Numbers have risen since the 1990s, helped by widespread insecticide resistance.
identification: Flat, oval, reddish-brown body about 4 to 7 millimetres long
Body swells and darkens after a blood meal
Tiny wing pads only; cannot fly
Short, broad head with four-segmented antennae
Nymphs smaller and pale straw-coloured until they feed

whyInteresting: Males mate by traumatic insemination, piercing the female's body wall with a needle-like organ instead of using her genital opening.
Adults can survive for months without feeding, especially in cool conditions.
It is not known to transmit disease to people, although bites can cause itchy welts and heavy infestations disturb sleep.
Its closest relatives feed on bats and birds, and it is thought to have first fed on humans in caves shared with bats.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds only on blood, mainly from humans, but also from bats, birds and other mammals. It pierces the skin with slender mouthparts, feeds for several minutes, then retreats to its hiding place for some days to digest.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few enemies are recorded. House spiders, centipedes, some ants and the masked hunter assassin bug are known to eat it. Its main defence is hiding in narrow cracks, and disturbed bugs release a strong-smelling alarm scent.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal, usually feeding in the hours before dawn. By day it clusters in cracks, seams and crevices near beds. There is no true seasonal dormancy, but in cool conditions it slows down and can survive months without feeding.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults commonly live several months, sometimes about a year, depending on temperature and access to blood meals.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The male mates by piercing the female's abdomen directly. She then lays a few eggs a day, a few hundred over her life, glued in cracks. Nymphs hatch in about one to two weeks and need a blood meal before each of five moults.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a narrower, pointed abdomen tip with a curved mating organ, while females have a broader, rounded abdomen and are slightly larger.

entries.name: Common Blackbird
entries.heroTitle: Common Blackbird — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A thrush that was once a shy woodland bird and has moved into towns across Europe over the last two centuries. The male's song is a slow, fluting warble delivered from a rooftop or treetop, mainly from late winter to midsummer. In cities some males sing at night near street lights.

Tail raised and wings drooped for a moment after landing
Runs or hops across grass, then stops with head tilted
Flicks dead leaves aside noisily under hedges
Flies off low with a loud, rattling alarm call

whyInteresting: Many birds from Scandinavia and northern Europe move south and west for the winter, while most in western Europe stay put all year.
Settlers took it to Australia and New Zealand in the nineteenth century, and it is now common in both.
It is widely regarded as the national bird of Sweden.
Birds with patches of white feathers turn up fairly often, especially in towns.
In mild winters town birds may start nesting weeks earlier than those in woodland.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Worms, insects, berries, and fallen fruit.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Cats, hawks, foxes, snakes, and nest predators threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Among the first birds stirring before sunrise and the last to go to roost. It sleeps in dense shrubs, ivy or evergreens, and birds settling for the night give a persistent 'chink-chink' call. In winter several may share a roost.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically about 3 years in the wild, with many young dying in their first year. Ringed birds have been recorded at more than 14 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female builds a mud-plastered cup of grass and twigs in a hedge, shrub or creeper. She lays 3 to 5 blue-green eggs freckled with reddish brown and incubates them for about two weeks. Chicks fledge after a further two weeks, and two or three broods are usual.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are black with yellow bills; females and juveniles are browner.

entries.name: Common Bream
entries.heroTitle: Common Bream — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Common Bream is a deep sifter, feeding patiently through soft bottoms where small repeated mouthfuls become a whole strategy.
identification: Deep, strongly flattened body that looks thin when seen head-on
Adults bronze-brown; young silvery
Long anal fin with more than 20 soft rays
Fins dark grey, never red as in roach or rudd
Scaleless keel on the belly behind the pelvic fins
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe. Slow lowland rivers, canals, lakes, reservoirs and flooded gravel pits with soft mud bottoms, often in nutrient-rich, murky water across much of Europe, and brackish parts of the Baltic Sea. Adults keep to deeper open water over mud.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe. Slow lowland rivers, canals, lakes, reservoirs and flooded gravel pits with soft mud bottoms, often in nutrient-rich, murky water across much of Europe, and brackish parts of the Baltic Sea. Adults keep to deeper open water over mud.

whyInteresting: Feeding shoals stir clouds of mud and send bubbles to the surface, and dense populations keep lakes so murky that bream are sometimes removed during lake restoration.
It hybridises readily with roach, and the hybrids can be hard to tell from either parent.
Young bream are easily confused with silver bream, which has a larger eye and reddish bases to the paired fins.
The jaws have no teeth; food is ground by pharyngeal teeth in the throat, as in other carp-family fish.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Young fish eat zooplankton. Adults take midge larvae, worms, small snails, mussels and crustaceans, pushing out a tube-like mouth to suck up sediment and sorting food from silt with the gill rakers.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pike, zander, perch and cormorants take young bream; otters, herons and large pike catch adults, and anglers fish for them widely. Dense shoals and the deep body of large adults limit which predators can swallow them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds most actively from dusk into the night and again at dawn, though in murky water shoals also feed through the day. Between feeding bouts they rest quietly in deeper water near the bottom.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly 10 to 15 years in the wild; ages above 20 years have been recorded in slow-growing northern populations.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning happens in late spring and early summer in weedy shallows, often noisily at night. Females shed tens of thousands to several hundred thousand sticky eggs onto plants, with no parental care, and the eggs hatch within about a week.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Outside spawning the sexes look alike. In the breeding season males develop hard white tubercles on the head and body, while females become full-bellied with eggs.

entries.name: Common Brittle Star
entries.heroTitle: Common Brittle Star — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Common Brittle Star AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: Common Brittle Stars use slender arms for crawling, feeding, and retreating into narrow shelter. Many brittle stars can shed damaged arms and regenerate them, making flexible reach and replaceable parts central to survival.
identification: Small disc, usually under 2 cm across, covered in short spines
Five thin arms bristling with long, glassy spines
Arms roughly four to five times the width of the disc
Colour highly variable: red, violet, orange, brown or banded
Crawls by rowing its arms, not on tube feet
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, north_atlantic, mediterranean. Rocky and mixed seabeds from the lower shore into deeper offshore water, especially gravel, shell and boulder ground swept by moderate currents. On parts of the Atlantic coast of Europe it can carpet the bottom in dense beds of many hundreds per square metre.

Rocky and mixed seabeds from the lower shore into deeper offshore water, especially gravel, shell and boulder ground swept by moderate currents. On parts of the Atlantic coast of Europe it can carpet the bottom in dense beds of many hundreds per square metre.

whyInteresting: Brittle stars form their own class, Ophiuroidea, separate from true starfish, with arms sharply set off from the disc.
It has no anus, so undigested waste leaves through the mouth.
Slits beside each arm base on the underside are used both for breathing and for releasing eggs or sperm.
Young brittle stars are often found clinging to the arms of adults in dense beds.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A suspension feeder. It raises two or three arms into the current and traps plankton and drifting organic particles on sticky tube feet and fine spines, then passes the food along the arm to the mouth. It also scavenges small scraps from the seabed.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Bottom-feeding fish, crabs and predatory starfish such as Luidia and Asterias eat it. Its main protection is concealment: the disc stays wedged among stones or tangled neighbours in a bed, with only the arms exposed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: In dense beds it feeds whenever the current runs, day or night. Solitary individuals shelter under stones and in crevices by day and come out more after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Poorly documented in the wild; growth studies suggest a lifespan of several years, probably under about ten.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Separate males and females shed eggs and sperm into open water, often in summer, where fertilisation takes place. The larva, a long-armed ophiopluteus, drifts in the plankton for several weeks before settling as a tiny juvenile. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look the same; sex can only be told from the gonads or when spawning.

entries.name: Common Buzzard
entries.heroTitle: Common Buzzard — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A broad-winged hawk about 50 centimetres long, with plumage that ranges from almost white to dark chocolate brown. Riding rising air over hillsides and fields, it can search a wide area for prey with hardly a wingbeat.
identification: Broad, rounded wings and a short, fanned tail
Wings raised in a shallow V when soaring
Dark wrist patches on a paler underwing
Pale band across the breast in many birds
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, central_asia. Mixed farmland with woods, copses and hedgerows, moorland edges and hilly country with scattered trees, from sea level into the mountains. It nests in woodland but hunts over open grassland and fields.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe, central_asia. Mixed farmland with woods, copses and hedgerows, moorland edges and hilly country with scattered trees, from sea level into the mountains. It nests in woodland but hunts over open grassland and fields.

whyInteresting: UK population estimates now rank it as the most numerous bird of prey in Britain, after it spread back into eastern England from the 1990s.
Birds from Russia and farther east winter as far away as southern Africa, while most Scandinavian birds move only to southern Scandinavia or western Europe.
In spring, pairs perform a rollercoaster display, climbing high then plunging in steep dives.
Eurasian Jays sometimes give a convincing imitation of its mewing call.
Eastern birds belong to a smaller, often rufous-tinged form known as the Steppe Buzzard.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Voles, mice and young rabbits make up much of the diet, with birds, reptiles, frogs, large insects and earthworms; carrion matters in winter. It hunts from perches, by soaring and hovering, and walks fields for worms.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Healthy adults have few natural enemies, though Eagle Owls and Goshawks occasionally kill them and crows mob them constantly. Illegal persecution, poisoned bait and road collisions are the main human threats.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active only by day, busiest from mid-morning into the afternoon. At night it roosts in a tall tree, usually inside woodland within its territory.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically around 8 to 12 years in the wild for birds that survive their first year; ringed birds have been recorded at over 25 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs build or reuse a bulky stick nest in a tree fork or on a crag, often decorated with fresh green leaves. Usually 2 to 4 eggs are incubated for about five weeks, mainly by the female, and chicks fledge at around seven to eight weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage does not differ between the sexes. Females average slightly larger, but sizes overlap and birds can rarely be sexed unless a pair sits side by side.

entries.name: Spectacled Caiman
entries.heroTitle: Spectacled Caiman — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: One of the most widespread and numerous crocodilians in the Americas, this caiman is named for a curved bony ridge between the eyes that looks like the bridge of a pair of spectacles. It copes with disturbed land better than most relatives, settling in cattle ponds, ditches and reservoirs as readily as in rivers and swamps.
identification: Bony ridge across the snout just in front of the eyes
Olive to grey-brown body with dark crossbands on the tail
Juveniles yellowish with bold black bands
Fairly short, broad snout with lower teeth mostly hidden when closed

Slow or still fresh water in the tropical lowlands of southern Mexico, Central America and northern and central South America, including the Magdalena, Orinoco and Amazon basins and the Pacific lowlands of Colombia and Ecuador. It uses marshes, oxbow lakes, flooded savanna, swamp forest and river margins with floating plants, and enters brackish lagoons.

Animals released from the pet trade have established populations in southern Florida and Puerto Rico.
The yacare caiman of the Paraguay basin was once treated as part of this species and is now usually ranked separately.
A flap at the back of the throat seals its airway, so it can open its mouth underwater without drowning.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Juveniles eat insects, snails and small crustaceans; adults add fish, frogs, water birds and small mammals. In the dry season adults gather where fish are trapped in shrinking pools, and small prey is swallowed whole.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tegu lizards and foxes have been recorded raiding nests, and herons, large fish and snakes take hatchlings. Jaguars, anacondas and people hunting for skins and meat kill adults. It submerges quickly, and cornered adults hiss and gape.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hunting happens mostly at night. By day it basks on banks and logs or rests in shallow water, and in severe droughts some animals shelter in mud or burrows and become dormant until rain returns.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is not well documented. It matures slowly, over several years, and captive animals can live for several decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In the wet season the female heaps leaf litter and mud into a nest mound and lays about 15 to 40 eggs, which incubate for roughly 70 to 90 days. She guards the nest, opens it when the young call, and hatchlings stay in groups near her for months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow considerably larger than females, reaching about 2 to 2.5 metres against usually under 1.5 metres, and have heavier, broader heads. Otherwise the sexes look alike.

White band near the edge split by a grey line

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger with black heads, limbs and forebody, and a pale, reddish, yellowish or grey rear body and tail depending on population; females and young are grey-brown with dark crossbands.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sparrowhawks, hobbies and other raptors take adults and young, while squirrels, corvids and mammals raid host nests containing cuckoo eggs. Host birds attack cuckoos near their nests, and a cuckoo usually slips away quietly.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are grey above with a grey chest. Females are similar but usually have a buff, barred wash on the breast, and some are a rufous-brown, barred form. The female's call is a loud, bubbling trill.

The species is a standard laboratory animal for the study of acoustic mate choice for exactly that reason.
Colour is highly variable between individuals, from grey to brown to distinctly green, matching whatever ground they grew up on.

analysis.summary: Among the heaviest of land mammals, with bulls commonly weighing 1,500 kilograms or more, it spends the day almost submerged because its thin outer skin loses water fast and burns in the sun. Glands in the skin ooze a reddish, acidic fluid that screens out ultraviolet light. Its nearest living relatives are whales and dolphins.

Calls made with the nostrils above the surface travel through air and water at once, so submerged animals hear them too.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Lions, crocodiles for young, drought, and humans threaten hippos. Territory protects access to the water they cannot live without.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They rest in water by day and graze mostly at night.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a gestation of about eight months, a cow gives birth to one calf, often in shallow water, and keeps it apart from the herd for its first weeks. Newborns weigh roughly 25 to 50 kilograms, and young calves rest on the mother's back in deep water.

It cannot blink, and cleans the clear scale over each eye by licking it.
Where it has been introduced, in Australia, Hawaii and the Pacific islands, it has pushed native geckos away from lit walls.
The name 'chichak' used across Malaysia and Indonesia copies the sound of its call.
Body colour pales at night and darkens in daylight, which helps a resting gecko match the surface it is on.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Cats, rats, snakes, large spiders, praying mantises and birds such as mynas and shrikes. A seized gecko sheds its tail, which keeps twitching while the animal escapes, and a shorter replacement grows back within weeks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal. It spends the day pressed into cracks, behind picture frames or under roofing and comes out at dusk, staying active through the night wherever a light draws insects.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around five years in the wild and up to eight or more in captivity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay two hard-shelled, round eggs at a time in a crevice or behind furniture, several times a year, and can store sperm for months. Eggs hatch after about six to nine weeks and the young receive no care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are slightly larger with a broader head and a row of pores on the underside of the thighs, and they are the ones that call and fight over feeding spots.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are smaller than females, with a less rounded abdomen, relatively longer legs and swollen palps. A male often lives for a time in a female's web.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active in daylight, especially in sun. At night and in bad weather it rests inside a small silk retreat spun in a crack, under a ledge or in a window frame.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Water fleas, copepods, small worms and insect larvae. Prey brushing a tentacle is paralysed by stinging cells, pulled to the mouth and swallowed whole.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Flatworms, some water snails and small fish eat hydras, and certain ciliates graze on them. Stinging cells deter many attackers, and damaged tissue is quickly regrown.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Although it has no brain, studies of this species found a sleep-like state: recurring periods of reduced movement that respond to some of the same chemicals that affect sleep in other animals.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Individuals in laboratory cultures show little or no sign of ageing and have been kept for many years; lifespan in the wild has not been measured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Most reproduction is asexual: buds grow from the body wall, form tentacles and detach as complete small hydras within a few days. In cold or stressful conditions it forms testes or ovaries, and fertilised eggs develop a tough shell that survives winter.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Non-breeding polyps all look alike. When breeding, testes form as small cones on the upper body and ovaries as larger swellings lower down; strains differ in carrying one or both.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are alike in size, colour and ear tufts, and cannot be told apart at a distance.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It rests near the surface between dives, and its feeding follows the movements of prey rather than a fixed daily pattern. How and when it sleeps has not been studied in detail.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult females are generally larger than males, common in baleen whales. Otherwise the sexes look alike and cannot be told apart at sea without a view of the underside.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds of prey, kingfishers, monitor lizards and domestic cats take them. It sprints into dense cover or under rubbish, and a seized tail can break off and wriggle while the skink escapes.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Strictly active by day. It emerges once the sun reaches the ground, and spends the night and heavy rain in crevices, under logs, stones or roots, or buried in leaf litter.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been well documented for this species, and no reliable age records are available.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry the young internally and give birth to litters of roughly two to eight fully formed babies, which are independent from birth and receive no care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males often have yellow, orange or reddish colouring on the sides of the head and neck and along the flanks, strongest in the breeding season. Females lack this colour and are plainer bronze-brown; both sexes have a dark band along each side.

entries.name: Common Swift
entries.heroTitle: Common Swift — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Sooty brown with a pale throat, it may hardly touch down between one breeding season and the next. Some adults have been shown to stay airborne for about ten months on end, through the journey to Africa and back, and young birds are thought to remain aloft for longer still, until they first breed.
identification: nearly constant flight
crescent wings
cavity nesting
and feeding on airborne insects
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, sub_saharan_africa. Breeds across Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, mainly in holes under roof tiles and eaves of towns, and also in cliffs and old tree holes. It feeds in open sky over any habitat, and winters over sub-Saharan Africa.

whyInteresting: Its scientific name Apus comes from Greek for 'without feet', from the old belief that swifts had none.
On summer evenings, parties of swifts race screaming around rooftops at high speed.
The feet are tiny with four forward-facing toes, built for clinging to walls rather than perching.
A pair collects airborne feathers, seeds and paper scraps to build its nest, cementing them with saliva.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It feeds on small flying insects and aerial plankton caught while flying. Aphids, flies, flying ants and ballooning spiders are taken high up in fine weather and low over water in cool, wet weather.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hobbies hunt swifts on the wing, and falcons, hawks, owls, and predators at nest cavities threaten Common Swift. Their main defence is speed; the loss of nest holes when old buildings are repaired is a bigger threat in many towns.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It is active on the wing through the day and able to sleep in flight during non-breeding periods. At dusk, flocks climb to one or two kilometres before spending the night aloft; breeding adults roost in the nest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Swifts can live for many years, sometimes more than a decade. The oldest ringed birds have reached about 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Each spring, females lay eggs in cavities and both parents bring balls of insects to the chicks. The 2 or 3 eggs are incubated for about 20 days, and the young fly after about 5 to 8 weeks, depending on how much food the weather allows.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are identical in plumage and cannot be told apart in the field.

entries.name: Common Tailorbird

analysis.summary: A small, restless warbler of South and Southeast Asian gardens that sews its nest. It pierces the edges of one or two large living leaves with its bill, pulls spider silk or plant fibre through the holes, and draws the leaves into a pouch that holds a soft cup.

Olive-green back and whitish underparts
Long tail often cocked upright and flicked
Loud, rapidly repeated towit-towit call

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Crows, snakes, cats and rats take eggs and young, and the plaintive cuckoo has been recorded laying its eggs in tailorbird nests. Adults scold loudly and flick their tails at intruders near the nest.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active through the day, busiest in the early morning. At night it roosts on a twig inside dense foliage.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No reliable figures exist for its lifespan in the wild or in captivity.

entries.name: Common Tenrec
entries.heroTitle: Common Tenrec — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Common Tenrecs are flexible island mammals that forage for insects, fruit, and small animals while using cover, torpor, and seasonal timing. Their power is not one trick; it is the ability to shift between hiding, feeding, resting, and defending as conditions change.
identification: No visible tail at the rear of the body
Long, tapering snout with long whiskers
Coarse grey-brown coat mixed with short spines
Crest of longer spines along the nape
Juveniles marked with pale stripes along the back

Juveniles are reported to rub together specialised quills on the back to produce high-pitched sounds, probably to keep in contact.
Its body temperature is low and fluctuates with the surroundings far more than in most placental mammals.
It is the largest living tenrec; big adults can weigh roughly 1.5 to 2.5 kilograms.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly earthworms and other soil invertebrates such as beetle larvae, found by rooting through soil and litter with the snout and whiskers, guided largely by smell. Small frogs, lizards and young rodents are taken when caught.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hunted by the fossa, dogs, birds of prey and snakes, and widely by people for meat. A threatened tenrec raises the spines on its neck, hisses, gapes to show long canine teeth and bucks its head upward at the attacker.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal, spending the day in a burrow. During the cool dry season, roughly May to October, it becomes dormant for several months in a burrow plugged with soil.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Few are thought to survive more than 2 or 3 years in the wild; captive animals are reported to have lived to about 6 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a gestation of about two months, females give birth to very large litters in a burrow, commonly 10 to 20 young and up to 32 recorded. Females have up to about 29 teats, and the young leave the nest within weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look much alike in coat and spines. Breeding females can be recognised by the long double row of teats on the underside; size differences are slight and poorly documented.

entries.name: Common Vampire Bat
entries.heroTitle: Common Vampire Bat — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Common Vampire Bat AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: One of only three bats that live entirely on blood, and the one that feeds mainly on mammals. A bat that misses two or three meals in a row can starve, and roostmates that fed well regurgitate blood to it, most often to relatives and to bats that have fed them before.
identification: A short, pug-like snout with a small, flattened nose pad
Two large, blade-sharp upper front teeth
Long, stout thumbs it uses to walk and jump on the ground
Greyish-brown fur, paler below, and no visible tail

whyInteresting: Heat-sensing pits around the nose let it locate warm blood vessels close to the skin.
Within minutes of starting to feed it passes dilute urine, shedding water weight so it can take off again.
A meal can amount to roughly half the bat's own body weight.
One anticoagulant in its saliva was named draculin.
It spreads rabies to livestock, a serious veterinary problem in parts of Latin America.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Drinks the blood of mammals, today mostly cattle, horses, pigs and other livestock. It lands near a sleeping animal, climbs on, shaves a small patch with its teeth, cuts the skin and laps the blood, which keeps flowing because of anticoagulants in its saliva.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, snakes, carnivores, humans, and failed feeding nights threaten vampire bats; reciprocal sharing buffers hunger risk.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal; bats leave roosts at night to feed and return before day, where social grooming and sharing continue.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Ringed wild bats have lived more than 15 years, and a captive bat has been reported to reach about 29 years; the typical span in the wild is shorter and not well measured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to a single pup and nurse it carefully, while social roostmates may maintain long-term bonds.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though females carry pups and play central roles in nursing and food sharing.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, owls, other birds, rats and domestic cats take it. It flees into cracks and can shed its tail, which wriggles to distract the attacker and later regrows.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly nocturnal in summer, though it often basks in sun at crevice entrances by day, especially in spring and autumn. It shelters in cracks and under bark or stones and is inactive in cold winter spells.

analysis.summary: Stone walls, rock faces and ruins across southern and central Europe are home to this slender, long-tailed lizard. It runs straight up vertical masonry, gripping rough surfaces with the sharp claws on its long toes, as it has no adhesive pads.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects and other small invertebrates: flies, beetles, ants, grasshoppers, caterpillars, spiders and woodlice. It hunts by sight, dashing from a basking spot to seize prey, and occasionally eats soft fruit.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Smooth snakes and whip snakes, kestrels, shrikes, crows, weasels and domestic cats all take them. A threatened lizard bolts for the nearest crack; if seized by the tail it sheds it, and the broken piece goes on twitching while the lizard escapes.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, emerging once the sun reaches its wall and retreating to crevices at night and in the heat of summer afternoons. Winter, from about November to February, is spent dormant in deep cracks, though in the south animals bask on sunny winter days.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating follows spring emergence. Females lay one to three clutches a year, more in the warm south, each of about 2 to 10 eggs, buried in loose soil or under stones.
