fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger-headed and more heavily built, often with bolder markings and blue spots along the edge of the belly. Females are slimmer, with a smaller head and cleaner stripes along the sides.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Flies by day, most actively in warm sunshine. At night and in dull weather it rests with wings closed beneath leaves in shrubs and trees.

analysis.summary: A crustacean only a few millimetres long whose females can breed for generation after generation without males, each brood made of genetically identical daughters. Its genome, published in 2011, was found to contain about 31,000 genes, more than the human genome.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A filter feeder: beating, leaf-like legs draw water through the carapace, and fine bristles sieve out algae, bacteria and organic particles, which are passed forward to the mouth.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Young fish, phantom midge larvae, backswimmers, dragonfly nymphs and hydra all eat it. Chemical cues from phantom midge larvae make young animals grow small spines on the neck, and where fish are present many populations sink to darker water by day.

entries.name: Common Wombat
entries.heroTitle: Common Wombat — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Common Wombat teaches Shelter through a solid body that builds safety downward. Strong claws, low stance, muscular shoulders, cube-like droppings, and deep burrows show refuge made slowly, claw by claw.
identification: Strong claws and shoulders dig extensive burrows in suitable soil.
A tough rear end can block tunnel entrances against threats.
Nocturnal grazing keeps the wombat close to its underground refuge.
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania, tasmania. Open forest, heathland, grassland, alpine slopes, farmland edges, and well-drained soils fit Common Wombats because burrows need diggable ground near grazing.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: australia_oceania, tasmania. Open forest, heathland, grassland, alpine slopes, farmland edges, and well-drained soils fit Common Wombats because burrows need diggable ground near grazing.

whyInteresting: Wombats are famous for cube-shaped droppings, which they often leave on logs and rocks as scent markers.
Their pouches open backward, helping keep dirt away while digging.
Burrows can provide shelter for other animals during heat or fire.
Unlike most marsupials, wombats have teeth that keep growing throughout life, much like a rodent's incisors.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, sedges, roots, bark, and tough plant material.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Dingoes, dogs, Tasmanian devils in some areas, humans, and vehicles can threaten wombats. Burrows, strong bodies, and rear-end blocking behavior protect them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Common Wombats are mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, resting in burrows by day and grazing at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Up to about 15 years in the wild. Captive wombats often pass 20, and one at Ballarat Wildlife Park in Victoria lived to 31.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry a single joey in a backward-facing pouch, then the young continues to use the burrow as it grows. Offspring make downward building essential because safety begins inside the earth.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males may be larger or more territorial.

analysis.summary: The largest pigeon in Europe, a heavy-bodied, long-tailed bird of woods, farmland and towns. In autumn, birds from the north and east of Europe move south-west in huge flocks, and very large numbers cross the western Pyrenees on peak days.

Broad white bar across the wing in flight
Grey body with pinkish-purple breast
Pale yellow eye
Long grey tail with a dark band at the tip

In display flight a male climbs steeply, claps its wings, then glides down.
Millions are shot each year across Europe, making it one of the continent's most hunted birds.
It has become a serious crop pest on farmland in parts of Europe.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Goshawks and peregrines take adults, and foxes catch birds on the ground. Crows, magpies, jays and squirrels raid nests. Flocks take off with a loud clatter of wings that alerts other birds.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. It roosts at night in trees, often in large communal roosts in woodland during winter, and rests in cover through the middle of hot days.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically about 3 years in the wild; British ringing records include birds of more than 15 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A flimsy twig platform in a tree or hedge holds 2 white eggs, incubated by both parents for about 17 days. Both feed the chicks on crop milk, and they fledge at about four to five weeks. Several broods a year are common.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot be reliably told apart in the field.

entries.name: Long-legged Fly
entries.heroTitle: Long-legged Fly — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A small, shining metallic green to blue-green fly of the Americas, standing high on long, slender legs. It belongs to the long-legged flies, the Dolichopodidae, and both adults and larvae are predators of smaller invertebrates.
identification: Bright metallic green to blue-green body
Very long, thin legs
Narrow wings folded flat over the back at rest
Small body, well under a centimetre long
Stands tall with the body raised well off the leaf
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Sunny upper surfaces of leaves on shrubs, tall herbs and low trees in gardens, parks, field edges and woodland margins, often near damp ground, in warm lowland areas of the Americas.

whyInteresting: The family name Dolichopodidae comes from Greek words meaning long foot, after the long legs shared by its members.
Its metallic sheen is structural colour made by the body surface rather than pigment, so the hue shifts between green and blue with the angle of light.
Adults often make short, jerky flights between nearby leaves and quickly return to sunlit perches on the upper surface.
Condylostylus is a large genus with a few hundred described species, most of them found in the tropical Americas.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults catch small soft-bodied insects such as aphids, small flies and mites on leaf surfaces, seizing them with the legs and mouthparts. The larvae live in damp soil or decaying matter and are thought to hunt small invertebrates there.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders, robber flies, dragonflies, lizards and small insect-eating birds are likely predators. It relies on quick reactions, hopping or darting off the leaf as a threat approaches.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, most of all in warm sunshine, when adults hunt and display on sunlit leaves. At night and in dull weather they rest on vegetation. In cooler parts of the range the winter is passed in the immature stages.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult lifespan for Condylostylus longicornis is unpublished; these metallic flies hunt small soft-bodied prey on sunlit leaves.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding of this species is poorly documented. Females are thought to lay eggs in damp soil, mud or decaying plant matter, where the larvae develop and pupate. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are similar in colour. Males have a genital capsule folded under the abdomen tip and, as in related Condylostylus, typically differ in antennae or leg bristles; sexing needs a close look or a lens.

entries.name: Cone-headed Grasshopper
entries.heroTitle: Cone-headed Grasshopper — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: This long, slender grasshopper has a head drawn out into a forward-pointing cone, with flattened, sword-shaped antennae at its tip. Held flat along a grass stem, its green or straw-coloured body becomes almost impossible to pick out from the leaves around it.
identification: Head extended into a long, pointed cone
Flattened, sword-shaped antennae
Long, thin hind legs
Narrow, pointed forewings
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe. Tall, warm grassland across southern Europe, from Mediterranean coasts north into the Hungarian plain: dry meadows, sandy and dune grassland, and rough lowland ground where grasses stand high through late summer. It has also been recorded in damper grassy places.

At the northern edge of its range it is thought to have declined where tall grassland has been lost.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds on grasses, chewing the leaf blades from the edge with strong mandibles.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: An adult that has been noticed is reported to edge round to the far side of its stem, keeping the stem between itself and the threat. The animals that hunt it have not been specifically documented.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day once the sun has warmed the grass, and largely inactive on cool mornings and dull days. It spends the night resting on grass stems within the sward.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About a year from egg to death, most of it spent as an overwintering egg; adults survive a few months from midsummer into autumn.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in pods in the soil in late summer and autumn. The eggs overwinter, and nymphs hatch in late spring, passing through several moults before becoming adult in summer. There is one generation a year.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are far bigger, often around twice the length of males, and heavier-bodied. Both sexes occur in green and brown forms.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grazes fine filamentous algae, cropping the thin turf from rock, rubble and dead coral with small mouth and comb-like teeth. It feeds almost continuously through the day.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predatory reef fish such as jacks, groupers and moray eels, and reef sharks, are its likely predators, and juveniles are vulnerable to many smaller predators. Staying in schools, keeping close to reef cover and fleeing into crevices are its main defences.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At night it stops feeding and shelters in reef crevices and holes, resuming grazing after sunrise.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is not well documented; it is thought to live for several years, possibly more than a decade.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawns in large aggregations, often around dusk, releasing eggs and sperm into open water with no parental care. The larvae drift in the plankton for roughly two months before settling in shallow water.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike and cannot be told apart in the field.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly insects, including beetles, grasshoppers and caterpillars, plus worms and some fruit. It drops from low perches onto prey on the ground or snatches it from foliage.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, owls, snakes and small carnivores take birds and nests, and it slips into dense cover when alarmed. Its biggest threat is trapping for the cage-bird trade, which has emptied many forests in Indonesia.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, including the dim light of early morning and dusk; it roosts alone or in pairs in thick, low cover.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly documented. Captive birds are commonly reported to live 10 years or more, far longer than most probably survive in the wild.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests are built in tree holes or dense cavities, mainly by the female. She lays about 3 to 5 eggs and incubates them for roughly 12 to 15 days; both parents feed the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are glossy blue-black above with a deep orange-chestnut belly and a longer tail. Females are grey-brown where males are black, with a paler buff-orange belly and shorter tail.

whyInteresting: Salmon farms in Norway and Scotland stock corkwing wrasse among their pens to pick sea lice off the salmon.
Like other wrasse, it swims mainly by rowing with its pectoral fins, using the tail for bursts of speed.
Like other wrasse, it has a second set of jaws in the throat whose teeth crush the shells of small crustaceans and molluscs.
Studies suggest that fish from Scandinavian and more southern coasts differ genetically, so moving wrasse between regions for fish farms is a conservation concern.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small crustaceans such as amphipods, isopods and shrimps, along with small molluscs and worms. It picks prey one item at a time from seaweed fronds, rock surfaces and crevices.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Likely predators include larger fish such as pollack, diving seabirds such as shags and cormorants, and seals. It darts into weed or a crevice when threatened.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active only in daylight. At night it rests motionless in a crevice or among seaweed, often lying on its side. In the coldest months it becomes sluggish and is thought to move into deeper water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually about 4 to 6 years in the wild; the oldest fish aged from their scales and ear bones are about 9.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning runs from about May to July. Several females may lay sticky eggs in one male's nest, where he tends them until they hatch after roughly one to two weeks. The larvae drift in the plankton before settling in weedy shallows.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Nest-building males turn bright green or blue in summer, with blue and red lines across the head. Females are mottled brown. Some small males look like females and spawn by slipping into other males' nests.

analysis.summary: At rest this small tortrix moth folds its wings steeply over the body like a roof and sits motionless on stems, dry bracts and dead leaves. In that position its dull, broken pattern passes for a fragment of withered plant.

Thread-like antennae lie back along the wings at rest

whyInteresting: Australian cotton growers know the caterpillar as the cotton tipworm.
A cotton plant that loses its growing tip to a caterpillar often responds by branching into several stems.
On cotton the damage is reported mainly early in the season, while the plants are still young.
In Australia, outbreaks on cotton have been linked to wet winters, which favour the mallow weeds the moth breeds on before the crop is sown.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars tunnel into the shoot tips, flower buds and seed capsules of mallow-family plants, including cotton, hibiscus, tree-mallow and wild mallows, eating the soft tissue inside. What the adult moths feed on is poorly recorded.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Parasitic wasps are known to attack tortrix eggs and caterpillars, and spiders, predatory bugs, birds and bats are likely to take caterpillars or moths. The caterpillar is protected mainly by feeding hidden inside a bud or capsule.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults fly after dark. They spend the day at rest on or near the food plant, while caterpillars feed out of sight at any hour.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults probably live one to two weeks. The cycle from egg to moth is thought to take about a month or a little more in warm weather, and longer in cool seasons.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid singly on shoot tips, buds and young capsules. The caterpillar bores in on hatching and, once fully fed, pupates in a silk cocoon in the damaged bud or in litter below. Several generations follow each year in warm climates.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are similar in size. Forewing pattern is reported to differ between the sexes, but telling them apart takes a close look at the settled moth or a specimen in the hand.

analysis.summary: At about 26 cm and 200 g the Cotton Pygmy Goose is the smallest waterfowl in the world, light enough to feed among floating lily leaves on ponds too choked with vegetation for a larger duck to use at all.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Water lily seeds and shoots, other aquatic plants, and some insects and crustaceans, picked from the surface while swimming among floating leaves. That feeding position is only available to something light enough not to sink the mat.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Marsh harriers and other raptors take adults, and snakes, monitor lizards and crows take eggs from cavities. Dense floating cover is the main defence, and it is very quick into the air.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, resting through the hottest hours on floating vegetation or a low branch, and roosting near or on the water at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around eight to ten years in the wild.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Six to twelve eggs in a tree cavity, sometimes well away from the water. Ducklings jump down and are led to the lily beds within a day of hatching.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Clear in the breeding season: the male has a glossy green-black cap, a dark neck collar and a bold white wing bar. The female is duller, with a dark eye-stripe and a much reduced wing bar.

It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, because its slow breeding leaves populations sensitive to fishing.
It is one of the rays most often kept in public aquarium touch pools, where the tail spine is usually trimmed.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Bivalves make up most of the diet, especially thin-shelled clams, along with crabs, shrimps and burrowing worms. Broken shell is reportedly spat out, with only the soft body swallowed.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large sharks, including bull and great hammerhead sharks, are its main natural predators, and many are caught by fisheries. A serrated, venomous spine near the base of the tail is its defence, backed by fast escape swimming.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Rest behaviour has not been studied in this ray. Schools are seen swimming and feeding in daylight, often close to the surface, and no regular resting site or time is known.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Growth bands in the vertebrae suggest wild rays live to roughly 18 years, perhaps a little more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females bear a single pup, rarely two, after a pregnancy of about 11 to 12 months. The embryo feeds first on yolk and then on nutritious uterine fluid, and pups are born in early summer in shallow bays, already roughly 30 to 45 cm across.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a pair of claspers beside the tail base. Females mature later and reach a slightly larger disc width; colour and shape are otherwise alike.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Unlike many cuckoos, it builds its own nest, a shallow platform of twigs in a tree or tangle, and raises its own young. Clutches are small, with eggs reported as white, and incubation and chick care are poorly documented.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in plumage.

entries.name: Crested Fireback
entries.heroTitle: Crested Fireback — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: This rainforest pheasant courts with sound as well as colour. Like other firebacks, a displaying male is reported to draw himself up and whirr his wings rapidly, making a loud rattle.
identification: Short, bushy crest held upright
Bare blue facial skin around the eye
Coppery-red lower back and rump in males
Scaled black-and-white underparts in females
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Crested Firebacks are native to the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Borneo, and nearby parts of Southeast Asia. They inhabit lowland tropical rainforest, swamp forest, forest floor, and dense primary or mature secondary woodland.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Crested Firebacks are native to the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Borneo, and nearby parts of Southeast Asia. They inhabit lowland tropical rainforest, swamp forest, forest floor, and dense primary or mature secondary woodland.

whyInteresting: Subspecies differ in the colour of the male's flanks and central tail feathers, which may be white or buff.
Males carry sharp spurs on the legs, used in fights with rival males.
At night it roosts off the ground in trees, flying up at dusk.
Clearance of lowland rainforest has led to its listing as Near Threatened.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Scratches through leaf litter for fallen fruit, seeds, termites, worms and other small invertebrates. It feeds on the ground, usually in small groups.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wild cats, snakes and birds of prey are likely predators, especially of chicks. It relies on running away through the undergrowth rather than flying. Snaring and loss of lowland forest are serious threats.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, mainly at dawn and in late afternoon. At night birds fly up to roost on branches above the forest floor.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been documented; ages reached in aviaries are not reliably reported.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding in the wild is poorly documented. The nest is a scrape on the forest floor, and captive hens lay about four to eight creamy eggs, incubated by the female for around three and a half weeks. Chicks follow the hen soon after hatching.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Strongly different. Males are larger and mostly blue-black with a long arched tail; females are rich brown with a shorter crest and tail.

entries.name: Crested Gecko
entries.heroTitle: Crested Gecko — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A tree-living gecko with a fringe of soft spines running from above each eye along the side of the head towards the neck, which gives it the look of heavy eyelashes. The spines are scales, flexible to the touch rather than sharp.
identification: Broad, triangular head with large eyes
Thick body on short, sturdy limbs
Pale stripe along each edge of the back in some animals
Colour ranges from grey and brown to orange or red
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Humid forest in the far south of New Caledonia's main island, Grande Terre, and on the Isle of Pines and some nearby islets. It lives mainly in shrubs, small trees and the lower forest canopy.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Humid forest in the far south of New Caledonia's main island, Grande Terre, and on the Isle of Pines and some nearby islets. It lives mainly in shrubs, small trees and the lower forest canopy.

A dropped tail does not grow back, and many wild adults are reported to be tailless.
Having no eyelids, it cleans and moistens its eyes by licking them with its tongue.
Colour shifts with activity: animals are usually paler when resting by day and darker and richer when active at night.
It is listed as Vulnerable, and the introduced little fire ant is regarded as a serious threat in its forests.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Introduced rats and cats are thought to take many; native birds and the larger New Caledonian giant gecko may take some. New Caledonia has no native predatory land snakes. By day it stays motionless in cover, its mottled colours blending with bark and dead leaves.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Emerges to climb and feed after dark. It spends the day asleep among leaves or in crevices, with its pupils narrowed to thin slits.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 15 to 20 years in captivity. Wild lifespan is not well documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay two soft-shelled eggs at a time and bury them in damp soil or leaf litter, producing several clutches in a season. In captivity eggs hatch after roughly 60 to 120 days, depending on temperature, and the young receive no care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have visible hemipenal bulges and pores.

entries.name: Crimson-fronted Barbet

analysis.summary: Heard far more often than it is seen, this barbet calls loudly from the treetops while its leaf-green plumage blends closely with the foliage. It is found only in Sri Lanka and is brightly marked on the head.

Black stripe through the eye
Stout, heavy bill for its size
Short tail and compact, chunky shape

whyInteresting: The Malabar Barbet of south-western India was once treated as part of this species but is now usually regarded as separate.
Coppersmith Barbets share its gardens in Sri Lanka and are told apart by their red breast patch and streaked underparts.
It is one of two barbets found only in Sri Lanka, the other being the larger Yellow-fronted Barbet.
At about 16 centimetres long, it is noticeably smaller than a common myna.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators of this barbet have not been documented. When disturbed it tends to sit still among the leaves or fly off calling.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Thought to roost at night in tree holes or dense foliage, it spends the day active in the canopy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan has not been documented for this species, and no reliable ages from ringed wild birds or captive birds have been published.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Both birds dig a nest hole in soft, dead wood of a branch or trunk. Clutches are usually two or three white eggs, and both parents share incubation and feeding.

entries.name: Crimson Sunbird
entries.heroTitle: Crimson Sunbird — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A small sunbird of southern and South-east Asia, the male brilliant crimson with a glossy green crown and tail. It feeds at flowers in gardens and forest edge, often perching beside the bloom rather than hovering.
identification: Crimson head, throat, breast and back in the male
Glossy green or violet crown and long tail in the male
Female plain olive above and paler yellowish below
Thin, strongly down-curved bill

Crimson Sunbirds range from the Indian subcontinent and Himalayan foothills through southern China and Southeast Asia to parts of Indonesia. They inhabit tropical and subtropical forest, forest edge, secondary woodland, mangroves, gardens and plantations where flowering shrubs and trees provide nectar and insects.

whyInteresting: The female builds a hanging, pear-shaped nest of plant fibres and cobweb, often with a small porch over the side entrance.
Several subspecies across its wide range differ in the extent of crimson and in the length of the male's tail.
Like many sunbirds, it sometimes pierces the base of long tubular flowers to reach the nectar.
Sunbirds resemble hummingbirds but are not closely related; the likeness comes from convergent evolution.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Nectar from flowers such as hibiscus, banana, coral trees and mistletoes, taken while perched or in brief hovering, plus small insects and spiders picked from foliage or caught in flight.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Small hawks, snakes, crows and other nest-raiding birds and mammals are its main threats, with eggs and chicks most at risk. Adults rely on speed and cover, and pairs call noisily at predators near the nest.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, most busy at flowers in the morning. At night it roosts alone among dense foliage. It does not migrate over most of its range or enter seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Aethopyga siparaja ringing lifespan remains sparse; males of this nectar-feeding sunbird wear scarlet heads across South and Southeast Asia.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nesting is by the female, which builds the suspended nest alone, often low in a shrub or garden plant. She lays usually two or three eggs and incubates them; the male may help feed the chicks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Strongly different: the male is crimson with a glossy green crown and long tail, while the female is dull olive-green with no red and a short tail.

entries.name: Crocodile Icefish
entries.heroTitle: Crocodile Icefish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: An Antarctic icefish whose blood has no haemoglobin, so it looks almost clear and carries only the oxygen dissolved in the plasma. A large heart, a high blood volume and unusually wide capillaries compensate, which works only because water near freezing holds a lot of oxygen.
identification: Long, flattened, crocodile-like snout with a wide mouth
Pale, almost translucent body
Pelvic fins set far forward, under the throat
Two separate dorsal fins, the first short and spiny
Large eyes set high on a long head
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: arctic_antarctic, southern_ocean. High-Antarctic continental-shelf waters, including the Ross and Weddell Seas, where the sea stays close to its freezing point of about minus 1.9 °C all year. It lives on or just above the seabed, mostly from a few tens to several hundred metres deep.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: arctic_antarctic, southern_ocean. High-Antarctic continental-shelf waters, including the Ross and Weddell Seas, where the sea stays close to its freezing point of about minus 1.9 °C all year. whyInteresting: Antifreeze glycoproteins in its body fluids stop ice crystals growing in seawater that sits just below zero degrees.
It has no swim bladder, so it is heavier than water and sinks when it stops swimming.
Its scaleless skin is thought to take up some oxygen directly from the surrounding water.
It belongs to the notothenioid fishes, the group that dominates fish life on the Antarctic continental shelf.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Krill, fish, and small crustaceans.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Weddell seals, penguins and Antarctic toothfish are known predators of icefishes on the Antarctic shelf, though which take this species most often is not well documented, and how it avoids them has not been studied in detail.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: A sit-and-wait fish that spends long periods resting on the seabed between short bursts of activity. Daily activity rhythms have not been studied in detail, and in the polar winter there is little light to set one.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Age data for this species are limited, and no reliable figures for its lifespan have been established.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay comparatively few, large yolky eggs. In the Ross Sea, egg nests on the seabed have been reported guarded by an adult, as in several other icefishes. Development in the cold water is thought to be slow, and the larvae drift in the plankton.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are not well described for this species. Mature males may have a taller first dorsal fin and longer pelvic fins than females, but this is not a reliable way to tell the sexes apart in the field.

entries.name: Crown-of-thorns Starfish
entries.heroTitle: Crown-of-thorns Starfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Crown-of-thorns Starfish feed directly on coral tissue and can damage reefs during population outbreaks. Their many arms, tube feet, stomach-feeding method, and painful spines make them powerful reef pressure points.
identification: Many arms, usually 13 to 20
Body commonly 25 to 35 centimetres across
Upper surface covered in long, sharp spines
Colour variable: purple, blue, red, grey or brown
Broad central disc with relatively short arms

Tropical coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea, on lagoon floors, reef flats and outer slopes, mostly in water shallower than about 30 metres. Young animals live hidden in coral rubble and crevices.

whyInteresting: It is among the largest starfish found on coral reefs.
It is thought to find coral and other crown-of-thorns starfish partly by chemical cues carried in the water.
Estimates suggest a single adult can strip several square metres of living coral in a year.
It has been recorded moving up to around 20 metres in an hour across the reef.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Live hard coral, with a preference for fast-growing branching and table corals such as Acropora. Each meal leaves a patch of bare white skeleton. When coral is scarce it will eat other reef organisms.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: The giant triton snail, humphead wrasse, titan triggerfish, starry pufferfish and harlequin shrimp all eat it, often only in part. It hides under coral by day and can regrow lost arms.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal, sheltering under coral ledges and in crevices by day. During outbreaks, crowded animals feed openly in daylight.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Thought to live up to about 8 years in the wild.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female can release tens of millions of eggs in a summer spawning, synchronised with males nearby. Larvae drift in the plankton for several weeks, then settle and graze coralline algae for months before turning to coral.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look identical from outside. The sexes can be told apart only at spawning, when each releases sperm or eggs, or by examining the gonads.

entries.name: Crystal Red Shrimp
entries.heroTitle: Crystal Red Shrimp — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Crystal Red Shrimp AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A red-and-white freshwater shrimp only 2 to 3 centimetres long, this is an aquarium-bred colour form of a small bee shrimp. The bold banding reportedly came from a red mutation bred in Japan and does not occur in the wild.
identification: Alternating bands of deep red and opaque white
Eyes on short movable stalks at the front of the head
Long antennae and a short pointed rostrum
Tiny fan-like claws on the first two pairs of legs
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: domestic_global. Kept only in aquariums: soft, slightly acidic fresh water at about 20 to 24 °C, with plants, moss, leaf litter and wood that grow the biofilm it grazes.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: domestic_global. Kept only in aquariums: soft, slightly acidic fresh water at about 20 to 24 °C, with plants, moss, leaf litter and wood that grow the biofilm it grazes.

Eyes on short movable stalks at the front of the head
Long antennae and a short pointed rostrum

whyInteresting: Breeders grade the shrimp by how much solid white the body carries, with the whitest animals valued most.
It does best in soft, slightly acidic water and is sensitive to changes in water chemistry.
It interbreeds readily with other bee shrimp colour forms, which is how many newer varieties were produced.
Freshly shed shells are often picked over and eaten, which is thought to return minerals to the shrimp.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grazes biofilm, algae and microorganisms from leaves, wood and stones, picking with tiny brush-tipped claws on its front legs. In aquariums it also eats decaying leaves and prepared food.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: With no wild population, its enemies are aquarium fish: almost any fish large enough will eat adults, and even small ones take the young. Keepers protect colonies with dense moss and shrimp-only tanks, and a startled shrimp shoots backwards with a flick of its tail.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: There is no clear daily rest; it grazes on and off through both day and night, pausing motionless on plants or wood between feeding bouts.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 1.5 to 2 years in aquariums.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female carries commonly 20 to 30 eggs under her abdomen for about a month, fanning them with her swimmerets. They hatch as miniature shrimp with no larval stage and receive no further care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger and deeper-bodied, with a broad lower edge to the abdomen for carrying eggs; developing eggs often show as a pale patch behind the head. Males are smaller and slimmer.

entries.name: Cat Flea
entries.heroTitle: Cat Flea — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A tiny, wingless, blood-feeding insect and the commonest flea on both cats and dogs worldwide. Its flattened body slips between hairs, and an elastic protein pad in the thorax powers jumps many times its own length onto a passing host.
identification: Reddish-brown to dark brown body, about 1 to 3 millimetres long
Body flattened from side to side
Row of dark comb-like spines along the lower edge of the head
Second comb of spines on the rear of the first thoracic segment
Head long and low, with a sloping forehead
Long, powerful hind legs
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: domestic_global. Homes, kennels, catteries and yards where cats and dogs live, and the dens of wild hosts such as foxes, raccoons and opossums. Eggs, larvae and pupae develop off the host in carpets, bedding, sofa crevices and shaded soil.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: domestic_global. Homes, kennels, catteries and yards where cats and dogs live, and the dens of wild hosts such as foxes, raccoons and opossums. Eggs, larvae and pupae develop off the host in carpets, bedding, sofa crevices and shaded soil.

whyInteresting: Females start laying within about two days of their first blood meal and can produce roughly 40 to 50 eggs a day at their peak.
Fully formed adults can wait inside the cocoon for weeks or months, emerging quickly when vibration, warmth or carbon dioxide signal a host nearby.
It carries the tapeworm Dipylidium caninum, which cats and dogs pick up by swallowing infected fleas while grooming.
It can transmit Rickettsia felis, which causes flea-borne spotted fever, and helps spread Bartonella henselae, the cause of cat-scratch disease.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults feed only on blood, piercing the skin of cats, dogs and other mammals, and sometimes biting people. Larvae live off the host and eat organic debris and the dried blood in adult flea droppings.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Grooming by the host kills many adults. Ants, beetles and mites eat eggs and larvae in bedding and carpets. Adults escape by jumping and slipping between hairs, and the tough, smooth body resists crushing.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It has no day-night sleep cycle; adults stay on the host and feed repeatedly. The only resting stage is the fully formed adult in its cocoon, which can wait there until a host is near.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Egg to adult takes about two weeks when warm, months when cool. Adults can live about two months on an ungroomed host, but grooming removes most within a week or two.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females start laying within a day or two of their first blood meal and lay many eggs daily. The smooth eggs fall from the host into bedding and carpets, where larvae feed, moult twice and spin silk cocoons. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger than males. The male's abdomen ends in an upturned tip, while the female's is rounded; the coiled male genitalia can be seen under a microscope.

entries.name: Cuban Hutia

analysis.summary: This stocky, short-tailed rodent is among the largest native land mammals still living in Cuba, often weighing several kilograms. Unlike many hutias of the Caribbean, which are rare or already gone, it remains widespread and locally common, climbing trees and scrambling over rocks with strong, curved claws.

whyInteresting: It is found only in Cuba and on a number of its offshore islands and cays.
Its dangers include owls, boas, feral cats, dogs, and humans.
It is a caviomorph rodent, related more closely to guinea pigs and South American spiny rats than to true rats.
Several subspecies have been described, some of them confined to particular groups of cays off the Cuban coast.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Hutia feeds on leaves, bark, fruit, seeds, roots, and tough local plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: The Cuban boa and owls are its native enemies. Feral dogs and cats, the introduced small Indian mongoose, and people hunting it for meat now add to the pressure. It retreats up trees or into rock crevices when threatened.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hutia rests in tree hollows, rock crevices, caves, and dense island cover. It is seen feeding mostly in the early morning and late afternoon, and several animals often share the same shelter.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot reliably be told apart in the field.

whyInteresting: Solenodons are among the few venomous mammals, and only two solenodon species survive today.
Their lineage is ancient and has survived while many relatives disappeared.
They forage by rooting and probing for invertebrates and small prey.
Cuban Solenodons are rare and threatened by introduced predators and habitat pressure.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Threats include dogs, cats, mongooses, habitat loss, and human pressure. Their defenses are secrecy, nocturnal movement, burrows, odor, and an unusual venomous advantage that makes the old body less helpless than it looks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Emerges after dark to root through leaf litter and soil. The day is spent in a burrow, a rock crevice, a hollow tree or a cave.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Poorly documented, but likely several years in the wild if predation is avoided. The lifespan why is resilience: survival is measured by keeping one rare advantage alive across hostile generations.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females produce small numbers of young, a slow strategy for a rare mammal.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are not strongly visible compared with the shared snout, teeth, and nocturnal toolkit.

entries.name: Cuban Tody
entries.heroTitle: Cuban Tody — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Cuban Tody shows that small does not mean minor. Its bright body and quick hunting turn compactness into charm and precision.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predation has been little studied. Snakes, rats and introduced mongooses are likely raiders of nest tunnels, and small hawks may catch adults; the bird relies on sitting still among the leaves.

analysis.summary: A cuckoo bee of the European spring. Its egg is laid in the nest cell of a mining bee, mainly recorded as Andrena nigroaenea or Andrena nitida, and the young larva uses long curved jaws to kill the host's egg or larva before eating the stored pollen.

Roughly 10 to 13 mm long

whyInteresting: It is so similar to Gooden's nomad bee that the two are usually separated only by examining small details under a lens.
Only the newly hatched larva has the long killing jaws; later larval stages lose them and simply eat the stored pollen.
Male nomad bees are known to give off scents resembling those of their host bees, and this species is thought to share the habit.
Adults are usually reported to appear a little later in spring than their host mining bees, once host nests are being stocked.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults drink nectar from spring flowers such as dandelions and blackthorn, and collect no pollen. Larvae eat the mixture of pollen and nectar that the host bee stocked in its cell.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders and robber flies catch adults. The bold yellow-and-black pattern resembles a wasp's and may deter some predators, and females can sting.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Flies only in warm sunshine during the day. Nights and cool, dull spells are spent clinging to a stem or leaf edge by the jaws alone, a habit typical of nomad bees.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults live for a few weeks in spring. The full life cycle takes one year, most of it spent developing and then overwintering underground in the host's cell.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: There is one generation a year. A female searches nesting banks for host burrows, slips in while the owner is out foraging and inserts each egg into the wall of a cell being stocked, laying in many separate cells.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are usually a little larger than males. As in all bees, males have 13 antenna segments and seven visible abdominal segments, while females have 12 and six and carry a sting.

analysis.summary: Small, heavily armoured wasps, with roughly 3,000 described species worldwide. Their brilliant green, blue, purple and red colours are structural, produced by thin layers in the cuticle that reflect light, so the colour shifts as the viewing angle changes.

whyInteresting: Most cuckoo wasps lay eggs in the nests of solitary bees or wasps, where their larvae eat the host larva or its food store.
When attacked by a host, many species roll into a tight ball protected by their hard, deeply pitted armour.
Most species cannot sting effectively; the female's ovipositor is a telescoping tube used for laying eggs.
Some species, in the subfamily Amiseginae, develop in the eggs of stick insects rather than in bee or wasp nests.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults visit flowers for nectar, often shallow ones such as umbellifers and spurges, and also take honeydew. In many species the larva first kills the host egg or young larva inside the sealed cell, then grows on the host larva or its stored food.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, spiders and robber flies catch adults, and the bees and wasps whose nests they enter bite and sting at them. The thick cuticle turns most stings, and adults escape with quick, darting flight.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active only in warmth and sunshine. On dull days and at night adults shelter in crevices and hollow stems or cling to vegetation.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults of most species live a few weeks. In temperate species the whole life cycle usually takes about a year, with the larva spending winter inside the host's cell.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female lays one egg, or occasionally a few, in each host cell, often while the owner is away. She gives no further care; the larva develops inside the cell, pupates in the host's cocoon and emerges as an adult, often the following season.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in colour and shape, and females are often slightly larger. Telling them apart usually needs a close look at the tip of the abdomen with a hand lens.

analysis.summary: A small, hardy wrasse of the north-west Atlantic, rarely more than about 30 centimetres long, found around rocks, weed and pilings. Unusually for a wrasse, it survives near-freezing winters by sheltering in crevices in a torpid state.

Spawning takes place in summer, and the small buoyant eggs drift in the plankton until they hatch a few days later.
Its closest large relative in the region is the tautog, a heavier wrasse that shares the same rocky coasts.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Picks mussels, barnacles, small crabs, amphipods, worms and other invertebrates off rocks, pilings and weed with its small, strong teeth, and takes fish eggs and scraps.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Cod, striped bass, sculpins and other larger fish take it, along with cormorants, gulls and seals. It relies on its camouflage and stays close to crevices and weed, darting into cover when threatened.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At night it rests motionless in crevices or among weed. In winter, when water falls to about 5 °C or below, it becomes torpid in rock shelters for months.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Reported to live up to about 10 years in the wild.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawns in late spring and summer in shallow coastal water, releasing small floating eggs that drift with the plankton and hatch within a few days. There is no parental care, and juveniles settle among rocks and eelgrass.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are much alike; coloration varies more with background than with sex, and the sexes are not reliably told apart in the field.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a slightly concave lower shell and a longer, thicker tail. Females have a flat lower shell and a short, slim tail.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly fruit plucked from canopy trees with the long bill, then tossed back and swallowed whole. Other aracaris also take insects and occasionally eggs or nestlings, and this species probably does too.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Specific predators are poorly documented. Forest raptors are likely threats to adults, and nest holes may be raided by monkeys and snakes. Groups give loud alarm calls and slip away into dense foliage.

whyInteresting: Horn growth stops each winter and leaves a ring, so a ram's age can be counted from its horns.
Rams settle rank by running at each other and clashing horns, a crack that carries far across mountain valleys.
Denali National Park in Alaska was founded in 1917 largely to protect Dall sheep from market hunting.
The species also includes the Stone sheep of northern British Columbia and southern Yukon, which has a grey to nearly black coat.
Rams and ewes live in separate groups for most of the year and come together for the rut in late autumn.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A grazer and browser of grasses, sedges, lichens, mosses, willows, and alpine plants. In winter it paws through thin snow on wind-blown ridges to reach dried grass and sedge stems. In spring many groups travel to mineral licks to eat salt-rich soil.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves are the main predator of adults, and bears take some; golden eagles, coyotes and wolverines take lambs, and hard winters with deep or crusted snow cause heavy losses. Feeding groups stay within reach of cliffs and run for them at the first alarm.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, it rests on open slopes with visibility, moving between feeding and escape terrain. Nights are spent bedded on ledges or in scraped hollows on steep ground.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Dall sheep can live into their teens. Rams as old as 16 and ewes as old as 19 have been recorded, although a 12-year-old sheep is already considered very old.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After mating in November and December and a gestation of about 170 to 175 days, females give birth to one lamb on safer steep terrain away from predators. Lambs arrive in late May or June, follow the ewe within a day and are weaned by autumn.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are much larger with massive curled horns; females have smaller horns and lead nursery groups. Rams weigh roughly 70 to 110 kilograms and ewes 45 to 60, and ewe horns are short, slender and only slightly curved.

whyInteresting: Unlike the familiar pond snails and ramshorns, which are hermaphrodites, river snails have separate males and females.
It breathes dissolved oxygen through a gill inside the mantle cavity instead of surfacing to breathe air like pond snails.
Females are reported to grow larger than males.
Its genus has a rich fossil record in south-east Europe, where Pliocene lake deposits preserve a famous series of gradually changing shells.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It probably gets much of its food by filtering, as other river snails do: fine particles, including algae and bacteria, are strained from water drawn over the gill, bound in mucus and swallowed.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Bottom-feeding fish, diving ducks and other waterbirds are likely predators, and muskrats are known to eat river snails in some areas. Threatened, the snail pulls its body into the shell and shuts the opening with its hard lid.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Its daily activity has not been studied. Like other river snails it probably grazes and filters over both day and night, and becomes largely inactive in winter, sheltering in bottom mud.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan has not been documented for this species; its slow growth to a large shell suggests individuals live several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Fertilisation is internal. The young are probably released over the warmer months, each a few millimetres long; brood size has not been documented in detail for this species.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: As in other river snails, males have a right tentacle shorter and thicker than the left, used in mating; in females both tentacles are alike. The shells look the same, so the sexes are hard to tell apart in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, snakes and small mammals are likely predators, and the chytrid fungus disease is a serious threat to wild populations. When disturbed it may flip onto its back, showing a black-and-white belly, and lie motionless.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active mainly by day, especially in damp or humid weather, sitting or hopping on the forest floor. Nights and cold or dry spells are spent sheltered under leaf litter, moss or logs.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raccoons, rat snakes and other nest robbers take eggs; hawks and owls take adults and ducklings, and large fish and alligators are reported to take ducklings. Flocks flush together with loud whistling, and adults lead broods into dense cover.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in plumage and size and cannot be told apart reliably in the field. Juveniles are duller, with grey bills and a pale, lightly barred belly.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Almost any green plant: leaves, shoots, flowers, fruit, seeds and bark of wild plants and crops, including millet, sorghum, maize, rice and vegetables. An adult eats roughly its own weight, about 2 grams, each day.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, snakes, spiders and wasps eat hoppers and adults; fly and beetle larvae destroy egg pods, and fungal disease spreads in crowded bands. Solitary locusts rely on camouflage, while in a swarm sheer numbers mean predators remove only a small fraction.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Swarms fly by day. They roost overnight in trees and bushes, bask in the early sun and take off once warm, usually a few hours after sunrise, settling again before dusk. Solitary adults fly mainly at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 3 to 5 months from egg to death, varying with weather: eggs hatch in around 2 weeks, hoppers take 30 to 40 days to become adults, and adults then live a few weeks to a few months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female bores into damp sand and lays a pod of eggs about 10 centimetres down, sealed with froth. Swarming females lay fewer than 80 eggs per pod and solitary females up to about 150, usually in two or three pods. Hoppers moult five or six times.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger than males. Mature swarming males turn bright yellow, while females yellow less strongly. The tip of the female's abdomen carries short, hard valves used for digging the egg hole.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Tubers, bulbs, roots, fungi, worms and insect grubs are dug from the soil, and acorns, fallen fruit, grass, eggs and carrion are taken from the surface. Farm pigs are fed mainly cereals and soya. Low-crowned, bumpy molars crush this mixed food.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Housed farm pigs face little predation. Free-ranging and feral pigs are killed by wolves, bears, large cats, dingoes and dogs, and piglets are taken by foxes and large birds of prey in some regions. Sows guard their litters aggressively, and a startled group bolts with a sharp alarm grunt.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active by day, with peaks in the morning and late afternoon, sleeping through the night in groups lying close together. In hot weather pigs rest in shade or mud through midday; feral pigs often become nocturnal where hunted.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 10 to 15 years, occasionally around 20, when kept as a pet or in a sanctuary. Most farm pigs are slaughtered at five to six months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Gestation lasts about 114 days. A sow builds a nest before giving birth to typically 8 to 14 piglets, and each piglet claims its own teat within days. Farm piglets are weaned at three to four weeks, while natural weaning takes about three months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow larger with tusks in wild-type forms.

entries.name: Domestic Rabbit
entries.heroTitle: Domestic Rabbit — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Domestic Rabbit descends from the European Rabbit and keeps its wild ancestor's senses: long ears that turn independently, eyes set high on the sides of the head, and a nose that twitches many times a second. It is a prey animal that goes on watching while it appears to rest.
identification: Long ears that swivel independently
Eyes set high on the sides of the head
Nose that twitches constantly
Powerful hind legs and a short upturned tail
Front teeth that never stop growing
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: domestic_global. Domestic Rabbits descend from the European Rabbit, whose native range is centred on the Iberian Peninsula and nearby parts of southwestern Europe and North Africa. Domesticated forms are now kept worldwide and occur around homes, farms, gardens, managed grassland and other human environments, while feral populations often favour open grassy ground with suitable soil for burrowing.

The ears carry a dense network of blood vessels and shed heat, which is why breeds from hot climates tend to have larger ears.
A contented rabbit leaps and twists in mid-air, a movement keepers call a binky.
Its teeth grow around two millimetres a week and are worn down only by chewing coarse hay and grass.
All domestic breeds, from the 1 kg Netherland Dwarf to the 7 kg Flemish Giant, come from the single European species.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grass and hay make up most of the diet, with leafy plants, herbs and bark. It re-eats soft droppings produced overnight, which passes food through the gut twice and recovers vitamins and protein made by gut bacteria.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, dogs, cats, stoats, ferrets, hawks and owls. A rabbit freezes first, then bolts in a zigzag for cover, and thumps a hind foot on the ground to warn others.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most active at dawn and dusk. It dozes in short spells through the day and night, often with eyes open, and sleeps deeply only where it feels safe, stretched on its side.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically eight to twelve years as a pet, with small breeds living longest; wild European rabbits rarely reach three.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A doe carries her litter for about 31 days and gives birth to four to twelve blind, hairless kits in a nest lined with fur pulled from her own chest. She nurses them only once or twice a day, and they are weaned at six to eight weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Does are often slightly larger than bucks and many develop a dewlap, a fold of skin under the chin. Bucks have a broader head and mark territory with a scent gland under the chin.

entries.name: Domestic Sheep
entries.heroTitle: Domestic Sheep — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Strongly gregarious, a sheep kept alone becomes visibly stressed, and grazing flock members stay within sight of one another. First kept for meat and skins some 10,000 to 11,000 years ago in south-west Asia, the descendants of wild mouflon were bred for wool only later.

Lanolin, the grease that waterproofs wool, is washed out of fleeces and used in skin creams.
A ewe learns the scent of her lamb within hours of birth and will usually butt away any other lamb that tries to suckle.
Dolly, born in Scotland in 1996, was a sheep and the first mammal cloned from an adult cell.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Dogs, wolves, coyotes, foxes for lambs, disease, and exposure threaten sheep. Grouping reduces individual risk.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Sheep graze by day and rest as a flock, with cycles shaped by safety and weather.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most sheep live about 10 to 12 years in good care, though commercial flocks rarely keep ewes beyond 6 or 7 years; a few have been recorded past 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After about five months' gestation a ewe bears one or two lambs, sometimes three or more depending on breed. Lambs stand within an hour and suckle soon after, and are usually weaned at three to four months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Rams are often larger and may carry heavier horns; ewes carry lambs and sustain the flock.

entries.name: Domestic Turkey
entries.heroTitle: Domestic Turkey — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Descended from wild turkeys domesticated in Mexico more than 2,000 years ago, this heavy farmyard bird forages in loose flocks, each bird lifting its head between pecks. The bare skin of the head and neck shifts between red, blue and white with the bird's state, so alarm shows across the flock at a glance.

Fleshy snood hanging over the bill
Broad tail raised into a fan in display
Bristle-like beard on the male's breast
Plumage white, bronze or black depending on breed

whyInteresting: Spanish ships carried domesticated turkeys from Mexico to Europe in the early 1500s, and colonists later took European-bred birds back to North America.
The snood of a displaying male lengthens and reddens as it fills with blood, then shrinks again when he relaxes.
Broad-breasted commercial strains carry so much breast muscle that males cannot mate naturally, so these flocks are bred by artificial insemination.
Gobbling is a male call; hens keep in touch with clucks, yelps and purrs instead.
The English name probably arose from confusion with guineafowl, which reached Europe through Turkish traders.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Omnivorous. Free-ranging birds graze grass and clover and peck up seeds, fallen fruit, insects, slugs and worms; farmed birds are fed mainly on grain and soya rations. Grit is swallowed to grind food in the gizzard.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, coyotes, dogs, raccoons and mink kill adults and poults, and hawks, owls and crows take chicks and eggs. Birds give sharp alarm calls, bunch together and run; lighter breeds fly up to a perch, but heavy commercial strains cannot.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At dusk birds settle on perches, rails or low branches, or on floor litter in the heaviest strains, and stay put until first light because they see poorly in the dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commercial birds are slaughtered at about three to five months. Heritage breeds kept into old age can reach 5 to 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A hen of a traditional breed lays 8 to 15 eggs in a scrape on the ground and sits for about 28 days. Poults walk and feed themselves within a day of hatching but need brooding for warmth for several weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males, called toms or stags, are much heavier, with a longer snood, larger wattle, leg spurs and a bristly beard on the breast; they strut with the tail fanned. Hens are smaller and plainer and rarely carry a beard.

entries.name: Downy Woodpecker
entries.heroTitle: Downy Woodpecker — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Downy Woodpecker teaches Precision Drumming through small-scale focus. Its compact body lets it work thin branches and smaller trunks, while tapping and drumming help it find hidden insects and communicate through wood. Its lesson is that precision can open spaces that larger force overlooks.
identification: Broad white stripe down the centre of a black back
Bill short, clearly less than the length of the head
Black wings chequered with rows of white spots
White outer tail feathers marked with a few black bars
High, descending whinny call and a sharp 'pik' note
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Open deciduous and mixed woodland, riverside willows and cottonwoods, orchards, parks and wooded gardens, from Alaska and Canada south through most of the United States. It is scarce or absent in the driest south-western deserts and in treeless country.

whyInteresting: It is the smallest woodpecker in the United States and Canada, about 14 to 17 centimetres long.
In winter males tend to feed on thin branches and weed stems while females work larger limbs and trunks.
Outside the breeding season it often travels in mixed flocks with chickadees and nuthatches.
Its plumage closely matches that of the larger hairy woodpecker, although genetic studies show the two are not each other's closest relatives.
Stiff bristle-like feathers over the nostrils keep out wood dust while it excavates.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly insects: wood-boring beetle grubs, ants and caterpillars. In winter it pecks open goldenrod galls for the fly larva inside, and takes berries, acorns, and suet and sunflower seeds at feeders.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: American kestrels, sharp-shinned hawks and Cooper's hawks take adults, while snakes and squirrels rob nest holes. A bird that sees a hawk slips round to the far side of the trunk or flattens itself against the bark and stays still.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Strictly a daytime bird. Each one sleeps alone in a tree cavity, and in autumn it chisels out fresh holes to use as winter roosts.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live only a few years. Banding records include a male that was at least 11 years old when recaptured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Both sexes excavate the nest hole in dead wood, which takes one to three weeks. The clutch is 3 to 8 white eggs, incubated for about 12 days by both parents. Nestlings leave at about three weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a small red patch on the back of the head, which females lack. Recently fledged young of either sex may show red on the crown instead.

analysis.summary: The Dragon Moray teaches threshold power. It does not need to patrol everywhere; it makes its chosen entrance unforgettable.

Hooked jaws that never fully close, exposing fang-like teeth
Orange to reddish-brown body covered in dark-edged white spots

Rocky and coral reefs in warm-temperate and tropical waters of the western and central Pacific, including southern Japan, Taiwan and Hawaii. It usually lives from a few metres down to several tens of metres, sheltering in holes and crevices.

A second set of jaws in its throat shoots forward to grip prey and drag it into the gullet, as in other morays.
Temminck and Schlegel described it scientifically from Japan in 1847, in their Fauna Japonica.
Its colours and rarity mean it often sells for high prices in the aquarium trade.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly small reef fishes, with crustaceans and probably octopus, seized in ambush from a hole or while it roams across the reef.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hardly any predation on this moray has been documented. Sharks, large groupers and bigger morays are the most likely enemies of adults, and an alarmed eel backs into cover rather than fleeing into open water.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Thought to be most active at night, when it leaves its hole to hunt. By day it usually rests in a crevice with only the head showing. No seasonal dormancy is known, and its daily rhythm has not been studied in detail.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Enchelycore pardalis lifespan are not published from otolith or aquarium series; the moray's hooked jaws and spotted pattern mark Indo-Pacific reef crevices.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Reproduction has not been studied in detail. Like other morays it is thought to release eggs into open water, where they hatch into transparent, leaf-shaped larvae that drift before settling on a reef.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes cannot be told apart in the field, and no external differences have been documented.

entries.name: Dragonface Pipefish

analysis.summary: The Dragonface Pipefish teaches aligned subtlety. It survives by becoming a line in the reef rather than a force against it.

Its species name, haematopterus, comes from Greek words meaning blood-red fin.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Picks tiny crustaceans such as copepods and amphipods from the bottom and the water just above it, sucking each one in with a quick snap of its tube-shaped snout.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Which animals prey on it has not been documented, though larger reef fishes probably take some. Its bony rings and thin shape make it an awkward meal, and its markings help it pass unnoticed against rubble.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Forages over the bottom by day. Night-time resting has not been described, though it probably settles among rubble and coral.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No ageing studies have been published for this pipefish, so its lifespan in the wild is unknown.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female transfers her eggs to the male, who carries them glued to a brood area on the underside of his trunk until they hatch. The young are released as tiny drifting larvae and get no further care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are similar in size and colour and are hard to tell apart unless a male is brooding eggs.

analysis.summary: A tiny, furry-winged moth fly of the family Psychodidae, now found in buildings almost worldwide. Its larvae grow in the slimy film lining sink drains, shower traps and sewage systems, which is why adults so often appear on bathroom walls.

Adults are weak fliers, often resting on bathroom walls near their breeding sites.
A female may lay hundreds of eggs on damp sludge around sewage and drainage.
From egg to adult takes roughly three to five weeks under warm, humid conditions.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Larvae feed on bacteria, fungi, algae and decaying organic matter in the gelatinous film inside drains, sewage filters and wet rotting material. Adults feed little, probably sipping liquids.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Its predators have not been studied in detail. House spiders catch adults on walls, and other insects in drains and sewage beds probably eat larvae. The hairy, water-repellent body sheds splashes, and adults escape with a short hop and flutter.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults sit still on walls and ceilings near drains by day and become more active in the evening and at night. Indoors it breeds all year; outdoors activity stops in cold weather.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults usually live about two weeks. In warm conditions the whole cycle from egg to adult can take only two to three weeks.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female lays clusters of tiny eggs, sometimes a hundred or more, on the slime film in drains and other wet organic places. Larvae hatch within a few days and feed for one to two weeks before pupating in the same film. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike to the naked eye. Under a hand lens the male shows clasping organs at the tip of the abdomen, which the female lacks.

entries.heroTitle: Driver Ant — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Driver Ant colonies use pheromone trails, mass recruitment, and aggressive defense to hunt, relocate, and protect the colony. Their power comes from synchronized movement rather than individual strength.

Soldiers with oversized heads and curved, sickle-shaped jaws
Workers have no eyes
Dense, fast-flowing columns several centimetres wide
Soldiers standing along trail edges with jaws raised outward

whyInteresting: A single colony can contain millions of workers, making driver ants among the largest insect societies known.
Winged males, called sausage flies in parts of Africa, are drawn to lights at night and fly off to find other colonies.
People in parts of East Africa have reportedly closed wounds by letting soldiers bite across the cut, then snapping off the bodies.
Households in the path of a raid sometimes leave for a few hours, and the ants clear cockroaches and other pests as they pass.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Earthworms, insects, spiders and other invertebrates make up most of the prey, with occasional small vertebrates that cannot escape. Raiding workers swarm over prey, cut it apart with their jaws and carry the pieces home.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Chimpanzees dip sticks into columns and nests to eat them, and pangolins and some birds also take them. Big soldiers line exposed trails with jaws open, bite hard and hold on, and workers often roof the trail with soil.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: There is no colony-wide rest: raids can run by day or night, though surface activity usually drops in hot sun. Between raids the workers cluster in the underground nest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Workers probably live a few weeks to a few months; queens are thought to live for several years, though exact figures for this species have not been measured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: One wingless queen lays eggs almost continuously, reportedly millions a month in driver ants, and workers tend the larvae and pupae. New colonies form by fission, a daughter queen leaving with part of the workforce.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Workers are sterile females varying greatly in size. The wingless queen is enormous, several centimetres long, and males are large, winged, sausage-shaped insects often drawn to lights at night.

entries.name: Dumbo Octopus
entries.heroTitle: Dumbo Octopus — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Named for the ear-like fins above their eyes, these are among the deepest-living octopuses known, recorded to about 7,000 metres. They swim by flapping the fins and pulsing the webbed arms, and they lack an ink sac, which would be of little use in total darkness.

A U-shaped internal shell remnant supports the fins, a structure most other octopuses have lost.
The genus is usually said to contain more than a dozen species, many known from only a handful of specimens.

The name fuciphagus means seaweed-eating, from an old belief that the nests were made of seaweed.
In some caves, harvesters climb rattan ladders and bamboo poles to collect nests high on the walls.
It is very hard to tell from other small swiftlets in the region by sight; nest type and calls are often more reliable.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Takes small flying insects such as midges, flies, flying ants, winged termites and tiny wasps, snapped up in the bill during long foraging flights. When feeding chicks it gathers many in the throat as a food ball.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Bat hawks and falcons catch swiftlets as they stream in and out of caves at dusk. Cave-dwelling racer snakes climb the walls to take eggs, chicks and roosting adults, and rats and owls hunt around colonies. Adults rely on fast, twisting flight.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It is active by day while feeding, returning to dark roosting or nesting sites. Birds pour out of the colony around dawn and return towards dusk, spending the night clinging to the rock wall or to the nest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan is poorly documented for this species; many small swifts and swiftlets live several years when they survive the risky juvenile stage.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In wild colonies, females lay small clutches in cave nests, often with both parents feeding the chicks. The clutch is usually two white eggs, laid in a nest cup that takes the pair several weeks to build.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In swiftlets, sexes are usually similar, with breeding role differences more visible than plumage differences. Male and female edible-nest swiftlets cannot be told apart in the field.

analysis.summary: Colour changes with age in this small heron of the Americas. First-year birds are entirely white; during their second year they moult into a patchy blue-and-white plumage before becoming fully dark, so one colony can hold birds of three quite different looks.

In high breeding condition adults grow long, loose plumes on the head and back, and the bare facial skin brightens.
After the breeding season young birds disperse widely, and white juveniles turn up well north of the breeding range in late summer.
The species name caerulea is Latin for dark blue, a reference to the adult plumage.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raccoons, crows, grackles, snakes and alligators take eggs and chicks at colonies, and alligators occasionally catch adults. Nesting in mixed heron colonies over water or on islands limits access for mammals, and disturbed birds flee with harsh squawks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At night it roosts communally in trees and shrubs, often on islands or over water, alongside egrets and other herons.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most wild birds probably live only a few years, although banded individuals have been recorded at more than 10 years old.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A clutch of usually 3 to 5 pale blue-green eggs is laid in a stick platform in a shrub or tree. Both parents incubate for about 3 weeks and feed the chicks by regurgitation; young clamber onto branches before flying at about 4 weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the same plumage at every age. Males average slightly larger, but the difference is not useful in the field.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly small fish such as killifish and mosquitofish, with shrimps, crayfish, frogs, tadpoles and aquatic insects. Besides standing still, it may dash through the shallows or open its wings to shade the water while it hunts.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raccoons, fish crows and snakes take eggs and chicks, and a colony can fail once low water or a causeway lets raccoons reach its island. Nesting in dense colonies on islands or over water keeps most mammals out, though storm surges can still wash out low mangrove nests.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It hunts through the day, including the half-light around dawn and dusk. Towards evening, small groups fly in loose lines to mangrove islands and shrubby swamps, where they perch for the night among other wading birds.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Poorly documented: too few banded birds have been recovered to give an average wild lifespan, though recoveries show that some live beyond a decade.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs build a stick nest in mangroves or shrubs within a colony, and the usual clutch is 3 or 4 pale blue-green eggs. Incubation by both parents takes about three weeks, and the young fly at roughly five weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is identical in both sexes. Males are on average a little larger and heavier, which is not visible in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, birds of prey, snakes and cats take bats at roosts and exits. Roosting deep in dark caves keeps them out of reach of most predators. People also fumigate or destroy cave colonies to protect orchards.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Roosts by day in caves, tombs, mines or buildings, hanging in dense clusters that can number thousands. It leaves after dark and returns before dawn.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive bats have lived more than 20 years; wild lifespans are shorter and less well documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually a single pup is born after roughly four months of gestation, sometimes twice a year. The mother carries it at first, then leaves it in the roost; it flies at about two months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are on average larger and heavier than females; otherwise the sexes look similar.
