fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Big eagles, jackals and larger wild cats take some, mainly the young. People shoot, trap and poison it as a threat to poultry and game, and many die on roads. When cornered it raises its coarse coat to look larger, growls, and bolts for dense cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Chiefly active by day, especially in the morning and late afternoon, it lies up through the night. Egyptian Mongoose rests in burrows, reeds, thickets, rock piles, and shaded cover.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly known; in captivity it has lived for about 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a gestation of about 11 weeks, the female gives birth in a den to usually two to four young. The mother does most of the rearing, and the young stay with her into their first year, until they can hunt for themselves.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are somewhat larger and heavier than females; the sexes are alike in colour and markings.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day along the water's edge, resting in shade near the water through the hottest hours. Where it roosts at night has been little studied.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Goshawks and eagle owls kill adults, while crows, martens and cats take eggs and young. Magpies answer with harsh chattering alarm calls and mob intruders in groups. People have long trapped and shot them to protect gamebirds and songbirds.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically around 5 years for birds that reach breeding age; the oldest ringed wild bird on record was over 21.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Both birds build the nest, a mud-lined cup roofed with thorny sticks. The female lays 5 to 8 greenish, brown-speckled eggs in April and incubates them alone for about three weeks while the male feeds her. Young fledge at around four weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females have identical plumage. Males average slightly larger and heavier, but the overlap is wide, so the sexes cannot be reliably separated in the field except by behaviour at the nest.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and chicks are taken by large gulls, crows, foxes and stoats, and adults occasionally by peregrines. Parents mob intruders with loud piping while chicks crouch motionless. In some estuaries, overharvesting of cockles and mussels has caused winter die-offs.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeding follows the tide rather than the clock, so birds work the shore by day and by night. Over high water they pack into dense roosts on shingle spits, saltmarsh or fields, standing on one leg with the bill tucked into the back feathers.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Many adults live about 10 to 15 years; ringed birds have been recorded at more than 40 years, among the oldest known waders.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually 3 eggs, sometimes 2 to 4, laid in a bare scrape and incubated by both parents for about 24 to 27 days. Unlike most waders, the parents bring food to the downy chicks, which fly at around 4 to 5 weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes share the same black-and-white plumage. On average females have a slightly longer bill, but the difference overlaps too much to sex most birds in the field.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in plumage and size. In the breeding season only the male gives the long song, which is the most reliable way to pick him out.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike, which is unusual among sparrows and the quickest way to separate this species from the House Sparrow, whose female is plain brown.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have no regular predator apart from people, who kill them by shooting, poaching and road traffic. Rival packs kill trespassers, and pups can be killed by bears. Wolves avoid people by moving at night and denning in remote cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly active from dusk to dawn in settled landscapes, and more by day in remote country. It lies up through the middle of the day in dense cover, and breeding females use a den in spring.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating falls between January and March and gestation lasts about 63 days. A litter of usually four to six pups is born blind in a den in spring, suckled for six to eight weeks and then fed on regurgitated meat by the whole pack.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and heavier than females, with a broader head; adult males range from about 30 kilograms in southern Europe to over 50 in the north and east. Coat colour does not differ between the sexes.

entries.name: European Eel
entries.heroTitle: European Eel — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A snake-shaped fish that grows up in the rivers, lakes and coasts of Europe and North Africa, then swims roughly 5,000 to 7,000 kilometres back across the Atlantic to breed. Spawning adults have never been observed; its breeding area was located because the smallest larvae ever netted came from the Sargasso Sea.
identification: Long, cylindrical body with slimy skin and tiny embedded scales
Dorsal, tail and anal fins joined in one continuous fringe
Lower jaw projecting slightly beyond the upper
Dorsal fin starting well behind the pectoral fins
Small, rounded pectoral fins just behind the gill opening
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, north_atlantic, mediterranean. Almost any fresh or brackish water linked to the sea: rivers, streams, lakes, ponds, canals, estuaries and coastal lagoons, from Scandinavia and Iceland to the Mediterranean and North Africa. Growing eels favour soft muddy bottoms, stony stretches and dense weed.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, north_atlantic, mediterranean. Almost any fresh or brackish water linked to the sea: rivers, streams, lakes, ponds, canals, estuaries and coastal lagoons, from Scandinavia and Iceland to the Mediterranean and North Africa. Growing eels favour soft muddy bottoms, stony stretches and dense weed.

whyInteresting: Listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN after the numbers of young glass eels reaching Europe collapsed from around 1980.
Eel farms cannot yet breed the species commercially, so they depend on wild-caught glass eels, and illegal export of glass eels to Asia is a major smuggling trade.
On damp nights eels can wriggle short distances over wet grass, reaching ponds not joined to any river.
Its flat, transparent, leaf-shaped larvae look so unlike adults that they were first described as a separate fish.
The mystery of eel reproduction drew many naturalists, among them a young Sigmund Freud, who dissected hundreds of eels searching for testes.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A night-feeding predator and scavenger that hunts largely by smell, taking insect larvae, worms, snails, crayfish, shrimps, small fish and frogs. Some eels develop broad heads and take larger prey, while narrow-headed eels eat mostly small invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Herons, cormorants, otters, pike and larger eels eat small eels. Greater threats are human: glass-eel fishing, dams and weirs, hydropower turbines, pollution and an introduced swim-bladder parasite. A thick coat of slime makes an eel slippery and hard for a predator to hold.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly nocturnal. By day it lies buried in mud or wedged under stones, roots and banks, and in cold winter water it becomes almost dormant.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild eels usually spend about 5 to 20 years in fresh water before their single migration to spawn. Captive eels that never migrated have been recorded living more than 50 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females are thought to release one to several million eggs in the Sargasso Sea and then die, with no parental care. The larvae drift on Atlantic currents towards Europe for perhaps one to three years before turning into transparent glass eels over the continental shelf.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females grow much larger, commonly 60 cm to over a metre, and migrate older; males rarely exceed about 45 cm. Sex is not fixed at hatching, and crowded waters tend to produce more males.

entries.name: European Field Cricket
entries.heroTitle: European Field Cricket — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: European Field Cricket AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: The male European Field Cricket digs a burrow, sits at its mouth and sings for weeks. He never leaves — the song brings females to him, and the burrow means a single step backwards ends any threat.
identification: Glossy black body, 20-26 mm, with a large rounded head
Yellow patch at the base of the forewings
Loud, even, ringing chirp repeated continuously
Sits at the mouth of a burrow in short turf and drops in when approached
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, mediterranean, north_africa_middle_east. Dry, short, well-drained grassland and heath on south-facing slopes with bare patches. Warmth and short turf both matter — the song carries and the burrow stays dry.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe, mediterranean, north_africa_middle_east. Dry, short, well-drained grassland and heath on south-facing slopes with bare patches. Warmth and short turf both matter — the song carries and the burrow stays dry.

whyInteresting: Only males sing, by rubbing a scraper on one forewing across a file on the other, and they can keep it up for hours.
The male holds one burrow for most of his adult life and sings from the entrance rather than searching for mates.
Chirp rate rises predictably with temperature, so the song is effectively a thermometer.
It needs short, well-grazed dry turf, and has declined sharply in Britain and northern Europe as such grassland has been lost.
Nymphs overwinter part-grown in their own small burrows and complete development in spring.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, leaves and some carrion and insect remains, taken within a very short distance of the burrow mouth. Feeding close in is what makes singing from a fixed position survivable at all.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, spiders and parasitoid flies that home in on the song itself. The burrow is the whole defence — a singing male is one step from being underground.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Sings by day and into the evening in warm weather, resting in the burrow overnight and during the hottest part of the afternoon.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About a year in total, with nymphs overwintering part-grown and adults living roughly two months in early summer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females insert eggs singly into soil with a long ovipositor after visiting a singing male. Nymphs dig their own burrows and overwinter part-grown, so the choice of a warm dry slope shapes the whole next generation.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have textured forewings bearing the file and scraper, and sing. Females have smooth forewings, do not sing, and carry a long straight ovipositor at the rear.

entries.name: European Flounder
entries.heroTitle: European Flounder — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: European Flounder accepts the seabed completely, flattening its life around camouflage, mud, and the patient search for bottom prey.
identification: Rows of small bony tubercles along the bases of the fins
Upper side dull brown or olive, often with faint orange spots
Blind side white
Lateral line nearly straight, with a slight curve above the pectoral fin
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, north_atlantic, mediterranean. Coastal seas, estuaries and lagoons of the eastern Atlantic, the Baltic and the Mediterranean, mostly shallower than 50 metres. It tolerates fresh water well and often moves far up rivers.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe, north_atlantic, mediterranean. Coastal seas, estuaries and lagoons of the eastern Atlantic, the Baltic and the Mediterranean, mostly shallower than 50 metres. It tolerates fresh water well and often moves far up rivers.

whyInteresting: Most have both eyes on the right side, but left-eyed fish are far commoner than in plaice or sole, and their share varies widely between populations.
Hybrids between flounder and plaice have been recorded, notably in the Baltic.
On the Solway coast of Scotland, people catch flounders by feeling for them with bare feet in the shallows, a practice called flounder tramping.
Because it lives in estuaries and tolerates pollution, it is used to monitor contaminants in European coastal waters.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Worms, small clams, shrimps, amphipods and other crustaceans, plus small fish. It feeds on the rising tide, moving onto mudflats as they flood.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Cod and other large fish, cormorants, herons, seals and otters take flounders. Its defence is to lie motionless against the bottom and dart away in a cloud of silt if found.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeding follows the tide more than the clock, and much of it happens at night. Between feeds it rests on the bottom, often buried in sediment with only the eyes showing.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live under 10 years; ages of about 15 years have been recorded, and females tend to live longer than males.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Adults move to deeper sea water to spawn in late winter and spring. A female releases hundreds of thousands to about two million floating eggs. Larvae swim upright at first; then one eye moves across the head and they settle in estuaries.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike. Females grow larger and males mature younger and smaller.

entries.name: European Greenfinch
entries.heroTitle: European Greenfinch — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: European Greenfinch is a seed specialist with bright edge confidence, using a strong bill and flock life around hedges, gardens, and trees.
identification: Stout-billed green finch
Bright yellow flash along the wing edge
Yellow patches at the sides of a forked tail
Dark patch between bill and eye, giving a frowning look
Long wheezing 'dzweee' note in spring
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, central_asia. Woodland edges, farmland with tall hedgerows, parks, orchards and gardens, especially where there are dense evergreen shrubs and conifers for nesting.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, central_asia. Woodland edges, farmland with tall hedgerows, parks, orchards and gardens, especially where there are dense evergreen shrubs and conifers for nesting.

whyInteresting: Formerly placed in the genus Carduelis, it now sits in Chloris.
Some northern birds move south and west for the winter, while most western European birds stay put all year.
Pairs often nest in loose groups, with several nests in neighbouring shrubs or along one stretch of hedge.
At busy feeders, birds squabble constantly, lunging at rivals with the bill held open.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds form most of the diet, cracked in the stout bill: dog's mercury, rose hip seeds, bramble and cereal grain, plus buds. At garden feeders it favours sunflower hearts.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sparrowhawks and domestic cats take adults; crows, magpies and squirrels raid nests. Since about 2006 the parasitic disease trichomonosis, spread at feeders, has caused steep declines in Britain. Flocks flee into dense cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At night greenfinches roost in dense evergreens, hedges or ivy, often in communal groups outside the breeding season.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically about 2 years in the wild; ringed birds have exceeded 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females build a cup of twigs and moss in a dense shrub and lay about 4 to 6 eggs, incubating them for roughly 13 days. Both parents feed the young on regurgitated seeds; they fledge after about two weeks, with two broods common.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are olive-green with bright yellow edges to the wings and tail. Females are duller and browner with faint streaking, and juveniles are more heavily streaked.

analysis.summary: European Herring Gull carries Coastal Opportunism through cliffs, harbors, roofs, and tide lines, reading human and marine edges for food and nesting chances.
identification: Pale gray wings
Strong coastal flight
Opportunistic feeding
Loud colony communication

whyInteresting: They nest on cliffs, islands, rooftops, and coastal structures.
They eat fish, shellfish, scraps, eggs, and many other foods.
Gulls can learn from human routines and repeated food sources.
Young birds take several years to gain full adult plumage.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat fish, marine invertebrates, eggs, carrion, refuse, and stolen food. A broad diet lets them exploit tides, fishing activity, and city edges.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, foxes, large gulls, nest disturbance, storms, pollution, and food shortages can threaten adults or chicks. Colonies and loud defense reduce some risks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are diurnal, feeding during daylight and roosting on water, rooftops, beaches, or open ground. Tide and human activity shape daily movement.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Large gulls can live for many years, sometimes decades, if they survive early life. Long learning time supports flexible coastal problem-solving.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs nest in colonies or loose groups and raise chicks that leave the nest area before full flight. Parents defend young aggressively.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger than females, but plumage is similar. Pair behavior, size, and calls often reveal roles more than color.

entries.name: European Hornet
entries.heroTitle: European Hornet — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: European Hornet teaches Night Reach. It is the only large social wasp in its range that keeps hunting after dark, taking a shift no other hornet works.
identification: The largest social wasp in Europe, up to 35 mm
Brown and yellow rather than the black and yellow of smaller wasps
Flies and hunts after dark, often coming to lights
Papery nests built in hollow trees, lofts and wall cavities
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, central_asia, east_asia, north_america. Woodland, parkland and older buildings with cavities, because Night Reach needs both a dark hunting shift and a dry hollow to nest in.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe, central_asia, east_asia, north_america. Woodland, parkland and older buildings with cavities, because Night Reach needs both a dark hunting shift and a dry hollow to nest in.

whyInteresting: It is the only European hornet that regularly forages at night, which is why it turns up at lit windows.
Despite its size it is markedly less aggressive than smaller wasps away from the nest.
A colony lasts a single season; only new queens survive the winter.
It is a major predator of other insects, taking large numbers of flies, wasps and beetles.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Large insects hunted on the wing, plus tree sap and fallen fruit for the adults' own sugar.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, badgers taking nests, and human destruction of colonies. Nesting deep inside a cavity is the defence, leaving a single guarded entrance.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: European Hornets are active by day and unusually far into the night, which is what separates them. Their rhythm stretches the working day at both ends.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: The colony lives one season and the queen a single year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The queen founds the nest alone and raises the first workers herself before laying full time.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Queens are much larger than workers; males appear late in the season and do not sting. The difference structures the entire single-season cycle.

entries.name: European Lobster
entries.heroTitle: European Lobster — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: European Lobster builds its life around shelter, strength, and territory, proving that a protected refuge can become the center of survival.
identification: Dark blue-black shell above, pale yellow underneath
Two claws of unequal size, one noticeably bulkier
Long reddish antennae sweeping forward
Broad segmented tail ending in a fan
Up to about 60 centimetres long, usually much smaller
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, north_atlantic, mediterranean. Rocky seabed with crevices, boulders and ledges it can use as dens, from the lower shore down to about 50 metres, more rarely deeper. It occurs along the eastern Atlantic coast from Norway to Morocco and in the Mediterranean.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe, north_atlantic, mediterranean. Rocky seabed with crevices, boulders and ledges it can use as dens, from the lower shore down to about 50 metres, more rarely deeper. It occurs along the eastern Atlantic coast from Norway to Morocco and in the Mediterranean.

behaviorTraits: Dark blue-black shell above, pale yellow underneath

whyInteresting: Cooking turns the shell red because heat releases the pigment astaxanthin from the protein that holds it blue.
Unlike the American lobster, it has no spines on the underside of its rostrum.
Egg-carrying females are often marked with a V-shaped notch in the tail fan and returned to the sea to protect breeding stock.
Newly settled juveniles hide in burrows and crevices and are so rarely found in the wild that their first years are poorly known.
Adults moult less and less often as they grow, so large lobsters may keep the same shell for a year or more.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Crabs, molluscs, sea urchins, starfish and worms make up most of the diet, with carrion and some algae. It searches by touch and smell on the seabed, crushing shells with one claw and tearing flesh with the other.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larvae and small juveniles are eaten by fish such as cod and wrasse; adults face conger eels, octopus and, above all, commercial fishing with pots. It backs into its den claws first and escapes by flicking its tail to shoot backwards.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly nocturnal. By day it stays in a crevice or dug-out den under a rock, claws at the entrance, and comes out after dark to forage. It becomes much less active in the coldest winter water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Age is hard to measure because moulting sheds the hard parts. Ageing studies suggest individuals can live 30 years or more, and some large lobsters may exceed 50; most in fished areas are caught far younger.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating follows the female's moult, and she stores sperm. She carries several thousand to tens of thousands of eggs under her tail for about 10 to 12 months; the hatched larvae drift in plankton for several weeks before settling on the seabed.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have larger claws and a narrower tail, while females have a broader tail for carrying eggs. The first pair of swimmerets is hard and rigid in males but soft and feathery in females.

entries.name: European Mole Cricket
entries.heroTitle: European Mole Cricket — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: European Mole Cricket AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: European Mole Crickets are burrowing insects built for soil. Their powerful forelegs, tunnels, and night calling make the ground both shelter and sound chamber.
identification: Large brown velvety insect about 4 to 5 centimetres long
Broad, shovel-like front legs with strong digging teeth
Hard, rounded shield covering the front of the body
Short forewings, with folded hindwings reaching past the abdomen
Two long tail filaments at the rear

whyInteresting: Males sing from a specially shaped burrow whose flared opening works like a horn, amplifying the song.
Its broad, shovel-like forelegs dig tunnels through soil, and it spends most of its life underground.
Females guard their eggs and young nymphs in an underground chamber, an unusual level of care among insects.
Adults can fly on warm evenings and can also swim reasonably well when their burrows flood.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Omnivorous: roots, tubers and seedlings, with earthworms, insect larvae and other soil animals caught underground. It feeds while tunnelling just beneath the surface.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Moles, shrews, hedgehogs and birds such as crows and storks take them. It escapes by retreating deep into its burrows and releases a foul-smelling brown fluid when handled.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Spends the day below ground in its burrows. Adults come to the surface after dark, and sometimes fly on warm nights.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: The life cycle usually takes about two years from egg to adult death, with nymphs and adults overwintering deep in the soil.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female digs an underground nest chamber and lays roughly 200 to 300 eggs, which she guards and keeps clean. Nymphs hatch after two to three weeks and stay near her briefly before dispersing.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a ribbed, sound-producing area on the forewings; females have a plainer vein pattern. Both sexes otherwise look similar, and females lack an external egg-laying tube.

entries.name: European Nightjar

analysis.summary: A migrant nightjar that spends the day on the ground or perched lengthwise along a low branch, eyes narrowed to thin slits. It usually settles among leaf litter, heather or fallen wood whose browns and greys match its own plumage.
identification: Long wings and tail with a flat head and tiny bill
Wide gape fringed with stiff bristles
Silent, buoyant, twisting flight at dusk
Pale moustache stripe and a buff line along the folded wing

whyInteresting: The churring song can run for several minutes without a break, switching between two pitches as the bird breathes in and out.
Males display by clapping their wings together above the back in flight.
Birds that breed in Europe spend the winter in Africa south of the Sahara.
The genus name Caprimulgus means goat-milker, from an old belief that these birds sucked milk from goats.
Some studies suggest egg-laying is timed so chicks hatch near the full moon, when parents can hunt longer.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly moths, with beetles such as chafers and dung beetles, caught in flight at dusk and at night. It hunts on the wing or sallies from a perch, and may fly a few kilometres from the nest to feed.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, crows and other corvids, and in places adders and other snakes take eggs and chicks. A flushed adult flutters off low or performs an injury-feigning display to draw danger from the nest.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hunts mainly in the first hours after sunset and before dawn, and more through the night when the moon is bright. Daytime is spent roosting, often at the same few favoured spots day after day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically about four years; ringed birds have been recorded living beyond ten years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: No nest is built: two mottled eggs are laid on bare ground among leaf litter or heather and incubated for about 17 to 18 days. Chicks fly at about two and a half weeks, and pairs often raise a second brood.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males show white spots near the wingtips and white tail corners, obvious in flight; females lack these white markings.

whyInteresting: Perch in Windermere, England, have been trapped and counted every year since the 1940s, one of the longest fish population studies anywhere.
In small, crowded ponds perch often become stunted, with many adults barely reaching hand length.
Schools usually contain fish of similar size, and the biggest perch tend to hunt alone.
It was chosen as the national fish of Finland in a public vote.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Young perch eat zooplankton, then insect larvae and shrimps. Larger fish turn increasingly to other fish, which they chase down by sight.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pike, zander, larger perch, cormorants, herons, grebes and otters all take perch. Young fish shelter in schools and weed beds, and the spiny front fin makes them awkward to swallow.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: A daytime hunter, busiest at dawn and dusk. At night schools break up and fish rest near the bottom or among plants.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly up to about 10 years; a few fish have been aged at over 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning takes place in shallow water in spring. The female lays tens of thousands of eggs, more in large fish, in a long, lace-like gelatinous strand draped over plants or branches; there is no parental care, and the eggs hatch in one to three weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike. Females grow faster and larger, while males mature earlier at a smaller size.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike from outside. Females grow larger and mature several years later than males, but an individual fish cannot be sexed by eye.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, mammals, spiders, parasitoids, weather, and humans can threaten nests or individuals. Group defense and hidden paper nests reduce the risk of losing the whole colony.

entries.name: European Wildcat
entries.heroTitle: European Wildcat — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: European Wildcat teaches Unmixed Line by disappearing in a way almost nothing else does. It is not being hunted out; it is being bred out, absorbed into the domestic cats it can still interbreed with, until the wild animal is a trace in someone else's bloodline.

whyInteresting: Its main threat is not persecution but hybridisation: it interbreeds with domestic cats, and the wild genome thins with every generation.
The Scottish population, known as the Highland tiger, is down to somewhere between 30 and 430 animals and is Critically Endangered nationally.
Felis silvestris grampia, long used as the Scottish wildcat's scientific name, is no longer accepted as a distinct subspecies.
It was never the ancestor of the house cat - that was Felis lybica, the African wildcat, split off as a separate species in 2017.
Kittens raised from birth by people stay wild; the species has resisted taming for as long as anyone has tried.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few natural predators as an adult; kittens are taken by foxes and birds of prey. The real pressure is habitat loss, road traffic, and the domestic and feral cats it interbreeds with rather than competes against.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: European Wildcats are largely nocturnal and crepuscular, lying up by day in rock crevices, hollow trees, dense thicket or old fox and badger earths.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most wild individuals live under 10 years; in captivity wildcats commonly live 12 to 15 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females raise a litter of two to four kittens alone in a well-hidden den, moving them if disturbed.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are noticeably larger and heavier-headed than females, but both sexes carry the same blunt ringed tail. The similarity fits a species identified by its markings rather than by its size.

featuredImage.alt: Evergreen Bagworm Moth AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: Bagworm Moth's power is Case-Worn Patience: portable silk cases covered in leaves, twigs, or debris. In trees and shrubs, this is not a decorative trait; it is how the animal turns case construction into survival. The lesson is specific: use the exact body, rhythm, or tool that your world rewards, instead of forcing a strategy built for somewhere else.
identification: Spindle-shaped silk bag covered in bits of leaves and twigs
Bags hang from twig tips, growing to about 5 centimetres long
Caterpillar pokes a mottled black-and-cream head and legs from the bag
Male moth has a black, furry body and nearly clear wings
Bags often clustered thickly on junipers and arborvitae

whyInteresting: Newly hatched caterpillars can hang from a silk thread and drift on the wind, which is how the species spreads between plants.
Each larva enlarges its bag as it grows and pushes its droppings out through a small opening at the bottom.
Bags are built from whatever plant the larva is feeding on, so bags on a juniper look different from those on a maple.
Heavy infestations can strip junipers and arborvitae so completely that the plants die, because these conifers rarely regrow from bare branches.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It mainly feeds on leaves. This diet is the reason the principle works: the animal's food is reached through case construction, so the lesson is not simply 'eat to live' but 'solve the meal with the exact tool your body has been given.'
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds tear open bags to reach the larvae, and parasitic wasps are major enemies, laying eggs in larvae or pupae inside the case. When disturbed, the caterpillar pulls back into its tough bag and closes the opening.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Caterpillars feed from late spring through summer, carrying their bags as they move; when resting they withdraw inside and hold the bag to a twig. Winter is spent as eggs sealed in the mother's old bag.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: One generation a year. Eggs last through winter, larvae feed for about three months, and adult males survive only a few days.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The wingless female stays inside her bag and releases a scent that draws males, which mate through its lower opening. She lays several hundred to about a thousand eggs in her pupal case, then dies. Caterpillars hatch in late spring and spin tiny bags within hours.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adults differ completely: the male is a small moth with a black, furry body and largely clear wings, while the female is grub-like, without functional wings, legs or eyes, and never leaves her bag.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Killer whales are probably its main natural enemy, and large sharks may take some. Far more are killed by people: hooked on longlines when they take bait and catch, taken in drive hunts in Japan, or entangled in nets.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hunts by night as well as by day, and groups have been followed feeding at all hours. When and how it rests is poorly known, though periods of slow, tightly grouped travel near the surface are thought to include rest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Maximum ages estimated from growth layers in teeth are around 60 years for females and somewhat less for males; typical lifespan in the wild is not well established.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: One calf is born after a pregnancy of about 14 to 16 months and nurses for up to about two years. Females give birth only every several years, and older females appear to stop breeding while living on for years.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow larger, reaching about 6 m against roughly 5 m for females; colour and shape are otherwise alike.

whyInteresting: It belongs to Ptilodactylidae, the toe-winged beetles, a damp-wood family most people never notice.
The fan antennae are not for display to predators. They increase surface area so a male can follow a pheromone plume that would be invisible to a simple thread antenna.
Larvae scrape film and decaying plant matter in permanently wet wood, so the species tracks seepages, swamp edges and waterlogged logs.
Adults come to lights in warm weather and are otherwise sitting still on the underside of a leaf.
serricollis refers to the saw-toothed edge of the thorax, a confirmation mark once you already have the beetle in hand.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults take little or no obvious food in the open; larvae graze decaying plant film in saturated wood. Finding a mate in that quiet habitat is the job the fan antenna was built for.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders and predatory beetles take adults that sit too long on a leaf. Remaining still, and signalling with chemistry rather than motion, is how they keep the loss rate down.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Night-active, coming to lights after dusk, and sitting still on foliage by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults live a few weeks in summer. Larvae may take a year in cold wet wood.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid in or on saturated decaying wood. The larva stays in that wet film until pupation, so a drying log ends the brood.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have the conspicuous fan antennae. Females have shorter, simpler antennae and are found closer to the wet wood.

analysis.summary: The Fancy Guppy teaches Bright Variation through a tiny livebearer whose fins, colours, and patterns turn smallness into attention. Its ornamental tails, quick social movement, and endless colour forms show that variety can be strength when it stays lively and readable. Its lesson is that small differences can keep a whole space awake.

In Trinidad streams above waterfalls, where large predatory fish cannot reach, males are far more colourful than those living below the falls.
Guppies moved to a predator-free stream evolve later maturity and larger young within a few years, one of the fastest cases of evolution watched in the wild.
Females prefer males with rare colour patterns, which keeps many patterns alive in one population.
It has been released in many countries to eat mosquito larvae, with mixed results and harm to native fish.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An omnivore that picks at algae, plant fragments and tiny animals: mosquito larvae, water fleas, worms and insect eggs. Its upturned mouth suits feeding at the surface.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pike cichlids, killifish, prawns, water bugs, kingfishers and herons. Guppies shoal tightly where predators are common, and a few fish swim out to inspect a predator before the group decides to stay or leave.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At night it rests near the bottom or among plants with fins lowered and colours dulled.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are about half the length of females, brightly coloured with long patterned tails, and have a rod-shaped anal fin used in mating. Females are larger and plain silver-grey, with a dark spot near the vent when carrying young.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, especially barn owls, snakes, introduced foxes and feral cats are its main predators. It forages under cover of darkness and shelters by day in soil cracks, under logs and stones, or in grass tussocks.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active at night through the wet season. By day it sleeps in tree hollows, sometimes sharing a hole with its mate and young.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Unusually long for its size: captive animals have been reported to live close to 30 years, and wild individuals have been recorded living more than ten years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating follows emergence from dormancy, and after a gestation of about two months the female gives birth to two or three young in a tree hole. Both parents care for them, and the male often guards the young while the female feeds.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are similar in size and colour and are not easy to tell apart in the field.

whyInteresting: It is usually cited as the world's smallest gliding mammal, with a head and body only about 6.5 to 8 cm long.
Its toe pads have fine ridges that grip smooth surfaces, and captive animals can climb vertical glass.
Outside its own genus, its nearest living relative is the feathertail possum of New Guinea, which has a similar tail but cannot glide.
Since about 2015, northern populations have been treated as a separate species, the narrow-toed feathertail glider.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Its food is nectar, pollen, insects, and small plant exudates. It laps nectar and pollen from eucalypt, banksia and grevillea flowers with a brush-tipped tongue, and licks sap, manna and honeydew from bark.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, snakes, and introduced cats and foxes kill feathertail gliders, and pet cats bring many in from bushland suburbs. It escapes by darting fast along branches or launching into a glide to another tree.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Strictly nocturnal, resting by day in nests or hollows, sometimes in groups. Nests of dry leaves fill small hollows, and in cold weather or when food is short it can drop into torpor for hours or days.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild animals have been recorded living about 5 years, and captive ones somewhat longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding females raise tiny pouch young that later shelter in nests. A litter usually has three or four young, which leave the pouch at about two months and stay in the nest a further month or so; a second litter can follow soon after.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are broadly similar, with the tail and glide design shared. Only females have a pouch, and males are not noticeably larger.

Some species build mud chimneys or hoods beside the burrow entrance, and females are drawn to males with these structures.
A male that loses his big claw grows a replacement that can look as large but is weaker, and rivals are often bluffed.
Their shell colour changes on a daily cycle, darkening by day and paling at night under the control of an internal clock.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Shorebirds, herons, gulls, raccoons, fish and larger crabs eat them. At a passing shadow or sudden movement the whole colony dashes underground, each crab usually running to its own burrow.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Activity follows the tides: crabs emerge to feed and display on exposed mud at low tide, mostly by day, then retreat into their burrows and plug the entrance as the water returns.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most species are thought to live about 1 to 3 years in the wild.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females mate at or in a burrow and carry thousands of eggs under the abdomen for about two weeks. The larvae are released into the water, often on night-time high tides, and drift as plankton for weeks before settling.

analysis.summary: The Two-spotted Cricket is a glossy black field cricket about 3 cm long, named for the pale yellow spot at the base of each forewing. Males sing by drawing a toothed vein on one wing across a scraper on the other, and listen with ears on their front legs.

whyInteresting: Its ears are thin membranes on the front legs just below the knee, linked by an air tube that helps it tell which side a sound comes from.
Chirp rate rises with temperature, because the wing muscles work faster when warm.
Males have three songs: a loud calling song, a softer courtship song at close range, and a sharp song used when fighting another male.
It is one of the most widely farmed insects, raised as food for pet reptiles and increasingly as food for people.
Two hair-covered tail filaments detect the rush of air ahead of a striking predator and trigger a jump within a fraction of a second.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An omnivore that eats seeds, seedlings, fallen fruit, leaves and fungi, along with dead insects and smaller live ones. It will eat its own shed skin and, when crowded or short of protein, other crickets.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, frogs, toads, spiders, shrews, mice and bats, and parasitic flies that track singing males by sound. A male falls silent the moment he senses footsteps or moving air.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hides under cover through the day and becomes active at dusk. Males sing mainly from early evening into the night, and singing slows as the air cools.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About two to three months as an adult, after six to eight weeks as a nymph; it breeds year-round in warm conditions and has no overwintering stage.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female pushes her long egg-laying tube into damp soil and lays eggs singly, several hundred to more than a thousand over her life. Nymphs hatch in about two weeks looking like small wingless adults and moult eight to ten times.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Only males sing, and their forewings are crinkled with the veins that make sound. Females have smooth wings and a long needle-like egg-laying tube between the two tail filaments.

During the twentieth century its breeding range spread west and south into central Europe.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sparrowhawks, goshawks and other raptors take adults; crows, magpies, jays and squirrels raid nests. Breeding birds dive at nest raiders with harsh calls and spatter them with droppings, which can foul the plumage of attacking crows and birds of prey.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. In winter, flocks gather at dusk to roost communally in thick hedges, scrub, young conifer plantations and, it is reported, sometimes on the ground in open fields.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live only two to three years in the wild; ringing records show a few birds surviving well beyond ten years.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look very similar. Males tend to have a cleaner grey crown with blacker streaking and slightly richer colours, but most birds cannot be sexed reliably in the field.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It feeds on krill, copepods, and schooling fish taken in large lunge-feeding passes. Krill dominate in the Southern Hemisphere, while North Atlantic whales also take herring, capelin and sand eels; feeding dives commonly reach about 100 to 200 metres.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Orcas attack calves and occasionally adults, and an adult's main defence is speed. Industrial whaling killed hundreds of thousands in the twentieth century; today ship strikes, entanglement and ocean noise are the main threats.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are usually slightly larger than males. The sexes otherwise look alike, though only males produce the loud, regular patterned song.

It is widely used in research on heat tolerance, because life on the shore exposes it to sharp temperature swings at low tide.
Its broad claws are not used to catch food and are thought to serve mainly in pushing and sparring contests with neighbours over space.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, shore crabs and shorebirds are likely predators. It escapes by scuttling sideways into crevices, and a seized claw or leg is readily shed and later regrown.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Activity follows the tides: it feeds when submerged and shelters motionless under rocks when the tide is out.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry clusters of eggs under the folded tail flap, typically for several weeks. The larvae hatch into the plankton, bearing very long spines, and later settle on the shore.

whyInteresting: It is the one large North American catfish that hunts live prey almost exclusively and largely ignores carrion.

Where it has been introduced outside the Mississippi basin it has emptied whole rivers of native fish.
Anglers call it mudcat, shovelhead and appaloosa catfish depending on the state.
Males clear a nest cavity and guard the eggs, fanning them until they hatch.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Live fish, taken whole at night — sunfish, shad, carp and smaller catfish, with crayfish when young.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have almost no predators beyond people; young are taken by larger fish, wading birds and turtles. Their defence is depth, cover and locking sharp pectoral and dorsal spines outward.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal. It spends the day motionless under cover and moves into shallower water to hunt after dark, which is why it is caught far more often at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Flathead Catfish can live more than 20 years, long enough for one fish to hold and defend the same deep-water lie season after season.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female lays her eggs in a cavity the male has cleared, and he stays to guard and fan the clutch. Fry shoal together in the shallows before dispersing to find lies of their own.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike, with males distinguishable mainly when guarding a nest. Both hunt the same way and hold the same kind of cover.

analysis.summary: A torpedo-shaped, silvery grey fish of warm and temperate coasts worldwide, usually 30 to 60 centimetres long. It grazes fine mud and algae rather than hunting, and moves freely between the sea, estuaries and fresh water.

Flathead Grey Mullet have an exceptionally broad natural distribution through tropical, subtropical and temperate coastal waters around much of the world. They inhabit estuaries, lagoons, river mouths, harbours and shallow coastal seas, frequently moving between marine, brackish and freshwater environments and feeding over sand or mud bottoms.

whyInteresting: Mullet often leap clear of the water, singly or in whole shoals, and the reason for this behaviour is still debated.
Adults gather in large shoals and move offshore to spawn at sea; the tiny young then drift back into estuaries and lagoons.
A thick-walled, gizzard-like stomach grinds the sand and mud it swallows, helping to break up algae and detritus.
Its salted, dried roe is prized as a delicacy, known as bottarga in Italy and karasumi in Japan.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults suck up detritus, diatoms, microalgae and small invertebrates from mud and surfaces, straining them through fine gill rakers. Young fish feed on zooplankton.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Dolphins, sharks and large fish such as bluefish take mullet, and ospreys, pelicans, herons and cormorants catch them near the surface. People fish heavily for the flesh and the roe. Schools scatter and leap clear of the water.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active in schools mainly by day, and sometimes feeds at night. How it rests is not well documented. There is no dormancy, though in cooler waters fish move to deeper water in winter.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live fewer than about 10 years; fish aged to around 16 years have been reported.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Adults move offshore in autumn and winter to spawn in large schools. A female releases hundreds of thousands to a few million floating eggs, and there is no parental care. Young fish drift inshore and grow up in estuaries and lagoons.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike, though females grow slightly larger. The sexes cannot be told apart in the field.

entries.name: Florida Scrub-Jay

analysis.summary: Found nowhere but Florida, this crestless blue jay lives in family groups on year-round territories. Grown young often stay home for a year or more, helping their parents guard the territory and feed new nestlings, and a son may eventually inherit part of the land.
identification: Blue head, wings and tail with no crest
Plain grey-brown back and shoulders
Whitish forehead and pale throat
Blue-grey band across the upper breast
Long, fairly slender tail

It has been listed as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act since 1987.
Families at Archbold Biological Station have been followed since 1969, one of the longest continuous studies of any bird.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects such as grasshoppers and caterpillars, spiders, small lizards, frogs, snakes and mice, and bird eggs make up much of the summer diet. Acorns dominate in autumn and winter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Cooper's hawks, sharp-shinned hawks and other hawks take adults; snakes, such as coachwhips and rat snakes, raid nests. Families give alarm calls and mob snakes together. Habitat loss and missing fire are the main threats.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Each bird spends the night hidden in dense oak foliage within its home territory, becoming active again at dawn.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live only a few years, but ringed birds in long-term studies have survived for more than a decade.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually 3 or 4 eggs are laid in spring in a twig cup set in a low oak; only the female incubates, for about 18 days. Parents and helpers feed the nestlings, which leave the nest at around two and a half weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike, though males are slightly larger. Only females give a distinctive rapid hiccup call.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Red-tailed hawks, great horned owls, bobcats, foxes, coyotes and dogs take fox squirrels, snakes raid nests, and people hunt them. A threatened squirrel slips round to the far side of a trunk or climbs high, chattering and flicking its tail.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, tending to start later in the morning than many squirrels. Nights, storms and hard cold are spent in a leafy drey high in a tree fork or in a tree cavity.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most wild fox squirrels live fewer than about 5 years, and many die in their first year; exceptionally, wild animals have passed 10.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating chases happen in midwinter and early summer. After about 45 days' gestation the female bears usually two to four young in a drey or cavity and raises them alone; their eyes open at about five weeks and they are weaned at roughly three months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in colour, pattern and size and are hard to tell apart at a distance; nursing females show visible teats on the belly.

whyInteresting: Development is direct: there is no free-swimming marine larval stage at all, which is the defining break from their coastal relatives.
Females carry the young under the abdomen after hatching, sometimes for weeks, before releasing them as functional crabs.
Many species dig burrows into banks and can survive out of water for long periods in humid conditions.
Because young cannot disperse by sea, populations are often confined to a single catchment or hill range — a large share of described species are threatened for that reason.
Freshwater crabs have evolved independently more than once, so the group as a whole is defined by habitat and life history rather than by a single ancestor.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Omnivorous scavenging — leaf litter, algae, snails, insect larvae and carrion, taken at night from the streambed and bank. A generalist diet is what makes a single small catchment enough to live in.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Otters, water birds, monitor lizards, snakes and larger fish. Burrows, hard carapace and nocturnal habits do the defending, and the mother's carrying of the young removes the most vulnerable stage from open water entirely.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Largely nocturnal, sheltering under stones or in burrows through the day and emerging to forage after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Several years for most species, with slow growth and relatively few young per brood compared with marine crabs.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Small clutches of large yolk-rich eggs, carried under the female's abdomen and hatching directly into miniature crabs that she continues to carry. Investment per offspring is high and the number is low, the opposite of the marine pattern.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males typically have a narrow triangular abdominal flap and larger claws; females have a broad rounded flap for holding eggs and young.

entries.name: Freshwater Crayfish
entries.heroTitle: Freshwater Crayfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Freshwater relatives of lobsters, armoured in a jointed shell and carrying a pair of large claws, which live on the beds of streams, rivers, lakes and ponds. Escape is a reflex, not a choice: a sudden touch fires giant nerve fibres running the length of the body, and the tail muscles contract within a few hundredths of a second.

Many species need clean, well-oxygenated water; others, such as swamp and pond species, tolerate still, muddy water. Some dig burrows in wet ground well away from open water. Diversity is highest in the south-eastern United States and south-eastern Australia.

whyInteresting: Before moulting, a crayfish stores calcium in two stony discs in its stomach, called gastroliths, then reabsorbs it to harden the new shell.
The giant freshwater crayfish of Tasmania is the largest freshwater invertebrate in the world, with old records of animals weighing about five kilograms.
A lost claw or leg regrows over the following moults, though the replacement is often smaller than the original.
Crayfish plague, a water mould carried by North American species, has wiped out many populations of Europe's native crayfish.
More than 600 species are known, and over half of them are native to North America.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Omnivorous scavengers and grazers. They shred dead leaves and water plants, scrape algae, catch snails, worms, insect larvae, tadpoles and small fish, and eat carrion. Food is held in the claws and passed to the mouthparts by the smaller pincered legs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Otters, mink, raccoons, herons, eels, trout, bass and other large fish eat them, and they are most vulnerable just after moulting, when the new shell is soft. Defences are hiding under cover, raised claws and a rapid tail-flip away from danger.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal. By day they shelter under stones, among roots or in burrows, and come out after dusk to feed. In cold water they become sluggish and may stay in their refuges for much of the winter.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Small species live about 2 to 4 years and many stream and river species 5 to 10 or more. The giant Tasmanian crayfish may live for several decades, possibly up to about 60 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After mating the female glues her eggs, from a few dozen to several hundred, to the swimmerets under her abdomen and carries them for weeks or months. Hatchlings resemble tiny adults and cling to her through their first moults before dispersing.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males generally have larger claws and a narrower abdomen; females have a broader abdomen for carrying eggs. In northern-hemisphere species the male's first swimmerets are hardened into rods used to transfer sperm.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Filter-feeding matters because the animal does not chase abundance; it receives tiny particles again and again. The diet explains why slow strength is built from repetition, not dramatic conquest.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators and humans matter because a quiet shell can survive natural danger for years yet be undone quickly by harvesting, pollution, or habitat damage. The defense is strong, but not invincible.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It has no human-like sleep rhythm; its pause is metabolic quiet, valve closure, and low-energy filtering.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Longevity is the whole point: decades or even centuries in related species make the shell a record of restraint. Time is not just survived; it becomes structure.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females release eggs into water or depend on host-fish stages in mussels, showing why reproduction needs the whole system to be healthy, not just one strong individual.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are usually not visually dramatic.

analysis.summary: The Fruit Bat teaches Renewal through night flight that spreads seeds, pollen, and future forest. Its fruit diet, wide travel, hanging roosts, and pollination or seed-dispersal work show that influence can happen after the animal has already moved on. Most roost in trees; some species roost in caves, rock clefts or under palm fronds.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pythons and other snakes, owls, eagles, monitor lizards and small carnivores take bats at roosts, and people hunt the larger species. Colonies take flight or shift noisily when disturbed, and roosting in large groups gives early warning.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active from dusk through the night, though a few island species also feed by day. They rest through daylight hanging from branches or in caves, many in colonies; small species often roost alone in foliage.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Varies with size: small species typically live a few years to about ten in the wild, while large flying foxes may reach 15 to 20; captive animals have lived over 30.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Most species bear a single young, once or sometimes twice a year, after a pregnancy of roughly four to six months. The young clings to the mother at first, then is left at the roost while she feeds, and flies at about two to three months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In many species males are larger, with bigger heads and canines. Males of epauletted fruit bats carry white shoulder tufts that they fluff out when displaying; in others the sexes look similar.

whyInteresting: Egg to reproductive adult takes about ten days at 25 degrees Celsius, and one female lays several hundred eggs.

It is drawn to fermentation rather than to fruit as such — the cue is the alcohol and acetic acid of rot, not sugar.
Larvae tolerate ethanol concentrations that kill most insects, which effectively reserves rotting fruit for them.
Roughly three quarters of known human disease genes have a recognisable counterpart in its genome.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders, predatory mites, parasitoid wasps and ants. There is no defence to speak of — the answer to being eaten is simply to have already reproduced.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Shows genuine sleep, with consolidated rest at night and a midday siesta, and this is a standard model for sleep research.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around 40 to 50 days as an adult in good conditions, and far less in the wild.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Several hundred eggs laid straight onto fermenting surfaces, in small batches across many sites. Nothing is invested per egg — the strategy is volume and speed, spread across as many patches as possible.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are slightly larger with a pointed, paler abdomen tip. Males have a rounded dark abdomen tip and sex combs — small black bristle tufts — on the forelegs.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in plumage and size. In the pair's duet the two sexes sing different parts at different tempos, so a practised listener can tell them apart by ear.

Several species, such as the winter moth and the cankerworms, can strip the leaves from orchard and forest trees in outbreak years.
Caterpillars of some emerald moths fasten fragments of petals and leaves to their backs as camouflage.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars chew the leaves, buds or flowers of trees, shrubs and herbs, and many species are restricted to a few host plants. Adults of many species sip nectar or sap through a coiled tongue; others have reduced mouthparts and do not feed.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, bats, spiders and parasitic wasps and flies are the main enemies. Many caterpillars stand rigid like a twig or drop on a silk line when disturbed; adults rely on bark-like patterns and can hear the calls of hunting bats.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most adults fly at dusk and through the night and rest by day flat against bark, walls or the undersides of leaves. A minority of species fly in sunshine. Many caterpillars feed at night and stay motionless by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults usually live one to three weeks. The whole life cycle typically takes a year or less, and temperate species pass the winter as an egg, caterpillar or pupa, depending on species; some have two or more generations a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay from a few dozen to several hundred eggs, singly or in batches, on or near the food plant. There is no parental care. Caterpillars moult several times, then pupate in soil, leaf litter or a loose cocoon among leaves.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males of many species have feathery antennae and slimmer bodies, while females have thread-like antennae and stouter abdomens. In some species, including the winter moth, females are wingless or have only wing stubs.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: There are no separate sexes: each individual has both reproductive roles, so size and condition matter more than male/female difference. Young adults produce only sperm at first and begin laying eggs when they are older and larger.

Non-feeding adult stage: the winged body is built for mating, not maintenance.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Nymphs feed on fine organic matter and algae in sediment, while adults usually do not feed. The diet supports Ephemerality because the winged stage exists for reproduction, not maintenance.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, birds, bats, spiders, dragonflies, and aquatic predators consume mayflies at every stage. Synchronized emergence overwhelms predators by turning timing into protection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults often emerge in evening or night swarms and live briefly, while nymphs spend months or longer underwater. Their rhythm is patience below, urgency above.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Giant Burrowing Mayflies may spend many months to a few years as aquatic nymphs, while adults often live only hours to days. That contrast is the heart of Ephemerality: long hidden preparation, brief visible purpose.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females release or deposit eggs back into water after mating, returning the next generation to the sediment world. Offspring begin where the adult dance ends.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males often form mating swarms and may have enlarged eyes or mating adaptations, while females carry eggs. The difference exists to complete the short adult mission quickly.

Its haemoglobin can carry oxygen and sulphide at the same time, holding the sulphide at separate sites so it does not poison the worm.

respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: As an adult it takes in no food. The plume absorbs hydrogen sulphide, oxygen and carbon dioxide from the water, and the blood carries them to a spongy organ called the trophosome, where the bacteria make sugars that the worm absorbs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Vent crabs and eelpout fish nip at the exposed plumes. When touched or shaded it snaps the plume back into its tube, and colonies are also lost when their vent stops flowing.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: There is no known sleep or day-night rhythm; sunlight never reaches the vents. Activity continues around the clock, driven by the chemistry of the vent water rather than by light.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No reliable lifespan figure exists: individual worms have not been followed from settlement to death, and the range of possible ages is unknown.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Sexes are separate. Females release fertilised eggs that develop into drifting larvae, which live on yolk reserves for an estimated several weeks and can be carried to other vents. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are separate but look alike from the outside; the sexes cannot be told apart in the field.

Heavy legs and strong grip for night climbing
Nocturnal habits that reduce exposure
Slow sturdy movement rather than delicate flight

Long, thin whip-like tail without a sting
First pair of legs long and used as feelers
Dark reddish-brown to black flattened body

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raccoons, armadillos, skunks, birds and larger arachnids may take it. Faced with a threat, it rears up and holds its heavy pincers open towards the attacker.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal. It spends the day in a burrow it digs with its pincers, or under logs, rocks and debris where the air stays humid, and emerges after dark to hunt.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Reaching adulthood is thought to take about four years, and individuals probably live around seven to eight years in total.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After mating the female retires to a burrow and carries a sac of roughly 30 to 40 eggs under her abdomen for weeks to months. Hatchlings climb onto her back and ride there until they moult, then disperse.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males tend to have larger, longer pedipalps than females; otherwise the sexes look very similar.

Short, broad snout rather than a long weevil beak
Straight, club-tipped antennae, not elbowed ones
Small body with rounded wing cases

whyInteresting: It belongs to the leaf-rolling weevils, family Attelabidae, whose females cut and fold leaves into tight parcels for their eggs.
The female slices across the leaf blade with her jaws, then folds and rolls the hanging part into a neat barrel.
Each leaf roll usually holds a single egg, sealed inside before the female moves on.
Males are thought to use their long necks in pushing contests with rival males.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults chew the leaves of their host plants. The larva feeds on the tissue of the rolled leaf its mother made, eating its shelter from the inside.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Specific predators have not been documented for this species. Birds, spiders, lizards and predatory insects are the likely threats, and the rolled leaf hides the larva from many of them, though tiny parasitic wasps attack leaf-roller eggs.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Like other leaf-rolling weevils, adults are thought to be active on leaves by day. Where and how they rest at night has not been documented for this species.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult lifespan has not been documented for this species.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female folds a leaf and winds it into a tight cylinder; as in related leaf-rollers, she usually lays a single egg inside. The larva grows and pupates within the roll, and the new adult chews its way out.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a noticeably longer neck than females, as in other long-necked leaf-rolling weevils; how large the difference is in this species is not well documented.

entries.name: Glass Catfish
entries.heroTitle: Glass Catfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Glass Catfish shows that transparency is not weakness. In the right group, being see-through can become part of the strategy.

Organs packed into a silvery pouch behind the head
Two long barbels pointing forward from the upper jaw
Long anal fin running most of the body's length
Hovers at a slant in midwater, tail lower than head

The skin has no scales and the body almost no pigment.
After death the flesh turns milky white and opaque within a short time.
The dorsal fin is reduced to a tiny stub that is easily overlooked.
In bright light the flanks flash rainbow colours, which a recent study traced to light being split by the banded structure of the swimming muscles.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Known mainly from aquarium fish, which take water fleas and other tiny crustaceans, mosquito and midge larvae and other small insects, with the occasional fish fry. It darts out from the shoal to snap up drifting prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: No predators have been recorded for this species in the wild. In aquaria a frightened shoal bunches tightly and moves into cover among plants or roots.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, unlike most catfish. In aquaria the shoal stops feeding after dark and stays close to cover, barely moving, until morning.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly reported to live about 6 to 8 years in aquaria. No figures are available for wild fish.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding in the wild has not been described. Spawning in aquaria is rare, and clutch size, hatching time and parental care have not been reliably recorded.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: No reliable outward differences are known. Females carrying eggs may look slightly fuller in the belly, but males and females are otherwise alike.

entries.name: Glass Octopus
entries.heroTitle: Glass Octopus — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A nearly transparent octopus of the open ocean, drifting through the dim twilight zone hundreds of metres down. Only the eyes, optic nerves and digestive gland show clearly; the rest of the gelatinous body lets light pass straight through.

Long, narrow, rectangular eyes
Opaque, spindle-shaped digestive gland visible inside
Eight short arms joined by a web
Reported to reach about 45 centimetres including arms

whyInteresting: It was described scientifically by the French zoologist Louis Joubin in 1918.
Live animals have rarely been seen; most specimens come from deep trawl nets or predators' stomachs.
Video of living glass octopuses filmed in the central Pacific in 2021 drew wide public attention.
It swims by jetting water from its mantle and pulsing its webbed arms.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Glass Octopus feeds on small crustaceans, fish larvae, and drifting deep-sea prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tunas and other large ocean fishes eat it, and specimens have been recovered from their stomachs. Near-transparency is its main protection from hunters searching the water around it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Its daily cycle of activity and rest has not been documented.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Midwater lifespan for Vitreledonella richardi is unpublished. Nearly transparent tissues and tubular eyes suit life in the open mesopelagic zone.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females are reported to brood their eggs held among the arms around the mouth. Clutch size and development time are not known.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have one arm modified for passing sperm packets to the female; other differences are not known.

whyInteresting: A bubble of air swallowed and held in the stomach keeps it buoyant at the surface of the sea.
Its colouring is countershaded: the blue underside faces the sky, while the silvery back faces down towards the deep.
It was long lumped with Glaucus atlanticus until a 2014 study showed it to be a separate species, possibly a complex of several.
Each individual has both male and female reproductive organs, and mating partners exchange sperm with each other.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It feeds on floating colonial hydrozoans, mainly blue buttons and by-the-wind sailors, gripping them and biting off pieces with its jaws.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Specific predators are poorly documented. Its countershading, blue on the side facing the sky and silvery on the side facing the deep, makes it hard to see from above or below.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No rest period has been recorded, and it is carried by wind and current at all hours.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Glaucus marginatus lifespan at death is unpublished; the blue nudibranch floats upside-down in surface currents and preys on siphonophores.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After mating, both partners can lay strings of eggs, which are attached to floating objects, reportedly including the remains of prey, and hatch into free-swimming larvae.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: There are no separate sexes: each individual has both male and female organs, so every adult looks the same.

entries.name: Globular Springtail

Unlike most insects, springtails keep moulting throughout adult life.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders, predatory mites, pseudoscorpions, ants and specialist beetles hunt it, including rove beetles that shoot out a sticky mouthpart.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Males leave sperm packets on the ground that females pick up. Eggs are laid in damp litter or soil and hatch into small versions of the adult, which grow through a series of moults with no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in the field; telling them apart requires microscopic examination.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger predatory fish and fish-eating birds are the likely wild predators, though records for this species are few. Shoaling and a dash for plant cover are its defences; in aquaria, large cichlids and other big tank mates may eat it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At night it hangs almost still near the bottom or among plants, and its colours often pale until the light returns.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females scatter a few hundred or more slightly sticky eggs among fine-leaved plants. There is no parental care and adults eat any eggs they find. Eggs hatch in about one to two days, and the fry swim freely a few days later.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger and deeper-bodied, especially when carrying eggs. Males are slimmer and are often said to have a longer, more pointed dorsal fin, though fin shape is not a reliable guide.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds on decaying leaves, rotting wood and the fungal growth on them, chewing litter into small fragments. Its droppings return that material to the soil, where microbes finish breaking it down.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Shrews, hedgehogs, badgers, ground-feeding birds, ground beetles and spiders take it. Its defences probably give less protection against the larger mammals than against small hunters.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active at night and on wet days, wandering over the litter surface. By day it rests under bark, stones and deep leaf litter, and in dry or frosty spells it retreats further into the soil.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid singly in spring and early summer, each sealed by the female in a small capsule of soil and her own droppings. Young hatch with fewer segments and legs than adults and add them at successive moults, probably taking a few years to reach maturity.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have 19 pairs of legs and females 17; the male's hindmost pairs form claspers at the tail end, which can be seen on an unrolled animal with a hand lens.

Young caterpillars skeletonise leaves, eating the surface and leaving a network of veins.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars eat the leaves of many trees and shrubs, especially hawthorn and blackthorn, also oak, willow, birch, rose and fruit trees. Adults are not thought to feed.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: The hairy caterpillars are avoided by most birds, though cuckoos eat them; parasitoid wasps and flies kill many more.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults fly at night and spend the day resting on leaves, twigs or fence posts, often on the underside of a leaf.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid in a flat batch on a leaf, covered with golden hairs. Caterpillars feed briefly in late summer, overwinter while small, and finish growing in spring before pupating in a cocoon among leaves. There is one generation a year.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger with a bigger gold tuft. Males have more strongly feathered antennae and usually one or two small dark marks near the rear edge of the forewing, which females normally lack.

entries.name: Golden-fronted Bowerbird

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are far smaller, about 3 to 5 millimetres against the female's 6 to 11, and much darker, with a reddish-brown front body and dark front legs. Only females are conspicuously white or yellow.
