Selective breeding began in China more than a thousand years ago, and the fish reached Japan in the 1500s and Europe in the 1600s.
Released pets grow far larger than tank fish, reaching 30 to 40 cm, and are treated as an invasive pest in lakes in Australia, Canada and the United States.

Open-ground feeding keeps the body exposed, so escape readiness matters constantly.
whyInteresting: Grasshoppers can jump many times their own body length.
Some species make sound by rubbing body parts together.
Outbreak years can reshape fields because heavy feeding pressure affects crops and grasses.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, leaves, crop plants, and other vegetation.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, reptiles, rodents, mantises, and parasitic insects keep pressure high. The grasshopper’s answer is not armor but a loaded leap and sudden relocation.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Grasshoppers are mostly active by day in warmth, when jumping and feeding work best. Cooler periods slow the body and make readiness harder.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Many grasshoppers live only a season as adults, with eggs carrying the species through harsh periods. The short adult window makes readiness a seasonal strategy, not a long slow plan.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in soil or plant material, often in pods or clusters. The next generation begins hidden below the open ground where adults feed, jump, and risk exposure.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often larger because egg production takes space and energy, while males may be more active in calling or courtship. Size and sound both connect directly to reproduction.

analysis.summary: One of the largest angelfishes of the western Atlantic, reaching about 60 cm, this reef fish lives largely on sponges. Few fish can digest sponge tissue, with its glassy spicules and chemical defences, and the grey angelfish browses it steadily across reefs and hard bottoms.

Each scale edged paler, giving a speckled look
Tail fin cut square, with a pale rear margin
Inner face of the pectoral fin yellowish
Juveniles black with yellow vertical bands

It is caught for food in parts of the Caribbean and collected for the aquarium trade.
Juveniles usually live in shallower, more sheltered water than adults, often among rubble and sea grass.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Sponges make up most of the diet, bitten off with small brush-like teeth. It also eats tunicates, algae, soft corals, bryozoans and other encrusting animals picked from rock and reef.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large groupers, sharks and barracuda are its likely predators as an adult. The deep, laterally flattened body and a sharp spine on each gill cover make it awkward to swallow, and it darts into reef crevices when chased.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds through the day and retires at dusk to a regular crevice or overhang in the reef, where it rests almost motionless overnight.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Aquarium specimens are reported to have lived more than 15 years. How long grey angelfish survive on wild reefs has not been measured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs spawn around dusk, rising together and releasing eggs and sperm into open water. The buoyant eggs hatch within about a day and the larvae drift in the plankton for several weeks before settling. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike and cannot be told apart in the field.

analysis.summary: Gray Whale expresses Benthicturn through long migration, mottled gray body, bottom feeding, and careful seafloor rolling make the Benthicturn principle specific rather than generic; body, habitat, and pressure all point back to the same lesson.

whyInteresting: Barnacles and orange whale lice crust its head and back, and one barnacle species lives only on gray whales.
The round trip between Arctic feeding grounds and Mexican breeding lagoons covers roughly 16,000 to 20,000 kilometres.
Instead of a dorsal fin it has a low hump followed by a row of bumps, called knuckles, towards the tail.
Most individuals feed lying on their right side, and their right-side baleen is often more worn.
In some Mexican lagoons, individual whales approach small boats and allow people to touch them.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Its main food is amphipods, small crustaceans, and seafloor invertebrates filtered from sediment. Most feeding happens in summer in the Bering and Chukchi Seas; some whales also take mysid shrimps and crab larvae nearer the coast, and little is eaten during migration.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Orcas are the only regular natural predator, ambushing calves on the northward migration; mothers keep calves close to shore and in shallows to reduce attacks. Commercial whaling nearly wiped it out, and ship strikes and entanglement in fishing gear are the main human threats today.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It rests near the surface or in quiet lagoons, migrating and feeding in seasonal rhythms. Resting whales lie almost still at the surface and blow at long intervals, and activity continues through both day and night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most estimates put the lifespan at about 50 to 70 years, based on growth layers counted in earplugs; a few individuals have been estimated at around 75 or older.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pregnant females give birth to one calf in warm lagoons and nurse it during migration. Gestation lasts about 12 to 13 months, most births in the Baja California lagoons fall in January and February, and calves are weaned at about 7 to 9 months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult females are often slightly larger than males. Otherwise the sexes look alike at sea, though mothers with calves head north later in spring than other adults.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Humans, disease, starvation, rival packs, and injuries threaten wolves. Cooperation spreads risk across the group.

entries.name: Grayling

analysis.summary: Grayling pairs elegance with current skill, using a high dorsal fin and fine feeding timing in clear, fast rivers.

whyInteresting: The genus name Thymallus refers to the smell of thyme said to come from a freshly caught fish.
In European river classification, the stretch between the upland trout zone and the lowland barbel zone is called the grayling zone.
British anglers have long called it the lady of the stream.
Spawning males hold small patches of gravel and chase rival males away from them.
Studies have found that grayling in separate river systems often differ genetically, so fish from one river are poor stock for another.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly bottom-living invertebrates such as caddis, mayfly and stonefly larvae, freshwater shrimps and small snails, picked from the gravel. It also rises to take insects from the surface, and large fish occasionally eat fish eggs and small fish.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pike, large brown trout, otters, goosanders, cormorants and herons take grayling, the young especially. Warming water, silt, pollution and weirs are serious threats. A shoal holds in deeper, faster water and scatters to the bottom or under cover when a shadow passes.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeding is mostly by day, from morning through to dusk. At night the fish are thought to drop close to the riverbed in slacker water and stay fairly still until morning.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly 5 to 7 years; in cold northern waters some fish have been aged at over 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning takes place in spring, roughly March to May, over shallow gravel. With the male beside her, the female presses her eggs into the gravel, typically a few thousand, more in larger females, and neither parent guards them. The eggs hatch in about two to four weeks, depending on water temperature.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The male's dorsal fin is taller and longer, reaching further back towards the tail, and in the spawning season he is more richly coloured. The female's dorsal fin is smaller and more rounded. During spawning the male curves his fin over her back.

analysis.summary: The largest grebe in Europe, a long-necked diving bird with legs set so far back that it can barely walk on land. At the climax of courtship a pair dive, surface with beakfuls of water weed and rise breast to breast, treading water.
identification: Long, slender white neck held upright
Pink, dagger-shaped bill
Dark crest and chestnut ruff in breeding plumage
White face and neck in winter, without the ruff
Sits low in the water and dives often

whyInteresting: In nineteenth-century Britain it was hunted close to extinction for its head plumes and dense breast feathers, which were sold as grebe fur.
Adults swallow their own feathers and feed them to their chicks; the feathers are thought to protect the gut from fish bones.
Julian Huxley's 1914 study of its courtship was one of the first detailed scientific accounts of bird display.
The toes are not webbed but fringed with broad lobes that spread on the back stroke and fold on the return.
Parents often split the brood, each adult feeding its own share of the chicks.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, aquatic insects, crustaceans, and amphibians.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, large gulls, raptors, pike, and egg predators threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds and displays by day and sleeps on the water, often well out from the shore, with the neck laid back and the bill tucked into the back feathers. Migrating birds travel mainly at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly given as about 10 to 15 years; few wild birds have been followed for long enough to be sure.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually 3 to 5 eggs are laid on a floating platform of water weed anchored among reeds. Both parents incubate for about four weeks, covering the eggs with weed when they leave. Striped chicks ride on a parent's back and are fed for about ten weeks.

entries.name: Great Crow
entries.heroTitle: Great Crow — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Great Crow butterfly flies slowly and openly in plain sight, which only works because it is genuinely unpalatable. Its dark wings and white spotting are a signal other butterflies have converged on, so the warning gets stronger the more species share it.
identification: Large dark brown to black wings with a soft blue or purple sheen
Rows of white spots along the wing margins
Slow, deliberate flapping flight, unbothered and low
Males carry hair-pencils extruded from the abdomen tip when courting
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, south_asia, australia_oceania. Coastal forest, mangrove edge, gardens and secondary growth where its larval fig and Apocynaceae hosts grow. Open, well-lit habitat suits a butterfly that does not need to hide.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia, south_asia, australia_oceania. Coastal forest, mangrove edge, gardens and secondary growth where its larval fig and Apocynaceae hosts grow. Open, well-lit habitat suits a butterfly that does not need to hide.

behaviorTraits: Large dark brown to black wings with a soft blue or purple sheen

whyInteresting: Adults take pyrrolizidine alkaloids from Apocynaceae and Asteraceae plants and store them, which makes them genuinely distasteful to birds.
Crows are models in a Mullerian mimicry ring, not mimics of it — several unrelated distasteful butterflies converge on the same dark, white-spotted pattern, so every one of them benefits.
Males use those same stored alkaloids to build the pheromone released from their hair-pencils during courtship.
The species roosts communally in the dry season, sometimes in large aggregations in sheltered gullies.
Larvae feed on figs and other latex-bearing trees, cutting leaf veins first to drain the sticky sap before eating.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults take nectar and, distinctively, dried plant material and withered Heliotropium and Crotalaria for the alkaloids themselves. Larvae feed on figs and related latex-bearing trees. The adult diet is where the defence and the courtship pheromone both come from.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few birds pursue an adult after one attempt. Larvae and pupae are taken by wasps and ants, and the slow adult flight only remains safe where local birds have already learned the pattern.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and roosts overnight in vegetation, gathering in sheltered communal roosts through the dry season.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults live several weeks to a few months, considerably longer than most butterflies of similar size, helped by having few pursuers.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid singly on the underside of host leaves. Larvae are conspicuously banded rather than camouflaged, carrying the same honest-signal strategy the adults use.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar; males are recognised by the paired hair-pencils they push out from the abdomen tip when courting, and often by a slightly stronger blue sheen.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A sit-and-wait and wandering feeder that takes beetles, ants, caterpillars and other ground insects. It snaps prey up with a flick of the sticky tongue.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hognose snakes, garter snakes, birds and mammals such as coyotes and raccoons eat toads, and tadpoles are taken by insects and birds. Glands in the skin release an irritating secretion, and a threatened toad puffs up with air.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active at night in warm, wet weather. Days, winters and long dry spells are spent inactive below ground.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Individuals in wild populations have been aged at up to about 10 years; most probably live fewer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding bursts follow heavy rains, in shallow temporary pools. A female lays thousands of eggs in long strings that hatch in a few days, and the tadpoles transform within about three to seven weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a dark throat patch covering the vocal sac and dark nuptial pads on the thumbs in breeding season. Females are usually larger with a pale throat.

entries.name: Great-tailed Grackle
entries.heroTitle: Great-tailed Grackle — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A large, long-legged blackbird of towns, farms and marshes. Males are glossy black with yellow eyes and a long, keel-shaped tail, and they deliver an extraordinary range of whistles, rattles, clacks and piercing shrieks from treetops, wires and lamp posts.

Glossy black male with violet-blue sheen
Pale yellow eyes in adults of both sexes
Brown female, much smaller than the male
Loud whistles, rattles and shrieks from exposed perches

Open country with scattered trees and water nearby: farmland, irrigated fields, cattle yards, city parks, lawns, car parks, marshes and mangrove edges, from the south-western and central United States through Mexico and Central America. It avoids dense forest and the driest desert.

whyInteresting: Around 1900 it bred in the United States only in southern Texas; following irrigation and the growth of towns, it now nests across much of the west and the Great Plains.
The Aztec ruler Ahuitzotl is recorded as having brought the birds from the Gulf coast to the Valley of Mexico about 500 years ago.
In experiments it has solved puzzles such as dropping stones into a tube of water to raise the level and reach floating food.
Until the 1970s it was treated as the same species as the boat-tailed grackle of the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
More females than males survive to adulthood, and a successful male may mate with several females nesting in his territory.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Omnivorous. It walks over lawns, fields and shorelines taking insects, grain, seeds and fruit, wades for tadpoles, small fish and snails, raids the eggs and nestlings of other birds, and scavenges food scraps in towns.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, owls, cats, raccoons and snakes take adults, eggs or chicks. It nests in colonies and roosts in large flocks, and birds mob an intruder together with loud alarm calls.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At dusk flocks gather in noisy communal roosts, sometimes thousands strong in winter, in city trees, reedbeds or on wires above lit car parks, and leave to feed at first light.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most wild birds probably live only a few years; ringed birds have reached at least 7 years, and older ages have been reported.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females build the nest and raise the young alone, often in colonies in trees or reeds. The clutch is usually 3 or 4 pale blue eggs with dark scrawls, incubated for about 13 to 14 days; chicks leave the nest after about two weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are glossy black with a violet-blue sheen, about 43 centimetres long including the very long tail. Females are roughly half the weight, dark brown above and buff-brown below, with a shorter tail. Both have pale yellow eyes.

entries.heroTitle: Great Tinamou — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Great Tinamous are ground-dwelling forest birds with secretive movement and strong voices. They feed among leaf litter and fruiting forest floors while using stillness and cover to avoid attention.
identification: Plump, chicken-sized body with almost no tail
Olive-brown back finely barred with black
Small head, rufous-crowned in many populations
Slim neck and grey-blue legs
Explosive, whirring take-off when flushed

whyInteresting: DNA studies place tinamous among the ratites, the group of emus and ostriches, making tinamous the only living ratites that can fly.
Tinamous are reported to have some of the smallest hearts, relative to body size, of any birds.
At around a kilogram, it is one of the largest tinamous.
About a dozen subspecies are recognised, differing mainly in crown colour and the tone of the upperparts.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fallen fruits and seeds, many swallowed whole, with insects and occasionally small frogs or lizards. It walks slowly, picking items from the ground.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Ocelots, margays, tayras, coatis, forest hawks and snakes take adults, eggs or chicks, and people hunt it. It freezes when alarmed, then walks or runs quietly away, flying only if pressed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and calls at dusk. Unlike most tinamous, it roosts off the ground at night, perching on low horizontal branches.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Its lifespan is poorly known; no reliable wild or captive age records exist for this bird.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female lays 3 to 5 glossy turquoise eggs on the ground, often between buttress roots, and may go on to lay for other males. The male alone incubates for about 16 days and guards the chicks, which run within a day.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike; females are on average slightly larger.

entries.name: Great Tit
entries.heroTitle: Great Tit — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Great Tit is a bold problem-solver, combining loud signals, flexible feeding, and quick learning to thrive around woods, gardens, and people.
identification: Glossy black head with large white cheek patches
Yellow underparts split by a black central stripe
Greenish back and blue-grey wings with a single white bar
Loud, ringing two-note song, often written tea-cher

In experiments at Wytham Woods near Oxford, a new way of opening a puzzle feeder spread from trained birds through wild flocks and persisted as a local tradition.
Many populations now lay earlier in spring than decades ago, tracking the earlier peak in caterpillar numbers.
In a Hungarian cave, great tits have been recorded killing and eating hibernating bats in late winter.
A single male may sing several distinct song types, switching between them during bouts.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: In spring and summer it gleans caterpillars, beetles, spiders and other invertebrates from leaves and bark. In winter it turns to seeds and nuts, especially beech mast, hammering them open held under a foot, and visits bird feeders.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sparrowhawks catch adults, while weasels, great spotted woodpeckers, squirrels and cats raid nests. A female disturbed in the nest hole hisses like a snake and lunges. Hard winters kill many birds.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active through the daylight hours. At night it roosts alone, usually in a tree hole, nest box or dense cover, and on winter nights it can lower its body temperature slightly to save energy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually 2 to 3 years in the wild, with most deaths in the first year; ringed birds have lived beyond 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female builds a moss and hair nest in a tree hole or nest box and lays usually 6 to 10 red-speckled white eggs. She incubates them for about two weeks; both parents feed the chicks, which fledge after about three weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a broad black stripe down the belly that widens between the legs; in females it is narrower and the cap is slightly duller.

entries.name: Greater Amberjack
entries.heroTitle: Greater Amberjack — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A powerful jack of reefs and open coastal water that can exceed 1.5 metres and 50 kilograms. Its muscular, streamlined body and stiff, deeply forked tail are built for sustained swimming, and hooked fish are known for long, deep-diving fights.
identification: Dark diagonal bar from the snout through the eye to the dorsal fin
Amber to yellowish stripe along the mid-flank
Olive to bluish-brown back fading to a silvery belly
No bony scutes along the base of the tail

analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_atlantic, mediterranean, north_pacific. Coastal and offshore waters over rocky reefs, wrecks and steep drop-offs, most often about 20 to 70 metres deep but recorded to over 300; young fish drift near the surface under floating seaweed and debris.

Large fish from some reefs can carry ciguatera, a toxin that passes up the food chain and causes food poisoning.
Spawning aggregations, with many adults gathering at the same offshore reefs, have been recorded in parts of the western Atlantic.
Juveniles under drifting weed have bold dark vertical bars, which fade as they grow.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly fish, especially schooling species, with squid and crustaceans; young fish take small invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large sharks and bigger predatory fish take some, especially juveniles. Fishing is the main pressure, and heavy catches have depleted stocks in some regions. Its defence is speed and the safety of numbers in a group.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It hunts mainly by day. Night behaviour is little documented; like other open-water jacks it probably keeps swimming rather than resting on the bottom.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Ageing studies have found fish of about 15 years or more; most caught fish are much younger.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning takes place in open water in spring and summer, with each female releasing very large numbers of small, buoyant eggs that drift with the plankton. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot be told apart from outside.

entries.name: Greater Bee Fly
entries.heroTitle: Greater Bee Fly — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Greater Bee Fly AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: The Greater Bee Fly feeds in the open by pretending to be something that stings. The long straight proboscis, the hovering, and the bee-like fur are all for the same job: take nectar in daylight without being worth attacking.
identification: Furred brown body, 10-15 mm, hovering like a small bumblebee
Long rigid proboscis held straight forward, never folded
Dark leading-edge band on the wing
Long dangling legs while hovering at a flower
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, north_america, north_africa_middle_east, central_asia. Sunny banks, woodland edge, gardens and dry grassland with early flowers and nearby mining-bee burrows. The adult needs nectar in the open; the larva needs a solitary bee nest in bare soil.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe, north_america, north_africa_middle_east, central_asia. Sunny banks, woodland edge, gardens and dry grassland with early flowers and nearby mining-bee burrows. The adult needs nectar in the open; the larva needs a solitary bee nest in bare soil.

behaviorTraits: Furred brown body, 10-15 mm, hovering like a small bumblebee
Long rigid proboscis held straight forward, never folded
Dark leading-edge band on the wing

whyInteresting: It is a fly, not a bee. The resemblance is Batesian mimicry: it has no sting, and predators that have met a bee leave it alone.
Larvae are parasitoids of solitary mining bees. The female flicks eggs toward a nest burrow while hovering, and the larva finds the host cell on its own.
The rigid proboscis is used like a straw. The fly never lands to feed if it can help it, which is why the hover is so steady.
It is one of the first large hoverers of European and North American spring, often out before most bees.
Males hold small territories in sunlit clearings and chase anything of similar size that crosses them.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults take nectar from primrose, bugle, lungwort, grape hyacinth and other early tubular flowers, hovering rather than landing. Larvae eat the pollen store and then the larva of a mining bee.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds and robber flies take adults that linger; the bee disguise is the main defence. Eggs and young larvae are lost to soil predators before they reach a host cell.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active in warm sun, hovering in the open through the middle of the day, and still on vegetation in cool or wet weather.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults live a few weeks in spring. The rest of the year is spent as a larva or pupa inside a bee nest.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female does not enter the host nest. She flicks eggs toward the burrow while hovering, and each larva must find a cell. Many eggs never reach one.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike. Males are the ones holding sunlit airspace and chasing other flies; females are the ones hovering over bare soil as well as flowers.

entries.name: Greater Fairy Armadillo

Pale, banded shell covering the back
Blunt vertical bony plate over the rump
Very large curved claws on the forefeet

It was formerly placed in the genus Chlamyphorus with the pink fairy armadillo, its closest living relative, and is still sometimes listed as Chlamyphorus retusus.
Its eyes are tiny and its ears barely visible, features suited to a life spent almost entirely underground.
So few have been studied that it has been listed as Data Deficient on the IUCN Red List.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Thought to feed mainly on insects and their larvae, especially ants and beetle grubs, and other soil invertebrates found while digging. Plant material may also be eaten; its diet has hardly been studied.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Natural predators have not been documented. When exposed it digs itself in quickly. Clearance of Chaco scrub for farming and ranching is the main threat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Surface activity has been reported mainly at night and after rain.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not documented, either in the wild or in captivity, where very few have been kept.

analysis.summary: Short, sharp spines cover the back of this Madagascar mammal, and it looks so like a European hedgehog that it is often mistaken for one. It is a tenrec, not a hedgehog; the two lineages evolved spines independently.

whyInteresting: Tenrecs are thought to have reached Madagascar from Africa once, tens of millions of years ago, then diversified into shrew-like, mole-like and hedgehog-like forms.
It belongs to the Afrotheria, the mammal group that also includes elephants, aardvarks and golden moles.
Its nearest relative is the smaller lesser hedgehog tenrec, Echinops telfairi, of the drier south and south-west.
It also lives in degraded forest, farmland and village gardens, and is widespread in Madagascar.
It is hunted for food in parts of Madagascar.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly insects, earthworms and other invertebrates rooted from leaf litter and soil with its snout, plus fallen fruit and carrion. It climbs well and also forages in bushes and low trees.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: The fossa, Malagasy civets, introduced dogs and cats, large boas and owls take it, and people hunt it for food. When threatened it raises its spines, jerks and hisses, then rolls into a tight ball.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly nocturnal, spending the day curled up in a burrow, tree hollow or tangle of roots. In the cool dry season it can drop into torpor for days, letting its body temperature fall to save energy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is not well documented; animals in captivity have lived for more than ten years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeds in the warm wet season after emerging from dry-season torpor. After a pregnancy of about two months the female gives birth in a nest in a burrow or hollow to usually one to five young, which have soft spines and are weaned within about a month.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike, with no reliable visible difference in size or colour in the field.

entries.name: Greater Honeyguide
entries.heroTitle: Greater Honeyguide — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A plain brown-and-white African bird that leads people to wild bees' nests. It flies up close with a persistent chattering call, then moves ahead from tree to tree, waiting whenever its follower falls behind. At the nest itself it is reported to fall quiet and perch close by.

Short, stout bill on a starling-sized body
Small yellow patch at the bend of the wing, often hidden
Plain grey-brown back and wings, without spots or bars

Males advertise with a repeated, far-carrying two-note song, often given from a favoured perch.
A 2023 study found that birds near Hadza honey-hunters in Tanzania respond best to the Hadza whistle, not to the Yao call used in Mozambique.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Bee stings are a real risk when it feeds at an open nest, and host birds such as bee-eaters and barbets chase it from their nest holes. Hawks and snakes are probable predators; it escapes with fast, direct flight into cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Greater Honeyguide rests in tree cavities, roost branches, and hidden woodland cover. It is active only by day and spends long spells perched quietly in the canopy between bouts of calling and feeding.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males have a black throat, a white cheek patch and a pale pink bill. Females are plainer grey-brown with a dark bill and no black throat, and juveniles are olive-brown with a bright yellow throat and breast.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Few ringing recoveries pin down adult lifespan in Rostratula benghalensis. Females are the brighter sex and leave males to incubate the eggs.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and soft-shelled young are eaten by ravens, foxes, rats and wild boar, and golden eagles break adults open by dropping them onto rocks. Collection for the pet trade, scrub fires, ploughing and overgrazing have thinned many populations.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: This tortoise is diurnal when temperatures suit, sheltering through extremes and sometimes hibernating or aestivating. Where winters are cold it spends them buried in soil; in hot lowlands it may stay active in winter and lie up through the summer instead.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually smaller than females and have a longer, thicker tail and a slightly concave plastron. Females have a flat plastron and a short tail; shell colour and pattern are alike in both.

Its green colour comes largely from a bile pigment, named micromatabilin after the genus.
Its bite can pierce human skin and may cause brief local pain, but it is not medically dangerous.
It belongs to the family Sparassidae, whose larger tropical members are the well-known giant huntsman spiders.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flies, bugs, small beetles and other insects and spiders. It builds no snare: it waits motionless on a leaf or stalks across foliage, then rushes out and seizes prey with its front legs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards and spider-hunting wasps are among its likely predators. Its leaf-green colour hides it on foliage, and when disturbed it darts to the far side of a leaf or drops into the vegetation below.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hunts mainly by day in warm weather and sits still on leaves between hunts. It is seldom seen in cool or dull weather, when it probably shelters deeper in the vegetation.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one to one and a half years. Spiderlings hatch in summer, overwinter as juveniles, mature the following spring and die after breeding.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After mating the female draws one or more leaves together with silk to form a nursery tent. She lays her egg sac inside and stays on guard until the spiderlings hatch and disperse.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult females are larger and plain bright green. Adult males are smaller and slimmer, with a bright red stripe edged in yellow running down the top of the abdomen.

analysis.summary: White grubs of this heavy green scarab live in the soil of the eastern United States. Each digs a vertical burrow, commonly 15 to 30 cm deep. In ground where grubs are numerous the tunnelling loosens and turns over the upper soil.

Broad, flat-backed body about 2 cm long
Small flat horn projecting from the front of the head

Full-grown grubs reach about 5 cm in length, more than twice as long as the adult beetle.
Despite its size the adult neither bites nor stings and is harmless to handle.
Egg-laying females are drawn to ground treated with manure or compost, so heavily fertilised turf tends to hold more grubs.
The grub is thick and cream-coloured with a brown head, and its swollen hind end looks dark where soil in the gut shows through the skin.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults eat ripe and rotting fruit such as figs, peaches, grapes and blackberries, and drink sap from wounded trees. Grubs eat decaying plant matter in the soil and thatch, along with some roots.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Crows, grackles, skunks, raccoons, moles and armadillos dig out the grubs. The wasp Scolia dubia stings grubs in their burrows and lays an egg on each. Grubs retreat down their tunnels when disturbed; adults take flight.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults fly in sunshine and are reported to pass the night in vegetation or thatch. Grubs do the reverse, staying down their burrows by day and coming to the surface after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: The whole life cycle takes one year. Roughly ten months of that are spent as a grub; adult beetles live for only a few weeks in summer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: One generation a year. Females burrow into the soil and lay about 60 to 75 eggs over roughly two weeks, in batches packed inside balls of earth. Eggs hatch in about two to three weeks. Grubs pupate in an earthen cell the following spring.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look much alike and are hard to separate in the field. Behaviour is the better clue: males fly low, back and forth over turf in search of females, which spend more time in the grass.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably around 20 years in the wild, where few ages are known exactly; zoo animals have reached about 35 to 37.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single infant is born after about six months' gestation, with black fur and a pink face. The mother carries it against her belly, later on her back, and nurses it for roughly a year; births come about two years apart.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males weigh about twice as much as females, roughly 20 kilograms against 10 to 12, and wear a cape of long silver-grey hair over the shoulders. Females are olive-brown without a cape, and have much smaller canine teeth.

entries.name: Happy-face Spider
entries.heroTitle: Happy-face Spider — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Happy-face Spider reminds us that not all influence is loud. Sometimes a small, unusual mark is enough to become unforgettable.
identification: Tiny body, about 5 mm long, pale and translucent yellow
Legs very long and slender for the body size
Red, black or white patches on the abdomen, differing between individuals
Many individuals are plain yellow with no pattern at all
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Wet and mesic native forest on the Hawaiian islands of Oahu, Molokai, Maui and Hawaii, mostly at middle elevations, where it lives on the undersides of leaves of native shrubs and trees.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Wet and mesic native forest on the Hawaiian islands of Oahu, Molokai, Maui and Hawaii, mostly at middle elevations, where it lives on the undersides of leaves of native shrubs and trees.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 88/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Tiny body, about 5 mm long, pale and translucent yellow
Legs very long and slender for the body size
Red, black or white patches on the abdomen, differing between individuals
Many individuals are plain yellow with no pattern at all
whyInteresting: Its species name, grallator, is Latin for a stilt-walker.
Studies found that the colour patterns are inherited differently on Maui and on the island of Hawaii, suggesting they evolved separately on each island.
Its body colour has been reported to change for a while after a meal, as the translucent body shows the food inside.
It was first described scientifically by the French arachnologist Eugene Simon in 1900.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small flying insects such as flies. It spins a sparse web of a few threads beneath a leaf, rests against the leaf surface and runs out to seize prey that touches the lines.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Insect-eating birds are thought to be the main predators. Its translucent body and hiding place under leaves make it hard to spot, and one idea is that its many colour patterns stop birds learning a single search image.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Daytime finds it pressed flat to a leaf underside beside sparse silk threads. Activity rises when prey strikes those lines, and no seasonal dormancy is reported.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Nobody has tracked marked Theridion grallator across successive years. Colour patches on the abdomen differ sharply among neighbouring Hawaiian forest individuals.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female guards her egg sac under a leaf and stays with the spiderlings after they hatch, and has been reported to catch prey for them until they disperse.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are typically a little larger than males. Mature males can be recognised by their swollen palps, the paired appendages in front of the legs.

entries.name: Hard-lipped Barb
entries.heroTitle: Hard-lipped Barb — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Thick, folded lips with a hard, horny edge let this silvery barb rasp thin films of algae, microbes and detritus from stones, logs and submerged plants. It is one of the commonest barbs in lowland waters of Southeast Asia.
identification: Long dorsal fin with many soft rays
Two pairs of short barbels around the mouth
Downward-facing mouth under a rounded snout
Fins often tinged red or orange
Flanks often marked with a dark stripe or rows of spots
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Rivers, streams, canals, lakes, reservoirs and swamps in lowland Southeast Asia, in clear to turbid water, often over rocky, sandy or muddy bottoms with submerged wood and plants.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Rivers, streams, canals, lakes, reservoirs and swamps in lowland Southeast Asia, in clear to turbid water, often over rocky, sandy or muddy bottoms with submerged wood and plants.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 28/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Long dorsal fin with many soft rays
Two pairs of short barbels around the mouth
Downward-facing mouth under a rounded snout
Fins often tinged red or orange
Flanks often marked with a dark stripe or rows of spots
whyInteresting: Known as nilem in Indonesia, it is farmed in ponds in West Java as a food fish.
Many older books call it Osteochilus hasselti, a name now usually treated as the same species.
It can reach about 30 cm, though most fish seen are 10 to 20 cm long.
The genus name Osteochilus comes from Greek words meaning bony lip.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Algae and diatoms make up most of what it eats, with detritus, fragments of higher plants, plankton and small invertebrates such as insect larvae taken along with them.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakeheads, large catfish and other predatory fish take it, as do herons, and people net and trap it widely. It often moves in loose shoals and darts to cover or deeper water when alarmed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active mainly in daylight. At night it is thought to rest near the bottom or among cover; its daily rhythm has not been studied in detail.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan has not been well documented, either in the wild or in aquariums.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawns at the start of the rainy season, often moving into flooded margins and scattering many small eggs over vegetation or the bottom. There is no parental care; eggs hatch quickly in warm water and the young grow fast.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Outside the breeding season the sexes look alike; ripe females are noticeably deeper in the belly.

entries.name: Harlequin Beetle
entries.heroTitle: Harlequin Beetle — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Harlequin Beetle shows how reach becomes advantage. Its long limbs and bold form make distance part of its strategy.
identification: Very large longhorn beetle, often about 4 to 8 centimetres long
Wing cases patterned in black, red and greenish-yellow
Long antennae, longer than the body in males
A sharp spine on each side of the thorax
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_america. Warm, humid lowland tropical rainforest, along with forest edges and clearings that still hold large old trees.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: south_america. Warm, humid lowland tropical rainforest, along with forest edges and clearings that still hold large old trees.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 45/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Very large longhorn beetle, often about 4 to 8 centimetres long
Wing cases patterned in black, red and greenish-yellow
Long antennae, longer than the body in males
A sharp spine on each side of the thorax
whyInteresting: Tiny pseudoscorpions ride under its wing cases, travelling between the dying trees where both the beetles and the pseudoscorpions breed.
Males have front legs that can be longer than the whole body, used in contests with rival males over females.
Females chew a groove into the bark of a suitable tree and lay their eggs in the wound.
Adults are often attracted to lights at night in forested areas, where most people encounter them.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults feed on sap seeping from wounds in tree bark and are reported at fermenting fruit. The larvae bore into the wood of dead or dying trees, often reported from figs and related trees.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Its natural predators are poorly documented, though birds and forest mammals probably take adults. Handled adults are reported to squeak and may bite. Forest clearance and collecting for the insect trade are the main human pressures.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are seen on tree trunks during the day and also fly after dark, when they are often drawn to lights. They rest pressed against bark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Larval development is thought to take several months to about a year inside wood; adult lifespan in the wild is poorly documented and probably a few months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female chews a small cut into the bark of a suitable dead or dying tree and lays an egg in it. The larva tunnels through the wood as it grows, then pupates in a chamber before emerging as an adult.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have front legs that can be much longer than the body, far longer than the female's. Females have a similar pattern and much shorter forelegs.

entries.name: Harlequin Filefish
entries.heroTitle: Harlequin Filefish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Harlequin Filefish teaches the price and power of specialization. Its life is closely tied to coral, making habitat part of identity.
identification: Bright green body covered in rows of orange spots
Long, tubular snout with a tiny mouth
Single slender spine on top of the head
Slender, laterally flattened body seldom longer than about 12 centimetres
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: indian_ocean, coral_triangle. Shallow coral reefs and sheltered lagoons with dense stands of branching and table Acropora coral, in clear tropical water from about 1 to 30 metres deep, from the Indian Ocean to the Coral Triangle.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: indian_ocean, coral_triangle. Shallow coral reefs and sheltered lagoons with dense stands of branching and table Acropora coral, in clear tropical water from about 1 to 30 metres deep, from the Indian Ocean to the Coral Triangle.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 45/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Bright green body covered in rows of orange spots
Long, tubular snout with a tiny mouth
Single slender spine on top of the head
Slender, laterally flattened body seldom longer than about 12 centimetres
whyInteresting: Experiments have shown that it takes on the smell of the coral it eats, which helps hide it from predators that hunt by scent.
Pairs are reported to stay together and to keep other pairs away from their patch of feeding coral.
It is a filefish, a family named for skin that feels rough like a file because of its tiny, spiny scales.
After mass bleaching in 1998 killed much of the Acropora around Okinawa, it is reported to have vanished from reefs where it had been studied.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Almost entirely the polyps of Acropora corals, nipped one at a time with a tiny mouth at the tip of a long snout. It feeds steadily through the day, taking bite after bite from the same colony.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Groupers, rockcods and other reef predators take small fish of this size. The greatest threat is coral bleaching, which kills its food and cover. When alarmed it retreats deep among the coral branches.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At night it settles deep among the branches of a coral colony and stays there until morning.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No peer-reviewed lifespan estimate exists for Oxymonacanthus longirostris; field work centres on its obligate feeding on Acropora polyps on Indo-Pacific reefs.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs have been observed laying eggs among tufts of algae near the coral, and the sticky eggs are left without parental care. They hatch after a few days into tiny larvae that drift in the plankton before settling on a reef.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look very alike. Slight differences in the colour of the belly patch and ventral flap have been described, but they are hard to see underwater.

entries.name: Harlequin Tuskfish
entries.heroTitle: Harlequin Tuskfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Harlequin Tuskfish teaches that boldness is stronger when it has ability behind it. Its colors draw the eye, but its real strength is controlled, practical force.
identification: Alternating orange-red and blue-edged white bands
Bright blue, tusk-like front teeth
Dark rear body with a pale-edged tail
Heavy head with thick lips
Juveniles show dark eye-spots on the fins
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: coral_triangle, australia_coastal. Coral reefs of north-eastern Australia, including the Great Barrier Reef, usually on reef slopes and lagoon floors with rubble, sand patches and coral heads, from a few metres down to about 35 metres.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: coral_triangle, australia_coastal. Coral reefs of north-eastern Australia, including the Great Barrier Reef, usually on reef slopes and lagoon floors with rubble, sand patches and coral heads, from a few metres down to about 35 metres.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 55/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Alternating orange-red and blue-edged white bands
Bright blue, tusk-like front teeth
Dark rear body with a pale-edged tail
Heavy head with thick lips
Juveniles show dark eye-spots on the fins
whyInteresting: It grows to about 30 centimetres, making it one of the larger colourful wrasses on reefs.
Divers often find individuals curious and approachable, and some have been seen following divers to snatch prey they disturb.
Prized in the aquarium trade for its colours, it will eat small crabs, shrimps and fishes kept in the same tank.
Adults are usually seen alone, moving close to the bottom rather than out in open water.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds on hard-shelled invertebrates: crabs and other crustaceans, molluscs, sea urchins and worms. It turns over rubble and bites prey free, crushing shells with its jaws and throat teeth.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults face few predators beyond reef sharks and large groupers; juveniles are taken by many reef fishes. It stays close to crevices and coral heads and darts into cover when threatened.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, cruising a home area of reef. At night it wedges into a crevice or under a ledge and rests.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Its natural lifespan has not been documented in the scientific literature.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Its spawning has not been described; like other wrasses it is thought to release floating eggs in the water column with no parental care, and the larvae drift in the plankton before settling on the reef.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look much alike. Related tuskfishes change sex from female to male as they grow, which is suspected but not confirmed for this species.

entries.name: Harnessed Moth
entries.heroTitle: Harnessed Moth — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Harnessed Moth keeps its warning in reserve. At rest the striped forewings read as broken ground; disturbed, it lifts them and shows scarlet hindwings that were not there a moment before. The second layer only works because the first one hid it.
identification: Cream forewings with a bold dark harness-like pattern of stripes
Scarlet to orange hindwings, hidden completely at rest
Stout furry body typical of a tiger moth
Caterpillar is a dense bristly woolly bear
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Meadows, old fields, roadsides, woodland edge and gardens across eastern North America. Open weedy ground supplies both the low host plants and the broken pale substrate the resting camouflage is matched to.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america. Meadows, old fields, roadsides, woodland edge and gardens across eastern North America. Open weedy ground supplies both the low host plants and the broken pale substrate the resting camouflage is matched to.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 22/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Cream forewings with a bold dark harness-like pattern of stripes
Scarlet to orange hindwings, hidden completely at rest
Stout furry body typical of a tiger moth
Caterpillar is a dense bristly woolly bear
whyInteresting: The startle display works because it is intermittent — a predator that has already assessed a scrap of bark gets a sudden new signal at the moment of contact.
Tiger moths of this group also produce ultrasonic clicks that jam or warn bats, so the species defends itself in sound as well as colour.
Larvae feed on a wide range of low plants including plantain, clover and dandelion, so they are not tied to any one host.
The caterpillar is a bristly woolly bear and overwinters part-grown, resuming feeding in spring.
The harness pattern that names it is variable enough that individuals can often be told apart.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Larvae eat a broad range of low herbaceous plants; adults feed very little. The generalist larval diet is what lets the species occupy ordinary disturbed ground almost anywhere.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Bats, birds and spiders. The layered defence covers different attackers — camouflage against a searching bird, the hindwing flash against one that has already committed, and ultrasonic clicks against bats that never see it at all.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal, flying and mating at night and resting by day on vegetation and leaf litter, which is when the forewing camouflage is doing the work.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults live one to two weeks. The full cycle runs about a year, with most of it spent as an overwintering larva.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid in clusters on host foliage. Larvae feed through summer, overwinter part-grown in litter and pupate the following spring, so the timing hangs on surviving winter rather than on finding food.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have more strongly feathered antennae for detecting female pheromone; females are somewhat heavier-bodied. Wing pattern is similar in both.

entries.name: Harp Sponge
entries.heroTitle: Harp Sponge — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Harp Sponge teaches structural patience. Its body is the strategy, shaped to catch what the deep water brings.
identification: One to several flat vanes radiating from the centre like spokes
A row of evenly spaced upright branches on each vane
A swollen round ball at the tip of each branch
Pale, almost translucent body standing up from the mud
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_pacific. Deep, soft muddy seafloor in the north-east Pacific off California, where it has been recorded at roughly 3,300 to 3,400 metres. It stands upright on the bottom, anchored in the mud by root-like rhizoids.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_pacific. Deep, soft muddy seafloor in the north-east Pacific off California, where it has been recorded at roughly 3,300 to 3,400 metres. It stands upright on the bottom, anchored in the mud by root-like rhizoids.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 90/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: One to several flat vanes radiating from the centre like spokes
A row of evenly spaced upright branches on each vane
A swollen round ball at the tip of each branch
Pale, almost translucent body standing up from the mud
whyInteresting: It was described as a new species in 2012 by a team that included researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute.
The largest specimens in the original description were up to about 36 centimetres long.
Researchers suggest its flat, comb-like vanes grow facing across the current, which would give the most surface for catching drifting prey.
It belongs to the Cladorhizidae, a family of deep-sea sponges that are almost all carnivorous.
Its common name comes from the upright branches, which recall the strings of a harp or lyre, the source of its scientific name.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Unlike most sponges, which filter water, it catches small drifting crustaceans on its branches with microscopic hooked spicules. Each catch is then wrapped in a thin membrane and digested slowly where it was snagged.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: No predators of this sponge have been recorded. It has only been seen a few times, filmed and collected by remotely operated vehicles, so almost nothing is known about what might feed on it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Has no sleep in any usual sense: it is a fixed, brainless animal living in constant darkness about 3,300 metres down. No daily or seasonal cycle of activity has been recorded, since only a few individuals have ever been observed.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan has not been documented for this species; how long it lives and how fast it grows are both unknown.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The swollen ball at the tip of each upright branch appears to produce packets of sperm, which are released into the water. Eggs have been found developing in swellings partway along the branches, suggesting fertilisation follows capture of another sponge's sperm packets.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: No differences between the sexes have been described, and it is not known whether each individual produces both sperm and eggs.

entries.name: Harris's Hawk
entries.heroTitle: Harris's Hawk — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A dark brown, long-legged hawk of dry country from the south-western United States to Chile and Argentina, Harris's hawk is one of very few birds of prey that hunt in groups. Parties of two to six birds surround a rabbit or hare, flush it from cover and take turns leading the chase, then share the kill.
identification: Dark brown body with chestnut shoulders and thighs
White rump and white tip to a black tail
Long yellow legs and yellow skin at the bill base
Often perched in groups of two or more
Broad, rounded wings with chestnut linings
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Semi-arid country with scattered tall perches: desert with saguaro cactus, mesquite and thorn scrub, dry savanna, and in South America open woodland, marsh edges and farmland. It lives mostly in the lowlands and increasingly in city suburbs with large trees.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Semi-arid country with scattered tall perches: desert with saguaro cactus, mesquite and thorn scrub, dry savanna, and in South America open woodland, marsh edges and farmland. It lives mostly in the lowlands and increasingly in city suburbs with large trees.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 39/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Dark brown body with chestnut shoulders and thighs
White rump and white tip to a black tail
Long yellow legs and yellow skin at the bill base
Often perched in groups of two or more
Broad, rounded wings with chestnut linings
whyInteresting: Birds sometimes stand on each other's backs on a perch, two or three high, a habit known as back-standing.
Sociable and easy to train, it is widely used in falconry and is flown at airports and landfill sites to scare away gulls and pigeons.
John James Audubon named the species after his friend and supporter Edward Harris.
Nesting has been recorded in most months of the year, and a group may raise two or even three broods in twelve months.
Studies of groups in Arizona and New Mexico found a rank order in which the breeding female was dominant over the males.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly medium-sized mammals such as cottontail rabbits, jackrabbits, ground squirrels and woodrats, along with quail and other birds, lizards and large insects. It hunts from perches or in low flight and seizes prey on the ground with its feet.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Great horned owls, coyotes and ravens take eggs, nestlings and occasionally adults. Group members join forces to mob intruders near the nest. Electrocution on overhead electricity poles, collisions and shooting are the main losses caused by people.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, hunting most actively in the cooler hours after dawn and before dusk and perching in shade through hot afternoons. Group members often roost together at night in tall trees, cacti or pylons. It is resident, with no seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Roughly 10 to 12 years in the wild for birds that reach adulthood, and often 20 to 25 years in captivity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Groups build a stick nest in a cactus, tree or pylon. The clutch of two to four eggs is incubated for about 35 days, and chicks fledge at around six weeks. Older offspring often stay on and help to feed later broods.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is alike in both sexes. Females are markedly larger, averaging about 1 kilogram against roughly 700 grams for males.

entries.name: Hawaiian Crow
entries.heroTitle: Hawaiian Crow — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Native only to Hawaiʻi Island, this large dark crow, the ʻalalā, disappeared from the wild in 2002 and has survived through captive breeding. A study published in 2016 found that almost all tested birds used sticks as tools to pry food from holes in wood, a skill seen in very few birds.
identification: Dull sooty brown-black plumage without strong gloss
Thick, deep bill with bristly feathers at its base
Rounded wings and a fairly short, rounded tail
Wide range of loud caws, croaks and gurgling calls
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Formerly dry and wet native forest on the western and southern slopes of Hawaiʻi Island, mainly at middle elevations where ʻōhiʻa and koa trees and a rich fruiting understorey grow.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america. Formerly dry and wet native forest on the western and southern slopes of Hawaiʻi Island, mainly at middle elevations where ʻōhiʻa and koa trees and a rich fruiting understorey grow.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 98/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Dull sooty brown-black plumage without strong gloss
Thick, deep bill with bristly feathers at its base
Rounded wings and a fairly short, rounded tail
Wide range of loud caws, croaks and gurgling calls
whyInteresting: It is one of the largest surviving native forest birds of Hawaiʻi, roughly the size of a carrion crow.
Seeds pass through its gut unharmed, so its loss from the wild affects how many Hawaiian forest plants spread.
The captive population is kept at two breeding centres, one on Hawaiʻi Island and one on Maui.
Hawaiian cultural tradition treats the 'alalā as an ʻaumakua, a family guardian spirit, for some families.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An omnivore that eats the fruits of many native plants, along with insects and other invertebrates, eggs and nestlings of other birds, and carrion. It forages from the ground to the canopy and probes bark and crevices.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: The native Hawaiian hawk, or ʻio, is its main natural predator. Introduced cats, rats and mongooses, avian malaria and toxoplasmosis also killed wild birds. It mobs hawks with loud calls and takes cover in dense canopy.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. Wild birds roosted overnight in forest trees, but their daily routine was never studied in detail.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive birds commonly live 15 to 20 years or more; how long wild birds lived was never measured well before the species vanished from the wild.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs build a stick nest in a tree. The female lays about 1 to 5 eggs and incubates them for roughly three weeks while the male feeds her. Young leave the nest at about 40 days and stay with the parents for months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the same dark plumage. Males are somewhat larger, with a heavier bill, but the difference is hard to see without both birds side by side.

entries.name: Hazel Dormouse
entries.heroTitle: Hazel Dormouse — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A small golden rodent of European woodland that spends much of the year in deep hibernation. From about October to April it lies curled in a nest on or under the ground, its body temperature falling close to that of the surrounding air.
identification: Rich golden-orange fur with a paler cream throat
Thick, fully furred tail about as long as the body
Large, prominent black eyes
Head and body only about 6 to 9 cm long
Small, rounded ears set close to the head
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe. Broadleaved woodland with a dense, varied understorey, especially coppiced hazel with bramble, as well as overgrown hedgerows, scrub and plantation edges. It occurs across much of Europe, from lowlands into hills.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe. Broadleaved woodland with a dense, varied understorey, especially coppiced hazel with bramble, as well as overgrown hedgerows, scrub and plantation edges. It occurs across much of Europe, from lowlands into hills.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 45/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Rich golden-orange fur with a paler cream throat
Thick, fully furred tail about as long as the body
Large, prominent black eyes
Head and body only about 6 to 9 cm long
Small, rounded ears set close to the head
whyInteresting: Hazelnuts it has eaten carry a smooth round hole with tooth marks angled around the rim, a sign used in surveys.
It lacks a caecum, the gut chamber many rodents use to ferment plant fibre, so it cannot digest tough leaves.
It moves along connected branches, so gaps in hedgerows and woodland can isolate populations.
British monitoring suggests numbers there have roughly halved since the year 2000.
In Britain it is legally protected, and disturbing or handling one requires a licence.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds in the branches on whatever is in season: flowers and pollen in spring, insects such as caterpillars and aphids in summer, then berries and hazelnuts to build fat before winter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, weasels, domestic cats and, while it hibernates on the ground, foxes and badgers may take it. If grabbed by the tail, the skin can slip off and let it escape.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal, climbing through shrubs and canopy after dark. By day it sleeps in a woven ball of stripped honeysuckle bark and leaves in a bush, tree hole or nest box, dropping into torpor on cold or wet days.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Up to about five years in the wild, which is long for such a small rodent; many die in their first winter.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually one litter a year, sometimes two, born in summer after a gestation of about 22 to 24 days. Litters are typically of three to five blind, naked young, which stay with the mother for around six to eight weeks.

entries.heroTitle: Himalayan Monal — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A pheasant of the high Himalaya that makes its living as a digger. The strong, curved bill turns over soil, and snow in winter, to reach buried food, leaving freshly dug patches across the slopes.

It is classed as Least Concern, being widespread along the Himalaya and still common in places.
Its metallic colours come from the microscopic structure of the feathers, not from pigment, so they shift with the angle of the light.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Himalayan Monal feeds on roots, tubers, seeds, berries, insects, and grubs dug from mountain soil.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Red foxes, yellow-throated martens and large eagles are its likely natural enemies, and people hunt it for meat and plumage. A bird put up from the ground hurtles away downhill, while a hen on eggs relies on her brown plumage and sits tight.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It feeds by day, mostly in the morning and late afternoon. Himalayan Monal rests in dense shrubs, forest floor cover, and tree roosts. In winter several birds may feed and roost near one another.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is not documented. In captivity monals have reportedly lived for around 15 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The hen lays 3 to 5 pale, brown-spotted eggs in a scrape on the ground, sheltered by a rock, bush or tree roots, and incubates them alone for about four weeks. Chicks walk and feed themselves soon after hatching and stay with her for several months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are iridescent green, purple and copper above and black below, with a plain cinnamon tail. Females are smaller and streaked brown, with a white throat and a short brown crest.

Its loud, rising, whistled calls carry far across valleys and are often the first sign of a covey.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Golden eagles are the main threat from the air; foxes, wolves and snow leopards take birds on the ground, and people hunt it locally. A bird on lookout gives an alarm call and the covey scatters.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Snowcock rests in rock shelters, slope hollows, and covey roosts in open high country. It is active by day, feeding most in the morning and late afternoon, and roosts at night on steep slopes or cliff ledges.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan figures for Tetraogallus himalayensis remain sparse. Coveys forage alpine slopes above the treeline and flush downhill when disturbed.

analysis.summary: One of very few venomous mammals, it delivers toxic saliva along a groove in each of its second lower incisors; the name Solenodon means grooved tooth. It looks like an oversized shrew, about 30 centimetres long without the tail and weighing up to around a kilogram. Its lineage split from that of shrews, moles and hedgehogs in the age of the dinosaurs.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Foraging starts after dark. The day is spent in a burrow, hollow log, rock crevice or cave, often with several family members sharing the same shelter.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Unknown in the wild. One captive animal lived about 11 years, though most have survived far less in captivity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Litters are of one or two young, sometimes three, born in a nest burrow, with up to two litters a year. The female has only two teats, set far back near the rump, and the young stay with her for several months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes look broadly similar. No consistent difference in size or coat colour is known, and they cannot be separated by sight in the field.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably up to about 10 to 15 years in the wild; figures specific to this species are scarce.

entries.name: Hoff Crab
entries.heroTitle: Hoff Crab — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds mainly on bacteria that grow on the dense bristles covering its underside, combing them off with its mouthparts. Sitting in warm vent flow supplies the chemicals those bacteria need to grow.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Seven-armed sea stars and sea spiders at the cooler edges of the vent fields have been reported feeding on these crabs. Other predators have not been documented.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It lives in permanent darkness with no day and night cycle, and no rest pattern has been documented.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Kiwa tyleri has no published lifespan figure; the yeti crab clusters on East Scotia Ridge vents among dense bacterial mats.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Egg-carrying females have been found away from the vents on cooler surrounding rock, suggesting they leave the heat to brood their eggs. Larval development has not been observed.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are reported to grow larger than females and to hold the warmest spots nearest the vent openings, while females and smaller crabs gather further out.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Honey Possum rests in small nests, shrubs, bark, and sheltered vegetation near flowers. fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Many live only a few years, but Tiny succeeds through energetic breeding and repeated use of small protected sites.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay several eggs in stick-filled cavity nests, with males often starting multiple dummy nests nearby.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes look similar, though males sing more persistently and compete around territories and nest sites.

analysis.summary: The caterpillar of this small grey moth never leaves home. It spins a silk case, coats the outside with sand grains, dust and lint, and drags it along walls as it feeds. The case is open at both ends, and the larva can turn round inside to put its head out of either one.

Only the head and front legs show when the larva walks
Adult forewings are grey with up to four dark spots
Hind wings carry a fringe of long hair-like scales

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Old spider webs are the larva's main food, along with wool, other animal fibres and the remains of dead insects. In one rearing study larvae ate wool but refused cotton.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Small parasitic wasps have been reared from the larvae. House spiders, geckos and ants probably take others. A threatened larva withdraws and pulls the underside of the case up to shut the opening.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: The larva's daily rhythm is poorly documented; it feeds and rests inside its case wherever it happens to be on a wall. Adult moths sit on walls and along floor edges with the wings folded.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Development from egg to adult takes roughly two to three months in laboratory rearing. How long the adult moth lives is not well documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female glues her eggs singly to debris in crevices and along the join of wall and floor; rearing studies report up to about 200. The larva passes through several stages over roughly seven weeks before pupating.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger than males, but both are small, with a wingspan of roughly a centimetre, and the sexes are hard to tell apart in the field.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults drink nectar and eat pollen from open, shallow flowers; females need pollen protein to mature their eggs. Larvae differ by species: many hunt aphids, others filter bacteria from stagnant water, feed in decaying wood or bore into plant bulbs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Crab spiders waiting on flowers, birds, dragonflies, robber flies and social wasps catch adults, and parasitic wasps attack the larvae. Wasp-like or bee-like colours make many birds hesitate, and adults escape by fast, agile flight.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, mainly in sunshine and warm, calm air. At night and in cold or wet weather adults rest on vegetation, often under leaves or on flower heads.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults typically live from a few days to a few weeks. Females of some species, such as the marmalade hoverfly, overwinter as adults and survive for several months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females of aphid-eating species lay single white eggs beside aphid colonies, often several hundred in a lifetime. The legless larva feeds for one to three weeks and then pupates, and several generations a year are common. Other species lay in wet, decaying matter.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In most species the male's eyes meet on top of the head, while the female's are separated by a gap. Females usually have a more pointed abdomen; colour patterns are otherwise similar.

entries.name: Human
entries.heroTitle: Human — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Humans are large upright primates that walk on two legs, leaving the hands free to carry, make and throw. A large brain, spoken language and the use of fire let people live in groups that share food, knowledge and the care of children.

Modern humans now occupy every major terrestrial region and an exceptionally broad range of environments, from tropical forest and grassland to deserts, high mountains, polar settlements and dense cities.

People cool themselves by sweating over almost the whole body, which allows long-distance running in heat that stops most mammals.
The whites of human eyes are unusually visible, so others can see where a person is looking.
All living people belong to one species that arose in Africa about 300,000 years ago.
Humans share about 98 to 99 percent of their DNA with chimpanzees and bonobos, their closest living relatives.
