fieldGuide.dietSummary: An omnivore that eats plants, fruit, seeds, roots, meat, fish, eggs, milk and honey, varying widely between cultures. Nearly all food is prepared first by cutting, grinding, fermenting or cooking, which makes it easier to chew and digest.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators today; big cats, crocodiles, bears and sharks occasionally kill people. Disease, accidents and other humans are far greater dangers. Defence relies on living in groups, building shelter and using tools and fire.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. Adults sleep about seven to nine hours in one block at night, usually in a fixed, sheltered place, and infants sleep far longer in shorter spells.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 70 to 80 years on average where health care is good, and rarely beyond 110; the oldest documented person lived to 122.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pregnancy lasts about nine months and usually produces one baby, born helpless and needing years of care. Children are raised by both parents, grandparents and others, and childhood lasts longer than in any other primate.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Men are on average about 10 to 15 percent heavier and several centimetres taller than women, with more facial and body hair and a deeper voice. Women have broader hips and live a few years longer on average.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small schooling fish, chiefly anchoveta and sardines, with some squid and crustaceans. It hunts by sight in pursuit dives, mostly within a few tens of metres of the surface, and usually feeds within a day's swim of the colony while raising chicks.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: At sea, sea lions, fur seals and sharks take adults; on land, gulls and foxes take eggs and chicks. Greater losses come from El Niño years, when warm water drives the fish away, and from drowning in fishing nets.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Birds leave for the sea around dawn and come ashore again by dusk. Nights are spent on land, in the burrow when breeding or standing on the rocks among the colony.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 15 to 20 years in the wild for birds that reach adulthood; zoo birds have lived past 30.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The clutch is two eggs, incubated for about 40 days by both parents in turn. Chicks leave for the sea at roughly 10 to 12 weeks. Eggs can be laid in most months, and a pair may raise two broods in a good year.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is the same in both sexes. Males average slightly larger, with a heavier head and deeper bill, a difference hard to judge unless the two birds of a pair stand together.

entries.name: Ili Pika
entries.heroTitle: Ili Pika — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Known only from the Tian Shan mountains of Xinjiang in north-west China, this large pika lives on bare rock faces and boulder slopes at roughly 2,800 to 4,100 metres. In the short summer it cuts vegetation and leaves it to dry on the rocks, building a store of hay for the winter.
identification: Rusty-red patches on the forehead, crown and neck
Large rounded ears, big even for a pika
About 20 centimetres long with no visible tail
Sits hunched on ledges close to a crevice
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: central_asia, east_asia. Cold rocky slopes and talus fields fit because preparation must happen before snow closes the menu.

whyInteresting: It was discovered in 1983 by the Chinese conservationist Li Weidong and formally described three years later.
Surveys suggest numbers have fallen sharply since the 1990s, perhaps to fewer than about 1,000 adults, and the IUCN Red List classes it as Endangered.
It does not dig burrows, using existing cracks and cavities in the rock instead.
Animals live at low density, well spaced along the cliffs, rather than in crowded colonies.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, herbs, leaves, and stored haypiles.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Weasels, foxes, raptors, climate warming, and habitat pressure threaten pikas, making rock refuge and stored food important.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Ili Pikas are active in cool alpine windows, feeding and gathering while sheltering in rocks when heat or danger rises.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They often live several years, if enough alpine vegetation, rock shelter, and cool conditions remain stable through seasons.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females produce litters in sheltered rock spaces, giving young immediate access to the same crevice refuge and prepared food landscape.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar to casual view; the shared preparation behavior matters more than visual difference in this small alpine mammal.

analysis.summary: At rest this big rainforest moth folds its brown forewings, each marked with a midrib-like line, and passes for a dead leaf. A fully grown caterpillar is reported to draw leaves together with silk to form the shelter in which it pupates.
identification: Very large moth with a broad, heavy body
Brown forewings with a pointed tip and fine mottling
Dark hindwings with a bright pinkish or orange patch
Large smooth caterpillar with eyespots on the front segments

whyInteresting: The bright hindwing patch stays hidden under the forewings at rest and shows only when the moth opens its wings.
The southern population, in south-east Queensland and north-east New South Wales, is the subspecies smithersi, known as the southern pink underwing moth.
The genus name Phyllodes comes from the Greek for leaf-like, after the shape and colour of the forewings.
It is among the moths recorded piercing citrus and other cultivated fruit, and the holes it leaves can let rot set in.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars eat the leaves of rainforest vines in the moonseed family; in eastern Australia the recorded host is Carronia. Adults pierce ripe and overripe fruit with a stout, toothed proboscis and suck the juice.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds and other insect-eaters take adults and larvae, and bats probably catch flying moths. A disturbed caterpillar arches its front end to show large eyespots. Clearing of lowland rainforest is the main threat to some populations.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults fly and feed at night and spend the day motionless among foliage or leaf litter, wings folded over the body.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long Phyllodes imperialis adults live is unpublished; the large larva pupates inside a shelter of folded leaves.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are thought to be laid singly or a few at a time on the host vine. Each caterpillar feeds alone through several moults, and there is no parental care after laying.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Reliable field marks separating males from females have not been documented in general sources; both sexes share the same wing pattern.

entries.name: Indian Earthworm
entries.heroTitle: Indian Earthworm — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Swallowing soil along with rotting leaves, this burrowing earthworm digests the organic part and leaves the rest as crumbly casts, mixing and loosening the soil as its tunnels let air and water in. It is common in moist soils of South and Southeast Asia and is widely used for teaching earthworm anatomy.
identification: Long, cylindrical body divided into about 100 to 120 ring-like segments
Brownish colour with a darker line along the back
Thickened glandular band, the clitellum, around segments 14 to 16
Rings of tiny bristles on most segments, felt when stroked backwards
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Damp, loose soil rich in decaying plant matter: garden beds, lawns, field margins, compost heaps and the banks of ponds and ditches, mostly in the upper layers of soil.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Damp, loose soil rich in decaying plant matter: garden beds, lawns, field margins, compost heaps and the banks of ponds and ditches, mostly in the upper layers of soil.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 8/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Long, cylindrical body divided into about 100 to 120 ring-like segments
Brownish colour with a darker line along the back
Thickened glandular band, the clitellum, around segments 14 to 16

whyInteresting: A single female genital pore lies on segment 14, and a pair of male pores open on segment 18.
Four pairs of spermathecae, small pouches that store sperm received from a partner, open in the grooves between segments 5 and 9.
Excretion is handled by three kinds of nephridia, septal, integumentary and pharyngeal, rather than by a single pair of kidneys.
A pair of short, conical intestinal caeca branches off the gut in segment 26.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Decaying leaves and other plant debris are its food. The muscular pharynx sucks material in, the gizzard grinds it, and the intestine digests it.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators include birds, frogs, toads, snakes and shrews, as for other earthworms of the region. When disturbed it retreats deep into its burrow and grips the tunnel wall with its bristles.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal: it stays in its burrow by day and comes near the surface at night, especially when the ground is wet.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild is not well documented; field estimates for this species are lacking, and it is generally thought to live about one to two years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Two worms exchange sperm when mating. The clitellum then secretes a cocoon that receives eggs and stored sperm; after roughly three weeks young worms hatch directly from it without a larval stage, textbook accounts giving from two to about twenty per cocoon, commonly around four.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: There are no separate sexes: every adult carries both male and female organs, so individuals cannot be told apart by sex.

entries.name: Indian Pied Myna
entries.heroTitle: Indian Pied Myna — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Indian Pied Myna AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A black-and-white starling of farmland and villages that lives socially all year. Flocks feed together by day and at sunset stream into shared roosts in dense trees, bamboo or reed beds, often mixed with other mynas, chattering loudly until dark.
identification: Black head, breast and back with a white cheek patch
Bare orange skin around the eye
Stout yellow bill with a reddish base
White wing bar and rump flash in flight
Walks with a jaunty, upright gait on the ground
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Pied Mynas are native to the Indian subcontinent and extend into parts of mainland Southeast Asia. They favour open farmland, grassland, wetlands, villages, gardens, and other human-modified habitats.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Pied Mynas are native to the Indian subcontinent and extend into parts of mainland Southeast Asia. They favour open farmland, grassland, wetlands, villages, gardens, and other human-modified habitats.

Bare orange skin around the eye

whyInteresting: Its song is a varied, liquid mix of whistles, chuckles and creaking notes, often given by pairs calling together.
Populations formerly lumped with it in Thailand, Java and Bali are now often treated as separate species.
It sometimes nests on buildings and utility poles as well as in trees.
Like many starlings, it pushes its closed bill into soil and then opens it, prising the ground apart to expose prey.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Forages mainly on the ground, walking and probing soil and short grass for grubs, earthworms, grasshoppers and beetles. It also eats fruit, grain and nectar, and follows livestock and ploughs for disturbed insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks and other raptors take adults, and crows and other nest robbers take eggs and chicks. Flocks give harsh alarm calls, gather to mob a predator, and fly up together when one attacks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active from dawn until dusk, often resting in shade at midday in hot weather. Nights are spent perched in dense cover.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No ringing series yet yields a firm lifespan for Gracupica contra; flocks stream at dusk into shared roosts in trees, bamboo or reeds.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Both birds build a large, untidy domed nest of grass, straw and rubbish in a tree, often near houses. The clutch is usually about four to six glossy blue eggs, incubated for roughly two weeks, and both parents feed the chicks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in plumage and size, and cannot be reliably told apart in the field.

entries.name: Indo-Pacific Horseshoe Crab

analysis.summary: Indo-Pacific Horseshoe Crab teaches Unchanged Design. Its body plan has worked for hundreds of millions of years, and it survives by ploughing soft mud that almost nothing else contests.
identification: Hinged horseshoe-shaped shell with a long rigid tail spine
Ten legs hidden beneath the shell, used to plough and to feed
Blue, copper-based blood
Mass spawning on tidal flats around the highest tides
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, south_asia, east_asia. Soft mud and sand in shallow coastal water, mangroves and estuaries, because Unchanged Design suits a life ploughing sediment where competition is thin.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia, south_asia, east_asia. Soft mud and sand in shallow coastal water, mangroves and estuaries, because Unchanged Design suits a life ploughing sediment where competition is thin.

whyInteresting: It is not a crab at all — horseshoe crabs are closer to spiders and scorpions.
Their blue blood clots around bacterial toxins, and the same reaction is used to test medical equipment for contamination.
The tail spine is not a weapon; it is a lever for righting an overturned animal.
They come ashore to spawn in numbers timed to the highest tides.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Worms, small molluscs and other soft-bodied animals crushed by the leg bases.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sharks, rays, sea turtles and shorebirds taking eggs and juveniles. The shell handles most of it; the real threats now are habitat loss and harvesting.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They move with the tides more than with the sun, ploughing the shallows and burying themselves when the water drops. Their rhythm belongs to the moon.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Tachypleus gigas moults many times across roughly a decade before breeding, and spawning adults are often aged ten years or more; a single wild maximum is still unsettled.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female crawls up the beach with a male clasped to her shell and digs a series of shallow nests in the sand, each thought to hold a few hundred eggs that he fertilises as they are laid. Tailless young hatch, reportedly after several weeks, and get no care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are noticeably larger; males have modified front claws for holding on during spawning.

entries.name: Indochinese Tiger
entries.heroTitle: Indochinese Tiger — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Indochinese Tiger is shadow power in forest form. Its stripes, muscle, and solitary stalking show that the greatest force is often the one the forest hides best.
identification: Striped forest camouflage
Solitary ambush hunting
Powerful muscular body
Silent padded movement
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Indochinese Tigers live in tropical and subtropical forests, rugged hills, and remote protected landscapes.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Indochinese Tigers live in tropical and subtropical forests, rugged hills, and remote protected landscapes.

Solitary ambush hunting
Powerful muscular body
Silent padded movement
whyInteresting: Indochinese Tigers are adapted to forests and rugged landscapes of mainland Southeast Asia.
Each tiger needs large territories and healthy prey populations.
Their stripes break up the body outline in shadow and vegetation.
They are highly threatened by habitat loss, poaching, and prey decline.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Takes mainly large hoofed mammals such as sambar, muntjac, wild pig and young gaur or banteng, stalking close under cover before a short rush that ends with a bite to the throat or neck. Smaller animals are taken when large prey is scarce.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adult tigers have few natural predators, but humans are the major threat through poaching, conflict, and habitat loss.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are often active at night, dusk, and dawn, resting in cover during hotter hours.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild tigers may live around 10 to 15 years, with longer lives possible in care. Their lifespan is tied to territory, prey, and secrecy — the hidden conditions behind visible strength.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Litters of usually two to four cubs are born blind after a gestation of about 100 to 110 days, in a den hidden in thick cover or among rocks. The mother raises them alone; they follow her on hunts from a few months old and leave at about two years.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger than females, but both carry stripes and solitary hunting skill.

entries.name: Io Moth
entries.heroTitle: Io Moth — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Io Moth teaches Illusion Defense through a sudden hidden face. Its quiet forewings can hide large hindwing eyespots until a bird or small predator gets too close, then the moth flashes a bigger-looking gaze to interrupt the attack. Its lesson is not brute strength; it is the power of surprise, timing, and a believable warning.
identification: Wingspan is roughly 5 to 8 centimetres.
Body and legs are stout and densely furred.
Each hindwing eyespot is black and blue with a white dash at the centre.
Full-grown caterpillars are pale green with a red and white stripe along each side.

whyInteresting: The species is named after Io, a priestess in Greek myth who was loved by Zeus and turned into a heifer.
Young caterpillars travel in single file, each following the one in front, as they move between feeding and resting places.
Numbers have fallen in parts of the north-eastern United States, and a parasitic fly introduced to control spongy moths is one suspected cause.
It belongs to the giant silk moths, the family Saturniidae, but is one of the smaller North American members.
Females release a scent after dark that males detect with their antennae and follow upwind.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars eat the leaves of a very wide range of trees, shrubs and herbs, among them willow, cherry, hackberry, redbud, elm, clover and maize. Adult moths have reduced mouthparts and do not feed.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, bats and small mammals take the adults, and parasitic flies and wasps attack the caterpillars. The caterpillar is armed with branching spines that carry venom and sting sharply on contact.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults fly at dusk and through the night, and often come to lights. By day they rest motionless on trunks, twigs or among dead leaves.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults live about one to two weeks. The full life cycle takes a year in the north, where the pupa overwinters; in the far south several generations fit into a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay clusters of about 20 or more eggs on the leaves or stems of a food plant, and these hatch in roughly one to two weeks. Young caterpillars are orange-brown and feed in groups, spreading out as they grow, then pupate in a thin, papery cocoon among leaf litter.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have bright yellow forewings and broad, feathery antennae. Females are larger, with reddish-brown to purplish-brown forewings and thin antennae.

analysis.summary: The shining blue of the male is made not by pigment but by a spongy layer of keratin and tiny air spaces inside each feather barb, which scatters blue light. Short, stout black bill

The only other member of its family is the Philippine Fairy-bluebird; the leafbirds were once grouped with them but are now kept separate.
The species name puella is Latin for girl.
It is not considered globally threatened, but it depends on tall forest and disappears where lowland forest is cleared.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly ripe fruit, especially figs, plucked in the canopy, with nectar taken from flowering trees and some insects, particularly when feeding young.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Specific predators of this species have not been documented, and how it responds to an attack has not been described.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, feeding in the canopy from early morning, with a quieter spell in the midday heat. Its night roosts have not been well described but are presumably in dense foliage of tall trees. It has no seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly documented: too few fairy-bluebirds have been ringed and recaptured to give a reliable age.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The nest is a shallow cup of twigs and rootlets, often lined with moss, placed in a fork of a sapling or small tree. The clutch is usually two eggs; incubation is thought to be by the female, and both parents feed the chicks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are brilliant blue above and velvety black below; females are dull turquoise-blue all over with darker wings and tail.

entries.name: Iridescent Shark
entries.heroTitle: Iridescent Shark — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Iridescent Shark teaches Schooling Momentum through active group life. Open-water swimming, silver movement, river origins, and schooling dynamics make individual motion stronger when it joins shared direction. Its lesson is that momentum grows when many bodies flow together.
identification: Shark-like outline with a tall, pointed dorsal fin
Smooth skin without scales
Two pairs of short barbels beside the mouth

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning and larval care have been little studied in this species. Each summer's bloom comes from young jellyfish released by small polyps fixed to hard surfaces on the seabed.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Male and female medusae are outwardly identical. Nothing distinguishes them because a bloom reproduces by broadcast rather than by pairing.

entries.name: Japanese Spider Crab

featuredImage.alt: Japanese Spider Crab AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: It has the greatest leg span of any living arthropod: large males are reported to reach about 3.7 metres from claw tip to claw tip, though the body between the legs is only about 40 centimetres across. It walks the seabed off Japan's Pacific coast, mostly at depths of roughly 50 to 600 metres.

The body is orange and the legs are blotched with white
Short spines and knobs cover the top of the shell
Two thin spines project forward between the eyes

analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: east_asia, north_pacific. Deep coastal waters, rocky seabeds, and continental shelf slopes near Japan.

whyInteresting: Adults are reported to move into shallower water, around 50 metres, to breed in spring, a season when fishing for them is closed in Japan.
Smaller crabs have been seen fixing sponges and other seabed animals to their shells, which helps to hide them.
In Japan it is called taka-ashi-gani, which means tall-legged crab.
It is the only living member of its genus; its closest relatives are known only as fossils.
The species name honours Engelbert Kaempfer, a German physician who wrote about the natural history of Japan in the late 1600s.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Japanese Spider Crabs can live for many decades, making Long-Reach Patience a deep-sea version of slow endurance.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males often have larger claws and longer legs, while females carry eggs; both show the long-reach body plan.

Thought to have reached Singapore as escaped cage birds around the 1920s, it is now often counted as the most numerous bird on the island.
An alternative English name is the white-vented myna.
It walks and runs across open ground rather than hopping, often in pairs or small parties.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not measured for wild birds of this species. A few years is probably typical, and captive mynas of this genus have lived beyond 10.

entries.name: Javan Pond Heron

analysis.summary: At rest it is brown and easily overlooked, but the wings and tail are pure white, so a bird put up from a paddy seems to change colour as it takes off. This small, stocky heron ranges from mainland South-East Asia to Java and Bali.

whyInteresting: Outside the breeding season it is almost impossible to tell from the Chinese pond heron where the two occur together.
Short legs keep it to very shallow water, and it often hunts from floating plants, banks or the low walls between rice paddies.
It is thought to have gained from the spread of irrigated rice, and it is not considered globally threatened.
It is one of six pond herons in the genus Ardeola, which also includes the squacco heron of Africa and Europe.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, snakes, monitor lizards, mammals, and nest predators threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds by day, most actively in the early morning and towards dusk. In the evening birds fly to shared roosts in trees, bamboo or mangroves, often alongside egrets.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not documented for this species. Judging by ringed herons of similar size, a bird that survives its first year may live around 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests in colonies, often mixed with egrets and other herons, in trees or bamboo near water. The clutch is usually 3 to 5 pale greenish-blue eggs laid on a platform of sticks, and both parents feed the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes look similar; breeding plumage matters more than sex. Males and females take on the same breeding colours and return to the same streaked brown afterwards, and no reliable way of sexing birds in the field is known.

entries.name: Javan Rusa Deer
entries.heroTitle: Javan Rusa Deer — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Javan Rusa Deer AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: In the rut a stag thrashes grass and bushes with his antlers and often walks about with a tangle of vegetation draped over them. For much of the year the sexes live apart: hinds and their young gather in herds on open grassland, sometimes dozens strong, while mature stags keep to themselves or to small groups.
identification: Stags' antlers are lyre-shaped with three points on each side
Coat is coarse and greyish-brown, paler on the belly
Ears are large and rounded
Build is stocky, with fairly short legs

analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia, java, bali. Savanna grassland, open dry forest, scrub and forest edge on Java and Bali, mainly in the lowlands. It does best where grassland and cover lie side by side.

whyInteresting: People have carried the species far beyond its home: introduced herds live wild in New Guinea, Australia and New Caledonia.
Dutch settlers took it from Java to Mauritius in the seventeenth century, and it is still ranched there for venison.
It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, because native populations on Java and Bali have declined.
Stags are noisy in the rut, giving loud, shrill bellows that carry across open country.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly a grazer, cropping grasses and herbs, with leaves, shoots and fallen fruit taken as well. It is reported to drink seldom, getting much of its water from its food.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hunting and the loss of grassland do more harm than any predator. Javan leopards and dholes are the natural predators, and pythons may take calves; a herd that senses danger bolts for cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active at dawn, dusk and through the night, grazing in the open, and becomes more nocturnal where it is hunted. It rests and chews the cud in shade or forest cover during the heat of the day. It has no seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 15 to 20 years in captivity. Wild deer seldom live as long, and good figures from the wild are lacking.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A hind carries a single calf, rarely twins, for about eight months. The calf lies hidden in cover for its first weeks and is weaned at around six to eight months. First breeding is reported at anywhere from under two years in well-fed herds to several years in poor conditions.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Stags carry antlers and are much the heavier sex, at up to about 150 kg. Hinds have no antlers, a slimmer neck and roughly half the weight.

entries.name: Javan Surili
entries.heroTitle: Javan Surili — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Found only on the island of Java, this monkey lives almost entirely on leaves. Its large, chambered stomach holds bacteria that break down tough foliage, so it can live on food that most monkeys cannot digest.
identification: Grey back, outer limbs and tail
White throat, chest and belly
Bare, dark grey to black face
Slender body with long legs for leaping
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Tropical rainforest in western and central Java, from remaining lowland patches up into montane forest at around 2,500 m. Most surviving groups live in hill and mountain forest on volcanoes, and it avoids open farmland and plantations.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Tropical rainforest in western and central Java, from remaining lowland patches up into montane forest at around 2,500 m. Most surviving groups live in hill and mountain forest on volcanoes, and it avoids open farmland and plantations.

whyInteresting: It is also known as the grizzled leaf monkey or Javan grizzled langur.
Groups are reported to be small, usually one adult male with several females and their young.
The species name comata means long-haired, a reference to the crest on its crown.
Its long tail cannot grip branches; it serves as a counterweight for balance when leaping.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly young leaves, with fruit, seeds and flowers eaten when available. It feeds in the canopy, pulling leafy twigs towards the mouth, and seldom comes down to the ground.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Forest loss and capture for the pet trade threaten it far more than natural enemies, though Javan leopards and large eagles such as the Javan hawk-eagle probably take some. Groups either freeze silently or flee through the canopy while the male calls in alarm.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, most active in the early morning and late afternoon, with rest in the canopy around midday. Groups sleep high in tall trees at night; sleeping sites are not well documented. There is no seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Presbytis comata still lacks published wild lifespan figures; its chambered stomach ferments tough leaves high in the Javan canopy.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single infant is born at a time. Newborns of surilis and related leaf monkeys of the genus Presbytis have very pale coats that darken with age, and this is thought to hold here too; gestation length and birth spacing are not well documented.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in colour; males are only slightly larger, and the sexes are hard to tell apart in the field.

entries.name: Javanese Grasshopper

analysis.summary: Mottled brown-to-green colouring, varying from one individual to the next, lets this large, heavy-bodied grasshopper blend with the stems and dead leaves where it rests. It often stays still until closely approached, then leaps or flies off.

Dark antennae, as the name nigricornis suggests
Peg-like spine on the underside between the front legs
Long wings reaching past the abdomen tip

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, mantises and spiders take nymphs and adults, and small wasps parasitise the eggs in the soil. Adults escape with a powerful jump and kick hard with the spiny hind legs when grabbed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, feeding in warm hours. At night it rests clinging to stems and leaves in the vegetation.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one generation a year: eggs spend several months in the soil, and nymphs and adults live for a few months above ground. Precise adult lifespan is not documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females push the tip of the abdomen into soil and lay a pod of eggs in foam. Wingless nymphs hatch and moult several times before reaching the winged adult stage; there is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are clearly larger and heavier than males, and have short pointed egg-laying valves at the abdomen tip.

entries.name: Jerusalem Cricket

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Skunks, owls, coyotes, foxes and snakes eat them. When threatened it rears up, kicks with its legs, bites hard and releases a foul smell.

It swims by rippling its soft second dorsal and anal fins, creeping towards prey without flexing its body.
Most are about 30 to 40 cm long; exceptional fish have been reported at up to about 90 cm.
It is a highly prized food fish in Europe, much of it landed as bycatch rather than by a directed fishery.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sharks and larger bony fish take it. A deep body and stiff dorsal spines make it awkward to swallow.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: A daytime hunter that stalks prey by sight. Its behaviour at night is little studied; it is thought to rest near the seabed. It has no dormancy, but in some areas moves inshore in summer.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike, though females are reported to grow larger on average.

entries.name: June Beetle
entries.heroTitle: June Beetle — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Stout brown scarab beetles of North American lawns, fields and woodland edges, which spend most of their lives underground as white, C-shaped grubs feeding on roots. New adults form in autumn yet wait in the soil through winter, surfacing on warm evenings in late spring to fly, feed on tree leaves and mate.

whyInteresting: Pyrgota flies are reported to attack the beetles in flight at night, laying an egg under the raised wing cases; the maggot kills its host from within.
Phyllophaga means leaf eater in Greek, after the adults' habit of stripping tree foliage at night.
In species with a three-year cycle the grubs feed most heavily in their second summer, when most of the damage to turf and crops is done.
Heavy grub feeding can sever grass roots so completely that the dead turf rolls back like a loose carpet.
Adults are also called May beetles or June bugs, after the months when they swarm to lights.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grubs chew the roots of grasses, cereals, maize, potatoes, strawberries and tree seedlings, along with decaying matter in the soil. Adults eat the leaves of oak, hickory, walnut, elm and other broadleaved trees and shrubs, feeding after dark.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, bats, skunks, raccoons, and parasitic wasps threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are nocturnal, flying from dusk and feeding in tree canopies at night, then dropping back to burrow into soil or hide under litter before dawn. Grubs feed near the surface in warm months and move deep below the frost in winter.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: One to four years from egg to adult depending on species and latitude, with three years typical in the north. Nearly all of it is spent as a grub; adults above ground last only a few weeks.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females burrow several centimetres into soil and lay a few dozen pearly white eggs, each in a small ball of earth. Eggs hatch in about three to four weeks, and the grubs moult twice over one to three years before pupating in an earthen cell.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males may fly more actively to find females.

whyInteresting: The bill is the diagnostic feature: much deeper and more curved than that of the Carrion or House Crow, and strong enough to open shellfish and carrion.
Urban birds in Japan have been recorded dropping walnuts onto pedestrian crossings and collecting the kernels when traffic stops.
It readily displaces smaller crows at food and will harass raptors many times its weight.
Populations have grown steeply alongside cities across Asia, in step with the amount of edible waste available.
It is one of the most abundant large birds across much of Asia, from lowland coast to Himalayan forest.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Anything: carrion, eggs, nestlings, shellfish, fruit, grain, insects and human refuse. The bill is what makes that breadth real, since the food most competitors cannot open is the food most reliably still there.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large raptors take adults occasionally, and eggs and nestlings are taken by other crows and by martens. Adults are bold, gather quickly to mob a threat and have few consistent predators.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, gathering into large communal roosts at dusk, often in city trees, and dispersing again at first light.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly fifteen to twenty years in the wild.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Three to five eggs in a bulky stick nest in a tall tree or on a pylon. Both parents feed the young, and pairs defend a wide area around the nest aggressively.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look the same; males average slightly larger with a marginally heavier bill, which is not reliable in the field.

entries.name: Kakarratul
entries.heroTitle: Kakarratul — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Kakarratul, the northern marsupial mole, is a small desert mammal that “swims” through loose sand. Its reduced eyes, powerful digging limbs, and secretive habits make hidden movement its main survival design.

No visible eyes and no external ear flaps
Horny shield covering the top of the snout
Two huge, spade-like claws on each forefoot

Many species migrate from the sea or large lakes up rivers to spawn over gravel or rock in fast water.
Some species leap clear of the water; Gulf and Atlantic sturgeons are well known for it, though the reason is still debated.
Electroreceptors on the underside of the snout help sturgeons detect prey hidden in mud.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Fish rest in reduced-activity rhythms rather than beds; shelter, depth, or bottom contact becomes the pause. That fits the lesson because safety is found by staying with structure.

No function has been demonstrated for the long snout, which is an extension of the head and not part of the mouth.
Caterpillars of Epipyrops moths live as parasites clinging to the bodies of lanternflies, and the moth's name means 'upon Pyrops'.
Excess sugar from the sap diet is expelled as droplets of honeydew, which can coat the bark and leaves below.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Sap drawn from the trunks and branches of trees, above all longan and lychee, with mango and other fruit trees also used. It pushes needle-like mouthparts through the bark.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators of this species are poorly recorded. An insect that is approached sidles round to the far side of the trunk, and if pressed it springs off and flies.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are seen by day, clinging head-up to trunks and feeding for long spells without moving. They rest where they feed, on the bark of the host tree.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one year from egg to death where it has been studied, in the north of the range. There is a single generation a year there: adults emerge around early autumn, overwinter and breed the following spring.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females glue their eggs to tree trunks in neat rows and coat them with white wax. In orchards where the species has been studied, batches of roughly 60 to 100 eggs have been reported, hatching after about three to four weeks. The wingless nymphs receive no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the same colours, wing pattern and long snout, and cannot reliably be told apart in the field.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Ripe fruit, especially figs, makes up most of the diet, with young leaves, flowers and insects. It feeds high in the canopy, often hanging by one arm to reach fruit at the tips of branches.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few predators can follow it through the high canopy; leopards, clouded leopards, large pythons and big eagles are possible threats, mainly to young animals. People are the main danger, through hunting, the pet trade and forest clearance. Alarmed gibbons call loudly and move off through the treetops.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Strictly diurnal. The family is usually on the move soon after dawn and retires to a tall sleeping tree by mid or late afternoon, well before dusk, where each animal sleeps sitting upright on a branch.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around 25 years is often cited for wild animals, and captive individuals have been reported living into their 40s.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single infant is born after roughly seven months of gestation, usually two to four years apart. It clings to its mother's belly, is weaned at around two years and stays with the family until roughly eight to ten years old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are similar in size and build, and coat colour is not linked to sex, so the sexes are hard to tell apart by sight. In a duet, the female sings the long rising great call.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Figs, mango, rambutan and langsat are among the fruit taken, with nectar and blossom from durian and coconut. Fruit is crushed against the roof of the mouth; the juice is swallowed and the fibre spat out as a flattened pellet.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: People are the chief threat: it is hunted for meat, shot or netted as an orchard pest, and its roost forest is being cleared. Pythons and large birds of prey are thought to take some at roosts. Disturbed colonies take flight together and circle before resettling.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal. Days are spent hanging in the crowns of tall trees in colonies of hundreds or thousands, dozing, grooming and squabbling over perches. The colony flies out around sunset and returns before dawn.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 15 years is the usual estimate for the wild; captive animals are reported to have lived past 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single pup is born after a pregnancy of about six months; births are reported mainly from March to May, though timing varies with region. The mother carries it on her chest for the first days, then leaves it at the roost; weaning comes at two to three months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look much alike. Males average slightly larger and have stiffer, thicker fur; neither difference is easy to judge on a bat hanging in a tree.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sharks, tunas, billfishes, dolphins and larger hairtails all prey on it. Its defences are fast bursts of swimming and a mirror-bright body that is hard to follow in open water.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No sleep state has been described. Between feeding bouts it is often seen hanging head-up and almost motionless in mid-water, holding position by rippling its long dorsal fin.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Age studies find most fish in catches under about 5 years old; ages up to around 15 years have been reported.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning is prolonged and peaks in warmer months. A large female can release tens of thousands of small floating eggs or more, and there is no parental care; eggs and larvae drift in the plankton.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are coloured alike. Females tend to grow larger and outnumber males among the biggest fish in catches.

whyInteresting: Most of the world population breeds in the north-western Hawaiian Islands, and Midway Atoll holds the largest colony.
At Kaena Point on Oahu, about a third of the pairs studied in the 2000s were two females raising a chick together.
Its white head and body, dark upperwings and dark smudge around the eye give it a gull-like pattern on a wingspan of about 2 metres.
Chicks are fed an energy-rich stomach oil and partly digested squid, brought back after trips lasting days.
Since about the 1980s it has also bred on islands off western Mexico, such as Guadalupe.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Squid are the main food, along with fish eggs, crustaceans, fish and other food taken from the surface. Much of it is caught at night, when squid rise towards the surface, and foraging trips can cover thousands of kilometres.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tiger sharks patrol the breeding atolls to catch fledglings on their first days at sea. Introduced rats and cats, and at Midway house mice, have attacked nesting birds; longline fishing gear, swallowed plastic and storm surges on low islands add to the losses.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Outside the breeding season it rarely comes to land, resting on the sea surface between long flights. At sea it is active by day and night, taking short sleeps on the water; breeding adults rest on or beside the nest at the colony.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Breeding adults often live 30 years or more. A female called Wisdom, ringed at Midway Atoll in 1956, was still laying eggs when over 70.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Each female lays a single egg, usually in November or December, and does not replace it if it is lost. Both parents incubate in shifts for about 65 days and then feed the chick, which fledges after about five to six months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike. Males are on average slightly larger with a heavier bill, but the difference is hard to see in the field.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult lifespan in the wild is not documented; most butterflies of this group live a few weeks as adults.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid on the young shoots and tendrils of the host vines, reportedly in batches rather than singly. Development from egg to adult takes about a month in warm weather, and there is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are bright orange above. Females are paler, with the orange largely replaced by greyish or greenish white.

Long front flippers used for swimming
A snake-like neck when the head is raised

analysis.summary: A slender houndshark of the Pacific coast of North America, usually 1.2 to 1.5 metres long and harmless to people. Schools are often sorted by size and sex, and may include smoothhounds and spiny dogfish swimming alongside.
Genetic studies have found several distinct populations along the California coast, which suggests that most individuals do not travel far.
Females are thought not to breed until they are at least ten years old, which makes the species slow to recover from heavy fishing.
Its species name semifasciata means half-banded, after the dark saddles that cross the back.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Crabs, shrimps, clams, fat innkeeper worms, fish eggs and small fish such as anchovies and herring. It feeds by suction, snapping the mouth open to pull worms out of their burrows, and it bites off the siphons of clams that stick up from the mud.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger sharks hunt it, among them the broadnose sevengill and the great white. Pups keep to eelgrass and very shallow water, where big predators cannot easily follow. People catch it for food, for sport and, as pups, for the aquarium trade.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Swims by day and by night, and can also lie still on the sand because it is able to pump water over its gills. In one study at Santa Catalina Island, sharks gathered in the shallows by day and spread into deeper water after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Estimated at up to about 30 years from growth studies; typical lifespan in the wild is not well known.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs hatch inside the mother and the young are fed by yolk, not a placenta. After 10 to 12 months she gives birth in spring to between 4 and about 30 pups, each roughly 20 centimetres long, in sheltered shallows.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males carry a pair of claspers along the inner edge of the pelvic fins. Females grow larger, reaching about 1.8 metres, while males seldom exceed about 1.5 metres.

featuredImage.alt: Lesser Banded Hornet AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: The Lesser Banded Hornet is unbothered while foraging and immediately serious near the nest. The aggression is not temperament — it is a boundary with a radius, and the whole colony reads it the same way.
identification: Black with one broad orange-yellow band across the abdomen
Large, 22-30 mm, with a heavy deliberate flight
Grey papery nest, often in a tree or under a building eave
Guards patrol at the nest entrance and face outward

whyInteresting: Alarm pheromone released by a disturbed guard recruits the rest of the colony within seconds, which is why one sting is often followed by many.
It can sting repeatedly, since the sting is unbarbed, unlike a honey bee's.
Foragers away from the nest are notably unaggressive and can be watched at close range on flowers.
Colonies hunt honey bees at hive entrances, and Asian beekeepers screen entrances specifically against them.
The single broad band is the field mark that separates it from the other Vespa species across its range.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, especially honey bees and other social wasps, chewed into a paste for the larvae; adults take nectar, sap and fruit. Hunting far from the nest is why foragers can afford to ignore everything on the way.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Honey buzzards raid nests, and birds take individual foragers. Coordinated mass defence is the colony's answer, and it is triggered by proximity rather than by threat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Foraging is diurnal, with guards active at the nest entrance around the clock and a marked increase in defensive response at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Workers live several weeks; a founding queen a year, overwintering alone and starting a new colony in spring.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single queen founds the nest and lays all eggs; workers rear the brood. New queens and males are produced late in the season and mate before the colony breaks up for winter.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Workers and queens are female and sting; the queen is noticeably larger. Males appear late in the season, have longer antennae and cannot sting at all.

whyInteresting: Until a taxonomic revision in the early 2000s it was treated as part of the Java mouse-deer, Tragulus javanicus, now regarded as a separate species.
Despite the name it is not a deer: mouse-deer are chevrotains, an ancient family that split early from other ruminants and never grew antlers.
It chews the cud, but its stomach has only three well-developed chambers rather than the four of cattle and deer.
In Malay and Indonesian folk tales, the clever mouse-deer Sang Kancil outwits crocodiles, tigers and other larger animals.
Males mark their ground and their mates with scent from a gland under the chin.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pythons, leopard cats and other wild cats, civets, large eagles and dogs all kill mouse-deer, and people snare and hunt them widely. When threatened it freezes in cover, then bolts, and an alarmed animal drums the ground rapidly with its hooves.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It is mostly crepuscular or nocturnal, resting hidden in dense cover. Daytime rest is spent lying among tangled roots, fallen logs or thickets, though some daytime movement occurs.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large birds of prey take adults, while eggs and ducklings are lost to predators on the ground and in trees. Hunting and netting by people are a major pressure in places. Flocks flush together at any alarm and circle high before settling.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Largely nocturnal feeders. By day flocks loaf on open water, banks or low branches over the water, dozing close together and moving to feeding areas around dusk.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild has not been well documented, and ringing records for this species are few.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding follows the monsoon in much of South Asia. The nest is in a tree hole, an old nest of another bird, or on the ground among reeds. Clutches usually hold about 7 to 12 white eggs, incubated for roughly three and a half weeks; both parents tend the ducklings.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in plumage and size; the sexes cannot be told apart reliably in the field.

Autumn storms occasionally drive wintering birds inland or onto coasts in large numbers, an event known as a wreck.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Around the colonies, gulls, skuas, foxes, owls, and harsh weather threaten Little Auk. Glaucous gulls snatch adults in flight, while nesting deep among boulders keeps eggs out of reach of most hunters.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: The bird rests at sea and in colony crevices, feeding during long polar daylight. In winter it lives entirely at sea, resting on the water through the long nights.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult survival rates suggest breeding adults live around 8 to 10 years on average; the maximum wild lifespan is not well documented.

analysis.summary: Sea Moth's power is Seafloor Walker: armored bottom-dwelling fish design and modified fins for walking. In sandy seafloor and rubble, this is not a decorative trait; it is how the animal turns armored walking fish into survival. The lesson is specific: use the exact body, rhythm, or tool that your world rewards, instead of forcing a strategy built for somewhere else.

Sea moths belong to the same order as seahorses and pipefishes, the Syngnathiformes, despite their very different body shape.
The small toothless mouth can be pushed forward to suck tiny worms and crustaceans out of the sand.
Adults are small, usually no more than about 10 centimetres long, and are often seen in pairs.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It mainly feeds on small bottom invertebrates. This diet is the reason the principle works: the animal's food is reached through armored walking fish, so the lesson is not simply 'eat to live' but 'solve the meal with the exact tool your body has been given.'
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger bottom-feeding fishes are the likely predators, though attacks are rarely recorded. It relies on keeping still against sand it matches, and its body of fused bony plates makes an awkward, hard mouthful.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active by day, shuffling slowly over the bottom as it feeds. At night it is reported to rest on the seabed, sometimes partly covered with sand.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Age and growth papers do not quote a lifespan for Eurypegasus draconis. Paired fish walk the sand on enlarged pelvic fins while hunting small crustaceans.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs spawn at dusk, rising together off the bottom to release eggs and sperm in open water. The eggs float in the plankton and the larvae drift before settling to the seabed. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are hard to tell apart in the field, and differences in colour or size have not been well described.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Large insects such as beetles and crickets, earthworms, and small mammals, especially voles and mice, with some small birds, lizards and frogs. Insects and worms dominate in summer, rodents more in winter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tawny Owls, Eagle Owls, Goshawks and Common Buzzards take adults, and martens and cats raid nests. When alarmed it bobs and sways its head, crouches flat, or slips back into its nest hole.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Rests by day in a tree hole, barn or rock cleft, often sitting at the entrance in the sun. Activity is mainly at dusk and at night, though it also hunts in daylight, especially when feeding young.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually around 3 to 5 years in the wild, with heavy losses in the first year; a few ringed wild birds have reached about 15 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid in a cavity in a tree, wall, bank or nest box with no added lining. The female usually lays 3 to 5 white eggs and incubates them for about four weeks while the male brings food; young leave the hole at around five weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is identical, and females average only slightly larger. Voice helps more than looks: in spring the male gives a drawn-out, rising hoot, and the female answers with a higher, often hoarser version.

Locusts are collected and eaten as a protein-rich food in parts of Asia and Africa.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Eats grasses and cereal crops such as rice, maize, millet, wheat, sorghum and sugar cane, chewing the leaves with strong jaws. Swarms can strip much of the green growth where they settle.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Storks, kites, bee-eaters and other birds, lizards, rodents and spiders eat nymphs and adults, while larvae of bee-flies and blister beetles feed on egg pods. Adults escape by flying; swarms overwhelm predators by sheer numbers.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, basking in morning sun to warm up before feeding. At night it roosts on grass stems and shrubs; solitary adults often migrate after dark, whereas swarms fly by day. In temperate regions winter is passed only as eggs.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: One generation takes a few months: eggs hatch in about two weeks in warm soil, nymphs develop for four to six weeks, and adults live one to three months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female digs the tip of her abdomen into moist, bare soil and lays a pod of several dozen eggs sealed with a frothy plug, repeating this several times. Wingless nymphs hatch, receive no care, and moult five times before becoming winged adults.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger and heavier, with short, pointed digging valves at the tip of the abdomen; males are smaller with a rounded, upturned tip. Mature males in swarms turn bright yellow.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are broadly similar; the blue areas are said to be less extensive or duller in females, but the difference is hard to judge in the field.

analysis.summary: Colonies of this northern Australian termite build flat, slab-shaped mounds up to about 4 metres tall, with the thin edges pointing north and south and the broad faces turned east and west. The broad sides catch the gentler morning and afternoon sun, while at midday only the narrow top edge faces it, so the mound heats less.

Surveys have found that the average compass bearing of the mounds differs slightly from one site to another.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grass is the staple, mostly dry and dead blades and stems, with some other plant debris. Workers collect it close to the mound, and microbes in their gut help break down the tough plant fibre.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Ants raid colonies, and echidnas break into mounds to feed. Birds, lizards and frogs pick off the winged reproductives when they leave the mound. Workers quickly seal any breach with fresh mud while soldiers guard the opening.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: The colony is active around the clock inside the mound, though individual termites rest in short bouts. Workers are thought to forage outside mainly at night or in cool, humid weather, travelling through covered galleries and avoiding open sun.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Figures for this species are not documented. Colony and queen longevity have not been measured for it; in many mound-building termites colonies persist for years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Winged males and females leave the mound in swarming flights, typically early in the wet season. After landing they shed their wings and pair off to found a new colony. Workers tend the queen's eggs and nymphs, and most young become workers or soldiers.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Unlike ant workers, termite workers and soldiers include both males and females, and they cannot be told apart in the field. The established queen is larger than the king, with an enlarged abdomen.

Some older works treated it as a form of the black rat, Rattus rattus, and the two can be hard to tell apart where they meet.
Many small-island populations were once described under separate names, and most are now included within this one species.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Oil-palm fruit dominates the diet in plantations, eaten both in the palm crowns and from loose fruitlets on the ground. Elsewhere it takes seeds, other fruit, young shoots, insects and other small invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes including pythons and cobras, leopard cats, civets and birds of prey hunt it. It stays hidden by day, moves under cover of vegetation at night and relies on fast climbing and dense frond piles to escape.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly nocturnal. It spends the day in nests of shredded vegetation hidden in dense undergrowth, frond piles or palm crowns, and comes out to forage after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been measured for this species; as with other small wild rats, most individuals probably live less than a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeds through much of the year where food is plentiful. Gestation is probably about three weeks, as in related rats, and litters are reported to hold around four to eight young, born blind and hairless in a grass or frond nest.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot be told apart in the field.

analysis.summary: A large, glossy black scorpion of South-east Asian rainforest that digs its own burrow beneath logs, stones and tree roots or into soft earth banks. The damp, sheltered chamber protects it from drying out, from heat and from many predators.

Pincers broad and heavily granular, much bulkier than the tail
Tail relatively slender, ending in a small sting bulb
Adults about 10 to 12 centimetres long

It is widely sold in the pet trade, and many animals sold under this name are wild-caught.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Against an attacker it pinches hard with its heavy claws first and uses its comparatively weak sting only after that. Its own enemies are barely recorded, though monitor lizards, birds and small carnivores are thought likely to take it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal. By day it stays inside its burrow, and after dark it sits at the entrance or wanders only a short way from it.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: In captivity it commonly lives about 5 to 8 years; lifespan in the wild has not been measured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to live young, usually about 10 to 35 after a pregnancy of several months. The white newborns climb onto their mother's back and ride there until their first moult, then stay near her in the burrow for some time.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are hard to tell apart at a glance. Males usually have longer comb-like pectines under the body, with more teeth, and adult females tend to be bulkier with a broader abdomen.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: 5 to 10 years in the wild when conditions are good.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Introduced red foxes and cats kill chicks and adults, foxes and goannas dig into mounds for eggs, and birds of prey catch young birds. Adults freeze or slip into cover when alarmed and fly up into trees if pressed. Fire and land clearing destroy habitat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, foraging mostly in the cooler morning and late afternoon and resting in shade through the heat. At night it flies up to roost on a branch in a tree or tall shrub.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults may live 25 years or more according to some estimates, but very few chicks survive their first year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female lays eggs singly, several days apart, through spring and summer, often 15 to 25 in a season. Incubation takes about two months; the chick digs itself out, receives no parental care, runs at once and flies within about a day.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look almost identical, and males are only slightly larger on average. At the mound the female can be recognised by her visits to lay, which come every few days through the breeding season.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Harpy-like raptors, cats, snakes, humans, and Atlantic Forest loss threaten sloths, making concealment and steady canopy grip essential.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Maned Sloths rest for long periods in trees, moving slowly when feeding, shifting branches, or descending only when conditions demand.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for many years, especially when forest remains connected enough for slow feeding, resting, and reproduction.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females bear one young at a time; in studied populations births have peaked between February and April. The infant clings to its mother's front, begins eating leaves within its first weeks and leaves her at about 9 to 11 months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males may show a darker mane or marking, while females are less marked; both carry the same slow Atlantic Forest strategy.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Shorebirds, rays and coastal fish, mostly taking juveniles. Its answer is armour, burial in mud, and a shell shape a bird's bill cannot get purchase on.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mangrove Horseshoe Crabs move with the tide rather than the clock, ploughing across flats on the flood and burying on the ebb.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for decades and take years to mature.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in sediment on the upper shore, often with a male attached, and the young pass through many moults.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger, and males have modified front claws for gripping a female's shell during spawning. The difference is functional, built for holding on through moving water.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: The diet covers fish, squid, crustaceans, and marine scraps taken by surface feeding or diving. Sprats, young herring and sandeels are the commonest prey, often caught in short wing-propelled dives.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: On land, skuas, gulls, rats, cats, and other colony predators threaten Shearwater. Adults are clumsy on the ground, and colonies on islands such as Lundy have grown after rats were removed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeding is by day at sea; in the evening birds gather in rafts offshore and come ashore only after dark, fewer on moonlit nights. Incubating birds and chicks spend the day underground in the burrow.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Birds usually start breeding at about five or six years old and can go on for decades; one ringed on Bardsey Island, Wales, was still alive more than 50 years later.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Each spring females lay one egg, often in a burrow, and both parents make long food trips. Incubation lasts about seven weeks; the fat chick is left alone for its last week or so and leaves at night about ten weeks after hatching.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look the same; studies at colonies report that the night calls of the two sexes differ.

analysis.summary: Roughly the size of a house cat, at about 2 to 5 kilograms, this forest cat spends much of its life in the canopy of tropical forest from the eastern Himalaya to Sumatra and Borneo. fieldGuide.dietSummary: Diet is known from few records: birds, squirrels, rats and other small rodents, and probably lizards and frogs. It is thought to hunt both in the trees and on the forest floor.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predation on it has never been observed in the wild. Clearing of forest for plantations and farmland, logging, and snares set for other animals, which also catch small cats, are the threats it faces.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Camera-trap studies in Thailand and Borneo recorded it mostly in daylight and around dusk, with fewer night records, which is unusual for a small cat. Its daytime and night-time resting places in the wild have not been described.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive marbled cats have reached about 12 years; how long they survive in the wild is unknown.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding is known only from a handful of captive births: gestation of roughly 66 to 82 days and litters of one or two kittens. Kittens open their eyes at about two weeks and begin taking solid food at around two months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes share the same coat pattern. Males may be slightly larger, but too few animals have been measured to be sure.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flying insects such as flies, moths, midges and small beetles caught in a vertical orb web. The spider waits out of sight holding a signal thread that runs to the hub, then rushes out to wrap prey in silk before biting it.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, mud-dauber and other spider-hunting wasps, and parasitoid wasps that lay eggs on or in spiders all take it. When disturbed on the web it usually drops to the ground on a silk line and keeps still.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active in the evening and at night, when it spins or repairs the web and may sit at the hub. By day it usually stays hidden off the web in its retreat.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one year from egg to death, of which only some six to eight months are spent out of the egg sac. Adults mature in late summer and rarely survive the first hard frosts.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In autumn the female lays her eggs in a silk sac hidden in a sheltered spot such as a curled leaf or bark crevice, and dies soon afterwards. The eggs overwinter and the spiderlings disperse in spring, often by ballooning on silk threads.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are much larger than males, with a swollen, rounded abdomen. Males are slimmer, with relatively longer legs and enlarged pedipalps that look like small boxing gloves at the front of the head.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Nymphs and adults both drink xylem sap through piercing mouthparts. Xylem is very dilute, so they process large volumes, and the species feeds on hundreds of different plants, from grasses to shrubs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders and birds take many adults, and solitary wasps of the genus Argogorytes pull nymphs out of their froth to stock their nests. Adults escape by leaping away or dropping from the plant.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are active by day on vegetation and rest motionless on stems and leaves at night and in cool weather. Nymphs stay inside their froth at all hours.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one year from egg to death. Eggs overwinter, nymphs take roughly one to two months to mature in spring, and adults survive several months, from early summer until autumn frosts.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating takes place in late summer. Females lay small batches of eggs in dead stems, stubble and crevices near the ground; these hatch the following spring, and the nymphs pass through five stages before the final moult to adult.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are slightly larger than males. Wing patterns vary widely in both sexes, but some of the darker colour forms occur mainly or only in females.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults feed mainly on the blood of mammals, slicing the skin with three toothed jaws. Young leeches take their first blood meals from frogs. A large meal can raise body weight roughly 8 to 11 times, and digesting it can take around six months.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, ducks, herons, water beetles and dragonfly larvae eat leeches, especially young ones. The greater threats are the loss of ponds, fewer grazing animals at the water's edge and past over-collection for medicine.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It rests under stones, among plants or in mud for long periods while digesting, and becomes active when ripples, warmth or scent signal a host. In winter it lies dormant, buried in mud below the reach of frost.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Slow-growing, taking at least two years to mature. Wild lifespan is uncertain; captive leeches have lived more than ten years, with reports of around 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In summer each leech leaves the water to lay spongy cocoons in damp soil or under stones just above the waterline. A cocoon holds about a dozen eggs on average. Young emerge as miniature leeches after several weeks and feed first on amphibians.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: There are no separate sexes. Every individual is a hermaphrodite with both male and female organs; two leeches pair to transfer sperm, and either can lay cocoons.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal, emerging around dusk and hunting into the night. By day it rests in wall crevices, behind shutters or under stones, and it becomes largely inactive in cold winter weather.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are sooty black with a black beak when breeding, while females are grey-brown and heavily streaked. Young males pass through partly black, blotchy stages before gaining full black plumage.

Honey is stored in clusters of egg-shaped pots made of wax mixed with resin, and is thinner and more acidic than honeybee honey.
Whether a female larva becomes a queen is thought to depend partly on her genes, and up to a quarter of females may emerge as queens.
A new colony is founded gradually: workers prepare and stock the new cavity over days or weeks before a young queen moves in.
Brazilian beekeepers keep species such as the mandaçaia, Melipona quadrifasciata, and the uruçu, Melipona scutellaris, in box hives for honey and crop pollination.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Workers collect nectar and pollen from forest trees, shrubs and crops, and can shake pollen out of flowers such as tomato and aubergine by vibrating their flight muscles. Larvae are fed once: each brood cell is filled with a pollen and nectar mix, given an egg and sealed.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tayras and other mammals break into nests for honey, ants and robber bees (Lestrimelitta) raid them, and phorid flies breed in the food stores. Spiders, assassin bugs, lizards and birds catch foragers. Unable to sting, workers guard the entrance and bite intruders.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Foragers fly by day, starting at or soon after dawn and often busiest in the cooler, more humid morning hours. The whole colony stays inside the nest at night, and flights fall away during heavy rain and cold spells.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Workers live roughly one to two months as adults. Queens live far longer, commonly one to three years and sometimes more, and a colony can persist for many years as queens are replaced.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The queen lays a single egg on the liquid food in each cell of a horizontal brood comb, and workers seal the cell at once. Growth to adult takes about five to seven weeks. Queens are reared in cells the same size as workers', and surplus young queens are killed.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Workers are females with pollen baskets on the hind legs. Males are similar in size but lack the baskets, have one more antennal segment and often a paler face. The laying queen has an abdomen so swollen with eggs that she cannot fly.

whyInteresting: This crab often clips and drags fallen mangrove leaves toward its burrow, shredding them there and helping to break down leaf litter in the intertidal zone.

Individuals frequently occupy and maintain the same burrow for long periods, defending the entrance against similar-sized neighbours with raised claws and sideways shoves.
By grazing algae and biofilm from mangrove roots, it reduces fouling on the root surfaces and influences how other small invertebrates colonise the intertidal habitat.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes similar in size and colour; males often have slightly larger, more robust claws. The most reliable difference is the broader, rounded abdominal flap in females versus the narrower, more triangular flap in males.

entries.name: Milk Snake
entries.heroTitle: Milk Snake — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Few American snakes range as widely: taken in its broad sense, this nonvenomous kingsnake occurs from south-eastern Canada to northern South America. It kills its prey by constriction. Over that span its size and colouring shift so much that northern and tropical animals can look like different snakes.
identification: Smooth, glossy scales without ridges
Red or russet saddles or rings bordered in black
Head barely wider than the neck
Belly chequered black and white in northern animals
Pale Y or V mark on the nape of eastern animals
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Fields, forests, barns, rocky edges, and hidden ground cover.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Fields, forests, barns, rocky edges, and hidden ground cover.

whyInteresting: The name comes from an old belief that it sucked milk from cows; the snakes found in barns were in fact hunting mice.
A disturbed animal vibrates its tail, which in dry leaves can sound like a rattlesnake, and may release a foul-smelling musk.
Adult length varies widely, from about 60 centimetres in some northern populations to more than 1.5 metres in the largest tropical ones.
A genetic study published in 2014 proposed dividing it into seven separate species, and authorities still differ on how many to recognise.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Rodents, lizards, birds, eggs, and smaller snakes.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, mammals, larger snakes, and humans threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly nocturnal in warm weather, and more often about by day in spring and autumn. Daylight hours are spent under logs, rocks or boards, or in burrows. Northern animals pass the winter underground below the frost line, sometimes sharing a den with other snakes.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: In captivity 15 to 20 years is common, and a few snakes have passed 20. No reliable figure exists for wild animals, which probably live less long.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay clutches of roughly 3 to 20 eggs in hidden, damp spots such as rotting logs, loose soil or under boards, and leave them. Hatching takes about two months. In the north, mating is in spring and laying in early summer; breeding times of tropical populations are less well documented.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes look similar; females may be heavier.

Their bite can be painful if handled carelessly.
