fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flies, bees, caterpillars, beetles, and other insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, mantises, wasps, and larger predatory insects can threaten assassin bugs. Stillness, camouflage, and a painful defensive bite help protect them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly active by day in warm conditions, waiting and hunting among plants.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Milkweed Assassin Bugs usually live through a seasonal insect life cycle from egg to nymph to adult. The lesson is built in a short window of patient ambush.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay clusters of eggs on plants, and nymphs hatch looking like smaller wingless hunters. The next generation begins directly among stems and prey routes.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though females may be larger when carrying eggs. The more important distinction is between nymph and winged adult.

entries.name: Yellow-spotted Millipede
entries.heroTitle: Yellow-spotted Millipede — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Anoplodesmus saussurii is a flat-backed paradoxosomatid millipede, shiny dark brown to black with bright yellow collum and paratergal marks, now widespread in humid tropical litter.

Bright yellow underside of collum and short paraterga
Light brown legs on a broad 21–33 mm frame
Smooth metaterga crossed by a deep transverse groove
Dense aggregations under decaying litter layers

whyInteresting: Millipede has a field-guide lesson based on ecology, not appearance alone.
Its habitat matters because the principle needs the right setting to become useful.
Its food and predators explain the pressure behind the behavior.
Its daily rhythm and reproduction show how the strategy continues over time.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Decaying leaves, fungi, and soft plant matter support the principle because the animal's feeding method shows how it turns available resources into survival instead of chasing a mismatched life.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, frogs, mammals, beetles, and ants threaten it. These dangers matter because they explain why its defenses, caution, grouping, camouflage, or speed are not decoration but necessary strategy.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal or damp-weather active fits because its activity rhythm places effort when the animal has the best chance to feed, avoid danger, or communicate clearly.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Published Indian life-history work puts adults at roughly four to six weeks after a six-to-seven-month path from egg through seven moults in humid litter.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: About twenty to twenty-five days after mating, females bury one hundred to four hundred eggs in earthen nests five to ten centimetres deep; a female may produce two to four egg masses.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences subtle; males often have modified legs. This matters because sex differences either create obvious signals or show that behavior, age, and place are more important than display.

entries.name: Mint Moth
entries.heroTitle: Mint Moth — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Few European moths are as easy to watch by day as this small member of the family Crambidae, which flies in full sunshine and is regularly noticed in gardens. Adults visit flowers openly in daylight and often settle long enough to be seen well.
identification: Purple to maroon forewings with a few golden-yellow spots
Dark hindwings crossed by a thin pale yellow band
Wingspan only about 15 to 20 mm
Rests with wings held flat and slightly spread
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe. Mint patches, herb gardens, meadow edges, and low vegetation.
analysis.nativeRange: Europe and nearby regions; exact range depends on local taxonomy and records.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 24/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

Wingspan only about 15 to 20 mm

whyInteresting: Moth-trappers also catch it regularly at light traps at night.
Its species name, aurata, is Latin for gilded, after the golden spots on the forewings.
The similar Pyrausta purpuralis has a broken band of larger yellow markings, which helps separate the two.
It was first described by the naturalist Giovanni Antonio Scopoli in 1763.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Nectar as adults; larvae feed on mint-family plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, predatory bugs, and parasitoid wasps threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Flies mainly from mid-morning to late afternoon when the sun is out, though some also fly after dark. In dull weather and at night it mostly rests among low vegetation, usually on or close to its food plants.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult lifespan has not been measured precisely but is thought to be a few weeks. In much of its range two generations fly each year, usually the first in May and June and the second in July and August.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid on the host plants. The caterpillars feed on leaves and flowers under light silk webbing, then pupate in a silk cocoon. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the same wing pattern and are hard to tell apart in the field; the female's abdomen is usually plumper.

entries.name: Mirror Spider
entries.heroTitle: Mirror Spider — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Mirror Spider is a lesson in adjustable visibility. It does not stay fixed; it changes how it reflects the world around it.
identification: Silver patches divided by thin lines of orange, red or yellow
High, rounded abdomen much larger than the head
Body only a few millimetres long
Comb of bristles on the hind legs, visible under a lens
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Foliage of shrubs and small trees in rainforest, moist open forest and leafy gardens, mainly in eastern Australia. It keeps to low shrubs and understorey plants.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Foliage of shrubs and small trees in rainforest, moist open forest and leafy gardens, mainly in eastern Australia. It keeps to low shrubs and understorey plants.

High, rounded abdomen much larger than the head

whyInteresting: The silver patches are made of guanine crystals, a nitrogen waste product stored in cells just beneath the skin.
It belongs to the comb-footed spider family, Theridiidae, the same family as the redback spider.
Its species name, argentiopunctata, means silver-spotted, from the Latin for silver and spotted.
Comb-footed spiders use the row of bristles on the hind legs to draw out sticky silk and fling it over struggling prey.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small flying and crawling insects that become caught in a sparse tangle of silk threads strung beneath a leaf.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: No predators of this species have been recorded, and whether its silver patches help it avoid birds, wasps or other hunters has not been tested.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Its daily rhythm has not been studied; by day it is usually found motionless in its web.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How many seasons Thwaitesia argentiopunctata lives remains undocumented. Silvery guanine plaques on the abdomen can shift with the spider’s state.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female wraps her eggs in a silk egg sac, as spiders do. Clutch size, the look of the sac and whether she guards it have not been described for this species.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males carry swollen, bulb-tipped palps at the front of the head, used in mating, which females lack. Males are thought to be smaller than females.

entries.name: Giant Hatchetfish
entries.heroTitle: Giant Hatchetfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Tubular eyes that point straight upward let it scan the dim light above for the silhouettes of prey. At around 10 centimetres, this deep-bodied fish of the ocean twilight zone is among the largest of the silver hatchetfishes.
identification: Deep chest tapering sharply to a narrow tail stalk
Mouth set almost vertically, facing up
Sharp keel along the lower belly
Blade-like bony ridge in front of the dorsal fin
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, south_atlantic, north_pacific, south_pacific, indian_ocean. Open ocean in tropical and subtropical seas, mostly in the dim midwater several hundred metres below the surface, well away from the coast and the seabed.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_atlantic, south_atlantic, north_pacific, south_pacific, indian_ocean. Open ocean in tropical and subtropical seas, mostly in the dim midwater several hundred metres below the surface, well away from the coast and the seabed.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 80/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Deep chest tapering sharply to a narrow tail stalk
Mouth set almost vertically, facing up
Sharp keel along the lower belly

whyInteresting: Its scales and silvery skin are delicate, so trawled specimens often arrive damaged, with much of the silver rubbed away.
Specimens are known almost entirely from deep trawl nets, so living animals are rarely seen.
The genus name Argyropelecus means 'silver hatchet', after its shape and sheen.
Despite the shared name, it is unrelated to the small freshwater hatchetfishes kept in aquariums.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small planktonic crustaceans such as copepods, ostracods and amphipods make up much of the diet, and larger individuals probably also take krill. Prey is picked off singly in midwater rather than filtered from the water.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few predation records exist for this species. It is a weak swimmer and relies on staying unseen rather than on escape.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nothing is known about rest or daily activity cycles in this deep-sea fish, which is almost never observed alive.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan has not been documented for this species; no ageing studies of wild specimens are known.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Reproduction has not been described for this species. Like other deep-sea hatchetfishes it is thought to shed eggs that drift in open water, but clutch size, spawning season and larval development are not documented.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike, and no external difference has been described; sex is found only by examining the gonads.

entries.name: Mistle Thrush
entries.heroTitle: Mistle Thrush — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Mistle Thrush is a bold berry defender, holding food-rich trees and singing into rough weather when many smaller birds stay silent.
identification: Bold berry-guarding thrush
Large grey-brown thrush with bold round breast spots
White underwings flashing in flight
White tips to the outer tail feathers
Dry, rattling alarm call
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east. Open woodland, parkland, orchards, churchyards, large gardens and farmland with tall trees, and conifer forest edges in the uplands. It needs short turf or open ground near the trees for feeding.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east. Open woodland, parkland, orchards, churchyards, large gardens and farmland with tall trees, and conifer forest edges in the uplands. It needs short turf or open ground near the trees for feeding.

whyInteresting: Its name, and the scientific name viscivorus, refer to eating mistletoe berries; the sticky seeds pass out in its droppings and can lodge on branches, helping to spread the plant.
The nest is often decorated on the outside with wool, feathers, paper or plastic.
Its flight is strongly bounding, with the wings closed briefly between bursts of flapping.
After breeding, families gather into loose flocks that feed on open fields in late summer.
Song phrases are short, loud and fluty, with pauses between them, delivered from the very top of tall trees.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Earthworms, insects, slugs and snails taken from short grass in spring and summer. In autumn and winter it turns to berries of mistletoe, holly, yew, rowan and hawthorn.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Parents defend the nest boldly, diving at crows, magpies, jays, squirrels, cats and even people that come close. Sparrowhawks take adults.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: A daytime bird that spends the night high in tall trees, often tucked into ivy or dense conifers.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Average life in the wild is around 3 years, although ringing has shown that some individuals survive for more than 10.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nesting starts early, often in March, in a tree fork well above the ground. The female lays 3 to 5 eggs and incubates them for about two weeks; both parents feed the young, which fledge at around two weeks old. Two broods are usual.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look the same in plumage and size and cannot be told apart in the field, although in spring only males give the full loud song.

entries.name: Mitred Parakeet
entries.heroTitle: Mitred Parakeet — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Noisy flocks of this green, long-tailed parakeet work through dry Andean valleys, usually in groups of a few birds to several dozen. Feeding birds stay alert, and an alarm screech from one of them sends the whole flock into the air together.
identification: Bright green body with a long, pointed tail
Red patches on the forehead and face
Pale bare ring around each eye
Horn-coloured hooked bill
Harsh, screeching flight calls
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_america. Dry montane valleys, cliffs and ravines, scrub, forest edges and cultivated land on the eastern slopes of the Andes, roughly from 1,000 to over 3,000 metres, in Peru, Bolivia and north-western Argentina.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: south_america. Dry montane valleys, cliffs and ravines, scrub, forest edges and cultivated land on the eastern slopes of the Andes, roughly from 1,000 to over 3,000 metres, in Peru, Bolivia and north-western Argentina.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 38/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Bright green body with a long, pointed tail
Red patches on the forehead and face
Pale bare ring around each eye
Horn-coloured hooked bill
Harsh, screeching flight calls
whyInteresting: The amount of red on the face differs from bird to bird, from a small forehead patch to scattered red feathers across the cheeks.
It is one of the larger parakeets in its genus, reaching about 34 to 38 centimetres long including the tail.
Some taxonomists now place it in the genus Psittacara rather than Aratinga.
Escaped cage birds have founded feral flocks outside its native range, including in parts of southern California and Florida.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, fruits, berries, nuts and flowers taken from trees and shrubs. It also raids crops such as maize and fruit orchards, climbing through branches with bill and feet.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Falcons and hawks are the likely predators of adults, though predation is little documented. Some birds are trapped for the cage-bird trade, and in farming areas flocks are sometimes persecuted as crop pests.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal. Nights are spent at communal roosts on cliff faces or in dense trees, where birds gather in the evening with much calling before settling.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild years for Aratinga mitrata remain unpublished; captive birds are often said to live about 20 years or longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests in crevices or holes in cliffs and sometimes in tree cavities. Clutches of about 2 to 4 eggs are reported; incubation and chick development in the wild are poorly documented.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike and cannot be told apart in the field.

entries.name: Mohol Bushbaby
entries.heroTitle: Mohol Bushbaby — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Mohol Bushbabies are nocturnal primates that use huge eyes, sensitive ears, and springing hind legs to travel after dark. Their small size works because sensing and leaping stay tightly connected.

Long, bushy tail, longer than head and body
Pale stripe down the nose between the eyes
Bright orange-red eyeshine in torchlight
Hops upright on the hind legs when on the ground

analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Dry savanna woodland in southern and south-central Africa, especially acacia thornveld and mixed bushveld, and riverine woodland; it avoids dense evergreen forest.

whyInteresting: It rubs urine onto its hands and feet, which may improve grip and leaves scent along its travel routes.
The thin ears can be folded and crinkled down against the head while it sleeps or pushes through thorns.
Its lower incisors and canines lie forward in a closely set tooth comb used in grooming.
A second, horny tongue beneath the main tongue is used to clean the tooth comb.
The name bushbaby is said to come from its loud calls, which some people compare to a crying child.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Gum oozing from acacia bark is the staple through the dry winter months. Insects such as moths and beetles are caught by hand, often snatched from the air.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, genets, snakes and small carnivores hunt them. When threatened they give loud, repeated alarm calls and retreat higher into thorny branches.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal. By day several animals sleep huddled together in tree holes, dense tangles or leafy nests, emerging around dusk.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Up to about 14 years in captivity; wild lifespan is less well known and probably shorter.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: There are often two birth seasons a year. After a pregnancy of about four months, one or two young are born and left in a nest while the mother forages; later she carries them in her mouth.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are slightly larger and heavier than females, but the sexes look alike in the field.

entries.name: Mojave Desert Tortoise
entries.heroTitle: Mojave Desert Tortoise — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Mojave Desert Tortoise AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A high-domed desert tortoise that can go for months without drinking. Its large bladder holds water that the body reabsorbs between rains. When rain does fall it drinks deeply from puddles, and individuals have been seen scraping shallow basins in the ground that fill with runoff.
identification: High-domed brown shell, often with visible growth rings on each plate
Flattened, heavily scaled front legs built for digging
Stumpy, elephant-like hind feet
Adult shell length roughly 20 to 35 cm

behaviorTraits: High-domed brown shell, often with visible growth rings on each plate
Flattened, heavily scaled front legs built for digging
Stumpy, elephant-like hind feet
Adult shell length roughly 20 to 35 cm
whyInteresting: The Mojave population has been listed as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act since 1990.
Growth is slow, and females typically do not breed until they are around 15 to 20 years old.
It is the state reptile of both California and Nevada.
A frightened tortoise may empty its bladder, losing a water store it may not be able to replace until the next rain.
One tortoise may use many burrows in a year, and a single burrow can be used by different tortoises at different times.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Desert grasses, wildflowers, cactus pads, and seasonal plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Ravens, coyotes, foxes, badgers, disease, vehicles, and habitat loss threaten tortoises; burrows and shells protect them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Activity peaks in cooler parts of day and wetter seasons, with long resting periods underground during heat or drought.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Desert Tortoises can live for many decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in soil nests, and hatchlings face heavy predation because their shells are still soft.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males often have longer gular horns and concave plastrons, while females invest heavily in eggs and nesting.

entries.name: Mongolian Gerbil
entries.heroTitle: Mongolian Gerbil — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A small burrowing rodent of the Mongolian and northern Chinese steppe that does not hibernate. Family groups share a burrow system and fill its chambers with seeds through the autumn, living on these hoards through winters far below freezing.
identification: Sandy-brown back with a pale greyish-white belly
Furred tail ending in a small dark tuft
Short, rounded ears and large dark eyes
Long hind feet and upright sitting posture
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: central_asia, east_asia. Mongolian Gerbil belongs to dry steppe and semi-desert.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: central_asia, east_asia. Mongolian Gerbil belongs to dry steppe and semi-desert.

Furred tail ending in a small dark tuft
Short, rounded ears and large dark eyes
Long hind feet and upright sitting posture
whyInteresting: The laboratory and pet gerbils kept worldwide descend largely from a small number captured in eastern Asia in the 1930s.
Groups defend their burrows and will attack gerbils from other families.
Its hearing is unusually sensitive to low-frequency sounds, which has made it a common subject of hearing research.
Some individuals, especially in laboratory strains, have brief seizures when startled or handled.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Eats seeds, leaves, stems and roots of steppe plants, sitting up to handle food in its forepaws. It gets most of its water from its food.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, polecats, snakes, owls and hawks such as buzzards hunt it. Alarmed gerbils drum their hind feet on the ground to warn others, then dive into the nearest burrow entrance.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and at dusk rather than at night. It retreats underground in the midday heat of summer, and in winter comes up only briefly in the warmest hours, resting in grass-lined nest chambers.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: In the wild many live less than two years; pets usually live two to four years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Litters of about four to six young follow a gestation of roughly 24 to 26 days. The young are born naked and blind, open their eyes at around three weeks and are weaned soon after; older siblings in the family group have been reported to help with the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are somewhat larger and have a bigger scent gland on the belly; otherwise the sexes look alike.

entries.name: Monito del Monte
entries.heroTitle: Monito del Monte — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Monito del Monte AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: Mouse-sized and big-eyed, this marsupial of the cool temperate rainforests of southern Chile and Argentina is the only living member of the order Microbiotheria. Its lineage is more closely related to Australian marsupials than to the opossums that share its continent.
identification: Black ring around each large eye

featuredImage.alt: Namib Desert Beetle AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A small black darkling beetle of the Namib, it carries rows of smooth bumps across wing covers that are otherwise coated in water-repelling wax. A 2001 study proposed that fog droplets gather on the bumps and roll along the waxy grooves towards the mouth.
identification: textured wing covers
fog-basking posture
desert walking
and scarce-water efficiency
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Namib desert dunes and gravel plains touched by coastal fog.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Namib desert dunes and gravel plains touched by coastal fog.

behaviorTraits: textured wing covers
fog-basking posture
desert walking

whyInteresting: The species name gracilipes means slender-footed, a reference to its long, thin legs.
It is described as flightless, with its wing covers fused over the body, so it travels entirely on foot.
Adults are roughly 2 centimetres long, about the size of a thumbnail.
It belongs to the darkling beetle family, Tenebrionidae, which is unusually rich in species in the Namib.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It is thought to feed mainly on detritus: windblown plant fragments, seeds and other dead organic matter that piles up at the bases of plants and in the lee of dunes.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: On the open sand, lizards, birds, spiders, and extreme dehydration threaten Namib Desert Beetle. It escapes by running to shelter under debris or burrowing into loose sand.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly a daytime beetle, it is active during cooler foggy or morning windows, hiding from heat later. Nights and the hottest hours are thought to be spent sheltered in sand or under plant debris.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild has not been documented for this species.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding is little studied; females lay eggs in sand or protected substrate where larvae develop hidden from surface extremes. The larvae are thought to live buried, feeding on organic matter before pupating in the sand.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike to the eye, and no field differences between them have been described.

analysis.summary: A small day-flying hawkmoth that passes for a bumblebee. The furry body is banded buff and dark, and the wings are mostly clear glass edged with a thin dark border, as the scales there drop off soon after it first flies.

wasp-like body mimicry
fast flower visits
and agile escape

whyInteresting: Its wings beat fast enough to make an audible hum while it hovers at a flower.
Young caterpillars leave small round holes in scabious leaves, a sign surveyors use to find breeding colonies.
The adult flight season is short, mainly May and June.
It is easily confused with the Broad-bordered Bee Hawkmoth, which has a much wider reddish-brown border to its clear wings.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults sip nectar while hovering, from flowers such as bugle, lousewort, ragged robin and viper's bugloss. Caterpillars eat the leaves of devil's-bit scabious, and in some areas field scabious.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders and parasitic wasps and flies are its main enemies. Adults rarely stay long enough at a flower to be caught. Loss of damp meadows has caused declines in parts of Europe.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Flies only by day, in sunshine. At night and in dull weather it rests hidden in low vegetation.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults probably live only two to three weeks. One generation takes about a year to complete.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid singly on the undersides of devil's-bit scabious leaves. The green caterpillar feeds on the leaves through summer, then pupates in a loose cocoon at the base of the plant, where it overwinters.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in the field. The male has a slimmer abdomen ending in a fuller tuft of hair-like scales.

entries.name: Neotropic Cormorant
entries.heroTitle: Neotropic Cormorant — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Neotropic Cormorant teaches Wing-Dry Reset through a small dark diver that must return to air after going under. Strong feet, hooked bill, underwater pursuit, and spread-wing perching show that deep work needs recovery before the next dive.
identification: Small dark diver: the body slips underwater after fish.
Wing-spread drying: recovery is visible on exposed perches.
River flexibility: it uses freshwater, brackish, and coastal feeding sites.

whyInteresting: Neotropic Cormorants are smaller than many larger cormorants.
They often perch low with wings spread after diving.
They can be found around rivers, ponds, lagoons, and urban water bodies.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, small aquatic animals, crustaceans, and amphibians.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, caimans, snakes, raccoons, gulls, and nest predators can threaten adults, eggs, or young. Colonial nesting and water escape help reduce risk.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Neotropic Cormorants are diurnal, diving and drying through daylight. Their rhythm repeats the recovery cycle: submerge, surface, spread, reset.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Few have been followed for life, though banded wild birds have lived more than a decade.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in colony nests built of sticks or vegetation, often near water. Chicks are fed by adults that must repeatedly reset after underwater hunting.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males may average slightly larger.

entries.name: New Caledonian Crow

featuredImage.alt: New Caledonian Crow AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: From the barbed edges of pandanus leaves, this black crow found only in New Caledonia cuts its own probing tools. The shapes it makes, from wide strips to narrow tapered and stepped probes, differ between parts of the island and seem to be passed on by learning.
identification: All-black plumage with a slight gloss
Straight, fairly short bill
Often seen holding a stick or leaf strip in the bill
Soft, quiet 'waak' calls
Medium-sized crow, around 40 cm long

Often seen holding a stick or leaf strip in the bill
Soft, quiet 'waak' calls
Medium-sized crow, around 40 cm long
whyInteresting: In experiments some birds used a short stick to fetch a longer one that could reach food.
Hand-raised young with no adult to copy still began probing with twigs, so some of the skill develops without teaching.
Its eyes give it an unusually wide binocular field for a crow, which researchers think helps it guide a tool.
Young birds often stay with their parents for a year or more, a long dependence for a crow.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Beetle larvae, other insects, snails, small animals, fruit and nuts. It extracts hidden prey from dead wood and crevices using tools it makes, hooked twigs and stepped strips cut from pandanus leaves.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, introduced mammals, nest predators, and habitat loss threaten crows; intelligence and careful tool traditions reduce exposure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal; it forages, crafts, and learns by day, resting in trees when tool use and visual searching stop.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Crows can live many years, giving Hooked Ingenuity time to develop through learning, practice, and social transmission.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in tree nests, and young learn foraging skills gradually from parents and surroundings.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes look broadly similar, with intelligence and learned behavior more important than strong visual sex differences.

entries.name: New Zealand Bellbird
entries.heroTitle: New Zealand Bellbird — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: New Zealand Bellbird AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A New Zealand honeyeater in which both sexes sing. Neighbouring populations use distinct song dialects, and females have their own distinct songs, making it a well-studied case of female song in songbirds.
identification: Olive-green body with darker wings and tail
Fine, slightly curved bill for probing flowers
Slightly forked tail
About 20 cm long, smaller and slimmer than a tui
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Forests, canopy edges, and fruiting trees.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Forests, canopy edges, and fruiting trees.

Fine, slightly curved bill for probing flowers
Slightly forked tail
About 20 cm long, smaller and slimmer than a tui
whyInteresting: It pollinates many native plants, including flax, kowhai, fuchsia and native mistletoes.
A brush-tipped tongue lets it lap nectar from flowers.
It disappeared from much of the northern North Island after European settlement, but persists on offshore islands and further south.
Joseph Banks, sailing with James Cook in 1770, wrote that its dawn chorus was the most melodious wild music he had ever heard.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, nectar, and insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Introduced ship rats, stoats, possums and cats take eggs, chicks and sitting females; the New Zealand falcon and probably the morepork also take birds. Adults scold and mob intruders, and nests are hidden in dense foliage.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal. It starts singing before dawn, feeds through the day and roosts at night hidden in dense foliage, usually well above ground.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Poorly documented; banding shows that some wild birds survive for several years, and a lifespan of up to about ten years is possible.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female builds a loose cup of twigs and grass, lined with feathers, in a tree fork or dense foliage. The usual clutch is three or four pinkish, blotched eggs, which she incubates for about two weeks; both parents feed the chicks, which fledge at around two weeks old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are olive-green with a purplish-blue sheen on the head and dark wings and tail. Females are duller and browner, with a narrow pale stripe across the cheek.

entries.name: Niger Triggerfish
entries.heroTitle: Niger Triggerfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Niger Triggerfish teaches Current Facing on the outer reef slope, holding position nose-first into moving water where the current does the work of finding food.
identification: Deep blue to blue-green body that shifts colour with mood and light
Deeply forked lyre-shaped tail with long trailing tips
Distinctly red teeth, visible at close range
A locking dorsal spine used to wedge itself into reef crevices
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: indian_ocean, south_pacific, red_sea, coral_triangle. Current-swept outer reef slopes and drop-offs.

Distinctly red teeth, visible at close range

whyInteresting: The first dorsal spine locks upright and is released by a smaller 'trigger' spine behind it, which is what names the family.
Once wedged in a crevice with the spine locked, it is extremely difficult to pull out.
Its teeth are genuinely red, unusual among reef fish.
It feeds mainly on plankton taken from current, unlike many triggerfishes that crush hard-shelled prey.
Body colour changes noticeably with mood, from deep blue to almost green.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Zooplankton and drifting algae taken from moving water, with some benthic invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Reef sharks, large groupers and jacks. Its answer is the crevice and the locking spine: it reverses in, locks up, and becomes effectively immovable.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Niger Triggerfish feed in open water by day and wedge into a reef crevice at night, locking the dorsal spine to hold themselves in place while they rest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan studies of wild Odonus niger appear lacking; adults wedge into reef crevices with a locking dorsal spine when threatened.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: They spawn on the reef, and the eggs are laid in and guarded around a nest site on the bottom.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look closely similar, with males often slightly larger and with longer tail filaments. The difference is minor because the species' key behaviour is shared by both.

entries.name: Night Parrot
entries.heroTitle: Night Parrot — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Night Parrots are elusive Australian desert birds associated with spinifex, night movement, and extremely low detectability. Their strength is secrecy: moving quietly, using cover, and surviving where attention itself can become danger.
identification: Plump, round-bodied parrot about the size of a large thrush
Green upperparts densely barred and mottled with black and yellow
Plain yellow lower belly
Short tail with darker bars
Mostly heard, giving double whistles and short croaking notes
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Old, long-unburnt spinifex hummock grassland on the stony plains and sand country of inland Australia, usually close to low chenopod shrubland, samphire or other succulent flats where the birds feed. Known sites lie in western Queensland and the arid interior of Western Australia.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: australia_oceania. whyInteresting: Dead birds found in western Queensland in 1990 and 2006 proved it survived, but live birds were not photographed until 2013, after roughly a century with few confirmed records.
Its closest relatives are the ground parrots of coastal south-eastern and south-western Australia, which share its ground-dwelling habits.
A private nature reserve in western Queensland was set aside after the 2013 rediscovery to protect the birds found there.
Scans of museum skulls suggest its visual brain regions are small for a night bird, so it may see poorly in the dark and risk flying into fences.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly seeds of spinifex and other grasses, gathered on or near the ground at night. It seems to drink rarely and is thought to take much of its water from succulent plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Feral cats and foxes are the main known threats, and owls and other native predators are thought to take some birds. Fire and heavy grazing that destroy old spinifex remove the cover it depends on.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Spends the day hidden inside a large, old spinifex hummock. It leaves the roost around dusk and may fly several kilometres to feeding areas before returning before dawn.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No band-recovery age is available for Pezoporus occidentalis. The parrot roosts by day inside dense spinifex and emerges after dark to feed.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests in a short tunnel pushed into a dense spinifex hummock, ending in a small chamber. Clutches of about two to four white eggs have been recorded; incubation and chick-rearing are poorly described.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike and cannot be reliably separated in the field.

entries.name: North American River Otter
entries.heroTitle: North American River Otter — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: North American River Otter AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: North American River Otters are skilled swimmers that hunt fish, crayfish, amphibians, and aquatic prey. Their play strengthens movement, social bonds, and water confidence rather than wasting energy.
identification: Long streamlined body about 90 to 130 cm including tail
Thick tail tapering to a point, about a third of length
Webbed feet and small rounded ears
Dense dark brown fur with a paler, silvery throat
Swims with only head showing, often snorting
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Rivers, streams, lakes, marshes and estuaries with good bank cover, and rocky sea coasts in Alaska and the Pacific Northwest. Dens are in old beaver lodges, burrows dug by other animals, root tangles and log jams near water.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america. Rivers, streams, lakes, marshes and estuaries with good bank cover, and rocky sea coasts in Alaska and the Pacific Northwest. Dens are in old beaver lodges, burrows dug by other animals, root tangles and log jams near water.

whyInteresting: Its ears and nostrils close when it dives.
Otters return again and again to shared latrine sites, often on points of land or beaver lodges, to leave scat and scent.
Reintroduction projects have returned it to many US states where trapping and pollution had wiped it out.
On some coasts, males live and travel in groups while females stay with their young.
In winter it keeps hunting under the ice, surfacing to breathe at open holes and cracks.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Slow-moving fish such as suckers, carp and sunfish make up most of the diet, caught in short underwater chases. Sensitive whiskers help it find prey in murky water, and it also takes crabs, birds and small mammals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few predators; bobcats, coyotes, wolves, alligators and large raptors can take young or unwary otters. Trapping, water pollution and road traffic are the main human threats. Otters escape by diving.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active at any hour, though mostly at dawn, dusk and night where people are near. It rests in dens, under logs or in dense vegetation, using many sites across its range.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually under 10 years in the wild, occasionally around 13; captive otters have lived past 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating is in spring, and delayed implantation stretches pregnancy to around 10 to 12 months. One to three pups, sometimes more, are born blind in a den. They swim at about two months and stay with the mother through their first year.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are somewhat larger and heavier than females; otherwise the sexes look alike.

entries.name: Northern Basket Star
entries.heroTitle: Northern Basket Star — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Northern Basket Star AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A brittle-star relative whose five arms fork again and again into ever finer branches. After dark it spreads them into a wide bowl facing the current, turning its whole body into a net for small drifting crustaceans.

Five-sided disc with raised ribs running out to each arm
Usually pale tan, beige or orange-brown
Spread arms can span several tens of centimetres

whyInteresting: The genus name Gorgonocephalus means Gorgon's head, after the snake-haired figure of Greek myth.
The common name comes from the way the curled, branching arms form a basket shape.
Individuals tend to climb to high points on the reef, lifting their arms into faster-flowing water.
Where currents run strongly, many basket stars can gather on the same outcrop.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Zooplankton such as copepods, krill and small shrimps, with some suspended particles. Prey touching a branch is gripped, wrapped by the coiling tips and passed inward to the mouth on the underside of the disc.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predation on adults is poorly documented; fish are thought to crop exposed branches. Lost branch tips can be regrown.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Rests by day with its arms rolled into a tight knot close to the disc, clinging to a rock, sponge or coral perch.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Growth rates of Gorgonocephalus eucnemis are poorly constrained by published lifespan. At night the branched arms unfurl into a plankton-catching basket.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Sexes are separate and spawn eggs and sperm into the water.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike and cannot be told apart in the field.

entries.name: Northern Bobwhite
entries.heroTitle: Northern Bobwhite — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Northern Bobwhites roost in a tight ring, tails to the centre and heads facing out. Every direction is covered, the birds share warmth, and the whole ring explodes outward at once if anything comes close.
identification: Small round quail, mottled brown, grey and chestnut
Clear rising two-note bob-WHITE whistle
Males have a white throat and brow, females buff
Explodes into fast low flight when flushed, then drops back into cover
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Weedy field margins, brushy fencerows, open pine woodland and early-successional grassland with bare ground between clumps. Patchy structure is essential — solid grass gives no room to move and no bare ground to feed on.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america. Weedy field margins, brushy fencerows, open pine woodland and early-successional grassland with bare ground between clumps. Patchy structure is essential — solid grass gives no room to move and no bare ground to feed on.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 34/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Small round quail, mottled brown, grey and chestnut
Clear rising two-note bob-WHITE whistle
Males have a white throat and brow, females buff
Explodes into fast low flight when flushed, then drops back into cover
whyInteresting: Coveys of ten to fifteen roost in a tight disc, tails inward and heads out, which covers every approach and conserves heat.
A flushing covey scatters in all directions at once, which makes it hard for a predator to fix on any single bird.
Coveys reassemble afterwards using a gathering call, so the scatter is deliberately temporary.
The population has fallen steeply across much of its range with the loss of weedy field margins and the spread of dense uniform grass.
The whistle is one of the most recognised bird sounds in the American South and is what names the bird.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, especially of legumes and weeds, plus insects in summer and green shoots. Coveys feed together and move between patches as a group, so watching and eating happen at the same time.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, foxes, bobcats, snakes and feral cats. The ring roost, the mass flush and the reassembly call are all group answers to a bird that individually has very little defence.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and roosts on the ground overnight in the covey ring, which is when the arrangement matters most.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually under a year in the wild, with very high annual turnover; some individuals reach five or six years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Twelve to sixteen eggs in a ground nest woven from grass with a partial roof. Chicks leave the nest within hours of hatching, and the male will incubate and raise a brood himself if the female starts a second clutch.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Clear. Males have a bright white throat and eyebrow stripe bordered in black; females have the same pattern in buff.

featuredImage.alt: Northern Elephant Seal AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A huge true seal of the eastern North Pacific that spends most of each year diving almost without pause. Dives commonly reach 300 to 800 metres and last around 20 minutes, with only a couple of minutes at the surface between them.
identification: Pups are black at birth and turn silver-grey after weaning
Hind flippers cannot be turned forward under the body
Large dark eyes set in a broad face
Moves on land by humping its body forward
Flicks sand over its back while resting

analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, north_pacific. Pacific beaches, rookeries, molting sites, and deep offshore feeding zones.

Hind flippers cannot be turned forward under the body

whyInteresting: Hunting cut the population to perhaps a few dozen animals by the 1890s; it has since recovered to well over 200,000.
Because the population passed through so few survivors, the species has unusually little genetic variation.
Each year it sheds its outer skin and fur in large sheets, a moult that takes about a month ashore.
Each adult makes two long migrations a year between beaches and feeding grounds, some covering over 18,000 kilometres in total.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, squid, rays, and deep-water prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Orcas and great white sharks take seals at sea, especially near rookeries. Pups can be crushed by fighting bulls or lost to storm surf.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: At sea it sleeps in short naps during deep dives, drifting or spiralling downwards, adding up to only about 2 hours a day. Ashore it rests for long periods on the beach.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Females can live about 20 years; males rarely survive beyond about 14 because of the strain of breeding.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single pup is born on the beach between December and February. The mother nurses it for about 4 weeks on very fat-rich milk without feeding herself, then mates and returns to sea.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males reach around 4 metres and 2 tonnes, several times the mass of females, and grow a long inflatable nose and a thick, scarred chest shield. Females are smaller and lack the nose.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeding takes up long motionless spells on a single twig through the day, most of all in warm weather. Night-time behaviour has not been studied.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: One generation a year in most of its range: eggs overwinter, nymphs grow through late spring and early summer, and adults survive into late summer or early autumn.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are placed in bark or twigs and survive the winter there. In spring the nymphs emerge and moult several times before the final moult to a winged adult.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females cannot be told apart in the field; both are pale green to whitish with the same waxy bloom.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Caimans, snakes, raptors and herons take eggs and chicks; adults are hunted by hawks. Adults call loudly and mob intruders, and chicks freeze or dive under vegetation with only the bill above the water.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds by day, often into dusk. Night roosting is poorly described but is thought to take place on floating vegetation or low marsh plants.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan is not well documented; long-term studies of colour-ringed birds in Costa Rica show that adults can hold territories for several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Four glossy brown eggs scribbled with black are laid on a flimsy floating platform. Incubation takes about four weeks, and the downy chicks feed themselves within hours; the female may lay clutches for up to four males holding territories inside hers.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is the same in both sexes, but females are much larger, often more than half again the weight of males.

Although hunted for meat, it remains fairly widespread, partly because it appears able to live in secondary forest and near farmland.

analysis.summary: A slim grey songbird with a long tail and white wing patches, found in gardens and open scrub. It builds its song from copied sounds, including other birds' calls, frogs and machinery, repeating each phrase several times before switching. A male may use 150 or more song types, and unmated males often sing through the night.

whyInteresting: Males keep adding sounds through life, so older birds tend to have larger repertoires.
In a Florida study, nesting mockingbirds learned to pick out individual people who had approached their nest and attacked them on later visits.
In the nineteenth century so many were trapped for sale as cage birds that the species became scarce around some eastern cities.
The scientific name Mimus polyglottos means many-tongued mimic.
The purpose of the wing-flash display is not settled; it may startle insects into moving or warn off predators.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Beetles, ants, grasshoppers, caterpillars and other invertebrates in spring and summer, caught mainly by running and lunging on open ground. In autumn and winter it switches largely to berries and other fruit and defends fruiting bushes.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, owls, cats and snakes take adults or young; jays, crows and squirrels raid nests. Adults mob and dive at intruders near the nest, striking cats, dogs and sometimes people.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, roosting at night in dense shrubs and trees. Unmated males often sing for hours after dark in spring and summer, especially on moonlit nights or near street lights.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly lives up to about 8 years in the wild; the oldest banded wild bird was over 14, and captives have reached 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Three to five blue-green eggs blotched with brown are laid in a twig cup low in a shrub. The female incubates for about 12 to 13 days, both parents feed the chicks, and young leave the nest at around 12 days. Pairs raise two or three broods.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is the same in both sexes, though males tend to be a little bigger. Both sexes sing, but males sing far more, and females sing mainly in autumn.

analysis.summary: Family ties among females hold the troops of this stocky macaque of mainland South-east Asia together. Females stay for life in the troop they were born into, so mothers, daughters and sisters form its lasting core, while males leave as they mature and must find a place in another troop. Troops commonly hold from a dozen to several dozen animals.

Flexible forest and forest-edge foraging
Social group life with rank, grooming, and warning signals
Strong memory for routes, food patches, and danger

whyInteresting: Northern Pig-tailed Macaques are Old World monkeys native to parts of mainland Southeast Asia.
They spend time both in trees and on the ground, which lets them use layered forest habitat.
Their diet is flexible and can include fruit, seeds, leaves, insects, fungi, and small animals.
Like many macaques, they learn heavily through social attention, repeated routes, and group experience.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit is often important, but Northern Pig-tailed Macaques also eat seeds, leaves, shoots, insects, fungi, eggs, and occasional small animals. That broad diet matters because it shows practical intelligence: the animal does not depend on one perfect food source, but keeps learning what each season and patch can offer.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, large snakes, raptors, feral or domestic dogs, and humans can threaten macaques, while habitat loss and conflict with people are major pressures. Group vigilance, alarm calls, climbing, retreat into cover, and social awareness all help turn individual risk into a shared survival problem.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Northern Pig-tailed Macaques are mainly active by day, feeding, traveling, grooming, and watching the group while light is available. At night they sleep in trees or sheltered forest positions, so their rhythm separates active social problem-solving from safer resting cover.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Northern Pig-tailed Macaques can live for decades in protected care, while wild lives are often shorter because of predation, disease, injury, conflict, and habitat pressure. The long potential lifespan makes learning valuable: memory, rank experience, and social judgment can keep improving over many seasons.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to a single infant after a long primate pregnancy, then carry, nurse, protect, and teach the young through close contact. Infant survival depends on maternal care plus the wider social setting, where grooming, tolerance, and group position shape early life.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are clearly larger and more heavily built than females, with much longer canine teeth.

Introduced pike in parts of south-central Alaska have sharply reduced native salmon and trout.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly fish, including perch, roach, whitefish and smaller pike, plus frogs, crayfish, ducklings and small mammals swimming at the surface. Prey is usually seized crosswise in the teeth, then turned and swallowed head first.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Perch, larger pike, herons and diving birds eat young pike; big adults fall mainly to otters, ospreys, eagles and people fishing. Young pike stay in dense weed, where their mottled green colouring hides them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hunts mainly in daylight and twilight, relying heavily on sight. At night it usually rests motionless near the bottom or among weed.

A female scatters tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand sticky eggs, depending on her size, attended by one or more smaller males, with no care. Eggs hatch in about two weeks, and larvae hang from plants by an adhesive gland.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes share the same colours. Females grow faster and larger, and the biggest pike are almost always female.

Annual growth rings on a male's horns can be counted to estimate his age.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. In the midday heat it lies up in rock shade or caves, and at night rests on ledges.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Roughly 10 to 15 years in the wild, fewer for most males; captive animals can live into their late teens.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After about five months of gestation, a female gives birth to one kid, occasionally twins, on sheltered rock. The kid can follow her over steep ground within days and nurses for several months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males weigh around twice as much as females and carry long, knobbed horns sweeping back in a semicircle, plus a dark beard. Females have short, thin horns and a plain sandy coat; males darken during the autumn rut.

The name quahog comes from a Narragansett word for the hard clam, a different species in another family.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Filter-feeding matters because the animal does not chase abundance; it receives tiny particles again and again. The diet explains why slow strength is built from repetition, not dramatic conquest.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators and humans matter because a quiet shell can survive natural danger for years yet be undone quickly by harvesting, pollution, or habitat damage. The defense is strong, but not invincible.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It has no human-like sleep rhythm; its pause is metabolic quiet, valve closure, and low-energy filtering.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Longevity is the whole point: decades or even centuries in related species make the shell a record of restraint. Time is not just survived; it becomes structure.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females release eggs into water or depend on host-fish stages in mussels, showing why reproduction needs the whole system to be healthy, not just one strong individual.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are usually not visually dramatic, which strengthens the lesson: this is not display-based survival but shared, hidden endurance built into the body plan.

whyInteresting: The Ocellated Antbird is an obligate army-ant follower, getting most of its food at raids of the army ant Eciton burchellii.
It eats insects and other small animals flushed by the ants, rather than the ants themselves.
Birds are reported to check army ant bivouacs early in the morning to find out which colonies are raiding that day.
It is the only species in the genus Phaenostictus and is usually dominant over smaller antbirds at ant swarms.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Cockroaches, crickets, katydids, spiders and other large arthropods make up nearly all of the diet. It pounces on them on the ground or takes them from low stems and leaves.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators are poorly documented; forest hawks, snakes and nest-raiding mammals are the likely threats. The larger danger is forest loss, since it disappears from fragments too small to support army ant colonies.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active only in daylight. Where it spends the night is little described, though roosts are presumably in dense understorey.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not well documented. Colour-ringed birds in Panama have been followed for several years, but a typical or maximum lifespan has not been published.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests are rarely found; clutches of 2 eggs have been recorded. Young stay with their parents for months, and sons often settle near them, so related birds forage at the same swarms.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look nearly identical. Females average slightly smaller, but they cannot be reliably told apart in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pressed by an attacker, it releases a foul-smelling fluid from a pair of white glands at the tip of the abdomen, may bring up a brown liquid from the mouth, and bites. Hedgehogs, shrews, toads and ground-feeding birds are its likely predators.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hunts on the ground after dark and spends the day hidden in a crevice or under cover. Adults shelter through the winter and become active again in spring.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About two years in all. The larva takes roughly five months to develop, and adults can survive a second winter.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating takes place in autumn. The female lays large eggs singly in damp soil, moss or leaf litter, and they hatch after about a month. The larvae live mostly underground, moult through three stages and pupate in the soil.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes are the same black all over and overlap in length. Telling a male from a female takes close examination of a specimen in the hand.

What sets off the synchronised landings is not fully understood; wind, the phase of the moon and scent signals have all been suggested.
Having covered her eggs, the female packs the sand down by rocking her body and thumping it with the edges of her shell.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are several times larger and heavier than males and do nearly all the web-building seen in late summer. Males are small, long-legged and wander in search of females, plucking the web to announce themselves.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Ord Kangaroo Rat rests in burrows with multiple entrances, nests, and seed caches. It forages at night and spends the day below ground; in the colder north it is thought to spend long spells underground in winter.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Litters usually hold three or four young, but range from one to six, born after a gestation of about 30 days. In the south females may raise two litters a year; young are weaned at around three to four weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are alike in colour and markings; males average slightly larger, but this cannot be judged in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, spiders and wasps catch adults, and ants carry off eggs and maggots. In shared carcasses, larvae of the hairy maggot blowfly prey on its maggots, and parasitoid wasps attack the pupae. Adults escape by fast flight.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Flies by day and is busiest in warm sunshine. At night adults rest on leaves, twigs, walls and ceilings near feeding sites, and they are sluggish in cool early mornings.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In males the eyes meet on top of the head, with a band of noticeably larger facets in the upper part; in females the eyes are separated by a clear gap.

Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Diatoms, dinoflagellates, other plankton and fine organic particles. The crab raises its antennae in the draining backwash, then wipes the trapped particles off with its mouthparts.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sanderlings, willets, godwits and gulls pick them from the swash, and surfperch and other surf fish feed on them; people collect them as bait. When exposed, a crab reburies itself within seconds.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Activity follows the rhythm of waves and tides rather than daylight, and no regular rest period is known.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one to three years; females tend to live longer than males, many of which survive only about a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry a bright orange egg mass tucked under the folded tail for several weeks. The hatched larvae drift in the plankton for months, which lets them colonise beaches far from where they hatched.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females grow much larger than males, reaching about 3.5 cm in body length; males are usually under about 2.5 cm.

entries.name: Pacific Parrotlet
entries.heroTitle: Pacific Parrotlet — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: At about 13 cm long it is one of the smallest parrots in the Americas, native to the dry country of western Ecuador and north-western Peru. Small flocks forage low, often dropping to the ground to pick up seeds.
identification: Short, wedge-shaped tail
Stubby, pale horn-coloured hooked bill
Bright green head and underparts
Nape and back greyer green than the head
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_america. Dry deciduous woodland, thorn scrub and cactus-dotted lowlands on the Pacific slope of the Andes, along with forest edges, riverside trees and orchards, mostly in the lowlands and foothills.

whyInteresting: It is one of the most widely kept small parrots and is often sold as the celestial parrotlet.
Breeders have produced blue, yellow, white and other colour forms that do not occur in wild birds.
It is common across much of its range and has moved into farmland, towns and gardens.
Flocks are often small, but dozens of birds may gather where seeding plants are plentiful.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Parrotlet mainly uses seeds, fruit, berries, blossoms, and tender plant material. That food pattern supports Flockspark because the animal must get energy in the same way its principle works: a small body can carry large social energy when attention is alive.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators are poorly recorded. Hawks and falcons are the likely threat to adults, and snakes and small mammals probably raid nest cavities. At an alarm call a feeding flock bursts up and dives into dense foliage.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Night roosts are poorly described; birds are thought to sleep in dense bushes or trees, and pairs may use cavities. By day flocks feed most in the morning and late afternoon.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Kept as pets, Forpus coelestis commonly live fifteen to twenty years; wild averages near ten years are cited from demographic summaries of this tiny Ecuadorian parrot.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests are placed in tree holes and other cavities. The female lays about four to six white eggs and incubates them for around 18 to 20 days, and the chicks leave the nest at about a month old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a bright blue streak behind the eye and blue on the rump and wing feathers. Females are green in those places, with at most a faint blue-green mark behind the eye.

Long, frilled oral arms and fine tentacles trailing several metres
Slow, rhythmic pulsing of the bell
Gathers in large seasonal aggregations along the coast

whyInteresting: Its trailing tentacles can extend several metres behind a bell only a third of a metre wide.
It occurs along the Pacific coast of North America, from California to Alaska.
It captures zooplankton, larval fish and other jellyfish with stinging cells on its tentacles.
Coastal blooms are driven by upwelling and wind, so numbers swing enormously between years.
Sea turtles and ocean sunfish both eat it.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Zooplankton, fish larvae, comb jellies and other small drifting animals caught on stinging tentacles.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Ocean sunfish, sea turtles and some seabirds. Its answer is not escape but expendability — a bell that keeps functioning with substantial damage, backed by a potent sting.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Pacific Sea Nettles pulse continuously day and night, rising and sinking in the water column rather than resting.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: The drifting medusa lives less than a year, but the seabed polyp stage persists for much longer, so the lineage outlasts any individual bell.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Males release sperm into the water and females take it in. The fertilised eggs develop into larvae that are reportedly brooded on the female's oral arms before release, and each larva then settles on rock as a tiny polyp that later buds off young jellyfish.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Male and female medusae look alike from outside the bell. Appearance carries no signal because reproduction is by broadcast, not courtship.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Reported prey includes small crustaceans such as amphipods and copepods, along with worms, picked off rock and kelp surfaces near its resting spot.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger fishes, seabirds and sea otters are thought to take it, though records are few. Its armoured, bumpy skin may make it hard to swallow.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: A slow, sedentary fish that spends long periods motionless, stuck to rock or kelp. A daily cycle of activity and rest has not been studied.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Its lifespan is unknown, because no published study has aged wild spiny lumpsuckers.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay masses of sticky eggs on rocks in shallow water, and the male is reported to guard and fan them until they hatch. The young are tiny, round versions of the adult.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Differences between the sexes are not well described; colour varies widely between individuals, from green and yellow to orange and brown.

entries.name: Paddyfield Warbler
entries.heroTitle: Paddyfield Warbler — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: In spring the male sings a rapid, chattering song, often from the top of a reed stem or a low bush. The rest of the time this small, plain-brown reed warbler keeps hidden in reeds and wet grass, where it is easily overlooked.
identification: Long pale stripe over the eye, edged above by a dark line
Warm rufous-brown upperparts, brightest on the rump
Short bill, pale below with a dark tip
Pale throat with buff-washed flanks

Pale throat with buff-washed flanks
whyInteresting: Its song is reported to include imitations of other birds' calls, woven into the rapid chatter.
When alarmed it often cocks its tail and raises its crown feathers, giving the head a peaked look.
At around 13 centimetres long it is one of the smaller reed warblers.
In Indian winter quarters it often shares wetlands with Blyth's reed warbler, a greyer relative that keeps more to bushes and trees.
The species name agricola is Latin for farmer, matching the cultivated rice fields in the English name.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly small insects and spiders, gleaned from reed stems, grass and leaves as it creeps through low, dense vegetation; it occasionally sallies out for flying insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Poorly documented. Small hawks and other bird-eating predators are the likely threat to adults, and nests are exposed to snakes, rodents and crows. It relies on dense cover and quickly drops out of sight when disturbed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, most vocal in the early morning. It roosts within dense reeds or grass and, like other small warblers, migrates at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan is not well documented for this species; ringing recoveries are few, and no typical wild lifespan has been established.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The nest is a deep cup woven around several upright reed stems above water or wet ground. Four or five eggs are typical, incubated for about 12 days, and both parents are reported to feed the chicks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot be told apart in the field by plumage.

entries.name: Pagoda Cup Coral
entries.heroTitle: Pagoda Cup Coral — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Pagoda Cup Coral AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: Pagoda Cup Coral teaches Tiered Collection in stone. Its plates step outward as they stack, giving the colony the tiered roofline that named it and giving every layer its own share of light.
identification: Stony plates stacked in stepped, overlapping tiers
Large fleshy polyps that stand well clear of the skeleton when extended
Grey-green to brown tissue over a heavy calcium carbonate frame
Tolerates turbid, lower-light water that many stony corals cannot
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: indian_ocean, south_pacific, coral_triangle. Sheltered, often turbid inshore reefs and lagoon slopes.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: indian_ocean, south_pacific, coral_triangle. Sheltered, often turbid inshore reefs and lagoon slopes.

Large fleshy polyps that stand well clear of the skeleton when extended
Grey-green to brown tissue over a heavy calcium carbonate frame
Tolerates turbid, lower-light water that many stony corals cannot
whyInteresting: Its stepped plates are why it is called a pagoda coral — each tier oversails the one below.
It carries unusually large polyps for a plating stony coral, and extends them well beyond the skeleton to feed.
It handles silty, turbid inshore water better than most reef-building corals.
Colonies can grow over a metre across in shallow, sheltered water.
Like other reef-building corals it depends on symbiotic algae in its tissue for most of its energy.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Sugars from symbiotic zooxanthellae, plus zooplankton and particulate matter caught by its large extended polyps.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Crown-of-thorns starfish, coral-eating snails and some butterflyfish. Its answer is structural — a heavy stony skeleton and tissue withdrawn into the plate when disturbed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Pagoda Cup Coral extends its polyps mostly after dark and withdraws them in bright daylight, so the colony changes appearance entirely between day and night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Colonies live and expand for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Colonies release eggs and sperm in seasonal mass spawning events, and larvae settle on hard substrate to found new colonies.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Colonies show no external difference between sexes. Nothing about the animal signals sex because spawning is synchronised by season and moon rather than by display.

entries.name: Painted Frogfish
entries.heroTitle: Painted Frogfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Painted Frogfish shows that patience becomes active when paired with the right lure. It does not chase; it invites opportunity closer.
identification: Rounded, lumpy body covered in loose, finely prickly skin
Skin often marked with rings or spots of contrasting colour
Very wide mouth angled steeply upward
Pectoral fins bent like arms, with an elbow-like joint

Very wide mouth angled steeply upward

whyInteresting: It can change colour over a period of days or weeks to match a new sponge or background.
Prey about as long as the frogfish itself can be swallowed, thanks to an expandable mouth and stomach.
It is a member of the anglerfish order and usually walks over the bottom on its pectoral and pelvic fins.
Adults reach about 30 centimetres, but most individuals seen by divers are much smaller.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
