Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small fish and shrimps that come close. It wiggles the lure on its first dorsal spine, then opens its huge mouth in a few thousandths of a second, sucking prey in whole.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few predators of adults are known; larger reef fish and other frogfish probably take some. Its defence is to stay still and camouflaged, and if disturbed it jets away by pumping water from small gill openings behind the pectoral fins.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No distinct sleep period has been described. It sits motionless on the same spot for long periods and can strike at prey by day or by night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: lifespan at death remains unrecorded for Antennarius pictus; divers know it as a slow ambush predator that lures prey with a waving illicium.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female releases her eggs in a floating, jelly-like raft that the male fertilises as it emerges. The raft drifts away, there is no parental care, and the larvae live in open water before settling on the reef.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes cannot be told apart reliably in the field, although a female swells visibly with eggs shortly before spawning.

entries.name: Painted Turtle
entries.heroTitle: Painted Turtle — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: North America's most widespread native turtle, a small pond species 10 to 25 cm long. It cannot produce its own body heat, so it climbs onto logs and banks to bask, often piled on top of other turtles, and only feeds well once the sun has warmed it.
identification: Smooth, low, olive to black upper shell without a central ridge
Red bars or crescents on the plates around the shell's edge
Yellow stripes on the head, red and yellow on neck and legs
Lower shell yellow to reddish, plain or with a dark central blotch
Slides into the water at the first sign of approach

whyInteresting: In the north, hatchlings often stay in the nest through their first winter and can survive body temperatures several degrees below freezing.
Nest temperature decides the sex of the young, with cooler nests producing mostly males and warmer nests mostly females.
A courting male swims in front of the female, facing her, and strokes her cheeks with his front claws.
Four forms are recognised, eastern, midland, western and southern, and the southern one is sometimes treated as a separate species.
It swallows food underwater and has difficulty swallowing on land.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Aquatic plants, insects, snails, carrion, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raccoons, foxes, herons, large fish, and egg predators threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nights are spent asleep underwater, resting on the bottom or wedged among plants and sunken branches. By day it alternates basking with feeding.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly 20 to 30 years in the wild for turtles that reach adulthood. Marked wild individuals have been recorded at more than 50 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In late spring and early summer females dig a flask-shaped nest in open, sunny soil, usually within about 200 metres of water. A clutch holds roughly 4 to 15 oval eggs, which hatch after about 70 to 80 days. One or two clutches a year are usual.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males often have longer front claws and tails.

entries.name: Pallas's Cat

whyInteresting: It is a true bug in the order Hemiptera, a relative of cicadas, leafhoppers and aphids.
In Florida it is regarded as a minor pest of landscape and nursery palms, and the damage is usually cosmetic rather than a threat to the palm.
Its close tie to palms helps separate it from other Florida flatids such as Metcalfa pruinosa, which feeds on many kinds of trees and shrubs.
Like other planthoppers, it has short antennae set on the sides of the head below the eyes, unlike the leafhoppers and cicadas.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Its predators have not been studied in detail. Spiders, anole lizards, lacewing larvae and lady beetles hunting on palm fronds are the likely enemies, along with parasitic wasps that attack planthoppers generally.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: There is no separate resting place: nymphs and adults stay on the undersides of the fronds by day and by night, sitting still between long bouts of feeding.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Individual lifespan has not been documented for this species, and no reliable estimate is available.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are thought to be laid on the host palm, and the wingless nymphs that hatch feed on the same fronds, moulting through several stages before gaining wings. Clutch size and development time have not been documented.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Differences between the sexes have not been described for field use. Adults appear alike, and separating them needs close examination of the tip of the abdomen.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Its breeding has not been studied in detail. Like other velvet ants, the female is thought to lay a single egg in a sealed cell of a ground-nesting host and leave; the young develops and pupates there without parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Only females are wingless and able to sting. In velvet ants generally, males have wings and cannot sting; the male of this species is seldom seen or described.

analysis.summary: Roughly 1,000 species of social wasp in the subfamily Polistinae are known as paper wasps. In many species several females found a nest together and settle rank by contests, the dominant one laying most of the eggs.

Many tropical paper wasps of the tribe Epiponini found new nests in swarms of many queens and workers, and wrap their combs in a paper envelope.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults sip nectar from flowers such as buddleia, thistles, knapweeds, hemp-agrimony and dandelions, and in autumn take juice from rotting fruit. Caterpillars eat the leaves of common nettle.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds such as tits and small mammals such as mice attack adults, including hibernating ones, while parasitic wasps and flies attack the caterpillars. A disturbed adult flicks its wings open and rubs them together to make a hissing sound.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Flies on sunny days and roosts at night with wings closed among vegetation. Adults hibernate from autumn to the first warm days of spring in hollow trees, sheds, outbuildings and houses.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults that emerge in late summer can live about ten to eleven months, most of it in hibernation. Development from egg to adult takes roughly two to three months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay batches of up to a few hundred green eggs under young nettle leaves in spring. The caterpillars live together in a silk web, splitting up as they grow, and pupate after about a month.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike. Females average slightly larger, but the sexes are hard to separate in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Specific enemies are not documented; night-hunting bats, and birds and monkeys searching foliage by day, are likely predators. fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active mainly at night, when it feeds and moves between leaves. The day is spent resting on a twig or among foliage with the forewings folded over the body.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan has not been documented for this species; large tropical katydids generally take several months to reach adulthood and then live for some weeks to months.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males carry a pair of slender copulatory rods at the base of the last walking legs; otherwise the sexes look similar in the field.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger and heavier-bodied with the brightest blue. Mature males are smaller and longer-legged, often duller or greyish, and carry swollen palpal bulbs at the tips of their pedipalps.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, feeding most in the early morning and late afternoon. At night it roosts in trees or thick cover, often returning to the same roosts. It does not migrate or hibernate.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Heavy losses to predators, hunting and hard winters mean most wild pheasants live less than two years, although some survive several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The hen makes a shallow scrape on the ground in tall cover and lays usually about 8 to 15 olive-brown eggs. She incubates alone for about 23 to 26 days. The downy chicks leave the nest soon after hatching and can flutter within about two weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes differ strongly. Cocks are larger and brightly coloured, with red face wattles and a very long tail. Hens are mottled buff and brown with a shorter tail.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly nocturnal. By day it rests on a leaf, often on the underside, and barely moves.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females can reproduce with or without mating. Hard eggs that look like plant seeds are flicked or dropped to the ground and take several months to hatch. The newly hatched nymphs are reddish brown and turn green once they begin feeding.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger and broader, with forewings covering most of the abdomen, and cannot fly. Males are smaller and slimmer, with long antennae and working hind wings.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults can be taken by larger raptors and other predators, while nests are vulnerable to snakes, birds and mammals. Territorial vigilance, mobbing and group defence can reduce those risks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active during daylight and particularly conspicuous around dawn when vocal activity is strong. At night it roosts in trees or other protected elevated positions.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In breeding plumage the male is black and white with tail streamers far longer than his body. Females, young birds and non-breeding males are streaky brown with a boldly striped head.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, octopuses, larger crustaceans, and habitat disturbance threaten pistol shrimp; burrows and sharp snaps reduce attack success.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Activity varies by species and shelter, but many forage from burrows and remain alert across day-night reef rhythms.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No growth-ring study has dated the lifespan of this snapping shrimp. One enlarged claw fires a cavitation bubble that stuns small prey in sandy burrows.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry eggs under the abdomen until larvae hatch and enter planktonic stages before settling.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes can be similar, though claw size and pair roles may differ; the snapping claw is the defining feature.

entries.name: Planarian
entries.heroTitle: Planarian — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Planarians are flatworms with powerful regenerative cells. Their bodies can restore lost tissue, making recovery depend on internal pattern, stem cells, and the ability to reorganize after damage.
identification: Flat, soft brown body up to about 2 centimetres long
Arrow-shaped head with two dark eyespots looking cross-eyed
Glides smoothly over stones on a film of mucus
Shrinks and turns away from bright light
Pale feeding tube visible on the belly when feeding

It lives on stones, submerged leaves and plant stems in shallow water.

The asexual strain carries a large chromosome rearrangement that the sexual strain lacks.
Starved worms shrink steadily over weeks instead of simply wasting away, then grow again once they are fed.
It moves by beating tiny hairs called cilia on its underside, not by muscular crawling alone.
Its gut splits into three main branches, one running forward and two back, the pattern that gives its order, Tricladida, its name.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A carnivore and scavenger that takes small invertebrates and dead animal matter. It feeds through a muscular tube, the pharynx, pushed out from the middle of its underside, and sucks in partly digested food.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, predatory insect larvae and other freshwater invertebrates eat flatworms of this kind. It coats itself in slime that may make it less palatable, and pollution or the drying of its small spring-fed waters also threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active in darkness, creeping out to feed at night and resting under stones and debris by day. Laboratory studies have described a sleep-like resting state in this species.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long a single worm lives in the wild is unknown. Asexual laboratory lines renew themselves by splitting and have been kept going for decades, but that figure describes the clonal line, not one individual.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Two strains exist. In the sexual strain two worms mate and exchange sperm, then each lays small egg capsules holding several embryos, which hatch as miniature adults after roughly two weeks in laboratory culture. The asexual strain reproduces by tearing itself in two.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: There are no separate sexes. Each sexual individual carries both male and female organs, and asexual worms develop no reproductive organs at all.

entries.name: Plantain Squirrel

analysis.summary: The Plantain Squirrel is the everyday tree squirrel of the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java and Borneo, olive-brown above with a cream and black stripe along each side and a rusty belly. It is bold, active by day and as much at home in a city park or coconut grove as in forest.

Long, bushy tail about as long as the head and body

It uses every level from the ground to the canopy but spends most of its time in small trees and the lower crown.

whyInteresting: Ants and other insects make up a real share of its diet, alongside fruit and seeds.
It is one of the few native mammals still seen daily in the parks and gardens of cities such as Singapore and Kuala Lumpur.
Belly colour varies across its many island forms, from orange to deep reddish-brown.
Researchers in Malaysia found that it uses different alarm calls for ground predators, birds of prey and snakes.
It is treated as a pest in coconut and cocoa plantations because it gnaws into the fruit.
The Black-striped Squirrel shares the side stripes but has a plain grey belly, where the Plantain Squirrel is orange to reddish underneath.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, seeds, buds, flowers, tree sap and bark, along with ants, termites, beetle larvae and the occasional bird's egg. Little of that list depends on old forest, which is why planted and regrown trees feed it just as well.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pythons and other tree-climbing snakes, hawk-eagles and serpent eagles, monitor lizards and domestic cats. Loud, repeated alarm calls and a fast dash to the far side of a trunk are its usual answers.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day with peaks in the early morning and late afternoon. It sleeps in a round nest of leaves and twigs built in a tree fork or dense crown, or in a tree hollow.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Poorly recorded in the wild and probably only a few years; related squirrels in captivity have lived close to ten.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female raises one to four young, most often two, in a leaf nest, and can breed at any time of year where food is steady. Year-round breeding is part of how it fills newly planted habitat so quickly.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in size and colour. When a female is receptive, several males follow and chase her through the trees.

analysis.summary: Clear, window-like patches break up the smoky dark forewings of this small planthopper, so that a resting insect looks like a scrap of torn, sun-flecked leaf. In the dappled light of a shrub its outline almost disappears.

Small white mark on the front edge of each forewing
Nymphs carry a fan of white waxy threads at the tail

It has been recorded established in north-western Italy, far outside its native Asian range.
It was first described by the British entomologist Francis Walker in 1851.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults and nymphs pierce stems and leaf veins to drink phloem sap. It feeds on a wide range of woody and herbaceous plants, including citrus, grapevine and other crops.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders, predatory bugs, birds and lizards take adults and nymphs, and, as in related planthoppers, parasitic wasps probably attack the eggs. Disturbed insects escape with a sudden jump and a quick, fluttering flight.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, feeding on stems and leaves. At night adults and nymphs stay still on the same plants. In temperate areas it passes the winter as eggs inside twigs.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Detailed figures have not been documented; development from egg to adult takes several weeks, and adults probably live for a few weeks to about two months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female cuts slits in green twigs with her ovipositor and lays her eggs in a row inside, covering the slits with fluffy white wax. The wingless nymphs moult several times, probably five as in related planthoppers, before becoming winged adults.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot be told apart in the field without close examination of the tip of the abdomen.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly fruit, plucked with the tip of the bill and tossed back into the throat. It also takes insects and, at times, eggs or nestlings of other birds.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Specific predators are poorly documented, though large forest hawks are likely. The main threat is clearance of its cloud forest, and it has been listed as Near Threatened.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, moving through the canopy in pairs or small groups from fruiting tree to fruiting tree. Where and how it roosts at night has been little described. It does not migrate or become dormant, though it may shift altitude with fruit supply.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long wild birds of this species live is unknown.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests in a natural cavity or old woodpecker hole in a tree. Clutches of two or three white eggs have been reported, and both parents are thought to incubate and feed the young, but breeding has been little studied.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike; the female's bill is said to average slightly shorter.

analysis.summary: A small livebearer from warm lowland waters of southern Mexico and northern Central America, and one of the most widely kept aquarium fishes. Wild fish are olive-grey with scattered dark spots, but the species carries many natural pigment genes, which breeders have used to produce red, gold, blue, black and patterned forms.

It is also kept in heated aquariums worldwide.

whyInteresting: Hybrids between platies and swordtails can develop melanoma from pigment cells, and such crosses have been studied as a cancer model since the late 1920s.
The species has three kinds of sex chromosome, W, X and Y, so sex is set by more than one chromosome combination across populations.
Many aquarium platies carry genes from crosses with the variable platy and swordtails, so pet-shop fish are often not pure southern platyfish.
A gene region called the P locus largely sets when males mature, so some males mature early at a small size and others late and large.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An omnivorous grazer that picks algae and soft plant material from surfaces and takes small insect larvae, worms and crustaceans. In the wild, plant matter and algae usually make up a large share of what it eats.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger fish, herons, kingfishers and predatory aquatic insects take wild platies, and adults of many fishes, their own species included, eat newborn fry. Platies escape by darting into dense plants, where the fry also hide.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At night it settles low in the water or among plants and moves very little, and its colours often look paler until light returns.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 2 to 3 years in aquariums, occasionally longer; lifespan in the wild has not been documented in detail.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Fertilisation is internal. After roughly four weeks' gestation, depending on temperature, a female gives birth to about 20 to 80 free-swimming young, and stored sperm lets her produce further broods without mating again. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are smaller and have a gonopodium, an anal fin reshaped into a narrow, rod-like mating organ. Females are larger and deeper-bodied, with a fan-shaped anal fin.

analysis.summary: Pairs of this small western Amazon monkey, each animal weighing about a kilogram, stay together for years and raise their young as a family. Mates keep within a few metres of each other through the day and, when resting side by side on a branch, often twist their long tails together.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly ripe fruit, topped up with young leaves, seeds, flowers and insects. The pair forages together in small fruiting trees and vine tangles, picking food by hand.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Likely predators include large forest eagles, ocelots and other wild cats, tayras and large snakes. Titis freeze, slip into dense cover and give alarm calls rather than flee in the open.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day with a long rest around midday. At night the family sleeps huddled together on a branch hidden among dense vines or leaves.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly documented; roughly 10 to 15 years is a plausible estimate, and captive animals generally live longer than wild ones.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single infant is born, usually once a year. The father does most of the carrying from the first days, passing the infant to the mother mainly for nursing, and older offspring stay with the family group for a year or more before leaving.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are the same colour and nearly the same size, and cannot be told apart reliably in the field.

Moths of the genus Agdistis are an exception, with narrow wings that are not divided into lobes.
Caterpillars of the sundew plume, Buckleria paludum, feed on the sticky leaves of carnivorous sundews.
The white plume moth of Europe, Pterophorus pentadactyla, is entirely white and is one of the easiest members of the family to recognise.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars eat leaves, buds, flowers or seeds, and some bore into stems; many species use only one plant genus or family, such as bindweeds or daisies. Adults of many species take nectar from flowers.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, bats, spiders, predatory bugs and parasitic wasps and flies take adults or caterpillars. The resting adult resembles a dry grass stem, and caterpillars of many species feed hidden inside buds, rolled leaves or stems.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most fly at dusk and through the night, and many come to lights. By day they rest on stems, leaves, walls and fences with wings rolled, flying a short distance if disturbed. A few species are active in daylight.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults of most species probably live a few weeks at most, and the whole life cycle takes from about two months to a year. Some, such as the common plume Emmelina monodactyla, overwinter as adults and live several months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs singly or in small groups on the food plant. Caterpillars feed on or inside it, then pupate attached to the plant, often exposed on a stem or leaf. Many species have one or two generations a year.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in wing shape and colour in most species. Separating them reliably usually means examining the tip of the abdomen under magnification.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Song thrushes and other birds, small mammals, ground beetles and other snail-eating insects take it. When disturbed it withdraws into its shell.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active mainly at night and after rain, when the ground is damp. On ordinary days it rests low among plant bases, under litter or beneath stones.

entries.name: Pompeii Worm
entries.heroTitle: Pompeii Worm — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Pompeii Worms inhabit deep-sea hydrothermal vents where hot mineral-rich water meets cold ocean darkness. Their bodies and associated microbes let them survive one of the narrowest and harshest animal habitats on Earth.
identification: Pale grey body up to about 13 cm long
Red, feathery gills at the front end
Short paired side lobes along the body carrying bristles
Lives with its rear end deep in a papery tube
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_pacific. Walls of active black-smoker chimneys on the East Pacific Rise, about 2,500 metres down. Colonies of papery tubes coat the chimney surface, where vent water flowing past can be very hot.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_pacific. Walls of active black-smoker chimneys on the East Pacific Rise, about 2,500 metres down. Colonies of papery tubes coat the chimney surface, where vent water flowing past can be very hot.

Short paired side lobes along the body carrying bristles

whyInteresting: A fleece of filamentous bacteria grows on its back, fed by mucus from glands along the body.
Early measurements suggested its tail end sits in water near 80 °C, but later work argues its tissues experience much less, and the figure remains debated.
It was described in 1980, and its name recalls Pompeii, the Roman town buried by volcanic ash.
The genus Alvinella is named after Alvin, the research submersible used to explore the vents.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Thought to graze bacteria and fine particles from the chimney surface around the tube mouth, using tentacles around the head.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators are poorly documented. Vent crabs are suspected of preying on it, and it retreats into its tube when disturbed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: There is no day or night at these vents, and no rest cycle has been described.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long this worm lives has not been measured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Sexes are separate and fertilisation is internal. In laboratory tests, embryos developed only in cool water and stayed dormant in near-freezing water, suggesting young may drift through cold deep water between vents.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look much alike, but males carry a pair of enlarged tentacles near the mouth, which are thought to play a part in mating.

entries.name: Pond Slider
entries.heroTitle: Pond Slider — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A freshwater turtle of the eastern and central United States and north-east Mexico that spends long hours hauled out on logs and banks, sometimes stacked on top of one another. Basking is also thought to help dry the shell, which may discourage algae and leeches. The name comes from its habit of sliding straight back into the water when disturbed.
identification: A red, orange or yellow stripe or blotch behind each eye, varying by subspecies
Olive to brown upper shell with yellow lines, darkening with age
Yellow lower shell, plain or marked with dark spots or smudges
Thin yellow stripes on the head, neck and legs
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Ponds, lakes, marshes, slow streams, logs, and sunny banks.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america. Ponds, lakes, marshes, slow streams, logs, and sunny banks.

whyInteresting: The red-eared subspecies is one of the most traded pet reptiles and is now established in many countries outside its native range.
Nest temperature sets the sex of the hatchlings: warmer nests produce mostly females, cooler nests mostly males.
Old males can become melanistic, with the shell and head markings darkening to almost black.
A courting male swims in front of the female and flutters his claws close to her face.
Young sliders eat mostly animal food and shift towards a diet dominated by plants as they grow.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Aquatic plants, algae, insects, snails, fish, tadpoles, and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raccoons, herons, large fish, snakes, birds, and humans threaten sliders; shell, basking awareness, and water retreat protect them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal basking is common; they rest underwater or in sheltered places when temperature and light make activity inefficient.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Pond sliders can live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females dig nests on land and lay clutches of eggs, leaving hatchlings to find water after emergence.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often smaller with longer front claws and thicker tails, while females grow larger for egg production.

entries.name: Popeyed Scorpionfish
entries.heroTitle: Popeyed Scorpionfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Popeyed Scorpionfish teaches that stillness does not mean helplessness. Its silence is guarded by camouflage and consequence.
identification: Branched, weed-like skin tassels over the head and body
Very deep, flattened body in side view
Tall spiny dorsal fin running along the back
Upturned mouth set under a steep snout
Colour pink, red, yellow, brown or purple, often with ringed spots
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: indian_ocean, coral_triangle. Coral and rocky reefs and nearby rubble or sand slopes with algae and sponges, usually from about 10 to 90 metres deep, across warm tropical waters from the western Indian Ocean to the Coral Triangle.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: indian_ocean, coral_triangle. Coral and rocky reefs and nearby rubble or sand slopes with algae and sponges, usually from about 10 to 90 metres deep, across warm tropical waters from the western Indian Ocean to the Coral Triangle.

whyInteresting: Rather than swimming, it usually moves by walking and hopping over the bottom on its pectoral and pelvic fins.
It has been seen shedding its outer layer of skin, a habit shared with some other scorpionfishes.
Its rarity and odd shape make it one of the most sought-after reef fishes among underwater photographers.
It belongs to Rhinopias, a small genus of about six scorpionfishes, all of them rarely encountered.

Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Eats small fishes, taken by a sudden gulp when they come within reach. It may also creep slowly towards prey, rocking gently like drifting weed.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Natural predators are not documented. Collection for the aquarium trade may be a local pressure on some reefs.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Its daily rhythm has not been studied; divers find it motionless on the reef by day, and it seems to rest in the open rather than in a shelter.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long it lives, in the wild or in aquariums, remains unknown for this rarely studied reef fish.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding has not been documented for this species; its eggs, larval development and any parental care remain undescribed.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: No reliable external difference between the sexes is known; colour varies widely between individuals regardless of sex.

entries.name: Portuguese Dogfish
entries.heroTitle: Portuguese Dogfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Portuguese Dogfish teaches quiet endurance. Its world is dark and pressurized, reminding us that some resilience is forged far below attention.
identification: Stout dark brown to blackish body with no anal fin
Two small dorsal fins, each with a tiny, easily missed spine
Large, smooth, overlapping scales giving a glossy skin
Large eyes set well forward on a short snout
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic. On or near the bottom of continental slopes and abyssal plains in the North Atlantic, mostly deeper than about 400 metres, in cold, permanently dark water.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_atlantic. On or near the bottom of continental slopes and abyssal plains in the North Atlantic, mostly deeper than about 400 metres, in cold, permanently dark water.

Large, smooth, overlapping scales giving a glossy skin
Large eyes set well forward on a short snout
whyInteresting: It is among the deepest-living sharks, recorded at nearly 3,700 metres in the Atlantic.
Its large, oily liver gives buoyancy and has been fished for squalene, an oil used in cosmetics.
The name coelolepis means hollow scale, after the shallow depression on each of its scales.
Its large eyes have a reflective layer behind the retina that helps gather faint light.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Hunts near the seabed for squid, octopus and bony fishes, and also scavenges; remains of whales and other large carcasses have been found in its stomach.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few natural predators are known, though larger deep-sea sharks may take it. Deep-water trawls and longlines are the real threat, and fishing has reduced numbers in parts of the north-east Atlantic.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Its daily activity cycle and resting behaviour have not been studied in the wild.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild is poorly known, as reliable ageing methods for this shark are lacking; it is thought to grow slowly and mature late.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Bears live young. Embryos develop inside the mother on yolk reserves, and litters commonly number around a dozen pups, though the count varies widely. There is no care after birth.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females grow larger than males. Males carry paired claspers on the inner edge of the pelvic fins.

entries.name: Postman Butterfly
entries.heroTitle: Postman Butterfly — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A black longwing butterfly, 6 to 8 cm across, marked with red and with yellow or white. Wherever it lives it closely matches the local form of another distasteful longwing, Heliconius erato, so a bird that has learned to avoid one leaves both alone.
identification: Many forms show a red forewing band and a yellow hindwing bar
Amazonian forms carry red rays fanning across the hindwing
Small red dots at the base of the hindwing underside
Wings black with red, yellow or white, never orange with black tiger stripes
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_america. Tropical forests, edges, gardens, and passionflower corridors.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: south_america. Tropical forests, edges, gardens, and passionflower corridors.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 19/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

Amazonian forms carry red rays fanning across the hindwing
Small red dots at the base of the hindwing underside

whyInteresting: About thirty geographic races have been named, differing in where red, yellow and white appear on the wings.
Its common name is said to come from the way it visits the same flowers on a fixed daily round, like a postman on a delivery route.
A gene called optix switches on the red parts of the pattern, a finding published in 2011.
During mating the male passes a scent to the female that makes her less attractive to other males.
The genome was sequenced in 2012 and showed that colour-pattern genes had passed between longwing species through occasional hybridisation.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Nectar and pollen resources; larvae feed on passionflower.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, spiders, and parasitoids threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal. Flight begins once the morning sun has warmed the vegetation, and by late afternoon adults go to a night roost on thin twigs or tendrils, singly or in small groups.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults can live for several months, and about six months has been reported. Most butterflies of similar size live only a few weeks.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female lays only a few eggs each day but goes on laying for months, placing each one alone on a growing tip of a passionflower vine. The spiny caterpillars pupate after about two to three weeks of feeding.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes wear the same colour pattern. Males carry a patch of pale, shiny scent scales on the upper hindwing where the forewing overlaps it, seen only when the wings are open or in the hand.

entries.name: Pot-bellied Seahorse
entries.heroTitle: Pot-bellied Seahorse — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Pot-bellied Seahorse teaches Carried Brood through the largest brood pouch of any seahorse — a male may carry over a thousand young at once, and does the whole pregnancy himself.
identification: The largest seahorse species, reaching around 35 cm
A deep, distinctly rounded belly that gives the species its name
A prehensile tail used to grip weed, sponge and jetty piles
Males carry a large sealed brood pouch on the front of the abdomen
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: australia_coastal, south_pacific. Temperate weed beds, sponge gardens, jetty piles and estuaries.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: australia_coastal, south_pacific. Temperate weed beds, sponge gardens, jetty piles and estuaries.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 70/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: The largest seahorse species, reaching around 35 cm
A deep, distinctly rounded belly that gives the species its name
A prehensile tail used to grip weed, sponge and jetty piles
Males carry a large sealed brood pouch on the front of the abdomen
whyInteresting: The male, not the female, becomes pregnant — the female deposits eggs into his pouch.
A single brood can number several hundred to over a thousand young.
It is one of the largest seahorses in the world.
It anchors with its tail rather than swimming, and can hold position in current all day.
It lives around southeastern Australia and New Zealand, including on jetty piles and sponge gardens.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small crustaceans, mysid shrimp and other tiny prey drawn in by a fast snap of the snout.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger fish, rays and crabs. Its answer is stillness and camouflage — held motionless against weed or sponge, it reads as part of the holdfast.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Pot-bellied Seahorses stay anchored to a holdfast day and night, feeding through the day and remaining gripped in place after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live several years, and males may carry multiple broods in a season.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The male carries the brood for around a month and then expels hundreds of miniature, independent seahorses.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger, have a longer tail relative to the trunk, and carry the brood pouch females lack. The difference exists because the carrying is the male's job.

entries.name: Potato Leafhopper
entries.heroTitle: Potato Leafhopper — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A tiny leafhopper of North American crops that cannot survive northern winters. Each spring, adults from populations along the Gulf of Mexico ride warm southerly winds hundreds of kilometres north, reaching crops across the eastern United States and Canada within weeks.
identification: Pale green, wedge-shaped body about 3 mm long
Clear wings folded tent-like over the back
Hind legs lined with rows of fine spines
Nymphs run sideways across the leaf when approached
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Open farmland, field edges, gardens, orchards and forest margins of eastern and central North America, where it lives on the leaves of crops, fruit trees and weedy herbaceous plants, mostly in lowland areas.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america. Open farmland, field edges, gardens, orchards and forest margins of eastern and central North America, where it lives on the leaves of crops, fruit trees and weedy herbaceous plants, mostly in lowland areas.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 7/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Pale green, wedge-shaped body about 3 mm long
Clear wings folded tent-like over the back
Hind legs lined with rows of fine spines
Nymphs run sideways across the leaf when approached
whyInteresting: Its saliva injures the plant, causing hopperburn: leaf tips turn yellow, then brown, in a V shape.
It is one of the most damaging insect pests of alfalfa and potato in eastern North America.
The species name fabae refers to beans, one of its many host plants.
Alfalfa varieties with sticky glandular hairs on the stems have been bred to resist its feeding.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Sap and cell contents from the leaves and stems of a very wide range of plants, reportedly more than 200, including alfalfa, potato, beans and apple. It slices into the plant tissue with its mouthparts and sucks up the fluids.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders, damsel bugs, lacewing larvae and birds eat adults and nymphs, and tiny parasitic wasps develop inside the eggs. Disturbed adults jump and fly off.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults and nymphs feed on leaf undersides by day and night through the warm months. Adults take off mostly around dusk, and in cool weather both stay still on the underside of leaves.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults live about a month; development from egg to adult takes about three weeks in summer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females insert eggs singly into leaf veins and stems, a few each day, and they hatch in about ten days. The wingless nymphs moult five times; several generations follow each other through one summer.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are hard to tell apart in the field; females are slightly larger.

entries.name: Potter Wasp
entries.heroTitle: Potter Wasp — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Potter Wasps are solitary builders that collect mud, form protective cells, and stock them with prey for young. Their care is architectural: clay, prey, and timing all have to meet.
identification: Usually black with yellow, white or orange bands
Forewings folded lengthwise at rest, looking narrow
Narrow waist, in some genera a long slender stalk
Carries balls of wet mud to the nest
Marble-sized mud pot with a flared neck, in Eumenes

Gardens, meadows, hedgerows, open woodland and scrub, wherever flowers, caterpillars and a supply of damp soil occur together. Depending on species, nests are fixed to twigs, stems, rocks and walls, or built inside beetle holes, hollow stems and other cavities.

whyInteresting: Potter wasps belong to Vespidae, the same family as hornets, yellowjackets and paper wasps, but they do not form colonies.
Over 3,000 potter wasp species have been named, and new ones are still being described.
When damp soil is scarce, females of some species carry water to the nest site and mix it with dry earth to make mud.
In species that nest in hollow stems, cells lie in a row divided by mud walls, and males often develop in the outer cells and emerge first.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults feed on flower nectar and sometimes honeydew. The female hunts small caterpillars, and in some species beetle larvae, stings them so they cannot move, and packs from one to a dozen or so into each cell for a single larva.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, mantises and robber flies take adults. Sealed nests are broken into by cuckoo wasps, parasitic flies and other parasitoids, which lay their own eggs inside. Females can sting but rarely do, having no colony to defend.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Flying and building take place by day in warm, sunny weather. Adults spend the night and cool spells gripping stems or sheltering in crevices.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Varies by species: most adults live a few weeks to about two months in summer. In many species the next generation spends the winter as a larva sealed in its cell, emerging the following year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Each female works alone. She hangs a single egg by a fine thread inside an empty cell, stocks the cell with prey and closes it with mud. The larva feeds, pupates and later chews its way out, with no further care from the mother.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are usually larger and have a sting. Males are smaller, often with more yellow or white on the face, and in many species the tip of the antenna is hooked or curled.

entries.name: Powder Blue Isopod
entries.heroTitle: Powder Blue Isopod — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Powder Blue Isopod AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A fine powdery bloom dusts the back of this small woodlouse, giving it the frosted, blue-grey look that its scientific name pruinosus, from the Latin for hoarfrost, describes. The bloom rubs off easily when the animal is handled, leaving a darker body showing through. Like all woodlice, it is a land-living crustacean, not an insect.
identification: Narrow, smooth oval body up to about 12 millimetres long
Tail section abruptly narrower than the body, giving a stepped outline
Relatively long legs for a woodlouse
Two short pointed prongs projecting beyond the rear end
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east. Powder Blue Isopods have an Old World native range centred on the Mediterranean region and adjacent parts of Europe and North Africa, although they are now widespread through human introduction. They inhabit moist leaf litter, soil, rotting wood, compost and debris, especially warm places where decaying organic material is abundant.

whyInteresting: It moults in two halves: the rear half of the old shell is shed first and the front half follows a day or so later.
Genetic studies suggest that the animals sharing this name are several closely related species and not a single one.
Some populations carry Wolbachia bacteria, which pass from mother to young through the eggs and can turn genetic males into functional females.
Soil scientists use it as a test animal when measuring how pesticides and metals affect life in the ground.
Breeders have selected orange and white colour forms from the usual blue-grey stock, and keepers add the animals to terrariums to clear up waste.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Dead leaves, rotting wood, compost, dung and the fungi growing on them are scraped up with small jaws. It also eats its own droppings and its cast skin, recovering nutrients and minerals that would otherwise be lost.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders, centipedes, ground beetles, toads, shrews and birds all eat woodlice, and the woodlouse spider specialises in them. This species cannot roll into a ball. It relies on speed, sprinting for the nearest crack the moment its cover is lifted.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal. It spends the day packed together with others under stones, boards and bark or deep in compost, which slows water loss, and comes out to feed after dark when the air is cooler and more humid.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one to two years in captive colonies; how long it lives in the wild is poorly documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female carries her eggs in a fluid-filled pouch under her body until pale, fully formed young crawl out, often a few dozen at a time. They start with six pairs of legs and gain the seventh after a moult. Several broods can follow in a warm year.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike from above. Turned over, a male shows a pair of long, pointed structures at the front of the underside of the tail section, and a breeding female shows a pale, swollen brood pouch between her legs.

White scalpel spine at the tail base, set off by yellow
Reaches about 23 cm, compact for a surgeonfish

entries.name: Prairie Vole
entries.heroTitle: Prairie Vole — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A small grassland vole in which a male and female usually stay together after mating and defend a shared territory. Laboratory work on this species showed that the bond depends on oxytocin and vasopressin acting on receptors in the brain's reward areas, a pattern largely missing in its promiscuous relative, the montane vole.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, owls, foxes, coyotes, snakes, and weasels threaten voles; burrows and shared vigilance protect the bond.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Prairie Voles usually live short lives in the wild, often months to a few years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females produce litters in grass nests, and males often help with young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar in appearance, while bonding behavior and parental roles make the difference that matters.

entries.name: Prevost's Squirrel
entries.heroTitle: Prevost's Squirrel — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Three sharply bordered colours divide the coat of this Sundaland tree squirrel, a pattern bold enough to stand out even in deep canopy shade. The borders are crisp rather than blended, so an animal can be picked out from the ground at a considerable distance.

White or cream stripe along each flank
Chestnut-red belly and inner legs
Long, bushy black tail held arched
Moves in quick dashes with frequent pauses on branches

whyInteresting: Many subspecies have been named across its islands, some with grey or grizzled backs rather than black.

It is widely kept in zoos, where its bold colours make it one of the best-known Asian squirrels.
The species name is generally taken to honour the French naturalist and illustrator Florent Prévost.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruits and seeds form most of the diet, with flowers, nectar and insects; tree sap and bird eggs are also reported. It is known to raid fruit crops and plantation trees.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Likely predators include hawk-eagles, tree snakes, civets and small cats, and many are trapped for the pet trade. It escapes by fast climbing and leaping between branches, flicking its tail when disturbed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, busiest in the morning and late afternoon. It spends the night in a leaf nest built high in the branches or inside a tree hollow.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around 15 years has been reported for a captive animal. Wild squirrels probably live much shorter lives, but no study has measured it.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Litters are small, usually one to three young, born in a nest after a gestation of about seven weeks. The young are raised by the mother and stay in the nest until they can climb well.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in size and colour.

entries.name: Leopard Cat
entries.heroTitle: Leopard Cat — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Hunting alone after dark, it creeps through dense undergrowth and pounces on rodents it has located by sound and sight. It is one of the most widespread small wild cats in Asia, ranging from tropical islands to snowy temperate forest.

Two dark stripes running from the eyes back over the head
Bold white streaks from the inner corners of the eyes
Rounded ears with a white spot on the back

It ranges from the lowlands into the hills and, in the Himalaya, to around 3,000 m.

The Bengal breed of domestic cat was developed from crosses between leopard cats and domestic cats.
The Iriomote cat, found only on one small island in southern Japan, is a population of this species.
Cats from the cold northern part of the range are larger, with thicker and greyer winter fur, than tropical cats.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly rats, mice and other small rodents, with birds, lizards, frogs, insects and sometimes fish. It climbs well enough to take some of its prey in trees.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few natural predators are recorded; leopards, clouded leopards and large pythons are the likeliest. People are the main threat, through forest loss, road traffic and trapping for fur and the pet trade. It stays in cover, moves at night and climbs to escape.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly nocturnal, with activity peaking around dusk and before dawn. By day it lies up in hollow trees, dense thickets, rock crevices or burrows dug by other animals.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive leopard cats can live well over 10 years. Wild lifespan is poorly documented and is probably shorter.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Litters are usually two or three kittens, born after a gestation of roughly 60 to 70 days in a den such as a hollow tree, burrow or rock cavity. The mother raises them alone, and the young become independent within several months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and heavier than females. Both sexes share the same coat colour and pattern.

entries.name: Fire-tufted Barbet

It is usually met singly or in pairs, but several may gather at one heavily fruiting tree.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Figs and other small fruits make up most of the diet, plucked while perched or while clinging to a fruiting branch. It also takes insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Its predators have not been well documented; forest hawks are likely to take adults, and snakes and small carnivores to raid nest holes. A resting bird sits motionless, and its plumage is hard to pick out among leaves.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, feeding and calling from early morning, often most vocal in the first hours of daylight. Night roosting has not been well described for this species. It is resident, with no seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been documented for this species, and no reliable ages from ringed birds have been published.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nest holes in dead trunks or branches have been reported, but clutch size, incubation and fledging periods in the wild are poorly recorded.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Male and female share the same plumage, and no field mark separates them.

entries.name: Psychedelic Frogfish
entries.heroTitle: Psychedelic Frogfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

Stubby, rounded body
Thick, limb-like pectoral fins
Broad, flattened face with forward-facing eyes

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female has been reported guarding an egg cluster tucked against her body, as other Histiophryne frogfishes do. Clutch size, hatching time and early development are not documented.

Neighbouring males often call in alternation, answering each other phrase by phrase.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, bats, spiders and mantises take adults and nymphs. Its green body is hard to pick out among leaves, and when handled it can bite hard.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Rests motionless among leaves in the canopy through the day and becomes active at night, when males call from dusk until the early hours.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one year from egg to adult death; the adult stage lasts from midsummer until the first hard frost.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay their eggs in autumn, and the eggs overwinter. Nymphs hatch in spring, feed in the trees and moult several times before becoming adults in midsummer.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Only males give the loud calling song, produced by a sound-producing area at the base of the forewings; females carry a broad, upcurved ovipositor.

entries.name: Spotted Barb

analysis.summary: Strong or sluggish currents, warm or cool water, and clear or muddy conditions are all tolerated by this small silvery barb. That tolerance lets it live in almost every kind of fresh water across its South-East Asian range, from hill country down to the coastal lowlands.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An omnivore that picks up aquatic insect larvae, worms, small crustaceans, algae, plant fragments and fallen land insects, feeding both in open water and by nosing along the bottom with its barbels.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Kingfishers, herons, snakeheads and other larger fish take it, and water snakes probably do too. It relies on moving in loose groups, fast bursts of swimming and quick retreats into roots, plants or rock gaps.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds and moves about by day. At night it becomes still, resting near the bottom or among vegetation and roots in quieter water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around five years in aquariums, according to keepers' reports; how long it lives in the wild has not been documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females scatter many small eggs over plants or gravel, where the males fertilise them. There is no parental care, and the eggs hatch within a few days into tiny larvae that feed on microscopic food.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look much alike. Mature females are deeper and fuller in the belly, especially when carrying eggs, while males stay slimmer.

entries.name: Purple-crowned Fairywren
entries.heroTitle: Purple-crowned Fairywren — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Purple-crowned Fairywren teaches that protection can be collective. Its strength comes from group care around a fragile home.

Pale buff to whitish underparts
Fine, dark, slightly pointed bill
About 14 to 16 cm long, nearly half of it tail

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Nest predators are thought to include snakes and butcherbirds, and hawks may take adults. The bigger threat is loss of riverside cover to cattle, fire and weeds. Group members give alarm calls and dive into the thicket.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Breeding males have a violet crown with a black centre and a black band through the eye. Females have a grey crown and a chestnut patch over the ear; non-breeding males lose the violet crown.

Luigi D'Albertis collected early specimens in the 1870s and asked that the species be named after the Marquis Francesco Raggi of Genoa.
Plume colour changes across the range, from deep red in the south to apricot-orange in the north-east.
Males take about five years or more to grow their full plumes, and until then look much like females.
Where their ranges meet it interbreeds with the lesser and greater birds-of-paradise, producing hybrids with intermediate plumage.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly fruit, including figs, nutmegs and the capsules of mahogany-family trees, together with insects and spiders picked from bark and foliage. Fruits are swallowed whole and the seeds dropped elsewhere, which spreads several forest trees.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Goshawks and other forest hawks are thought to be the main predators of adults, and snakes may take eggs and chicks. People have long hunted displaying males for their plumes, worn in ceremonial headdresses. At an alarm call the males scatter into cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Strictly diurnal. Calling starts soon after first light, feeding in the canopy fills much of the day, and nights are spent roosting in forest trees.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not measured in the wild. In zoos, birds-of-paradise of this genus are reported to have lived for more than 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female builds a bowl-shaped nest in a tree fork and raises the brood alone. She lays one or two pale, streaked eggs, incubates them for about 18 to 20 days, and feeds the chicks in the nest for roughly three weeks more.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and carry all the ornament: an iridescent green throat, long flank plumes and two wire-like tail feathers. Females are maroon-brown with a dark face and a dull yellow crown and nape, and have no plumes.

Its song is a thin, drawn-out whistle of about two seconds, repeated at intervals and heard far more often than the bird is seen.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It eats insects, worms, small invertebrates, and forest-floor prey. Food is picked from leaf litter, fallen logs and low plants as it walks steadily through the understorey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Its natural predators are poorly recorded; snakes and small forest carnivores are likely threats to nests. The main danger is clearance of lowland forest for logging and plantations, and when disturbed it walks or runs away through cover rather than flying.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It is mostly active by day in cover, but hard to observe because it stays low and hidden. Where it roosts at night has rarely been recorded.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: lifespan for Eupetes macrocerus remains unlisted in ringing catalogues; the rail-babbler walks forest floors of the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, and Borneo.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Little is known of its breeding: nesting is hidden in dense forest cover, with young protected by secrecy and placement. The few nests described have been placed low, close to the forest floor.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in the field, and any plumage differences between them are slight.

Like other land crabs of its family, it is thought to draw water from damp ground through tufts of hairs near the bases of its legs.
The Dutch zoologist Jan Adrianus Herklots gave the species its scientific name in 1851.
Its closest well-known relative is the blue land crab of the Caribbean and the Atlantic coast of the Americas, in the same genus.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An omnivorous scavenger that feeds mostly on fallen leaves, fruit and other plant matter, adding insects, small animals and carrion when it finds them. Food is gathered near the burrow, and some is reportedly dragged inside.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators of adult crabs are poorly documented, though people are reported to collect them for food in parts of West Africa. When threatened it bolts for its burrow or turns to face the attacker with claws raised and spread.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly nocturnal. The day is usually spent in the cool, humid burrow, and the crab comes out after dark or on overcast, rainy days.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Published wild years for Cardisoma armatum are absent; captive crabs are often said to reach about 10 years, though reports stay informal.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry large numbers of eggs under the broad abdominal flap and walk to salt or brackish water to release the hatching larvae. The larvae are thought to drift as plankton for several weeks before tiny crabs come ashore.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Turned over, males show a narrow, triangular abdominal flap and females a wide, rounded one. Males may also have one claw noticeably larger than the other.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Rainbow Scarab mainly uses dung and organic matter used for feeding and nesting. That food pattern supports Soilshine because the animal must get energy in the same way its principle works: hidden work can still carry color, value, and ecological purpose.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Burrows keep adults and larvae out of reach much of the time. Above ground, birds and insect-eating mammals such as skunks are thought to take adults, though records are few. Livestock wormers passed in dung can harm dung beetle larvae.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day in warm sunshine. Nights and cool or rainy days are spent in burrows in the soil.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: One generation takes about a year, most of it spent underground as larva and pupa; adults are thought to live a few months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female shapes dung into brood balls, coats each in soil and lays a single egg inside. The larva feeds on the dung within its ball, then pupates there, so each female produces only a few young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males carry a long, curved horn on the head and a flattened, angular thorax; females have only small bumps on the head.

Eight short arms and two longer tentacles around the mouth
whyInteresting: The first video of a living individual, filmed in 2020 at about 850 metres off the Great Barrier Reef, showed it holding its head upward.
Its empty coiled shells, only about 2 to 3 centimetres across, float after death and wash up on tropical beaches far more often than the animal is seen.
It is the only living species in its family, the last survivor of a once much larger group of shelled squid relatives.
The name Spirula means little spiral, after the shape of its shell.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Little is known of its feeding. Stomach contents suggest it takes small zooplankton, mainly tiny crustaceans, caught with its eight arms and two longer tentacles.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Its remains turn up in the stomachs of predatory fishes and other deep-sea hunters. When threatened it can release a cloud of ink.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It appears to migrate daily, sinking deeper by day and rising towards shallower water at night. Whether it has any resting phase is not known.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Estimated at about 1 to 1.5 years from growth studies; its lifespan in the wild has not been confirmed.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Where and how it breeds is not known. Its eggs have apparently never been found in the wild, and the youngest individuals caught already carry a small chambered shell.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Mature males have arms modified for passing sperm packets to the female; otherwise the sexes are hard to tell apart.

entries.name: Ray
entries.heroTitle: Ray — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Ray teaches Bottom Glide through a flattened body that belongs to the sea floor. Its wide fins, smooth swimming, bottom resting, sand-coloured concealment, and low movement show that protection can come from staying close to the surface beneath you. Its lesson is that concealment works best when motion fits the ground.
identification: Gill slits on the underside, not on the sides
Pectoral fins joined to the head, often forming a flat disc
Eyes on top; in most, mouth and nostrils underneath
Tail thin and whip-like in stingrays, thick and muscular in guitarfishes

Most live on or near the sea floor over sand, mud, gravel, seagrass or reef, from shallow bays and estuaries down to the deep continental slope. Skates are commonest in cooler and deeper water, while manta and devil rays roam the open ocean.

whyInteresting: Jelly-filled pores on the snout, the ampullae of Lorenzini, detect the faint electric fields produced by the muscles of buried prey.
Openings called spiracles behind the eyes draw in water for breathing, so bottom-living rays can lie still without taking in sand through the mouth.
Sawfishes look like sharks but are rays, and all species are now seriously threatened.
Devil rays often leap clear of the water and fall back with a loud slap, sometimes many in the same area.
Manta rays are reported to have among the largest brains relative to body size of any fish.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Most eat bottom animals such as clams, crabs, shrimps, worms and small fish, often uncovering them by flapping the fins or blowing water into the sand. Eagle rays crush shellfish with plate-like teeth, and manta and devil rays filter plankton.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large sharks, hammerheads especially, are the main natural predators, along with bigger fish and some marine mammals. Defences include burying in sediment, the venomous tail spines of stingrays and the shocks of electric rays. Fishing and bycatch now threaten many species.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Many rest lying still or buried on the bottom by day and feed at dusk and through the night, though some forage mainly in daylight. Manta rays and other open-water species keep swimming to breathe.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Varies widely: many smaller rays and skates live about 10 to 20 years, while manta rays are thought to live 40 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Skates lay eggs in tough, horned capsules left on the sea floor. Most other rays give birth to live young; stingray mothers feed embryos with a milky uterine fluid. Litters are usually small, often a handful of pups, and there is no care after birth.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a pair of rod-like claspers on the inner edge of the pelvic fins, used in mating. Females are often larger, and in many skates males carry extra rows of hooked spines on the wings.

analysis.summary: Razorfish teaches Vertical Movement by swimming head-down in tight synchronised groups, so a school of fish reads as a patch of seagrass or a cluster of urchin spines.

Sharp-edged belly, which is what names it
Moves in tightly synchronised groups

Groups shelter among the spines of long-spined sea urchins and match their angle.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Razorfish stay in their vertical groups day and night, drifting close to the shelter they mimic after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No age study of razorfish is known, and how long they live in the wild or in aquariums is unknown.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: They spawn in open water and the larvae are planktonic before joining groups on the bottom.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike. The absence of difference is essential — a school only disappears if every fish in it looks the same.

entries.name: Red Admiral
entries.heroTitle: Red Admiral — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Red Admiral is a velvet-black butterfly crossed by a scarlet band, found across Europe, North Africa and North America. It is a strong migrant that pushes north each spring, and its caterpillars grow up hidden one by one inside folded nettle leaves.

White spots near the forewing tips

Eggs are laid singly on nettle leaves, so each caterpillar starts life alone.
Adults feed readily on fermenting fallen fruit and oozing tree sap as well as flower nectar.
Males hold sunlit perches in the afternoon and fly up to chase rivals and other passing insects.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars eat stinging nettle and related plants such as pellitory and false nettle, feeding from inside the folded leaf that shelters them. Adults drink nectar from ivy, buddleia, thistles and asters, and gather at rotting fruit and sap runs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, dragonflies and wasps take adults, and parasitic wasps and flies attack the caterpillars. The leaf tent is the main defence of the young, and the bark-coloured underside hides a resting adult once the wings close.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and fond of basking with wings spread in the sun. It roosts overnight with wings closed on trunks, in foliage or in sheltered corners, and some adults pass the winter dormant in mild regions.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: A summer adult usually lives a few weeks, while those that migrate and overwinter can last several months. Egg to adult takes roughly one to two months in warm weather.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female lays her green, ribbed eggs one at a time on separate nettle leaves rather than in a batch. Each caterpillar therefore builds and lives in a tent of its own, with no siblings beside it.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike, with females slightly larger on average. Behaviour separates them better than pattern: males hold afternoon perches and chase intruders, while females spend their time searching nettle beds.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Workers may live weeks to months, while queens and colonies can last longer when nesting sites remain warm, hidden, and connected to food.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Queens lay eggs in protected nest spaces, and workers move larvae or food as conditions change. Offspring stay hidden until the colony route expands.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Queens, males, and workers differ strongly in form and role; most visible ants are sterile female workers following trail information.

entries.heroTitle: Red-backed Fairywren — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A tiny wren of northern and eastern Australian grassland in which breeding males turn glossy black with a scarlet to orange back. Not every male changes: many young males breed in plain brown plumage, while females tend to favour black-and-red males, which in studies also fathered more chicks in other pairs' nests.

Black bill in breeding males, paler brownish bill in females

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small insects, spiders, and seeds.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Feral cats, snakes, birds of prey and other larger predatory birds take adults, eggs and chicks. Group members give sharp alarm calls and dive into dense grass, and pairs hide their nests deep in tussocks or low shrubs.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active throughout the day, foraging most busily in the morning and resting in shade during the midday heat. At night the family group roosts in dense grass or low shrubs, often perched close together.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild is poorly documented and no reliable figure can be given; many birds die within their first year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female builds a domed grass nest low in dense cover and incubates a clutch of about three eggs alone. Both parents feed the chicks, and in some groups a helper, usually a young male, joins in.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are plain brown above and pale below and never show red or black. Only breeding males carry the black-and-red plumage.

Squarish tail, ochre-yellow beneath with a broad dark tip

It belongs to a small genus of just two species; its only relative, the blue-bearded bee-eater, lives mainly further north in Asia.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Bees, wasps, hornets and other large flying insects, plus beetles and cicadas. It waits on a perch and makes short sallies to catch prey in the air, then beats it against a branch to remove stings.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Loss and fragmentation of lowland forest is the main pressure on the species. Natural predators are not well documented, though forest hawks probably take adults and snakes probably raid nest burrows.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, mainly in the morning and late afternoon, and roosts in the forest at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long it lives in the wild is not known; there appear to be no longevity records for the species.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs dig a nest tunnel into an earth bank or cutting. Clutch size, incubation and chick development are poorly documented for this species.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In most descriptions males have a lilac-pink forehead and females a red one. Otherwise the sexes look alike.

entries.name: Red-bellied Pacu
entries.heroTitle: Red-bellied Pacu — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A large relative of the piranhas, growing to about 80 centimetres and 20 kilograms or more. Square, molar-like teeth crack hard seeds and nuts, and many seeds are thought to pass through its gut unharmed, letting it carry them far from the parent tree.
identification: Deep, laterally flattened, almost disc-shaped silvery-grey body
Red or orange chest and belly, strongest in young fish
Small fleshy adipose fin without rays behind the dorsal fin
Blunt, rounded head with a fairly small mouth

Red-bellied Pacu are native to tropical South American river systems, especially the Amazon basin; historically the name has also been applied broadly around Orinoco populations now subject to taxonomic refinement. They inhabit large rivers, floodplains and seasonally flooded forests where fruits, seeds and other food fall directly from overhanging vegetation.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: During high water it eats fruits and seeds in flooded forest, with leaves, flowers and some insects, snails and small fish. When low water cuts it off from the forest it eats less and is thought to draw on fat laid down during the floods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators of young fish likely include piranhas, large catfish, caimans, river dolphins and fish-eating birds, while adults are taken mainly by people, who fish them heavily for food. Sheer size puts adults beyond most river predators.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Thought to be active mainly by day, feeding under the forest canopy and along channel edges, and to rest in deeper or sheltered water at night; its daily rhythm in the wild is little studied.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Adults migrate upstream as the water begins to rise and spawn in open river channels, releasing very large numbers of small eggs that drift towards flooding plains. There is no parental care; the young grow up among flooded vegetation.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: No outward feature that separates males from females has been described; in the breeding season a female full of eggs may simply look plumper.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Titi monkeys can live well over a decade, with captive individuals sometimes living much longer.

entries.name: Red-billed Oxpecker
entries.heroTitle: Red-billed Oxpecker — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds of prey are likely predators of adults, while snakes and other nest raiders reach eggs and chicks in tree holes. Riding a large mammal offers some safety, and at danger the bird flies up from its host and circles before settling again.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It is diurnal, feeding on hosts by day and roosting or nesting in cavities. Groups gather in trees or reedbeds to roost, and some birds have been recorded spending the night on resting antelope or giraffe.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult lifespan is poorly documented for this species; ringing studies have not yet produced reliable survival figures.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Paired females lay eggs in tree cavities lined with hair from host animals. Clutches are usually 2 to 5 eggs, incubated for about 12 days, and helpers from the group, often older offspring, help feed the chicks until they fledge at about four weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in plumage and size. Juveniles differ, with a dark brownish bill and no bare yellow ring around the eye; the adult colours develop over several months.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predation on it is poorly documented. Forest clearance and hunting are the main pressures, and the IUCN has assessed it as Near Threatened.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal. Males gather at display trees before first light and are most active in the early morning, then the birds feed in the canopy. Night roosts in the forest have not been described, and there is no seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan remains unknown: no long-term ringing study has followed birds on these islands.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female alone builds a cup nest, incubates and feeds the young; males take no part. Clutches are small, reported as one or two eggs, and nesting in the wild is little studied.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult females lack the male's plumes and tail wires and are mostly brown with a darker face.
