whyInteresting: At 53 to 56 centimetres long, it is among the smallest of the world's geese.
Most of the world population winters near the western Black Sea coast in Bulgaria, Romania and Ukraine.
Until the middle of the twentieth century the main wintering area lay by the Caspian Sea, and the flocks shifted west after farming there changed.
Migrating flocks stop to rest and feed on the steppe lakes of northern Kazakhstan on the way between Siberia and the Black Sea.
Breeding success rises in years when lemmings are abundant, because Arctic foxes then take fewer eggs and goslings.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A grazer of grasses, sedges, leaves, seeds, and agricultural crops in winter. On the breeding grounds it eats cotton-grass and sedge shoots; wintering flocks near the Black Sea feed on winter wheat, barley and spilt maize.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Arctic foxes are the main predators of eggs and goslings, and gulls and skuas take some as well. On the wintering grounds adults are lost to illegal shooting, often among flocks of legally hunted geese, and to disturbance. The species is listed as Vulnerable.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly diurnal, feeding and resting in flocks with constant watchfulness. In winter, flocks leave at dawn to graze on fields and return at dusk to roost on the open water of lakes and coastal lagoons.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild has not been well documented; captive birds are reported to live 15 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In June, females lay eggs in tundra nests, often near protective birds of prey or steep terrain. The clutch is usually 3 to 8 eggs, incubated by the female alone for about 25 days. Goslings leave the nest within a day and fly at 5 to 6 weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: sexes look similar, so loyalty is shown through pair behavior and flock coordination. The sex notes keep the field guide specific without forcing a display story where none exists. That difference keeps Pairwatch tied to real biology rather than a loose label.

identification: Small, compact bird with a black eye-stripe and white brow
Rusty orange underparts and blue-grey back
Climbs head-down on trunks and branches
Nasal, tinny yank-yank call, like a tiny toy horn

whyInteresting: It descends trunks head-first, gripping with one foot high and one low, which lets it see into bark crevices from above rather than below.
It smears sticky conifer resin around its nest hole entrance and flies straight in without touching the sides.
It caches seeds in bark crevices through autumn and relies on them heavily in winter.
In years when conifer cone crops fail, large numbers move far south of the usual range in what birders call an irruption.
It will excavate its own nest cavity in soft dead wood rather than only using existing holes.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects and spiders prised from bark in summer; conifer seeds and cached food in winter. The head-down approach is what gives access to prey sheltering on the upper side of crevices and flakes.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sharp-shinned Hawks and small owls take adults; squirrels and woodpeckers raid nests. The resin barrier at the nest entrance deters climbing predators and insects alike.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, roosting in cavities overnight, sometimes in the nest hole outside the breeding season.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically six to seven years in the wild.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Five to six eggs in a cavity the pair often excavates themselves in soft dead wood, with the entrance ringed in resin. Both parents feed the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a black crown and brighter rust underparts; females have a grey crown and paler, washed-out underparts.

When the cone crop fails across a wide area, large numbers leave and irrupt far beyond their usual haunts.
North American birds fall into several vocal types with distinct flight calls, and some of these types differ in bill size and preferred conifer.
Flocks often come down to roadsides and puddles to drink and to take grit and salt from the ground.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly seeds taken from the cones of spruce, pine, larch, fir and hemlock, often while the cones are still closed on the tree. It also eats some other seeds, buds and insects such as aphids.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults are taken by hawks such as sparrowhawks and goshawks, and by falcons and owls. Squirrels, crows and jays raid nests. Feeding flocks call constantly and burst into the canopy at an alarm call.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, feeding from soon after dawn. At night flocks roost in dense conifer foliage, usually high in the trees.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most wild birds probably live only about 2 to 4 years; ringing shows that a few survive considerably longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding can happen in almost any month when cones are plentiful, including late winter. fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are brick red to orange-red with darker wings; females are olive-green to greyish with a yellowish rump. Young birds are streaked brown, and first-year males may show patchy orange or yellow.

analysis.summary: A medium-sized freshwater turtle native to the Mississippi valley and Gulf of Mexico drainages, named for the red stripe behind each eye. Released pets have established populations on every continent except Antarctica, making it one of the most widespread turtles.

whyInteresting: The name slider comes from its habit of sliding off a basking log into the water at the first sign of disturbance.
Nest temperature decides the sex of the hatchlings: warm incubation produces mostly females, cooler incubation mostly males.
Adult males grow very long front claws, which they flutter in front of a female's face during courtship.
Older males often darken to almost black, a change that can hide the red ear stripe and the yellow shell lines.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Omnivorous. Young turtles eat mainly insects, snails, tadpoles and small fish; adults take more water plants and algae, along with carrion. It usually swallows food underwater.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raccoons, skunks and foxes dig up nests, and herons, large fish, snakes and bullfrogs take hatchlings. Adults face alligators and people. It slides off its basking spot into water at the slightest alarm and withdraws into the shell.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, alternating basking and feeding. At night it sleeps underwater on the bottom or floating near the surface. In the north of its range it becomes largely inactive in winter, resting in mud on the bottom.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly lives 20 to 30 years in the wild, and captive turtles often live longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females come onto land to dig a nest and lay usually about 6 to 12 eggs, sometimes several clutches a season. Eggs hatch after about two to three months, and nest temperature sets the sex, warmer nests giving more females. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have very long front claws, used to flutter at a female's face in courtship, and longer, thicker tails. Females grow larger. Old males often darken to a dull, blackish colour.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, mantises, dragonflies, and larger robber flies can threaten them. Fast flight, strong legs, and aggressive predation reduce risk.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Red-footed Cannibalflies are diurnal, hunting from sunny perches in warm weather. Their rhythm belongs to bright air and sudden interception.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults are on the wing for a few weeks in summer. The larvae develop in soil or rotting wood, and how long that stage lasts has not been measured for this species.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are broadly similar, though females may be heavier when carrying eggs. The capture equipment—legs, flight, and piercing mouthparts—defines both sexes.

whyInteresting: Workers change jobs as conditions demand, moving between nest maintenance, midden work, patrolling and foraging.
The rate at which foragers return with food sets how many more go out, so colonies forage less on dry days.
Patrollers leave the nest first each morning, and foragers only set out once patrollers have returned safely.
Each colony has only one queen, and when she dies the colony gradually dies out because no replacement is adopted.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds of grasses and desert annuals make up almost all the food, carried home one at a time in the jaws. Foragers also pick up dead insects, and stored seeds are husked and chewed inside the nest.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Horned lizards eat large numbers of foragers, and some birds and spiders also take them. Workers defend the nest with a very painful sting, and entrances are plugged with soil in bad conditions.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Foraging happens by day, mostly in the morning, with a smaller bout in late afternoon in hot weather. Workers stay underground through the midday heat and overnight.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Colonies and their queens commonly live 15 to 30 years; workers live about a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A new queen mates during a summer mating flight after rain, sheds her wings and digs a founding burrow alone. She raises the first workers from her own reserves, and the colony takes about five years to produce winged queens and males.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Workers and queens are female; queens are larger with a bulkier thorax and bear wings until mating. Males are winged, slimmer and darker, and appear only around mating flights.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, insects, honeydew, carrion, and household scraps.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, armadillos, phorid flies, other ants, pathogens, floods, and humans threaten colonies; stings and swarming defend Fiery.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Fire ants work in cycles across day and night depending on heat, moisture, and food, resting in the mound during dangerous extremes.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Workers live weeks to months, queens can live years, and colonies persist by replacing individuals through constant brood production.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Queens lay large numbers of eggs, while worker females rear larvae, defend the mound, and move brood when conditions change.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Workers are sterile females, queens are reproductive females, and males are produced mainly for mating flights.

entries.name: Red Junglefowl
entries.heroTitle: Red Junglefowl — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The wild bird from which domestic chickens descend, domesticated in Asia several thousand years ago. Unlike farmyard birds it is slim, shy and a strong flier.
identification: Rooster's golden-orange neck hackles over dark underparts
Long, arched, glossy green-black tail feathers in males
Red comb and facial wattles, largest in males
Slate-grey legs, spurred in adult males
Slim, upright build, lighter than most farm chickens
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, south_asia. Forest edges, bamboo thickets, secondary growth, scrub and overgrown clearings, often near cultivation, from lowlands up into the Himalayan foothills.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia, south_asia. Forest edges, bamboo thickets, secondary growth, scrub and overgrown clearings, often near cultivation, from lowlands up into the Himalayan foothills.

whyInteresting: A large genetic study published in 2020 pointed to the subspecies Gallus gallus spadiceus, of mainland Southeast Asia, as the main source of domestic chickens.
Five subspecies are usually recognised across its range.
A rooster that finds food calls and repeatedly picks it up and drops it, a display called tidbitting that draws hens to him.
Birds dust-bathe in dry soil, working it through their feathers, which is thought to help control lice and mites.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, grain, fallen fruit, shoots, termites, other insects and worms, found by scratching leaf litter and soil with the feet. Birds have been reported gathering at seeding bamboo.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators include leopards, jungle cats, mongooses and birds of prey, while snakes and small carnivores take eggs and chicks. Hunting and interbreeding with free-ranging village chickens threaten wild populations.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Roosts at night well above the ground in trees or bamboo clumps. By day it is busiest in early morning and late afternoon.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly documented and probably only a few years for most birds; captive junglefowl have lived about 10 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The hen lays usually about four to seven eggs in a scrape hidden under vegetation and incubates alone for about three weeks. Chicks are downy and leave the nest soon after hatching, following the hen, who broods and guards them.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Hens are smaller and plain brown with a small comb and no long tail. After breeding, roosters replace their bright neck hackles with short dark feathers for a few months, an eclipse plumage domestic cockerels lack.

entries.name: Red Lady Beetle
entries.heroTitle: Red Lady Beetle — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Red Lady Beetle AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A small, glossy ladybird whose red wing cases carry no spots at all, it hunts aphids from the tropics of South America to the warmer parts of North America. Both the adults and the larvae are predators, working through aphid colonies on crops and wild plants.
identification: Wing cases plain red to orange-red with no spots
Black shield behind the head edged and marked with white
Rounded, strongly domed body about 4 to 6 millimetres long
Larvae elongate and spiny, shaped like tiny alligators
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Sunny, open places where aphids build up on plants: maize, cotton and citrus fields, orchards, gardens, roadside weeds and grassland, from lowland tropics into warm-temperate regions.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Sunny, open places where aphids build up on plants: maize, cotton and citrus fields, orchards, gardens, roadside weeds and grassland, from lowland tropics into warm-temperate regions.

whyInteresting: In parts of the Americas it now shares crops with the introduced harlequin ladybird, which has been recorded eating its eggs and larvae.
When aphids run short, larvae and adults will eat ladybird eggs and pupae, including those of their own species.
Adults fly readily between fields as aphid numbers rise and fall, so local numbers can change within days.
In the United States it is sometimes called the spotless lady beetle.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly aphids, found on growing tips and the undersides of leaves. It has also been recorded taking psyllids, whitefly, insect eggs and small caterpillars, and adults supplement this with pollen and nectar when prey is scarce.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, lacewing larvae and parasitic wasps attack it, and ants guarding aphids drive it away. Like other ladybirds, a grasped adult can bleed drops of bitter yellow fluid from its leg joints, and its red colour warns of this.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hunts in daylight, most actively in the warm hours. At night and in cool or wet weather it rests motionless under leaves or in plant crevices, and in cooler areas adults may shelter together through winter.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult lifespan in the wild is not well documented. Laboratory-reared adults commonly live one to a few months, and development from egg to adult takes only a few weeks in warm conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay small clusters of upright yellow eggs on leaves close to aphid colonies. Larvae hatch within a few days, pass through four growth stages in about two weeks, then pupate fixed to a leaf or stem.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are very similar and hard to tell apart in the field without close examination. As in many ladybirds, females are often slightly larger.

entries.name: Red-lipped Batfish
entries.heroTitle: Red-lipped Batfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Red-lipped Batfish teaches Batfish Authenticity through a fish that walks its own floor instead of swimming like everyone else. Red lips, leg-like fins, seafloor hunting, and Galapagos strangeness make difference functional.
identification: Bright red lips that make the face unmistakable.
Modified fins used for walking-like movement on the seafloor.
Bottom-dwelling ambush lifestyle rather than open swimming.
Unusual body shape suited to Galapagos reef and sandy bottoms.
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_america, south_pacific. Galapagos reefs, sandy bottoms, rocky seafloor, ledges, and deeper coastal habitats.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: south_america, south_pacific. Galapagos reefs, sandy bottoms, rocky seafloor, ledges, and deeper coastal habitats.

whyInteresting: Red-lipped Batfish are associated with the Galapagos region.
They are poor swimmers compared with many fish and often move along the bottom.
Their pectoral and pelvic fins help them walk or prop themselves on the seafloor.
They use a lure-like structure to help attract prey near the mouth.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger fish, sharks, eels, octopuses, and habitat disturbance can threaten batfish. Camouflage, stillness, and bottom-hugging movement help protect a strange body.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Red-lipped Batfish are slow bottom-active hunters, with activity shaped by prey and shelter rather than dramatic day-night display.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Red-lipped Batfish likely live for several years, though exact wild lifespan is not well known.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Reproduction in this species has hardly been studied. Eggs are thought to be released into open water, where the larvae drift in the plankton before settling on the bottom as young fish.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar from casual observation. The lesson comes from the shared seafloor body plan rather than sex-specific display.

entries.name: Red Lory
entries.heroTitle: Red Lory — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A brush of fine papillae tips the tongue of this nectar-feeding parrot of the Moluccas, about 30 cm long. It sweeps nectar and pollen from open blossoms, so flocks travel from one flowering tree to the next.
identification: Plumage almost entirely bright scarlet red
Blue patch under the tail
Blue in the wing with black-tipped flight feathers
Orange-red bill and a medium-length, rounded red tail
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Red Lories are native to the Maluku Islands of Indonesia. They inhabit tropical lowland forest, secondary woodland, mangroves, plantations, gardens, and other areas with flowering and fruiting trees.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Red Lories are native to the Maluku Islands of Indonesia. They inhabit tropical lowland forest, secondary woodland, mangroves, plantations, gardens, and other areas with flowering and fruiting trees.

Blue patch under the tail
Blue in the wing with black-tipped flight feathers

whyInteresting: Several island populations differ slightly in shade and size, and some authors have treated them as separate subspecies.
It is among the lories most often kept in aviaries outside its native islands.
Its species name, bornea, is thought to come from an early mistaken belief that the bird came from Borneo.
Young birds are reported to be duller than adults, with a darker bill and less intense red.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Nectar and pollen from flowering trees, especially coconut palms and native blossoms, along with soft fruit, flowers and probably some insects. Birds clamber through the crown, often hanging upside down to reach blossoms.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Flocks screech in alarm and fly off fast at the first sign of danger. Birds of prey probably take adults, and climbing snakes and mammals can reach eggs and chicks in nest hollows. People are the larger pressure, through trapping for cage birds and forest clearance.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, flying between flowering trees from early morning. At night birds roost in trees, often in groups; its roosting habits are poorly documented.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive Eos lories often reach 15 to 25 years or more; how long wild birds live has not been recorded.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests in a hollow high in a tree. The usual clutch is two white eggs, incubated for about 24 to 26 days in captive records; the chicks leave the nest at roughly two months old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike and cannot be reliably sexed by plumage in the field.

entries.name: Red-necked Phalarope
entries.heroTitle: Red-necked Phalarope — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Red-necked Phalaropes feed by spinning in circles on water, bringing small prey within reach. Females are often brighter, and males do much of the incubation and chick care.
identification: Needle-thin, straight black bill
Rufous-orange band down the side of the neck in breeding plumage
White throat and dark back with buff stripes
Lobed toes and buoyant swimming like a tiny gull
Winter: grey above, white below, black patch through the eye

Breeds on low Arctic and subarctic tundra, bogs and marshes dotted with small shallow pools. Outside the breeding season it lives far out at sea, gathering in large flocks where currents and upwellings concentrate plankton at the surface.

whyInteresting: Phalaropes are sandpipers that took to swimming, and belong to the family Scolopacidae.
On the breeding grounds it is often very tame, feeding within a few metres of people.
The genus name Phalaropus means coot-footed, a reference to the lobed toes.
In Britain it breeds only in small numbers, mainly on Shetland.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: On the breeding grounds it eats mosquito and midge larvae and other small insects; at sea, copepods, krill and other tiny crustaceans. It pecks rapidly at the surface and moves each item up its thin bill using the water's surface tension.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Arctic foxes, skuas, jaegers and gulls take eggs and chicks; falcons such as merlins catch adults. Nests are hidden in grass tussocks, and adults give alarm calls and distraction flights when predators come near.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: On breeding grounds with near-constant daylight it may feed at any hour, resting briefly on pool margins. At sea flocks rest floating on the water, sleeping with the bill tucked into the back feathers.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Ringing recoveries are few for a bird that winters at sea, but ringed adults have been recorded living more than 5 years, and the true maximum is probably higher.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The usual clutch is four olive eggs blotched with brown, laid in a grass-lined scrape near water and incubated for about 18 to 21 days. Chicks leave the nest within a day and find their own food; some females go on to lay a clutch for a second male.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are slightly larger, with a dark grey head and rich orange neck; males have a duller, patchier head and neck. In winter plumage the sexes look alike.

entries.name: Red-necked Wallaby
entries.heroTitle: Red-necked Wallaby — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A medium-sized wallaby of eastern Australia and Tasmania, named for the reddish-brown fur across its nape and shoulders. The Tasmanian form, known as Bennett's wallaby, has a thicker, shaggier coat that suits its cold, wet highland habitat.
identification: Pale grey-white chest and belly
White stripe along the upper lip
Black paws, feet tips and nose
Grizzled grey body fur
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania, tasmania. Eucalypt forest and woodland with a dense shrub understorey, and coastal scrub, next to open grassy areas where it feeds. In Tasmania it ranges from coastal heath up into highland grassland and forest.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: australia_oceania, tasmania. Eucalypt forest and woodland with a dense shrub understorey, and coastal scrub, next to open grassy areas where it feeds. In Tasmania it ranges from coastal heath up into highland grassland and forest.

White stripe along the upper lip
Black paws, feet tips and nose
Grizzled grey body fur
whyInteresting: Mainland females can breed at any time of year, whereas Tasmanian females give birth mostly in late summer.
Animals released in New Zealand in the 1870s founded a wild population in South Canterbury, and escapes from collections have produced small, scattered populations in Britain.
Adults are usually solitary but may gather loosely where grazing is good.
Males spar by standing upright and grappling, pushing and kicking at each other.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grazes grasses and herbs, and browses on leaves of shrubs. It feeds in open pasture and clearings, usually close to cover.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Dingoes and feral dogs take adults, while foxes and wedge-tailed eagles mainly take joeys and young animals. Tasmania has no dingoes, and there dogs, eagles and road traffic are the main threats. When alarmed it thumps the ground with its hind feet and bounds into cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active at dusk, night and early morning, though often out in the late afternoon. It rests by day in dense scrub or forest cover.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around 9 years in the wild; captive animals may reach about 15.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a pregnancy of about 30 days a single joey is born and spends roughly nine months in the pouch, then suckles at foot for several more months. Development of a second embryo can pause until the pouch is free.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are noticeably larger than females and more muscular in the forearms and chest.

entries.name: Red Palm Weevil
entries.heroTitle: Red Palm Weevil — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Red Palm Weevil AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A large rust-red weevil whose larvae tunnel through the soft tissue inside a palm's trunk and crown. Damage stays hidden for months, and by the time the central fronds wilt the tree is often beyond saving. It attacks coconut, date and oil palms among others.
identification: Rusty-red body, roughly 2.5 to 4 cm long
Long, curved snout
Black spots on the thorax, variable in number
Elbowed antennae set near the base of the snout
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_africa_middle_east, south_asia, southeast_asia. Palm plantations, date groves, coastal coconut stands and ornamental palms in parks and streets. Native to south and south-east Asia, and now widespread in date-growing regions of the Middle East and North Africa.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_africa_middle_east, south_asia, southeast_asia. Palm plantations, date groves, coastal coconut stands and ornamental palms in parks and streets. Native to south and south-east Asia, and now widespread in date-growing regions of the Middle East and North Africa.

Long, curved snout

whyInteresting: Males release an aggregation pheromone that draws both sexes, and it is used as bait in monitoring traps.
The crunching of larvae feeding inside a trunk can sometimes be heard or picked up with acoustic sensors.
The fat larvae of this and related palm weevils are eaten as food in parts of south-east Asia.
Moving infested young palms and offshoots for planting has carried it far beyond its native range.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Larvae feed on the palm's soft, sugary internal tissue, above all the growing point in the crown and the bases of leaf stalks, and leave chewed fibres behind. Adults take fermenting sap at wounds and cut surfaces.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Recorded natural enemies include predatory earwigs, parasitic nematodes and fungal diseases such as Beauveria, several of which have been tested as control agents. Adults are protected by a hard, thick body shell.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are active and fly mainly by day, sheltering in leaf axils and crowns at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults commonly live two to three months. Egg to adult takes roughly three to four months, depending on temperature.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female uses her snout to make holes in wounds or soft tissue and lays eggs singly, commonly around 200 to 300 in her life. Larvae pass through a variable number of moults before pupating in an oval cocoon woven from palm fibres.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a row of short bristles along the upper side of the snout near its tip; females have a longer, thinner, bare and more curved snout.

analysis.summary: Females scrape fibres from weathered wood, chew them with saliva into pulp and spread the pulp into thin grey paper. From it this large wasp of the eastern and southern United States builds a single comb of six-sided cells, open underneath and hung from one narrow stalk.
identification: Head and body are rust-red with few or no yellow marks
The wings are smoky black and fold lengthwise at rest
Long hind legs trail below the body in flight
The abdomen tapers at both ends behind a narrow waist

whyInteresting: Unlike many paper wasps, it usually builds its nest in enclosed shelters such as hollow trees, wall cavities, or sheds.
Colonies are founded in spring by mated queens that spent the winter hidden in sheltered places.
Nests may be founded by a single queen or by several cooperating females, with one dominant female laying most of the eggs.
It closely resembles its relative Polistes perplexus, and the two species are often confused where their ranges overlap.

entries.name: Red Sea Urchin
entries.heroTitle: Red Sea Urchin — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Red Sea Urchins are spiny kelp-forest grazers that can live for a very long time. Their survival depends on patient movement, defensive spines, rock grip, and steady feeding on algae and kelp.

Colour from bright red to dark burgundy or purple
Tube feet visible between spines, gripping rock

Experiments found that old urchins regrow lost spines and tube feet about as well as young ones.
Tiny stalked pincers among the spines, some venomous, clear debris and fend off small animals.
It was long placed in the genus Strongylocentrotus before being moved to Mesocentrotus.
Where sea otters have returned, red urchin numbers have fallen and kelp forests have grown back.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly drift kelp: fronds carried by the current are trapped with spines and tube feet and chewed. When drift is scarce, groups roam out to graze attached kelp, and dense aggregations can strip reefs into bare barrens.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sea otters, sunflower sea stars, California sheephead, spiny lobsters and wolf eels eat them, and they are fished commercially for their roe. Adults wedge into crevices and swing their spines towards a threat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Movement and feeding are slow and continue by day or night, with no regular rest period.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Growth is slow and large individuals can be decades old; radiocarbon dating of the biggest urchins has estimated ages of more than 100 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Each female releases millions of eggs into open water, where they are fertilised by sperm shed from nearby males. The larvae drift for several weeks before settling, and young urchins often shelter beneath the spine canopy of adults.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look identical; sex shows only in the gonads or during spawning.

analysis.summary: Red Slender Lorises are nocturnal primates that rely on deliberate climbing, sharp vision, and careful reach. Their slow movement is controlled, not weak, because every branch and prey item is tested in darkness.

Its large, forward-facing eyes have a reflective layer behind the retina, producing bright eyeshine when caught in a torch beam.
It is listed as Endangered, threatened largely by loss and fragmentation of Sri Lanka's wet-zone forests.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly insects, especially ants and beetles, grabbed with both hands after a slow approach. It also eats other small invertebrates, and has been reported to take small vertebrates and bird eggs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, snakes and civets are likely predators, and domestic dogs and cats kill some. Forest loss, electrocution on power lines and road traffic are serious threats. Its main response is to freeze.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Sleeps through the day curled into a tight ball, gripping a branch in dense vine tangles or foliage, sometimes in small groups.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive Loris tardigradus have reached about twenty-two years at the Duke Lemur Center; wild ages are less certain. Slow climbing and a toxic bite mark its nocturnal foraging.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually one infant, occasionally twins, after a gestation of about five and a half months. The infant clings to its mother's belly, is later left on branches while she feeds, and is weaned at around six months.

entries.name: Red Slug
entries.heroTitle: Red Slug — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Arion rufus is a large European slug, orange to brick-red, that is helpless on a dry afternoon and unstoppable on a wet night. The trail is the method; the weather is the permission.
identification: Large slug, 10-15 cm when extended, orange to brick-red
Coarse skin tubercles, a long foot fringe
Breathing hole (pneumostome) on the right side of the mantle
No keel on the back, unlike Limax

analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe. Damp woodland, gardens, hedges and compost in Europe. Day cover under logs and pots; night feeding on the surface after rain.

whyInteresting: It is native to Europe and easily confused with the Spanish slug Arion vulgaris, which is the more invasive of the two.
The colour stays even when the animal is contracted, which helps separate it from some brown Arion.
It can eat fungi, carrion and seedlings as well as leaves, which is why a wet garden sees so much damage in a night.
This capture sat on the hidden slug group key; that key is not this species and is not aliased here.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, fungi, seedlings, decaying matter and occasional carrion, rasped on a wet surface. Dry food is not used because dry skin is fatal.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hedgehogs, frogs, ground beetles and thrushes. The main defence is to be out only when those hunters are less effective and the mucus trail holds.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Night-active and wet-weather-active. Hidden under cover through dry days.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: A year or more. Adults are the large red animals of late summer and autumn.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid in clusters in damp soil or under wood. A dry spell at hatching kills more than any predator.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: There is no useful field difference. Both individuals in a pairing are hermaphrodites.

entries.name: Red-spotted Guard Crab
entries.heroTitle: Red-spotted Guard Crab — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Red-spotted Guard Crab AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A small crab that spends its adult life inside a single branching coral colony and defends it. When a crown-of-thorns starfish or a coral-eating snail approaches, the resident crabs pinch its tube feet or spines and push it away, and corals holding guard crabs suffer less damage from these predators.
identification: Smooth, broad carapace with a wide, straight front edge
Pale cream body densely covered in small red spots
Stout, smooth claws held folded in front of the body
Sits wedged deep among coral branches, rarely in the open

Shallow tropical coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific, on reef flats, lagoons and upper reef slopes, where it lives inside colonies of branching cauliflower and bush corals, mainly of the genus Pocillopora.

whyInteresting: Like other guard crabs of its genus, it is thought to feed largely on mucus and fat-rich tissue produced by its host coral, along with particles trapped on the coral.
Each coral head usually holds a single adult pair, which chases off other adults of its own species.
Experiments on Pocillopora corals found that colonies hosting guard crabs coped far better with smothering sediment than colonies without them.
When its host coral bleaches or dies, the crab loses both shelter and food and must move to a new colony.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It prods the coral surface with its legs, which prompts the polyps to release mucus and small fatty bodies. The crab gathers these to its mouth, along with plankton and detritus trapped on the colony.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predation on it has been little studied; reef fishes and octopuses are the likely predators. It rarely leaves its coral, retreating deep among the branches where larger animals cannot reach it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It stays among the branches of its host coral by day and night. Daily activity rhythms and rest have not been studied in this crab.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long this crab lives has not been documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: As in other true crabs, the female carries her fertilised eggs under her folded abdomen until they hatch. The larvae drift in the plankton before settling onto a suitable coral and moulting into juvenile crabs.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: From above the sexes look alike. They can be told apart only by the abdomen folded under the body, which is narrow in males and broad and rounded in females.

entries.name: Red-spotted Purple
entries.heroTitle: Red-spotted Purple — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The dark, southern form of Limenitis arthemis, a North American admiral butterfly. Its blue-black wings resemble the distasteful Pipevine Swallowtail, which it mimics. Further north it grades into the White Admiral, the same species with a broad white band across the wings.
identification: Black upperside with iridescent blue to blue-green on the hindwing
No tails on the hindwings
Red-orange spots near the base and edge of the underside
Wingspan roughly 7 to 9 centimetres

analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america. Deciduous and mixed woodland, forest edges, stream corridors, clearings and leafy suburbs, from lowlands into low hills.

No tails on the hindwings
Red-orange spots near the base and edge of the underside

whyInteresting: A young caterpillar eats a leaf down to the midrib and rests on the bare vein, which it lengthens with silk and droppings.
The third-stage caterpillar survives winter in a hibernaculum, a leaf tip rolled and tied to the twig with silk.
Rare hybrids with the Viceroy, a close relative in the same genus, have been recorded.
The caterpillar carries a pair of knobbed, bristly horns on the thorax, just behind the head.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars eat the leaves of wild cherry, willows, poplars, birches and other trees. Adults rarely visit flowers, drinking instead from tree sap, rotting fruit, dung, carrion and damp mud.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds are the main predators of adults, while parasitic wasps and flies attack eggs and caterpillars. Adults escape with fast, gliding, twisting flight.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults fly in sunshine by day. At night and in dull weather they are thought to roost with wings closed beneath leaves in trees and shrubs.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults usually live about two to four weeks. In single-brooded northern populations the full life cycle takes a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay single eggs on the tips of host-tree leaves. Caterpillars pass through five stages before pupating in a hanging chrysalis; there are one to three broods a year, more in the south.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look almost identical; females tend to be slightly larger with broader wings.

entries.name: Red Swamp Crayfish
entries.heroTitle: Red Swamp Crayfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Red Swamp Crayfish AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: Dark red and usually no more than about 12 centimetres long, this freshwater crayfish comes from the swamps and ditches of the southern United States and north-east Mexico. It survives seasonal drying by digging a burrow down to the water table and waiting out the dry months in the damp chamber at the bottom.
identification: Dark red body, often almost black on older adults
Claws covered in raised bright red bumps
Black wedge-shaped stripe along the top of the tail
Long, fairly narrow claws held forward
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Slow or still fresh water with soft mud bottoms: cypress swamps, marshes, roadside ditches, ponds, rice fields and sluggish streams on lowland coastal plains. It copes with warm, oxygen-poor and seasonally drying water better than most crayfish.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america. Slow or still fresh water with soft mud bottoms: cypress swamps, marshes, roadside ditches, ponds, rice fields and sluggish streams on lowland coastal plains. It copes with warm, oxygen-poor and seasonally drying water better than most crayfish.

Claws covered in raised bright red bumps
Black wedge-shaped stripe along the top of the tail
Long, fairly narrow claws held forward
whyInteresting: It is the main crawfish of Louisiana, farmed on a large scale in flooded rice fields and ponds.
Deliberate introductions for farming and the aquarium trade have made it one of the most widespread invasive freshwater animals in the world.
Mature males alternate between a breeding form and a non-breeding form, switching when they moult.
Where it has been introduced it can strip out water plants and eat amphibian eggs and tadpoles, changing whole pond communities.
Blue and other unusual colour forms turn up in the wild and have been bred for aquariums.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An opportunistic omnivore that eats rotting plant matter, water plants, algae, snails, insect larvae, worms, tadpoles, small fish and carrion. It walks the bottom picking at food with its small front legs and seizes larger items with the claws.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Herons, egrets, ibises, raccoons, otters, turtles and fish such as bass, catfish and gar all eat it, and people harvest it in large numbers. Threatened, it raises its open claws toward the attacker or escapes backwards with a rapid flip of the tail.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly active at dusk and through the night, spending the day in its burrow or under debris. Laboratory studies of this species have described a sleep-like resting state with reduced responsiveness.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually 1 to 2 years in the wild; some individuals, especially in captivity, have been reported to live about 4 to 5 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After mating the female glues her fertilised eggs, usually a few hundred, to the swimmerets under her tail and carries them, often while sheltering in a burrow. The eggs hatch in about two to three weeks in warm water, and the young cling to her through their first moults.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males have larger claws, small hooks at the base of some walking legs, and the first two pairs of swimmerets hardened into rigid mating structures. Females have a broader tail and soft, feathery swimmerets.

entries.name: Red-tailed Black Shark
entries.heroTitle: Red-tailed Black Shark — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Red-tailed Black Shark AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A small river fish of the carp family from central Thailand, unrelated to true sharks. In aquaria it grazes rock and wood with an underslung, rasping mouth. Fish farms breed it by the thousand, yet it was listed as extinct in the wild until 2011, when a surviving population in the Chao Phraya basin was recognised and the species was re-listed as Critically Endangered.
identification: Velvet-black body and fins, apart from the tail
Deeply forked tail, bright red to orange
Tall, triangular dorsal fin held stiffly upright
Downturned mouth with two pairs of short barbels
Slender body reaching about 12 to 15 centimetres
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Lowland rivers and streams of the Chao Phraya basin in Thailand, over rock and sand, and probably the adjoining floodplains in the wet season.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Lowland rivers and streams of the Chao Phraya basin in Thailand, over rock and sand, and probably the adjoining floodplains in the wet season.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 17/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Velvet-black body and fins, apart from the tail
Deeply forked tail, bright red to orange

whyInteresting: Hugh M. Smith described the species in 1931 and reported it as not uncommon in Bueng Boraphet swamp and in the Chao Phraya as far south as Bangkok.
In aquaria young fish tolerate one another, and aggression towards their own kind grows as they mature.
An albino form, pale pinkish white with the red tail retained, has been bred for the aquarium trade.
Keepers report that the red of the tail fades towards pale orange when a fish is stressed, ill or kept in poor water, and deepens again as it recovers.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Keepers feed it a mixed diet of algae and plant matter with insect larvae, small crustaceans and worms, and it readily takes prepared foods. Its diet in the wild is poorly documented.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: What preys on it in the wild is not on record. Its decline there is blamed mainly on dams and the draining of swamps in the Chao Phraya basin. A startled fish bolts for the nearest crevice.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: In aquaria it is on the move through the day and busiest around dusk, withdrawing to shelter between bouts and at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly 5 to 8 years in aquaria, and sometimes reported beyond 10; no figure exists for wild fish.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning in the wild has never been described. On fish farms, breeders use hormone injections to bring adults into condition; the eggs are scattered, receive no care and hatch within a few days. Breeding in home aquaria is rare.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Colour is the same in both sexes. Mature females tend to be deeper-bodied and rounder in the belly and males slimmer, but young fish cannot be told apart by eye.

entries.name: Red-tailed Tropicbird
entries.heroTitle: Red-tailed Tropicbird — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Red-tailed Tropicbirds nest on remote islands and fly far over open ocean for fish and squid. Their long tail streamers and bright white body turn distance, flight control, and courtship display into one oceanic form.
identification: Heavy, pointed red bill
Black crescent through and behind the eye
Mostly white wings with little black
Silky white body, often with a rosy tinge when breeding
Harsh ratcheting calls over the colony
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: indian_ocean, north_pacific, south_pacific. Warm tropical and subtropical waters of the Indian and Pacific Oceans, often far from land. It breeds on remote islands and atolls, nesting on shaded ground beneath shrubs, in crevices or under rock overhangs.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: indian_ocean, north_pacific, south_pacific. Warm tropical and subtropical waters of the Indian and Pacific Oceans, often far from land. It breeds on remote islands and atolls, nesting on shaded ground beneath shrubs, in crevices or under rock overhangs.

whyInteresting: Polynesian peoples prized its two red tail feathers for ornaments and ceremonial regalia.
Its legs are set so far back that it cannot walk properly on land and shuffles forward on its belly.
In courtship flights pairs circle above the colony, and birds can appear to fly backwards as they hang in the wind.
Tropicbirds are not close relatives of other seabirds and form their own order, Phaethontiformes.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flying fish and squid make up most of the diet, with other small fish. It hunts in daylight, spotting prey from high above the water and seizing it just below the surface.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults face few natural enemies, but introduced rats and cats kill eggs, chicks and sometimes adults on nesting islands. A sitting bird will not leave the nest, screaming and biting at anything that comes close.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day over the sea. Away from the colony birds are thought to rest on the water at night, while breeders sit tight in their shaded nest sites.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Long-lived like most seabirds; banded breeding adults have been recorded at more than 20 years, but typical lifespan in the wild is not well quantified.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Each pair produces a single blotched egg, which the parents take turns to incubate for about 6 weeks. Both feed the chick, which leaves the nest after roughly 3 months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adults of both sexes look alike and cannot be reliably told apart in the field.

entries.name: Red Tegu
entries.heroTitle: Red Tegu — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: One of the largest lizards in South America, native to the dry Chaco and scrub of Argentina, Bolivia and Paraguay. Big males reach about 1.2 metres or a little more and can weigh several kilograms. Its species name, rufescens, means reddish, and it is the reddest of the tegus.

Juveniles brown with pale bands, reddening as they grow
Small, bead-like scales in neat rows across the back
Thick, muscular tail tapering to a fine tip
Heavy body on short, strong legs with long claws

whyInteresting: A cornered animal lashes out with its tail, and the tail can break off and partly regrow.
Its skin is used for leather, and tegu skins were exported from Argentina and Paraguay in very large numbers during the 1980s.
Until 2012 it was classified in the genus Tupinambis, alongside the tegus of the Amazon basin.
Where its range meets that of the black-and-white tegu in Argentina, hybrids between the two have been reported.
It swallows fruit whole and is thought to spread the seeds of the plants it feeds on.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, eggs, insects, small vertebrates, and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Young tegus are probably taken by birds of prey, snakes and carnivorous mammals; grown adults have few recorded predators. People also hunt it for meat. A threatened tegu runs for its burrow, and if cornered it hisses, puffs up and bites.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and underground at night, in a burrow it digs or takes over. During the cool, dry months of the southern winter it stays in the burrow, dormant, for weeks or months at a time.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is not well documented; in captivity animals commonly reach 15 to 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating follows emergence in spring. The female lays a clutch often put at 20 or more eggs in a burrow, and hatching takes roughly two months. She is reported to line the nest with plant material and to stay and guard it, though observations for this species are few.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow larger with broader heads and jowls.

The skin of the back carries a fine pattern of grooves that resembles the veins of a leaf.
Colour appears to vary by locality: slugs from one district often look alike, while those from different districts can differ markedly.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grazes the thin film of microscopic algae, fungi and bacteria on tree bark, rocks and logs, rasping it off with its radula.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards and introduced rats are likely predators, but attacks are poorly documented. When disturbed it contracts and produces thick, sticky mucus that makes it hard to grip.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active at night and on wet days. In dry weather it shelters under logs, loose bark and leaf litter, climbing trees again once rain returns.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid in moist, sheltered places after mating, but clutch size, incubation time and early development are poorly documented.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Every red triangle slug carries both sperm and eggs, so there is no visible male or female form to compare.

entries.name: Red-veined Darter
entries.heroTitle: Red-veined Darter — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: It travels more like a migrant bird than most dragonflies do. Breeding in warm temporary pools across Africa, the Mediterranean and the Middle East, this red darter moves north in spring and summer and reaches northern Europe in some years.

Red veins on the forewing leading edge in males
Yellow patch at the base of the hindwings
Pale yellow wing spot edged with black

Red veins on the forewing leading edge in males
Yellow patch at the base of the hindwings

whyInteresting: Immature males are yellowish and only turn red as they mature.
In Britain it has occasionally bred after large arrivals, though such colonies have rarely lasted.
It is often among the first dragonflies to breed in newly dug ponds and flooded pits with little vegetation.
Its species name honours the French entomologist Boyer de Fonscolombe.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults catch midges, mosquitoes, small flies and other soft-bodied flying insects in flight. Larvae hunt small aquatic invertebrates on the pond bottom.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds such as hobbies, bee-eaters and wagtails catch adults, and spiders and frogs take them near water. Larvae are eaten by fish and larger insect larvae, and shelter in silt and debris on the bottom.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Flies only in sunshine and warmth. At night and in cloudy weather it roosts clinging to grass stems or shrubs, often away from the water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults usually live a few weeks; in warm water the whole cycle from egg to adult can take roughly three months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs fly in tandem, the male holding the female, while she taps her abdomen on open water and releases eggs. Larvae grow quickly in warm pools, allowing more than one generation a year in the south.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Mature males have a bright red abdomen and red wing veins. Females are yellowish-olive to light brown with yellow veins.

analysis.summary: Crested and dark-headed, this bulbul lives closely alongside people in South Asia. It nests in hedges, creepers and garden shrubs, sometimes even in potted plants on verandas, and forages through gardens, orchards and roadside scrub.

Crimson patch under the base of the tail
Brown body with pale scaly edging on back and breast
White rump shows clearly in flight
Dark tail with a white tip

Crimson patch under the base of the tail
Brown body with pale scaly edging on back and breast
White rump shows clearly in flight
Dark tail with a white tip
whyInteresting: It is among the recorded hosts of the pied cuckoo, though babblers are that cuckoo's main hosts in South Asia.
Regional subspecies differ in crest shape and in how dark the back and head are.
It is among the birds that spread lantana seeds, helping the invasive shrub spread.
Where its range meets that of the white-eared bulbul in the north-west, the two have been recorded hybridising.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Eats fruit and berries, flower nectar and petals, buds and young shoots, and insects gleaned from foliage or caught in short flights from a perch.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Shikras and other small hawks take adults, while crows, snakes and cats raid nests. Jacobin cuckoos lay eggs in its nests. Pairs give harsh alarm calls, mob intruders near the nest, and dive into dense shrubs.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active from first light to dusk, with most feeding in the cooler hours. At night it roosts in dense shrubs, bamboo or creepers, often in loose groups outside the breeding season.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is not well documented, and published ages from ringed birds are scarce.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The nest is a small, neat cup of rootlets and grass, and the usual clutch is 2 or 3 pinkish, red-spotted eggs. Incubation takes about two weeks, both parents feed the young, and chicks leave the nest after roughly 10 to 14 days.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is identical in both sexes, so pairs cannot be sexed by sight.

entries.name: Red-winged Blackbird
entries.heroTitle: Red-winged Blackbird — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A marsh-nesting blackbird of North America whose glossy black males carry scarlet shoulder patches edged with yellow. Each male sings from a cattail or fence post with wings half spread and the patches flared, and may hold a territory containing several nesting females. Males whose patches were blackened in experiments often lost their territories.
identification: Male glossy black with red, yellow-edged shoulder patches

Territorial males chase crows, herons and hawks, and will strike people or horses that come too close to the nests.
Males can cover the red with body feathers, showing only the yellow border, when trespassing on another male's ground.
Females have a chattering song of their own, often given in answer to a singing male.
It is among the most abundant land birds in North America, with a breeding population estimated at well over one hundred million.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, including dragonflies, caterpillars and beetles, dominate in summer, some exposed by pushing the closed bill into a plant stem and opening it. Seeds of grasses and weeds and waste grain make up most of the winter diet.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks and owls take adults, while snakes, raccoons and marsh wrens destroy eggs and nestlings; cats hunt near towns. Territorial males dive at intruders, and neighbouring males often join in the mobbing.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. Outside the breeding season it gathers at dusk in communal roosts in marshes and thickets, often shared with grackles, cowbirds and starlings; breeding birds roost on or near the territory.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically around 2 to 4 years in the wild; the oldest ringed bird on record was over 15 years old.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female weaves a cup nest low among marsh stems and lays 3 or 4 pale blue-green eggs marked with dark scrawls. She incubates for 11 to 13 days, and chicks leave the nest at about 11 to 14 days old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are glossy black with red and yellow shoulder patches. Females are smaller, streaked dark brown above and below with a pale eyebrow, and are often mistaken for large sparrows.

entries.name: Redclaw Crayfish

analysis.summary: Rivers in its tropical home stop flowing in the dry season and shrink to warm, muddy waterholes low in oxygen. This large freshwater crayfish survives in them where many animals cannot. It is a weak digger for a crayfish, relying on existing cover instead of deep burrows.

Body blue-green to dark brownish green
Claws long and fairly slender, not broad
Shoots backward with tail flicks when alarmed

Water colder than about 10 degrees Celsius kills it, which confines wild populations to warm climates.
Large males have been recorded at around 500 to 600 grams.
Lost claws and legs regrow over successive moults.
It was little known outside northern Australia until farming trials began there in the 1980s.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly decaying plant material and the microbes growing on it, along with water plants, algae, small invertebrates and carrion. It feeds along the bottom, shredding food with the claws and mouthparts.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Cornered, it rears up with claws raised and open. Large fish such as barramundi, eels, turtles, cormorants, herons and water rats all eat crayfish, and people trap them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It hides through the day and walks out to feed from dusk, returning to shelter before sunrise. Activity falls in cool water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably four to five years at most; reliable ages for wild animals are lacking.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding takes place in the warmer months, and a female may raise several broods in a season. Depending on her size she carries roughly 300 to 1,000 eggs under the tail for about six to ten weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Mature males have a soft red patch on the outer edge of each claw, which females lack. Males also grow heavier, with larger claws. Reproductive openings sit at the base of the last pair of walking legs in males and the third pair in females.

analysis.summary: Redwing is a winter-moving thrush that reads berries, weather, and night migration, proving that timing can be as important as strength.

Bold creamy-white stripe above the eye
Rusty-red flanks and underwing
Breast streaked rather than spotted
Pale stripe running below the cheek

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Earthworms and other soil invertebrates taken by running and pausing on open ground, plus hawthorn, rowan and holly berries once frost hardens the soil. In summer it eats insects, caterpillars and snails.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sparrowhawks and other raptors take adults, while crows and small mammals raid nests. Flocks give thin alarm calls and dive into cover. Hard frost and deep snow can kill large numbers when food is locked away.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds by day in winter and gathers at dusk to roost communally in thick hedges, scrub or evergreen plantations, often alongside other thrushes.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live only 2 to 3 years in the wild, though ringing shows that a few survive much longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The nest is a grass cup with a mud layer, low in a tree or shrub or on the ground. Usually 4 to 6 eggs are incubated by the female for about 12 to 14 days; both parents feed the young, which fledge after roughly two weeks. Two broods are common.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the same plumage. Only the male gives the full song, a short varied phrase that differs between regions and even between neighbouring birds.

analysis.summary: One of the largest rays, this manta usually spans 3 to 3.5 metres across the fins and rarely up to about 5. It lives around coastal reefs and islands and feeds by filtering plankton, unfolding two fleshy lobes beside the mouth to funnel water in.

White underside with scattered dark spots
Wide mouth at the front of the head
Mostly white or pale area around the mouth
Short whip-like tail with no sting

whyInteresting: Divers identify individual reef mantas from the spot pattern on the belly, which stays the same through life.
It was recognised as a separate species from the larger giant oceanic manta only in 2009.
Females usually give birth to a single large pup after a pregnancy of about a year, often with gaps of several years between births.
When plankton is dense, groups sometimes feed in a spiralling chain called cyclone feeding.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Filters zooplankton such as copepods, krill, shrimp larvae and fish eggs from the water, swimming open-mouthed along reef edges and at the surface. It also feeds near the seabed and after dark on plankton rising towards the surface.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large sharks, such as tiger and bull sharks, and orcas attack it; many reef mantas carry healed bite scars. Target fishing for the gill plates, bycatch and boat strikes are the main human threats. Its defences are large size and fast escape swimming.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and night, following plankton: it often visits cleaning stations in daylight and feeds in shallow water after dark. It must keep swimming to breathe, and how or whether it rests is not well documented.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not precisely known. Photo-identified individuals have been resighted over more than 30 years, and lifespan is commonly estimated at 40 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females mature late, at roughly 8 to 15 years, and are followed by chains of courting males. A single pup, already well over a metre across, is born fully formed and independent; no care follows, and young often use sheltered shallow bays.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males carry a pair of claspers, finger-like extensions of the pelvic fins beside the tail base. Females grow slightly larger, and mature females often show mating bite scars near the tip of the left pectoral fin.

entries.name: Reef Stonefish
entries.heroTitle: Reef Stonefish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A thickset, warty ambush fish of Indo-Pacific shallows and one of the most venomous fishes known. Each of its dorsal spines, usually about thirteen, carries a pair of venom glands. Nothing is injected on purpose: the weight of a foot or hand drives a spine in and squeezes the glands, and stings cause intense pain and have killed people.
identification: Lumpy, warty skin that breaks up any smooth outline

Small eyes placed high on the head
Mottled grey, brown or reddish colour, often with algae growing on it
Large, rounded pectoral fins spread on the bottom

Shallow reef flats, coral rubble, sand and lagoon floors of the tropical Indo-Pacific, from the Red Sea and East Africa across the Indian Ocean to the western Pacific. It usually lies from the intertidal zone to about 30 metres deep, often beside coral heads or rocks.

whyInteresting: It has been reported to survive out of water for many hours when stranded on a reef flat by a falling tide.

Very hot water, as hot as can be borne without scalding, is standard first aid for a sting because the venom proteins are heat-sensitive.
Stonefishes are usually placed in their own family, Synanceiidae, close to the scorpionfishes and lionfishes.
Adults usually measure about 30 centimetres, with the largest reported near 40 centimetres.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small fishes, shrimps and other crustaceans that wander within reach. Lying motionless, it engulfs them with an extremely fast upward gulp of its large mouth, the whole strike lasting a fraction of a second.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few animals eat adults, though bottom-feeding rays and sharks have been reported taking them. When disturbed it does not flee but holds its ground and raises the dorsal spines. People catch it for food in parts of Asia and for the aquarium trade.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeding is reported to peak at night, though it will strike at prey that comes close at any hour. By day it lies half buried in sand or wedged among rubble, often staying in the same spot for long periods.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been well documented. Aquarium specimens have been reported to live around 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning in the wild has rarely been observed. Fertilisation is external, no parental care is known, and the young are thought to drift as planktonic larvae before settling on the bottom.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: No reliable external difference between males and females is known, and the sexes cannot be told apart in the field.

entries.name: Reeves's Muntjac
entries.heroTitle: Reeves's Muntjac — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: One of the smallest deer, standing about half a metre at the shoulder, Reeves's muntjac is best known for its voice. An alarmed or excited animal gives a single loud, harsh bark and repeats it every few seconds, sometimes for many minutes on end. Both bucks and does bark, and the sound carries far through woodland.
identification: Hunched stance, with the rump higher than the shoulders.
Russet-brown coat in summer, duller and greyer in winter.
Broad tail raised when fleeing to show a white underside.
Slit-like scent glands sit below each eye.

Bucks fight mainly with their tusks rather than their antlers, and older males often carry torn ears and scars.
It lives alone, in pairs or as a doe with her fawn, and does not form herds.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Dogs, leopards, foxes, large cats, humans, and pythons can threaten muntjacs. Barking warns before danger gets close.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Muntjacs are often crepuscular or nocturnal, moving in quiet hours.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly around 10 to 13 years. Exceptional wild animals have been recorded at 16 years for bucks and 19 for does.

Flat, rounded body with a whip-like tail
Serrated spine set well back along the tail
Pale, almost white underside

It often lies in shallow water near the banks and moves onto newly flooded ground in the wet season.

Like other river stingrays, it sheds its tail spine from time to time and grows a replacement.
People wading in South American rivers shuffle their feet to avoid treading on buried rays, whose stings are painful and slow to heal.

entries.name: Rhinoceros
entries.heroTitle: Rhinoceros — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Rhinoceros teaches Grounded Force through a massive herbivore body that makes panic break around its weight. Its thick skin, horn, low stance, grazing life, and defensive charge show that power is most convincing when rooted and direct. Its lesson is that strength does not need to rush when it is difficult to move.

African species use savanna, grassland and dry bush; Indian rhinos live in floodplain tall grass and swamp. The Javan and Sumatran rhinos live in dense lowland and hill rainforest. All need water and mud for wallowing.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: All are plant-eaters. White and Indian rhinos mainly graze short and tall grasses; black, Javan and Sumatran rhinos browse leaves, twigs, shoots and fruit, gripping them with a pointed upper lip. Adults eat large amounts daily.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Healthy adults have almost no natural predators, but lions and spotted hyenas in Africa and tigers in Asia kill calves. Mothers guard calves closely and charge threats. Poaching for horn is the greatest danger to every species.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most feed in the cooler morning, evening and night and rest through midday, lying down in shade or wallowing in mud. They doze standing or lying, often in the same resting places.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single calf is born after a pregnancy of about 15 to 16 months. It can walk within hours, is suckled for a year or more and stays with its mother for two to four years, until the next calf arrives.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males of most species are larger and heavier than females. Indian rhino males develop massive neck folds and larger incisor tusks; in African species females often have longer, thinner horns.

Wings clap loudly on take-off
whyInteresting: Pigeons drink by sucking water up with the bill held under the surface, whereas most birds must scoop and tilt the head back.
Racing pigeons commonly fly at about 70 to 90 kilometres per hour, and faster with a following wind.
Charles Darwin bred fancy pigeons and used their many varieties as evidence in On the Origin of Species.
A pigeon named Cher Ami carried a message in 1918 that helped to rescue nearly 200 trapped American soldiers.
In laboratory tests, pigeons learned to sort paintings by Monet from paintings by Picasso.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, grains, buds, and urban scraps.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Peregrine falcons, hawks, cats, rats and humans. Pigeons feed and fly in flocks, where many eyes spot danger, and burst into fast, clattering takeoff when a predator appears.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal; pigeons feed and commute by day, then roost on sheltered ledges that repeat the city-cliff pattern.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Feral pigeons often live a few years in the wild and longer in protected settings; Urban success comes from constant reuse of safe sites.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually lay two eggs in simple ledge nests, and both parents feed chicks with crop milk.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males are often slightly larger and more display-heavy during courtship.

entries.name: Rock Ptarmigan
entries.heroTitle: Rock Ptarmigan — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Rock Ptarmigan live in Arctic and alpine habitats where the background changes sharply by season. White winter feathers and mottled summer colors help the bird stay hidden on snow, rock, and tundra.
identification: Plump grouse about 35 cm long
White wings in every season
Black outer tail feathers show in flight
Low croaking, rattling call
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, europe, central_asia, east_asia, arctic_antarctic. Open, stony ground above the treeline and on Arctic tundra, with dwarf shrubs, mosses and boulder fields. In Scotland it lives mainly above about 700 metres, and in the Alps higher still.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, europe, central_asia, east_asia, arctic_antarctic. Open, stony ground above the treeline and on Arctic tundra, with dwarf shrubs, mosses and boulder fields. In Scotland it lives mainly above about 700 metres, and in the Alps higher still.

Black outer tail feathers show in flight
Low croaking, rattling call
whyInteresting: Thick feathers cover the feet and toes, spreading its weight on snow like snowshoes.
It moults three times a year, not twice, passing through distinct autumn, winter and summer plumages.
Males in spring have been seen deliberately dirtying their white plumage, which makes them harder to spot against melting snow.
Some populations, such as Iceland's, rise and fall in cycles of about ten years.
In Japan the alpine population is protected as a Special Natural Monument.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Buds, catkins and twigs of dwarf willow and birch sustain it through winter. In summer it eats leaves, flowers and berries such as crowberry and bilberry, and chicks take insects in their first weeks.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Gyrfalcons and golden eagles hunt adults, and arctic and red foxes and stoats take birds on the ground; ravens, gulls and skuas raid nests. A threatened bird crouches still, then bursts into flight at close range.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. In winter it often roosts in a burrow dug into soft snow, which gives shelter from wind and cold.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live only about two to three years in the wild; some reach about eight.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female lays about six to ten eggs in a shallow scrape and incubates alone for about three weeks. Chicks leave the nest within a day, feed themselves and can flutter within about ten days, while she guards them.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Winter males have a black stripe from the bill through the eye, which females lack. In spring males show a larger red comb, and summer females are more finely barred in gold and black.

entries.name: Roe Deer
entries.heroTitle: Roe Deer — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Small and slender, the roe deer stands about 65 to 75 centimetres at the shoulder and weighs 15 to 30 kilograms. It lives across most of Europe. It is the only deer in which the fertilised egg pauses for months before developing: does mate in midsummer, but the embryo does not implant until about January.
identification: Reddish-brown summer coat, grey-brown in winter
Pale rump patch and no visible tail
Black nose and moustache stripe above a white chin
Short, upright antlers with up to three points
Large ears edged with dark hair
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe. Deciduous and mixed woodland with a dense shrub layer, young plantations, hedgerows, scrub and reedbeds, usually next to fields or meadows where it feeds. It is common in farmland dotted with small woods and occurs from the lowlands to the tree line in European mountains.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe. Deciduous and mixed woodland with a dense shrub layer, young plantations, hedgerows, scrub and reedbeds, usually next to fields or meadows where it feeds. It is common in farmland dotted with small woods and occurs from the lowlands to the tree line in European mountains.

Short, upright antlers with up to three points

whyInteresting: During the rut a buck may chase a doe round and round a tree or bush, wearing circular tracks known as roe rings.
It is the most numerous deer in Europe, with a population estimated at more than 10 million.
In summer roe deer live alone or in small family groups, but in winter they gather in larger parties on open fields.
Fawns hidden in long grass stay put when danger approaches, and many are killed by mowing machines in hay meadows each spring.
Bambi, in the 1923 Austrian novel by Felix Salten, was a roe deer.
