fieldGuide.dietSummary: A selective browser that picks buds, shoots and leaves of bramble, ivy, herbs and young trees, adding grasses and crops in spring and acorns, fungi and berries in autumn. It feeds in short bouts, nibbling as it walks.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves and lynx take adults, while foxes, wild boar and dogs kill fawns. Road traffic and hunting account for many deaths. Roe deer rely on keen hearing and smell to detect danger early, and seldom feed far from thick cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active in bouts throughout the day and night, with peaks at dawn and dusk. Between feeds it lies up in dense cover or long grass to ruminate. Heavily disturbed populations become more nocturnal.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually 7 to 10 years in the wild, with a few reaching about 15. Many fawns die in their first year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating takes place in July and August, and one to three spotted fawns, most often twins, are born the following May or June. They lie hidden alone for the first weeks while the doe returns to suckle them.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Bucks carry short antlers, usually with three points each, which are shed in late autumn and regrown in velvet over winter. Does have no antlers and in winter show a tuft of hair below the rump patch. Bucks are slightly heavier.

entries.name: Roloway Monkey
entries.heroTitle: Roloway Monkey — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A long-tailed forest guenon found only in Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire, dark grey with a white chest and a rusty patch on the lower back. Troops usually contain a single adult male, keep to the upper canopy and often travel alongside other monkey species.
identification: Bold white beard and dark face that stand out through canopy shade
Group calls and social movement through high forest routes
Fruit-and-seed foraging that keeps the troop coordinated across trees
Arboreal agility tied to recognition and shared alertness
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Roloway Monkey usually lives in Upper Guinea forests, mature canopy, and forest edges in West Africa.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Roloway Monkey usually lives in Upper Guinea forests, mature canopy, and forest edges in West Africa.

Arboreal agility tied to recognition and shared alertness
whyInteresting: It was formerly treated as a subspecies of the Diana monkey, Cercopithecus diana.
The Sassandra River in Côte d'Ivoire roughly divides its range from that of the Diana monkey to the west.
The IUCN Red List places it among Africa's Critically Endangered primates.
Like other guenons, it has cheek pouches in which it can store food while foraging.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Roloway Monkey feeds on fruit, seeds, leaves, insects, and canopy foods gathered in groups.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Crowned eagles and leopards are the expected natural predators, and the adult male gives loud alarm calls when danger is seen. Far more are lost to bushmeat hunting, and the clearing of forest for farms and timber has left only scattered groups in a few forests.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active, sleeping in trees and moving through canopy with group calls, so cohesion is renewed every time the troop travels.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive Roloway monkeys are reported to live into their twenties, but survival in the wild has not been recorded.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually have one infant that clings and learns group signals over time, turning cohesion into something taught body-to-body.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger; both sexes use visible markings and calls for recognition through leaves.

entries.name: Rose-ringed Parakeet
entries.heroTitle: Rose-ringed Parakeet — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Rose-ringed Parakeet teaches adaptable confidence. It survives by reading human-shaped landscapes, using a clear voice, social movement, and flexible feeding to make new places work.
identification: Pale yellowish-green plumage all over
Long, tapering tail with bluish central feathers
Hooked bill with a red upper mandible
Pale eye surrounded by a thin orange-red ring
Fast, direct flight on rapidly beating pointed wings
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_asia, sub_saharan_africa. Lightly wooded country, savanna, riverside trees, farmland, and towns and gardens, mostly in the lowlands. The native range runs in a belt across Africa south of the Sahara, from Senegal to Ethiopia, and through the Indian subcontinent. It avoids dense rainforest.

The native range runs in a belt across Africa south of the Sahara, from Senegal to Ethiopia, and through the Indian subcontinent. It avoids dense rainforest.

whyInteresting: In India most nesting takes place in the dry months, from about December to May.
Four subspecies are recognised, differing slightly in size and in bill and plumage colour.
Escaped and released cage birds have founded breeding populations in many cities outside the native range, among them London, Brussels and Amsterdam.
Captive birds can learn to imitate human speech, and the species has been kept as a cage bird for many centuries.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, grain, fruit, buds, flowers and nectar. It climbs through the branches using bill and feet, often holding food in one foot to bite at it. Flocks also feed in crops such as sorghum, maize and sunflower, and in orchards.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Nest holes are raided by crows and snakes, and adults fall to hawks, falcons and owls. People trap it for the pet trade and kill it as a crop pest. A flock that spots a bird of prey takes off together, screeching.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Flocks spend the night in communal roosts in tall trees, often in towns, where hundreds or thousands may gather. Birds are active from first light and feed through the day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive birds commonly live 20 years or more; how long wild birds survive has not been well measured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests are in tree holes, often old woodpecker or barbet holes that the pair enlarges, and sometimes in gaps in walls. The female incubates 3 or 4 white eggs, occasionally more, for a little over three weeks. Young leave the nest at about seven weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males have a black chin stripe that runs into a narrow black and rose-pink collar. Females and young birds lack the collar or show only a faint paler green one. Males gain theirs in their second or third year.

entries.name: Rosy Tetra
entries.heroTitle: Rosy Tetra — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Shoals of this small characin hang loosely in midwater and, at any alarm, close up and turn together so that no single fish stands out. About four centimetres long, with a rose-tinted body and red fins, it comes from forest streams of the Guianas in north-eastern South America.
identification: Deep, flattened body tinted translucent pink
Black blotch on the dorsal fin, edged with white
Red pelvic, anal and tail fins
Small adipose fin between dorsal fin and tail
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: domestic_global. Slow, shaded forest streams and backwaters in the Guianas of north-eastern South America. It is usually described from quiet water among sunken wood, leaf litter and marginal plants, though the wild microhabitat has been little surveyed.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: domestic_global. Slow, shaded forest streams and backwaters in the Guianas of north-eastern South America. It is usually described from quiet water among sunken wood, leaf litter and marginal plants, though the wild microhabitat has been little surveyed.

behaviorTraits: Deep, flattened body tinted translucent pink
Black blotch on the dorsal fin, edged with white
Red pelvic, anal and tail fins
Small adipose fin between dorsal fin and tail
whyInteresting: The species was described in 1909 by the American ichthyologist Marion Durbin, from fish collected in what was then British Guiana.
Most rosy tetras sold for aquaria are bred on fish farms, not caught from the wild.
Aquarium keepers often confuse it with the ornate tetra, a close relative of similar colour, and the two are sold under each other's names.
Keepers report that the colours are strongest in soft, acidic water stained brown by leaf litter, and look washed out in hard water under bright light.
Its genus, Hyphessobrycon, is one of the largest among the characins, with well over a hundred small South American species.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An omnivore that picks small food from midwater and the surface: insect larvae, tiny crustaceans, worms and some plant matter. The wild diet has been little studied, and most of what is known comes from aquarium fish.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger predatory fishes and fish-eating birds are the likely predators, though none has been recorded in detail for this species. Frightened fish dash into plant thickets or under sunken branches.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. After dark it hangs almost motionless close to plants or the bottom until the light returns.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is not documented. Aquarium fish commonly live several years, with about five years often quoted by keepers.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: An egg-scatterer. In aquaria a pair spawns among fine-leaved plants, the female releasing small adhesive eggs that hatch in about a day to a day and a half. The parents give no care and will eat any eggs they find.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are slimmer and brighter, with the dorsal fin drawn out into a long point. Females are deeper-bodied, with a shorter, rounded dorsal fin.

entries.name: Rougheye Rockfish
entries.heroTitle: Rougheye Rockfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A deep-slope rockfish of the North Pacific, it grows so slowly that females are thought to reach maturity only at around 20 years old. It lives near the bottom on steep, rocky ground, mostly at roughly 200 to 500 metres, from Japan across the Aleutians to the Pacific coast of North America.
identification: Row of 2 to 10 small spines on the lower rim of each eye
Pinkish-red to orange-red body, often with dusky blotches
Large, spiny head and stout, deep body
Grows to about 90 cm, large for a rockfish
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_pacific. Deep, rocky, cold, or river-bottom habitat matters because fast tactics fail there. Rougheye Rockfish fits Deep-Rock Years because the environment rewards armored patience, slow growth, and precise use of depth.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_pacific. Deep, rocky, cold, or river-bottom habitat matters because fast tactics fail there. Rougheye Rockfish fits Deep-Rock Years because the environment rewards armored patience, slow growth, and precise use of depth.

whyInteresting: Fish once all called rougheye were split into two species in 2008, so many older records mix it with the blackspotted rockfish.
Like other rockfish it bears live young: eggs are fertilised and hatch inside the female, which then releases swimming larvae.
Fish hauled up from depth usually suffer swollen swim bladders and bulging eyes, so few survive being released.
It is caught in Alaskan trawl and longline fisheries under tight catch limits.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Takes shrimps, krill, crabs and small fishes near the bottom, catching them with a quick lunge and a gulp of its large mouth.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few recorded natural predators; large fish and deep-diving marine mammals may take some. Young fish are more exposed. Fishing is the main threat, since slow growth makes stocks slow to recover. It shelters close to rocks and sponges.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Its daily activity rhythm is poorly known. Survey footage shows it resting on or beside boulders, corals and sponges on the slope, and it stays at depth all year.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often several decades and sometimes more than a century; one Alaskan fish was aged at about 205 years from ear-bone growth rings, a figure some researchers treat with caution.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females bear live young. Females store sperm after mating, and the eggs are later fertilised, develop and hatch inside the mother; she then releases large numbers of tiny swimming larvae, which drift in the plankton before settling near the bottom, where young fish live shallower than adults and move deeper with age.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot be told apart from outside; females appear to reach slightly larger sizes.

entries.name: Rove Beetle
entries.heroTitle: Rove Beetle — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: This rove beetle carries pederin, a toxin more potent by weight than cobra venom, in its own body fluid. It never bites or stings — the harm only happens if you crush it against your skin, which makes it one of the few animals dangerous purely by being broken.
identification: Slender orange-and-black beetle with very short wing cases
Most of the abdomen left exposed behind the short elytra
Runs quickly with the abdomen raised, ant-like
Strongly attracted to lights after dark
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: mediterranean, europe, north_africa_middle_east. Damp ground near water — irrigated fields, marsh edges, riverbanks and gardens with moist litter. Wet soil supports the small prey it hunts and stays soft enough to move through.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: mediterranean, europe, north_africa_middle_east. Damp ground near water — irrigated fields, marsh edges, riverbanks and gardens with moist litter. Wet soil supports the small prey it hunts and stays soft enough to move through.

Most of the abdomen left exposed behind the short elytra
Runs quickly with the abdomen raised, ant-like

whyInteresting: Its haemolymph contains pederin, weight for weight more toxic than cobra venom, and the beetle produces it with the help of a symbiotic bacterium.
It does not bite or sting. Skin blistering, called Paederus dermatitis, happens only when a beetle is crushed or brushed hard against skin.
The short wing cases are the family signature and let the abdomen flex freely, which is why it can run into crevices most beetles cannot.
It is drawn to lights, which is how most human contact happens — a beetle lands on someone at night and is swatted.
Adults and larvae are both predators, hunting other insects in damp leaf litter and soil.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small insects and other invertebrates hunted actively in leaf litter and topsoil by both adults and larvae. It is a hunter that carries a defence it never uses offensively — the toxin does nothing to help it feed.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders and larger predatory insects. Pederin makes an individual a bad meal after the fact rather than during, so the protection is at the population level: predators that learn, stop.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day in litter and strongly drawn to artificial light after dark, so encounters cluster around lit rooms and porches at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Several months to a year, with the whole life cycle spent in and around damp soil.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid singly in damp soil and the larvae are predatory from hatching. Pederin is passed to the eggs by the female, so the young are chemically defended before they have eaten anything.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike. Only females actually synthesise pederin at full concentration, via the symbiotic bacterium they also pass to their eggs.

entries.name: Royal Flycatcher
entries.heroTitle: Royal Flycatcher — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A tropical forest flycatcher with a crest that normally lies flat, giving the head a hammer shape. In display, or when handled, it opens into a wide fan of red, orange or yellow feathers tipped with blue-black, and the bird may sway its head slowly from side to side with the bill open.
identification: Long, broad, flat bill fringed with bristles
Plain brown upperparts with small buff spots on the wings
Bright cinnamon-rufous rump and tail
Underparts ochre-buff, paler on the throat
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical forest understory, humid edges, and streamside trees.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical forest understory, humid edges, and streamside trees.

Plain brown upperparts with small buff spots on the wings
Bright cinnamon-rufous rump and tail

whyInteresting: Populations in Mexico and Central America, western Ecuador and Peru, and Brazil's Atlantic Forest are treated as separate species by some authorities.
The birds of the Atlantic Forest and of western Ecuador and Peru are considered threatened by forest loss.
Long placed among the tyrant flycatchers, it is now often put in a small family of its own, Onychorhynchidae.
The genus name Onychorhynchus means nail-bill, from Greek words for claw and beak.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flying insects such as flies, beetles, dragonflies and butterflies. It watches from a perch in the lower and middle forest levels, often over a stream, then sallies out to snatch prey in the air or from leaves.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators are poorly documented; forest raptors are likely for adults. Hanging the nest from a thin branch, often over water, is thought to keep climbing predators such as snakes and monkeys away.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, hunting from perches in the lower forest, often beside streams. Where it roosts at night has not been described; small forest flycatchers usually sleep perched in dense vegetation. It is resident and has no dormant season.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long royal flycatchers live is not known with any reliability.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The nest is a long, loose bag of plant fibres, sometimes a metre or more long, hanging from a branch or vine with a side entrance. The usual clutch is two eggs, and the female is thought to incubate and feed the young largely alone.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes differ in crest colour: males have a scarlet crest and females a yellow to orange one. Otherwise they look alike, so the sexes can be told apart only when the crest is raised.

analysis.summary: A bright orange butterfly of tropical America, reaching south Florida, with a long, dagger-like tail on each hindwing. Its caterpillars feed on wild figs, so it is most common in hammocks and forests where fig trees grow.

Females lay their eggs singly on the soft new leaves of fig trees.
There are several generations a year, and adults can be seen in any month in south Florida and the tropics.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars eat the leaves of wild figs such as the strangler fig. Adults drink nectar from flowers such as Cordia and Lantana and sip moisture from damp ground.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards and spiders take adults, and parasitic wasps and flies attack caterpillars. Adults rely on fast, gliding flight and the leaf-like underside; caterpillars bear long spines.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Flies only by day, most actively in warm sunshine. At night and in dull weather it rests with wings closed beneath leaves. It breeds through the year in warm regions and has no dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult lifespan in the wild has not been documented; it probably lives a few weeks.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs singly on the young leaves of fig trees. The caterpillars feed on the foliage and form chrysalises hanging from the plant, with no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look similar; females are slightly larger and a little paler than males.

entries.name: Ruddy Darter
entries.heroTitle: Ruddy Darter — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A small darter dragonfly, about 3.5 cm long, found across much of Europe and into North Africa. It often breeds in shallow pools that shrink or dry out in late summer: by the time the water drops, most larvae have already emerged as adults.
identification: All-black legs without pale stripes
Club-shaped red abdomen in males
Red face and red-brown eyes in males
Small amber patch at the hindwing base

whyInteresting: The name sanguineum comes from the Latin for bloody, after the colour of mature males.
It often shares ponds with the common darter, and the two fly together in late summer.
Recording schemes show its range in Britain spreading northwards in recent decades.
Newly emerged adults often feed away from water in sheltered woodland rides before returning to breed.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults catch small flying insects such as midges, gnats and mosquitoes, seizing them in the air. The aquatic larvae eat small invertebrates among the submerged vegetation.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds such as hobbies and wagtails, frogs, spiders and larger dragonflies take adults. Larvae are eaten by fish and water beetles. Adults escape with fast, jinking flight.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active in sunshine and warmth. It roosts overnight and in dull weather perched in tall grass, bushes or trees near water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: The whole life cycle takes one year; adults live a few weeks on the wing.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs lay eggs in tandem, the female flicking them over damp mud, dry vegetation or shallow water at the margin. Eggs overwinter and hatch in spring, and larvae develop through summer in a few months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Mature males are deep red; females and young males are ochre-yellow to golden brown.

analysis.summary: A small, short-tailed dove of open country from Mexico to northern Argentina, common around farms, gardens and towns. Males are warm rufous with a blue-grey crown, and both sexes show black spots on the wing and black underwing linings in flight.

Female duller, grey-brown with only a rufous tinge

Black underwing linings visible in flight

whyInteresting: It builds a flimsy platform of twigs and grass, usually low in a shrub or small tree, and normally lays two white eggs.
Both parents incubate and feed the chicks on crop milk, and pairs may raise several broods in a year where conditions allow.
The song is a soft, monotonous series of two-note coos, often written as 'ca-woo', repeated from a perch through much of the day.
When flushed, pairs and small groups burst up on whirring wings and drop back to the ground a short distance away.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Eats mainly small seeds of grasses and weeds, picked from bare or sparsely vegetated ground while walking; it also takes some grain and occasional small invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks and falcons take adults, while snakes, monkeys, opossums and domestic cats raid nests or catch birds on the ground. It relies on its ground-coloured plumage and a fast, whirring take-off into nearby cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, feeding from early morning until dusk and resting in shade during the hottest hours. It roosts at night perched in shrubs and trees. It has no seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is not well documented. Small doves of this kind often live only a few years, although individuals can survive longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Builds a flimsy platform of twigs and grass in a shrub, tree or vine tangle and usually lays two white eggs. Both parents incubate for about two weeks and feed the chicks crop milk; young leave the nest within about two weeks, and several broods may be raised each year.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are rufous with a blue-grey head. Females are plainer grey-brown, with much less rufous and no contrasting grey crown.

entries.name: Ruff
entries.heroTitle: Ruff — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Male Ruffs develop dramatic collars and use different reproductive strategies at leks. Their shorebird life combines wetland feeding with social competition shaped by costume, timing, and position.
identification: Small head on a long neck, with a short, slightly drooping bill
Upright, pot-bellied stance that gives a hunch-backed look
Scaly upperparts, each dark feather neatly edged with buff
Oval white patches either side of the dark tail in flight
Leg colour ranging from greenish to yellow or orange
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, central_asia, sub_saharan_africa. Breeds in lowland wet grassland, marshy tundra and damp hay meadows with short vegetation across northern Europe and Asia. Outside the breeding season it uses shallow freshwater margins, flooded fields, rice paddies and salt-pan edges, and most of the population winters in Africa south of the Sahara.

whyInteresting: Males and females tend to winter apart: many males stay further north, in Europe or northern Africa, while most females travel on to West and southern Africa.
It is one of the quietest waders and rarely calls, even when flushed.
DNA studies led to its move from its own genus, Philomachus, into Calidris alongside the stints and other sandpipers.
The species name pugnax is Latin for combative or fond of fighting.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects and their larvae, especially flies and beetles, dominate in summer, picked from the surface or probed from soft mud. In winter it takes much more plant food, including seeds, rice and spilled grain, along with worms and small molluscs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, gulls, skuas, crows and falcons take adults, eggs or chicks. Nests are hidden in tall grass, and a flock rises and wheels tightly together when a falcon attacks. Drainage and intensive farming of wet meadows are the main threats to breeding numbers.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly diurnal. Outside the breeding season birds gather at night in dense communal roosts, standing in shallow water or on bare islands and mudflats where ground predators cannot approach unseen.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live only a few years in the wild; ringed Ruffs have been recorded surviving beyond 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female alone makes a shallow, grass-lined scrape hidden in a tussock and usually lays 4 eggs, incubating them for about 3 weeks. The downy chicks leave the nest within a day, feed themselves under her guard and fly at around 25 to 28 days.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are clearly larger than females, which are called reeves. In breeding dress males grow bare yellow to orange facial warts and head tufts whose colour varies from bird to bird; reeves stay mottled grey-brown all year.

analysis.summary: A small sengi of dry East African scrub, weighing around 50 grams, that runs on long hind legs along narrow trails it keeps clear itself. Each day it sweeps twigs and fallen leaves off these paths with its forefeet, so that it can sprint along them without tripping.
identification: Long, flexible, trunk-like snout that constantly twitches
Large dark eyes set in a pale eye-ring
Long hind legs and a bounding, springing gait
Soft greyish to reddish-brown fur
Thin, sparsely haired tail

A pair shares one territory, and field studies found that each partner chases off intruders of its own sex.
Partners in a pair spend most of their time apart and are seldom seen together.
It picks up ants and termites with a long, slender tongue that flicks out beyond the tip of the snout.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Ants, termites, beetles, spiders, and small invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds of prey, mongooses, genets and small cats hunt it. When alarmed it drums its hind feet on the ground, then bolts at high speed for the nearest cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most active in the cooler morning and late-afternoon hours. It rests mostly at night and through the midday heat, on the ground in the shade of thick bushes, though some activity after dark has been recorded, especially on moonlit nights.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is short and poorly measured, probably one to two years for most animals; captive animals commonly live several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs breed several times a year. After about two months of gestation the female bears one or two fully furred young with open eyes, which can run within hours; she visits them only briefly to nurse.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike and are similar in size, so they cannot be told apart in the field.

analysis.summary: The Rufous Potoo teaches that stillness is a skill. Its body becomes part of the forest by holding the right shape at the right time.
identification: Rich rufous to chestnut plumage all over
Rows of white, black-edged spots on underparts and shoulders
Small for a potoo, roughly 21 to 25 cm long
Minute bill above an enormously wide mouth
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_america. Humid lowland rainforest of the Amazon basin, including terra firme forest with a dense, shaded understorey and forest along streams. It usually perches in the lower and middle storeys rather than the high canopy.

whyInteresting: The upper eyelids have small notches, as in other potoos, which are thought to let it detect movement while its eyes look closed.
It is one of the least-known potoos, and much of what is known comes from sound recordings rather than sightings.
Potoos form their own family, Nyctibiidae, found only in the American tropics, and are related to nightjars.
Its song has been described as a series of soft, hollow hooting notes given from the forest interior at night.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flying insects, probably mainly moths and beetles as in other potoos, taken at night in short sallies from a perch and snapped up in the air.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators have not been recorded. Owls, forest hawks, snakes and monkeys are likely threats. By day it relies on camouflage, sitting upright and motionless on a perch, and flies off only if closely approached.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal. It rests through the daylight hours alone on a perch, eyes almost closed, and begins feeding at dusk.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Neither wild nor captive lifespan figures exist for Nyctibius bracteatus. By day it freezes upright on stubs, matching bark and broken wood.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding is barely described. Other potoos lay a single egg in a small depression on a branch or stump without building a nest, and this species is presumed to do the same.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are not known to differ in plumage or size in any way that can be seen in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Herons, hawks, snakes and small carnivorous mammals are likely predators, and rising water can flood nests.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It is active in dense cover, often crepuscular, calling more often than seen. Birds also forage and call through the day, and rest hidden low in thick vegetation.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Laterallus melanophaius remains without a published lifespan in wild studies; this small rail skulks through marshy grass and reedbeds of South America.

whyInteresting: When handled or jostled by a rival it may chirp, a rasping sound thought to be made with the ridges on its claw.
Adults breathe air and will drown if held under water for long.
It carries a small store of water inside its shell to keep the gills and abdomen damp, topping it up at pools.
To moult it buries itself in damp sand for weeks, sheds its hard outer skeleton and usually eats it afterwards.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An omnivorous scavenger. It eats fallen fruit, seeds, dead leaves, stranded seaweed, carrion and dead fish, finding food largely by smell and picking it apart with its claws.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Its answer to a threat is to pull back into the shell and block the opening with a claw, or to let go of its foothold and drop. Shorebirds, larger crabs, rats and monitor lizards eat adults, and fish take the drifting larvae.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active mainly at night. Days are spent buried in damp sand or tucked under debris, often in clusters, which limits water loss. It comes out at dusk and is busiest on humid nights.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not measured in the wild. Captive animals are reported to live ten years or more when kept well.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating takes place on land. The female carries the eggs, often hundreds or more, on her abdomen inside the shell, then walks to the water's edge to release hatching larvae. These drift in the plankton for several weeks before settling, taking a tiny shell and coming ashore.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike from outside the shell. Females have a pair of small genital openings at the base of the rear walking legs and feathery limbs on the abdomen for holding eggs, visible only when the crab extends.

entries.name: Russian Desman
entries.heroTitle: Russian Desman — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Russian Desmans are semi-aquatic relatives of moles. They use riverbank burrows, webbed feet, and touch-sensitive snouts to locate aquatic invertebrates in murky water where vision is limited.
identification: Tail flattened side to side, scaly and nearly as long as the body
Dense glossy fur, dark brown above and silvery grey below
Tiny eyes and no visible external ears
Body roughly 20 centimetres long
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, central_asia. Slow rivers, oxbow lakes, floodplain ponds and backwaters with well-vegetated banks, mainly in the Volga, Don and Ural basins of Russia and Kazakhstan; it formerly lived in the Dnieper basin as well. It needs firm banks to dig in and water that does not freeze to the bottom.

analysis.summary: Skin colour tracks body temperature in this heavy-bodied, plant-eating lizard of the central Saharan uplands. A cold animal is dark and absorbs sunlight quickly after the desert night; as it warms, the skin pales and reflects more of the heat, slowing further warming.

It was long treated as a subspecies of the North African spiny-tailed lizard Uromastyx acanthinura before being recognised as a separate species.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults are almost entirely vegetarian, biting off leaves, flowers and seeds of desert shrubs and grasses. Juveniles are thought to eat a larger share of insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds of prey, snakes and small carnivores such as foxes take these lizards. Threatened, it bolts into a burrow or rock crevice, inflates its body to wedge itself in, and lashes the spiny tail at anything that follows.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, emerging after sunrise to bask and sheltering through the hottest midday hours. Nights are spent in a burrow or deep crevice, and it stays underground for weeks in the cool season.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No wild lifespan figure has been published for this species. Keepers report spiny-tailed lizards of the genus Uromastyx living 15 years or more in captivity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females dig a nest burrow and lay a single clutch a year, reported as roughly 5 to 15 eggs, which take about two to three months to hatch. The hatchlings receive no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are usually larger and more brightly coloured than females, with prominent pores on the underside of the thighs. Colour varies a great deal between individuals, so it is not a reliable guide to sex on its own.

entries.name: Sailfin Tang

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large raptors are a major danger, along with snakes and wild cats. Troop members watch the sky and give sharp alarm calls, at which the whole group drops into dense cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active from dawn to dusk, resting in shade during the heat of midday. At night the troop sleeps in tall trees, huddled in small clusters along the branches.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around 15 years is often cited for wild animals, though figures are uncertain; captives have lived more than 20 years.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger than females. Before the mating season adult males put on weight around the shoulders and upper arms, becoming noticeably bulkier.

entries.name: Salmon Shark

analysis.summary: A stocky mackerel shark of the cold North Pacific, it keeps its swimming muscles, eyes, brain and gut far warmer than the sea around it. Dense networks of fine blood vessels work as heat exchangers, holding in the heat its muscles produce, so it can chase fast fish in water only a few degrees above freezing.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Salmon Shark rests in continuous swimming in open water rather than fixed shelter. It is active by day and by night, and tagged sharks make repeated dives between the surface and a few hundred metres.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Ageing from growth bands in the vertebrae gives maximum ages of roughly 20 to 30 years, with estimates differing between studies and regions.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females mature at a larger size than males, and males carry paired claspers on the pelvic fins. The sexes are strongly segregated: catches in the western North Pacific are mostly males, while females dominate in the east.

analysis.summary: Generally regarded as the largest deer native to South and Southeast Asia: a big stag can stand 1.5 metres at the shoulder and weigh around 300 kilograms. For all that bulk it is secretive, and in most forests it is heard far more often than it is seen.

Animals shipped to Australia and New Zealand in the 1800s founded wild herds that are still hunted there today.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tigers, leopards, dholes and crocodiles all hunt sambar, and people hunt it throughout its range. An alarmed animal stamps a forefoot, raises its tail and gives a loud, ringing bark. Pursued by dholes, it often backs into water and strikes out with its forefeet.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active from dusk to dawn, and more strictly nocturnal where it is hunted. The day is spent lying up in dense thickets or tall grass.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Seldom more than about 12 years in the wild; captive animals have lived into their mid-twenties.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually a single calf, born after a pregnancy of about eight months. It lies hidden in thick cover for its first weeks, starts on solid food within a fortnight or so, and stays with its mother for a year or more.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Stags are much larger and carry antlers, which are shed and regrown, and grow a thick mane on the neck in the rut. Hinds are smaller and antlerless. Hinds and young live in small groups, while adult stags are mostly solitary.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Coyotes, foxes, raccoons, ravens and bobcats take eggs and chicks; golden eagles and coyotes occasionally kill adults. Parents stand tall with wings spread, call loudly and kick at intruders approaching the chicks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, flying out to fields after sunrise and back before dusk. At night flocks stand in shallow water on sandbars or marsh flats, often on one leg with the head tucked.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Survival past the first year is the main hurdle. Typical adult lifespan in the wild is not well measured, but banded wild birds have lived more than 30 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs usually lay 2 eggs on a mound of marsh vegetation, and both parents incubate for about 30 days. The downy chicks leave the nest within a day, fly at about 2 months, and stay with their parents until the next spring.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike, though males average slightly larger. Paired birds are easiest to tell apart in the unison call: the male gives a single low note to each pair of higher calls from the female.

analysis.summary: A leatherleaf slug whose mantle has spread into a tough, leathery skin covering the entire back, from just behind the head to the tip of the tail. The flat, elongated body gives the species its name: linguaeformis means tongue-shaped.

whyInteresting: Unlike many slugs, which keep a small shell plate hidden in the body, it has no shell of any kind as an adult.
It has no lung and takes in oxygen through its skin, as other leatherleaf slugs do.
Its family, Veronicellidae, is a separate branch of air-breathing gastropods from garden slugs, so its slug shape evolved independently.
Telling it from similar leatherleaf slugs usually needs dissection of the reproductive organs, since colour and shape overlap.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grazes at night, rasping with its radula at the leaves of low-growing plants, including seedlings and crops, and eating decaying plant material on the ground.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: No predator has been recorded for this species in particular, though ground-feeding birds and toads probably take it. When touched it contracts into a stiff, flattened shape and coats itself in sticky mucus.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds mainly at night, and also on overcast, rainy days. By day it burrows a short way into moist soil or lies flattened beneath stones, and dry spells keep it underground.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Its lifespan, in the wild or in captivity, is poorly documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid in clusters in moist soil or under litter, and the young hatch as small copies of the adults. Clutch size and growth rates are poorly known for this species.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: A hermaphrodite: each adult carries both sexes, with the male opening near the head and the female opening partway along the right underside, so there are no separate sexes.

entries.name: Sargassum Fish

analysis.summary: The Sargassum Fish turns habitat into identity. It survives by becoming so well matched to its surroundings that the environment itself becomes protection.

Arm-like pectoral fins that grip seaweed
Short lure on the snout above the mouth

It rarely leaves the weed; currents carry it along with the mats, and storms sometimes strand it near coasts or on beaches.

It has been seen to shift colour gradually to match lighter or darker weed.
Although it looks nothing like one, it belongs to the anglerfish order, Lophiiformes, alongside the deep-sea anglers.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An ambush hunter of small shrimps, crabs and fishes that live in the weed. It creeps close, then opens its mouth so fast that prey is sucked in, and it can swallow animals close to its own size.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Dolphinfish, tunas, jacks and other open-sea hunters feed around floating weed. When chased it has been seen clambering out of the water onto the weed mat and staying there briefly.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Rest and activity cycles have not been described. It spends long periods motionless, gripping the weed with its fins, whether waiting for prey or at rest, by day and by night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been documented, and no ages have been determined.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females release many thousands of tiny eggs embedded in a floating, jelly-like raft that drifts with the weed. There is no parental care; larvae live in the plankton before settling onto floating weed.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike, though a female close to spawning swells noticeably as her eggs develop.

analysis.summary: Iron sulphide is built into the skeleton of this deep-sea gastropod. In some populations the outer layer of its three-layered shell and the scales on its foot are mineralised with it, making it the only living animal known to do so.
identification: Foot covered in hundreds of overlapping hard scales called sclerites
Scales and shell black at the Kairei vents, white at Solitaire
Coiled shell with a small, low spire
Shell up to about 4.5 cm across
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: indian_ocean. Black-smoker vent fields on Indian Ocean ridges at roughly 2,400 to 2,900 metres, clustered on chimney walls where warm, sulphide-rich fluid mixes with cold seawater. It is known from just three vent fields.
analysis.nativeRange: Indian Ocean hydrothermal vent systems where the species is known.

The iron-sulphide coating on the scales of black snails is reported to be magnetic.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Relies on bacteria living inside a greatly enlarged gland in its oesophagus. The bacteria use chemical energy from vent fluids to make food that the snail absorbs, and its digestive tract is reduced.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Crabs and vent predators able to handle shells threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nothing is known of any rest or activity rhythm in this snail, which has only been watched during brief visits by submersibles and remotely operated vehicles.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not well known, likely tied to vent stability. Individual lifespan has not been measured, as no ageing study of this snail has been published.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Each snail is thought to be a simultaneous hermaphrodite. Eggs develop into larvae that drift away from the vent, the only way new vent fields can be reached, but how long they spend in the plankton is not known.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: No separate male or female form exists to tell apart: each adult is thought to carry both sets of reproductive organs.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are yellowish to olive-brown rather than red, and their abdomen is slightly thicker than the male's.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are alike in size and colour, and they cannot be separated by eye in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sharks and large groupers are the likeliest predators, though few attacks have been recorded. Like other filefishes it can raise its long head spine, and a threatened fish may wedge itself into a crevice with the spine erect.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active in daylight, browsing slowly over reef and seagrass. Where it spends the night is not well documented, though resting fish are thought to shelter close to the reef after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No reliable estimate of its lifespan is available, for wild fish or for those kept in aquariums.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding has rarely been observed, and eggs are thought to be laid on the bottom. Young fish spend a long open-water stage sheltering beneath floating weed, driftwood and debris before settling on reefs.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes cannot be told apart by appearance.

An isolated population lives on coastal dunes in Buenos Aires Province, Argentina, far from the main range.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, pumas, birds of prey and domestic dogs kill armadillos, people hunt them for meat, and many die on roads. A threatened animal runs for the nearest burrow or wedges itself into loose soil, leaving only the armoured back exposed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Field studies in Argentina have found it mostly nocturnal in the hot summer and active more by day in winter. It rests in burrows it digs itself, often under shrubs.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been documented. Animals kept in zoos have been reported living more than 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Litters are usually of one or two young, born in a nest inside the burrow after a gestation of roughly two months. The young are born with soft shells that harden as they grow, and they are weaned within a couple of months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike and cannot be told apart in the field.

The nerve circuits that drive its rhythmic wingbeats have been studied for decades as a model of how simple nervous systems control movement.
In Japan it is known as kurione, and crowds watch for it under the winter drift ice off Hokkaido.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Almost entirely sea butterflies of the genus Limacina. Three pairs of sticky tentacles shoot out from the head to grip the prey's shell, and small hooks pull the soft body out to be swallowed whole.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Little has been documented about what eats it. Plankton-feeding fish and baleen whales are likely consumers, and any defences it has are poorly known.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No sleep cycle has been described; it beats its wings more or less continuously to stay in the water column, speeding up sharply when it strikes at prey.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Studies suggest a life cycle of about 1 to 2 years, varying with water temperature and food supply; lifespan is not precisely known.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating is reciprocal, each partner fertilising the other. Floating jelly-like egg masses hatch into larvae that have a small shell, which is shed as they develop into adults.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: There are no separate sexes: every adult is a simultaneous hermaphrodite, so no male and female forms exist.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Jorunna parva lifespan has never been tabulated; this tiny dorid nudibranch is recognised by its fuzzy rhinophores and sponge-grazing habit.

whyInteresting: Its sinking shells and faecal pellets carry carbon from the surface towards the deep sea.
High-speed filming published in 2016 showed it swims with a clap-and-fling wing stroke also used by tiny flying insects.
Young animals make up most of the population through the dark polar winter and are thought to live partly on stored fat.
Arctic populations are thought to spawn mainly in spring and summer, when the plankton bloom provides food for the larvae.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Hangs in the water and spreads a sheet of sticky mucus, often much larger than itself, that traps phytoplankton, tiny animals and drifting particles. It then draws the web back in and eats it along with the catch.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: A specialist hunter, the naked pteropod Clione limacina, feeds largely on it; fish such as herring, cod and salmon, seabirds and baleen whales also take it. When disturbed it pulls its body into the shell and sinks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No sleep state has been described. Many populations move up towards the surface at night and down to deeper water by day, and individuals often drift motionless with the wings held out.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one to two years; many Arctic populations complete a generation in roughly a year, though growth and timing vary with region and food.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Each animal begins adult life as a male and later becomes female. Eggs are released in floating gelatinous strings, and the young hatch as tiny swimming larvae called veligers that grow their own shells, with no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: No separate males and females exist; an individual's sex depends on its age and size, so sexes cannot be told apart by appearance.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Copepods, small crustacean larvae, fish eggs and fish larvae. Two long tentacles fringed with sticky colloblast cells trap prey, then the tentacle is reeled in and wiped across the mouth.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Other comb jellies of the genus Beroe swallow it whole, and fishes such as mackerel and herring are reported to eat it. Without stinging cells, it has no active defence.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeding and swimming carry on through day and night; with a nerve net and no brain, it shows no identified sleep-like rest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably a few months, possibly up to about a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Each animal produces both eggs and sperm and releases them into the water. The young hatch as a tiny cydippid that already looks like the adult and grows into it directly, with no metamorphosis.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Each animal is a hermaphrodite, so there are no separate males and females.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds on the richest top layer of the mud, using a ring of tentacles around the mouth to push sediment in and digest its organic matter. It appears to favour freshly fallen debris from the sunlit surface over older material.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Deep-sea fish, crabs, and other seafloor predators threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No rest cycle is known. It has a nerve ring but no brain, and in the dark abyss it has been seen crawling and feeding whenever observed.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan has not been measured for this species, and no established method yet exists for ageing an individual deep-sea sea cucumber.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Reproduction has rarely been studied. Like most sea cucumbers it is thought to have separate sexes and to release eggs and sperm into the water, where fertilised eggs develop into drifting larvae.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are not visibly distinct in normal viewing.

entries.name: Secretarybird
entries.heroTitle: Secretarybird — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Secretarybird was created to be the champion of Specific Force. The blueprint skips the usual rules for hunting birds—instead of flying high and grabbing prey with its claws, this bird was dropped onto the wide-open ground to solve one scary problem: venomous snakes. By giving it super-long, powerful legs, the design proves that a single, perfect, stomping tool can easily defeat a dangerous enemy that other animals are afraid to touch.
identification: Very long stilt-like legs
Powerful snake-stomping kicks
Crested head feathers
Ground-hunting raptor lifestyle

They can deliver rapid forceful kicks to subdue prey.
Their name is linked to the quill-like crest feathers.
They roost and nest in trees despite hunting mainly on the ground.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A diet of snakes and lizards justifies the giant legs. The bird does not dive from the clouds like an eagle; it solves its dinner problems with quick, perfectly aimed karate kicks on the ground.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: To keep the babies safe from sneaky ground predators, the design puts their big nests high up in thorny trees, creating a safe fortress in the sky.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It hunts during broad daylight so it can easily spot squirming snakes in the grass before delivering its quick, definitive stomp.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Living over ten years shows that having one perfect superpower keeps the bird safe from injury and saves a lot of energy over its lifetime.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Laying eggs high up in the trees keeps the chicks perfectly safe while they grow the long legs they will need to rule the ground later.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Moms and dads look exactly the same because the snake-stomping leg design is an important tool that both parents need to use every day.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds and other plant material are characteristic foods for many Lygaeidae, accessed with piercing-sucking mouthparts. fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, predatory insects and small reptiles may take them. Small size, camouflage, hiding in vegetation or litter and in some species chemical or visual defences reduce predation.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Activity varies across the family and climate. Many are encountered during the day on plants, soil or litter, with individuals sheltering when conditions become unsuitable.

whyInteresting: Its baleen fringes are unusually fine, pale and woolly, among the finest of any rorqual.
The name comes from the Norwegian word for pollock, a fish that arrived off Norway at the same season as the whales.
It is famously irregular, arriving in large numbers in an area one year and then staying away for years.
Its flanks often carry pale oval scars from the bites of cookiecutter sharks.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It takes copepods, krill, small fish, and other small schooling or planktonic prey. Calanus copepods are a staple in the North Atlantic, while North Pacific sei whales are reported to eat anchovies, sauries and some squid.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Orcas prey on calves and may attack adults, which rely on speed to escape. Heavy whaling in the 1950s to 1970s, after blue and fin whales had been depleted, cut numbers sharply; ship strikes and entanglement are current threats.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It rests at sea between feeding and travel, often moving with prey conditions. Most feeding takes place in the upper few tens of metres, and how it sleeps has not been studied.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: It can live for many decades, commonly estimated around 60 years or more. Most individuals are thought to become sexually mature at around 8 to 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Adult females bear a single calf and nurse it before it feeds independently. Gestation lasts about 11 to 12 months, the newborn is about 4.5 metres long, and weaning comes at roughly 6 to 9 months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult females are generally larger than males. The sexes otherwise look alike and cannot be told apart at sea.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, assassin bugs and parasitoid wasps. Most vertebrates learn after one attempt, which is what makes an unpleasant-but-harmless defence work; parasitoid wasps, which attack the eggs, are unaffected by it.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are similar; females are usually slightly larger and broader, and the sexes are separated reliably only by the shape of the abdomen tip.

In winter herds use wind-blown slopes where snow lies thin.

whyInteresting: Siberian Ibex inhabit rugged mountain regions and rely on climbing, herd awareness, and endurance in harsh terrain.
Outside the rut, adult males and females live in separate herds on different parts of the mountain.
Rival males rear onto their hind legs and bring their horns crashing down on each other.
It is the largest member of the goat genus Capra by body weight in many accounts.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, shrubs, herbs, lichens, buds, and tough alpine plants support terrain mastery because feeding requires moving carefully through sparse high places.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snow leopards and wolves are the main hunters, with golden eagles taking kids and hunting by people an important threat. Herds keep lookouts, give whistling alarm calls and escape onto steep rock.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Daytime is when it feeds, with peaks after dawn and before dusk and a long midday rest lying on slopes. Nights are spent bedded on or beneath cliffs.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 10 to 15 years in the wild, with few males reaching the upper end; captive individuals have lived to around 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating takes place in late autumn and early winter. After a gestation of around six months, females give birth in May or June, usually to a single kid, sometimes twins, which can follow its mother over rock within days and is weaned by autumn.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males can weigh twice as much as females or more and carry thick, scimitar-shaped horns that may exceed a metre along the curve, with a long dark beard. Females have short, slender horns, usually no more than about 30 to 35 centimetres.

Small agile body for mountain forest movement
Musk gland used in scent communication
Secretive browsing in cold forests

whyInteresting: Male musk deer have tusk-like canine teeth rather than antlers.
They produce musk from a gland, historically valued by humans.
They are solitary and secretive compared with many deer.
They move through steep forest and rocky slopes with agility.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat leaves, shoots, lichens, grasses, mosses, and seasonal browse.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators include lynx, wolverines, foxes, wolves, and humans. Their defenses are concealment, agility, freezing still, and climbing through broken terrain rather than standing in open combat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly crepuscular or nocturnal, resting hidden by day and feeding in safer dim light. The rhythm makes alternate strategy clearer: avoid the obvious contest and use the time that fits the body.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often around 10 to 14 years where protected. The lifespan why is that unusual tools can endure if the animal keeps choosing terrain and timing that make those tools useful.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to one or two fawns hidden in cover. Offspring start with concealment rather than weaponry, showing that survival begins before display appears.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have the prominent tusks and musk gland role; females lack the same display emphasis.

entries.name: Siberian Sturgeon
entries.heroTitle: Siberian Sturgeon — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Growth is slow in the cold Siberian rivers, so this bottom-feeding sturgeon takes many years to reach breeding condition. Females in the northern rivers may be 15 to 20 years old or more before they first spawn.
identification: Five rows of bony plates along the body
Long, pointed snout with four barbels underneath
Shark-like tail with a longer upper lobe
Grey to brown back and pale belly
Long, slender body tapering to the tail
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: central_asia, east_asia. Large, cold rivers of Siberia, from the upper tributaries down to brackish estuaries such as the Ob Gulf, plus lakes such as Baikal. Adults keep to the bottom of deep channels over sand, silt and gravel, and most populations live entirely in fresh water.

whyInteresting: It is one of the most widely farmed sturgeons, raised in many countries for meat and caviar.
Its skeleton is mostly cartilage rather than bone, a feature it shares with other sturgeons.
Scientists read a sturgeon's age from growth rings in a cross-section of its pectoral fin ray.
Hybrids with other sturgeon species occur readily in fish farms.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It feeds on the bottom, locating prey by touch and taste and sucking it up through a protrusible mouth. Insect larvae, molluscs, crustaceans and worms make up most of the diet, with small fish in larger adults.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and larvae are eaten by other fish, but adults have few natural enemies. Overfishing, poaching for caviar, dams that block spawning runs and pollution have caused steep declines, and wild populations are listed as endangered.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Daily rest patterns in the wild are poorly known. In winter many fish gather in deep river pits and feed little until the ice breaks up.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Maximum ages of around 60 years have been reported; most wild fish today are much younger because of fishing.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females shed tens of thousands to several hundred thousand sticky eggs over gravel in fast current, usually in late spring or early summer. Eggs hatch in one to two weeks depending on temperature, and there is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike from outside and cannot be told apart reliably in the field; females generally grow larger.

entries.name: Signature Spider
entries.heroTitle: Signature Spider — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Argiope anasuja sits at the centre of a garden orb with a pale signature on the silk. The mark is not decoration. It is widely read as a warning that stops a bird flying through the web.
identification: Yellow-and-black Argiope, female much larger than the male
Stabilimentum as an X, a zigzag, or a disc at the hub
Orb built in a garden gap, hedge or low tree
Sits head-down at the hub by day
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_asia. Gardens, hedges, forest edge and village gaps across South Asia. A sunny opening between stems is the site.

whyInteresting: It is the common signature spider of South Asian gardens.
Several Argiope species write on the web; this one is A. anasuja, not the European Wasp Spider.
Males are tiny and wait at the edge. Mating is brief and often fatal for them.
The web is rebuilt often; the signature is rewritten each time.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flying insects caught in the orb — flies, bees, moths. The spider waits at the hub rather than hunting on foot.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds and parasitic wasps. The stabilimentum is aimed at the birds; it does nothing against a wasp that walks the silk.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-sitting at the hub. Night is when much of the rebuilding happens.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Females live several months through a warm season. Males are shorter-lived.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Egg sacs are placed near the web in silk. The female guards them, so a garden that is sprayed loses both the hunter and the next brood.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are the large yellow-and-black spider at the hub. Males are a fraction of the size and sit at the edge.

entries.name: Silky Carpenter Ant
entries.heroTitle: Silky Carpenter Ant — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Silky Carpenter Ant AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: Fine golden hairs lie flat over the abdomen of this large black ant, found from Mexico to northern Argentina, and flash in sunlight as it runs over bark. Workers of one colony come in a continuous range of sizes, from slim minors to big-headed majors. As in other carpenter ants, the majors are thought to do most of the guarding and the cutting up of large prey.
identification: Head and thorax are black and duller than the abdomen
Front corners of the thorax form sharp, angular shoulders
Largest workers are well over a centimetre long, with broad heads
Single narrow waist segment between thorax and abdomen
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical forest, forest edge and wooded savanna from the lowlands into the foothills. Colonies occupy cavities in the trunks and thick branches of living or dead trees, and workers forage over bark, foliage and the ground nearby.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical forest, forest edge and wooded savanna from the lowlands into the foothills. Colonies occupy cavities in the trunks and thick branches of living or dead trees, and workers forage over bark, foliage and the ground nearby.

Single narrow waist segment between thorax and abdomen
whyInteresting: Like other carpenter ants it has no sting, and defends itself by biting and spraying formic acid from the tip of the abdomen.
The name sericeiventris means silky belly, from the Latin words for silken and belly, after the golden hairs on the abdomen.
Its larvae spin silk cocoons before pupating, as in most other ants of its subfamily, the Formicinae.
Workers often travel along regular trails on trunks and branches between the nest and trees where they collect honeydew.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Omnivorous. Workers collect honeydew from treehoppers and other sap-sucking bugs, drink nectar from glands on leaves and stems, and hunt or scavenge insects. Liquid food is carried home in the crop and shared mouth to mouth.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Anteaters, woodpeckers, lizards, spiders and raiding army ants are the likely enemies of a large tree-nesting ant like this one. Lacking a sting, defenders bite hard and spray formic acid into the wound, and alarmed workers pour out of the nest together.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Workers forage by day, with traffic on the trunk heaviest in the warm hours. At night most withdraw into the nest galleries, where the brood is tended at all hours.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No figures are published for this species. In carpenter ants generally, workers live for some months and queens for several years, in some species more than ten.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: As in other carpenter ants, a mated queen is thought to shed her wings, seal herself in a cavity and rear the first workers from her own reserves. Eggs pass through grub and cocooned pupa stages. Later the colony raises winged queens and males, which leave on mating flights.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Workers are wingless females. Queens are larger, with a bulkier thorax, and bear wings until mating. Males are winged, slimmer and smaller-headed than queens, and appear only at mating time.

entries.name: Silver Argiope
entries.heroTitle: Silver Argiope — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Silver Argiope writes a bold zigzag of white silk across the middle of its web. The decoration does not catch anything — the leading explanation is that it stops birds flying through a web they would otherwise never see.
identification: Silvery-white carapace with a banded, angular abdomen
Sits head-down at the hub with legs paired into an X
Bold zigzag silk band, the stabilimentum, across the web centre
Shakes the whole web violently when disturbed
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Sunny scrub, garden edges, cactus and open shrubland where there is a clear gap between plants to span. An exposed, well-lit site is precisely where a large web most needs marking, because it is where birds fly fastest and see least.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Sunny scrub, garden edges, cactus and open shrubland where there is a clear gap between plants to span. An exposed, well-lit site is precisely where a large web most needs marking, because it is where birds fly fastest and see least.

Bold zigzag silk band, the stabilimentum, across the web centre

whyInteresting: The zigzag band is called a stabilimentum, and it reflects ultraviolet strongly — the strongest evidence is that it warns birds off rather than attracting prey.
Threatened, the spider whips the entire orb back and forth until its own outline blurs, then drops on a line if that fails.
Females are several times the size of males, and a male approaching a female plucks the web in a specific rhythm to avoid being taken as prey.
It rebuilds or repairs the orb frequently, so the decoration is re-drawn rather than maintained.
Found from the southern United States through Central and South America and across the Caribbean.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flying insects taken in the orb — grasshoppers, flies, bees and wasps — wrapped in silk on contact and fed on at the hub. The web does all the hunting, so everything depends on it staying intact.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wasps, birds and lizards take adults, and mud-dauber wasps provision nests with them. The web-shaking display, and the stabilimentum keeping birds from blundering through, are both defences of the web as much as the spider.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Sits at the hub day and night without a real rest period, most active in the warm middle of the day when insects are flying.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Females live about a year, reaching full size in a single season; males live only a few weeks after their final moult.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female builds a papery egg sac attached near the web and guards it. Spiderlings disperse by ballooning on silk threads, so each one starts its own web somewhere else entirely.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Strongly different. Females reach roughly 12 mm with the silver carapace and banded abdomen; males are around 4 mm, slender and plain, and are the ones seen at the edge of a female's web.

entries.name: Silver Dollar Fish

analysis.summary: A close relative of the piranhas and pacus, in the same South American family, it uses sharp, closely set teeth to crop plants rather than flesh. Adults reach at most about 14 centimetres long.
identification: Flat, disc-shaped body almost as deep as it is long
Plain bright silver sides, sometimes with faint grey spots
Long, low fleshy fin between dorsal fin and tail
Saw-edged keel of small scutes along the belly
Small head with a short, blunt snout

analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: domestic_global. In the wild it is recorded from the Tapajós River basin in Brazil, where it lives in warm, soft, slightly acidic water along well-vegetated margins and side channels.

whyInteresting: The common name comes from its resemblance to the large silver dollar coin of the United States.
Several species of Metynnis are sold under the same name, and they are hard to tell apart without close examination.
The species was first described in 1923 by the German ichthyologist Ernst Ahl.
Its scientific name argenteus is Latin for silvery, after the plain bright sides of the fish.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves and stems of water plants form most of the diet, with algae, seeds and some small insects and worms taken as well. In aquaria it will strip soft-leaved plants down to the stalk.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators of wild fish are not recorded in detail for this species, though larger predatory fish and fish-eating birds are the likely ones. A frightened fish dashes for plant cover, and in aquaria a sudden shadow or movement overhead is enough to set it off.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, cruising the middle and upper water in a group. After dark the fish slow down and hang almost motionless near plants or the bottom until the light returns.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around 10 years in aquaria, and sometimes more; lifespan in the wild has not been documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are scattered among plants, with around 2,000 reported from a single aquarium spawning. They sink, hatch in about three days, and the fry swim freely roughly a week after spawning. The parents give no care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a longer anal fin with a curved front edge, tinged with red or orange, most strongly at breeding time. In females the fin has a straight edge and little or no colour. The sexes are otherwise alike in size and shape.

entries.name: Silver Pheasant
entries.heroTitle: Silver Pheasant — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: This large pheasant spends most of its life walking the floor of evergreen hill forest in southern China and mainland South-east Asia. More than a dozen subspecies have been named across that range, and males differ noticeably between them in the pattern of their plumage.
identification: Bright red legs in both sexes
Pale horn-coloured bill
Bare red skin around the eye, largest in males
Male's white upperparts crossed by black lines, heavier in some subspecies
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, east_asia. Evergreen and mixed broadleaf forest on hills and mountains, often with bamboo or dense undergrowth, from the lowlands up to about 2,000 metres, in southern China, Hainan and mainland South-east Asia.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia, east_asia. Evergreen and mixed broadleaf forest on hills and mountains, often with bamboo or dense undergrowth, from the lowlands up to about 2,000 metres, in southern China, Hainan and mainland South-east Asia.

whyInteresting: Its image was embroidered on the rank badges worn by fifth-grade civil officials in Ming and Qing dynasty China.
It has long been one of the pheasants most often kept in aviaries, and it breeds readily in captivity.
Where its range meets that of the Kalij Pheasant in Myanmar, birds with intermediate plumage occur, and some ornithologists have treated the two as one species.
Outside the breeding season it often moves in small parties, commonly a male with several females.
It is classed as Least Concern, although it has declined locally where forest is cleared or hunting is heavy.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, fallen fruit and berries, shoots, leaves, insects and worms, found by scratching through leaf litter with the feet and picking from the forest floor.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopard cats, civets, birds of prey and snakes are its likely natural enemies, and eggs and chicks are the most exposed. Snaring and hunting by people are a threat in parts of the range. A startled bird usually runs into cover, flushing on noisy wings only when pressed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, feeding mostly in the early morning and late afternoon on the forest floor. At night it flies up to roost on branches in trees. It does not migrate or enter any seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive birds are commonly reported to live about 10 to 15 years; lifespan in the wild has not been documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The hen makes a shallow scrape on the ground in dense cover and incubates alone. Captive hens typically lay about six to eight buff eggs, incubated for about 25 days; the downy chicks leave the nest soon after hatching and follow her.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are mainly white and black and considerably larger. Females are olive-brown with a much shorter tail and a brown crest.

entries.name: Silverfish
entries.heroTitle: Silverfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Silverfish are ancient, wingless insects with flattened bodies, quick movement, and a talent for disappearing into cracks. Their survival power is low-profile persistence: they avoid light, feed on overlooked starch-rich materials, and keep going in spaces most animals ignore.
identification: Carrot-shaped, flattened body about 1 to 2 centimetres long
Silvery-grey metallic scales covering the whole body
Three long bristle-like tails at the rear
Long, thread-like antennae
Fast, wriggling fish-like run and no wings

Silverfish belongs in homes and forests, and that environment explains the principle of Paper-Crack Continuance: the animal succeeds only when its body and behavior fit that setting. whyInteresting: Mating is indirect: the male leaves a sperm packet on the ground under silk threads, and the female picks it up.
Unlike most insects it keeps moulting throughout adult life, reportedly dozens of times.
Silverfish belong to an ancient lineage of wingless insects that branched off before insects evolved wings.
It needs high humidity, roughly above 75 percent, which is why damp rooms suit it best.
