fieldGuide.dietSummary: Starchy and sugary material: paper, book bindings and wallpaper paste, flour, cereals, dandruff, hair and dead insects. It can digest cellulose and survives many months without food.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: House spiders, spitting spiders, house centipedes and earwigs catch them. Its defences are speed, a flattened body that slips into narrow cracks, and loose scales that rub off in a predator's grip.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal and strongly light-shy. By day it rests in cracks, behind skirting boards, under loose wallpaper or among stored papers, coming out after dark to feed.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly 2 to 3 years, and up to about 8 years has been reported under laboratory conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay small batches of eggs in crevices, usually fewer than 100 in a lifetime. The young hatch after several weeks as small whitish copies of the adult and gain scales and colour as they moult.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in size and silvery scaling. Adult females carry a short, pointed ovipositor under the tip of the abdomen, visible with a hand lens.

entries.name: Silvery Gibbon
entries.heroTitle: Silvery Gibbon — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A small grey ape found only in the forests of western and central Java. Pairs of most gibbon species sing duets, but here the female does nearly all the singing, giving loud solo bouts of rising notes that end in a bubbling trill. Males call seldom, and are reported to do so mostly before dawn.
identification: long arms
silver fur
loud calls
swinging travel
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Silvery Gibbon usually lives in tropical forest canopy, especially mature lowland and hill forest.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Silvery Gibbon usually lives in tropical forest canopy, especially mature lowland and hill forest.

silver fur

whyInteresting: It is classed as Endangered; estimates of the wild population run from about 2,000 to 4,500, many of them in Gunung Halimun Salak National Park.
A family of two adults and their young defends a territory of a few tens of hectares.
Unlike the great apes it builds no sleeping nest, resting upright on a branch on the hardened sitting pads of its rump.
On the ground or along a broad branch it walks upright on two legs with the arms raised for balance.
In Indonesia it is known as owa jawa, the Javan gibbon.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Silvery Gibbon feeds on fruit, leaves, flowers, and occasional small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, pythons and large eagles are the likely natural predators, though attacks are rarely seen. Keeping to the upper canopy and sleeping in tall trees puts the apes out of reach of most hunters. Forest loss and the capture of infants for the pet trade are greater dangers.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Silvery Gibbon is diurnal, singing and foraging through the canopy by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around 25 to 35 years is the usual estimate for wild animals, though few have been followed for life. Captive animals can live longer, with ages over 40 reported.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a pregnancy of about seven months, females usually raise one infant at a time with family support. Births are about three years or more apart. The infant is weaned at around 18 months to two years, and young leave the family at roughly eight to ten years old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes are silvery grey with a darker cap and a black face, and both weigh roughly 6 kilograms, so in the treetops they are hard to tell apart by sight. Overall the sexes are similar, with pair bonds more important than dimorphism.

entries.heroTitle: Angoumois Grain Moth — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Angoumois Grain Moth AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A small straw-coloured moth whose caterpillar completes its whole growth inside a single cereal grain. It hollows out the kernel as it feeds and pupates there, so an infested grain can look whole from outside until the adult emerges.
identification: Narrow buff or straw-coloured forewings, sometimes with a few dark specks
Hindwings end in a sharp, finger-like point
Very long fringes of hair along the hindwing edges
Small, with a wingspan of roughly 1 to 2 cm

whyInteresting: Its common name comes from Angoumois, a former province of south-west France, after damaging outbreaks there in the eighteenth century.
It is mass-reared on grain as a host for Trichogramma wasps, which are released to control moth pests in crops.
In bulk stores it mainly infests the top layer of grain, because the moths cannot work their way deep into the mass.
Infested grain loses weight and quality and gives off a musty smell.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars eat the starchy interior of whole cereal grains, including wheat, maize, rice, barley and sorghum. They cannot attack ground flour. Adults live briefly and feed little, if at all.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tiny parasitoid wasps attack the eggs and the larvae inside kernels, and predatory mites and spiders take other stages. In stores, drying, cooling and fumigation of the grain are the main threats to its populations.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults rest by day on sacks, walls and grain surfaces and become active at dusk and after dark, when they fly and mate.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults usually live about one to two weeks. Egg to adult takes roughly five weeks in warm conditions and much longer in cold stores.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female lays on average several dozen eggs, sometimes a few hundred, on or between grains. The eggs are white when laid and turn reddish before hatching. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are slightly larger with a heavier abdomen; otherwise the sexes look alike and are hard to tell apart without handling.

analysis.summary: Tiger Beetles are visual hunters that chase small insects in bursts. Their speed is so extreme relative to their size that they must pause and re-aim, making pursuit a rhythm of sprint, reset, and strike.
identification: Brilliant metallic green all over
Up to six small white spots near the wing-cover edges
About 10 to 14 millimetres long
Long, slender legs and large bulging eyes

whyInteresting: Its green colour is produced by fine layers in the outer shell that reflect light, not by pigment.
The larva braces itself in its burrow with hooks on a hump on its back, so struggling prey cannot pull it out.
Adults bite readily when handled and can give a sharp nip to a person's finger.
In much of its range, adults appear in spring woods as early as April.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults run down ants, caterpillars, small flies and spiders on the ground and seize them in their mandibles. Larvae wait at the mouth of a vertical burrow and snatch insects that walk past.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, robber flies and spiders are among the hunters that take adults. A disturbed beetle flies off low and fast, landing a few metres ahead, often facing back towards the threat. Larvae in their burrows are attacked by parasitic wasps and flies.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active only in warm sunshine. At night, and on cool or cloudy days, adults shelter under leaf litter, bark or in shallow holes in the soil; larvae stay in their burrows.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Development from egg to adult usually takes one to two years, mostly as a larva in a burrow. Adults are active for a few months in spring and early summer, and some are thought to overwinter as adults first.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female digs a small hole in soil and lays one egg at a time. The larva passes through three larval stages and pupates underground, with no care from the parents.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look very similar. Males are usually a little smaller, and their front feet are broader and padded, which helps them hold the female during mating.

White lines through the body resembling a ribcage

Each zooid stands separately, joined to others only at its base

whyInteresting: It was formally described as a new species only in 2024.
Its name joins the Latin for bone with panda, yet the white lines that look like bones are reported to be blood vessels.
As a tunicate, it belongs to the invertebrate group most closely related to animals with backbones.
Its clear outer tunic contains cellulose, a material that almost no animals other than tunicates can make.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A filter feeder: each zooid draws seawater in through one siphon, traps plankton and fine organic particles on a sheet of mucus inside its body, and expels the filtered water through a second siphon.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators of this recently described sea squirt have not been documented. When touched, the zooids contract and close their siphons.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Sea squirts have no sleep cycle; the zooids keep pumping water by day and night, pausing only briefly when they contract.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Neither zooid nor colony lifespan are published for Clavelina ossipandae; the tunicate forms white colonies with panda-like black and pink markings on Japanese Pacific coasts.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Colonies grow by budding new zooids from creeping stolons at the base. Sexual reproduction in this species has not been described in detail; in its genus, embryos are brooded inside the parent and released as tiny tadpole-shaped larvae that soon settle.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: There are no separate males and females: as in other sea squirts, each zooid is thought to carry both male and female organs.

Shallow, sheltered coastal water on seaweeds, hydroids and bryozoans, and on man-made surfaces such as mussel ropes, fish-farm cages, buoys and marina pontoons. Native to the north-west Pacific around Japan, it is now established in the North Atlantic and north-east Pacific.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No rest cycle has been documented for it; it spends long periods clinging motionless to a single perch.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Short-lived; most are thought to live only a few months, with several generations a year in warmer water.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female carries her eggs in a brood pouch on the underside of the middle of her body. Young hatch as tiny versions of the adult with no swimming larval stage, and may cling to her briefly.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow much larger than females and have huge, spined grasping front limbs and dense hairs on the front body segments. Females are smaller and carry a brood pouch.

entries.name: Tobacco Grasshopper

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, frogs, mantises, spiders and parasitic flies and wasps take nymphs and adults. It relies on keeping still, then hops a short way or slides round to the far side of a stem when approached.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, feeding mostly in warm hours. At night and in heavy rain it sits motionless on stems and the undersides of leaves in the same patch of vegetation.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults probably live for a month or two, and the full cycle from egg to adult takes a few months, so several generations likely follow each other each year in warm lowlands.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females push the abdomen into moist soil and lay pods of usually a few dozen eggs in a frothy coating. Nymphs hatch after a few weeks, look like small wingless adults and moult several times before maturing.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are much larger and heavier than males, roughly one and a half times the male's length. Mating pairs are easy to spot because the small male rides on the female's back, sometimes for hours or days.

Four-wing agility: the body can hover, dart, stop, and redirect quickly.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Slender Skimmers are active by day, especially in warmth and sunlight.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Most land snails rasp soft leaves, seedlings, fungi, algae and decaying plant matter; many also gnaw limestone, bones or empty shells for calcium. Some snails are predators, including cone snails that harpoon fish.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Song thrushes, hedgehogs, shrews, toads, slow worms, ground beetles and glow-worm larvae. A snail withdraws into its shell and may froth mucus at the opening; thrushes answer by smashing the shell on a stone.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Land snails are active on damp nights and after rain. In dry or cold weather they seal the shell opening with a dried mucus plate and lie dormant, for months if necessary.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Garden snails usually live two to five years; large species such as the Roman snail can pass ten, and some reach twenty or more in captivity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Most land snails are hermaphrodites, each animal both male and female, and a mating pair usually fertilise each other. Each then lays dozens of small round eggs in a hole dug in damp soil, and the hatchlings emerge with a tiny transparent shell.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In most land snails there are no separate sexes to tell apart. Many freshwater and sea snails do have males and females, which generally look alike from outside.

analysis.summary: Silver-blue at sea, this Pacific salmon turns brilliant red with an olive-green head in the weeks before spawning, as pigments from its crustacean diet shift from muscle to skin. Most runs depend on lakes, where the young grow for a year or more before going to sea.

Carcasses of spawned-out sockeye carry nitrogen from the ocean into streams and fertilise trees along the banks.
Snake River sockeye swim about 1,400 kilometres inland to Redfish Lake in Idaho, climbing about 2,000 metres.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Brown and black bears, bald eagles, gulls and wolves take spawning adults; seals, sea lions and salmon sharks hunt them at sea. Trout, char and mergansers eat eggs and young. Young fish leave lakes in schools, largely at night.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Juveniles in lakes rise towards the surface at dusk and dawn to feed and sink into deep, dark, cold water by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live 4 or 5 years, with a range of about 3 to 7. All die within weeks of spawning.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female digs several nests in gravel with her tail and lays roughly 2,000 to 4,500 eggs in total, guarding them until she dies. Eggs hatch in winter; the young stay in the gravel on their yolk until spring.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: At sea the sexes look alike. On the spawning grounds males develop a humped back and a hooked jaw with enlarged teeth, while females stay smaller-headed and less humped.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Feral cats, brought to Socorro by people, are thought to have killed off the ground-feeding doves, after sheep grazing had stripped much of the forest understorey. Birds raised for release will need cat-free habitat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day; at night it roosts on branches off the ground. Socorro Dove rests in trees, shrubs, and protected aviary or future island cover.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs build a flimsy twig platform in a shrub or low tree and usually lay two white eggs. Both parents incubate for about two weeks and feed the chicks on crop milk.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are very similar; males are said to be slightly brighter, but the difference is small and hard to judge in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolf spiders, the mirid bug Cyrtorhinus lividipennis, which eats its eggs, ladybirds, tiny egg-parasitic wasps and fungal diseases all kill it, and farmers spray insecticides. A disturbed hopper leaps away or sidles round the stem.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are much larger with enlarged noses and fight for breeding access; females are smaller and invest heavily in pups.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in plumage, and size differences are slight, so birds cannot reliably be sexed in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, toads and digging mammals take it, and it has specialist enemies: the fly Ormia depleta finds calling males by ear and deposits larvae on them, and the wasp Larra bicolor paralyses it to feed its young. Its main escape is a rapid retreat down the tunnel.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a sound-producing file and a clear, drum-like area on the forewings that females lack, so wing venation separates the sexes; otherwise they look alike.

A rolled animal may leave a slit open and snap it shut on a probing paw.

Short, stiff tail covered in knobbly armour.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly diurnal in mild conditions, retreating into shade or crevices during heat or cold. In the hottest, driest months it may stay inactive for long spells.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long it lives in the wild is not known; no field study has followed individuals over their full life.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding females lay very small clutches, often single eggs, in protected soil. Several clutches may be laid in a season, and the eggs take roughly three to four months to hatch.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult females are often larger than males, a common tortoise pattern linked to egg carrying. Males usually have a longer tail and a slightly concave underside.

entries.name: Spectacled Bear
entries.heroTitle: Spectacled Bear — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: South America's only native bear is also the last survivor of the short-faced bear lineage. It climbs into fruiting crowns and bends or breaks branches into a rough platform on which it feeds and rests, sometimes staying for days while a tree is in fruit. In the Andes it ranges from foothill forest to above 4,000 metres.
identification: Shaggy coat is black to dark brown.
Any pale cream markings sit on the face, muzzle and chest.
Muzzle is short and broad for a bear.
Ears are small and rounded; the tail is very short.
Stands roughly 60 to 90 centimetres at the shoulder.

analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: south_america. Andean cloud forests, mountain slopes, páramo edges, and dense vegetation fit Spectacled Bears because climbing and plant foraging define their world.

whyInteresting: The pale facial markings differ on every bear, and researchers use them to tell individuals apart in camera-trap photographs.
It does not hibernate, because food is available throughout the year where it lives.
Large jaw muscles and broad cheek teeth let it grind tough, fibrous plant material that few other carnivores could eat.
It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, mainly because of habitat loss and conflict with farmers.
The species lives along the Andes from Venezuela south through Colombia, Ecuador and Peru to Bolivia.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adult bears face few predators, but cubs may face pumas, jaguars, or humans. Climbing and secrecy protect them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are often active by day or twilight depending on disturbance. Their rhythm follows fruit, cover, and mountain weather.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is not well known and is usually put at around 20 years; zoo animals have lived into their thirties.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Birth follows mating after about five and a half to eight and a half months in captivity, a spread thought to reflect delayed implantation. One to three blind cubs of roughly 300 to 350 grams are born in a sheltered den and stay with the mother for a year or more.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males typically weigh 100 to 200 kilograms and can be about twice as heavy as females. Coat and markings do not differ between the sexes.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It tends to forage slowly over the seabed at night and spends much of the day still among rocks and weed.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow larger, longer claws. Females have a broad, rounded abdomen that covers the eggs, while the male's is narrow and triangular.

entries.name: Spider Monkey
entries.heroTitle: Spider Monkey — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Seven species of long-limbed monkeys in the genus Ateles, among the largest primates of the American tropics at roughly 6 to 11 kilograms. They swing beneath branches by their arms, using the prehensile tail as a fifth grip, and can cross gaps of several metres in the canopy.

Hook-like hands with the thumb tiny or missing
Coat black, brown, reddish or golden, depending on species
Often hangs by the tail alone while feeding

Tall tropical forest from southern Mexico through Central America to the Amazon basin and the Pacific lowlands of Colombia and Ecuador. Most species keep to the upper canopy of mature evergreen rainforest; a few also use seasonally dry or swamp forest.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. whyInteresting: Spider monkeys live in fission-fusion communities: a group of roughly 20 to 40 splits into small, shifting parties that forage separately by day.
In most spider monkey communities the females leave their birth group to join another, while males stay for life.
Females usually give birth to a single infant only every three years or so, one of the slowest breeding rates among monkeys.
Hunting and forest loss threaten several species; the brown spider monkey of Colombia and Venezuela is listed as Critically Endangered.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly ripe, fleshy fruit, which usually makes up most of the diet, with young leaves, flowers, seeds, aerial roots and occasional insects. Parties travel long distances each day between fruiting trees such as figs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, pumas and harpy eagles and other large eagles are natural predators. When threatened, spider monkeys bark, shake branches and break off dead wood, dropping it towards an intruder on the ground.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, feeding most in the early morning. At night small parties sleep high in tall trees, often returning to favoured sleeping trees within their range.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Roughly 20 to 25 years in the wild; captive animals have lived beyond 40 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Gestation lasts about seven and a half months. The single infant clings to its mother's belly at first, later riding on her back, and stays dependent for well over a year. Females first give birth at about seven or eight years old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are similar in size and colour. Females have a long, pendulous clitoris that is often mistaken for a penis, so the sexes are easily confused in the field.

entries.name: Spinifex Hopping Mouse

analysis.summary: Moving in long, bounding hops on its hind legs, this small rodent forages over open sand in Australia's arid interior. Weighing roughly 30 to 45 grams, it is among the most widespread native rodents of the inland deserts.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably one to two years in the wild; captive animals have lived several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding can happen in any season when rain produces food. Litters are usually three or four young after a gestation of about a month, and the young are weaned at around four weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: No visible difference between males and females has been described; sexing a mouse requires handling it.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Spinner Dolphins often feed at night and rest or socialize by day in sheltered waters. Their rhythm separates deep work from visible joy, making the leap a daytime signal after hidden effort.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hunts by day when pollinators fly. At night it stays still at its perch, clinging to the plant it hunts from.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, basking on sandbars, logs and mud banks and foraging in shallows. Nights are spent on the bottom in quiet water, and through northern winters it stays dormant under water for months.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Poorly documented; individuals are thought to live for at least about 20 years, but reliable wild figures are lacking.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females dig nests in sunny sand or gravel banks in early summer and lay a clutch of roughly a dozen to over twenty brittle-shelled, spherical eggs. There is no parental care; hatchlings emerge after about two to three months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females grow much larger, with shells about twice the length of males. Adult males keep the juvenile pattern of small dark spots and rings on an olive shell and have longer, thicker tails; females become blotched and mottled.

entries.name: Spinybacked Orbweaver
entries.heroTitle: Spinybacked Orbweaver — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A small orb-weaver whose female has a hardened, flattened abdomen that works as a shell. From above she looks more like a seed or a burr than a spider, and the stiff, spiny shell is thought to make her an awkward mouthful for birds and lizards.
identification: Six stout spines around the shell's edge, often red-tipped
Shell white, yellow or orange with neat black spots
Female body wider than long, about 1 centimetre across
Short dark legs tucked under the broad body
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Spiny Orb-weaver belongs in forest edges, gardens, orchards, shrubs, and open gaps where orb webs can catch flying insects.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Spiny Orb-weaver belongs in forest edges, gardens, orchards, shrubs, and open gaps where orb webs can catch flying insects.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 19/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Six stout spines around the shell's edge, often red-tipped
Shell white, yellow or orange with neat black spots
Female body wider than long, about 1 centimetre across
Short dark legs tucked under the broad body
whyInteresting: The species name cancriformis means crab-shaped, from the broad, angular outline of the female.
Its dangers include birds, wasps, lizards, ants, and larger spiders.
Small tufts of fluffy silk are placed along the web's threads, possibly making the web visible so that birds avoid flying through it.
Males have been seen hanging on a single thread at the edge of a female's web while waiting for a chance to mate.
The species ranges from the southern United States through Central America and the Caribbean into South America.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Spiny Orb-weaver feeds on small flies, mosquitoes, moths, wasps, and other insects trapped in orb webs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Like many orb-weavers, a disturbed female probably drops from the hub on a silk line and climbs back once the danger has passed. Spider-hunting wasps, including mud daubers, have been recorded carrying this species off to stock their nests.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Spiders do not sleep as mammals do. The female stays at the hub day and night, repairing or rebuilding damaged web in place, and leaves it mainly to lay her eggs.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Under a year in total. Adults live only a few months, and males die soon after mating.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female lays a cluster of roughly a hundred to a few hundred eggs on the underside of a leaf and wraps it in a loose mass of fluffy silk. She dies soon afterwards, and the spiderlings hatch and disperse without any care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are tiny, about 2 to 3 millimetres long, longer than wide and without the large spines, and are easily overlooked. Females are several times larger and carry the spiny shell.

entries.name: Splendid Garden Eel
entries.heroTitle: Splendid Garden Eel — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Splendid Garden Eel AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: The Splendid Garden Eel teaches anchored alertness. It does not chase the ocean; it positions itself where the current brings what it needs.
identification: Bright orange body ringed with narrow white bands
Pencil-thin body standing upright out of the sand
Large eyes on a short, blunt snout
Head bent into the current, body curved like a question mark
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: coral_triangle. Open sand and fine rubble slopes beside coral reefs in the Coral Triangle, where a steady current flows. Colonies are usually found fairly deep, often below about 25 metres.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: coral_triangle. Open sand and fine rubble slopes beside coral reefs in the Coral Triangle, where a steady current flows. Colonies are usually found fairly deep, often below about 25 metres.

whyInteresting: Colonies can hold dozens of individuals, each rising from its own burrow a short distance from its neighbours.
Mixed colonies with spotted garden eels are often reported, the two kinds rising side by side on the same slope.
The burrow walls are thought to be stiffened with mucus from the skin, which stops the sand tube collapsing.
Garden eels are thought to dig their burrows tail first, driving a stiffened tail tip down into the sand.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Zooplankton such as copepods and tiny crustacean and fish larvae, picked out of the water one item at a time.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predatory fish hunting over the sand are the main threat. When a predator or a diver comes near, it sinks backwards into its burrow within moments and stays hidden until the danger has passed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, when it rises from the burrow to feed. At night it withdraws completely below the sand and rests inside the burrow.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Its lifespan is unknown; no ages have been reported from the wild or from the colonies sometimes displayed in public aquariums.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A transparent, leaf-shaped leptocephalus larva, the kind produced by all true eels, drifts in open water before changing shape and settling onto sand. Courtship and spawning have not been described in detail.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike, and the sexes cannot be told apart in the field.

entries.name: Splendid Toadfish
entries.heroTitle: Splendid Toadfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Splendid Toadfish shows that brilliance can live close to the ground. Its lesson is not to confuse low visibility with low value.
identification: Broad, flattened head with a very wide mouth
Fins edged with bright yellow
Fleshy barbels fringing the lower jaw and cheeks
Eyes set high on top of the head
Head patterned with fine, wavy pale and dark lines
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic. Coral reefs of the Caribbean, known almost entirely from around the island of Cozumel off Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. It lives in crevices and under ledges and coral overhangs, at depths easily reached by recreational divers.

whyInteresting: It was not described scientifically until the 1970s, despite living on some of the most visited reefs in the Caribbean.
It has none of the hollow, venom-bearing spines found in a few other toadfish genera.
It is also known as the Cozumel toadfish.
Most toadfishes are drab browns and olives, and it is usually described as the most brightly coloured member of the family.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Diet has not been studied in detail. It is thought to take crabs, shrimps, small fish and other animals that pass the mouth of its shelter, seizing them in a sudden lunge.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Its predators have not been documented; larger reef fishes such as groupers are plausible threats. It spends most of its time inside a crevice or under a ledge with only its head showing, and withdraws when approached.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Usually seen by day resting in a crevice or under a ledge with only the head showing. Its activity has not been studied, but it is thought to forage mostly around dusk and at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Its lifespan is unknown; ages of wild or captive fish have not been reported.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Toadfishes typically lay large, sticky eggs in a sheltered nest that the male guards. This species is presumed, not confirmed, to do the same, as its reproduction has not been studied.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Differences between males and females have not been described, and the sexes cannot be told apart in the field.

entries.name: Spotted Dove
entries.heroTitle: Spotted Dove — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Gardens, villages and city streets across South, Southeast and East Asia hold this slim, long-tailed dove. It feeds on open ground within a few metres of passers-by, and its soft, rolling coo is among the most familiar bird sounds of towns in its range.
identification: Black half-collar dotted with white on the hindneck
Long, graduated tail with white-tipped outer feathers
Pinkish-buff head and underparts; brown back
Dark bill and reddish-pink legs
Juveniles lack the spotted collar

whyInteresting: Like other pigeons, both parents feed the nestlings crop milk, a fatty secretion from the lining of the crop.
It drinks by dipping the bill and sucking water up continuously, without tipping the head back as most birds do.
Released birds have founded lasting populations outside Asia, including in Australia, New Zealand, Hawaii and Mauritius.
Adults are about 30 centimetres long, much of it tail, and weigh roughly 150 grams.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds of grasses and weeds, spilt grain and fallen fruit, picked up one at a time while walking. Insects are taken occasionally, and it comes readily to grain put out for poultry.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: When alarmed it bursts almost vertically into the air with a clatter of wings. Hawks and falcons take adults, while crows, snakes, cats and rats take eggs and nestlings.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, feeding mainly in the morning and late afternoon and resting in shade at midday. It roosts at night in trees and dense shrubs, singly or in pairs. It is resident, with no seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild and captive lifespans are not well documented for this species.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The nest is a thin platform of twigs in a tree, shrub or on a building ledge. Two white eggs are incubated by both parents for about two weeks, and the young fledge roughly two weeks after hatching. Pairs in warm regions raise several broods a year.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot be reliably told apart by plumage in the field. During courtship it is the male that bows and coos in front of the female.

entries.name: Spotted Eagle Ray
entries.heroTitle: Spotted Eagle Ray — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Spotted Eagle Ray AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A large eagle ray whose biggest adults span up to about 3 metres across the disc, it regularly launches itself clear of the surface, sometimes several times in a row. Why it leaps is not understood; escaping predators and shedding parasites have been suggested, but neither is confirmed.
identification: Dark back densely marked with white spots and rings
Flat, rounded snout like a duck's bill
Head projecting clearly in front of the disc
Very long, thin whip-like tail
Pale white underside

analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_atlantic, south_atlantic, indian_ocean. Spotted Eagle Ray belongs to reefs, sandy flats, and warm open water.

Flat, rounded snout like a duck's bill
Head projecting clearly in front of the disc
Very long, thin whip-like tail
Pale white underside
whyInteresting: Researchers identify individual rays by their spot patterns, which differ from ray to ray.
It is often seen in groups, sometimes of dozens of rays, especially when travelling.
A small dorsal fin sits far back, at the base of the tail just ahead of the spines.
Its tail spines are thought to be shed and replaced from time to time, as happens in stingrays.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Hard-shelled prey dominates: clams, oysters, snails and other molluscs, with shrimps, crabs and small fish. It roots in sand with its snout, then crushes shells between fused, plate-like teeth and spits out the fragments.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large sharks, including tiger, bull and great hammerhead sharks, are its main natural predators. It can outpace many attackers, and the long tail carries one or more venomous spines near its base.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active mainly during the day, cruising along reef edges and over sand flats and moving into shallow bays with the tide. Its behaviour at night is poorly documented.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild is poorly documented, and no reliable figure has been established.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Live-bearing: embryos develop inside the mother, nourished first by yolk and then by uterine fluid. Litters are small, typically up to about four pups, after a gestation of roughly a year.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males carry a pair of claspers, the rod-like mating organs beside the base of the tail; females lack them. Otherwise the sexes look alike.

entries.name: Spotted Gar
entries.heroTitle: Spotted Gar — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A long, armoured fish of weedy, still water, it hunts by hanging almost motionless beside plants or sunken timber, its spotted flanks lost among the stems. When a small fish drifts within reach, the narrow jaws swing sideways and snap shut on it with rows of needle-like teeth.
identification: Long, cylindrical body covered in shiny diamond-shaped scales
Round dark spots on the head, body and all fins
Fairly short, broad snout for a gar
Dorsal fin set far back, directly above the anal fin
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Clear, quiet, heavily vegetated water: backwaters, oxbow lakes, swamps, bayous, sloughs and slow river margins across the Mississippi basin, the Gulf coastal drainages and parts of the Great Lakes. It tolerates slightly brackish coastal water.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america. Clear, quiet, heavily vegetated water: backwaters, oxbow lakes, swamps, bayous, sloughs and slow river margins across the Mississippi basin, the Gulf coastal drainages and parts of the Great Lakes. It tolerates slightly brackish coastal water.

Fairly short, broad snout for a gar

whyInteresting: Its eggs are toxic, and eating gar roe can make people and other mammals ill.
Its genome was sequenced in 2016 and serves as a reference for comparing ray-finned fishes with land vertebrates.
Gars belong to an old lineage whose fossils reach back more than 100 million years.
Its hard, interlocking scales are coated with ganoine, an enamel-like mineral layer.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly small fish such as shad, minnows and young sunfish, with crayfish and shrimp. A caught fish is worked round in the jaws and swallowed head first.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Young gars are eaten by larger fish, herons and other wading birds; adults face alligators and people. When disturbed it retreats into dense weed cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeding peaks at dusk and through the night. By day it often rests near the surface among vegetation or logs, drifting almost still.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Females outlive males: ages in the high teens have been recorded for females, while males rarely seem to pass about 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning runs from spring into early summer in shallow, weedy water, where a female scatters often thousands of sticky eggs over plants, attended by several males. There is no parental care; the larvae cling to vegetation with an adhesive pad on the snout until they can swim.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in colour and pattern. Females grow larger and heavier than males of the same age.

entries.name: Spotted Garden Eel
entries.heroTitle: Spotted Garden Eel — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Spotted Garden Eel AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A slender conger eel of Indo-Pacific reefs that spends its adult life with its tail anchored in a sand burrow lined with its own mucus. Hundreds live side by side, each rising from its hole to face the current and pick passing plankton. The whole colony sinks out of sight when a large fish or diver approaches.
identification: Pencil-thin body up to about 40 centimetres long
White body densely covered with small black spots
Larger black blotches at the gill opening and mid-body
Large eyes and short, upturned mouth
Sways upright from a sand burrow, facing the current

Sandy slopes and flats beside coral reefs where a steady current flows, usually between about 7 and 45 metres deep. It occurs from the Red Sea across the Indian Ocean to southern Japan, northern Australia and the islands of the western Pacific.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania, indian_ocean, north_pacific, coral_triangle, red_sea, southeast_asia_coastal, australia_coastal. whyInteresting: The eel digs tail-first with its hard, pointed tail and cements the burrow walls with mucus.
From a distance a colony looks like a bed of seagrass waving in the current, which is how garden eels got their name.
Colonies range from a few dozen to several thousand eels, spaced so that neighbours are just out of reach of each other.
In strong currents the eels shorten and curve their bodies, staying closer to the burrow to reduce drag while still feeding.
In aquaria, males have been seen to move their burrows closer to a female and to drive off rival males.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Zooplankton, mainly copepods and other tiny drifting crustaceans, along with fish eggs and larvae. Each eel picks items one at a time by sight from the water flowing past, without leaving its burrow.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predation is poorly documented; larger fish that hunt over sand are the likely threat. At any approach, including a diver's, the eels sink tail-first into their burrows and re-emerge slowly once the disturbance has passed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds by day with most of the body out of the burrow. At night, and whenever threatened, it withdraws completely into the sand.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Aquarium and wild lifespan work has not produced a species figure. Colonies stand from sandy burrows, picking plankton as currents pass.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Neighbouring males and females stretch from adjacent burrows and entwine to spawn without leaving the sand. Eggs and the transparent, leaf-shaped larvae drift in open water before young eels settle and dig a burrow; there is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in colour and pattern and are hard to separate by eye.

entries.name: Spotted Handfish
entries.heroTitle: Spotted Handfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Spotted Handfish teaches local responsibility. Its survival depends on a specific seafloor world, reminding us that small habitats can hold huge value.

Arm-like pectoral fins with hand-shaped tips, used to walk over the seabed
Small lure-tipped spine above the mouth, followed by a crest-like dorsal fin

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Natural predators are not well documented. Its main threats are introduced northern Pacific seastars, which eat the stalked sea squirts it uses as egg sites, silt and pollution, and swinging boat moorings that scour the seabed. It relies on camouflage and keeping still.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Its daily activity cycle is not well documented. It lives permanently on the seabed, resting motionless on the silt between slow bouts of walking, and has no known seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild is not well documented; it is thought to live several years, possibly up to about a decade.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawns in spring, around September and October. The female wraps a mass of roughly 80 to 250 eggs around the stalk of a sea squirt or plant and guards it for about seven to eight weeks. Young hatch as tiny, fully formed fish with no larval stage.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike; any differences in size or colour are not well documented.

analysis.summary: A lanternfish reaching only about 10 cm, it is studded with round light organs along the belly and flanks that give off a blue-green glow. Their pattern is fixed for each lanternfish species, and the light from the underside is thought to hide its outline against the dim water above.

Big, thin scales that rub off easily
Dark back above silvery flanks
Small fleshy adipose fin in front of the tail

whyInteresting: Its name punctatum means spotted, after the rows of light organs dotted along its body.
It was described by Rafinesque in 1810 and is the type species of the genus Myctophum.
Early sonar operators recorded a false sea floor by day, a scattering layer now known to be formed partly by lanternfishes.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Squid, tunas, hake, cod, dolphins and seals all eat it, and surface-feeding seabirds catch fish that come close to the top at night. No specific escape behaviour has been described.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Daylight hours are passed in deep, dim water below the reach of most sunlight. No sleep-like resting state has been described for any lanternfish.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan is poorly known; like most lanternfishes it is thought to live only a few years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning in the North Atlantic is thought to peak in late winter and spring. Eggs are shed into open water and drift in the plankton, and the larvae grow near the surface without any parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Mature fish carry a luminous gland on the tail: in males it sits above the base of the tail, in females below it, so the sexes can be told apart in the hand.

analysis.summary: Spotted Lanternflies are plant-feeding planthoppers with spotted forewings and vivid hindwings. Their survival depends on jumping, clustering on host plants, and using visual disruption when attention closes in.
identification: Pinkish-grey forewings with black spots and brick-patterned tips
Red hindwings with black spots and a white band
Adults about 2.5 centimetres long, holding wings tent-like
Young nymphs black with white spots; late nymphs red, black and white
Leaps strongly when approached rather than walking away

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are slightly larger and have red coloration at the tip of the abdomen, which males lack; males have a more pointed abdomen tip.

analysis.summary: A chocolate-brown crow speckled with white, the nutcracker spends autumn burying conifer seeds and hazelnuts in thousands of small caches. Uneaten seeds left in the ground grow into new Arolla and Siberian pines.

entries.name: Pit-trapping Antlion
entries.heroTitle: Pit-trapping Antlion — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Known mainly from its larva, a relative of the lacewings that hunts from a hole of its own making. Shuffling backwards in a tightening spiral, it flicks sand out with its head until a steep-sided cone is left, then buries itself at the bottom. When prey struggles on the slope it throws more sand to bring it down.
identification: Larva is oval, grey-brown and bristly, with long sickle-shaped jaws.
Larvae walk only backwards.
Adult resembles a slender grey damselfly with short, clubbed antennae.
Adult wings are clear and unspotted, folded roof-like over the body at rest.
Adult flight is weak and fluttering.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Ants and other small crawling insects. The larva digs a cone-shaped pit in dry sand and waits buried at the bottom; prey slipping on the loose walls tumbles into its jaws and is sucked dry.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, spiders, parasitic wasps, and disturbance threaten antlions. Buried stillness keeps the hunter hidden.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Larvae wait for long periods in pits, while adults are often active at dusk or night. Their rhythm is patient construction followed by sudden capture.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males and females look alike in the field, with the same grey body and clear wings; telling them apart needs close examination of the abdomen tip. Larvae cannot be sexed by sight.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Bulls are taller and heavier than cows and live alone or in loose male groups, coming into musth with fluid streaming from a gland between eye and ear. Only a small minority of bulls carry tusks; cows lack tusks or have short tushes.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have huge eyes that meet on top of the head and clear wings; females have a small head with small eyes, a larger body and smoky brown wings.

whyInteresting: Newly emerged flies pump haemolymph through the soft stalks to inflate them, and they harden at that length permanently.
Males settle contests by facing each other and comparing span; the narrower male almost always withdraws without contact.
Females actively prefer wide-eyed males, and eye-span reflects the conditions the male grew up in, so it cannot be bluffed.
Flies gather at night in aggregations on hanging rootlets and fine vegetation over streams, often dozens together.
It is a standard model in the study of sexual selection and honest signalling for exactly these reasons.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fungi, bacteria and decaying plant material, with larvae developing in rotting vegetation. Growing well on a poor diet is precisely what a wide eye-span advertises, which is why the signal is honest.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders, birds and predatory insects. The stalks make flight less agile, so the ornament costs real safety — which is part of what makes it a reliable signal.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Aggregates at night on hanging rootlets, disperses to feed by day, with the male contests concentrated around dawn as the roost breaks up.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Several months as an adult, considerably longer than most small flies.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid in rotting vegetation where the larvae develop. Larval nutrition determines adult eye-span, so the conditions of the offspring's development set what it will be able to advertise later.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Strong and the whole point. Males have dramatically longer eye stalks, often exceeding body length; female stalks are much shorter and roughly proportionate.

In its brain the star is mapped as a set of separate stripes, one for each ray, taking up a large share of the touch cortex.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, hawks, foxes, mink, snakes, and wetland disturbance threaten moles; tunnels and fast touch reduce exposure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It does not hibernate and forages through the year, by day and by night, in short bouts separated by rest. Between bouts it sleeps in a ball of dry grass and leaves, usually in a chamber in raised, drier ground above the water level.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live several years, with survival tied to wet soil, prey supply, and protection inside tunnel systems.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually produce one litter per year in a nest chamber, with young developing in protected tunnels.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes look similar, though males may show breeding-season reproductive changes.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Many Berytidae feed on plant sap, seeds or other plant resources, while some supplement this with mites and small insects. Because feeding varies within the family, AnimalDex avoids reducing the whole group to either pure herbivores or predators.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders and other arthropod predators can take them. Their tiny narrow body, muted colours and extremely delicate profile make them difficult to pick out among stems and plant fibres.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Family-wide sleep behaviour is poorly suited to a single statement. Individuals commonly become inactive while remaining attached to vegetation.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: There is no defensible single lifespan estimate for the entire Berytidae family.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in locations associated with their host vegetation. Hatchlings are nymphs with the same general long-legged body plan, becoming progressively more adult-like with successive molts.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexual differences vary among species and are usually too subtle to use as a family-level field mark.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Specific predators have not been documented, though larger deep-sea fishes are presumed to take it. Its black skin reflects very little light, which makes it hard to see by the glow of other animals.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Rest or sleep has not been documented in this deep-sea fish. It lives below the reach of sunlight, so there is no daylight cycle at its usual depth.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long it lives is unknown; no age study of this dragonfish has been reported.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning has never been seen. Eggs are presumed to float free and hatch into larvae that grow in the plankton before descending, as in other dragonfishes.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Differences between males and females have not been well described in this species.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No reliable figures exist for how long wild birds live.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs build a cup nest in a tree fork or thick shrub, often near water. The clutch is reported to be usually two or three eggs, and both parents are reported to feed the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot reliably be told apart in the field.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Its lifespan is unknown, because wild crabs are hard to age and few have been followed over time.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Streaked Gurnards stay on the bottom through the day and night, resting on their fin rays rather than settling into cover.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A scavenger and opportunist predator. It eats carrion and seal afterbirth, takes seabird eggs and chicks, kills weakened birds, digs grubs and other invertebrates from the ground, and picks through tideline refuse and farm scraps.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have almost no natural predators, and threats to eggs and chicks are poorly documented. People were the main threat: Falklands farmers shot many birds and paid bounties on them, and birds that stood their ground near people were easy to kill.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, often in loose groups. At night birds roost on cliff ledges, rocky outcrops and tussac-grass slopes, often communally outside the breeding season.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No reliable figures exist for how long wild striated caracaras live, as few birds have been followed from hatching to death.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs nest on cliff ledges or among tussac grass, timing breeding to the seabird season from about October. The female usually lays 1 to 3 eggs; both parents feed the chicks on food taken from nearby colonies.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adults of both sexes look alike; females average larger. Juveniles are distinct, plain brown with darker faces and a pale tail tip, taking several years to gain adult plumage.

fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Tree kangaroos can live for many years, especially in protected conditions. The long arc suits reinvention: a rare future is built slowly in the canopy.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females raise a single joey in the pouch, giving it long protected development before independence. The pouch makes upward life possible before the young can climb well.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger than females, but both carry the same climbing design. The sex difference matters less than the shared body plan turned toward trees.

analysis.summary: A tailless fruit bat of Neotropical forest that builds its own shelter. It bites a line of cuts across the ribs of a large leaf, often a palm or banana leaf, until the leaf folds down into a tent that hides the bats and sheds rain.
identification: Two bold white stripes on each side of the face
Thin white stripe running down the middle of the back
Prominent spear-shaped nose leaf
Grey-brown fur and no visible tail
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical forests with broad leaves, palms, and sheltered understory roosts.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical forests with broad leaves, palms, and sheltered understory roosts.

whyInteresting: Figs are among its main foods, and it often carries a fruit away to a feeding perch rather than eating in the tree.
Seeds dropped beneath its feeding perches help spread fig trees and other forest plants.
It can make several differently shaped tents, depending on the kind of leaf it cuts.
Groups move between several tents within their home area, and a single tent may stay in use for weeks.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly soft fruit; nectar, pollen and insects are reported to be taken at times. Like other fruit bats of its family, it chews fruit to squeeze out juice and soft pulp and spits out wads of fibre.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, owls and hawks take roosting or flying bats. Roosting groups stay alert under the tent, dropping out and flying off as soon as the leaf is disturbed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Spends the day hanging in small groups under a leaf tent, leaves after dusk to forage through the night, and returns to a tent before dawn.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Marked Uroderma bilobatum colonies have not supplied a published maximum age. Day roosts form under leaves chewed into tent-like folds in Neotropical forests.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females bear a single pup, often twice a year in step with fruiting seasons, and gather in maternity groups under tents. The pup clings to its mother at first and is thought to be left at the roost later, while she forages.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look very similar in colour and markings.

analysis.summary: A flat, spiny lizard of the southern plains and northern Mexico, coloured like the soil it sits on. When a coyote or dog grabs it, it can raise blood pressure in its head until vessels near the eyes burst, squirting a jet of blood that tastes foul to canids.

Dark blotches with pale rear edges on the back
Two rows of fringe scales along each side
Broad, pancake-flat body

whyInteresting: In rain it arches its back and lowers its head so water runs along grooves between the scales to its mouth.
It is the state reptile of Texas and has declined in much of its former range.
Spreading red imported fire ants and insecticide use are thought to be major causes of that decline.
Zoos in Texas have raised young for release at sites where the species had disappeared.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Harvester ants form the bulk of the diet, taken one at a time at trail edges and nest entrances; thick mucus in the mouth protects against stings. Beetles, grasshoppers and other small insects are also eaten.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, roadrunners, shrikes, snakes, coyotes and foxes hunt it. It first freezes against the soil; if grabbed, it tilts to present its horns, and puffs up with air to look too large to swallow.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, basking in the morning and sheltering from midday heat. It buries itself shallowly in loose soil at night and spends winter dormant underground.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably about 5 to 8 years in the wild; this is poorly measured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females dig a burrow in loose soil in late spring and lay a large clutch, often about 20 to 40 eggs. The eggs hatch after several weeks, and the hatchlings receive no care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females grow somewhat larger than males. Males have enlarged scales behind the vent and more obvious femoral pores on the undersides of the thighs.

entries.name: Texas Tortoise
entries.heroTitle: Texas Tortoise — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The smallest of North America's gopher tortoises, with a domed, yellowish-brown shell about 15 to 22 centimetres long. Unlike its relatives it rarely digs a deep burrow. It scrapes out a shallow resting place, called a pallet, under a bush or prickly pear and returns to it again and again.

Shell rarely longer than 22 centimetres

Rival males ram each other and try to hook and overturn the opponent with the projection on the lower shell.
It stores water in its bladder and may empty it when alarmed, losing a reserve that it needs to get through dry periods.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grazes grasses, low herbs and fallen flowers, and eats the pads, blossoms and red fruits of prickly pear cactus, which also supply much of its water.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and hatchlings are taken by raccoons, skunks, coyotes, foxes, snakes and birds of prey; adults, protected by the shell, have few natural enemies. Road traffic, brush clearance and illegal collecting are the main threats.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. In hot months it moves in the morning and again in late afternoon, sheltering through midday under shrubs or cactus in its pallet. It stays inactive during cold winter spells.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Thought to live several decades, possibly up to about 60 years; firm data from the wild are scarce.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay small clutches of about 1 to 5 eggs, usually 2 or 3, between spring and late summer, sometimes more than one clutch a year. The hard-shelled eggs hatch after roughly three to four months, and hatchlings receive no care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a concave underside to the shell, a longer tail and a longer, more deeply forked projection at the front of the lower shell. Females have a flat underside. Males tend to be a little larger.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards and spiders prey on it. When threatened it may rock like a stem in the wind or spread its wings.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It stays on its perch through day and night, as mantises do not sleep in a fixed cycle. Hunting is mostly by day; males may fly towards lights at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably about a year from egg to death, with adults surviving a few months; wild data are scarce.

entries.name: Yam Hawk-moth
entries.heroTitle: Yam Hawk-moth — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A large, fast-flying hawk-moth of the tropics and subtropics. By day it rests motionless on a leaf or stem with its narrow wings swept back into a tight triangle, and the olive-green to brownish forewings, crossed by paler streaks, blend into the foliage around it.

Narrow, pointed forewings with a straight outer edge
Stout, torpedo-shaped body tapering to a point
Wingspan about 10 to 13 cm

Its range runs from India and Sri Lanka through southern China and South-east Asia to northern Australia.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults hover in front of flowers at dusk, drinking nectar through a long coiled tongue. Caterpillars eat the leaves of yams and of aroids such as taro, and have been recorded on a few other plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Like other large hawk-moths, adults are likely taken by birds, bats and lizards, and caterpillars by parasitic wasps and flies. Adults escape by fast, darting flight. A threatened caterpillar can pull in its head and swell its front segments, showing eyespots.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Flies mainly at dusk and in the first hours of darkness, and stays inactive through the daylight hours.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long adults live in the wild is not documented for this species; in many hawk-moths adults live only a few weeks.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs singly on the leaves of food plants. The caterpillar grows large and carries a short horn at the tail end; when fully grown it pupates in a loose cocoon among leaf litter on the ground.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are alike in colour and pattern and are hard to tell apart in the field.

whyInteresting: A thin white stripe runs along the cutting edge of the upper bill near the gape.
A 2013 study measured its flight as among the most energy-costly of any bird, because its short wings suit swimming.
In Britain it is called Brünnich's guillemot, after the Danish zoologist Morten Brünnich.
In winter it moves south to ice-free waters of the North Atlantic and North Pacific, many staying close to the pack ice edge.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It feeds on fish, crustaceans, squid, and other marine prey caught by diving. Arctic cod is important in many colonies; it swims with its wings and regularly feeds more than 100 metres down.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Both on the cliffs and at sea, gulls, skuas, foxes at colonies, and marine predators threaten Thick-billed Murre. Glaucous gulls take many eggs and chicks from the ledges, polar bears raid some colonies, and people hunt it in Greenland and eastern Canada.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It rests on sea cliffs or ocean surface between dives and colony duties. Feeding is mostly in daylight, but it also dives in dim light, and outside the breeding season it lives entirely at sea.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: An adult can live for decades, as many alcids rely on long adult survival. Ringed birds have been recorded at more than 20 years of age.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Each summer females lay a single pointed egg directly on cliff ledges, with both parents caring. The pair takes turns incubating for about a month.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females have identical plumage in summer and winter, and cannot be separated at a colony by sight.

entries.name: Treehopper
entries.heroTitle: Treehopper — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Thorn Bugs are treehoppers with enlarged pronotal shapes that can mimic plant thorns. Their plant-feeding life depends on staying close to stems, blending into host plants, and making predators hesitate.
identification: Plate behind the head extends over the body as a thorn, hump or horn
Small body, mostly 2 to 15 millimetres long
Sits lengthwise on stems, often clustered with nymphs
Jumps suddenly when disturbed, then flies

whyInteresting: Many species communicate by vibrations sent through the plant stem; in the thorn bug Umbonia crassicornis, nymphs send a coordinated burst of them when a predator approaches.
In Bocydium the helmet carries a cluster of small hairy balls on stalks, one of the strangest shapes in the family.
Nymphs lack the adult's enlarged helmet, and in many species carry spines or bristly outgrowths instead.
Scientists have described more than 3,000 treehopper species.
How the helmet evolved is still debated; one study proposed it grows from a wing-like outgrowth, a view others have challenged.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Both adults and nymphs pierce stems with a needle-like beak and drink the sugary sap flowing through the plant. They excrete the surplus sugar as honeydew, which ants, wasps and bees often collect.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, spiders, assassin bugs and hunting wasps eat them, and tiny parasitic wasps attack the eggs. Defences include a hard, often spiny shield over the body, keeping still, a sudden jump, and in many species attendant ants that drive off attackers.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day and night are spent on the host plant, with long periods of feeding without moving. Most walking, flying and signalling happens by day in warm conditions.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults typically live a few weeks to a few months. Many temperate species complete one generation a year, overwintering as eggs, while tropical species may breed continuously.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females cut slits in stems or leaf veins and insert batches of eggs, in some species covering them with a frothy secretion. In many species the mother sits over her eggs and nymphs for weeks, kicking or buzzing her wings at attackers. Nymphs moult five times.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are generally a little larger than males. In some species, such as the thorn bug Umbonia crassicornis, the male's horn differs from the female's in shape and colour; in many others the sexes look alike.

analysis.summary: Thorny oysters, a family of bivalves nearly all in the genus Spondylus, fix one valve to rock or reef and grow long spines or frills from the upper valve. Many species have bright red, orange, purple or yellow shells, colours that often show only once the encrusting sponges and algae are scraped away.

Unequal valves, the lower one usually deeper than the upper
Inner shell surface white, usually with a coloured margin
Mantle edge often brightly coloured and fringed when the valves gape

Once cemented, a shell's shape follows the surface beneath it, so shells of one species can vary widely.
Spines tend to grow longest in sheltered water, while shells from rough water usually have short, worn spines.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, crabs, snails, sea stars, and humans threaten it.

whyInteresting: The male glues his nest of plant fragments together with spiggin, a sticky protein made in his kidneys.
He fans water through the nest with his pectoral fins, keeping the eggs supplied with oxygen.
Niko Tinbergen's experiments showed that males attack crude models with a red underside more readily than lifelike models without red.
Freshwater populations founded since the last Ice Age have repeatedly evolved fewer armour plates, through changes in the same gene.
Males court with a zigzag dance, then lead the female to the nest and point at its entrance with the snout.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small invertebrates picked from plants, the bottom or open water: water fleas, copepods, midge larvae, worms and small snails, plus fish eggs and fry, including those of other sticklebacks. It hunts by sight, hovering before a quick snap.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pike, perch, trout, herons, kingfishers, grebes and otters all take it, and dragonfly larvae eat the young. When seized it locks its dorsal and pelvic spines upright, which makes it hard to swallow, and bony side plates resist teeth.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, feeding in loose shoals outside the breeding season. At night it rests close to the bottom or among water plants.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually 1 to 3 years in the wild, with many fish dying after a single breeding season. Ages of 4 to 5 years are known from some populations and from aquaria.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female lays commonly 50 to 200 eggs in a nest at one visit and may spawn several times in a season, in different nests. She gives no care. Eggs hatch in about a week at 18 to 20 °C, and the fry leave a few days later.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In the breeding season males develop a red throat and belly, bright blue eyes and a blue-green sheen on the back. Females stay silvery with faint dark bars and look plump when full of eggs.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish-eating neighbours such as snakeheads, herons, kingfishers and water snakes are its likely predators, and people catch it for food. It keeps to dense vegetation and darts into cover when alarmed, though its need to surface for air exposes it to birds.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Even at night it rises now and then to gulp air, hanging almost motionless among plants between visits to the surface, with its colours paled. Feeding and courtship take place by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 4 to 6 years in aquaria; wild lifespan is not well documented and is probably shorter.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The male blows a floating nest of mucus-coated bubbles among surface plants and wraps around the female beneath it as she releases eggs, which can number a thousand or more. He guards the nest; eggs hatch in about a day and fry swim freely a few days later.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a longer, pointed dorsal fin and a slimmer body. Females have a shorter, rounded dorsal fin and a deeper, fuller belly, most obvious when carrying eggs.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Domestic cats, Cooper's and sharp-shinned hawks and owls take adults; rat snakes, raccoons and squirrels raid nests. Brown-headed cowbirds lay eggs in its nests. It scolds intruders with harsh chatters and slips into cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, feeding low in cover. At night it roosts alone or with its mate in cavities, old nests, dense vines or sheltered corners of sheds and porches.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live only 2 to 3 years in the wild; banded birds have occasionally reached about 6 years or more.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in plumage. Males average slightly larger, and only the male sings the loud full song, so voice is the best field clue.

identification: Long cheek fur widens the face beneath small, narrow eyes.
Muzzle, crown and back are tan to rusty; the flanks are grey.
Bushy tail is grey with a white tip.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly diurnal or crepuscular, often active when pikas are active.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Poorly documented. Up to about 8 to 10 years is often quoted, but most wild foxes are thought to die before five.

Ixodes uriae lives on seabirds in the Arctic and sub-Antarctic, surviving harsh cold in nesting colonies.
Oxpeckers in Africa remove ticks from large mammals, although they also feed on wounds and blood.
Bites of the lone star tick, Amblyomma americanum, are linked to alpha-gal syndrome, a delayed allergy to red meat.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: All active stages feed only on blood. Hard ticks cut the skin, cement their mouthparts in and feed for days; soft ticks usually feed for minutes to hours, often at night.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, ants, spiders, beetles and fungi kill ticks, and the parasitic wasp Ixodiphagus lays its eggs inside them. Ticks rely on their small size, a tough body and retreating to damp litter.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No true sleep. Between feeds they rest in leaf litter or host shelters to regain moisture; many species also stop activity during winter or dry seasons.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Hard tick life cycles usually take one to three years; some soft ticks are reported to survive for several years, fasting for long periods between meals.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female hard tick feeds once as an adult, drops off and lays one batch of often thousands of eggs, then dies. Soft ticks lay several smaller batches. Six-legged larvae hatch, then moult into nymphs and adults.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In hard ticks, the male's hard shield covers the whole back, while the female's covers only the front, so her body can swell greatly while feeding.

analysis.summary: A small, deep-bodied barb from the streams of Sumatra, gold with four black vertical bars and red-edged fins. It lives in shoals that keep a strict pecking order, and the fish chase and nip one another throughout the day to hold their rank.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger predatory fish such as snakeheads, fish-eating birds and water snakes are the likely predators in its native streams, though few records exist. It answers with tight shoaling, bars that break up its outline, and a dash into plants or roots.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At night the shoal settles low among plants or near the bottom and hangs almost still, and the colours fade until light returns.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Roughly 5 to 7 years in aquaria; lifespan in the wild has not been documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: An egg scatterer with no parental care. A female sheds several hundred sticky eggs among plants, usually in the morning; they hatch in about one to two days and the fry swim freely a few days later. Adults eat any eggs they find.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger and rounder in the belly, with paler fins. Males are slimmer and more intensely coloured, and in breeding condition the snout and the edges of the fins turn bright red.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs and invest in nesting choices that protect the next generation. For Trustvoice, the nest, clutch, and chick stage show how the principle must be carried into care, not just adult survival.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females may differ in size, markings, calls, or breeding roles depending on the species. For Trustvoice, any sex difference matters only when it changes protection, display, parenting, or movement.

Red-edged fins and a red-margined forked tail
Deep-bodied cyprinid to about 30 cm
Almost always in a shoal, turning as one
Constantly on the move in open midwater

It is a strong jumper and will clear the surface of an open tank or a low weir.
It eats plants as readily as insects, and will strip soft aquarium plants overnight.
Barbonymus schwanenfeldii is also sold as a tinfoil barb; that one has black markings on the tail lobes.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger river predators take them, which is what the shoal is for. Their answer is not armour or speed but numbers and a synchronised turn.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, settling low in the water and in cover through the night while the shoal stays loosely together.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Tinfoil Barb live around eight to ten years, so a fish spends its whole life inside a shoal it grows up in.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are scattered over vegetation in the flood season and left; there is no parental care. Juveniles form tight shoals immediately, so the cover starts before anything else does.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Outside the breeding season the sexes are almost impossible to tell apart; ripe females become noticeably fuller in the belly.

whyInteresting: It is a soft coral, so it has no stony skeleton — the shape is held by water pressure and microscopic sclerites in the tissue.
Sheddings happen every few weeks and strip away settled algae, silt and film.
Symbiotic zooxanthellae inside its tissue provide most of its food from sunlight.
It releases terpenoid compounds into the water that discourage neighbouring corals from crowding it.
A single colony can spread more than half a metre across the cap.
