fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly sugars from symbiotic zooxanthellae, supplemented by dissolved organic matter and fine plankton captured by the polyps.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Nudibranchs, some butterflyfish and grazing snails. Its answer is chemical rather than physical — unpalatable terpenoids in the tissue, plus a shedding cycle that removes anything settling on it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Toadstool Leather Coral has no sleep in the animal sense, but polyps retract at night and during shedding, so the colony visibly cycles between open and closed.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Colonies persist for decades and keep expanding.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Colonies broadcast eggs and sperm into the water on seasonal spawning nights, and can also grow new colonies from fragments of the cap.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Colonies are usually of a single sex but look identical from the outside. Appearance carries no signal here because reproduction is chemical and seasonal, not visual.

Tail as long as the body, carried in an S or C
Lives in mixed-sex troops in forest and temple grounds

whyInteresting: It is endemic to Sri Lanka and does not occur as a wild population anywhere else.
Three subspecies track wet-zone, dry-zone and highland forest and are already isolated from one another.
Troops raid fields and temples, which is why the species is both sacred and persecuted.
The toque is visible from the front even on a moving animal, which is how you separate it from a Long-tailed Macaque at a distance.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, leaves, insects, crops and temple offerings. A troop that can switch from forest fruit to stolen rice is the one that still holds the village edge.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, eagles and village dogs take isolated animals. The troop and the trees are the defence; a macaque on the ground alone is the one that is lost.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal. Troops forage through the day and sleep in tall trees or on temple roofs.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Fifteen to twenty years in the wild when a troop holds a safe roost.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single young is the usual birth. The infant stays with the mother in the troop, so the quality of the remaining forest decides whether it is raised at all.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are slightly larger and leave the natal troop. Both sexes wear the toque; it is not a sex mark.

entries.name: Trashline Orb-weaver
entries.heroTitle: Trashline Orb-weaver — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Many webs of this small orb-weaver carry a vertical band of rubbish through the middle: sucked-out insect husks, shed skins and scraps of plant, bound together with silk. The spider sits in a gap in the band with its legs folded, and its mottled body is hard to tell from the debris around it.

Body is mottled in silver-grey, brown and black
Orb web is small, with closely spaced spiral threads
Body is under roughly a centimetre long

whyInteresting: Observers have recorded that webs differ between individuals: some carry a line of debris, while others have only a band or spiral of plain silk.
When the web is renewed the debris line is usually left in place and the new spiral is spun around it.
It finds trapped insects by touch, not sight: struggling prey sends vibrations along the radial threads to the spider waiting at the hub.
Only the spiral threads of the web are sticky; the spokes and the hub are dry silk that the spider can run along freely.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small flying insects such as midges, flies, leafhoppers and tiny wasps that strike the sticky spiral. Each catch is bitten, wrapped in silk and carried to the hub to be eaten.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: A disturbed spider may shake the web so that its outline blurs, or drop to the ground on a safety line and lie still. Birds, spider-hunting wasps, jumping spiders and lizards are the likely predators.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Stays at the hub by day and by night instead of retiring to a leaf shelter. Like other spiders of its genus it is thought to renew a damaged web in darkness or around dawn.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not well documented. It probably lives about a year, as most small orb-weavers do, with females outlasting males by some weeks.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female makes several small egg sacs in succession and fastens them into the line of debris, where they pass for more rubbish. Spiderlings hatch inside the sac, stay near it briefly and then disperse. Egg numbers for this species are not well recorded.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are the larger sex and are the ones seen in webs. Adult males are considerably smaller and slimmer, with swollen palps, and spend their short adult life wandering in search of females.

entries.name: Tree Frog
entries.heroTitle: Tree Frog — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Most members of this large family are climbers. Each toe pad is covered in flat-topped cells separated by channels of thin mucus, which lets a frog cling to wet leaves, bark and even glass. Hylidae, which in many classifications includes the Australasian tree frogs and the leaf frogs, holds roughly 1,000 species, most of them in Central and South America.
identification: Round adhesive discs on the tips of fingers and toes
Slim body with long hind legs
Large eyes, often with horizontal pupils
Smooth skin, commonly green, grey or brown
Males call loudly from vegetation near water
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america, europe, north_africa_middle_east, south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania. Trees, shrubs, reeds and tall herbs close to fresh water, from tropical rainforest canopy to temperate woodland, marsh edges and gardens. Most breed in ponds, swamps, flooded ditches or slow streams; some use water held in bromeliads and tree holes. A few species live on the ground.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america, south_america, europe, north_africa_middle_east, south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania. Trees, shrubs, reeds and tall herbs close to fresh water, from tropical rainforest canopy to temperate woodland, marsh edges and gardens. Most breed in ponds, swamps, flooded ditches or slow streams; some use water held in bromeliads and tree holes. A few species live on the ground.

behaviorTraits: Round adhesive discs on the tips of fingers and toes

whyInteresting: An extra short segment of cartilage between the last two bones of each digit lets the toe pad swivel flat against a surface.
Several species, including the grey tree frogs of North America, can change colour between green, grey and brown.
The grey tree frog and the spring peeper survive winter with part of their body water frozen, protected by glycerol or glucose in the tissues.
Red-eyed tree frog embryos can hatch early and drop into the water when a snake or wasp attacks the egg clutch.
A chorus of spring peepers, frogs only about 3 centimetres long, can be heard from several hundred metres away.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults eat flies, moths, crickets, beetles, ants, spiders and other small invertebrates, caught with a flick of the sticky tongue or a lunge from a perch. Large species sometimes take smaller frogs. Tadpoles of most species graze algae and detritus.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds, bats, large spiders and bigger frogs eat adults; fish, dragonfly larvae and water beetles eat tadpoles. Tree frogs rely on camouflage and stillness by day and leap away when found, and some produce distasteful or irritating skin secretions.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most are nocturnal. By day they sit pressed against a leaf, stem or bark, or inside a tree hole, with the limbs folded under the body to limit water loss. Temperate species hibernate under litter, logs or soil.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Variable and poorly documented for most species. Few European tree frogs aged in the wild have been older than about six years, while captive animals of that species are reported to have lived more than 15 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Most females lay eggs in still water, from a few hundred to a few thousand depending on species, singly, in clumps or as a surface film. Tadpoles typically transform in one to three months. Leaf frogs attach their eggs to leaves overhanging water.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are usually larger than males. Breeding males have a vocal sac, often visible as loose, darker or yellowish throat skin, and many develop rough pads on the thumbs for gripping the female.

It is also widely known as the white-bellied pangolin.
It has no teeth; a muscular stomach, often holding swallowed grit, grinds up its insect food.
Thick eyelids and closable nostrils guard it against biting ants while it raids a nest.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Tree Pangolin feeds on ants, termites, and social insects gathered with a long sticky tongue.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Rolling into a ball defeats most natural predators but lets hunters simply pick it up. It can also release a foul-smelling secretion from glands near the tail.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Tree Pangolin rests in tree hollows, vine tangles, burrows, and curled resting places. Mainly nocturnal, it leaves its daytime shelter after dark to forage both in trees and on the ground.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single young is born after about 150 days' gestation, with soft scales that harden within days. It rides on its mother's back or tail as she forages and is weaned at around 3 months.

Glossy, rounded abdomen
Reddish-brown front body
Legs plain orange-brown

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small crawling arthropods caught in its irregular web, including ants, beetles, woodlice, ticks and other spiders. It throws sticky silk over prey with its hind legs before biting.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Other house spiders, including cellar spiders, and house centipedes are likely predators. It stays hidden in a retreat at the web's edge and drops away when disturbed.

Many photographed females show orange or reddish edges to their flanges, colours that in other net-winged beetles advertise distasteful body fluids.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators have not been recorded, and how this beetle defends itself has not been studied.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Its daily cycle has not been studied. Females are seen by day on logs and move very slowly, staying in the same small area for long periods.

Carpenter bee eggs are among the largest laid by any insect, more than a centimetre long in the biggest species.
As in other large carpenter bees, males are thought to hold small territories near flowers or nest sites, hovering in place and chasing off other insects.
Tunnels are often reused and lengthened by later generations, so one piece of old timber can hold many galleries.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, spiders, ants, and parasites threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active in daylight, mainly in warm, sunny weather. Nights and spells of heavy rain are spent inside the nest tunnel.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult longevity for Xylocopa latipes is unpublished. Related large carpenter bees typically live several months to about a year while nesting alone in timber.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females can sting and build nests; males cannot sting.

entries.name: Tropical House Gecko

featuredImage.alt: Tropical House Gecko AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: The Tropical House Gecko is a small, pale, big-eyed lizard that came from Africa and now lives on buildings across much of the tropical Americas. It spends the day in cracks and roof spaces and comes out at night to hunt on lit walls and ceilings.

Broad toe pads on every foot
Pale grey-brown skin with dark chevron bands

Houses, outbuildings, walls, tree trunks and rock faces in warm, humid lowlands, and now a familiar sight on buildings through the Caribbean, Central and South America and Florida. It favours walls with a lamp to hunt by and cracks close at hand to hide in.

Houses, outbuildings, walls, tree trunks and rock faces in warm, humid lowlands, and now a familiar sight on buildings through the Caribbean, Central and South America and Florida. whyInteresting: It is native to sub-Saharan Africa, is thought to have crossed the Atlantic on ships, and is now established from Florida to Brazil.
Each toe pad carries rows of plates covered in microscopic hairs that grip by molecular attraction, which is why it can run across a ceiling or a window pane.
It changes shade, turning pale and almost pinkish-white at night and darker with clearer bands by day.
It is a vocal lizard, and males give soft chirping calls during encounters with rivals and mates.
The tail breaks off when grabbed and keeps twitching to distract a predator, and a new one grows back.
The Mediterranean House Gecko looks similar but is pinkish and spotted with prominent pale warts, where the Tropical House Gecko usually shows dark V-shaped bands across the back.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Moths, flies, mosquitoes, cockroaches, ants, termites, spiders and other small invertebrates, and occasionally a smaller gecko. Most are caught within a short dash of a light, so the hunting ground is chosen for the gecko by the lamp.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, larger lizards, owls and other birds, rats, large spiders and house cats all take it. Hunting in the open on a lit wall is a risk, offset by staying within a quick run of a crack.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal, emerging around dusk and staying active through much of the night. By day it hides in crevices, behind shutters and pictures, under bark and in roof spaces.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably three to five years for most wild individuals, and somewhat longer in captivity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female lays two round, hard-shelled eggs at a time and can produce several clutches a year in warm climates. Several females often use the same sheltered crevice, and the young hatch fully independent and begin hunting the same walls.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males have a broader head, a swollen tail base and a row of pores in front of the vent and along the thighs that females lack. Males are territorial and will chase a rival off a good lit patch of wall.

featuredImage.alt: Tropical Leatherleaf Slug AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: This land slug has no shell at all; a tough, leathery mantle covers the whole of its back instead. Beneath it lies an unusually narrow sole, only a few millimetres wide in adults, on which the animal glides by waves of muscular contraction.
identification: Thin pale stripe along the middle of the back
Dark brown to black upper surface with a fine, grainy texture
Flattened, elongated oval, about 5 to 8 centimetres long
Only the tentacle tips show beyond the mantle edge
No breathing hole visible on the right side
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Tropical Leatherleaf Slugs are native to tropical parts of Asia and have spread widely through other warm regions. They favour humid gardens, agricultural land, forest edges, plantations, leaf litter and disturbed vegetation, hiding in damp shelter during dry periods and becoming most active at night or after rain.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Tropical Leatherleaf Slugs are native to tropical parts of Asia and have spread widely through other warm regions. whyInteresting: It can host the rat lungworm, so gardeners in affected regions are advised to wear gloves and to wash salad leaves thoroughly.
It belongs to the Veronicellidae, the leatherleaf slugs, a family found mainly in the tropics.
The eyes sit at the tips of the upper pair of tentacles; the lower pair is forked at the tip.
The thick skin is thought to slow water loss, letting it tolerate drier conditions than most slugs.
It is thought to travel between countries hidden in the soil of potted plants.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Living and decaying leaves, seedlings, soft stems and fallen fruit are rasped away with a toothed radula. In gardens and nurseries it feeds on lettuce, cabbage, beans and many ornamental plants, and is treated as a pest.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few records name its predators; toads, rats, ground-feeding birds and predatory beetles, which eat slugs generally, are the likely ones. A touched slug contracts into a firm oval, draws its tentacles under the mantle and gives off sticky mucus.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeding begins after dusk and ends before sunrise. Daylight hours are spent pressed to the underside of stones, logs, boards and flowerpots or down in soil cracks, and in the dry season it lies buried and inactive.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long this slug lives is poorly known, and no well-established lifespan figure is available for it in the wild or in culture.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Every individual can lay eggs after mating. The eggs are laid in a cluster in damp soil or beneath litter and left untended, and the young hatch as miniature slugs. Clutches of several dozen eggs have been reported.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: None to see: this slug is a hermaphrodite, each animal carrying both male and female organs.

entries.name: Tufted Capuchin
entries.heroTitle: Tufted Capuchin — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A stocky, black-capped monkey of South American forests, it forages with unusual force for its size. Strong hands rip open dead branches, palm leaf bases and bamboo stems to reach the insect larvae hidden inside.

Squirrel monkeys often travel with tufted capuchin groups, following them through the canopy and feeding alongside them.
Long known as Cebus apella and much used in tool-use studies, it moved with the other robust, tufted capuchins into the genus Sapajus around 2012.
It is widespread, ranging across much of the Amazon basin and the Guianas.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Tufted Capuchin mainly uses fruit, nuts, seeds, insects, eggs, small animals, and hard foods opened with skill.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, ocelots, harpy eagles, snakes, and humans pressure Tufted Capuchin.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, travelling and foraging from dawn until late afternoon. At dusk the group settles in tall trees, often in palm crowns or large emergent trees, and sleeps on branches with members sitting close together.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly documented, but captive tufted capuchins have been recorded living more than 40 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single infant is born after a pregnancy of about five months, usually about two years after the previous birth. It rides on its mother's back for the first months, other group members sometimes carry it, and weaning comes at around a year.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are clearly heavier than females, often by a quarter or more, with larger heads, heavier jaws and usually more prominent tufts on the crown.

entries.name: Tufted Gray Langur
entries.heroTitle: Tufted Gray Langur — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Tufted Gray Langur AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: The Tufted Gray Langur is the pale, black-faced leaf monkey of south-eastern India and Sri Lanka's dry zone, named for the pointed tuft of hair on its crown. Large troops move between the canopy and the ground through the day, often with spotted deer feeding underneath and both species listening for the other's alarm.

Pointed tuft of hair on the crown
Grey-brown back with paler cream underparts
Very long tail, longer than head and body

Open woodland with clearings suits a monkey that feeds both in the canopy and on the ground, which is where the deer find it.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: south_asia. Dry-zone forest, scrub, riverine woodland and the edges of villages, temple grounds and ancient ruins in south-eastern India and Sri Lanka. whyInteresting: A chambered stomach full of bacteria ferments tough mature leaves, letting it live on foliage that most monkeys cannot digest.
Spotted deer follow feeding troops to eat the leaves, flowers and fruit that the monkeys drop from the canopy.
Its harsh barking alarm is one of the most reliable signs that a leopard is on the move, and trackers in Sri Lankan national parks listen for it.
The Sri Lankan population is a separate subspecies, Semnopithecus priam thersites.
Females other than the mother regularly carry and mind a young infant, a habit shared across the gray langurs.
The Purple-faced Langur, the other leaf monkey in Sri Lanka, is darker brown to black with white whiskers and no crown tuft, and keeps more to the trees.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly leaves, with fruit, flowers, buds and seeds taken in season, all broken down by fermentation in a chambered stomach. It is a wasteful feeder, dropping much of what it picks, and that fallen food is what draws the deer in beneath the troop.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards are the main predator, and pythons and village dogs also take langurs, mostly young ones. The shared alarm matters most on the ground, where a langur is furthest from the safety of a tree.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, with feeding peaks in the early morning and late afternoon and a long rest through the midday heat. The troop climbs into tall trees before dusk and sleeps high on the branches.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around 20 years in the wild is a good age for a gray langur, and captive animals have reached about 30.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female usually gives birth to a single infant after a pregnancy of about six and a half months. Other females in the troop carry and mind the baby from early on, so care of the young is shared in much the same way the watch is.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are noticeably larger and heavier than females but share the same colouring. Troops hold many adult females with one or several adult males, and surplus males form bachelor bands.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Takes nectar from flax, kowhai, rata, pohutukawa and other flowering trees with a brush-tipped tongue, and also eats fruit and insects. It pollinates many native plants and spreads seeds.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Introduced ship rats, stoats, possums and cats take eggs, chicks and sitting birds, and the New Zealand falcon and swamp harrier take adults. Predator control has helped numbers recover in many areas.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, often singing well before dawn and sometimes at night. It roosts in dense foliage after dusk.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: A population-level lifespan for Prosthemadera novaeseelandiae is still unsettled. Adults defend nectar trees with loud, complex song across New Zealand forest.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female builds a bulky nest of twigs and grass in a tree fork and incubates two to four eggs for about two weeks. Both parents feed the chicks, which fledge after about three weeks; two broods a season are common.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is alike in both sexes, but males are clearly larger and heavier than females, and females can look slightly duller.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults feed mainly on fish such as sand eels, sprat, gobies and small whiting, with some squid and crustaceans. Young turbot eat small crustaceans and worms. Prey is seized with a wide, protrusible mouth.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Young turbot are taken by larger fish and probably by diving seabirds such as cormorants; large adults have few natural enemies, though seals are known to eat flatfish. Fishing is the main pressure, as it is a valuable catch in trawls and set nets.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Long spells are spent resting motionless on the bottom. Juveniles feed mainly by day; the daily rhythm of wild adults is poorly known.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Up to about 25 years has been reported, but in fished waters most turbot are caught well before 15.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning runs from about April to August in the North Sea. Females shed millions of small floating eggs with no parental care. The larvae drift for weeks, then the right eye moves over to the left side and the young settle on shallow sandy shores.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females grow faster and larger than males; otherwise the sexes look alike.

Stocky build with a short, square-ended tail
whyInteresting: The yellow flank plumes fade to white in museum skins, which is why early describers named it melanoleucus, meaning black and white.
It is the only species in the genus Seleucidis.
During courtship the male swings his body to brush the wires repeatedly across the female's face and throat.
It is assessed as Least Concern, but it depends on lowland swamp forest that is being cleared in parts of its range.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly fruit taken in the canopy and mid-storey, supplemented with insects and other arthropods gleaned from foliage and bark. Nectar has also been recorded in the diet.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Natural predators have been little studied; birds of prey and tree-climbing snakes are the likely threats, and nests are probably the most exposed stage. Displaying males are wary and drop into cover when disturbed. Some local communities hunt males for their plumes.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal. Males call and display from bare dead treetops mainly at first light, then feed through the day. Night roosts in the swamp forest have not been described, and there is no seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No ages from wild birds or from aviaries appear to have been reported, and how long it lives remains unknown.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female alone builds the nest, incubates and feeds the young; the male plays no part after mating. The clutch is reported to be a single egg, and incubation and fledging periods are poorly documented.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes differ strongly. Only the male has black and yellow plumage, a green-edged breast shield and the wires; the female is brown above with a blackish head and pale, barred underparts.

analysis.summary: A plant-sucking mite less than half a millimetre long that is among the arthropods with the most recorded cases of pesticide resistance. Short generations and very large populations let resistant strains build up within a few seasons of repeated spraying.

Greenish-yellow body with a dark patch on each side
Round, translucent eggs among the webbing under leaves
Adults have eight pale legs and move slowly over the leaf

Its genome, published in 2011, was reported as the first complete genome of any chelicerate.
Its silk comes from glands opening on the palps near the mouthparts, and it lays threads as it walks.
Its genome carries unusually large families of genes for breaking down plant toxins.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Pierces individual leaf cells with needle-like mouthparts and sucks out the contents, leaving pale specks that merge into bronzing. It has been recorded on more than a thousand plant species.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predatory mites such as Phytoseiulus persimilis, tiny black Stethorus ladybirds, predatory thrips and lacewing larvae all eat it. Its dense webbing slows many predators, and colonies disperse when attacked or crowded.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No day and night rest cycle has been described; feeding and egg-laying continue around the clock. In autumn, short days send mated females into winter dormancy in leaf litter, bark crevices or greenhouse structures.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult females live about two to four weeks and males less. Egg to adult takes about a week near 30 °C and two to three weeks in cool weather.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female lays several eggs a day, commonly around 100 in her life, on the leaf underside among the webbing. Unfertilised eggs become males and fertilised eggs females. Young pass through a six-legged larva and two eight-legged nymphal stages.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger and oval with a rounded rear; males are smaller, more active and have a tapering, pointed abdomen. Only females turn orange-red for winter.

analysis.summary: One of Europe's largest butterflies, with a wingspan of roughly 7 to 9 centimetres and two slender tails on each hindwing. Its rapid, gliding flight around Mediterranean treetops makes it easy to notice but hard to follow.
identification: Dark brown upperside with a broad orange border
Underside marbled brown with white and orange bands
Small blue-grey spots near the hindwing tails above
Four-horned head on the green caterpillar

whyInteresting: It is the only European member of Charaxes, a genus with well over a hundred species, most of them African.
Adults are drawn to spilled wine and beer, which collectors have long used as bait.
Caterpillars rest on a pad of silk spun on a leaf, returning to it between meals.
Because its caterpillars feed almost entirely on strawberry tree, its distribution largely follows that shrub around Mediterranean coasts.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults rarely visit flowers; they suck juices from rotting fruit such as figs, from tree sap and from dung. Caterpillars feed on the leaves of the strawberry tree.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds and lizards take adults, and caterpillars are hunted by birds and parasitic wasps. Adults rely on fast, powerful flight; the green caterpillar is hard to see against strawberry-tree leaves.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active in sunshine through the middle of the day. At night and in dull weather adults rest in tree canopies with wings closed, the patterned underside blending with bark and leaves.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults usually live a few weeks. The autumn brood overwinters as a caterpillar, spending roughly six months in the larval stage.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay single pale, rounded eggs on the upper side of strawberry-tree leaves. There are usually two broods a year; caterpillars from the second brood grow slowly through winter and pupate in spring as green hanging chrysalises.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are similarly patterned, but females are larger, with broader wings.

entries.name: Umbrella Cockatoo

analysis.summary: In alarm or display, the broad, rounded crest of this large white cockatoo lifts from lying flat into a full half-circle of white feathers around the head. About 46 centimetres long, it lives only in the northern Moluccas of Indonesia.

Broad, rounded wings beaten in shallow flaps between glides
Short, square-ended white tail

Chicks hatch with closed eyes and only a sparse covering of yellowish down.
It is also widely known by the name white cockatoo.
Outside the breeding season it may gather in small loose groups at feeding trees.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, nuts, fruits and berries are taken in the canopy, cracked or peeled with the heavy bill and held in one foot. Insects and their larvae are also eaten, and birds raid maize and fruit crops near forest.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Natural predators have been little studied; large birds of prey probably take some adults and nests are exposed to climbing predators. Trapping for the cage-bird trade and forest loss are the serious threats, and the species is listed as Endangered.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: At dusk pairs and small groups fly to tall forest trees to roost, often using favoured trees again. By day they are active, and noisiest early and late.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been documented. In captivity many live 40 to 60 years, and a few are reported to have lived longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs nest in a hollow high in a large tree. The usual clutch is two white eggs, incubated by both parents for about four weeks, and the chicks stay in the nest for around three months while both adults feed them.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is identical. Adult males usually have a dark brown to black iris, while females have a reddish-brown one, and males tend to have a slightly larger head and bill.

entries.name: Underwing Moth
entries.heroTitle: Underwing Moth — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Underwing Moths teach Hidden Flash: camouflage handles the ordinary moment, while the colour stays hidden until the instant it is useful.
identification: Cryptic grey, brown or bark-patterned forewings
Brightly coloured and boldly banded hindwings in many species
Hindwing colour normally hidden completely while resting
Broad triangular moth shape when the wings are spread
Many species rest flat against tree bark during the day
Species-level identification can be difficult without seeing the hindwings
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: central_asia, east_asia, europe, north_africa_middle_east, north_america. Catocala is principally a Northern Hemisphere genus. Adults commonly spend daylight hours resting against trunks, branches and other surfaces where their cryptic forewings blend into the background. That habitat is the reason Hidden Flash works: the moth begins the encounter by being difficult to see at all.

whyInteresting: Catocala is a very large genus containing more than 250 described species.
The common name Underwing comes from the brightly patterned hindwings concealed beneath the much duller forewings.
A resting Underwing can be exceptionally difficult to notice because its forewing pattern resembles bark.
When disturbed, many Underwings suddenly expose their brightly coloured hindwings before covering them again after landing.
The abrupt switch from hidden bark camouflage to bright colour may interfere with a predator's ability to keep track of the moth.
Underwing species have some unusually dramatic English names, including Sweetheart, Girlfriend, Bride, Widow, Tearful, Mournful, Dejected and Inconsolable Underwings.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adult Underwing Moths feed primarily on sugary liquids such as tree sap and fermenting or ripe fruit. Their caterpillars feed on the leaves of woody plants, with different Catocala species associated with trees and shrubs including oaks, willows, poplars and other hosts. The group-level entry therefore represents a feeding strategy shared broadly across a diverse genus rather than one exact host plant.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, bats and other insect predators hunt Underwing Moths. Their first defence is cryptic forewing camouflage while resting. When disturbed, the sudden appearance of strongly contrasting hindwing colour can create a radically different visual target before the moth lands and hides the colour again.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Primarily nocturnal as adults. During daylight they commonly remain still on bark or other camouflaging surfaces with the hindwings completely covered.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan varies among the many Catocala species, so AnimalDex does not assign a false genus-wide lifespan estimate. Like other moths they spend substantial portions of the life cycle as egg, caterpillar and pupa before the adult flight period.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs associated with the woody host plants used by the caterpillars. Host preference differs between Catocala species, which is another reason a genus-level capture should not invent species-specific reproductive ecology.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Male and female appearance varies by species and there is no single reliable visible sex difference that applies across the whole Catocala genus. AnimalDex therefore avoids presenting one species' sexual dimorphism as a characteristic of every Underwing.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Kept animals are mostly active from dusk and through the night. In the wild they are thought to spend daylight hours in a burrow dug into a damp bank, or under stones, roots and leaf litter, where the air stays humid.

analysis.summary: A monitor lizard of the African savannah belt south of the Sahara, usually under 1 m long. Unlike most monitors it feeds mainly on hard-bodied invertebrates, cracking snail shells and beetles with blunt, rounded rear teeth.

whyInteresting: It is also called Bosc's monitor, after the French naturalist Louis Bosc, who described it in 1792.
Field studies in Ghana found that it builds up fat reserves while insects are plentiful in the wet season and draws on them when food is scarce.
It is among the reptiles most heavily exported from West Africa for the pet trade, many as hatchlings from ranched eggs.
Like all monitor lizards it is listed by CITES, so international trade in it must be licensed and recorded.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Forages on foot through grass, leaf litter and loose soil for millipedes, grasshoppers, crickets and other invertebrates. Small vertebrates and eggs are taken occasionally.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Young fall to birds of prey, snakes and carnivores; adults face larger raptors and mammals. A cornered lizard hisses, puffs up its body, lashes its tail and bites.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, with most activity in the warmer part of the morning. Nights are spent under cover, often in a tree hollow or rock pile.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive animals have lived for more than 10 years; lifespan in the wild is poorly documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay clutches that can exceed 20 eggs in burrows or dug chambers. Incubation takes several months, and the young hatch around the start of the rains, when insect food is plentiful. The hatchlings receive no care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike. Males tend to grow larger with broader heads, but they are hard to tell apart without close examination.

whyInteresting: It was long treated as two species, the Red-backed Hawk of lower ground and the Puna Hawk of the high Andes; many authorities now merge them.
It builds a stick nest on a cliff ledge, in a tree or on a tall cactus, and usually lays two or three eggs.
Small mammals, especially rodents, are its main prey, along with birds, lizards and large insects, often caught after hovering on the wind.
Birds breeding in the far south of Patagonia partly move north in winter, while Andean birds are largely resident.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly rodents such as leaf-eared mice and tuco-tucos, and introduced rabbits in parts of Patagonia; it also takes small birds, lizards, snakes, beetles and grasshoppers, usually seized on the ground after a short stoop.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Healthy adults have few natural enemies. People are the main threat: some birds are shot or poisoned near livestock farms, and pairs dive at intruding raptors and people near the nest.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, hunting mostly once the morning air has warmed and the wind has risen. It roosts at night on cliff ledges, in trees or on rocky outcrops, often near the nest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No single lifespan fits this hawk complex; birds from coastal scrub to high Andean puna are often still treated as one variable form.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female does most of the incubating while the male brings food. Nestlings grow up over several weeks and stay near the nest for a period after fledging; exact incubation and fledging times are poorly documented.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger and heavier than males, as in most hawks. Pale, dark and barred forms occur in both sexes, so size and back colour, not the underparts, separate them.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Larvae chew keratin-rich dried animal matter: wool, fur, feathers, silk, dead insects, old bird nests and museum specimens. Adults feed on pollen and nectar, especially from white flowers such as hogweed and other umbellifers.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few enemies are documented. Spiders and predatory insects take adults, and small parasitic wasps attack larvae. Larvae defend themselves by raising tufts of barbed hairs that entangle ants and other attackers, and adults drop and feign death when disturbed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are active by day and fly towards light, often gathering at windows. Larvae stay hidden in dark crevices, and in temperate climates they spend winter as larvae, pausing development until spring.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: The life cycle usually takes about a year, but can stretch to two or three years in cool conditions or when food is poor. Adults live only a few weeks.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After mating, females lay a few dozen eggs on or near larval food such as wool, fur or bird-nest material. Larvae hatch within a few weeks, moult several times over many months, and pupate inside the last larval skin. There is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in the field; females average slightly larger, and reliable separation needs magnification of the underside.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger reef predators, including groupers and sharks. Its answer is the same stillness it hunts with — an unmoving lizardfish is very hard to find.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Variegated Lizardfish rest on the bottom around the clock, hunting during daylight and remaining settled on sand at night.

entries.heroTitle: Variegated Meadowhawk — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Most meadowhawks live and die near the pond they emerged from. The Variegated Meadowhawk treats a continent as one habitat, riding fronts south in autumn and returning north to breed, so a drying marsh is a reason to leave rather than a reason to fail.
identification: Slender dragonfly, 38-42 mm, with a yellow-and-brown or red abdomen
Yellow wash at the base of each wing, strongest on the hindwing
Face pale, eyes reddish-brown in mature males
Often seen well away from water, including over roads and fields
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america. Ponds, marshes, irrigation ditches and temporary wetlands across North America, plus the fields and coasts it crosses between them. Permanent water is useful; the ability to leave when it fails is the point.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_america. Ponds, marshes, irrigation ditches and temporary wetlands across North America, plus the fields and coasts it crosses between them. Permanent water is useful; the ability to leave when it fails is the point.

whyInteresting: It is one of the few North American dragonflies with a regular long-distance migration, moving with weather fronts rather than along a fixed corridor.
Autumn swarms can appear far from any breeding pond, including over the ocean and high mountain passes.
Males do not hold a territory the way pond dragonflies do. They find females at water and leave.
Nymphs develop in shallow, often temporary, wetlands, so the adult's willingness to travel is what keeps the species in contact with water that is not there year-round.
Colour changes with age: young adults are yellow-brown and mature males redden, which is why the same species is described as both.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small flying insects taken on the wing — midges, mosquitoes and other flies — both at water and along the migration route. Feeding away from a territory is what makes a long crossing possible.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds take migrating adults in numbers; fish and aquatic insects take nymphs. There is no nest to defend, so the answer to pressure is to keep moving.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, most visible in warm sun, roosting in low vegetation at night and riding weather systems when a front is moving.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults live several weeks to a few months; the migratory circuit is completed by more than one generation in a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are dropped into shallow water or damp mud. Nymphs can finish in a single season in a warm wetland, which is why a temporary pool is enough.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Mature males become redder on the abdomen; females and young adults stay yellow-brown with darker side stripes. Both sexes carry the yellow wing-base wash.

Bright red eyes
Blue lines on the legs and claw joints
Last pair of legs flattened into broad swimming paddles
Carapace up to about 10 centimetres across

whyInteresting: It supports a valuable fishery, and much of the catch from Scotland and France is exported live to Spain and Portugal.
Older books list it as Liocarcinus puber or Macropipus puber; the genus Necora now contains only this species.
Mass deaths in some populations have been linked to infection by a parasitic dinoflagellate, Hematodinium.
Females carry masses of orange eggs tucked under the abdomen, mainly through late winter and spring.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An omnivore that eats brown seaweeds alongside mussels, barnacles, small crabs and worms, crushing shells with its claws. It also scavenges dead animals on the seabed.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Octopuses, conger eels, cod and other large fishes eat it, and otters take it on some coasts; it is also caught commercially in pots. Threatened, it rears up with claws spread wide and nips hard, or swims off using its paddle legs.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active at night and around dusk, sheltering under boulders and in weed-covered crevices by day. It is less active in the coldest months but has no true dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not well documented. Growth studies suggest most wild crabs live only a few years, but reliable ages are lacking.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating takes place soon after the female moults, while her shell is still soft, and the male guards her. She carries a large mass of eggs under her abdomen for several weeks, and they hatch into planktonic larvae that drift before settling on the shore.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow larger, with bigger claws. Turned over, the male's abdomen is narrow and pointed, while the female's is broad and rounded for carrying eggs.

entries.name: Velvet Worm
entries.heroTitle: Velvet Worm — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Velvet Worm carries Sticky Aim through a specific body plan, habitat choice, and survival rhythm. The principle is visible in how it feeds, moves, avoids danger, and places the next generation.
identification: Soft, cylindrical body covered in fine velvety papillae
Between 13 and 43 pairs of stubby, unjointed legs
A pair of fleshy, ringed antennae on the head
Most species only a few centimetres long
Slow, flowing walk with the body extending and contracting
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania, north_america, south_america, south_asia, southeast_asia, sub_saharan_africa. Humid forests, rotting logs, leaf litter, and damp crevices fit Sticky Aim because the body dries easily and ambush needs moisture.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: australia_oceania, north_america, south_america, south_asia, southeast_asia, sub_saharan_africa. Humid forests, rotting logs, leaf litter, and damp crevices fit Sticky Aim because the body dries easily and ambush needs moisture.

whyInteresting: Velvet worms catch prey by squirting sticky slime from a pair of glands beside the head, entangling insects and other small animals.
They breathe through many tiny openings that cannot be closed, so they lose water quickly and need humid shelter.
They walk on stubby, unjointed legs called lobopods, with the number of leg pairs differing between species.
Velvet worms form their own phylum, Onychophora, and are thought to be close relatives of arthropods and tardigrades.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small insects, termites, and other invertebrates support Sticky Aim by rewarding a sudden adhesive slime cast at close range.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders, birds, centipedes, reptiles, and drying conditions threaten velvet worms; hidden damp shelter protects the soft body.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal, leaving cover in humid darkness when prey is close and dehydration risk is lower.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Many velvet worms can live several years, with slow hidden life making Sticky Aim a patient ambush strategy.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Depending on species, females may lay eggs or give birth to live young; reproduction is tied to protected humid microhabitats.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often larger in many velvet worms, while males may have specialized reproductive structures.

entries.name: Vendace
entries.heroTitle: Vendace — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Vendace depends on clean, deep lake systems, showing how small plankton-feeders can reveal the health and fragility of a whole water body.
identification: Small slender silvery fish, usually 10 to 20 centimetres
Lower jaw projecting beyond the upper jaw
Small fleshy adipose fin before the tail
Dark bluish-green back over bright silver flanks
Many long, fine gill rakers inside the gill cover
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe. Open water of cool, deep, clear lakes low in nutrients across northern Europe, from the Baltic basin through Fennoscandia and north-western Russia, with outliers in northern Germany, Poland and England's Lake District. Some populations also live in the brackish northern Baltic Sea.

whyInteresting: Known in Finland as muikku, it is a traditional food, often fried whole in butter or rye flour.
Its bright orange roe is sold in Sweden as löjrom, and roe from the Kalix area holds protected origin status.
Derwent Water now holds Britain's main surviving native stock, since the Bassenthwaite Lake population has not been found in recent surveys, making it one of the country's rarest freshwater fish.
Year-class strength swings widely, so a lake's stock can rise or collapse within a few seasons.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds almost entirely on zooplankton, especially water fleas and copepods, strained from open water with long, closely packed gill rakers while swimming in shoals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pike, perch, trout, zander and burbot eat adults, and cormorants take them near the surface. Other fish eat the eggs, and introduced ruffe are thought to do so in some lakes. Nutrient enrichment, silt and warming water remove the cold, well-oxygenated depths it needs.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Shoals follow a daily vertical cycle, staying deep and dark by day and rising towards the surface after dusk to feed. How much they rest at night is not well documented.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live only a few years, commonly about 3 to 5; ages near 10 have been recorded but are rare.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawns in late autumn or early winter, scattering eggs over gravel or sand with no parental care. The eggs develop slowly in cold water, often under ice, and hatch in spring. Many females mature at one or two years old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike for most of the year; in the spawning season small pale breeding tubercles appear on the scales, usually more prominent in males.

entries.name: Venus' Flower Basket
entries.heroTitle: Venus' Flower Basket — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Venus' Flower Basket AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: Glass Sponges form intricate silica frameworks in cold or deep seas. Venus’ Flower Basket shows how fragile-looking architecture can become strong when geometry, filtration, and deep-water stability work together.
identification: Curved, hollow tube shaped like a narrow vase
Walls form a fine square-grid lattice of glass
Top sealed by a sieve-like lid
Tuft of long, hair-like glassy spicules at the base
Spiral ridges winding around the outer wall
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_pacific, southeast_asia. Soft, muddy seafloor of the western Pacific, mainly around the Philippines and southern Japan, at depths of roughly 100 to 1,000 metres. It stands upright in the sediment in cold, dark, slow-moving water.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: north_pacific, southeast_asia. Soft, muddy seafloor of the western Pacific, mainly around the Philippines and southern Japan, at depths of roughly 100 to 1,000 metres. It stands upright in the sediment in cold, dark, slow-moving water.

behaviorTraits: Curved, hollow tube shaped like a narrow vase
Walls form a fine square-grid lattice of glass
Top sealed by a sieve-like lid
Tuft of long, hair-like glassy spicules at the base
Spiral ridges winding around the outer wall
whyInteresting: Young shrimp often enter the basket, grow too big to leave through the lattice, and live out their lives inside as a pair.
In Japan, dried baskets with their pair of shrimp inside have traditionally been given as wedding gifts.
The long anchoring spicules carry light along their length, and researchers have compared them with manufactured optical fibres.
Its skeleton is built from thin layers of silica bonded with organic material, which makes it far tougher than solid glass of the same size.
Computer flow studies published in 2021 suggest the spiral ridges create slow eddies inside the body cavity, which may help it feed.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A filter feeder that draws seawater in through the pores of its walls and strains out bacteria and fine particles of organic matter. Flagellated chambers inside the body wall drive the current and capture the food.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Natural predators of this species are poorly documented, though sea stars are known to feed on some glass sponges. Bottom trawling can damage the sponge beds, and dried skeletons have long been collected for sale.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: As a sponge it has no nervous system and does not sleep. Water is drawn through its body walls day and night, with no known daily period of rest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No one has measured how long this species lives, so it is unknown whether individuals typically last for years or for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Reproduction of this species is poorly known. Glass sponges as a group are thought to brood embryos inside the body and release swimming larvae that settle and grow into new sponges; no brood sizes are recorded for this species.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: No visible differences between the sexes are known, and how sex is organised in this species has not been well documented.

analysis.summary: Vernal Pool Fairy Shrimp hatch from drought-resistant eggs when seasonal pools fill. Their delicate swimming, fast growth, and resting eggs fit habitats that exist only for a short window.
identification: Slender, translucent body up to about 2.5 cm long
Eleven pairs of beating leaf-like legs
Compound eyes on short stalks
No shell covering the body

Seasonal rain pools in grassland over clay or hardpan soil, in California's Central Valley, surrounding foothills and coastal ranges, and a small area of southern Oregon. Pools are often small and shallow, with clear to tea-coloured water, filling in winter and drying by late spring.

whyInteresting: It swims upside down, belly uppermost, rowing with its beating legs.
It was not formally described as a species until 1990.
Fairy shrimp are branchiopod crustaceans, related to brine shrimp and water fleas.
Its tough eggs may be carried to new pools in mud on the feet of birds and grazing animals.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: It filters algae, bacteria, protozoa and fine detritus from the water with its leaf-like legs, which beat in rhythm and push food along a groove to the mouth.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Backswimmers, dragonfly larvae, diving beetles, salamander larvae, wading birds and ducks eat them. Loss of vernal pools to farming and building is the main threat, and it is listed as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Rest has not been documented; while the pool holds water they swim almost continuously, day and night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults can mature in about three weeks and live until the pool dries, usually a few weeks to about four months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry eggs in a brood sac beneath the body and drop them to the pool floor, or they are released when the female dies. Not all eggs hatch after the next rains, so some remain for later wet seasons.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have greatly enlarged second antennae used to clasp females during mating. Females have a brood sac behind the legs.

Black, bare face
Tail about as long as the body
Hind legs much longer than the arms

whyInteresting: The name sifaka comes from its alarm call, a sneezing shi-fak.
Females are dominant over males and usually feed first.
Groups usually hold about 2 to 12 animals.
It is reported to go without drinking through much of the dry season, taking its water from leaves.
In parts of southern Madagascar, local taboos against hunting it are thought to have helped protect some populations.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, flowers, fruit, bark, and seasonal plant foods support Sideways Grace by rewarding agile travel between feeding trees.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fossas, raptors, snakes, dogs, humans, and habitat loss threaten sifakas; group vigilance and leaping protect them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal; sifakas feed, sun, groom, and travel by day, resting in trees when movement and visibility fall.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live into their teens or longer in protected conditions, making Sideways Grace a learned group rhythm.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to one infant that clings to the mother and later rides as it learns leaping routes.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar in appearance, with social rank and scent behavior often more important than size differences.

analysis.summary: Different predators get different alarm calls from this savanna monkey. A leopard alarm sends troop members up into trees, an eagle alarm makes them look skyward and dive into bushes, and a snake alarm has them stand upright to scan the grass.

whyInteresting: A female's social rank is largely inherited from her mother's rank within the troop.
Infants give eagle alarms to many harmless birds and even falling leaves, and only with age narrow them to real threats such as martial eagles.
Troops defend their home ranges against neighbouring troops, and females take an active part in these encounters.
In dry East African savannas, gum oozing from acacia trees becomes an important food in the dry season.
Troops usually hold from about 10 to 50 animals, sometimes more.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruits, leaves, seeds, flowers, insects, and occasional small prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, eagles, pythons, baboons, dogs and humans. Vervets give distinct alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, each triggering a different escape, and the group keeps watch while foraging.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal; troops feed and travel by day, then sleep in trees where social spacing and alarm awareness remain important.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually about 10 to 12 years in the wild; captive vervets have lived beyond 20 years and reportedly to about 30.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to one infant and raise it within a social troop where relatives and group life shape survival.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and often move between troops, while females remain in natal groups; both rely on social reading.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit and insects matter because the bird must fuel movement, color, and display without abandoning the trees. The diet explains why Velvet Stage is not empty glamour: the body earns its signal by constantly finding energy in the canopy.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators are not well documented. Birds of prey such as goshawks are likely to take adults, and snakes and other nest raiders threaten eggs and chicks. It keeps to dense foliage, and loss of lowland rainforest reduces its range.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, with displaying males busiest in the early morning. At night it roosts in the rainforest canopy or mid-storey; it has no seasonal dormancy, though males display mostly in the breeding months.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild is not well documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female alone builds the nest, incubates and raises the young; the male takes no part after mating. The nest is a cup of leaves and vine stems in dense foliage, usually holding one or two eggs.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are velvet black with an iridescent blue-green crown and throat. Females are grey-brown above and buff below with dark chevrons and a pale eye stripe.

Glossy black body and legs with no pale hair bands
Dark wings that shine violet-blue in sunlight
Heavy, direct flight, often hovering in front of flowers

whyInteresting: It has spread north through Europe in recent decades and has been recorded breeding in southern Britain.
Old nests are often reused and extended by later bees, so a single timber can end up holding several tunnels.
On mild, sunny winter days, overwintering adults sometimes leave their shelters and can be seen flying.
Before take-off on cool mornings it can warm its flight muscles by shivering them, without beating its wings.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults take nectar and pollen from a wide range of flowers, favouring large blooms such as wisteria, sage, lavender, legumes and thistles. At deep flowers it often bites a slit near the base and drinks nectar without pollinating.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds such as bee-eaters catch adults in flight, and brood cells can be attacked by parasitic insects. The female guards her nest entrance and can sting if handled, though she seldom does.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Flies by day, mostly in warm sunshine. Nights and cool spells are spent inside a nest tunnel or another cavity in wood.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About a year as an adult: bees emerging in late summer overwinter, breed the following spring and early summer, and then die.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Each female nests alone, stocking a row of cells with a loaf of pollen and nectar and laying one egg on each. Larvae feed on the loaf and pupate in the cell.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are black all over, antennae included. Males have an orange-red band near the tip of each antenna and, like all male bees, cannot sting.

entries.name: Violet Sea Snail

analysis.summary: A purple ocean snail that spends its adult life upside down at the surface, hanging from a raft of bubbles it makes itself. Its foot traps air in mucus that hardens as it dries, and without the raft it sinks.
identification: Thin, fragile violet shell up to about 4 centimetres
Low spire, the shell wider than it is tall

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Violet Sea Snail mainly uses floating cnidarians such as Portuguese man o war relatives and other soft-bodied prey. fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, seabirds, turtles, storms, and loss of the bubble raft pressure Violet Sea Snail.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No sleep or rest cycle has been documented; it drifts and feeds whenever prey comes within reach, day and night.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike and cannot be told apart from the shell.

entries.name: Vulture Bee
entries.heroTitle: Vulture Bee — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A small stingless bee of Neotropical forests that is reported to collect no pollen at all. Workers slice flesh from dead animals with toothed mandibles, carry it home in the crop and store it, processed with their own secretions, in wax pots inside the nest as protein for the colony.
identification: Small, dark bee crowding onto fresh carcasses
Noticeably smaller and more compact than a honeybee
Hind legs never carry pollen loads
No working sting; handled workers bite instead

Foragers recruit nestmates to a find, and a crowd of workers has been reported stripping a small carcass within hours.
A 2021 study of carrion-feeding stingless bees found acid-loving gut bacteria similar to those of vultures and hyenas, which may help them cope with rotting meat.
Researchers looking for vulture bees commonly attract foragers with baits of raw meat.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Protein comes from the flesh of dead vertebrates of many kinds. For energy, workers also gather sugary liquids, reported to include nectar and fruit juices.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders and other insects take foraging workers, and ants and robber bees may raid nests. The colony relies on guards at the nest entrance and on sheer numbers.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Foragers work carcasses during daylight and return to the nest by dusk. At night the colony stays inside its cavity nest, where workers rest on the combs.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not documented for this species. Workers of stingless bees generally live from a few weeks to about two months, while a colony with its queen can persist for years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single egg-laying queen lays into wax brood cells that workers first fill with processed food, then seal. Each larva feeds alone on that store and pupates in the cell, with no further care until it emerges.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The queen is much larger, with a swollen abdomen, and seldom leaves the nest. Workers and males are similar in size and hard to tell apart in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, other wild cats, jackals and large eagles such as martial eagles hunt it. Groups give loud alarm calls, usually run rather than fly, and fly up into trees when pressed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal. Groups forage in the cooler morning and late afternoon, rest in shade at midday, and roost together high in tall trees at night.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests are scrapes hidden in grass or under a bush. Clutches are commonly 4 to 8 cream eggs, incubated by the female for about 24 days; chicks leave the nest soon after hatching and feed themselves under group protection.

Albino and pied forms are bred for the aquarium trade.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Walking Catfish mainly uses fish, insects, crustaceans, mollusks, detritus, and plant material.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Herons, cormorants, otters, water snakes and larger predatory fish eat it, young fish most of all. Its pectoral spines can be locked erect, making it awkward to swallow.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly active at night and around dusk, when it feeds along the bottom. By day it lies in mud, among plant roots or in holes in the bank, and in the dry season it may stay buried in damp mud until the rains return.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning takes place in the rainy season in flooded shallows and rice fields. fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes share the same grey-brown colouring. Males have a longer, pointed genital papilla behind the vent, while in females it is short and rounded, and ripe females look noticeably fuller in the belly.

entries.name: Wandering Glider
entries.heroTitle: Wandering Glider — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Wandering Glider rides weather systems rather than fighting them, riding monsoon winds across open ocean between continents. It travels further than any other insect by treating the wind as the vehicle rather than the obstacle.
identification: Golden to amber body, roughly 45 mm long
Unusually broad hindwing bases built for gliding, not chasing
Rarely seen perched — almost always soaring in loose groups
Hovers and drifts high over open ground rather than patrolling water

Open country, coastlines and any temporary standing water. Permanence is not required and is arguably a disadvantage — this species specialises in pools that appear after rain and vanish again, which is where it faces no established competitors or fish.

behaviorTraits: Golden to amber body, roughly 45 mm long
Unusually broad hindwing bases built for gliding, not chasing
Rarely seen perched — almost always soaring in loose groups
Hovers and drifts high over open ground rather than patrolling water
whyInteresting: Its multi-generational circuit between India and East Africa is the longest known migration of any insect, several thousand kilometres across open ocean.
It breeds in temporary rainwater pools, which is why it can colonise puddles, tyre ruts and rooftop tanks nothing else has reached yet.
The broad hindwings let it glide for long stretches on rising air, so it burns far less energy per kilometre than a hawking dragonfly.
Larvae can complete development in as little as five weeks, fast enough to finish before a seasonal pool dries out.
It is the most widely distributed dragonfly on Earth, found on every continent except Antarctica.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small flying insects taken on the wing, largely midges and mosquitoes, caught while gliding rather than by pursuit. Feeding this way costs very little energy, which is what makes an ocean crossing survivable at all.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, larger dragonflies and spiders' webs take adults; fish and aquatic beetles take larvae wherever a pool lasts long enough for them to arrive. Breeding in short-lived water is itself the main defence.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and most visible in the warm hours, roosting in vegetation at night, though migrating swarms will keep moving into dusk when the wind is favourable.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults live a few weeks to a couple of months, so the full migration circuit takes several generations to complete — no individual makes the whole journey.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are dropped straight into temporary pools with the female tapping the water surface in flight, spreading a clutch across several pools rather than committing it all to one that might dry.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are similar and both golden; males tend to be a slightly deeper amber and are the ones that hold loose airspace over a breeding pool.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Largely nocturnal feeder. By day, dense flocks stand or sit packed together on banks, mud bars and floating mats at the water's edge, resting and preening.

whyInteresting: Wasp Moth is a common-name group rather than one single genus.
Several different arctiine lineages contain moths that independently resemble wasps.
Amata species are classic Old World examples and belong to Syntomini.
Ctenuchina and Euchromiina contain many of the best-known American and tropical wasp moths.
The Virginia Ctenucha has a metallic blue body and conspicuous contrasting head while still being a moth.
The Polka-dot Wasp Moth combines dark metallic colouring, pale spots and a bright red abdomen.
Many wasp moths fly during daylight, making their visual mimicry useful under the same conditions in which predators encounter real wasps.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adult diets vary, but many visit flowers for nectar or other sugary resources. Caterpillar host plants vary strongly between species and genera. AnimalDex therefore avoids assigning one narrow host plant or larval diet to the whole Wasp Moth group.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, spiders and other insect predators can take these moths. Their standout defensive strategy is visual signalling: many resemble stinging wasps through body shape, colour, transparent wings and movement. Some members may also possess chemical defences of their own, but that cannot safely be generalized to every species represented by this group.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Many classic Wasp Moths are unusually active during daylight compared with the stereotypical nocturnal moth. Resting behaviour varies between species and regions.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: There is no meaningful single lifespan for the Wasp Moth group because it contains many species across several lineages. AnimalDex therefore does not assign a false group-wide lifespan.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs on or near the host plants required by their caterpillars, but host selection and reproductive details vary substantially by species. There is no prolonged parental care after egg laying.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences vary strongly among genera. In some species males have more elaborate antennae or scent-producing structures involved in courtship, but there is no single visible male-female difference that can be applied safely to every Wasp Moth.

analysis.summary: A large orb-weaving spider of European grassland; the female is banded in yellow, black and white like a wasp. She hangs head down at the centre of a web crossed by a vertical zigzag of thick white silk. What the silk band does is still debated: luring insects, warning birds off the web and hiding the spider have all been proposed.

Legs ringed with dark and pale bands
Often rests with legs held in pairs, forming an X
Female abdomen is a long oval, not globular

Over recent decades it has spread north from the Mediterranean region to reach the Baltic coast and southern Scandinavia.
Females often seize and eat the male during mating.
A mating male commonly breaks off the tip of his mating organ inside the female, which hinders males that arrive later.
Newly emerged young climb grass stems and let the wind carry them away on threads of silk.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasshoppers and crickets are the main prey, with flies, bees and other insects that jump or fly into the low web. Struggling prey is swathed in broad bands of silk first and bitten afterwards.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds and spider-hunting wasps take spiders from the web, and parasitic wasps lay their eggs in the egg sacs. A female that is pressed hard drops from the hub on a line into the grass below.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: There is no separate retreat: the female stays on her web through day and night. The web is usually renewed around dawn or dusk, which takes about an hour.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one year from egg to death. Adults mature in summer and none survive the winter; males die first, soon after the mating period.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid in late summer in a brown, papery, flask-shaped sac hung in the grass near the web, typically holding a few hundred eggs. The young hatch within weeks but stay inside through winter and leave in spring. The sac is not guarded.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females reach about 15 mm in body length and carry the bright bands. Males are about 5 mm long, pale brown and slender, and are easily overlooked at the edge of a female's web.

entries.name: Water Bear

analysis.summary: Water Bears, or tardigrades, survive harsh conditions by entering cryptobiotic states where metabolism nearly stops. Their toughness comes from reducing activity until water and safety return.
identification: Principle in the body: Water Bears, or tardigrades, can enter cryptobiotic states that help them survive drying, freezing, radiation, and other extremes.
Habitat power: life in moss and water films makes Cryptobiosis Courage useful instead of symbolic.
Daily behavior: extreme survival is the repeated action that makes the lesson visible.
Survival pressure: threats from small invertebrates keep the power honest and necessary.
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america, europe, sub_saharan_africa, south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania. The habitat is not background decoration; it is the pressure that makes 'Resilience sometimes means reducing everything to the minimum that can continue.' useful, because extreme survival only makes sense in a place where food, shelter, and danger meet that way.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Its diet of algae, microbes is part of the lesson because feeding is where the power becomes practical. Water Bear does not eat randomly; the food source rewards the same skill described by Cryptobiosis Courage, whether that means patience, precision, cooperation, hidden movement, display, or endurance. The meal shows why the principle feeds the animal instead of remaining an abstract idea.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators and threats such as small invertebrates explain why the power has consequences. The animal's lesson is not just about success; it is also about avoiding the cost of being seen, rushed, isolated, or poorly placed. That pressure keeps Cryptobiosis Courage sharp, because the wrong timing or wrong signal can turn survival into exposure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Rest around dormancy supports the same pattern: Water Bear needs a safe reset point that matches its way of moving and feeding. Its sleep or resting rhythm reinforces Cryptobiosis Courage because the animal cannot keep using its power without a place to pause, hide, conserve energy, or return to the group before the next active phase.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Its lifespan and pace should be read through the principle rather than as a plain number. A life built around extreme survival depends on repeating the same successful pattern across seasons: find the right habitat, use the right food, avoid the right threats, and keep the power of Cryptobiosis Courage working long enough to reproduce.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Offspring strategy connects to the lesson because young animals must inherit more than genes; they must enter the same ecological problem. For Water Bear, nesting, eggs, larvae, young, or maternal investment all matter because the next generation has to learn or physically carry the same relationship between moss and water films, algae, microbes, safety, and Cryptobiosis Courage.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Laboratory stocks of Hypsibius exemplaris reproduce by parthenogenesis; males are not a regular field character for this species.
