whyInteresting: Gerridae are commonly called Water Striders or Pond Skaters.
Their legs are covered in microscopic water-repellent structures that help prevent them from breaking the surface.
Water Striders detect vibrations travelling across the water surface and use them to locate prey, predators and other striders.
The middle legs provide much of the propulsion while the hind legs help steer.
Many species prey on insects trapped at the water surface.
Some Gerridae live on streams, ponds and lakes, while the related ocean-skating genus Halobates includes insects that live on the open sea.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly small insects and other arthropods found struggling on or immediately beneath the water surface. Water Striders detect vibrations through their legs, approach the source and use the front legs and piercing mouthparts to capture prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, frogs, aquatic insects, birds and other predators can take Water Striders. Rapid surface acceleration, sensitivity to vibration and the ability to move across water without entering it provide their main defences.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Activity varies among species and conditions. Water Striders spend resting periods stationary on the surface, near vegetation or along sheltered margins rather than maintaining constant movement.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs on aquatic vegetation or other objects near the water depending on species. Young hatch as wingless nymphs that already live and move on the water surface, passing through successive molts before adulthood.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences vary among Gerridae and can involve body size, abdominal structure and mating-related morphology. Those characters are often too subtle to serve as family-wide phone-camera field marks.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A fruit eater that plucks fruits in flight or from a perch and swallows them whole, later regurgitating the large seeds. Fruits of the laurel and incense-tree families are thought to be important.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predation has hardly been studied. Forest raptors are the likely threat to males calling from exposed treetop perches, while the female's green plumage helps hide her at the nest.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal. Males spend long periods of the day on high, exposed perches, calling at intervals. Where birds roost at night has not been described, and it has no seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan is not documented for this species, wild or captive.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female alone builds a small, flimsy twig nest, incubates and feeds the young. The clutch is a single egg, and the chick is thought to be raised largely on fruit.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Only adult males are white and carry a wattle. Females are olive-green above with yellowish, olive-streaked underparts. Young males resemble females and are thought to take several years to become white.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Many species chew the fine roots of grasses, cereals, vegetables and tree seedlings with strong mandibles. Others eat decaying plant matter, compost or rotting wood. Microbes in an enlarged hindgut help to digest the tough plant fibre.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Moles, shrews, skunks, badgers, wild boar, crows, rooks and starlings dig grubs out of turf. Ground beetles, parasitic wasps and flies, nematodes, fungi and bacterial diseases kill many more. Grubs have little defence beyond staying buried.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Grubs live in darkness and feed whenever the soil is warm and moist, with no clear day and night cycle. In temperate regions they burrow deeper in winter and lie inactive until the soil warms in spring.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: The larval stage lasts about one year in many species, such as the Japanese beetle, and three to four years in cockchafers. Adult beetles usually live only a few weeks to a few months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Adult females burrow into soil and lay eggs singly or in small clusters, commonly a few dozen in total depending on the species. Eggs hatch in about two to four weeks. Larvae pass through three growth stages, then pupate in an earthen cell.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Male and female grubs look alike to the naked eye. Differences appear in the adult beetles, where males of many chafers have larger, fan-like antennae and males of some scarabs carry horns.

entries.name: White-rumped Vulture

analysis.summary: A large Asian vulture with blackish plumage and a white back, and the smallest of the Gyps vultures in the region. whyInteresting: Unlike the many Gyps vultures that nest on cliffs, it nests in trees.
In the 1980s it was thought to be one of the most numerous large birds of prey in the world, with a population estimated in the millions.
It has been listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN since 2000.
Captive breeding centres in India and Nepal have released young birds into areas kept free of diclofenac, where meloxicam, a painkiller found safe for Gyps vultures, is promoted instead.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Almost entirely carrion, mostly dead cattle and water buffalo left in fields or at village carcass dumps, plus wild hoofed mammals. It feeds on soft muscle and internal organs and does not kill live prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Healthy adults have few natural enemies. The collapse of its population in the 1990s and 2000s was caused by diclofenac, a veterinary painkiller that causes fatal kidney failure in vultures eating treated carcasses; veterinary use was banned in India, Nepal and Pakistan in 2006. Poisoning and loss of nest trees also threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day only. It roosts overnight in tall trees, often in groups, and stays perched in the early morning until the ground warms enough to give it rising air for soaring.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Poorly documented in the wild. Individuals are thought to live about 20 years or more, but reliable figures from marked wild birds are lacking.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single egg is laid in a large stick nest, mostly between October and March. Both parents incubate it for about 45 to 50 days and feed the chick by regurgitation until it fledges after roughly three to four months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike. Age is easier to judge: juveniles are browner and streaked, lack the white back and rump, and take about four to five years to reach adult plumage.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: White Seabream feed by day and settle among rocks and crevices at night, dropping into the same broken ground they spend the day working.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for a decade or more.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike, and the species is a protandrous hermaphrodite — some fish begin as males and later function as females. Appearance stays constant because nothing about the strategy depends on being recognised.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves, coyotes, bobcats, bears, cougars where present, humans, vehicles, and harsh winters pressure White-tailed Deer.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Its food is flying insects captured during rapid aerial movement. Beetles, flying ants, termites, bees and flies are taken, often high in the air.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fast flight leaves adults with few natural enemies, though falcons, hawks, and other aerial predators threaten Needletail Swift. In Australia, deaths from collisions with windows, wires and wind turbines have been recorded.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It is diurnal and strongly aerial, resting mostly around nesting or roosting sites. Wintering birds in Australia have been found roosting in the tall canopy of forests.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot be told apart in the field.

analysis.summary: Hidden under pale, bark-coloured forewings, the hindwings of this large underwing are black crossed by a broad white band, unlike the red or orange of most of its relatives. The band flashes into view when the moth takes off and vanishes as it lands.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars eat the leaves of poplars, aspens and willows. Adults sip sap from wounded trees and juice from fermenting fruit, and readily come to sweet baits painted on trunks.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds search trunks for resting moths, and bats take them in flight. A discovered moth bolts in a fast, erratic flight and quickly resettles on another trunk, where it becomes hard to follow.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It flies at night, from dusk onwards. Daylight hours are spent resting on the trunks of trees with the body pressed close to the bark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults probably survive for several weeks, since they feed as adults. There is one generation a year, so the whole life cycle takes about twelve months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid in late summer in bark crevices of host trees and hatch the following spring. The grey caterpillars feed through spring and early summer and pupate in a loose cocoon among leaves or debris.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are very similar in pattern and size, and are hard to separate in the field.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural enemies, and most losses are of eggs and small cygnets. Parents defend eggs and cygnets fiercely, hissing and charging with raised wings. Collisions with power lines and lead poisoning from swallowed shot kill many birds.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Whooper Swan rests in open water, ice edges, reed beds, and paired roosting sites. Active by day; in winter flocks leave farmland feeding sites at dusk to spend the night together on lakes or estuaries.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most wild birds probably live around 10 years; ringed individuals have been recorded at more than 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually 4 to 6 eggs in a large mound of plant material beside water. The female incubates for about 5 weeks while the male guards, and the grey cygnets fly at around 12 to 13 weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: No plumage difference separates the sexes. The male is on average bigger and heavier, but the sizes overlap widely.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Wild Boar feeds on roots, tubers, acorns, fruit, insects, eggs, carrion, crops, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves are the chief natural predator across much of the range, with tigers and leopards in parts of Asia; foxes, lynx and eagles take piglets. People now kill the most, through hunting and traffic. Sows defend their young fiercely, and a cornered boar will charge.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Wild Boar rests in thickets, wallows, reed beds, and sheltered ground nests. Where hunted it feeds mostly at night and around dusk, but in undisturbed places it is also active by day.

fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and heavier than females, and adult males carry long lower tusks that curve up and out of the mouth. Adult males usually live alone outside the breeding season.

Short, rounded wings with a fluttering, swallow-like flight
whyInteresting: Adults weigh only about 30 to 50 grams, making it one of the smallest seabirds.
Its keen sense of smell, unusual among birds, helps it find patches of food at sea.
It readily follows ships and feeding whales, picking plankton from the churned water.
It is named after Alexander Wilson, the Scottish-American ornithologist of the early nineteenth century.
It is often described as one of the most numerous seabirds in the world, with a population in the millions.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Picks tiny prey from the sea surface while fluttering low with wings raised and feet pattering on the water: krill and other small crustaceans, small fish and squid, and oily scraps.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Skuas are the main predators, catching adults and chicks at the breeding colonies. Late snowfalls that block nest crevices kill many eggs and chicks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds mainly in daylight at sea and rests on the water. At colonies, birds stay hidden in their nest crevices by day and fly in and out at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably around 10 years on average once adult, which is long for so small a bird; the maximum age is not well established.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single white egg is laid in a crevice or burrow and incubated by both parents for roughly 40 to 50 days. Both parents feed the chick on regurgitated food and oil until it flies at about 50 to 60 days old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot be told apart in the field.

Compact rounded body under 10 cm long

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are most active at dawn and dusk and through the night, staying underground while raptors hunt.

fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females raise small litters in a burrow chamber and can breed again quickly.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are closely similar in size and coat; both moult on the same daylight cue.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults are probably taken by small forest hawks, forest-falcons and snakes, and nests are raided by snakes, birds and small mammals. Few attacks have been documented; adults stay close to cover and dart away quickly.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, with males displaying most intensely in the early morning. At night birds roost perched on branches in dense cover.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Average wild lifespan is not known; ringing studies in Ecuador have followed males holding display sites for several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female nests alone. She builds a small, shallow cup slung in a low fork, usually lays two eggs, and incubates and feeds the chicks without help from the male.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are olive-green above and pale yellow below, with shorter tail filaments and none of the male's red or black. Young males look like females at first and gain adult colours gradually over several years.

analysis.summary: A heavy-bodied wolf spider that hunts on the ground without a web, running down its prey rather than trapping it. It spends much of its life in a silk-lined burrow dug into open soil, emerging after dark to search the surrounding ground by sight and touch.

whyInteresting: It was designated the official state spider of South Carolina in 2000.
A reflective layer behind its large eyes makes them shine green in a torch beam, so it can be found at night by eyeshine.
Mature males wander widely in late summer and autumn in search of females, and often turn up inside houses and garages.
Its size and hairy legs lead many people to mistake it for a tarantula, although it belongs to a different family, the Lycosidae.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly insects such as crickets, grasshoppers, beetles and caterpillars, plus other spiders; small frogs or lizards are occasionally reported. It hunts by pursuit or short ambush near its burrow, seizing prey with its legs and biting.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, toads, shrews, centipedes and spider-hunting wasps take it. It escapes by sprinting into its burrow; cornered, it rears up to show its fangs and may bite. The bite is painful to people but not dangerous.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal, hunting on open ground after dark. By day it rests in its burrow or under stones and debris, often waiting just inside the entrance.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually about 1 to 2 years; females tend to outlive males, which often die within months of reaching maturity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female spins a round egg sac and carries it attached to her spinnerets for several weeks. The hatched spiderlings, often more than a hundred, climb onto her back and ride there for roughly a week before dispersing.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are smaller and slimmer, with relatively longer legs and swollen pedipalp tips used in mating; females are much bulkier, especially in the abdomen.

whyInteresting: It was formally described only in 2006, although divers and underwater photographers had known it for years.
Its species name, photogenicus, refers to how often it had been photographed before scientists named it.
It shelters in burrows in soft sand and can disappear completely below the surface when disturbed.
It is most often seen hunting in the open around dusk and dawn, spending much of the day hidden.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small fish, shrimps and crabs. It hunts by spreading its arm web over holes and crevices in the sand, then probing inside with its long arm tips.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish and other predators hunt it on open sand. It retreats into its burrow, and its bold banding may warn off or confuse attackers; mimicry of venomous animals has been suggested but not shown.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most active around dawn and dusk. For much of the day it stays hidden in its burrow in the sand.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan has not been measured. Most small shallow-water octopuses live about a year, and this species is probably similar.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Males pass sperm with a modified arm. The female lays small eggs, and the hatchlings drift as plankton before settling on sand. As in most octopuses, adults probably breed once and die.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike; the male can be told by the modified tip of one arm used in mating.

entries.name: Wood Turtle
entries.heroTitle: Wood Turtle — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A medium-sized freshwater turtle whose rough carapace is built from raised, pyramid-shaped scutes, each ringed with growth lines. The skin of the neck and front legs is washed orange or red, and it is among the most land-going of the freshwater turtles in its range.

Yellow plastron with a large black blotch on each scute
Black head without bold markings above
Shell usually about 14 to 20 centimetres long

Females often travel along rivers to the same sandy nesting sites year after year.
Hatchlings have long tails and grey, plain shells that gradually gain the adult's sculpted texture.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Omnivorous: earthworms, slugs, snails, insects, tadpoles and carrion, with berries, mushrooms, leaves and algae. It forages mostly on land in summer and in the water in spring and autumn.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raccoons, skunks, foxes and other mammals raid nests and kill young, and raccoons maim some adults by chewing off legs or tails. It withdraws into its shell or dives. Road traffic, farm mowing and illegal collecting kill many more.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, often basking on logs or banks in the morning. Nights are spent in shallow water or under vegetation, and from late autumn to spring it hibernates underwater on stream bottoms, often beneath banks or roots.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild turtles commonly live 40 years or more; a captive individual has been reported at about 58 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females dig nests in open sand or gravel, often on riverbanks, in late spring or early summer, laying about 4 to 18 eggs. Hatchlings emerge after roughly two to three months. Females may not breed until about 12 to 20 years old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger, with a broader head, a concave plastron and a longer, thicker tail. Females are smaller with a flat plastron.

Their breathing surfaces sit on the underside of the abdomen, and many species have tiny air tubes there, but the thin outer skeleton loses water quickly, so their lives are shaped by the need for damp shelter.

Seven pairs of similar walking legs
One obvious pair of jointed antennae
Pill woodlice roll into a tight ball when disturbed

whyInteresting: They do not produce urine; much of their nitrogen waste leaves the body as ammonia gas.
Many eat their own droppings, recovering nutrients that passed through the gut the first time.
They moult in two halves, shedding the rear half of the skin first and the front half a day or two later.
A woodlouse that has turned bright blue or violet is usually infected with an iridovirus, which is fatal.

fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, centipedes, beetles, and small mammals threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active at night, when the air is cooler and damper. By day they stay hidden in damp, dark shelter, though some come out in daylight during wet weather.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most common species live about 2 to 3 years; some, such as the common pill woodlouse, have been recorded living four years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry fertilised eggs in a fluid-filled brood pouch under the body. Young hatch there and leave as tiny pale mancas with six pairs of legs instead of seven, gaining the last pair at a later moult. Broods range from a few to more than a hundred young, depending on species and female size.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar, with subtle abdominal differences.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mayfly, stonefly and caddisfly larvae are the main food on the rivers. On winter mudflats it sweeps its bill sideways through the soft film of mud, taking small worms, crustaceans and insect larvae.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Introduced stoats, cats, ferrets and hedgehogs take eggs and chicks, and black-backed gulls and harriers also hunt them. Floods and weed spread on riverbeds destroy nests. Adults lure intruders away with distraction displays.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds mainly by day. In winter large flocks roost packed together on shell banks at high tide, often flying in tight swirling formations before settling.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Ringed birds have lived beyond 10 years, though many live fewer.

entries.name: Yellow-legged Gull
entries.heroTitle: Yellow-legged Gull — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A large gull of the Mediterranean and the Atlantic coasts of southern Europe, long treated as a form of the herring gull. It is a generalist that fishes for itself, scavenges at harbours and rubbish tips, robs other seabirds of their catch and takes eggs, chicks and small birds.
identification: Adults have bright yellow legs and feet
Back and upperwings are mid-grey, darker than a herring gull's
Yellow bill carries a large red spot near the tip
Wingtips are black with small white spots
Head stays largely white in winter
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, mediterranean. Rocky coasts, sea cliffs, offshore islets, beaches, saltpans, lagoons and harbours, and inland along large rivers, lakes and reservoirs. Colonies nest on islands and cliffs and, increasingly, on rooftops in coastal cities.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe, mediterranean. Rocky coasts, sea cliffs, offshore islets, beaches, saltpans, lagoons and harbours, and inland along large rivers, lakes and reservoirs. Colonies nest on islands and cliffs and, increasingly, on rooftops in coastal cities.

whyInteresting: Karl Michahelles, a nineteenth-century German zoologist and physician, is commemorated in the scientific name.
After breeding, many Mediterranean birds move north in late summer to the coasts of France, the Low Countries and southern Britain.
Young birds are mottled brown and take four years to gain the grey and white adult plumage.
At some Mediterranean seabird colonies it has been culled to protect rarer species such as Audouin's gull.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, crabs, molluscs and other shore animals, along with refuse, carrion and insects. It plunges for fish near the surface, picks over the tideline at low water and hawks swarming ants in flight.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Healthy adults have few natural enemies, though eagle owls and peregrines take some. Foxes, rats and neighbouring gulls eat eggs and chicks. Colonies answer an intruder with alarm calls and repeated dives, striking with the feet, while chicks crouch in cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Daylight hours are spent feeding and loafing, though some birds feed at night around lit harbours. At dusk flocks gather to roost on islets, breakwaters, saltpans, reservoirs and rooftops.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Many adults live well over 10 years, and ringing recoveries show that some pass 15. Most deaths come in the first year or two.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs build a mound of plants and debris on the ground, a ledge or a roof. Usually three olive-brown, blotched eggs are laid between mid-March and early May and incubated by both parents for about four weeks. Chicks fly at five to six weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is identical in the two sexes. Males are larger, with a heavier bill and a flatter crown, a difference easiest to see when a pair stands together.

entries.name: Yellow Mongoose
entries.heroTitle: Yellow Mongoose — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Yellow Mongoose teaches Anchoring through a small explorer that never forgets the burrow. Open foraging, social groups, sentry behavior, and den return show that wide movement becomes safer when refuge stays known.
identification: Burrow systems create a reliable refuge near exposed foraging grounds.
Sentry behavior and group awareness help manage open-country risk.
A small agile body can explore widely because safety remains close.

whyInteresting: Yellow Mongooses often use burrows made by other animals as well as their own systems.
They are active by day more than many small carnivores.
They live in southern African dry grassland and scrub habitats.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, beetles, rodents, reptiles, eggs, birds, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jackals, raptors, snakes, wild cats, and domestic dogs pressure Yellow Mongooses to stay near burrows and use group alertness. The anchor is what makes exploration possible.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Yellow Mongooses are mostly diurnal, foraging by day and retreating to burrows for rest and danger. Their rhythm repeats the pattern: go out, check risk, return.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild has not been documented; captive yellow mongooses have reportedly lived to around 12 to 15 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth in underground dens, and young begin life inside the anchor before exploring outside. Offspring make the burrow more than shelter; it is the starting point for all risk-taking.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are broadly similar, though males may be slightly larger.

entries.name: Yellow Sac Spider
entries.heroTitle: Yellow Sac Spider — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Yellow Sac Spider AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: A hunting spider of warm grassland, best known for the nursery the female builds. Before laying, she bends the tops of tall grasses or herbs together into a closed ball a few centimetres across, lines it with dense silk and seals herself inside with her eggs.
identification: Orange to reddish-brown carapace, brighter than the abdomen
Reddish chelicerae ending in black fang tips
Front legs clearly the longest of the four pairs
Adults up to about 15 mm long
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: europe, central_asia. Warm, dry, sunny open ground with tall grasses and herbs: meadows, dry grassland, heath, fallow fields, road verges and railway embankments, mainly in the lowlands.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: europe, central_asia. Warm, dry, sunny open ground with tall grasses and herbs: meadows, dry grassland, heath, fallow fields, road verges and railway embankments, mainly in the lowlands.

whyInteresting: Its bite is one of the few from spiders in its range that easily pierces human skin, causing burning pain and local swelling that usually fades within days.
It has been found further north than before in recent decades, a change often linked to warmer summers.
It belongs to the family Cheiracanthiidae, and was long placed with other sac spiders in Clubionidae.
With no web to signal a catch, it probably relies more on touch and vibration than on sight when hunting at night.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An active hunter that builds no capture web. At night it roams grass stems and leaves, seizing insects and other small arthropods and subduing them with a quick venomous bite.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Likely predators, as for other grassland hunting spiders, include birds, spider-hunting wasps and other spiders. Its main defence is keeping still and out of sight among grass stems and leaves.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hunts at night from late spring into autumn and spends the day in a small silk tube spun in a folded leaf or among grass heads. Young spiders pass the winter inactive in thicker silk cells low in grass tussocks or plant litter.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one year: young hatch in late summer, overwinter as juveniles, mature the next summer and die after breeding.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating takes place in early summer. The female guards her egg sac inside the sealed nest for weeks without feeding and usually dies there; the spiderlings have been reported to feed on her body before they disperse.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger, with a stout, pale olive-yellow abdomen. Males are smaller and slimmer, with longer legs, longer projecting chelicerae and swollen palps.

entries.name: Common Seahorse
entries.heroTitle: Common Seahorse — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A fish that swims upright, pushed along by a small fin on its back that beats many times a second while the body stays stiff. In place of scales it has rings of bony plates under the skin. It lives along shallow coasts from the Indian Ocean to the western Pacific.
identification: Deep, thick-set body with a low, rounded coronet
Skin smooth, with low rounded bumps rather than sharp spines
Thick snout that barely narrows along its length
Yellow, cream, brown or blackish, often with fine dark spots
Usually about 10 to 17 centimetres from coronet to tail tip
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania, indian_ocean, north_pacific, coral_triangle, southeast_asia_coastal, australia_coastal. Seagrass, mangroves, coral rubble, and sheltered shallow coasts.
analysis.nativeRange: Indo-Pacific coastal waters, depending on population and taxonomy.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 75/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

Thick snout that barely narrows along its length

whyInteresting: Each eye swivels independently, so it can watch for prey and for danger in different directions at once.
It has no tail fin and no pelvic fins, and steers with a pair of small fins just behind the head.
The name kuda is the Malay word for horse.
It has been recorded in estuaries and the lower reaches of rivers, where the water is brackish.
International trade in all seahorses, dried or alive, has been regulated under CITES since 2004.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small crustaceans such as copepods, amphipods and mysid shrimps, along with fish larvae. It waits for prey to drift close, then snaps the head upward and sucks the animal in through the tubular snout. Having neither teeth nor a stomach, it feeds often.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger fish, crabs, rays, and habitat loss threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeding is done mainly in daylight, since it hunts by sight, and nights are spent resting low among the vegetation. Its daily routine in the wild has been studied far less than that of aquarium animals.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not measured in the wild. Seahorses of this size are estimated to live about 3 to 5 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pregnancy lasts roughly two to four weeks, shorter in warmer water. A brood usually numbers in the hundreds, and broods of more than a thousand have been recorded from large males. The newborns are under a centimetre long, fully formed, and receive no further care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males carry the brood pouch; females deposit eggs.

entries.name: Yellow Tang
entries.heroTitle: Yellow Tang — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Yellow Tang teaches Reef Current Flow across Hawaiian reef, gliding with the surge rather than fighting it and turning that saved effort into a full day of grazing.
identification: Uniform bright yellow body, unmistakable on a reef
White scalpel spine at the tail base
Snout drawn out for reaching algae in crevices
Pale with a dark horizontal stripe at night

whyInteresting: It fades at night, developing a dark lateral stripe, and brightens again at dawn.
It cleans algae off the shells of green sea turtles, which visit reef to be groomed.
It is most abundant on the reefs of Hawaii.
Its long snout lets it reach algae that blunter grazers cannot.
Its scalpel spine is white against yellow, and easy to see when raised.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Filamentous algae and seaweed grazed from reef rock, plus algae taken off turtle shells.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Groupers, jacks and reef sharks. Its answer is a dash into coral and a raised tail blade rather than sustained speed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Yellow Tangs graze through the day and wedge into reef crevices at night, changing colour so completely that they are hard to recognise.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Yellow Tangs can live over thirty years in the wild.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning takes place in open water around dusk, in groups or in pairs, with no parental care. The larvae drift for roughly two months before settling on shallow reef, where young fish often shelter among finger coral.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look identical, with males slightly larger and performing a rapid colour-flashing display when courting. The difference appears only in behaviour, and only briefly.

entries.name: Yellow-vented Bulbul
entries.heroTitle: Yellow-vented Bulbul — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Few birds follow forest clearance as closely: it is among the first to settle on newly cleared land and often becomes one of the most numerous birds around houses. Pairs will nest in hedges, ornamental shrubs and even hanging pot plants beside doors and windows.
identification: Dark brown crown that can be raised into a short crest
White stripe above the eye with dark lores
Bright yellow undertail feathers below whitish underparts
Plain grey-brown back, wings and tail
Slim songbird about 20 centimetres long

whyInteresting: By swallowing small fruits whole and passing the seeds, it spreads shrubs and pioneer trees into disturbed ground.
Outside the nesting season small groups gather at fruiting trees, sometimes mixing with other bulbuls.
Birds of the Philippines and those of the Sunda region differ in face pattern, and some authorities treat them as two species.
In gardens it will come to cut fruit such as banana or papaya put out on a feeder.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small berries, figs and other soft fruits make up much of the diet, with nectar and petals from flowering shrubs and insects picked off foliage or caught in short sallies from a perch.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes and crows raid nests for eggs and chicks, and coucals and squirrels probably do too, while small hawks and domestic cats take adults. Adults give harsh scolding calls and gather to mob a snake or cat near the nest.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, busiest in the first hours after dawn and again in late afternoon. At night it roosts in dense shrubs or trees, sometimes close to other bulbuls.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is not well documented; reliable ages from ringed birds have not been published.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The nest is a neat cup of grass, rootlets and leaves placed low in a shrub, hedge or potted plant. Clutches are usually two or three eggs, and both parents feed the chicks, which leave the nest after roughly two weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in plumage; the sexes cannot be told apart reliably in the field.

Drops into the coral branches the moment a larger fish approaches
Deep, laterally compressed damselfish body about 13 cm long

Males clear a patch of hard substrate, then guard the sticky eggs laid on it until they hatch.
It is one of the damselfishes most often seen over branching Acropora in the Coral Triangle.
The yellow belly is easiest to see from below, against the light.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Zooplankton taken from the current, with some algae and small benthic invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Groupers, lizardfish, trevally and other reef hunters. Its answer is not speed over distance but distance kept short — it never puts more water between itself and the coral than it can cross in a moment.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Yellowbelly Damselfish are active by day and settle deep into coral branches at night, wedging into a crevice where a hunting predator cannot follow.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Yellowbelly Damselfish live several years on a reef.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay adhesive eggs on a cleared patch of substrate and the male guards and fans them until hatching.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look closely alike, with males distinguished mainly by nest-guarding behaviour. The similarity fits a species whose survival rests on a shared shelter rather than on display.

entries.name: Yellowfin Surgeonfish
entries.heroTitle: Yellowfin Surgeonfish — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: One of the largest surgeonfishes, reaching roughly 60 to 70 cm, this purplish-grey reef fish ranges more widely in depth than most of its relatives. It feeds in sheltered lagoons only a metre or two deep and has been recorded on outer reef slopes well below 50 metres.
identification: Outer part of each pectoral fin bright yellow
Yellow patch in front of the eye
Purplish-grey to dark brown body without stripes
Deeply crescent-shaped tail fin
Pale band often visible across the tail base

analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: indian_ocean, north_pacific, coral_triangle. Sand and rubble bottoms beside coral reefs, in bays, harbours, channels and lagoons. Young fish stay in shallow, sheltered and often turbid inshore water.

whyInteresting: It is often reported feeding in mixed groups with other surgeonfishes over open ground rather than alone.
It is reported to have a thick-walled, gizzard-like stomach that grinds the sediment swallowed with its food.
Individuals are reported to shift quickly between darker and noticeably lighter shades, especially when feeding or disturbed.
It is taken for food by spear and net fishers in many parts of its range.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly diatoms, detritus and filamentous algae taken from sand and hard surfaces, with hydroids and scraps of fish flesh also recorded in its gut. Unlike many surgeonfishes, it does not rely mainly on crops of seaweed on rock.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Reef sharks, groupers and other large predatory fishes are its main threats, and young fish are taken by a wider range of hunters. It stays close to schoolmates and can slash an attacker with the sharp, blade-like spine on each side of the tail base.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, feeding over sand and rubble. At night it retreats into the reef and rests in crevices or beneath overhangs.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: A long-lived reef fish: otolith ageing of fish from Hawaii has reported individuals up to about 29 years old. Lifespan elsewhere in its range is less well studied.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Adults gather to spawn in open water, releasing eggs and sperm that drift away with no parental care. The flat, transparent larvae spend weeks in the plankton before settling on shallow reefs as young fish.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike, and the sexes cannot be told apart in the field.

entries.name: Yellowjacket & Hornet
entries.heroTitle: Yellowjacket & Hornet — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Yellowjackets and hornets are social wasps whose colonies usually start from a single queen in spring and grow to hundreds or many thousands of workers by late summer. In warm climates some yellowjacket colonies survive winter, gain extra queens and build nests of enormous size.
identification: Wings folded lengthwise into pleats when at rest
Kidney-shaped eyes with a deep notch on the inner edge
Many species boldly patterned black with yellow, white or orange
Narrow waist between thorax and abdomen
Hornets are the largest, some queens exceeding 3 centimetres

whyInteresting: Nest paper is made from wood fibres that workers scrape from posts and dead wood and chew with saliva.
In temperate yellowjackets and hornets the colony dies in autumn, and only mated queens survive winter, hibernating in sheltered spots.
Unlike a honeybee, a worker's sting is barely barbed, so she can sting more than once.
Potter and mason wasps belong to the same family but are solitary, building small nests of mud.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults live mainly on sugars from nectar, ripe fruit, honeydew and sap. Workers hunt flies, caterpillars and other insects, and yellowjackets also scavenge meat, chewing it into paste for the larvae, which give the adults a sugary saliva in return.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Honey buzzards in Europe and Asia dig out nests for the grubs, and badgers, bears and skunks raid ground nests; bee-eaters and other birds take adults. Colonies answer with massed stings, and warning colours teach predators to leave them alone.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Workers forage in daylight and spend the night inside the nest. Some hornets, including the European hornet, also fly after dark and come to lighted windows.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Workers live roughly two to five weeks in summer, and males a few weeks. Queens live about a year, from emerging in late summer through hibernation to the end of their colony the next autumn.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The founding queen builds a small comb and lays one egg per cell. Larvae hatch after about a week and are fed chewed prey; the first workers emerge after roughly a month. Late in the season the colony raises males and new queens, which mate before winter.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Queens are the largest members of a colony; workers are smaller females. Males have longer antennae, with 13 segments against the female's 12, one more visible abdominal segment, and no sting.

fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Yeti Crabs live in constant deep darkness, so their rhythm follows vent chemistry, temperature, and food growth rather than day and night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long this vent crab lives is not known; no individual has been aged, in the wild or in captivity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry eggs under the abdomen like other crabs, and larvae likely disperse through deep water. Offspring must eventually find the rare chemistry of vents.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are subtle in general appearance, though females carry egg masses. The shared hairy-claw strategy matters more than display.

entries.name: Zebra Danio
entries.heroTitle: Zebra Danio — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Zebra Danio is a tiny, fast, blue-and-silver striped minnow from the streams and rice fields of South Asia, and one of the most widely kept aquarium fish. Under the name zebrafish it is also among the most studied animals in science, valued for see-through embryos and an ability to regrow damaged organs.
identification: Five dark blue stripes running from gill to tail
Stripes continuing across the tail and anal fins
Slim torpedo-shaped silver-gold body
Small upturned mouth with fine barbels
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_asia. Slow streams, ditches, ponds, floodplain pools and rice paddies in India, Bangladesh and Nepal, mostly in the Ganges and Brahmaputra basins. It favours shallow, still or gently moving water with plants along the margins and a silty bed.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: south_asia. Slow streams, ditches, ponds, floodplain pools and rice paddies in India, Bangladesh and Nepal, mostly in the Ganges and Brahmaputra basins. It favours shallow, still or gently moving water with plants along the margins and a silty bed.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 15/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Five dark blue stripes running from gill to tail
Stripes continuing across the tail and anal fins
Slim torpedo-shaped silver-gold body
Small upturned mouth with fine barbels
whyInteresting: Its embryos are transparent and develop outside the mother, so a beating heart can be watched under a microscope within about a day of fertilisation.
Roughly 70 percent of human genes have a counterpart in the zebrafish genome.
Young fish learn the look of the companions they grow up with and later prefer to shoal with fish of that pattern.
The first fluorescent GloFish sold in pet shops were Zebra Danios carrying an added gene for a fluorescent protein.
The spotted Leopard Danio is not a separate species but a colour form of the Zebra Danio.
The Giant Danio is sometimes confused with it but grows to around 10 cm and has broken blue and yellow lines and spots rather than five clean stripes.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An omnivore taking zooplankton, insect larvae, small insects that fall on the surface, worms and algae. It feeds mainly in the upper water and at the surface.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakeheads, freshwater garfish, knifefish, kingfishers and pond herons, with dragonfly larvae taking the young. Shoaling is the everyday defence, and the capacity to regrow a torn fin means a narrow escape need not be a lasting handicap.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At night it enters a sleep-like state, hovering almost motionless low in the water with slowed responses, and the species is used in sleep research for that reason.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About two to three years is typical, and up to five in good aquarium conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females scatter a few hundred non-sticky eggs over the bottom in shallow water, usually in the first minutes after dawn, and the parents give no care and will eat the eggs. The young hatch in two to three days and carry the same capacity for repair from the start.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger, rounder-bellied and more silvery between the stripes. Males are slimmer and more torpedo-shaped, with a gold or pinkish cast between the blue lines and on the fins.

entries.name: Zebra Dove
entries.heroTitle: Zebra Dove — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: The Zebra Dove teaches Quiet Presence through striped camouflage and soft daily song. It lives close to gardens, paths, and human places without needing to dominate them, using gentle calls and modest coloring to belong without forcing attention. Its lesson is that calm consistency can make a presence feel safe.
identification: Fine black-and-white barring on the neck sides and flanks
Blue-grey face with bare blue skin around the eye
Long, narrow tail with white tips to the outer feathers
Brown upperparts crossed by thin black bars
Small and slender, about 20 to 23 centimetres long
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Open lowland country with scattered trees and scrub, farmland, village edges, parks and gardens, from peninsular Myanmar and southern Thailand through the Malay Peninsula to Sumatra, Java, Bali and Lombok. It keeps out of closed forest.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Open lowland country with scattered trees and scrub, farmland, village edges, parks and gardens, from peninsular Myanmar and southern Thailand through the Malay Peninsula to Sumatra, Java, Bali and Lombok. It keeps out of closed forest.

whyInteresting: In Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia it is kept for cooing contests, and birds with prized voices change hands for high prices.
Birds released in Hawaii in the 1920s founded a population that is now among the commonest birds in the islands.
It was once treated as a single species with the peaceful dove of Australia and the barred dove of eastern Indonesia.
Like other pigeons it drinks by sucking water up with the bill held down, without tipping the head back.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small seeds of grasses and weeds, picked from the ground while walking with quick, short steps. Insects and other small invertebrates are taken now and then.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Trapping for the cage-bird trade removes large numbers. Natural predators include hawks, cats and snakes, with crows and rats robbing nests. A disturbed bird bursts up from the ground and flies fast and straight to the nearest tree.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, feeding mostly in the early morning and late afternoon and resting in shade in the heat of the day. At night it roosts in dense foliage of trees and shrubs. It is resident, with no seasonal dormancy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Poorly documented in the wild. Captive birds often reach 10 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The nest is a thin platform of twigs and grass in a bush or tree. Two white eggs are usual, incubated by both parents for about two weeks. The chicks are fed at first on crop milk and leave the nest at around two weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike and cannot be reliably told apart in the field. In display it is the male that bows, raises the tail and coos.

entries.name: Zebra Moray Eel
entries.heroTitle: Zebra Moray Eel — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

featuredImage.alt: Zebra Moray Eel AnimalDex species guide

analysis.summary: Zebra Moray teaches Striped Blending inside reef crevices, where dense white banding on a dark body dissolves against broken coral until the eel moves.
identification: Dark brown to black body ringed with dozens of narrow white bands
Blunt, rounded snout unlike the pointed jaws of fish-eating morays
Flat, pebble-like teeth for crushing shells
Reaches about 1.5 m
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: indian_ocean, south_pacific, coral_triangle, red_sea. Reef crevices, rubble and coral heads.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: indian_ocean, south_pacific, coral_triangle, red_sea. Reef crevices, rubble and coral heads.

Blunt, rounded snout unlike the pointed jaws of fish-eating morays
Flat, pebble-like teeth for crushing shells
Reaches about 1.5 m
whyInteresting: Its teeth are flattened plates rather than fangs, built to crush rather than grip.
It eats crabs, urchins and molluscs rather than fish.
The banding is dense and irregular, which breaks its outline against coral rubble.
It is far less aggressive than most morays of its size.
Like other morays it has a second set of pharyngeal jaws that pull food back down the throat.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Crabs, shrimp, urchins and molluscs crushed with flat pebble-like teeth.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large groupers and sharks. Its answer is the crevice: an eel wedged into rock with only its head showing is a difficult target.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Zebra Morays rest in crevices through the day and become more active at night, when the crustaceans they hunt are out.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been measured. Aquarium specimens are reported to have lived for well over a decade, some reportedly 20 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Adults spawn by releasing eggs and sperm into open water, with no parental care. The eggs hatch into transparent, leaf-shaped leptocephalus larvae that drift in the ocean for months before settling on the reef.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike. Appearance carries no sex signal because a crevice-dwelling ambusher gains nothing from being distinguishable.

entries.name: Eared Dove
entries.heroTitle: Eared Dove — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A medium-sized, grey-brown dove found across South America and into the southern Caribbean, from the Lesser Antilles to Tierra del Fuego. Where grain crops are grown it can become enormously abundant, nesting in huge colonies and feeding in flocks on fields.
identification: Grey crown and plain brown back
Black spots on the wing coverts
Two short black lines on the side of the face, one below the ear
Pinkish-buff breast and belly
Iridescent purple-bronze patch on the side of the neck
Wedge-shaped tail with pale or cinnamon outer tips
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_america. Open and semi-open country from the lowlands into Andean valleys: farmland, grassland, savanna, dry scrub, towns and city parks. It avoids dense forest and nests in shrubs, trees or on the ground.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: south_america. Open and semi-open country from the lowlands into Andean valleys: farmland, grassland, savanna, dry scrub, towns and city parks. It avoids dense forest and nests in shrubs, trees or on the ground.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 10/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

whyInteresting: Pairs can raise several broods in a year, and breeding may continue in almost every month where food is plentiful.
Like other pigeons, both parents feed the young on crop milk, a nutritious secretion from the lining of the crop.
It belongs to the same genus, Zenaida, as the North American Mourning Dove, one of its closest relatives.
It has adapted well to towns and cities, feeding on lawns and pavements and nesting in street trees and on ledges.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly seeds, picked from the ground while walking: grasses, weeds and cultivated grain such as sorghum, wheat, maize and sunflower, including spilled grain after harvest.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Falcons and hawks take adults, and snakes, opossums, cats and birds raid nests. At large colonies predators gather around the edges. It escapes with a fast, direct flight with a clatter of wings.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, feeding most in the morning and late afternoon. At night it roosts in trees and dense shrubs, often communally in large numbers. It does not hibernate.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been well documented, and no reliable typical or maximum ages from ringed birds have been published.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The nest is a flimsy platform of twigs in a shrub, tree or on the ground. Two white eggs are usual; both parents incubate for about two weeks and feed the young on crop milk. Pairs may nest several times a year.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are similar. Males have a greyer crown, a pinker breast and a stronger neck gloss; females are slightly duller and browner.

entries.name: Zoanthid
entries.heroTitle: Zoanthid — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: Zoanthid teaches Held Ground as a mat rather than a monument. No single polyp is much, but a colony spreads across bare rock, closes ranks when disturbed, and defends its patch with chemistry instead of size.
identification: Colonies of small polyps, each a disc of tentacles 5-20 mm across
Polyps joined at the base by a shared mat of tissue
Whole colony closes at once when disturbed
Extremely variable colour, often ringed in contrasting bands
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: indian_ocean, south_pacific, coral_triangle, north_atlantic. Shallow, well-lit reef flats, rubble and rock walls with steady water movement.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: indian_ocean, south_pacific, coral_triangle, north_atlantic. Shallow, well-lit reef flats, rubble and rock walls with steady water movement.
analysis.rarityReason: AnimalDex canonical rarity score: 36/100, maintained by the live indexed species profile.

behaviorTraits: Colonies of small polyps, each a disc of tentacles 5-20 mm across
Polyps joined at the base by a shared mat of tissue
Whole colony closes at once when disturbed
Extremely variable colour, often ringed in contrasting bands
whyInteresting: Many zoanthids carry palytoxin, among the most poisonous non-protein substances known, and aquarium keepers have been hospitalised handling colonies in a closed room.
Polyps in a colony are connected by a shared tissue mat, so the colony behaves as one animal.
Palythoa and Protopalythoa embed sand grains in their tissue, which makes them tougher than they look.
Symbiotic algae in the tissue supply much of the colony's energy.
The colour morphs sold in the aquarium trade are variants, not separate species.
respectfulSpotting: Observe from a respectful distance and avoid changing the animal's behavior.
Do not block feeding, shelter, nesting, or travel routes.
Use a live camera capture without handling or staging wildlife.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Sugars from symbiotic zooxanthellae, plus plankton and particulate matter caught by the polyps.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Nudibranchs and a few specialised snails and butterflyfish. Its answer is chemical: palytoxin makes a colony a poor meal, and the whole mat closes at once when something touches it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Zoanthids have no sleep in the animal sense, but polyps open in good light and current and close tight at night or when disturbed, so a colony visibly changes shape through the day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Colonies persist for many years and keep spreading.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Colonies grow mainly by budding new polyps off the shared mat, and also spawn into the water column.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Polyps show no external difference between sexes. Appearance carries no signal because the colony spreads mostly by budding rather than by pairing.

entries.name: Oriental White-eye
entries.heroTitle: Oriental White-eye — Identification, Habitat, Animal Power & Facts

analysis.summary: A tiny warbler-like songbird, yellow-green above with a ring of white feathers around each eye. It is rarely seen alone: small parties move through foliage together, calling constantly, and often join other small birds in mixed feeding flocks.
identification: Bold white ring around the eye
Bright yellow throat and undertail
Yellow-green upperparts and pale greyish belly
Short pointed black bill
Warbler-sized, about 10 centimetres long
analysis.habitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Open woodland, forest edges, scrub, mangroves, plantations, parks and gardens, from the lowlands into the hills and, in the Himalaya, to around 2,000 metres or more.
analysis.nativeRange: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Open woodland, forest edges, scrub, mangroves, plantations, parks and gardens, from the lowlands into the hills and, in the Himalaya, to around 2,000 metres or more.

whyInteresting: Flock mates often preen each other, a behaviour that helps keep small parties together.
By taking nectar it carries pollen between flowers of the trees it visits.
In parts of the Himalaya some birds are thought to move to lower altitudes for the winter.
It is trapped for the cage-bird trade in parts of its range.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small insects and spiders gleaned from leaves and twigs, plus nectar from flowers and soft fruit and berries. It hangs from twigs to reach undersides and probes blossoms with a brush-tipped tongue.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Small hawks such as the shikra take adults, and crows, treepies, snakes and squirrels raid nests. Parties keep up contact calls, give sharp alarm notes and dive into dense foliage when a hawk appears.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day. At night birds roost in dense foliage, and several birds are often reported perching pressed side by side along one branch.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild has not been reliably documented for this species; most wild birds probably live only a few years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The small cup nest is slung from a forked twig. Two or three pale blue eggs are usual; both parents incubate for about 10 to 12 days and feed the young, which fledge after roughly another 10 days.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike and cannot be told apart in the field.
